First thing first, the art is amazing. Unlike most early access games this is nearly a finished product and will give you many, many hours of play at its current state and more later on when new content is added. This game is brutal. I have seen many people see this in a negative light, but peronally I think it adds to the fun of these kinds of games. People who have said things about RNG most likely aren't utilizing all the game mechanics and upgrades as these help out a lot. I have already completed all the Caretaker Goals that are currently in the game and I'm still playing because it's that addicting. Going into a dungeon with 0 stress and full health and then coming out barely sane and needing a few rounds at the bar to shake off your friends death is a most pleasing experience. I'm excited to see where the devs take the rest of the game, ie: flushing out mechanics, fixing small issues, adding new dungeons, classes and monsters, but the game is already very enjoyable as it is. I have already reccomended it to several friends and will continue to reccomend it to fans of dungeon crawling rougelikes looking for a new experience.

Coming from a guy who hated Minecraft and Terraria, I love this game. It takes away what I feel as blandness that came from the other two games, Starbound offers both the freedom that the others do as well as goals. The feeling of wanting to play rather than "I need to finish." Fantastic game, best indie I've played.
EDIT:
Well it's been a couple years now. Occasionally I check in to see any new content. Once I was pleasantly surprised with a rather large update, giving it a central hub, some missions, and some updated gameplay. Still, it quickly became a bore yet again. Chucklefish tried too hard with this game, and to this day, it has been one of the greatest gaming disappointments I have felt. Maybe, just maybe, it will be a finished, satisfying game one day. But until then, it's just a slightly unique, lackluster Terraria.

Okay, it's time for another revision of this update since it's official release.
Starbound has once more become great again. What do I mean by that? It's content, of course? Now, before I really get into it, this is not going to be compared to Terraria which is a completely different game with a completely different purpose. With that out of the way, let's do this!
Hunger is back! With the addition of new modes (survival, casual, hardcore), the hunger system is definitely back except in casual mode. Farming now has a purpose again.
The ship system is still the same as it pretty much was pre-release; however, there's the addition of gaining crew members via random quests you do for people in settlements. One of my weirdest moments was getting a crew member who I originally gained as a colony tenant. It's now safe to say that her priority is defending her home colony from dangers both foreign and.. foreign. But, at any rate, there's still nothing entirely enticing you to actually settle down on a planet minus the scavaging considering your ship turns into a mobile home after a while. The interface is new in that you can see the orbits of planets, your ship trajectory, randomly right click in a solar system to move there for no reason at all, see what planets are in each solar system, visit space stations, asteroid fields, etc. It's all new and enticing.
Colonies are easy to establish. Put in basic furniture items, a tenant deed, and boom! You have +1 tenant. You will randomly get requests from them to farm, add new furniture to their home, get them a specific item to add to their shop if they're a merchant, or even somehow join your colony.
The music is still boring to me after all these years, but that's my personal pickiness considering I always change the game music in almost any game I can afford to. The music isn't [bad], I just don't enjoy it. Who knows? You might.
The combat is revamped slightly as well. Special abilities for weapons, new weapons, varied weapon choices, defensive capabilities, specialized gear, etc. It's still jump, dodge, shield, swing, but each weapon choice leaves you with new avenues on how to handle one-on-one encounters or mob encounters. Even bosses become fun the longer they go on. I, myself, use weaker weapons on bosses to draw out the fight.
If you beat the main story which is semi-lame, then you get more content added in the form of vaults that you much attain a key for by means of material farming. Once inside, you have a limited time to complete each vault before you get locked out. The encounters are random, the fights are a struggle, but the rewards are worth it. Terraformers that alter planets' biomes to upgrading legendary equipment that's below tier 6. Just as well, there are still challenge dungeons littered around the solar systems in planets for you to find for unique pieces of gear.
The building is still the same, really. New blocks add new building ideas, but it's your creativity or lack thereof that determine what you do/don't do.
Planets may contain settlements that'll net you new schematics, crew members, items, gear, or even pets via quests. They're simple, copy/paste quests but there's enough there that'll leave you still wanting to do them (maybe) for that random thing you may not have known you needed.
Then, of course, there's mods. There's 2 types of people in the Starbound community: those who think mods are essential to enjoy the game and those who add mods to simply spice things up. If you find yourself someone who is amongst the prior then perhaps gaming isn't your thing if you cannot appreciate a game for what it offers; however, if you're amongst the latter then there's aplethora of mods here to mix up your experience. While I could easily cut out every mod I have subbed to and still enjoy myself, well.. I don't want to break my saves, basically.
Starbound is a game about exploration- which there's plenty of- and finding ways to have fun doing it. Between the mini-games, excavating fossils, combat, building, farming, questing, and modding, you'll more than find something to do. While I personally find this game a very enjoyable experience, I know several out there will label me a fanboy and eventually they'll bring in the Terraria comparisons. Let me tell you; don't. I reward good games and devoted devs with my time and loyalty and Chucklefish has earned that. Starbound isn't perfect and I understand this, but it keeps me hooked and it may keep you hooked as well.

Just realized I haven't reviewed this one.
After some glitches on PC (square monitor = lockpicking doesn't work, unless you window it), I got super absorbed yet again in to the fallout universe.
This game though has so much more content packed in at evert turn though.
If you go wandering around (as you occasionally can, and are encouraged to do), you'll stumble on a plethora of story and world building.
This game brings something new and untested to the Fallout 4 formula (like boats did to assassin's creed).
You can build your own village, and have it protect itself against raiders (or help them out). In turn they'll help you out to defend against random encounters by bombardment, and possibly walking up and joining in?
I don't really know, because what actually happened, was in my playthrough, I built a sky-fortress-come-power-armour-garage that I didn't let any of my NPCs in, then built some turrets, and pretty much left them to themselves, while I explore this beautiful world.
The main storyline makes sense, and they let you choose your own path. So when presented the choice, I shot my own son in the face after spending most of the storyline looking for him. It might have let's say cut the story short a bit, but still feel justified in this course of action, and the payoff wasn't bad either.
I also really liked the "chinese take" in this one with the submarine mission. It felt like it brought a new perspective in to it.
Now all we need for the next game, is some Tom Lehrer music!
PS: Loading screens at the start, and switching areas one of the best (least irritating) I've seen, pretty much ever. They can occasionally be a tad long. But it's not Xcom2 long.
PPS: Tip for new players: You might want to find a new settlement "out of the way" from your main one as soon as possible, then send Preston Garvey there. I swear, I spend half the time dodging him, so he doesn't give me another damn "the wasteland is in trouble" quest.

If you feel like taking a break from non-stop killing, you can. That really helps. Then again, if you want nothing but the FPS experience, you can do that too. Nothing requires that you build towns and establish settlements. That's up to you. I've really enjoyed that balance.

This game reminds me alot of xcom, only as a Lovecraftian RPG instead of grid based SRPG.  You have a base that you have to build up with resources earned, recruit new troops (who die alot), upgrade you gear, train them, and send them into missions with very high rates of permadeath.  But there's the added twist of managing the stress of battle, which can have very negitive effects on your troops if not handled properly.
I love this game for the most part, but it can get a pretty frustrating.  I don't really mind hard, but alot of the difficultly comes from arbitrary dice rolls and not from bad tactics.  You can be doing great, but suddenly you get in a battle with a group of scrubs, and everyone of them pulls a critical on you healer.  Four criticals in a row, while 5 of your attacks are dodged.  And now your healer is dead, your party is in freak out mode from stress and not responding to your commands.  And now and entire mission goes down the toilet because the enemy got on a mysterious hot streak of criticals, all focused on one person in your team that goes from full health to dead in one or two turns.....
But that aside, its still a great game that has kept me coming back for more punishment.  I think since its still in early release, alot of these issues will be hammered out by the official release, and it will be Game of the Year material.
I recommend  putting it on your wishlist for a few months for them to iron out some of the flaws, and then diving into an increadible RPG experience.

This is the latest entry in the Dark Souls series (quite possibly the final for a long time). Let me quickly introduce you to what this game actually is:
A "Souls" game (DemonSouls;DarkSouls;Bloodborne)  is a unique type of action RPG which focuses a whole lot on gameplay and good mechanics. It is more or less a linear experience with a level design that connects levels together in some sort of "inter-conected" world (very clever indeed). It has a very dark artistic theme, a lot of death and eerie stuff, complete with an amazing orchestral/epic soundtrack (with lots of cool vocals) and great sound design. "Souls" games are thus caracterized by their visual and sonorous beauty, compelling gameplay and mechanics and intelligent level-design overall.
I'm here to tell you if Dark Souls 3 achieves what it's predecessors did.
Dark Souls 3 feels new and refreshing compared to the other souls games, it has effectively mixed multiple elements from the older games to create this feeling :
- Spells now use "Mana" ; You can exchange Boss Souls for gear and weapons or spells (Demon's Souls)
- Faster gameplay (Bloodborne)
- Good old Dark Souls
The result should be nothing short of amazing right? Well it is poorly executed in some areas:
- Spells and Miracles are bad in PvP. Most of them use up too much of your Ashen Estus Flasks and deal poor damage, not to mention those that do deal damage are impossible to land a hit with. In most cases you will run out of flasks before your ennemy dies (especially if he has some means to heal himself).
Even in PvE i haven't found spells that perticularly interested me or were that fun to use... ( i still used a mage and miracle user once or twice for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles though. )
(of course you can use Wrath of the Gods, possibly a Crystal/Simple Estoc or some lightning based builds... but that's about it)
- The Poise system is non existant in this iteration of the game, or at least doesn't work the way it used to. Equipping armour doesn't seem to make you less vulnerable to hit-stun weapons such as the Estoc. You can get stun-locked easily if you aren't carefull. I find this change to be odd, but it didn't really affect me since i prefer using Hyper-Armor to tank through ennemy hits (a few frames in your attack animation with large weapons in wich you can't be hit-stunned). Otherwise dodging or outranging your opponents still work well. I still have to say that i feel the commitment to attack animations isn't as punishing as in say Dark Souls 2 since you recover really fast and can immediately turn your character around in the next attack effectively making you impossible to backstab (exept in extreme circumstances ).
- Boss Souls weapons are fun to use in PvE, so fun to use in fact that i started neglecting all other weapons. Crafting my own weapons and upgrading them with my ores was most of the time worse than my newest boss weapon. Especially enchantments like Blessed which are completely useless.  I even used Boss weapons in PvP ,DragonSlayer's Swordspear and Two Princes' Greatsword being my favourites.
- Some Bosses are uninspired or just a bit too easy for my taste. Some of the Lords of Cinder are surprisingly bad. Some bosses such as Lothric, Soul of Cinder, or Nameless King are weirdly some of the best bosses in the series IMO. It is very inconsistent to say the least.
Despite it's flaws Dark Souls 3 remains one of the best RPG released in 2016. It is beautiful and has awsome and epic boss battles. It's ending boss is incredible and worthy of an end game boss (Soul of Cinder who represents all player fighting styles mixed together which makes for a thrilling boss fight), a real challenge with epic music and multiple forms increasing in difficulty as it tries to stop you from achieving your goal.  Despite the lack of real story, it still has the interesting characters who speak with a weird accent and the bits and pieces of information that you can link together and imagine what you want for a story.
Dark Souls 3 won't hold you hand and will let you play the game the way you want to, feel free to disregard my opion on PvP combat and create your own meta if you wish, there are tons of possibilities. After all Dark souls is known for having a  lot of potential for trolling and other fun stuff because of it's sheer amount of customization.
All I can say is ... I want more . 8/10

In Broken Hills, humans and mutants could learn to live peacefully together, and spread a message of tolerance to the world beyond – or a race war could erupt, killing everyone.
In Fallout 4, instead of all this, you get settlement construction. Settlements are a place to store companions you're not using. Not that they mind if you're not actually constructing anything.

While not a bad game by any means Darkest Dungeon is a slow, grueling, and needlessly-punishing experience. I first played Darkest Dungeon back in early access, and I thought it was a pretty decent concept. I'm a fan of games that are generally very difficult and punishing, as it can make your victory seem that much more satisfying. I'm also a fan of this type of dark medieval fantasy setting, so I'll admit the artstyle, audio and general atmosphere were definitely a huge draw as well. The game has definitely improved over the years, especially by adding much needed content, but it has not improved certain aspects that I found to be heavily flawed when I first played it.
In Darkest Dungeon you build a party of 4 heroes and send them down into a spooky dungeon to gain treasure and experience (assuming they accomplish their task). They will encounter various enemies, usually in groups of 2 to 4, who will aim to either kill your party members or cause immense "stress" by being exceptionally spooky. A character who's stress meter reachers 100 will then have their "resolve tested", which will usually lead to some kind of mental breakdown like fear or paranoia that will last for the rest of the dungeon. This will cause them to misbehave during combat, skipping turns, attacking allies, etc. which makes them very unreliable. Players are expected to manage their heroes' stress levels in the same way they manage their hit points.
Assuming one of your characters dies, it's not game over. In fact, the game is designed to allow you to lose party members by the handfuls. Despite only using 4 at a time to explore dungeons with, you can recruit dozens of heroes to sit in town as back-ups. And furthermore since highly-stressed characters need to rest up in town, you will generally have not one but many parties of heroes to do dungeons with. Your town acts as the game's progression; use the treasure you find in dungeons to buy new gear, learn and upgrade your heroes' skills, unlearn bad traits, cure diseases, and quickly undo stress with a trip to the tavern. The town itself can be upgraded too to give more options to the player in terms of what can be purchased and upgraded, and even if everyone dies you'll still have your town to work with; making it a somewhat permanent form of progression.
In a typical roguelike, dying is the end: you die, you start over. That means that in order for the game to feel fair in its difficulty, the player should never die simply because they got unlucky. However in Darkest Dungeon since (in the standard difficulty setting) you have as much time as you need and no limit on how many heroes are allowed to die... the game is not afraid to utterly slaughter your party members. This leads to some very annoying and unfair deaths, such as all 4 monsters in the enemy team attacking one of your heroes and killing them before you have a chance to respond. Situations like that are not the player's fault and there is literally nothing you can do to prevent such a thing. Deaths like these are supposedly justified because you've got plenty more heroes at your disposal; it's not like it's game over just because you lost 1 hero, right?
What makes a roguelike good is the possibility of being dealt a bad hand, possibly one of the worst, and still having a reasonable chance of winning. In every roguelike/roguelite I've ever played there has been a significant element of randomness that factored into the player's success. In most of the better games, that randomness can be mitigated by various elements so that you never feel like you lost a game because you had bad luck. In Faster Than Light, players manage the randomness by being prepared for the worst, spending their scrap wisely, and properly micromanaging their crew and doors. In Binding of Isaac, you can beat the game with poor upgrades simply by playing very carefully and being skilled at dodging enemy's attacks. In traditional roguelikes (like Tales of Maj'Eyal) you've usually got a myriad of scouting, positioning and utility skills to ensure that bad luck is almost never the reason you died.
In Darkest Dungeon, however, there are consistently situations where you lose a hero or are forced to abandon the dungeon because of bad luck. While losing a single hero may not be the end of the game, it can be very frustrating to lose a character you've invested so much time into, especially when you had very little control (if any at all) over their fate. The main problem is that the combat is incredibly simple. There's very little room for actual skill to come into the equation. Outside of just knowing the best hero party compositions and not making any obvious mistakes, there's really nothing that significant you can do to increase your chance of winning a fight. This style of turn-based combat was designed to work with story-driven RPG games where "losing" was virtually impossible, and even if you did lose you could just continue from a saved game or a checkpoint. It just doesn't work for a highly-punishing roguelite.
The game can feel very tedious at times due to the extremely slow sequencing. Loading screens, menu transitions, walking and combat animations are rather sluggish and make up about 90% of the game. There's some mods on the workshop that make walking and combat a bit faster, but it's far from ideal. In your first few hours you won't mind because the game has a great artstyle and you won't mind basking in the atmosphere, but once you've played for awhile you'll find it's slow pace to be a nuisance. Especially if one or more of your heroes was killed and you're thinking about how much time you've just wasted as a result.
I also felt that the game was very lacking in hero customization. Each character can pick 4 combat and camping skills out of 7, and equip them with 2 trinkets (your choices are rather limited as there's almost always an obvious best option for these). That's it. That's the only character customization you get. You can use the sanitorium to "lock" their randomly generated positive traits in so they're not replaced by other ones, but that's too finnicky and random of a system for me to consider it a form of true character customization. The only real customization you get is deciding which 4 heroes to use together, and I'll admit that is my favorite part of the game, but I just wish it was more in-depth.
I generally don't recommend this game because of luck is the primary deciding factor in a player's success, especially when there are so many other much better rogulike/lites out there. This game will quite literally test your patience.

If there's one game I would recommend buying this quater for those of you who enjoy a sprinkle of masochism in their video games, then I have to recommend this one.
Starting at the top with the visuals. The best way I can find it is to suggest it evokes the ideas of an old, rusted cleaver, caked with blood, in that it's purpose is often clear and intentionally threatening, adding perfectly to the atmosphere of the game itself.
The Gameplay itself a solid system with which to base a game like this, revolving around preserving your heroes and completing your tasks during dungeons, with battles that often exacerbate your worries and frustrations, but that generally have an underlying system allowing to learn about your enemies and compensate for their actions.
Outside of the dungeons the gameplay revolves around distrubting your limited reasorces, often involving power-now upgrades versus things that will be useful in the future, complicated by the need to launch your missions with enough reasources in-dungeon to allow your heroes to succeed with minimized risks.
Heroes in general have a wide variety of skills, though I have found some to far outweigh others in-slot, though generally heroes have atleast two ways they can be played, with areas of grey inbetween.
The supposed elephant in the closet however is the early access, and while I haven't gone all the way through the game, I feel like currently I have reached close towards the end, but I rather expect to be surprised a few more times before the next wave of content is released.
Summing up: The game is brutal and callous towards your existance, but as you are a human who can think and maximize your reasources you will be able to learn and overcome, but it will take some time and it won't be gentle.

TL;DR at bottom.
Ah, Fallout 4.  This game can be a divisive one, some people love it, some people hate it for what it has done to such a prolific series.
For starters, the gameplay is vastly improved, an absolute improvement to previous 3D Fallout titles.  VATS is no longer a crutch, it's often more fun to use your FPS skills to actually aim for your opponents rather than hitting the VATS key to stop time to hit your opponent due to atrocious shooting mechanics.
Next up, a divisive issue with this game, the removal of RPG mechanics in favor of a more streamlined approach.  If you've played a previous Fallout title, you are familiar with skills and tag skills. You start out with a certain set of skill points distributed across several skills, and you choose a couple to give a  boost to. You then earn points with each level you can distribute to the various skills to specialize your character, and pick a perk based on your skills and S.P>E.C.I.A.L to add new abilites to your character every couple levels.  In Fallout 4, the skill system is scrapped in it's entirety for a system reliant entirely on S.P.E.C.I.A.L and perks.  This system certainly allows for a more streamlined and casual friendly level system, but it suffers from one critical flaw: no level cap.  Without a level cap, if you play long enough, your character looks just like everone elses character, and specialization is effectively not possible.
That's enough on the RPG part of the game, onto another divisive issue: Voiced protagonist.  In previous game by Bethesda, your character was mute, speaking through text prompts you would choose to advance the conversation. In Fallout 4, your character actually has a voice!  This poses a few problems. While the voice actors certainly do a good job with the lines, you can choose an option meaning to sound one way, and instead it comes out souding an entirely way.  In addition to this, the normal text prompts are replaced with a 4-option dialog wheel. Yes, No, Sarcastic, Maybe, that's it.  Personally, my biggest problem with the system is the incredibly limited dialog choices it leaves.  Which brings me to the next portion of my review.
The Story. Oh boy, this one's a doozy.  The story starts off ok, not great, but you almost don't expect it to be anymore coming from this company.  Halfway through, assuming you have missed spoilers for this long, you'll probably figure out the main twist well before it's shown, it's very predictable.  Another problem goes back to the lack of dialog options, the game pushes you toward the end so hard that the 4 options often end with the same result!  Furthermore, the skill and special checks that peppered the previous titles are largely gone, only Charisma checks remain save for maybe 2 bona-fied skill checks in side quests, and even then they aren't hard checks, just a chance of working.  Onto the ending, it's terrible. The end of the story, while not bad, feels unfinished.  No matter which faction you choose, the ending generally turns into kill the other factions, become leader or high ranking member chosen faction, and.....do nothing? The Commonwealth looks exactly the same afterward, you make no difference, and you can't make a difference in your new role with the faction.
Onward we must go, the story's ok, but you don't realy care about that, do you?  The world is amazing, I love frollicking through the streets of Boston, the atmosphere is superb and I'll go ahead and say Bethsoft nailed it. But the rest of the game....there's just not much there.  For the size of the world, you'd expect there to be, and they can be very repetitive. One such side quest involves a certain  NPC sending you off to defend and build settlements every single time you see him. I just avoid that guy honestly.  Though I will admit there are some great side quests in this game, just not enough.
Overall, I'd say the game was never finished. Bethesda might have bit off more than they could chew, or maybe they simply didn't care.  With large swaths of unfinished terrain outside of the game's map, an ending that felt rushed and unfinished, and unfullfilling side quests, I can't see how this game could possibly be the finished product they wanted it to be.
All in all, I enjoyed the game, but I can't see much potential for replayability.  If you just like the idea and the world of Fallout or just want to mod it, go for it, but if you enjoy the RPG aspects, a good story, and like to replay your games, go back to Skyrim or Fallout 3/New Vegas.
TL;DR:
Great gameplay, simplified RPG that suffers from lack of a level cap, limited dialog and a bad story without a fully fleshed out world leave this game feeling unfinished and hinder replayability. Still incrdibly fun the first time and mods do help somewhat.

While not a bad game by any means Darkest Dungeon is a slow, grueling, and needlessly-punishing experience. I first played Darkest Dungeon back in early access, and I thought it was a pretty decent concept. I'm a fan of games that are generally very difficult and punishing, as it can make your victory seem that much more satisfying. I'm also a fan of this type of dark medieval fantasy setting, so I'll admit the artstyle, audio and general atmosphere were definitely a huge draw as well. The game has definitely improved over the years, especially by adding much needed content, but it has not improved certain aspects that I found to be heavily flawed when I first played it.
In Darkest Dungeon you build a party of 4 heroes and send them down into a spooky dungeon to gain treasure and experience (assuming they accomplish their task). They will encounter various enemies, usually in groups of 2 to 4, who will aim to either kill your party members or cause immense "stress" by being exceptionally spooky. A character who's stress meter reachers 100 will then have their "resolve tested", which will usually lead to some kind of mental breakdown like fear or paranoia that will last for the rest of the dungeon. This will cause them to misbehave during combat, skipping turns, attacking allies, etc. which makes them very unreliable. Players are expected to manage their heroes' stress levels in the same way they manage their hit points.
Assuming one of your characters dies, it's not game over. In fact, the game is designed to allow you to lose party members by the handfuls. Despite only using 4 at a time to explore dungeons with, you can recruit dozens of heroes to sit in town as back-ups. And furthermore since highly-stressed characters need to rest up in town, you will generally have not one but many parties of heroes to do dungeons with. Your town acts as the game's progression; use the treasure you find in dungeons to buy new gear, learn and upgrade your heroes' skills, unlearn bad traits, cure diseases, and quickly undo stress with a trip to the tavern. The town itself can be upgraded too to give more options to the player in terms of what can be purchased and upgraded, and even if everyone dies you'll still have your town to work with; making it a somewhat permanent form of progression.
In a typical roguelike, dying is the end: you die, you start over. That means that in order for the game to feel fair in its difficulty, the player should never die simply because they got unlucky. However in Darkest Dungeon since (in the standard difficulty setting) you have as much time as you need and no limit on how many heroes are allowed to die... the game is not afraid to utterly slaughter your party members. This leads to some very annoying and unfair deaths, such as all 4 monsters in the enemy team attacking one of your heroes and killing them before you have a chance to respond. Situations like that are not the player's fault and there is literally nothing you can do to prevent such a thing. Deaths like these are supposedly justified because you've got plenty more heroes at your disposal; it's not like it's game over just because you lost 1 hero, right?
What makes a roguelike good is the possibility of being dealt a bad hand, possibly one of the worst, and still having a reasonable chance of winning. In every roguelike/roguelite I've ever played there has been a significant element of randomness that factored into the player's success. In most of the better games, that randomness can be mitigated by various elements so that you never feel like you lost a game because you had bad luck. In Faster Than Light, players manage the randomness by being prepared for the worst, spending their scrap wisely, and properly micromanaging their crew and doors. In Binding of Isaac, you can beat the game with poor upgrades simply by playing very carefully and being skilled at dodging enemy's attacks. In traditional roguelikes (like Tales of Maj'Eyal) you've usually got a myriad of scouting, positioning and utility skills to ensure that bad luck is almost never the reason you died.
In Darkest Dungeon, however, there are consistently situations where you lose a hero or are forced to abandon the dungeon because of bad luck. While losing a single hero may not be the end of the game, it can be very frustrating to lose a character you've invested so much time into, especially when you had very little control (if any at all) over their fate. The main problem is that the combat is incredibly simple. There's very little room for actual skill to come into the equation. Outside of just knowing the best hero party compositions and not making any obvious mistakes, there's really nothing that significant you can do to increase your chance of winning a fight. This style of turn-based combat was designed to work with story-driven RPG games where "losing" was virtually impossible, and even if you did lose you could just continue from a saved game or a checkpoint. It just doesn't work for a highly-punishing roguelite.
The game can feel very tedious at times due to the extremely slow sequencing. Loading screens, menu transitions, walking and combat animations are rather sluggish and make up about 90% of the game. There's some mods on the workshop that make walking and combat a bit faster, but it's far from ideal. In your first few hours you won't mind because the game has a great artstyle and you won't mind basking in the atmosphere, but once you've played for awhile you'll find it's slow pace to be a nuisance. Especially if one or more of your heroes was killed and you're thinking about how much time you've just wasted as a result.
I also felt that the game was very lacking in hero customization. Each character can pick 4 combat and camping skills out of 7, and equip them with 2 trinkets (your choices are rather limited as there's almost always an obvious best option for these). That's it. That's the only character customization you get. You can use the sanitorium to "lock" their randomly generated positive traits in so they're not replaced by other ones, but that's too finnicky and random of a system for me to consider it a form of true character customization. The only real customization you get is deciding which 4 heroes to use together, and I'll admit that is my favorite part of the game, but I just wish it was more in-depth.
I generally don't recommend this game because of luck is the primary deciding factor in a player's success, especially when there are so many other much better rogulike/lites out there. This game will quite literally test your patience.

If there's one game I would recommend buying this quater for those of you who enjoy a sprinkle of masochism in their video games, then I have to recommend this one.
Starting at the top with the visuals. The best way I can find it is to suggest it evokes the ideas of an old, rusted cleaver, caked with blood, in that it's purpose is often clear and intentionally threatening, adding perfectly to the atmosphere of the game itself.
The Gameplay itself a solid system with which to base a game like this, revolving around preserving your heroes and completing your tasks during dungeons, with battles that often exacerbate your worries and frustrations, but that generally have an underlying system allowing to learn about your enemies and compensate for their actions.
Outside of the dungeons the gameplay revolves around distrubting your limited reasorces, often involving power-now upgrades versus things that will be useful in the future, complicated by the need to launch your missions with enough reasources in-dungeon to allow your heroes to succeed with minimized risks.
Heroes in general have a wide variety of skills, though I have found some to far outweigh others in-slot, though generally heroes have atleast two ways they can be played, with areas of grey inbetween.
The supposed elephant in the closet however is the early access, and while I haven't gone all the way through the game, I feel like currently I have reached close towards the end, but I rather expect to be surprised a few more times before the next wave of content is released.
Summing up: The game is brutal and callous towards your existance, but as you are a human who can think and maximize your reasources you will be able to learn and overcome, but it will take some time and it won't be gentle.

Just realized I haven't reviewed this one.
After some glitches on PC (square monitor = lockpicking doesn't work, unless you window it), I got super absorbed yet again in to the fallout universe.
This game though has so much more content packed in at evert turn though.
If you go wandering around (as you occasionally can, and are encouraged to do), you'll stumble on a plethora of story and world building.
This game brings something new and untested to the Fallout 4 formula (like boats did to assassin's creed).
You can build your own village, and have it protect itself against raiders (or help them out). In turn they'll help you out to defend against random encounters by bombardment, and possibly walking up and joining in?
I don't really know, because what actually happened, was in my playthrough, I built a sky-fortress-come-power-armour-garage that I didn't let any of my NPCs in, then built some turrets, and pretty much left them to themselves, while I explore this beautiful world.
The main storyline makes sense, and they let you choose your own path. So when presented the choice, I shot my own son in the face after spending most of the storyline looking for him. It might have let's say cut the story short a bit, but still feel justified in this course of action, and the payoff wasn't bad either.
I also really liked the "chinese take" in this one with the submarine mission. It felt like it brought a new perspective in to it.
Now all we need for the next game, is some Tom Lehrer music!
PS: Loading screens at the start, and switching areas one of the best (least irritating) I've seen, pretty much ever. They can occasionally be a tad long. But it's not Xcom2 long.
PPS: Tip for new players: You might want to find a new settlement "out of the way" from your main one as soon as possible, then send Preston Garvey there. I swear, I spend half the time dodging him, so he doesn't give me another damn "the wasteland is in trouble" quest.
FUN A must buy! well worth the price

I has been a while, but I can honestly say that this game rocks my socks off.
I have been playing it on and off and every time I took some time off the developers tweaked and added to the game on such a regular basis that everytime I returned to it I pretty much had to relearn the game. Not that I mind, hell I love the fact that the developers continue to tweak, bugfix and add to the game.

-New characters: the houndsmaster with his best friend and the shapeshifting abomination.

TL;DR at bottom.
Ah, Fallout 4.  This game can be a divisive one, some people love it, some people hate it for what it has done to such a prolific series.
For starters, the gameplay is vastly improved, an absolute improvement to previous 3D Fallout titles.  VATS is no longer a crutch, it's often more fun to use your FPS skills to actually aim for your opponents rather than hitting the VATS key to stop time to hit your opponent due to atrocious shooting mechanics.
Next up, a divisive issue with this game, the removal of RPG mechanics in favor of a more streamlined approach.  If you've played a previous Fallout title, you are familiar with skills and tag skills. You start out with a certain set of skill points distributed across several skills, and you choose a couple to give a  boost to. You then earn points with each level you can distribute to the various skills to specialize your character, and pick a perk based on your skills and S.P>E.C.I.A.L to add new abilites to your character every couple levels.  In Fallout 4, the skill system is scrapped in it's entirety for a system reliant entirely on S.P.E.C.I.A.L and perks.  This system certainly allows for a more streamlined and casual friendly level system, but it suffers from one critical flaw: no level cap.  Without a level cap, if you play long enough, your character looks just like everone elses character, and specialization is effectively not possible.
That's enough on the RPG part of the game, onto another divisive issue: Voiced protagonist.  In previous game by Bethesda, your character was mute, speaking through text prompts you would choose to advance the conversation. In Fallout 4, your character actually has a voice!  This poses a few problems. While the voice actors certainly do a good job with the lines, you can choose an option meaning to sound one way, and instead it comes out souding an entirely way.  In addition to this, the normal text prompts are replaced with a 4-option dialog wheel. Yes, No, Sarcastic, Maybe, that's it.  Personally, my biggest problem with the system is the incredibly limited dialog choices it leaves.  Which brings me to the next portion of my review.
The Story. Oh boy, this one's a doozy.  The story starts off ok, not great, but you almost don't expect it to be anymore coming from this company.  Halfway through, assuming you have missed spoilers for this long, you'll probably figure out the main twist well before it's shown, it's very predictable.  Another problem goes back to the lack of dialog options, the game pushes you toward the end so hard that the 4 options often end with the same result!  Furthermore, the skill and special checks that peppered the previous titles are largely gone, only Charisma checks remain save for maybe 2 bona-fied skill checks in side quests, and even then they aren't hard checks, just a chance of working.  Onto the ending, it's terrible. The end of the story, while not bad, feels unfinished.  No matter which faction you choose, the ending generally turns into kill the other factions, become leader or high ranking member chosen faction, and.....do nothing? The Commonwealth looks exactly the same afterward, you make no difference, and you can't make a difference in your new role with the faction.
Onward we must go, the story's ok, but you don't realy care about that, do you?  The world is amazing, I love frollicking through the streets of Boston, the atmosphere is superb and I'll go ahead and say Bethsoft nailed it. But the rest of the game....there's just not much there.  For the size of the world, you'd expect there to be, and they can be very repetitive. One such side quest involves a certain  NPC sending you off to defend and build settlements every single time you see him. I just avoid that guy honestly.  Though I will admit there are some great side quests in this game, just not enough.
Overall, I'd say the game was never finished. Bethesda might have bit off more than they could chew, or maybe they simply didn't care.  With large swaths of unfinished terrain outside of the game's map, an ending that felt rushed and unfinished, and unfullfilling side quests, I can't see how this game could possibly be the finished product they wanted it to be.
All in all, I enjoyed the game, but I can't see much potential for replayability.  If you just like the idea and the world of Fallout or just want to mod it, go for it, but if you enjoy the RPG aspects, a good story, and like to replay your games, go back to Skyrim or Fallout 3/New Vegas.
TL;DR:
Great gameplay, simplified RPG that suffers from lack of a level cap, limited dialog and a bad story without a fully fleshed out world leave this game feeling unfinished and hinder replayability. Still incrdibly fun the first time and mods do help somewhat.

I have my early access review below, quoted.  I had suggested the game then.  Times changed, development created frustration, and then when it launched it did so at a cheaper  price than we paid for early access.
If I had it to do again, I wouldn't buy the game.
"I have been told it's very similar to Terraria, but I have no experience with that game and only a small amount with Minecraft.   Why? These games bore me to tears typically.   I get on, play for 20-30 minutes and then lose interest in them.  Nothing usually catches me.
But yet the early beta of Starbound has been exceptionally fun to me.   I'm not really sure which point appeals to me the most, so I'm going to just discuss the parts that I enjoy.
The first one is the variety of species, both for your own character and as inhabitants of the various worlds.  It's fun to run into an Apex (Ape People) science facility on one planet, then stumble into a prison on another with every species you can think of held captive.  And that's not even including the wide array of native animals you find on every planet.  I've yet to see the same exact alien on multiple planets that wasn't a major species of humanoid.
Another interesting aspect is that you can travel all these worlds, with each one being different in one way or another.  Exploring them, harvesting on them, hunting on them.  And then just return back to your ship whenever you're on the surface from any part of the world by simply having Scotty beam you up. (Disclaimer: It's not actually Scotty, but we can pretend.)   You can decorate your ship (And they are working on adding ship customization due to the popularity of the ship customizing mods that are available) and turn it into a mobile base of operations, a home, a giant storage facility, whatever.
The downside is the way that advancement is basically throttled by boss fights.  You can gather and create a ton of things, but eventually to advance to the next tech tier you have to build a specific boss summoning item from your current tier.  Defeat the boss, get their drop, and use it to create the next tech tiers item and advance forward.   I hate this aspect because it takes away a lot of control in a sandbox experience.
With things like building your own Mechs, customizing your space ship, and flying hoverbikes on the horizon? I'm excited to see the beta advance further.  But be warned! The game is currently wiping characters in the early beta, though that won't be lasting much longer."

This latest update has changed Starbound completely. In a good way, of course.
There is so much new, everything shown in Starbound news, everything the team was working on!
I've been playing around 12 hours non-stop and can only leave a positive review to this.
Sure, there are bugs and crashes, but again, this is in beta version and will further on improve!
Now, to the review itself:
You start in a broken ship which you have to fix up in order to start travelling. Before you travel you gather resources and minerals that are needed to fix up the ship so it can move. This is basically your first quest which involves exploring of your starting planet and digging from surface down to the core of the planet.
You then are sent to a mysterious gate that leads to an outpost where you see a gathering of multiple races, such as glitch, human, avian, floran, hylotl, apex who give you quests and missions that let you proceed further into the game.
The entire concept is mostly exploring. You get all your gear through mining for ores and occasionally bumping into chests which have a rare chance of having a rare weapons and cosmetics which makes the game more fun. Besides, if you explore further down, you may find some small labs of sorts that have these chests and other items aside!
Some of the quests involve finding an item, such as an Avian Moon Emblem which can only be found at Avian Tombs which take time to search for.
This kind of quests is ideal for Starbound due to the fact that it forces the player to explore non-stop in order to proceed further through and upgrade their gear, matter manipulator and even the ship.
This was about gameplay.
Races:
There are 7 races - Glitch, Human, Avian, Floran, Apex, Hylotl, Novakids.
All of them have their own styles of gear and ships, later on will also have special race abilities!
Planets:
Before you randomly click on a planet to travel to you are meant to see how dangerous it is, you can't just go on a planet with high radiation while wearing only iron tier gear!
They divide in following difficulties: Harmless, Mostly Harmless, Moderate, Dangerous, Extreme.
You start on Harmless, it also however has almost nothing on it, apart from weak monsters and some trees. Mostly Harmless has stronger gear, monsters and even dungeons you can visit. And so it goes on... There also are different types: Forest, desert, arid, ocean, snow, snow ocean, jungle and extreme planets with lava on surface with no air to breate with enormously high temperature. There also are moons where you can gather up with fuel for your ship! They however dont have any ore.
Other than that, all of these have their own weather. An example would be sand storms in desert, rain in ocean and forest, snow storm in frozen planets, etc.
There is still some stuff lacking however. It can't be called a FULL game, but it can be called a descent game. Even though the updates aren't so frequent, why do you people just whine about it? Starbound isn't the only game in the world, why keep so many hopes on a single early access game?
As for the new winter update content itself, there is a lot you can talk about, but it is always better to play the game to see it all yourself!

What can I even say about Trove? I've been with the game since closed beta, and I don't even know how many hours I've played. I guess if I had to TL;DR this review, I'd just say "Play this goddamn game."
On the surface, Trove looks like Minecraft Clone #437, and while Trove definitely takes cues from Minecraft, it's anything but a clone. Trove retains Minecraft's basic system of breaking and picking up blocks for later use, but makes some improvements I find to be very nice.
-Blocks aren't a defined material; they're just different colors. This gives greater flexibility when building
-You can gather blocks further away with the help of frickin' laser beams
In addition, you get a persistent plot of land on which you can build whatever you like. Furthermore, this plot of land can be moved to any other empty plot you find, and anything you built on it moves right along with it. If you're not content just building on that little plot of land, though, you can make a Club, Trove's answer to guilds, and get an entire persistent world on which to build with your friends.
The building really isn't the main attraction of Trove, though. At least not for me. For me, the combat and dungeons are the best part. Combat handles like a cross between a third person shooter and your standard MMO combat; aim with the mouse, attack with the left mouse button, and use abilities with RMB and the number keys. While the combat system isn't especially deep, it's quite simply FUN, and if you get bored with one class, there are 10 more at the time of my writing this, with more to come. The dungeons, like combat, aren't incredibly nuanced things, but from the moment you finish the tutorial, you can head off to find a dungeon to run, since all of the procedurally generated worlds are jam-packed with dungeons, with mercifully few random mobs to slog through in between. Dungeons are varied, and while you're likely to find some repeats, the enemies and bosses change every time, so you never play quite the same thing twice.
So that's enough of the sales pitch. Let's get into the pros and cons.
PROS
+Fun combat
+Fun, unique classes
+Great sense of humor
+Lots to do
+Great character customization
+Constantly updating
+Player-made dungeons and equipment
+Great graphics
+Free to play, not pay to win
CONS
-Can get a bit repetitive after several hundred hours
-It takes a little longer than I'd like to get new classes without using real money
-Servers are a little clogged post-launch
Long story short, you're missing out if you don't give this game a try.

Soooo, turns out the "next generation of open-world gaming" does not include an ending, and gives you no real agency.
To elaborate: Fallout used to be all about choices. From the original Fallout all the way up to New Vegas, your actions had consequences. Your decision to visit a place (or not), help a town (or not), kill someone (or not) had an impact on everything that followed. Doors would open or close depending on what kind of a wastelander you chose to be.
Not least, the ending would always be different. You could look back upon your journey as a paragon of virtue, a harbinger of doom, or a chaotic jester. With your help, Shady Sands could evolve into a teeming hub of trade and progress, capital of a budding republic. Or you could let the town and its people wither and die. In Broken Hills, humans and mutants could learn to live peacefully together, and spread a message of tolerance to the world beyond – or a race war could erupt, killing everyone.
In Fallout 4, instead of all this, you get settlement construction. Settlements are a place to store companions you're not using. Not that they mind if you're not actually constructing anything.

I have my early access review below, quoted.  I had suggested the game then.  Times changed, development created frustration, and then when it launched it did so at a cheaper  price than we paid for early access.
If I had it to do again, I wouldn't buy the game.
"I have been told it's very similar to Terraria, but I have no experience with that game and only a small amount with Minecraft.   Why? These games bore me to tears typically.   I get on, play for 20-30 minutes and then lose interest in them.  Nothing usually catches me.
But yet the early beta of Starbound has been exceptionally fun to me.   I'm not really sure which point appeals to me the most, so I'm going to just discuss the parts that I enjoy.
The first one is the variety of species, both for your own character and as inhabitants of the various worlds.  It's fun to run into an Apex (Ape People) science facility on one planet, then stumble into a prison on another with every species you can think of held captive.  And that's not even including the wide array of native animals you find on every planet.  I've yet to see the same exact alien on multiple planets that wasn't a major species of humanoid.
Another interesting aspect is that you can travel all these worlds, with each one being different in one way or another.  Exploring them, harvesting on them, hunting on them.  And then just return back to your ship whenever you're on the surface from any part of the world by simply having Scotty beam you up. (Disclaimer: It's not actually Scotty, but we can pretend.)   You can decorate your ship (And they are working on adding ship customization due to the popularity of the ship customizing mods that are available) and turn it into a mobile base of operations, a home, a giant storage facility, whatever.
The downside is the way that advancement is basically throttled by boss fights.  You can gather and create a ton of things, but eventually to advance to the next tech tier you have to build a specific boss summoning item from your current tier.  Defeat the boss, get their drop, and use it to create the next tech tiers item and advance forward.   I hate this aspect because it takes away a lot of control in a sandbox experience.
With things like building your own Mechs, customizing your space ship, and flying hoverbikes on the horizon? I'm excited to see the beta advance further.  But be warned! The game is currently wiping characters in the early beta, though that won't be lasting much longer."

This latest update has changed Starbound completely. In a good way, of course.
There is so much new, everything shown in Starbound news, everything the team was working on!
I've been playing around 12 hours non-stop and can only leave a positive review to this.
Sure, there are bugs and crashes, but again, this is in beta version and will further on improve!
Now, to the review itself:
You start in a broken ship which you have to fix up in order to start travelling. Before you travel you gather resources and minerals that are needed to fix up the ship so it can move. This is basically your first quest which involves exploring of your starting planet and digging from surface down to the core of the planet.
You then are sent to a mysterious gate that leads to an outpost where you see a gathering of multiple races, such as glitch, human, avian, floran, hylotl, apex who give you quests and missions that let you proceed further into the game.
The entire concept is mostly exploring. You get all your gear through mining for ores and occasionally bumping into chests which have a rare chance of having a rare weapons and cosmetics which makes the game more fun. Besides, if you explore further down, you may find some small labs of sorts that have these chests and other items aside!
Some of the quests involve finding an item, such as an Avian Moon Emblem which can only be found at Avian Tombs which take time to search for.
This kind of quests is ideal for Starbound due to the fact that it forces the player to explore non-stop in order to proceed further through and upgrade their gear, matter manipulator and even the ship.
This was about gameplay.
Races:
There are 7 races - Glitch, Human, Avian, Floran, Apex, Hylotl, Novakids.
All of them have their own styles of gear and ships, later on will also have special race abilities!
Planets:
Before you randomly click on a planet to travel to you are meant to see how dangerous it is, you can't just go on a planet with high radiation while wearing only iron tier gear!
They divide in following difficulties: Harmless, Mostly Harmless, Moderate, Dangerous, Extreme.
You start on Harmless, it also however has almost nothing on it, apart from weak monsters and some trees. Mostly Harmless has stronger gear, monsters and even dungeons you can visit. And so it goes on... There also are different types: Forest, desert, arid, ocean, snow, snow ocean, jungle and extreme planets with lava on surface with no air to breate with enormously high temperature. There also are moons where you can gather up with fuel for your ship! They however dont have any ore.
Other than that, all of these have their own weather. An example would be sand storms in desert, rain in ocean and forest, snow storm in frozen planets, etc.
There is still some stuff lacking however. It can't be called a FULL game, but it can be called a descent game. Even though the updates aren't so frequent, why do you people just whine about it? Starbound isn't the only game in the world, why keep so many hopes on a single early access game?
As for the new winter update content itself, there is a lot you can talk about, but it is always better to play the game to see it all yourself!

Woe be the heroes, those poor souls who descend into these odious crypts of unimaginable horrors in search of treasure and glory.  Woe be those who return, should they return, as though they may bring glittering treasures and experience from below, they will also be the bearers of the scars wrought of terror and despair.  Send them not lightly as surely these items can be used to improve these heroes, at what cost do they come?  Physical wounds heal freely, but calm of spirit is sought through both debauched and pious vices, acts which often bring scars of their own.
I actually agree with many of the people who do not recommend this game, your mileage may vary.  The RNG is really, really cruel and some things need to be disconnected from it.  However, even without tuning the difficulty works.  This is Lovecraftian horror, everything is out of your control and the things that are within your control seem to barely matter.  Darkest Dungeon is a mean game.  It never gives you a break, never extends a helping hand and constantly demands sacrifice.  On some levels it can be deceptively simple: combat, skills, levelling and equipment are all boiled down into simple upgrade paths, and yet range and targets, party orientation and stress mean this is no point-click-win adventure.  Sometimes all options suck.  Do you retreat?  Press on?  Let someone break?  Let them die?  Do you risk your strong?  Or send an untrained face into the fire?  Every detail has a cost, nothing comes for free and the longer you spend in the dungeon the worse it is going to get.  This management is the hardest part of the game and you often make due with anyone not drinking, praying or being admitted which can cost you even more if you don't plan accordingly.
That's not to say it's perfect, but if Cthulu set in a medieval setting at all appeals to you, this is probably worth picking up.  The setting is perhaps the game's biggest initial strength—this isn't Tolkien-inspired fantasy, it has room to breathe and it takes in the fresh air.  Though I hope the developers take the criticism to polish the rough edges before launch, I strongly recommend this title.

I've heard a lot of things about Fallout 4. How Bethesda messed up, how Fallout 3 and NV were better.
Well I can't really confirm or deny that last part, because German censoring laws are weird and I'm not going to play a game with horrendous German dub voices. Anyway.
So, that leaves me being a first time player of the Fallout series, starting off with 4. Thus, I don't know anything BUT 4 and cannot say if Bethesda messed it all up. They probably did, but I don't care.
In short, I think this is a great game. I have a lot of fun with it. I'd recommend you get it on sale or off of key-dealers because it's not actually worth 60€.
Fallout 4 is a narrative RPG that lacks the RPG feeling a bit. I do agree that a Karma system, like the one seen in Mass Effect (again, can't speak for FO3 or NV), with the entire Paragon/Renegade thing, would have been highly beneficial, as it would have allowed for more character development of the player character. But Bethesda has always lacked the ability to really create an in-depth player-character, as has been shown with Skyrim. It's really up to you to imagine a story around your character. It's not optimal, but hey.
So yes, Fallout 4 definitely falls short in the category "player character". But what it lacks there it makes up for with it's many, many characters, specifically the companions, that now have their own moral likes and dislikes, with a built in sort of karma system that varies from companion to companion. So really, the company you keep in this game defines your character, because they seem to be the only ones that reflect your choices at all.
The companions, with their new likes and dislikes, feel very interactive, at least to me. Each of them is unique and likeable in their own way, with backstories and their own struggles. They are the ones developing over the course of your story, not the player. While I agree that that simply shouldn't happen, with an open world game it can be rather hard to create the same sort of variety and uniqueness of player characters you can see in more linear titles. In the end though, I find myself playing for the companions, not my player character.
The main quest was alright. It wasn't the best, necessarily, but it wasn't bad. What I loved were the personal quests for characters, be it companion or random stranger. Some of those quests left me deeply conflicted
and were genuinly fun.
Fallout 4 also has many tone-shifts. It can go from grind quest "shoot-em-up" to more quietly disturbing in moments.
About those grind quests....
I do not understand why every single place I visit has to be riddled with ghouls, mirelurks or raiders. Because really, some of the locations are horrifying even without things trying to kill you. Sombre things like an entire family dieing, families seperated and dieing, people subjecting themselves to radiation and dieing, and just a whole lot more tragic dieing all over the place. Because Fallout 4 does the entire "scary without monsters" well. They just throw the goddamn monsters in anyway, which I think to be tedious and wholly unnecessary, but what can you do.
Nontheless, I felt deeply affected by many a story of the Commonwealth. Even if I had to fight an ungodly amount of mirelurks to be able to feel anything for the sceneary.
But, at the same time, there are certain stories that just wholly ripped me out of my immersion.
Then there are the glitches. The cars falling out of the sky. Carla's brahmin chilling in the living room of a house in Sanctuary. Marcy standing on a roof. Nick air-swimming. Preston sitting on air, phasing through walls or sitting inside tables. Yeah, it's a bit broken sometimes. Also, the engine seems to have trouble with light on object in dark rooms for some reason.
But really, while it breaks the immersion, it can be hella funny to see a flying deathclaw satisfyingly splat onto the dusty floor of the Commonwealth. It's part of the fun of a Bethesda game, to be honest.
Point being, it's sometimes hilarious and I'm fine with glitches.
People often critisize how Bethesda is still using the Morrowind engine. I don't see the issue- after all, Valve still uses Source, do they not? Really, it has no impact on the game, and as someone who has a Skyim and a Fallout 4 game going, I don't really notice that they run on the same engine. They improved the engine, that's all that matters, and it looks far nicer. Overall that's fine.
What is not fine is that I get 40FPS on Low/Medium graphics with a PC that gets 60FPS on higher-end games. What is also not fine is that my high res texture mod gets better performance than the default textures on low.
Also not fine is the fact that settlement building, something which has a very high importance in Fallout4, is so unbearable, what with placement issues and other nonsense that makes it frustrating to do anything with.
But what's great? There's official mod support now. Which means that almost everything I've mentioned can be ironed out.
And while the FPS is horrible, at least for me, the atmosphere is wonderful. No ENBs are required to make this game picturesque, especially in the indoor areas.
Now, keep in mind I'm judging whether or not this game will be worth your time, not if it's a really good game. Because it's not. It lacks a lot and can get very tedious after a while. The mods balance all that out and make it worth your time.
I know that I've bashed this game a lot, but I still think it's a good game. I like the plot. I like the characters. I love my companions, the stories, modding my weapons till they are dreadfully OP...
It's fun
That's all I know, that's all I care about
Also don't do Preston's radiant quests if you value your nerves. They don't do anything, are repetitive, tedious, and are good for nothing but EXP grinding. Also they bug out, saying you failed when you didn't. There's a reason why Preston Garvey has a meme now.

This game is a difficult game to recommend, which is a shame, because I'd really like to.
The Art Style and Atmosphere are terrifically dark and grimy, the soundtrack is top-notch and I'm a particular fan of the Affliction and Stress system.
However, the game has issues, mainly stemming from the RNG, and the extent to which the game seems to rely upon it for its difficulty. It's hard to think of an aspect of the game that doesn't work by a Random Number Generator. Combat varies wildly from outright disaster to legendary success seemingly regardless of player input, for instance. In addition, the game suffers from a lack of content, with only three dungeons currently available, all of which do tend to get a bit samey even with procedural generation. In its current state, the game is a bit overpriced for what is currently offered.
The combat can be immensely confusing as well, with the functions and effects of some stats remaining very much a mystery for much of the game, and learning how all of the different classes work together can be quite overwhleming.
Other minor issues include annoying dialogue bubbles both in and out of dungeons that start off quite cool, but quickly become repetitive, and combat animations that also leave something to be desired.
However, I have still found the game to be hugely enjoyable, despite all of the critiscisms above. I have not been particularly irritated by RNG thus far, and the Stress and Afflictions have been a big selling point for me ever since I first heard about the game, although I know some players haven't enjoyed them as much as I have. I have found the combat fun, and the town that acts as your Hub is really cool. Upgrading it as you play is really fun, although the amount of options can make it confusing at first.
All in all, while I have enjoyed the game immensely myself, I can't recommend it currently no matter how much I might want to. If you're a fan of roguelikes and dungeon-crawling RPGs, then you might want to give this a go if you think you can put up with the games current issues, as many have. However, if you feel a bit concerned about any of the aforementioned issues, then you may want to back off, and wait for the full release.

TL, DR:
Get the vanilla game only if it's on sale. (6/10)
Pros:
- Combat is pretty solid for a non-shooter.
- Some companions are pretty funny.
- Weapon and armor customization is decent.
- You do feel like a badass.
- Diamond City changes decorations if the in-game date is on Halloween or Christmas, so that's nice.
- Caps and ammo are easier to obtain as opposed to previous games.
- Codsworth can say common names.
Meh:
- Story is okay (and highly predictable).
- Some quest activation takes a bit of hunting for the right situation at the right time which can be infuriating at times, especially if you're a completionist
- Other companions are pretty lame, not as much character building as compared to Fallout New Vegas.
- The lack of diversity of companion affinity forces you to play nice most of the time.
Cons:
- The entire settlement building mechanic. From the premise, to the actual building, to the crappy snapping, to the irritating radiant defence quests, to Preston Garvey becoming my most hated character very quickly... The settlement building is just
.
- Speech checks are on RNG instead of hard stats.
- Simplified perk system compromises on the core of Fallout games
- You actually make no impact with your choices because the game almost ends in the same way no matter what you do.
- Season pass is daylight robbery.
- Almost all the DLCs are overpriced and not worth buying.
As some reviewers have noted here, flak is shot at Fallout 4 because of its "lack" compared to the previous Fallout titles. For myself personally, I have completed Fallout 3, New Vegas and Fallout 4, clocking enough time to finish every main quest (vanilla and DLC) for each game on the console and buying from Steam during a sale was only for the mods and messing around with the game.
For new players:
If this is your first Fallout experience, get Fallout 4 on a sale. I think it's quite gentle on new players in the form of simplified mechanics and making Fallout more combat-based rather than "conversation-based" or "stealth-based". There is little need to sneak (since silenced weapons are hard to make in early-game anyway) and unless you're playing on Very Hard or Survival, you would survive just about any humanoid that the game throws at you (if you face a Deathclaw then... sorry.)
It's still quite a rich (albeit cliche) experience with decent graphics and pretty solid weapon and armor customization. The settlement building gets irritating after a while, but for myself, I base my entire collection of loot in one settlement, fortified a few settlements (Sanctuary and the few settlements around Sanctuary) and ignored the rest because the settlement quests usually interrupts the general flow of the game.
Get it when it's on sale but
. Besides Automatron and Far Harbor, the other DLCs are completely overpriced and not worth it (Nuka World is... debatable). The season pass at that price is practically daylight robbery - you could get another AAA title with that money and enjoy yourself way more than you would with the season pass.
The vanilla game is enough to introduce you to the Fallout world and when you're done with Fallout 4,
which will complete your experience and leave you wanting more (with Fallout 3, 2 and 1).
For Fallout fans and players familiar to the series:
Yes, in all honesty, Fallout 3 and New Vegas was better than Fallout 4 because of the RPG intricacies that FO3 and NV offers - from using your skill points more wisely to perks being linked to both SPECIAL points and skills, it causes the player to be more strategic and directed in their playstyle - do I go for stealth? do I focus on a melee build? do I focus on a "trader" build maxing Barter, Speech, Medicine and Repair?... these questions made me truly enjoy Fallout and increases replayability because usually about 50-60% through any runthrough, I find myself wondering if other builds can finish some quests or the entire game faster.
Fallout 4 just kills that. And it gets frustrating because builds cannot be clearly defined from their simplified perk system and the starting SPECIAL distribution is just... wrong. No longer can I max my Intelligence stat and still have decent points for the other SPECIALs, but now I have to compromise even more. It'll be helpful if the compromise actually affects the way quests turn out, but it doesn't because mainly, speech options are now on probability rather than hardened statistics. Yes, while I can always quicksave on conversations and reload if I don't get the outcome I want, it's not the point when I have max Charisma and still fail speech checks more often than I should (failing a yellow check once made me stop playing for the day).
I think what Bethesda has done well in this title is to polish up the combat system (except weapon damage but more on that later). VATS become spur of the moment decisions (which made me spend less time in VATS and more time actually on ADS), combat feels more smooth with AI being slightly smarter, taking cover, flanking you, throwing grenades to flush you out... not as good as any FPS out there but it's still something. The combat AI from previous games is quite laughable as you can pick them off easily since they hardly take cover and if you die in previous games, it's because you failed to spot an enemy standing in the open. In Fallout 4, combat actually feels fun (which made me drop the stealth build) and at times (especially at one point in the Automatron DLC), I was tempted to lower the difficulty for that fight because I kept getting swarmed and was forced into a literal corner.
However, from the simplified perk system, weapon damage becomes pretty silly as you have to specialize in a type of weapon (semi-automatic rifles, automatic weapons, pistols, explosives) relatively early on in the game because weapon damage is directly linked to perks instead of previous installments where your skills have a slightly smaller multiplier towards weapon damage (weapon damage is more dependent on the weapon itself). The diversity of weapons felt shrunk in Fallout 4 so I find it irksome that I have to rely on perks to improve my damage output on a pretty decent mid-game unique weapon instead of finding a slightly better gun.
Some companions are pretty amusing though and I think the voice acting is relatively decent on that front (unless one compares to RPGs with great voice work like Mass Effect, then it falls pretty flat)
Hopefully Bethesda works with Obsidian again for the next title, and that we would get a better game worth its weight in the future. But for this, I do not recommend Fallout 4 unless it's on a huge sale or Bethesda lowers the price of the DLCs to complete an expensive experience.

This game is a difficult game to recommend, which is a shame, because I'd really like to.
The Art Style and Atmosphere are terrifically dark and grimy, the soundtrack is top-notch and I'm a particular fan of the Affliction and Stress system.
However, the game has issues, mainly stemming from the RNG, and the extent to which the game seems to rely upon it for its difficulty. It's hard to think of an aspect of the game that doesn't work by a Random Number Generator. Combat varies wildly from outright disaster to legendary success seemingly regardless of player input, for instance. In addition, the game suffers from a lack of content, with only three dungeons currently available, all of which do tend to get a bit samey even with procedural generation. In its current state, the game is a bit overpriced for what is currently offered.
The combat can be immensely confusing as well, with the functions and effects of some stats remaining very much a mystery for much of the game, and learning how all of the different classes work together can be quite overwhleming.
Other minor issues include annoying dialogue bubbles both in and out of dungeons that start off quite cool, but quickly become repetitive, and combat animations that also leave something to be desired.
However, I have still found the game to be hugely enjoyable, despite all of the critiscisms above. I have not been particularly irritated by RNG thus far, and the Stress and Afflictions have been a big selling point for me ever since I first heard about the game, although I know some players haven't enjoyed them as much as I have. I have found the combat fun, and the town that acts as your Hub is really cool. Upgrading it as you play is really fun, although the amount of options can make it confusing at first.
All in all, while I have enjoyed the game immensely myself, I can't recommend it currently no matter how much I might want to. If you're a fan of roguelikes and dungeon-crawling RPGs, then you might want to give this a go if you think you can put up with the games current issues, as many have. However, if you feel a bit concerned about any of the aforementioned issues, then you may want to back off, and wait for the full release.
