834.6 hours in Fallout 4 (current, and still climbing)
---I will preface this.  I am an Elder scrolls fan.  I bought Fallout 4 to hold me over till Elder Scrolls 6.---
TL;DR at bottom.
I love this game.  I had no idea I'd put in almost twice the hours into this game than one of my favorite franchises.  I took Bethesda on their word and good faith that they usually nail the value of their season passes (IMO and at the time), and I paid $30 for my season pass about a week after I bought the game.  I anticipated getting a good bit of time into this game, but nowhere near what I have now.
Fo4 did what Fo3 and NV failed to do: draw me in.  It gave me more than just running around, killing stuff, and questing.  When I got bored of slaughtering raiders (and getting slaughtered by a random deathclaw) I would go and work on my settlements.  That helped significantly to fill the gap in when I just wanted to take a break from story and questing.
Pros:
-The graphics are beautiful.  Yes, they could always be better, but some folks were complaining about "they're just slightly better than Skyrim" well Skyrim also looked pretty danged good when it was released. Install some graphics mods and get over yourself.
-Combat is fluid and smooth.
-There's a good variety of enemies to get killed by.
-Piper and Curie.
-Loads of stuff to do outside of combat.  Far Harbor and Nuka World added great amounts of new territory to tear through.
-Most of the DLC is great.  Far Harbor added a good bit of new territory and enemies and had some beautiful surroundings at times, Nuka World is just downright fun and also had loads more area to run through, and is where I spent most of my time outside of the commonwealth. Automatron was great with new enemies and robot building, but I really don't use any of the stuff from Wasteland/Contraptions Workshop. The Vault Tech workshop was good in the vast expanse that it allows you to build your vault (it's seriously huge) but I am not good enough with digging through everything or coming up with floor plans to actually build my own vault well.  It has a couple of quests to do, and the experiments weren't really that in depth, but overall, the sheer amount of exploration and items added for settlement building is good.
-Mods.  Mods, mods, mods and mods.  Don't like something in the game? Stop complaining about it and mod it! Seriously it's a fool proof design and it's not that hard.  Playing this without mods, graphical or game changing, is severely limiting the potential.  Think the graphics are "too Skyrim?" Mod it! There's dozens of graphics mods out there supporting 4K textures.  PC is too potato? Mods! There's a lot of performance enhancing mods (though I ran it on a mediocre system and still had good framerates, some people just can't be pleased).
-Characters are loveable, voice acting is good, and you get to listen to Civilization by Danny Kaye.
-Melee is viable.  Close range is viable.  Long range is viable.  Build how you want.
-Special melee attacks are FUN.  I always enjoy doing a little dodge and then watching my character grab a gunners leg and throw them on their back.
-Some of the dialogue is just so much better with it being voiced by the survivor.
-The looting system is downright boss.  Good job, Beth.
Mediocres (not great, but not really bad):
-Story.  A lot of "True one-and-only original super maximum over-fans" of the Fallout series would claim that there isn't really any story, it's not that good, or it's just all a rehash of NV.  They haven't been paying attention.  Pretty much ALL of today's sotries, whether on TV, in games, or in books are ALL rehashed in some way shape or form.  It's not an exact cookie cutter like CoD though.  The story is engaging, it has plot, has some twists and turns, and has multiple paths you can take, though most of them just involve blowing someone/thing up.
-The factions.  I literally hate all of the factions except for the minutemen.  But I hate Preston and his whiney "I have two more settlements for you to help, yesterday!"  I usually side with the MM to destroy the big bad baddies and then turn around and kill the RR because they're a bunch of mentally impaired vending machine liberators regardless.  Screw the BoS.
-Dialouge interface.  One thing I did like about 3/NV was sometimes the slew of dialogue choices you could make, often causing me to have to scroll through the options.  Mods can fix this somewhat. Otherwise, there's still only so many ways you can say Yes/No.  4 options should almost always be enough, with only a couple of instances optioning 5.
-The settlement building can be downright frustrating, but I'd much rather this than that archaic weapon repairing crap.  It's like minecraft that doesn't suck.  Until you can't get the snap points lined up just right.  If you're OCD avoid this feature.
-I wish there were more guns and ammo types in this game, though what they provide is sufficient.  Mods fix the rest.
-There's a decent amount of armors, but a lack of color changing options (mods fix this too) make you not want to really wear certain things sometimes.
Cons:
-Minutemen radiant quests.  Screw you, Garvey.  And you stupid settler that keeps letting yourself get kidnapped 3 times a week, just die already.  You'd be more useful that way.
-Brotherhood of Steel.  Just give me the power armor and get off my lawn.
-Elder Maxon:  PMS with a mohawk.
-Railroad. Machine programming is not emotion. "Free the vending machines! Be one with Professor Goodfeels!"
-"Hardcore/original/serious/real/legit/trueblood" Fallout fans.  They spit in their own food and claim Todd Howard made them do it.  Yes, some complaints are legit, and yes some of their points are valid.  Yes, even "I didn't like it just because I didn't like it" is legitimate if you truly think that way, but don't be so rabidly hellbent on trying to prove other people's OPINIONS wrong because you disagree.
Overall, I give this game a solid 8 Wendy's crispy chicken sandwiches (unmodded, 9 modded), out of 10.  For the amount of time I put into this game, I say $90 well spent for over 800 (and growing) hours of amusement.  This game helped me get through a surgery that debilitated me for almost 6 months and kept me out of work for another 3.  Yes I had a lot of free time to play it, but the game kept drawing me back to make me WANT to play it, a desire I haven't had in a long time.  It pulled me away from Skyrim, a game that I was in love with, to a franchise I really had trouble getting into.  I am now excited for the next Fallout releases, something that I couldn't really say before Fo4.
Yes, some things could be better. Some things could be much less annoying.  But there is a solid foundation here to make it into something better. If you're one of those "purists" who don't believe in playin with mods, that's your right to do so, but I feel you are doing yourself a great disservice.
A few quotes I wish to address:
"Fallout 4 isn't that great of a game, it's only a 7/10 at best." A 7/10 still warrants a second playthrough by just about any standard.
"I spent over 2/3/400 hours in this game and it's just no good." Then why were you playing it that long? You should be questioning a majority of your life choices.
"Fallout 4 is just a complete rehash of 3/NV."  All stories can be summed up when overgeneralized. "Something happened, the end."
TL;DR: I basically love almost everything about this game.  What I don't like can generally be fixed with mods, but each person should decide how they want to handle it.  Grab it on sale for the base game and you have a great deal, grab Far Harbor, Nuka World and maybe VT Workshops on sale if you can and you'll have a real good deal.

A 2D RPG with wonder background and character art that makes you want to play more to see more of the game. the game is in early access on stem started on Feb 3. Each character has there own and unique look and way to play, as each character class is unique from each other in look, camp skills , battle skills, attack and damage animations. That includes  player characters, NPCs and enemies units. Even that it may be still  frame animation, there is enough different animations to keep the game to the game play  and flow smooth  in battle and out.
The Estate
The game centers around the family estate which acts as your hub were you do everything from. A lot like the village from the monster hunter games or majula from dark souls 2.  the estate holds 7 places (so far) , 2 are for stress relief, one is for hiring new units which are random after every dungeon raid. 2 are for leveling up your character in both skills and equipment upgrades. One is for buying items that show up randomly after every dungeon raid and the last one is for the removal of bad traits.
Characters
There are 15 different character classes so far, each one is unique and plays different from others. Two of the most notable things are the stress system and the traits system. The trait system has both good and bad , which your units start with and gain as you play them. Say if your plague doctor (a unit from the game) reads interacts with a bookshelf in a dungeon they may gain a good train which lets them do more damage to undead or on the other hand they interact with a iron maiden and it is trapped they will gain a bad trait which let them to become a higher target for trap when they go off.
With the stress system there is a bar under your units life bar that show how the stress level goes up as you are in a dungeon , as you wonder about and as you fight. Once the stress bar fills one of two thing can happen, good or bad. Good is when your stress fills and your units becomes brave or determine, which lowers that units stress greatly and your parties stress a bit and gives that unit that was stressed a buff to help them in the battle. Bad is when your stress fills and your unit becomes a fearful or hopeless. Your unit gives more stress to other units in your party, and the unit that is stressed gains debuff that lowers the attack or there defense or makes them change your party’s formation which can do a lot to ruin a battle.

EDIT: I changed my recommendation to 'No', because I read a review that said we should be sending a signal to BGS that this (Fallout 4) isn't a good direction to take this franchise (less RPG elements, less choice (next to none here) and too much radiant quests (the Far Harbor DLC was in a good direction again though)). So there, just so you know this is not a good representation of a fallout game, you're free to like it (I sort of do), but the franchise is stumbling and sidetracking here.
Lots of design decisions feel lazy.
For example: instead of having loot spread out realistically throughout an entire location in places where it would make sense, there is usually just 1 singular "dungeon end, you did it" chest placed... where else? At the end of a dungeon...
Thus, you can only enter most locations (75%) from 1 direction through 1 entrance, and go through them in just 1 direction, aided (???) by conveniently barred doors, to preserve that end chest feeling.
Another example: sometimes you come across legendary enemies, these are randomly encountered (not placed like bosses), have increased stats, 'mutate' (a.k.a. regain all their health on death, which is stupid) and drop a random weapon or armor having a random "enchantment" I'm not kidding, you can get a "Fat Man of Healing", a launcher which deploys miniature nuclear warheads... ...that heal friends. Or, you can get a radiation gun that does extra damage to ghouls... ...which are immune to radiation... <sigh>.
So yes, it's totally RNG, you can get overpowered combinations (e.g. explosive bullets minigun) or something that's no help at all, and larger enemies do not drop better gear. That awsome minigun can be looted off a mutated roach, or a hulk-like (yes, green-skinned) superhuman. No risk vs reward.
Did I mention that these (sometimes) awesome weapons, armors and enemies look identically to their normal counterparts? Yeah, the only way to know these things are thougher and cooler is the name overlay when aiming at them.
Most RPG elements are weak, the voiced protagonist (nice experimental addition that's not used to full potential) required the developer to develop (what else?) linear conversations. They want to tell a story, not you, you just choose in what flavour you say "yes". There are always 4 dialogue options, which are: "Yes" (progress the quest), "No" (hold progress on the quest to say "Yes" later), "Sarcastic" (slightly funnier version of "Yes") and a question (which returns the conversation to "Yes", "No" and "Sarcastic".
I could talk about more things that irk me, but thats probably personal opinion. Not everybody experiences the game in the same way.
Back to the question at hand, it's quite a good game if you have no experience with the previous Fallout titels (or Elder Scrolls titles, which are from the same developer: Bethesda Game Studios), and you like open world shooters (like lets say Borderlands 2, much less humour in here though...)
My expectations of this game where a best of both worlds of both Fallout 3 (excellent game world design, by BGS) and Fallout New Vegas (excellent story, characters, good world, interesting factions, by Obsidian), instead, BGS looked mostly to experimental stuff and renewing the trusty formula (e.g. voiced protagonist), which is commendable. Sadly, not everything worked out as good as they would have wanted.
On a last note, be wary of the DLC Season Pass. The most worthwhile DLC is Far Harbor (better then the base game in story, characters, ...), the other ones feel (and most probably are) rushed (because the developer wanted the prestige of being able to say that they could release 1 dlc per month, unfortunately, that meant half of the dlc's being glorified mods, seemingly made by unpaid interns).

Sad to say this, but right now I would not recommend buying this game (that is in Early Access).
This game has very good artwork and style, has great atmosphere of grimdarkness. However, from gameplay standpoint it's not that great.
If you expect to have procedurally generated loot (as in most rogue-likes), then you are wrong. Basically you loot money, resources to upgrade your town and trinkets (most of them do more harm than good or are simply worthless). No lootable weapons, no lootable armor. Basically all heroes of same class that you hire are utterly disposable and similar to one another - only difference between them is different set of skills unlocked at the begining, but you ultimately can unlock any skill.
Overall, this game has 3 major issues right now:
1. Lack of content. Basically you have 3 really different dungeons, several types of enemies, several types of traps/"crates" and that's all. Most of gameplay time you will be grinding for money/resources to upgrade you town.
2. Game is utterly random. By saying random I mean totally, completely random. There are a lot of people reporting that situations when you have 10+ misses in a row are commonplace. There is no consistency in this game - basically one time you just die on a boss with no chance of survival at all (he crits all his attacks, you try to retreat and fail) - next time with similar party setup and level you just steamroll this boss with lucky crits. Even hunger system works totally random - you can eat your food, make one step (!) and be forced to eat again - just because (as game code indicates hunger works as another "invisible" trap, that's all)
3. Game is really not balanced. Start of the game is very hard, but as you approach end it is more and more easier. There are a lot of loopholes in gamedesign, like stun-lock healing in battles and grind of first dungeon with 0 level heroes with no food and torches (heroes doesn't cost anything at all, they are infinite). Class balance is also not good, there are obvious good choices and obvious bad choices gameplay-wise (I look at you, plague doctor, from lore standpoint I wanted to take you in party, really!)
Saying all of that, I recommend to wait and see if devs are able/willing to improve this game.

Ah Starbound, where do I begin?
I'll say this right up front. This game is TOTALLY FREAKING AWESOME! I love it! It's like a combination of Terraria and Minecraft. Let's break the game into different sections before my final thoughts.
Story: There is no story. None whatsoever. Nope. Nada. None. I FREAKING LOVE IT! Games with stories (in my opinion) restrict you to completing the game before getting what you really want. Starbound, like Terraria and Minecraft, allow you to go at your own pace. There's no "Oh sorry! You can't get this badass looking sword unless you beat the game. Good Luck!" There's none of that. Sure you have to defeat bosses to get to other sections of the galaxy, but still, it's not required. Nothing is required to progress in this game. You can stay on tier 1 planets for half the game if you like! Onto the next catagory!
AI (Artificial Intelligence): The randomness of the AI is FREAKING HILARIOUS!!!! Some I just look at and go, "How did the creators of this game make something that freaking ugly?" The peaceful AI just make the game look more "pretty" I should say. They're OK, but, I don't know. The hostile AI however freaking wants to kill you, eat all your limbs away, then chuck the rest of you into a fire. I'm actually kind of terrified when a hostile attacks me. My thoughts when a hostile attacks me: "I love Starbound! This is so much fun! Wait, is that combat music? Oh crap. Oh god. THERE'S 4 OF THEM! NONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONO!!!!!!!!!!!!!!" The AI is good. Onto the next catagory!
Gameplay/Controls: The controls are much like those of Terraria. They are basic, and simple to remember. The gameplay is absoulutely splendid! That's all I have to say. Nothing more. Onto the next topic!
Randomness: This game is CRAZY RANDOM!!! Some of the names of the weapons I get are like, "Poopy Eyecutter" or "Boring Tickler". Those are the names I laugh at and go, "Why?" There are other names, too. Like "Bloody Dismemberer" and "Stabby Stabber". Those are the names where I go, "That sounds badass!" I once got a weapon called "Kill Killer". After reading the name I said, "This is a keeper. No doubt." Onto my Final Thoughts!
Final Thoughts: Four words: GET. THIS. GAME. NOW!!!!!!
Story: 10/10 (Even though there is none.)
AI: 8/10
Gameplay/Controls: 10/10
Randomness: 10/10
Overall Score: 95/100

Darkest Dungeon is an incredibly addicting game. The tactical mechanics and resource management are quite fun. The diversity of character classes and abilities means that there are many ways to form a competitive party that is fun to play.
I LOVE the constant auto-save and perma-death features. While I enjoyed getting to spend some more time in the Fallout universe, the faults in this game lead me to give it only a weakly positive review.  For fans of Bethesda games, you will see a lot that is fimiliar, for good and bad.
Pros:
-The world is full of interesting places to explore, and the backstory of what was happening at each loction before or after the war are well-written and funny as always.
Mixed:
-The shooting mechanics are improved from Fallout 3, but are still not satisfying compared to any modern shooter.
-The main story quest (finding your son), while theoretically compelling, doesn't mix well with a game where you spend huge amounts of time aimlessly wandering the wasteland.  I guess he will be fine until I get around to looking for him.
-Weapon and armor crafting.  While the customization is nice, it leads to a miserable experience sorting through items in shops, plus it guarantees that most characters will need half their perk points invested in the crafting and lockpicking/hacking perks.
-Settlement building.  The idea is cool in theory.  Rebuild parts of the wasteland and have your own settlements going, which can produce some loot and send reinforcements in the area.  In practice, however, this process is pretty annoying.  The console-ized building controls are inexcusably bad, and despite amassing huge amounts of raw materials, you can still only build stuff that looks like crap that was half-destroyed in the war.  Also, your settlers end up being needy whiners, constanly needing babysitting when they get kidnapped or attacks by raiders.  Bethesda should have stuck to only 4 or five really cool settlements that you could build up, and let them be more self-sufficient once they get going.
-All the factions kinda suck, and by the end of the game i really didn't want to be allied with any of them.  I finally just had to pick a side and push through the end because I wanted to be done with it.  At the beginning, they make sense, as they all have their own goals, but by the end of the game they all require the genecide off everyone else.
Cons:
-Lengthy loading times pop up any time you move to a new area.  If this only happened during fast travel that would be reasonable, but even popping in or out of a little two room house on the wasteland sometimes requires loading.  Surely a modern game engine should be able to load assets in the background.  If you are playing on a system with a low end graphics card, sometimes the game gets frozen loading and never finishes.
-The game is just as buggy as always for Bethesda, even though I played it a year after release.  Minor graphical glitches wouldn't be a big deal, but the quest scripts frequently break, requiring you to find an old save to load if you  want to continue. Really breaks the immersion.
-Characters are just as wooden as ever, with crappy animation and bad pathfinding.  You have a wide choice of sidekicks, which you will never travel with because they spend all of their time blocking doors you want to go through.  Thankfully, there is a perk which lets you carry more stuff when alone, so you can live without your packhorse companions.
In the end, I enjoyed much of my time in the game because I love the Fallout universe, but it's getting hard to stomach all of the problems with the Fallout/Elder Scrolls games.  I think I'm going to have to hold off on any future titles until they finally build a new engine and get a more focused approach to their game design.  I simply don't have enough time anymore to play something like this which serves more quantity than quality.

My current records in Steam...
83 minutes in Fallout 3 (not accurate, played non-steam versions and "beat it," twice)
21 hours in Fallout NV (again, not accurate)
500+ hours in Skyrim
834.6 hours in Fallout 4 (current, and still climbing)
---I will preface this.  I am an Elder scrolls fan.  I bought Fallout 4 to hold me over till Elder Scrolls 6.---
TL;DR at bottom.
I love this game.  I had no idea I'd put in almost twice the hours into this game than one of my favorite franchises.  I took Bethesda on their word and good faith that they usually nail the value of their season passes (IMO and at the time), and I paid $30 for my season pass about a week after I bought the game.  I anticipated getting a good bit of time into this game, but nowhere near what I have now.
Fo4 did what Fo3 and NV failed to do: draw me in.  It gave me more than just running around, killing stuff, and questing.  When I got bored of slaughtering raiders (and getting slaughtered by a random deathclaw) I would go and work on my settlements.  That helped significantly to fill the gap in when I just wanted to take a break from story and questing.
Pros:
-The graphics are beautiful.  Yes, they could always be better, but some folks were complaining about "they're just slightly better than Skyrim" well Skyrim also looked pretty danged good when it was released. Install some graphics mods and get over yourself.
-Combat is fluid and smooth.
-There's a good variety of enemies to get killed by.
-Piper and Curie.
-Loads of stuff to do outside of combat.  Far Harbor and Nuka World added great amounts of new territory to tear through.
-Most of the DLC is great.  Far Harbor added a good bit of new territory and enemies and had some beautiful surroundings at times, Nuka World is just downright fun and also had loads more area to run through, and is where I spent most of my time outside of the commonwealth. Automatron was great with new enemies and robot building, but I really don't use any of the stuff from Wasteland/Contraptions Workshop. The Vault Tech workshop was good in the vast expanse that it allows you to build your vault (it's seriously huge) but I am not good enough with digging through everything or coming up with floor plans to actually build my own vault well.  It has a couple of quests to do, and the experiments weren't really that in depth, but overall, the sheer amount of exploration and items added for settlement building is good.
-Mods.  Mods, mods, mods and mods.  Don't like something in the game? Stop complaining about it and mod it! Seriously it's a fool proof design and it's not that hard.  Playing this without mods, graphical or game changing, is severely limiting the potential.  Think the graphics are "too Skyrim?" Mod it! There's dozens of graphics mods out there supporting 4K textures.  PC is too potato? Mods! There's a lot of performance enhancing mods (though I ran it on a mediocre system and still had good framerates, some people just can't be pleased).
-Characters are loveable, voice acting is good, and you get to listen to Civilization by Danny Kaye.
-Melee is viable.  Close range is viable.  Long range is viable.  Build how you want.
-Special melee attacks are FUN.  I always enjoy doing a little dodge and then watching my character grab a gunners leg and throw them on their back.
-Some of the dialogue is just so much better with it being voiced by the survivor.
-The looting system is downright boss.  Good job, Beth.
Mediocres (not great, but not really bad):
-Story.  A lot of "True one-and-only original super maximum over-fans" of the Fallout series would claim that there isn't really any story, it's not that good, or it's just all a rehash of NV.  They haven't been paying attention.  Pretty much ALL of today's sotries, whether on TV, in games, or in books are ALL rehashed in some way shape or form.  It's not an exact cookie cutter like CoD though.  The story is engaging, it has plot, has some twists and turns, and has multiple paths you can take, though most of them just involve blowing someone/thing up.
-The factions.  I literally hate all of the factions except for the minutemen.  But I hate Preston and his whiney "I have two more settlements for you to help, yesterday!"  I usually side with the MM to destroy the big bad baddies and then turn around and kill the RR because they're a bunch of mentally impaired vending machine liberators regardless.  Screw the BoS.
-Dialouge interface.  One thing I did like about 3/NV was sometimes the slew of dialogue choices you could make, often causing me to have to scroll through the options.  Mods can fix this somewhat. Otherwise, there's still only so many ways you can say Yes/No.  4 options should almost always be enough, with only a couple of instances optioning 5.
-The settlement building can be downright frustrating, but I'd much rather this than that archaic weapon repairing crap.  It's like minecraft that doesn't suck.  Until you can't get the snap points lined up just right.  If you're OCD avoid this feature.
-I wish there were more guns and ammo types in this game, though what they provide is sufficient.  Mods fix the rest.
-There's a decent amount of armors, but a lack of color changing options (mods fix this too) make you not want to really wear certain things sometimes.
Cons:
-Minutemen radiant quests.  Screw you, Garvey.  And you stupid settler that keeps letting yourself get kidnapped 3 times a week, just die already.  You'd be more useful that way.
-Brotherhood of Steel.  Just give me the power armor and get off my lawn.
-Elder Maxon:  PMS with a mohawk.
-Railroad. Machine programming is not emotion. "Free the vending machines! Be one with Professor Goodfeels!"
-"Hardcore/original/serious/real/legit/trueblood" Fallout fans.  They spit in their own food and claim Todd Howard made them do it.  Yes, some complaints are legit, and yes some of their points are valid.  Yes, even "I didn't like it just because I didn't like it" is legitimate if you truly think that way, but don't be so rabidly hellbent on trying to prove other people's OPINIONS wrong because you disagree.
Overall, I give this game a solid 8 Wendy's crispy chicken sandwiches (unmodded, 9 modded), out of 10.  For the amount of time I put into this game, I say $90 well spent for over 800 (and growing) hours of amusement.  This game helped me get through a surgery that debilitated me for almost 6 months and kept me out of work for another 3.  Yes I had a lot of free time to play it, but the game kept drawing me back to make me WANT to play it, a desire I haven't had in a long time.  It pulled me away from Skyrim, a game that I was in love with, to a franchise I really had trouble getting into.  I am now excited for the next Fallout releases, something that I couldn't really say before Fo4.
Yes, some things could be better. Some things could be much less annoying.  But there is a solid foundation here to make it into something better. If you're one of those "purists" who don't believe in playin with mods, that's your right to do so, but I feel you are doing yourself a great disservice.
A few quotes I wish to address:
"Fallout 4 isn't that great of a game, it's only a 7/10 at best." A 7/10 still warrants a second playthrough by just about any standard.
"I spent over 2/3/400 hours in this game and it's just no good." Then why were you playing it that long? You should be questioning a majority of your life choices.
"Fallout 4 is just a complete rehash of 3/NV."  All stories can be summed up when overgeneralized. "Something happened, the end."
TL;DR: I basically love almost everything about this game.  What I don't like can generally be fixed with mods, but each person should decide how they want to handle it.  Grab it on sale for the base game and you have a great deal, grab Far Harbor, Nuka World and maybe VT Workshops on sale if you can and you'll have a real good deal.

Ah Starbound, where do I begin?
I'll say this right up front. This game is TOTALLY FREAKING AWESOME! I love it! It's like a combination of Terraria and Minecraft. Let's break the game into different sections before my final thoughts.
Story: There is no story. None whatsoever. Nope. Nada. None. I FREAKING LOVE IT! Games with stories (in my opinion) restrict you to completing the game before getting what you really want. Starbound, like Terraria and Minecraft, allow you to go at your own pace. There's no "Oh sorry! You can't get this badass looking sword unless you beat the game. Good Luck!" There's none of that. Sure you have to defeat bosses to get to other sections of the galaxy, but still, it's not required. Nothing is required to progress in this game. You can stay on tier 1 planets for half the game if you like! Onto the next catagory!
AI (Artificial Intelligence): The randomness of the AI is FREAKING HILARIOUS!!!! Some I just look at and go, "How did the creators of this game make something that freaking ugly?" The peaceful AI just make the game look more "pretty" I should say. They're OK, but, I don't know. The hostile AI however freaking wants to kill you, eat all your limbs away, then chuck the rest of you into a fire. I'm actually kind of terrified when a hostile attacks me. My thoughts when a hostile attacks me: "I love Starbound! This is so much fun! Wait, is that combat music? Oh crap. Oh god. THERE'S 4 OF THEM! NONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONONO!!!!!!!!!!!!!!" The AI is good. Onto the next catagory!
Gameplay/Controls: The controls are much like those of Terraria. They are basic, and simple to remember. The gameplay is absoulutely splendid! That's all I have to say. Nothing more. Onto the next topic!
Randomness: This game is CRAZY RANDOM!!! Some of the names of the weapons I get are like, "Poopy Eyecutter" or "Boring Tickler". Those are the names I laugh at and go, "Why?" There are other names, too. Like "Bloody Dismemberer" and "Stabby Stabber". Those are the names where I go, "That sounds badass!" I once got a weapon called "Kill Killer". After reading the name I said, "This is a keeper. No doubt." Onto my Final Thoughts!
Final Thoughts: Four words: GET. THIS. GAME. NOW!!!!!!
Story: 10/10 (Even though there is none.)
AI: 8/10
Gameplay/Controls: 10/10
Randomness: 10/10
Overall Score: 95/100
For this game being in beta (I think it's in beta) it's really up there with the greats! Good job Starbound creators! Love your game!

UPDATE 8/13 - I had to switch to a thumbs down after kicking on the game from being away for over a year. RNG town events?  Christ.  I went into a dungeon with a couple of my top old characters who were kitted out, 2 of them died in one battle that wasn't even a boss, and I don't suck it was just a string of RNG.  Salt adds a lot to a meal but when you keep pouring it on, you kill all possibility of fun.  Bummer because with added content and classes I thought the game would get better, instead it is just punishing unfairly and without player recourse.  I hope this game is studied in game design school as RNG done wrong.
Now for my old review.. the game that could have been:
Incredibly polished for early access.  It will also mop the floor with you in terms of difficulty (at least at this early stage).  The ambiance is that of unyielding despair, with no option to correct a mistake or revert a save.  Make no mistake, this game will punish you with RNG and make you die (or live in famine) with the consequences.  It also forces you to be strategic with every resource you have, from gold, to heroes.
The biggest thing it has going for it right now is the art style, which for all intents and purposes is complete.  The combat system is neat, but needs balancing.  Having played for about 10 hours over 2 games, there was only glimpses where I went from feeling underwater, to breathing air, only to have something pull my legs back to the abyss.  The thing is... I think this game would be boring if it were easy.  It would simply become a grind of leveling up each class, getting them some equipment, and beating some bosses.  Wait... where have I done that before?

The Beta of StarDrive allows players to explore the expanse of the universe in glorious, pixelated 2D! Part of the recent emergence of "Mine, Craft, Explore" games, a trend ignited by the advent of Minecraft some 4 years ago, this game will seem familiar to players of those type of games, in particular Terraria.
You will scavenge for resources, mine your way into the earth with increasingly costly mining tools, and fend off creatures with a wide variety of different weapons. Much like it's other 2D brother, Terraria, the focus of Starbound seems to be concentrated more on the combating of Boss characters, or it's variation on hostile-infested dungeons. Although mention must be made of the extensive list of different decorative items the game sports, allowing you to build any number of marvellous space-bases and underground compounds.
The game's biggest draw seems to be the thousands upon thousands of procedurally generated planets, that the player is free to explore at will, provided they have the resources to make the trip there. Each planet comes with different climates and a diverse set of unique creatures, procedurally generated from many different physical traits and abilities, that inhabit the world.
With all of that said, it would seem that Starbound should be an amazing experience, with a near endless arsenal of new experiences, creatures and tools. The reality though, is that once you've seen 2 or 3 worlds, you've seen them all. The procedural generation may lead to an innumerable amount of different variations, but the worlds end up feeling very same-y, and you'll find yourself barely taking note of the nth iteration of 'bunnies with lizard tails'. The only thing that's genuinely worth discovering after a while are the different dungeon areas, and I imagine that novelty will wear thin once you've found all the different 'types'.
The weapon/tool/gear progression can be a bit tedious, having to rely on collecting tons and tons of resources to craft the next tier, or on sheer luck of finding a chest with something that isn't terrible. You'll spend a lot of time digging up what you need for the next armour set so you can advance to a higher difficulty planet where you repeat that process again. On the upside, there are a lot of unique weapons generated in dungeons making those even more exciting and valuable to find. Especially early on, though, you'll spend a lot of time in the ground.
With the game in early Beta, and the developers still working hard on improving on the many aspects of play, Starbound could have a bright future ahead of it, but it definitely has some hurdles to overcome to transcend being simply a novel variation in a genre that's seen better, more streamlined experiences.

Fallout 4, what is it? To put it simply,
Fallout 4 is a game with many things to do, that much is certain. Currently, the game is highly modifiable and will only increase in the time coming (Disclaimer: You can't find mods on the workshop, Google it, Bing it, what ever you use). Alas, Fallout 4 is not quite is expansive as previous Bethesda games in some ways. Compared to my
, you'd notice that my Fallout 4 play time is rather miniscule, this is due to the fact that, to me, the game doesn't have as much replayability (keep in mind this is a rather biased opinion since they're two completely different games). I'll go into more detail in the
and
below.
Voiced player characters: I was scepticle when I first started playing the game and there were actual voices for your character compared to previous Bethesda games. I enjoyed giving my character their own voice and personality, to add a little spark to the game, that option is now gone in Fallout 4.
Graphics: For the true PC gamer, the graphics may seem a bit off at places, for example low detail. I had to include this here as a statement for there being a high quality texture FREE DLC pack in the making, if not released already, for Fallout 4,
Base building: Base building is new to Bethesda's games and you can expect some trouble to come with that. It's fun at times but good God prepare to clench your mouse real hard at times. It's extremely finicky at times and so I just stopped using it after a while.
Physics: The engine for Fallout 4 has been improved upon since Skyrim. I'm not entirely sure if this is the case, but Fallout 4 has felt more
than its ancestor counterpart, which is a big deal.
The Minutemen: I enjoyed the Minutmen storyline
. It was just a tad bit in depth and not as serious as,
the Brotherhood, which made it just a little more enjoyable. The reason the Minutemen is on the Cons list is because of Preston. Radiant quests are fun, sure, but please take him away.
Storyline length: Yet again, compared to Skyrim, Fallout 4's storyline felt a bit short. You had one objective and you knew it from the beginning. I finished the storyline in a mere matter of hours, luckily the side quests protected its♥♥♥♥♥♥
Melee weapons: Just, don't use them. There is almost never a moment where you will be using melee weapons in the base game. Originally there was, The Combat Zone, but for some reason the devs decided to cut it. Long range weapons will always over power a melee weapon, no matter what.
Saving: First off, I save a lot, in case there's a puzzle or something that I want to redo; I do that a lot in games. Thing is, if you save and come across an enemy that you can't possibly beat no matter what you do right afterwards, you're gonna be in a loop. I had the same problem in previous Bethsoft games, and that aint fun.
Hacking: Man, I struggled with this at first. The tutorial for hacking is a pile of text, that's it. I had to actually go on Google to figure out how to actually work the hacking component effectively, and I don't want that from any game unless it's about an easteregg a la Call Of Duty.
Loadtimes: Oh my gaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaawd. Count those 'a's, multiply the time it took you by roughly one thousand and then you have how long it takes to load a scene in this game. This was the major down put for me on this game that's slowed my play time. I have a reasonably good computer (in profile) and this should not take long. Even having an SSD doesn't exactly help much. Say for example; you're walking the commonwealth and come across a building with an accessable door, head in there, place is small as hell and there's one enemy within it and a few caps, leave and- OOOOOOH LOADING TIMES THAT'S GREAT LET ME JUST GO MAKE MYSELF SOME POPCORN. I.e. it's♥♥♥♥♥♥
I liked this game, don't get me wrong, but I just don't think I got my money's worth out of it. Skyrim (eugh) is a whole lot cheaper but in some ways feels a lot bigger. I do recommend this game, sure, but I'm not going to be hanging on to it for very long, I'd rather wait for the next TES game. Thanks for sticking along through this massive review, by the way, it took a while to write, enjoy your Gaben provided goodness.

Drain you of your sanity, face the Thing That Should Not Be!
Was this an Early Access game?  My goodness, I must not have noticed because it is utterly phenomenal and I can't put it down.
In Darkest Dungeon, you are the heir to a ruined estate which just so happened to be built on top of the ancient ruins of Lovecrafian abominations.  Its up to you to hire poor saps to throw their lives away in randomly generated dungeons while managing dwindling food, light, and the very sanity of your army.
When characters die, they stay dead.  When characters live, they recieve randomly generated strengths and weaknesses.  That amazing sword loving warrior you love so much?  He's seen too much combat and goes easily insane.  Will you drop the money to send him to therapy while letting weaker teammates dungeon crawl in his place?  Will you work him to death?  Will you fire him and seek a replacement?  Or will you continue to invest money and time on keeping him physically and emotionally strong?  Who knows?  Maybe he or she will gain permanent perks, courage and resiliency and you tangle with Cthulhu...
The loot is composed primarily of two things, standard gold for buying precious rations for dungeon crawling, and your family heirlooms, which help restore your estate to its former glory.  Heirlooms permanently repair and upgrade your estate, giving you access to better weapons, more fresh meat---er, I mean recruits for dungeon crawling, and better, more effective treatments as your favorite allies start going insane.
I've seen Sanity in other cosmic horror games, and I haven't seen it used this effectively since Eternal Darkness.  In this game, its called Stress, and no matter what you do, it will accumulate on your characters.  You walk through a hallway?  That's stressfull.  You step on a trap?  That's really stressful!  You get struck by a critical hit?  Your entire party will be terrified?  Upon reaching 100 Stress, your character will likely go insane and recieve randomly generated Afflictions that will cause you to lose control of them.  Not only that but their actions and words drag down the emotional state of the team they are in.  This makes stressed out characters extremely toxic to your team.
And that doesn't even cover the audio and visuals.  A dynamic narrator depicts what is going on with a distinct Lovecraft taste.  Hellboy style 2D artwork coupled with great music.  This game just oozes character.  Buy it now, because I only see it getting better in the future!

Trove - A Voxel MMO RPG by Trion Worlds
Short version:
A building, exploring & collecting game best described as silly fun.
Long version:
I've been playing Trove for about 2 and a half months now. Its very fun a fun game but not without faults.
Building - This has improved recently but even before this was very capable and this shows. While permanent building is restricted to cornerstones (your own private house) and club worlds, the amount of creativity is astonishing. People have made some truly amazing club worlds. There is a club world full of music, others with boat & wing race courses and some truly awe inspiring creations.
Adventuring - There are no quests besides the tutorials designed to teach you the game. You just go out and find things to kill. Small lairs, huge dungeons and later on shadow arenas. Until you get towards the end game content (more on that later) its a very casual and relaxed game. While you dont form patries, working in groups is rewarding and allows you to push forward a little faster.
Collecting - As you progress through the game you earn mastery points. Mastery levels unlock various rewards (like wings at 20 and access to challenges at 30) with the untimate goal to reach max mastery (currently 200). Raising your mastery can be sped up a little with items from the shop but almost everything can be obtained in-game through work, trading or bought from the shop with in-game credits.
End game - End game currently is completing hourly challenges, shadow arenas and Uber 6 dungeons to get better gear and upgrade items. Challenges are admittedly a bit is a mess with huge zergs of adventurers rushing around a biome stripping it bare like a swarm of locusts. Its a mad rush to earn dragon caches but the best way to earn materials and resources required to upgrade gear.
Pay2Win & RNG - Is it Pay2Win? In a word, no. There is no 'win' in trove. Even when PvP is added this shouldnt change. You can buy a patron pass that gives more XP, extra jump but none of these give you any kind of real advantage.
Trove contains a lot of RNG. Dragon caches, adventure boxes, chaos chests, miner's troves, shadow caches, nightmare boxes and radiant caches (all earned in different ways) are all RNG boxes and rarely drop good items. None require money to open and are mostly just a bit of fun with a chance to get a cool mount, pair of wings or something equally as fun.

Darkest Dungeon is incredibly difficult for all the wrong reasons. It gives you the illusion of strategy but in reality you have barely any choice of what happens to you and your party in this game. The randomness in this game is totally out of control. You could go into a fight completely fully healed only to have your party order randomly completely rearranged (which is incredibly important) which will most likely lead to multiple party members dying.
1) Surprises in Combat
Whenever you encounter an enemy, you have a random chance of surprising them, while they also have a chance of surprising you. You can be surprised even with maximum torchlight (which is supposed to give you a boost to surprising THEM) which, like I said before, will rearrange your party. This is incredibly important because certain abilities your party members can use can only be used in certain party arrangements. For example, the crusaider can only attack in the first 2 party slots. When your crusaider is scrambled from the front spot to the very back, it can take up to 2 rounds of combat to move him back to his spot, making him completely useless for the time being. By that time though, you'll probably be dead already anyway.
2) Crits and Dodges
Crits and dodging attacks is pretty standard for RPGs. In this game though, where you could possibly go to full to 0 health from 1 critical attack, they do not belong and they definitely should not happen nearly as often as they do. I've been crit 4 times in a row in a single round of combat. Your party members all gain stress when someone gets crit too, so thats makes matters even worse. Your whole party could become completely stressed and almost dead from one round of combat if the game hates you enough (it will). Dodging attacks also happens way too often, even with accurate attacks. All attacks have a base accuracy score, from 0-100, based on the % chance of it hitting. Though it doesn't matter most of the time because monsters have a dodge score, which depending on how high it is means they have the potential to always dodge your attacks.
TL;DR: only buy this game if you enjoy playing 100% perfectly only to be ♥♥♥♥ed by the randomness with there being nothing you could have done different to change the outcome (which is always you dying)

It's a bit too early to fully review this game, however I must say that the Beta is going quite well. It hooked me upon starting on my first world...although not everything is implimented yet there is still quite a LOT of content in the game.
I have not reached the endgame, but I have watched countless streams of people who were in that part of the game.
A warning to all: the game is in the first phase of Beta, wipes are EXPECTED. Don't go building an epic Glitch castle and then cry your heart out when that save is wiped. The devs experiment a LOT to get the right balence and feel to the game, and wipes are going to happen in order for you to fully experience those changes.
If you are on the fence about buying: price probably won't change, so you could check back later and then buy it prior to release. (although you should test it and get a feel for things...don't go too deep, you might burn yourself out before full release)
Yes; this game looks similar to another game in the genre called Terraria (if you have not heard of that, go search it NAO), however both games branch off in quite different paths. In Terraria, you stay in one area...map is pretty small compared to Starbound, and it's more focused on just mining and obtaining gear so you can slay bosses and stuff...eventually making your own utopia (I guess)
Starbound, however: you start on one planet, as soon as you get your bearings, you check your star map on your ship...you'll notice how quickly things change. Millions...no...Trillions of planets out there await your beloved starship's arrival and your feet to touch the ground. There will be harsh enviroments...which will require special equipment and tactics. Monsters are fierce and also randomly generated. You'll probably won't be able to come across the same monster on a different planet.
There are several sectors in this vast universe you explore...each one getting harder as you progress. Tread lightly, traveler: you might come across a hostile pack of monsters, a mini boss, or even a sacrificial cult of bird-people worshipping the sun.
Good luck, and explore safely.

-Despite the fact that Fallout 4 may not fit in Fallout frachise, this could still be a great game.
Sure it's a little over-simpilified, and lack of options to make it a real RPG, make 'your character' more like 'the character'
-Story is okay, and there are a lot of side quests that more than main quests and enough to drown you. So I never got nothing to do in this game. Although many times they don't make a difference, it's still fun to discover some interesting little stories or mysteries around the wasteland.
-Craft & Building system, well, it looks simple, just gather components and craft and gather more components and craft more stuff so you can gather even more components and carft even more stuff that might be useful, make it much more complicated than I imagine (sometimes, I feel scrapping for components is wierd, can you really build those fancy stuff from junk?).
-Now Settlement building also take a part in game, it's just like babysitting, full of trouble, bugs everywhere, but still have something to enjoy. Sometimes building structures really annoys me when I can't place them at where they supposed to be, and settlers just simply can't take care of themselves, so they keep telling Preston they need help and then Preston ask you to take care those crap (the thing is sometimes I'd like to help them because I literally didn't have anything to do), even a settlement with super defense would be harassed by few enenies. Although it has a lot of terrible points, a well-built settlement still proves a nice shelter for a rest and stock up, and it's sometimes fun playing with settlers like playing with puppets. And Bethesda released 3 DLCs for and only for building them?
-SPECIAL skills/perks are what should mainly save me while wandering around the wastes, I enjoy picking perks and then blow s**t up, every single one of them makes the game more fun to play. Not much more to say about this, you can pick them however you like (and you take full responsibility to your decision).
-I barely see any personality on my characters, they can chose to act completely different in similar situations, most times though, doesn't affect the game, you still gotta do what you gotta do... People always look at you the same way, unless, you murdered them (all).
You have to chose between factions in order to 'finish' the game, two of them must die(except from the Minutemen, who ask you gather all those settlements), no other way out, probably because 'War never changes'. Either ending you chose, makes game different but probably make you feel the same, it's just your personal preference.
In the end, I couldn't call this game perfect, either have eveything to be an RPG, but it's still a good one, I can tell that my hours spent with it worthed it.
EDIT: Ignore the crappy ''creation club'' as much as you can, and for as long as you can, even though it takes extra 2 GBs on your hard drive.

It may not be a very popular opinion given the seemingly untouchable legacy of Fallout: New Vegas, but I think Fallout 4 is more tailored for players like me than its renowned predecessor. My Fallout fandom began with the very first entry, and I've played each subsequent entry extensively. I'm not what you'd call a fanboy, but I am very familiar with the series as a whole.
What do I like about it so much? Well, I can't say that this will be a good reason for everyone looking for an open world adventure, but the primary reason I have roughly 600+ hours poured into it (only 529 of them may be logged in to Steam, but that only reflects the hours I was playing while conencted to Steam's network-- I have Comcast so its sometimes hit or miss)  is the collecting of resources and building settlements. I will be the first to admit that the vanilla settlement mechanics are rather shallow and limited, even with all the expansions, but even without mods, (I am currently in the middle of a 'clean' no mod playthrough) its still a blast to explore The Commonwealth and finally collect junk and build with purpose. I love arming and outfitting my ragtag group of settlers across the wasteland one by one, building their homes, and overcoming the admittedly wonky settlement building system like I would a puzzle game. I honestly think they could make a standalone settlement building game and it would be really fun as long as they added more variety and more settlement options. But, they said from the beginning that this was all optional content so I can understand why they didn't spent more development time and resources on it. Even if it is my favorite part.
The gunplay is improved from previous entries, acting as a double-edged sword. Yes, it confirms that the series will ever stray further from its turn-based RPG roots, but all it is, is a refined version of what Fallout 3 and New Vegas were already attempting to do. Fallout 4 also provides what I believe to be far and away the best perk system in any action/rpg game I've ever played. There's no cap to your characrer's level, only your interest level. There are a lot of paths and perks to choose from, and sometimes its a difficult decision to make. I loved building robots, too. So many robots and so many sweet mods and weapons for them.
I can't vaunt this game entirely though. It may be my favorite Fallout game by far, but it still suffers from the pitfalls typical to any other Bethesda game. Its more polished, but there's still plenty of those game-breaking bugs to encounter, sketchy clipping and eye-rolling enemy AI-- seriously, its infuriating to have a raider armed with a rocket launcher charge at you and fire a rocket at point-blank range just to kill you as if they were on some suicide mission. I get the whole crazy suicidal raider angle, but I don't think that was their intent. A lot of the time you end up firing your gun at something that's just pushing up against you rather than making tactical decisions and finding cover. If things like that (understandably) ruin games for you, then beware. Oh, and if you hate bullent sponges, then this may not be for you. There's still a pretense of hit points and armor values residing in its mechanics. Your AI companions are useless aside from getting perks for maxing their affinity and carrying extra weight, and in combat situations all but impotent unless you construct a cool robot that can use decent weapons. Your companions eat up any ammo for the weapons you give them, and they switch back to their pea-shooter defaults pretty fast. (at least that's been my experience) I have yet to make use of the DLC content that allows you to pit raiders and settlers against wasteland creatures in any meaningful way-- it's just dumb and not implemented very well at all. A good idea, but not very well executed.
The litany of quests are for the most part pretty forgettable story-wise, and the voice acting for a lot of the characters, the main male and female included, are bland and rigid. But hey-- I've never known anyone who played an Elder Scrolls or Fallout game for its  gripping story; that's usually just the glue to hold the gameplay together. Its hard to make your character anything but a polite (sometimes sickeningly polite) do-gooder-- even the 'renegade' dialogue options aren't as nasty and mean as you'd want them to be if you want to play as a truly gritty, sadistic kind of guy. And that Preston Garvey... the man needs some serious acting lessons.
But like I said, for me, Fallout 4 was all about the exploration, the collecting, and the perk management; and at the core of it all, that's what makes the post Fallout 3 games so fun. I have a warehouse that's slowly accumulating more and more complete power armor sets, and some pieces that I'm still searching for. I'd still love to see a story-driven intellectual tactitcal foray into the wastelands along the lines of Pillars of Eternity--- its what drew me to the series in the first place. But I'm pretty content with what they made here. There's things in Fallout 4 that I can't do in any other game right now until someone ambitious enough steps up and tries to take an edgier, more dark approach to open world RPG's.

Starbound, however: you start on one planet, as soon as you get your bearings, you check your star map on your ship...you'll notice how quickly things change. Millions...no...Trillions of planets out there await your beloved starship's arrival and your feet to touch the ground. Trove is a classic example of a simple game idea with good execution. The game knows exactly what it wants to be, and is it.
Grinding is a big part in Trove, so if you don't like to grind, this game probably isn't for you. However, there are several ways to grind items in this game. Examples would be; by fishing you can also get ores, or by opening chests you get randomly by mining or doing dungeons. This way, you can still get items by doing different activities, so you won't get bored of doing the same stuff over and over again. This leads me to my following point:
Even though there a plenty of ways to accomplish the same goal, there are many things that may need improvement. Fishing is a bit boring, it's easy profit, but it becomes too repetitive. You just buy lures, and fish. It takes about 20-30 seconds for a fish to take the bait, and you repeat. To make a decent amount of Glims (in-game currency, next to Flux), you will probably be doing this for the next half an hour. This also leads me to my following point:
Trove is a simple game, and that's a good thing! However, a bit more complexity introduced in an intuitive manner so it isn't too hard to learn, would also work. You only have 4 abilities per class, next to a "Dash" ability (defaults to Shift) on every class. However, in my opinion, a way to customize abilities, get new ones or swap them would be nicer. It gets a bit repetitive, and after about level 4, your only reason to level is to get extra stat increments, Mastery points or a new costume (1 every 10 levels -- 20 is the max level). Also other things like Club Worlds lack a bit of customization (like customizing ranks and permissions.)
However, this might just be me. I fully understand if people prefer the simplicity.
I felt I needed to elaborate mostly on the negative points, however, that might make it seem like it's a negative game, which it's not. At all. Trove is a great game, the open world(s) are full of fun adventures, different objectives in every biome, different ways to do things, many blocks to collect and build and fun things to discover. This all results in a really fun and social game for almost all ages to enjoy. With the (almost) weekly updates they push out, this experience will stay fresh and interesting. I can't wait to find out what Trion has planned next for this very big potential game.

Although negitive reviews make some good points, some of the stuff they mention is just flat out wrong (i.e. how skills/perks have no affect on the game.  This statment is compltely false).  After some of these people put 500+ hours into the game these negivitve reviews can seem like an "emo-rant" after these people explored everything the game had to offer and didn't feel like they got the 1,500 hours worth like FO3 or NV.  What I mean by that is a lot these people are just slamming things they didn't like without really giving a "pros/cons" reasoning behind it.  In other words, it's not really a review of the game, but rather a rant on why they don't like it.
Something else I've always wondered when people have hundreds of hours in a game but post a bad review is, "What? Every minute you spent in the game was anger and frustration?  That after realizing what a horrible game it was in the first 50 hours (and that's being very generous) you put in 450 more just despising every moment of the game?".  With all that being said, I can't argue the fact that after a play through or two, I had a feeling like I didn't get as much as I did in the last couple of Fallouts, but that was after putting in almost 200 hours at that point.  Even if I stopped playing there, saying that it wasn't worth the money would be a ludicrous statement.  Hell, with most games nowdays I'm happy if it translates to $1 a hour (as in $60 = 60 hours of playtime) becuase, lets be honest, that's rarely the case.
Is this the best Fallout ever made, simply put, no.  And stements about the reduction in RP (weather it's dialog, character creation/playability, or the story in general) are spot on.  In fact, it really is the one HUGE glaring problem with this game.  Seeing as how Bethesda built their name on providing the best open world RP experience money can buy, it's a huge negitive for this iteration of Fallout.  However, it's still a damn fun game! Even after putting in hundreds of hours and realizing all of it's faults.  Besides, show me the person who DIDN'T have a lundry list of problems with Skyrim, FO3 or NV after putting in that amount of time!  All of those games were modded to hell and back by the communtiy to fix things Bethesda couldn't, or didn't want, to fix.
All in all, there is no good reason for most people who give a "thumbs down" to do it other than the fact that they're looking through nestalgia glasses.  I'm not saying that's the only reason (obviously), but it's a big one.

Constantly running from city to city in order to find leads to your son? And in comparison, hunting down the man who shot you in the head in New Vegas? As a consumer, I do not care so much about the main character's son, and you can somewhat expect a certain ending - you either find your son, or you don't. Having to hunt down the man you shot you in the head is much more compelling. Do we find him, and how do we go about confronting him? Do you show mercy or malice? What if he's a leader of a gang - do we have to face that too? Anything outside of the story for Fallout 4 is simply much more interesting and desirable.
Fallout 4
have gameplay elements which attempt to become unique to its components. Customisation your weapon and armour
seem exciting, as video gamers have a natural interest to become stronger and more "epic", and being able to form a city to which people can build a society from the ground up
sound fun and empowering. And of course, they are! In fact, many of my hours were spent constructing aeshetically pleasing settlements, simply because I found it enjoyable. However, nothing felt polished.
Upgrading gear felt like there was much to be had, as, at the end of the day, there is only one acceptable combination of attachments to provide the strongest arsenal. It would have been much more interesting to see several optimal builds, such as having a shotgun with a high rate of fire but low damage, but then another shotgun with more damage but small ammo capacity. Settlement building is has many bugs - vending machines would sometimes only be allowed to be placed a few feet from the wall, and doors were essentially a no go. This makes main cities, such as Diamond City, redundant as well, as merchants can exist in settlements which offer
. You would only go there for questing, nothing else!
There is much more that could be mentioned about this game, but the other games in the franchise are much more enjoyable to play. If this is the first one of the series that you have an interest in playing, consider starting somewhere else first.

It may not be a very popular opinion given the seemingly untouchable legacy of Fallout: New Vegas, but I think Fallout 4 is more tailored for players like me than its renowned predecessor. My Fallout fandom began with the very first entry, and I've played each subsequent entry extensively. I'm not what you'd call a fanboy, but I am very familiar with the series as a whole.
What do I like about it so much? Well, I can't say that this will be a good reason for everyone looking for an open world adventure, but the primary reason I have roughly 600+ hours poured into it (only 529 of them may be logged in to Steam, but that only reflects the hours I was playing while conencted to Steam's network-- I have Comcast so its sometimes hit or miss)  is the collecting of resources and building settlements. I will be the first to admit that the vanilla settlement mechanics are rather shallow and limited, even with all the expansions, but even without mods, (I am currently in the middle of a 'clean' no mod playthrough) its still a blast to explore The Commonwealth and finally collect junk and build with purpose. I love arming and outfitting my ragtag group of settlers across the wasteland one by one, building their homes, and overcoming the admittedly wonky settlement building system like I would a puzzle game. I honestly think they could make a standalone settlement building game and it would be really fun as long as they added more variety and more settlement options. But, they said from the beginning that this was all optional content so I can understand why they didn't spent more development time and resources on it. Even if it is my favorite part.
The gunplay is improved from previous entries, acting as a double-edged sword. Yes, it confirms that the series will ever stray further from its turn-based RPG roots, but all it is, is a refined version of what Fallout 3 and New Vegas were already attempting to do. Fallout 4 also provides what I believe to be far and away the best perk system in any action/rpg game I've ever played. There's no cap to your characrer's level, only your interest level. There are a lot of paths and perks to choose from, and sometimes its a difficult decision to make. I loved building robots, too. So many robots and so many sweet mods and weapons for them.
I can't vaunt this game entirely though. It may be my favorite Fallout game by far, but it still suffers from the pitfalls typical to any other Bethesda game. Its more polished, but there's still plenty of those game-breaking bugs to encounter, sketchy clipping and eye-rolling enemy AI-- seriously, its infuriating to have a raider armed with a rocket launcher charge at you and fire a rocket at point-blank range just to kill you as if they were on some suicide mission. I get the whole crazy suicidal raider angle, but I don't think that was their intent. A lot of the time you end up firing your gun at something that's just pushing up against you rather than making tactical decisions and finding cover. If things like that (understandably) ruin games for you, then beware. Oh, and if you hate bullent sponges, then this may not be for you. There's still a pretense of hit points and armor values residing in its mechanics. Your AI companions are useless aside from getting perks for maxing their affinity and carrying extra weight, and in combat situations all but impotent unless you construct a cool robot that can use decent weapons. Your companions eat up any ammo for the weapons you give them, and they switch back to their pea-shooter defaults pretty fast. (at least that's been my experience) I have yet to make use of the DLC content that allows you to pit raiders and settlers against wasteland creatures in any meaningful way-- it's just dumb and not implemented very well at all. A good idea, but not very well executed.
The litany of quests are for the most part pretty forgettable story-wise, and the voice acting for a lot of the characters, the main male and female included, are bland and rigid. But hey-- I've never known anyone who played an Elder Scrolls or Fallout game for its  gripping story; that's usually just the glue to hold the gameplay together. Its hard to make your character anything but a polite (sometimes sickeningly polite) do-gooder-- even the 'renegade' dialogue options aren't as nasty and mean as you'd want them to be if you want to play as a truly gritty, sadistic kind of guy. And that Preston Garvey... the man needs some serious acting lessons.
But like I said, for me, Fallout 4 was all about the exploration, the collecting, and the perk management; and at the core of it all, that's what makes the post Fallout 3 games so fun. I have a warehouse that's slowly accumulating more and more complete power armor sets, and some pieces that I'm still searching for. I'd still love to see a story-driven intellectual tactitcal foray into the wastelands along the lines of Pillars of Eternity--- its what drew me to the series in the first place. But I'm pretty content with what they made here. There's things in Fallout 4 that I can't do in any other game right now until someone ambitious enough steps up and tries to take an edgier, more dark approach to open world RPG's.
