This is a living review, I will continue to update it as my experience evolves; see comments for additional updates.
TL; DR Overall, the game is fun and I can foresee getting many hours of solid gameplay out of it which is why I have recommended it.  Be prepared to experience the consensus "cons"; which can be blisteringly frustrating in the early game.  If you think those things will be enough to trump the enjoyment you would get from the things the game does well, do not purchase it.
The most common criticisms of Darkest Dugeon are the inability to turn off combat animations, combat speed, dialogue animations causing you to be unable to interact with anything until completed, and RNG.  All of these things exist in varying degrees.
Combat animations + dialogue have the potential to draw combat out for far too long.  The animations themselves, while cool, can start to feel really repetitive if you're having a bad stroke of RNG (missing a lot, despite a high chance to hit).  They also are very herky-jerky (there's a zoom during an animation) that leaves me feeling like I'm rocking on a boat.  If I play on an empty stomach, sometimes I feel slightly nauseous.
The chat bubbles also leave something to be desired.  They become repetitive very quickly and interupt the flow of exploration and combat.  I suspect they were included to create atmosphere, but I find they actually detract from it because of how herky-jerky they become - this causes your immersion to be regularly broken up/halted.  This is typically only an issue if your party is afflicted by negative quirks or your torchlight is dimming.  Characters become more talkative when things are going poorly.
RNG.  I originally wrote that I didn't find this particularly irritating and chalked up the experience to most people just being unfamiliar with game mechanics (IE Chance to Hit, Resistances, etc).  I've chosen to recant that.  RNG is crippling, but only in the early game.  Darkest Dungeon's biggest  problem, in my opinion, is the early vs late game balance.  Early on, resources are tight.  You don't have a ton of gold that can afford you to recoup your losses if you have to abandon a mission.  You don't have a town that has been upgraded to reduce the cost of removing negative quirks/high stress levels.  Due to this, you often feel overwhelmed - particularly if you have a bad stroke of RNG (IE. You get crit multiple times early in a dungeon, multiple characters have very high stress levels from it, etc).  Later in the game, once you've upgraded your town some, prices aren't has crippling (maybe 750-1000 gold instead of 1500) AND you're getting more money from missions.  In addition, you might be able to remove quirks from 2 characters at a time, instead of just one.  As the game progresses, you almost start to feel overpowered - not in the traditional sense, as things can still go terribly wrong, but when compared to your early experience where EVERY thing feels stressful.
Getting crit increases stress by 15-20.  Landing a crit reduces stress by 5-10.  Therein lies many of the inherent problems in every facet of this game.  When something goes wrong it is always nearly TWICE as punishing as the beneficial aspect of something going right.
My personal biggest qualm has to be the lack of an easy way to discern combat attack order.  There exists a "SPD" stat, which I assume is speed and I also assume determines attack order.  Rifling through each monsters' stat in an effort to figure out what will be attacking when is not an intuitive, efficient, or easy system.  It also feels like the order isn't static, as the encounter progresses the same monster isn't always attacking in the same spot (or so it seems - I could be incorrect in this claim).  The reason this is problematic is because it forces you to pay astronomically close attention/have an excellent memory of when something attacked to determine whether you should disable (stun) or gamble for a kill (powerful regular attack).  This becomes further complicated when trying to "combo" attacks.  IE. Stun with a character so another class that has an attack with a dmg increase against stunned targets can eliminate it.  Since combat positioning matters, if I stun, then my character gets pushed into a different position, and the new position renders me unable to use my bonus dmg against stunned targets attack, I have essentially wasted that initial action.
Beyond some of these troubling mechanics, most of which I foresee being tweaked to be less punishing/better tuned, the game has some very neat features.  Stress, while annoying to some, was a big selling point for me.  I would like to see stress become more balanced around fight/flight.  What I mean by that is, currently, it feels like the vast majority of stress mechanics are negative.  Indeed, I would say upwards of 80% of the time my characters have become stressed they have suffered negative mechanics as opposed to positive.  I would like to see this number brought closer to 50/50.  Not to get too invested in "real life" comparisons, since this game is hardly reminscent of "real life", but stress serves a pretty strong evolutionary purpose and definitely is not something that is 80% negative (even if it has been shown to reduce your life span).  The same could be said of what happens when you "gamble" on opening chests/sarcophagus.  It feels, more often than not, like this is a greater risk than potential reward.
Combat positioning and class synergy are very cool.  Unfortunately, I don't think they are explained in a proficient way for new players which leaves one floundering in the dark for quite some time.  This type of trial and error experience feels a little bit exhausting.  Perhaps the addition of a tutorial or "practice" mode that has some examples of "combos" would be helpful.  IE. a guide that says, "Try using class X ability Y following using class Z ability T".
The town is also neat.  The availability of upgrades makes it highly customizable and meaningful.  Much like the class system and synergy, though, it can feel quite confusing and overwhelming.  Resources are definitely finite early on and with so many different options and features to upgrade, I have often felt at a bit of a loss.  Discerning what is important in the early game versus what can be ignored until resources start to become plentiful in the late game is extremely difficult.
I've heard some argue that upgrading character abilities and weapons/armor doesn't feel worth it for the cost.  I whole-heartedly disagree.  Upgrades are ABSOLUTELY worth it.  Sure, your damage doesn't go up astronomically, but your accuracy does.  Accuracy, to me, is probably the most important stat.  Also, they aren't that pricey as long as you invest in reducing cost - something that I think people aren't doing.
Class balance could be improved.  There are a few classes that just feel worthless when compared to their counterparts.  I think both Plague Doctor and Leper are worthless.  Jester, other than people abusing their "stress heal" mechanic, leaves a lot to be desired as well.
Ultimately, this game is really about two phases of gameplay.  Early game is soul-crushing and you feel like a victim to every mechanic.  When I read negative reviews, I can see why people are frustrated.  Early game can be THAT frustrating.  Frustrating to the point of wanting to smash your keyboard against the wall.  Most of these things are resolved by mid-late game, though.  If you survive early game, Darkest Dungeon opens up and becomes incredibly fun.  My hope is we will see some tuning regarding early versus late game.  I suspect we will.
If you don't think early game will be too frustrating or are willing to soldier through that frustration, pick up Darkest Dungeon.  The game is done remarkably well and, despite being in an older genre, has a lot of innovation which makes it stand out from its peers.
It's more retro-futuristic post apocalyptic training for year three of Trump's presidency.

I bought this game after my son told me about it. I'm a big fan of H.P.  Lovecraft and rpg's, so I thought that this would be right up my alley.
I think the game is great. I love the cel shaded artwork and the dark story is absolutely riveting. The voice acting is a little stilted, but still very well done.
There are a couple sore spots in the game for me which I shall outline now:
1- The difficulty is absolutely BRUTAL. I don't mean that in a light way... It is really tough, and you should not choose this game if you prefer a light workout.
2- The players collect stress too quickly for me. I like the idea of stress in the game causing hardships for the characters, but having a new character go completely insane 3 or 4 rooms into the ruins? Maybe it's just me, but I think it's a little excessive.
3- If you're not playing close attention, you may repeat a command you used in a previous battle sequence. In this game you choose what you want to do when your turn to attack comes... ok, fair enough, you do that in all these games, however, your previous choice does not default back to a set starting point- the last action you did with that character stays selected and if you are not watching closely you may, for example, heal when you meant to attack.
I'm glad to be involved with this early access game, and I hope they continue to work on it. I am enjoying it, dispite the above items. Keep plugging away, Red Hook... I'll be looking forward to your next update!
P.S. nice company name... 'Red Hook' with the tentacle... As a Lovecraft fan, I salute you.

It may not be a very popular opinion given the seemingly untouchable legacy of Fallout: New Vegas, but I think Fallout 4 is more tailored for players like me than its renowned predecessor. My Fallout fandom began with the very first entry, and I've played each subsequent entry extensively. I'm not what you'd call a fanboy, but I am very familiar with the series as a whole.
What do I like about it so much? Well, I can't say that this will be a good reason for everyone looking for an open world adventure, but the primary reason I have roughly 600+ hours poured into it (only 529 of them may be logged in to Steam, but that only reflects the hours I was playing while conencted to Steam's network-- I have Comcast so its sometimes hit or miss)  is the collecting of resources and building settlements. I will be the first to admit that the vanilla settlement mechanics are rather shallow and limited, even with all the expansions, but even without mods, (I am currently in the middle of a 'clean' no mod playthrough) its still a blast to explore The Commonwealth and finally collect junk and build with purpose. I love arming and outfitting my ragtag group of settlers across the wasteland one by one, building their homes, and overcoming the admittedly wonky settlement building system like I would a puzzle game. I honestly think they could make a standalone settlement building game and it would be really fun as long as they added more variety and more settlement options. But, they said from the beginning that this was all optional content so I can understand why they didn't spent more development time and resources on it. Even if it is my favorite part.
The gunplay is improved from previous entries, acting as a double-edged sword. Yes, it confirms that the series will ever stray further from its turn-based RPG roots, but all it is, is a refined version of what Fallout 3 and New Vegas were already attempting to do. Fallout 4 also provides what I believe to be far and away the best perk system in any action/rpg game I've ever played. There's no cap to your characrer's level, only your interest level. There are a lot of paths and perks to choose from, and sometimes its a difficult decision to make. I loved building robots, too. So many robots and so many sweet mods and weapons for them.
I can't vaunt this game entirely though. It may be my favorite Fallout game by far, but it still suffers from the pitfalls typical to any other Bethesda game. Its more polished, but there's still plenty of those game-breaking bugs to encounter, sketchy clipping and eye-rolling enemy AI-- seriously, its infuriating to have a raider armed with a rocket launcher charge at you and fire a rocket at point-blank range just to kill you as if they were on some suicide mission. I get the whole crazy suicidal raider angle, but I don't think that was their intent. A lot of the time you end up firing your gun at something that's just pushing up against you rather than making tactical decisions and finding cover. If things like that (understandably) ruin games for you, then beware. Oh, and if you hate bullent sponges, then this may not be for you. There's still a pretense of hit points and armor values residing in its mechanics. Your AI companions are useless aside from getting perks for maxing their affinity and carrying extra weight, and in combat situations all but impotent unless you construct a cool robot that can use decent weapons. Your companions eat up any ammo for the weapons you give them, and they switch back to their pea-shooter defaults pretty fast. (at least that's been my experience) I have yet to make use of the DLC content that allows you to pit raiders and settlers against wasteland creatures in any meaningful way-- it's just dumb and not implemented very well at all. A good idea, but not very well executed.
The litany of quests are for the most part pretty forgettable story-wise, and the voice acting for a lot of the characters, the main male and female included, are bland and rigid. But hey-- I've never known anyone who played an Elder Scrolls or Fallout game for its  gripping story; that's usually just the glue to hold the gameplay together. Its hard to make your character anything but a polite (sometimes sickeningly polite) do-gooder-- even the 'renegade' dialogue options aren't as nasty and mean as you'd want them to be if you want to play as a truly gritty, sadistic kind of guy. And that Preston Garvey... the man needs some serious acting lessons.
But like I said, for me, Fallout 4 was all about the exploration, the collecting, and the perk management; and at the core of it all, that's what makes the post Fallout 3 games so fun. I have a warehouse that's slowly accumulating more and more complete power armor sets, and some pieces that I'm still searching for. I'd still love to see a story-driven intellectual tactitcal foray into the wastelands along the lines of Pillars of Eternity--- its what drew me to the series in the first place. But I'm pretty content with what they made here. There's things in Fallout 4 that I can't do in any other game right now until someone ambitious enough steps up and tries to take an edgier, more dark approach to open world RPG's.

Pros:

As such, he can't do anything to release his stress unless I pay gold. And because my party members feel like big piles of meat to throw in the grinder, I can't help but laugh at his misery.
Cons:
- I feel it's a bit too RNG-Based for some of the fights. I feel I'm either going to do a ton of damage, next to no damage, or I'm going to miss.

Overall, I recommend this game wholeheartedly. It's fun, addicting, it's very difficult, and I feel its dark atmosphere also has its hilarity.

The vast majority of us steam users have been stung by the early access model with one game or another.  I promised myself with my last early access purchase that I would never do it again.
I am so glad I relented and purchased Darkest Dungeon.
I won't go into detail about the game as it has already been said but I will state that this is a shining example of how Steam early access should work.
What we basically have here is an extremly polished production with amazing atmosphere, exceptional narration, top notch art style and just an all round brilliant game. It highlights horribly just how dire the majority of early access titles are with many of them being little more than demo's.
If I had to be hyper critical, I would say that the game is sometimes brutal to the point of being a little unfair. I love the challenge and brutality as it really forces you to think about each turn carefully, but on occasion, your party can be at the point of being wiped out before you have had the chance to do anything to prevent it and therefore it is completely out of your control and no matter how good of a tactician you are, it is unavoidable. I accept that some may love the uncertainty of this mechanic but for me, the luck / skill ratio is a little lob sided towards luck rather than skill.
That being said, I absolutely love this game and the above is just a small niggle I have with the game and it is overwhelmed by all the good points that I could highlight about the game which has already been stated on earlier reviews.
If like me you have your own horror stories regarding early access and you are hesitant to purchace this game as a result, I can assure you that if the genre of this game appeals and you like a challenge, you will almost certainly love this game.
I'd also like to note that the devs deserve a great deal of credit for not releasing this too soon on early access and waiting until the game was completly playable and polished.
This game has toppled Wastleland 2 from the top spot of my best early access purchaces.

Fallout 4 tries to be Skyrim, but fails.
Fallout 4 is a messy game with lots of new elements poorly executed, but if you're looking for an open world game similar to Skyrim you might like this. It's not Skyrim, though, and it fails in most areas where Skyrim succeeds.
The ability to go off and explore is nice, but in this case it detracts from the game - you don't move from one element of the story to the next at a good pace. The story isn't well integrated into the game. It starts out in a compelling way, but the momentum of the story is lost as you move through the world.
If you're looking for a story-driven game, this isn't it. The story gets lost in the muddle of the open-world.
Geez, update your game engine. Combat is horrible.
Bethesda seems to be using their old game engine, but they added so many "features" to it, you're always stopping gameplay to pull up this weapon or that buff or to go into VAT. There's a quickbar feature, and that helps, but not enough. You'll still be stopping the fighting because you've decided you need a mine instead of a grenade or a machine gun instead of a pistol or a shotgun or a pipe gun or a laser gun or a...
I've never liked stopping combat - it feels like cheating.
In addition to that, the character movements are lame, very dated, imo. Characters don't take cover, they jump in the same lame way they did about a decade ago, and stealth is just you crouching - there aren't any cool stealth kills like many games have, now.
Female characters move like guys, which is lazy.
If you're looking for an open world game, this might be okay for you.
This game is a mess, though, and lacks modern gameplay elements, especially in combat, kinda a critical part of the game. Bethesda needs to update their game engine, add new combat elements, add female animations so it has broader appeal, and focus on the story and the RPG.
It's still a playable game, but meh.

This is a living review, I will continue to update it as my experience evolves; see comments for additional updates.
TL; DR Overall, the game is fun and I can foresee getting many hours of solid gameplay out of it which is why I have recommended it.  Be prepared to experience the consensus "cons"; which can be blisteringly frustrating in the early game.  If you think those things will be enough to trump the enjoyment you would get from the things the game does well, do not purchase it.
The most common criticisms of Darkest Dugeon are the inability to turn off combat animations, combat speed, dialogue animations causing you to be unable to interact with anything until completed, and RNG.  All of these things exist in varying degrees.
Combat animations + dialogue have the potential to draw combat out for far too long.  The animations themselves, while cool, can start to feel really repetitive if you're having a bad stroke of RNG (missing a lot, despite a high chance to hit).  They also are very herky-jerky (there's a zoom during an animation) that leaves me feeling like I'm rocking on a boat.  If I play on an empty stomach, sometimes I feel slightly nauseous.
The chat bubbles also leave something to be desired.  They become repetitive very quickly and interupt the flow of exploration and combat.  I suspect they were included to create atmosphere, but I find they actually detract from it because of how herky-jerky they become - this causes your immersion to be regularly broken up/halted.  This is typically only an issue if your party is afflicted by negative quirks or your torchlight is dimming.  Characters become more talkative when things are going poorly.
RNG.  I originally wrote that I didn't find this particularly irritating and chalked up the experience to most people just being unfamiliar with game mechanics (IE Chance to Hit, Resistances, etc).  I've chosen to recant that.  RNG is crippling, but only in the early game.  Darkest Dungeon's biggest  problem, in my opinion, is the early vs late game balance.  Early on, resources are tight.  You don't have a ton of gold that can afford you to recoup your losses if you have to abandon a mission.  You don't have a town that has been upgraded to reduce the cost of removing negative quirks/high stress levels.  Due to this, you often feel overwhelmed - particularly if you have a bad stroke of RNG (IE. You get crit multiple times early in a dungeon, multiple characters have very high stress levels from it, etc).  Later in the game, once you've upgraded your town some, prices aren't has crippling (maybe 750-1000 gold instead of 1500) AND you're getting more money from missions.  In addition, you might be able to remove quirks from 2 characters at a time, instead of just one.  As the game progresses, you almost start to feel overpowered - not in the traditional sense, as things can still go terribly wrong, but when compared to your early experience where EVERY thing feels stressful.
Getting crit increases stress by 15-20.  Landing a crit reduces stress by 5-10.  Therein lies many of the inherent problems in every facet of this game.  When something goes wrong it is always nearly TWICE as punishing as the beneficial aspect of something going right.
My personal biggest qualm has to be the lack of an easy way to discern combat attack order.  There exists a "SPD" stat, which I assume is speed and I also assume determines attack order.  Rifling through each monsters' stat in an effort to figure out what will be attacking when is not an intuitive, efficient, or easy system.  It also feels like the order isn't static, as the encounter progresses the same monster isn't always attacking in the same spot (or so it seems - I could be incorrect in this claim).  The reason this is problematic is because it forces you to pay astronomically close attention/have an excellent memory of when something attacked to determine whether you should disable (stun) or gamble for a kill (powerful regular attack).  This becomes further complicated when trying to "combo" attacks.  IE. Stun with a character so another class that has an attack with a dmg increase against stunned targets can eliminate it.  Since combat positioning matters, if I stun, then my character gets pushed into a different position, and the new position renders me unable to use my bonus dmg against stunned targets attack, I have essentially wasted that initial action.
Beyond some of these troubling mechanics, most of which I foresee being tweaked to be less punishing/better tuned, the game has some very neat features.  Stress, while annoying to some, was a big selling point for me.  I would like to see stress become more balanced around fight/flight.  What I mean by that is, currently, it feels like the vast majority of stress mechanics are negative.  Indeed, I would say upwards of 80% of the time my characters have become stressed they have suffered negative mechanics as opposed to positive.  I would like to see this number brought closer to 50/50.  Not to get too invested in "real life" comparisons, since this game is hardly reminscent of "real life", but stress serves a pretty strong evolutionary purpose and definitely is not something that is 80% negative (even if it has been shown to reduce your life span).  The same could be said of what happens when you "gamble" on opening chests/sarcophagus.  It feels, more often than not, like this is a greater risk than potential reward.
Combat positioning and class synergy are very cool.  Unfortunately, I don't think they are explained in a proficient way for new players which leaves one floundering in the dark for quite some time.  This type of trial and error experience feels a little bit exhausting.  Perhaps the addition of a tutorial or "practice" mode that has some examples of "combos" would be helpful.  IE. a guide that says, "Try using class X ability Y following using class Z ability T".
The town is also neat.  The availability of upgrades makes it highly customizable and meaningful.  Much like the class system and synergy, though, it can feel quite confusing and overwhelming.  Resources are definitely finite early on and with so many different options and features to upgrade, I have often felt at a bit of a loss.  Discerning what is important in the early game versus what can be ignored until resources start to become plentiful in the late game is extremely difficult.
I've heard some argue that upgrading character abilities and weapons/armor doesn't feel worth it for the cost.  I whole-heartedly disagree.  Upgrades are ABSOLUTELY worth it.  Sure, your damage doesn't go up astronomically, but your accuracy does.  Accuracy, to me, is probably the most important stat.  Also, they aren't that pricey as long as you invest in reducing cost - something that I think people aren't doing.
Class balance could be improved.  There are a few classes that just feel worthless when compared to their counterparts.  I think both Plague Doctor and Leper are worthless.  Jester, other than people abusing their "stress heal" mechanic, leaves a lot to be desired as well.
Ultimately, this game is really about two phases of gameplay.  Early game is soul-crushing and you feel like a victim to every mechanic.  When I read negative reviews, I can see why people are frustrated.  Early game can be THAT frustrating.  Frustrating to the point of wanting to smash your keyboard against the wall.  Most of these things are resolved by mid-late game, though.  If you survive early game, Darkest Dungeon opens up and becomes incredibly fun.  My hope is we will see some tuning regarding early versus late game.  I suspect we will.
If you don't think early game will be too frustrating or are willing to soldier through that frustration, pick up Darkest Dungeon.  The game is done remarkably well and, despite being in an older genre, has a lot of innovation which makes it stand out from its peers.

I bought this game after my son told me about it. I'm a big fan of H.P.  Lovecraft and rpg's, so I thought that this would be right up my alley.
I think the game is great. I love the cel shaded artwork and the dark story is absolutely riveting. The voice acting is a little stilted, but still very well done.
There are a couple sore spots in the game for me which I shall outline now:
1- The difficulty is absolutely BRUTAL. I don't mean that in a light way... It is really tough, and you should not choose this game if you prefer a light workout.
2- The players collect stress too quickly for me. I like the idea of stress in the game causing hardships for the characters, but having a new character go completely insane 3 or 4 rooms into the ruins? Maybe it's just me, but I think it's a little excessive.
3- If you're not playing close attention, you may repeat a command you used in a previous battle sequence. In this game you choose what you want to do when your turn to attack comes... ok, fair enough, you do that in all these games, however, your previous choice does not default back to a set starting point- the last action you did with that character stays selected and if you are not watching closely you may, for example, heal when you meant to attack.
I'm glad to be involved with this early access game, and I hope they continue to work on it. I am enjoying it, dispite the above items. Keep plugging away, Red Hook... I'll be looking forward to your next update!
P.S. nice company name... 'Red Hook' with the tentacle... As a Lovecraft fan, I salute you.

Pros:
- It's fun watching your party bicker amongst each other/refuse each other's help resulting in their death.
- It makes you realize what type of heart you need when you any rogue-like: One that's willing to lose everything for an inch of progress.
- It's ridiculously addicting.
- It's difficult.
- This is the only game where I can have a leper in my party who has satanophobia, zoophobia, who's paranoid over EVERYTHING, who's addicted to gambling and can only gamble to reduce his stress, but can't gamble because he has another negative that says he can only drink in town. As such, he can't do anything to release his stress unless I pay gold. And because my party members feel like big piles of meat to throw in the grinder, I can't help but laugh at his misery.
Cons:
- I feel it's a bit too RNG-Based for some of the fights. I feel I'm either going to do a ton of damage, next to no damage, or I'm going to miss.
- The difficulty can spike ridiculously high out of nowhere, causing your 'okay' party to fall to the brink of madness...or wipe in a single combat phase. And while that can halt progression, I can't help but laugh whenever I see my party wipe, and come back to town to a bunch of new folks saying, 'Hey, I'm here to get gold/Hey, I heard there was money in this gig?'
Overall, I recommend this game wholeheartedly. It's fun, addicting, it's very difficult, and I feel its dark atmosphere also has its hilarity.

The vast majority of us steam users have been stung by the early access model with one game or another.  I promised myself with my last early access purchase that I would never do it again.
I am so glad I relented and purchased Darkest Dungeon.
I won't go into detail about the game as it has already been said but I will state that this is a shining example of how Steam early access should work.
What we basically have here is an extremly polished production with amazing atmosphere, exceptional narration, top notch art style and just an all round brilliant game. It highlights horribly just how dire the majority of early access titles are with many of them being little more than demo's.
If I had to be hyper critical, I would say that the game is sometimes brutal to the point of being a little unfair. I love the challenge and brutality as it really forces you to think about each turn carefully, but on occasion, your party can be at the point of being wiped out before you have had the chance to do anything to prevent it and therefore it is completely out of your control and no matter how good of a tactician you are, it is unavoidable. I accept that some may love the uncertainty of this mechanic but for me, the luck / skill ratio is a little lob sided towards luck rather than skill.
That being said, I absolutely love this game and the above is just a small niggle I have with the game and it is overwhelmed by all the good points that I could highlight about the game which has already been stated on earlier reviews.
If like me you have your own horror stories regarding early access and you are hesitant to purchace this game as a result, I can assure you that if the genre of this game appeals and you like a challenge, you will almost certainly love this game.
I'd also like to note that the devs deserve a great deal of credit for not releasing this too soon on early access and waiting until the game was completly playable and polished.
This game has toppled Wastleland 2 from the top spot of my best early access purchaces.

Genre: Turn-based RPG
Modes: Single-Player
Intro:
Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based RPG, with semi-random dungeons in which you strive to keep your entire roster healthy, geared up, powerful but most importantly (emphasis on MOST): SANE!
I truly don't consider this game rogue-like at all. If it is, then Diablo's a "rogue-like" too. Pretty much the same elements are randomized which are layouts, enemies per combat (not enemy types per dungeon) and characters for hire. If there was no character choice whatsoever, be it for hire or the actual party exploring, then yes, it would be "kinda rogue-like". But you choose every important decision and the randomized features are also randomized in most other games.
Graphics:
It sports a beautiful, gritty and dark hand-drawn 2D style for graphics, and uses engaging quick camera zoom-ins to keep the player engaged when doing actions. 2D doesn't really get better than this when it comes to exploiting 3D features such as turning the sprites a little during the zoom-ins, and multiple layers of sprites. The drawings are crisp and perfect for the style. It's beautiful and encaptures what the game's about perfectly.
Gameplay:
In town, you manage your roster of adventurers in levels, gear, skills and upgrades and provisions for the next mission. You also have to manage your currencies to upgrade buildings which allow for easier management as the game gets harder. The balance seems fair, but you will be fighting stress for a while until you find your golden setup.
Ailments:
Your characters get affected by the usual RPG standards. Bleeds, "Blight" which is kind of light poison, and stress. Your characters' stress goes up and down constantly. Some abilities help relieve it, enemies also have abilities to increase it. It goes up naturally the more your torch goes out while exploring.
Stress is the game's main enemy for (I assume) a long time. It doesn't reset when you go back in town. In fact, there are buildings dedicated for stress relief, as mentionned earlier, for a price and locks out the character for the next run (until fully restored). Once max stress is reached, it kind of reminds me of the usual "Confusion" status effect in traditional RPGs, but not as restrictive. You may still control the character, but they will act "strange".
Exploration:
Outside of town and combat, you control the party in 2D, left and right. You must explore rooms and the pathways in-between. There is a torch meter that constantly runs out when you move. The brighter it is, the less stress your characters get by simply moving and the more scouting you can do. The dimmer it is, the faster your characters go crazy. Scouting happens in non-combat rooms when your torch is full or near full and reveals tiles around the room you are in, on your mini-map. Some characters have abilities that will increase the torch meter.
In Combat:
It's very much like any traditional RPG with stats such as: Damage, Accuracy, Critical Chance, Dodge and Speed. They govern what they usually do. Speed governs turn order/frequency. Dodge and Accuracy somewhat counter each other. Critical hits also inflict or restore stress. Get crit, gain stress; Do crits, relieve stress.
There are 10 character classes and each feel, and bring very unique elements to the table. It is, again, standard fares as far as what you would expect from a class. For instance, Crusaders feel like Paladins. They have higher HP and their abilities mostly consist of damage and aid. Plague Doctors literally take care of everything related to "plague" (status effects). They cure them, and inflict them (and have creepy plague doctor masks). The Jester is your best friend. I'll leave it at that :)
Conclusion:
I give this game a very solid and well-deserved 8/10. The one element that makes me love it so, is also the one element that makes it imperfect, for me, as well. It's a stressful game if you value your characters' lives. It will remind you of playing XCOM in Iron Man mode very much. The world is out to kill you, and it's pretty good at it. I love the challenge, but it's doing some work on my anxiety. In terms of price/quality/hours you can get out of it? Hell yeah. I will play this a lot and so should you!

So, what's the REAL story on the various systems of Fallout 4, and do they hold up under scrutiny?  Most of the rhetoric you'll read is from either fanboys who hate the game, or fanboys who love the game.  But to really understand it you only need a handful of objective, critical points.
I'm running F4 on an aging machine, so I can't speak properly as to its technical execution.  What I can tell you is that I had numerous hard crashes after extended play, and I suspect a memory leak somewhere, but more importantly, the loading screens have been labeled god awful by just about everyone.  What else everyone agrees on is the game is STILL laden with bugs - rather serious ones that affect actual gameplay, particularly surrounding the DLCs.  What's more, Bethesda has shown very little inclination of fixing them in recent months, and the unofficial patch mod equally so.  Do these bugs destroy the game?  Not particularly, but they do help knock it down a few pegs.
The atmosphere was more or less done right.  I always thought Fallout 3 should have been darker and more intense, and I couldn't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about the cowboys and gambling from New Vegas.  If those two statements sound like something you would say, you're going to LOVE this game. I spent 100 hours fighting and looting across former Boston before I even began the story, and I regret none of it.
Companions are all essential, and give you a perk when affinity is maxed out.  You can outfit them with equipment using a button instead of guesswork this time, along with other commands, and they are SLIGHTLY better at getting the ♥♥♥♥ out of the doorways.  You can even put them into a suit of power armor, and they won't use up fusion cores wearing it either.
There's a lot that could be said about settlements.  It's the primary reason most DLCs are so controversial - because they mostly focus on this mechanic.  If you didn't like this part of the game, you were SOL for half of them.  Building walls doesn't mean anything unless you're personally there to defend camps when they come under attack.  Attacks seem to be random, regardless of a camp's defense rating.  It's not supposed to be this way, but it is.  The robot settlers from the Automatron DLC STILL WON'T DO JOBS PROPERLY.
My major beef is the actual construction system lacked polish.  I built a basic setup on almost every settlement in the game, and there is a ton of them.  My biggest gripes were the snap-to grid, being unable to delete certain items (there's a mod for this) and generally puzzling omissions from the build menu along with the garbage UI.  I spent countless hours just trying to get things to line up, and would fail anyway.  I almost felt as though the devs were trolling me.  When all was said and done, I discovered the tracking system for each settlement's resources from the Pip-Boy was heavily bugged, only being corrected upon visiting the actual settlement.
If you enjoy building bases or homes of any kind in any other game, Fallout 4 is going to earn a B, possibly a C rank for you.  There's a build limit for every site because Bethesda still insists on using the old engine.  It'll keep you for quite a few hours if you enjoy such things, but lacks any substantial reward that would matter in end-game.
Combat this time is, of course, heavily modified depending on your gear.  V.A.T.S. and its slow-motion has been improved with a manual critical hit that charges up, but being an old FPS'er, I never used the system anyway.
The game features a legendary looting system.  Occasionally (frequency depends on the difficulty setting) tougher enemies will pop up with one unique piece of gear that has a particular perk or stats on it.  Unfortunately there wasn't enough diversity in the system, and I can tell you you'll be getting mostly the same crap at level 90 as you were at level 20.  The best gear in the game still has specific names and locations, just like always.
Conversations give obtuse options instead of telling you exactly what you're going to say.  There's a mod that fixes this, but what concerns most people is how little the dialogue choices actually affect anything in the game.
Crafting and modifying things in the game is superb.  Not only settlements, but weapons, armor, building robots as settlers or companions, cooking, chemistry, and power armor all require raw components.  You'll never look at coffee mugs or TV dinner trays the same way again.  EVERYTHING has a purpose, and those particular crafting systems run deep.  This is where the game shines, but it does hit a ceiling in some cases.  Once the best mods are on all of your chosen gear, there's no reason to engage the system anymore.  Most aspects of your gear are completely configurable, including the many power armor sets in the game, which actually feel like power armor for the first time.  These are the systems that will keep you hooked for awhile.
There is a lot of debate about how they essentially took skills out of the game and replaced it with only the perk system.  There is no level cap.  Let's be honest here.  The only people who hate the change are the ones who like to make 3-5 characters to experience every type of gameplay in previous titles.  The same people who enjoyed the possibility of gimping their characters and starting over.  While the game has problems with diversity anyway, I am the opposite.  If I play one character long enough, I expect to be able to do mostly everything.  As such, I had no problems with this particular change.
The game has three types of storytelling.  The primary story is... alright.  It has good ideas - but badly structured and delivered as a morally-gray pile of mush.  Whatever character you're playing as in your head will most certainly have to do things that don't fit during this questline.  Unlike previous games, alignment doesn't seem to matter, almost all the factions are mundane, and you're treated to carbon copy canned endings with no cutscenes regarding your many adventures.
Many of the side-quests, and the DLCs tend to be quite a bit more interesting in the short term, and were an effort to add this value back into the game after the fact with mixed results.  In case you were wondering, every DLC adds much needed items to the settlement system, but only Automatron, Nuka-World, and Far Harbor had their own stories.
The environmental storytelling, on the other hand, is excellent.  As you wander the wasteland you get a genuine feeling for what people were doing at the time the bombs fell, and if you take the time to really LOOK for these stories (most people don't), the game is a lot richer.
I'm vastly disappointed by the lack of good mods for the game.  I get the feeling Bethesda was relying upon them to fix many bugs and add a lot of content, and the modders simply... didn't.  As such, many elements of F4 are knocked down from what should have been an A down to a B or a C because of hurried, sloppy implementation.
Is it a good open-world apocalyptic fps game with heavy crafting and building components?  Mostly.  For every thing the game does well, it would have done another equally well if it hadn't half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it with bugs or lack of polish.  When you've built every settlement up and have gone through the somewhat short main questline, done the DLCs, and have been to at least 90% of the locations, the game feels like it lacks staying power.  You'd have to role-play to stay interested, and unlike previous Fallout games, it won't really help you with that.
Is it a good Fallout game?  Questionable.  If you want a deep and winding storyline with lots of choices that matter that moulds itself around your role-play or style, this isn't it.  That's what the previous games had, and it's not here.
Hopefully this analysis will dispel some of the rampant fanboy fog surrounding the game.  I advise picking it up, along with the DLCs, during a very good sale, 40 bucks for the lot of it, tops.

Let me tell you a story...Once upon a time, there was a duo. They were known as Red and Blue. They made Terraria. An amazing game which went on to sell over a million, but who cares about sales right. The game itself was awesome. Well it was certainly a new form of playing a sandbox game. Metriodvania, sandbox, creativity and building all put into one. With bits of zeldaesque powerups and item collection thrown in. This game had it all. Proving to be quite an oppenent to minecraft. Now now, the game was updated till the Red (the lead dev) had a child. So updates stopped and so the game (as great as it was) become sorta boring. You see if minecraft ceased updating then it too would become boring (also if it had no mod support).
Now boring stuff aside. Starbound is the dream game created by Tiy. Not red or even blue (though blue helped out). Tiy was a humble fella. A mere art designer for the previous game he worked on. Starbound mixes the best of Terraria, minecraft and various other games into one awesome combination. And hell, it's even got some real good art work thrown in.
This game is awesome! Procedureally generated universe. With over a quintillian planets. If such a value exists. Randomly generated weapons and monsters. It is in early beta at the time of this review. So contains a lot of bugs and incomplete features. Nonetheless, the game is brawl to play.
Now if my wall of text is not enough to sway you into playing this game. Clearly nothing will. As for me. I'm going to enjoy it ;)
So it has been a little over year since my review (I think?). What are my opinions of the game right now? Well first of all, let me say that the game has gone into a sort of development hell though it has recovered from it and is now back to where it should be. The game will always have a special place in my heart. I for one backed it's mini kickstarter afterall. I do feel that the game has slowed down but it has started to pick up pace again.
A huge update hit (Winter update) and anouther one is on its way. So I look to this game with huge optimism and reccomend people get it either now or wait till the next big update. (which is not long away).

There are 10 character classes and each feel, and bring very unique elements to the table. It is, again, standard fares as far as what you would expect from a class. For instance, Crusaders feel like Paladins. They have higher HP and their abilities mostly consist of damage and aid. Plague Doctors literally take care of everything related to "plague" (status effects). They cure them, and inflict them (and have creepy plague doctor masks). The Jester is your best friend. I'll leave it at that :)
Conclusion:
I give this game a very solid and well-deserved 8/10. The one element that makes me love it so, is also the one element that makes it imperfect, for me, as well. It's a stressful game if you value your characters' lives. It will remind you of playing XCOM in Iron Man mode very much. The world is out to kill you, and it's pretty good at it. I love the challenge, but it's doing some work on my anxiety. In terms of price/quality/hours you can get out of it? Hell yeah. I will play this a lot and so should you!
You'll laugh, you'll cry, you might even throw your controller. It's a really good time.

I love this game. Some people complain about the difficulty, but I think they're overstating it. It's true that not every quest ends in riches, and sometimes heroes die due to the capricious whims of the RNG, but overall, if you play smart and know when to hold 'em and when to 'fold em you'll succeed. I'm glad this is a game where sacrifices have weight and success is not guaranteed.
The gameplay itself has you managing a roster of adventurers. Every week you send a team of four of them out to complete a mission, while tending to the fragile psyches of those you leave behind. As your team travels into the dungeon they accumulate stress, which can eventually lead them to snap and cause problems for your whole party. This adds a really intersting dimension to Darkest Dungeon as its not just the combat that you need to worry about. It makes it viable to bring things like a jester in your party (who, while not quite as useful in combat as a crusader, does wonders for party morale.) Successful quests will leave you with gold (which you can use to upgrade characters skills, weapons, and armor, as well as to lower their stress) and heirlooms (which let you upgrade the buildings in town.) Slowly but surely your band of misfit heroes can be made into a formidable fighting force.
Right now the game is in early access, which means only ten of the 15 classes are implemented (although, as you can imagine, even with ten classes the number of different parties you can put together is pretty large.) Additionally, each class has 8 skills (although they can only have four equipped at a time.) This means that your two crusaders may not be exactly identical, or that you can bring a Bounty Hunter that fights from the front and another that prefers to stand in the back. It's an intersting system and lets you arrange your group of adventurers in all sorts of ways.
Don't listen to the haters. This game is only too hard if you can't handle dissapointment and don't think tactically. If your a fan of XCOM or roguelikes, this game comes highly recommended.

I don't normally write reviews, nor do I play "Mine & Craft" games apart from a single title by Mojang, but here is my review for you!
After several hours on just a couple planets, I am still blown away by the game. It's super simple if you just want a little cobblestone shack on the first planet you land on, and it feels very comfortable do so with my experience in the genre, but if you look outwards, a whole different game awaits you! Prisons full of hostile inmates, planets with tons of lava right on the surface, friendly shops, and so much more! The game is as complex, or as simple as you want to make it, with a great soundtrack to boot!
Even though the game is in early testing, there are a few bugs, but for the most part, the game is very solid! The quests only go as far as to teach you how to summon your first boss fight (Which ended up destroying my little cobblestone shack). Combat itself is not all too bad, can seem like trading blows at some points early on, but with a bit of skill and timing, you can get though most mobs with little difficulty. Upgrading your items rather then just creating a better item by itself is a good concept, it gives you something to work for. Mining is actually fun! I spent a lot of my time so far just seeing how low I can go, which by the way, is pretty dang deep! Having to keep track of hunger, AND not freezing to death just brings one more aspect to a great genre!
All around, this game is super solid for it's stage in development, and there will be one more character wipe coming, but if you have the $15 to drop, you will not be let down by this gem that is Starbound!

A promising start with some rough edges but plenty of content still to come. Part of me wants to keep playing and see how it all goes, part of me doesn't want to get too far into something that may yet get a massive overhaul or reset. The terrible perils of Early Access!
The look and tone of the game are wonderful so far. Bleak, black, broken - it's got great style that matches the Lovecraftian theme that's carried in the writing and sound design as well. The music doesn't stand out quite as strongly for me - it's thematic and well done just not something that will sweep you away. The subtleness is probably intentional though and is reminiscent of a few tracks in Diablo. Later I'll have to just listen to the soundtrack without distraction.
The writing is wonderfully melodramatic. Bombastic metaphors and exaggerated emotion that just feels very right from a place that's supposed to be dripping with madness. Having a character snap under the stress, become sadistic and drive another character to snap who eventually commits suicide? I love it. This is certainly an aspect of the game I hope gets a lot more attention as it's a weakness in many games that you get the same line of dialogue a few hundred times before you're done and just don't care any more, it's no longer flavour but annoyance.
The weak parts that have nagged at me the most have been interface based, just not enough feedback on what this-or-that really means or does. For example, embarking on a mission, it took a minute before I got that you were supposed to drag the characters to the open slots the first time and it was something that caught two friends of mine whom I already convinced to try the game. Similarly there's no feedback I noticed about shovels being consumable or that your supplies were use-or-lose by the end of the mission.
Thankfully the crash-to-desktop bug I was suffering has already been patched and it's good to see that progress is still being steadily made toward completion - something which has been a problem for a few titles, particularly kick-started ones.
The balance of the game is something which, if it weren't still alpha, should be a concern. In particular, at the moment, random events seem to play far too strong a roll in success. A couple of lootings gone bad and the entire mission can come crashing down no matter what equipment or characters were brought. Maybe this is smoothed out as characters reach higher levels and stabilize. Maybe the stress system will get a total overhaul. Since half the classes are yet to be added, and I can only imagine some more diversity of enemies and abilities as well, it's just something that has to be accepted as a work in progress - something that many people seem to forget about the Early Access system.
Overall, if you can live with some rough patches and don't mind playing something that's in development, it's worth checking out. If you prefer a finished game, I'd recommend wishlisting and coming back to check on every few weeks, but certainly don't forget about it.

Ok first and foremost, im not particualarly a fan of Roguelikes. I love to be able to start from where i left off. I get emotionally attached to my characters and i like being the savior of the universe, with no help from some stinkin friends!!
That said, i love this game. Bought it yesterday and played it,non stop, for about 10 hours afterwards.
The only bug i have had so far is i got shorted on one trip into the dungeons and somehow only 3 characters showed up on a trip to kill one of the bosses or mini bosses. I thought after reading all the comments on the game that id be meat. Turns out  i  must have had a killer 3 party members(one lvl 1 2 lvl 2, unsure of the exact party makeup but def had a vestal for healing 2 of the 3 were def maxed on armor and 2nd lvl spells) I believe the boss was the necromancer. But with stuns, which i expected to fail half of the time, it was a pretty easy beatdown. (one hit would stun first 2 combatants) Im sure it was also combined with the luck i had in finding the boss in one of the fist 5 rooms.
and so far, i am loving the gameplay, style, music, voiceovers and yes even the banter amuses me wholeheartedly.
Sure its rough at the start, but shouldnt all games be? Yes you have to run from battles and possibly give up on quests before your done with them and either retrain or party up your toons to get rid of stress/personality disorders you can accrue, and you WILL accrue A LOT of them if your not careful.
Someone likened it to an adventuerer simulator? Not a bad analogy. You can expand your roster(so far i have a pool of 13, 3 to choose from at any given time, but also can be expanded), build your city up to be able to get rid of personality traits that can cripple you in battles, releive stress after a dungeon crawl and build your abilities.
I reccomend getting all the different classes and having fun with each, as they all have differing enough abilities that they all have SOME use, albeit, not all are as fun to use. (and im sure everyone has a favorite/least favorite class, which is what every game SHOULD have!)
At this point ive only "lost" 1 starting character and 1 character from stupidity of not running. Any other than the ones ive re-named for myself have been "let go" by me because of the playstyle or just not wanting to relieve their stress. ;)
Ive found if you have a deep roster of characters you like and some throwaways, you can run dungeons to stock up on cash and prizes while using said cash and prizes to upgrade your "mains".
Do be aware once your mains hit a certain level they will not go back into beginner dungeons. (veteran 3 was when i found out that they refuse to go back into lvl 2 and 1 type dungeons) So if youll probably end up not using your mains when you hit up some of the bosses for the first few levels.
I also realize im just scratching the surface of the game even after 10 hours of romping around dungeons, sometimes barely making it out alive, and sometimes..well not everyone makes it out.
Do you have to pay attention? HELL YES.  Can it be frustrating? also HELL YES. Is it SUPER HARD? I wouldnt say so.
Its a CHALLENGE, something that is sorely missed in alot of the AAA titles nowadays and i thank god we have a few indie devs that get that and make the games THEY want to make while hoping we as a community like it to.
And for whatever reason this game just has "it" for me.

I don't normally write reviews, nor do I play "Mine & Craft" games apart from a single title by Mojang, but here is my review for you!
After several hours on just a couple planets, I am still blown away by the game. It's super simple if you just want a little cobblestone shack on the first planet you land on, and it feels very comfortable do so with my experience in the genre, but if you look outwards, a whole different game awaits you! Prisons full of hostile inmates, planets with tons of lava right on the surface, friendly shops, and so much more! The game is as complex, or as simple as you want to make it, with a great soundtrack to boot!
Even though the game is in early testing, there are a few bugs, but for the most part, the game is very solid! The quests only go as far as to teach you how to summon your first boss fight (Which ended up destroying my little cobblestone shack). Combat itself is not all too bad, can seem like trading blows at some points early on, but with a bit of skill and timing, you can get though most mobs with little difficulty. Upgrading your items rather then just creating a better item by itself is a good concept, it gives you something to work for. Mining is actually fun! I spent a lot of my time so far just seeing how low I can go, which by the way, is pretty dang deep! Having to keep track of hunger, AND not freezing to death just brings one more aspect to a great genre!
All around, this game is super solid for it's stage in development, and there will be one more character wipe coming, but if you have the $15 to drop, you will not be let down by this gem that is Starbound!

Straight away you can tell this game is brimming with potential, and it is fun to play right now as well. However, you can also easily tell that (in its current state) it will likely get annoyingly repetitive down the road. I know every game is repetitive to a degree as such are video games, but considering the scope of the game it seems like it will be annoyingly so.
As of right now, the game feels like it would be perfect on a tablet. But, with more depth I think it could surely be a hallmark pc rpg.
It's got fun turn based combat that in my opinion needs more clarity. It has interesting classes that upon my initial impressions seem fairly balanced. It obviously took cue from XCOM:EU and it's associatied Long War mod in that you hire random recruits and your current party members get "worn out" and must relieve their stress after excursions, requiring you to shuffle your party members per dungeon.
It I has very unique mechanics where your party brings torches into the dungeon and as you progress the torch begins to burn out. As it burns out, the scenery gets realistically darker and subsequently the challenge becomes tougher while yielding better rewards. You can control this game mechanic by bringing consumbale torches and use them to replenish the torch gauge. Also, as you progress through each dungeon and fight monsters, your characters become stressed out which is represented by stress points. These stress point go up to until they reach their cap (though there are spells to heal your stress) and once reaching that cap, your character gets a random affliction which can be extremely good or extremely unhelpful. To get rid of their affliction, or to relieve them of their stress entirely, you must wait until you're back in town where you can send them to the tavern or a church type building. These buildings have a few options each how you'd like to relieve the stress of your party member, and they can be upgraded to be more effective.
Each character also has positive and negative traits and gain more traits as you complete dungeons with them. Negative traits can be cured from another building back in town for a fee, which can also be upgraded to be more effective. The characters can learn about 7 skills each, but can only bring 4 skills with them during each adventure. Depending on the skills you choose, the character will have preferences where they like to be positioned in combat. Some skills can only be used when the character is standing in the right position (yes you can move positions during combat but it costs that characters turn) and likewise some abilities can only hurt enemies that are standing in the right position. The position in combat looks something like this from a side scroller perspective: Your team -4,3,2,1 >< 1,2,3,4 - enemy team. It's actually really unique and opens up a lot of possibilites.
All this creativity ties in so well for the game, and I really have big hope that will progress positivly and expand in both scope and depth. With how much potential it has, it shouldn't have much of a problem. For now, it's a very fun game to play while you're taking a break from another game or if you're like me then in between LoL matches.

A fun roguelike where everything is trying to kill your characters horribly and when nothing is trying to kill them you have to worry about them going insane. As you work your way through the various dungeons your characters get stressed out from almost dying, causing them to develop various afflictions and quirks which can alter there stats and behaviours.
The behaviours for one character will even affect the others in the same party. Example: After becoming too stressed out my Crusader became abusive and would start yelling at any other party member that didn't kill an enemy on a successfuly attack. This then caused my Highwayman to become paranoid and start ignoring my commands so he could accuse everyone else in the party of trying to kill him. All these accusations then sent my Plague Doctor into a spiral of Hopelessness weaking all his ablilities.
Then comes the town meta which lets you recurit and upgrade characters and also reduce the stress of those who returned alive from previous missions. Reducing stress is quite interesting, as some of your characters quirks and afflictions determine the ways they can and can't reduce their stress. Reducing stress takes a character out of play for one exepedition and sometimes when you get back they may have even gained new quirks.  Here is my favourite example: One of my Lepers (yes Leper is a character class) was at maximum stress after we returned from a boss battle. So naturally I went to reduce his stress, this being the first time I had to do this for this character I found out that he was a Nymphomaniac and could only reduce stress at the brothel... yep. After I came back from another expedition his stress was completely gone. However he must have had such a great time that he developed the quirk of being sluggish which reduced his speed and accuracy stats.
I love this game so much.

I want to start by saying that I am a HUGE Fallout fan and lore nerd. Now, I must admit that I have not played Fallout and Fallout 2 (I did pick them up in a sale, but I'm having the age old issue of finding time to play them), and have still not finished Fallout 3 (although I did watch a full playthrough of it, and I'll probably finish it soon if I have the time). Now we all know the huge hype surrounding this game. Everyone's mind was running wild at the new additions and fixes Bethesda could have done to the series, to finally make it the be-all and end-all of all RPGs. However, Bethesda seems to have either forgot what people like about Fallout (even what Fallout is in the first place), or they just decided they don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the fans, and made a dumbed down piece of crap for the masses to gobble up. Probably the latter. Due to its size, I think the best way to evaluate this game is by examining each of its aspects.
Shooting: The shooty shooty action has certainly improved since Fallout 3 and New Vegas. It definitely feels significantly more responsive and punchy. However, it doesn't really compare to other modern games. Besides, there's even been mods that improve the gunplay of New Vegas by adding some much needed recoil to the weapons, so I can't see anyone liking this game due to its guns feeling nice to shoot. It also suffers from having a pretty small variety of weapons compared to New Vegas, and of course the unique weapons look exactly like their common counterparts! Yay!
RPG elements: This is no doubt the worst part of Fallout 4. It's beyond me why Bethesda decided to remove almost every single RPG element from the game. In New Vegas there are so many different ways to differentiate your character, by picking from a huge array of traits, skills and perks, but it looks like Bethesda didn't get the damn memo on how to make a good RPG. Half the perk tree is devoted to just simple stat increases, like getting more scrap from stuff, or dealing more damage, and perks related to crafting more advanced mods for your weapons. And of course there's the obligatory completely useless perks such as seeing the path to your nearest objective! Gee thanks Bethesda! It just doesn't feel like your character progresses in any meaningful way in this game.
Exploration: Remember how good Bethesda was at making interesting worlds for you to explore? Well, they failed this time around. The Commonwealth feels incredibly bland in comparison to the Capital Wasteland, even the Mojave, and especially compared to Skyrim. There's just too many "filler" locations full of raiders and ghouls, with interesting places that you actually want to explore immediately after getting the first glimpse of them being few and far between. So many areas of the map feel almost identical to each other, giving you no incentive to just head out in some random direction to see where you end up.
Story and quests: This game's story is simply mediocre. Fallout 3's story is certainly better, with New Vegas being leagues ahead. Don't even get me started about the New Vegas DLC blowing this game's story out of the water. Since the beginning of the game, your character is forced into a very specific role, removing the freedom to make absolutely any character you would like. You always have to be a parent looking for their child. The ending is simply crap. Completely unsatisfying, and does not give you a nifty slideshow like Fallout 3 and New Vegas to make you feel that the choices you made had some impact on the world. Moreover, the vast majority of quests in this game are bland "go to this place, kill everything inside (and possibly grab some item) and come back for your reward". Was Bethesda really working on this game for 5 years, or was most of the time spent modifying the engine so it wouldn't die on them, and then put the quests in at the last minute?
Customisation: Now this is one aspect of Fallout 4 I really liked. I'm a sucker for deep customisation for your weapons and other equipment, and this game certainly has a lot of that. Probably the reason why Bethesda didn't include that many weapons was because they can all be customised to different extents, allowing you to personalise them for your own gameplay style. It's certainly nice to be able to stick to your favourite weapons throughout the game by upgrading them so they are still a viable choice down the line. Some more cosmetic customisation would also have been great, but what's already in the game is pretty good.
Power armour: I love power armour. It's one of my favourite things about Fallout. Seeing these images of people wearing these indestructible mech suits, transforming them into walking tanks, is actually pretty representative of how power armour in this game feels like. This is another thing I really liked about this game. The fact that power armour is no longer just a regular outfit makes it feel much more immersive using it, and looking at a dashboard instead of your normal HUD definitely gives you the amazing feeling of being a walking tank, blasting anything in your way with a hail of gunfire from your minigun. The modifications you can make to your suits is also very cool, allowing you tailor it specifically to your playstyle. Blowing people and creatures up (or smashing their skulls in using a super sledge) never felt better! It would be the best part of Fallout 4 for me if it wasn't for one little thing. Power armour is completely ♥♥♥♥ing neutered because of how Bethesda decided to put it
. You get power armour right at the beginning of the game, and constantly bump into other suits, either abandoned at the side of the road (because if you came across power armour in a nuclear apocalypse, of course you would leave it exactly where it was, untouched), or more uncommonly used by raiders. The satisfaction you got from acquiring power armour and using it for the first time is completely gone.
Settlement building: I always enjoy being able to construct my own base and fill it with useful stuff and trophies I've acquired along the way in any game. Yes, I enjoy my occasional dose of modded Minecraft, deal with it! Settlement building in Fallout 4 though? It's something else. Firstly, it's incredibly obvious that the UI was made for consoles. It's extremely annoying to use on a PC, constantly wasting your time digging through menus to find the stuff you want. As if it wasn't for that, it only "just works" whenever the ♥♥♥♥ it wants to. I've had countless issues with stuff not snapping to each other for no apparent reason, and with not being able to place stuff where you want even though it seems perfectly reasonable. Spend some time making a house, and as soon as you start getting ambitious about your build, you slam headfirst into the build limit, because consoles. Thankfully there's mods which fix that. I can't even count the number of times I've loudly exclaimed about the stupidity of Bethesda because the pieces provided are lacking in order to build a house that doesn't look like♥♥♥♥♥♥ or other times not providing parts which would make building some stuff so much more convenient. For example, why are vaults the only structures you can build that don't require having 15 billion wires around so you can take power to where you need it?
DLC: This game's DLC is simply poop. Far Harbor and Automatron are the only ones really worth a damn. It just falls flat on its face compared to the DLC of New Vegas. Half of it could have basically been added by mods anyway.
Make no mistake, Fallout 4 is basically a first person shooter with RPG elements, and a pretty mediocre one at that. I don't know why I spent over 400 hours in this game (I probably wasn't bored to death because I enjoy FPS), but as soon as I finish Nuka World, I know that I'll never replay it like I did with New Vegas and Skyrim. I hope Bethesda have learned their lesson.

All in all, I would definitely recommend you give this game a try.

To begin with, Fallout is my favorite game series. Fallout 1 and 2 is still interesting to play, despite that it was released in 1997-1998. Fallout 3 have some problems, but it brought a new life into Fallout series and I like it, Fallout: New Vegas is still a brilliant and my favorite game in the series, that just can't get boring. It is amazing RPG game (just like first two) and it has everything what I liked in the third one (thank you, Obsidian). After New Vegas I was waiting for Fallout 4 and finally in 2015 Bethesda announced Fallout 4. I was excited, I wanted it so badly. When it was released, I played it a lot and realized that Fallout 4 is not what I've been waiting for...
1. Shooting - In Fallout 3 and New Vegas this part of the game was a weak. I always used VATS for a help (actually, this is the main point for a VATS). And yeah, Fallout 4 greatly improved shooting.
2. Character customization - As we all know, it is very important in RPG games to create a character that you want. In previous Fallout games it was poorly made game part. Now it's comfortable, similar to Sims 4. It's not ideal, but it's still good.
3. Companions - Every companion in this game is pretty interesting, I like that all of them reacts to your actions.
1. Dialogue System - After incredable dialogues in other Fallout games, why the hell they made dialogue system like it was in Mass Effect? Seriously, without dialogue mod I can't even understand what my character is going to say after my chosen option. For example, typical Fallout 4 dialogue: [ - Do you know something about the Railroad? ] And your answers: [ Railroad?] [Sarcasm] [Yes] [No]. And it even doesn't have any influence. Just compare it with New Vegas dialogues, where even your skill build had influence.
2. Very often the game just don't give you another choice - Yes and it's sad, because in the previous ones there was a lot of quests that had a lot of options how to complete the quest. In Fallout 4 you  just do what the quest says. For example: You can't decline Minutemen offer for a help. You must do what the quest says to do. And that's it.
3. Immortal NPC characters - Another disappointment of the game. You can't kill an important character. For example: Preston Garvey - the most annoying character that I've ever seen. I wanted to kill that fool, because I don't want to keep this idiot and all minutemens alive, because I think that they are too weak to survive and fight against the other survivors. But what do you think? The game says that it's very important character and you can't kill him. Why? Because another settlement needs your help! Role-Play....
4. No Original Quests - Well, yeah, I don't actually remember an interesting quest from this game. Most of them were just boring. Go there and bring me that or kill someone. Where's your imagination, Bethesda?
5. Storyline - In Fallout 3 we were looking for father. Now we are looking for son. What's next? In Fallout 5 our mother gonna leave us? For real, I don't have any motivation to look for my newborn baby, because I don't even know where he is and my wife is dead. Why I can't just forget the past and live a new life? In Fallout 3 our father was our idol, he always been with us, so there was motivation to find him at least.
6. Skills - Science, Repair, Speech, Barter, Survival, Unarmed... In previous games there was skills that affected the whole game. It was an important part of the series and I don't understand why in Fallout 4 there is no skills anymore. It's a big reason why Fallout 4 is not RPG game.
7. Endings - After completing previous Fallout games, we could see the cutscene (or whatever it is) where the game shows how we affected the world. In Fallout 4 there's no that thing (because it's not RPG). The one of the endings just shows how our son dies. And that's it... I completed the whole game to see how my son dies... I thought that after that I can do with Synths and whole Institute whatever I want. But no! The game just ends! Just imagine that Fallout New Vegas ends when you find and kill Benny. What a disappointment...
Gun modifications
Building
The whole Boston City
Some Characters can say your name
Pip-Boy Mobile App
To sum up, I can't recommend it for all Fallout fans and for those who liked Fallout for it's RPG part. It's a big disappointment for me. It's not RPG anymore, it's just a open world shooter. Fallout 4 is a bad Fallout game and the worst game in series, but when you stop comparing it with previous ones it's not that bad. You may like it. But I don't.
P.S. I think that the game title should be changed to "Another Settlement Needs Your Help".
P.S.S. Waiting Fallout from Obsidian Entertainment. Bethesda, let them show you how to make true RPG Fallout game.

I recomend this game because its concept is ever-expanding; allowing for nigh limitless gameplay while not sacrificing visuals or responsiveness. This game has a soul. The progression from nothing to badass is too short, but with planned future updates I feel this will be sorted out or expanded. Traveling from one randomly generated planet to another feels like an adventure. Every new place brings new dangers and rewards. You will actually need to be careful in your exploration. This game does not hold your hand (despite one of the better tutorial systems I've seen) and I found myself dying more as a result of bad decision-making. Going out into the wilds without bandages, or other health items will be treacherous. This is great for pacing and progression if it weren't for the necessary evil of character wipes that will occur during the beta period while the developers are still hashing out bugs and introducing new content. Beta is beta and for now I will leave this game alone, but you can guarantee that I'll be picking it up again after the next major update (or you know... tomorrow).
