I want to start by saying that I am a HUGE Fallout fan and lore nerd. Now, I must admit that I have not played Fallout and Fallout 2 (I did pick them up in a sale, but I'm having the age old issue of finding time to play them), and have still not finished Fallout 3 (although I did watch a full playthrough of it, and I'll probably finish it soon if I have the time). Now we all know the huge hype surrounding this game. Everyone's mind was running wild at the new additions and fixes Bethesda could have done to the series, to finally make it the be-all and end-all of all RPGs. However, Bethesda seems to have either forgot what people like about Fallout (even what Fallout is in the first place), or they just decided they don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the fans, and made a dumbed down piece of crap for the masses to gobble up. Probably the latter. Due to its size, I think the best way to evaluate this game is by examining each of its aspects.
Shooting: The shooty shooty action has certainly improved since Fallout 3 and New Vegas. It definitely feels significantly more responsive and punchy. However, it doesn't really compare to other modern games. Besides, there's even been mods that improve the gunplay of New Vegas by adding some much needed recoil to the weapons, so I can't see anyone liking this game due to its guns feeling nice to shoot. It also suffers from having a pretty small variety of weapons compared to New Vegas, and of course the unique weapons look exactly like their common counterparts! Yay!
RPG elements: This is no doubt the worst part of Fallout 4. It's beyond me why Bethesda decided to remove almost every single RPG element from the game. In New Vegas there are so many different ways to differentiate your character, by picking from a huge array of traits, skills and perks, but it looks like Bethesda didn't get the damn memo on how to make a good RPG. Half the perk tree is devoted to just simple stat increases, like getting more scrap from stuff, or dealing more damage, and perks related to crafting more advanced mods for your weapons. And of course there's the obligatory completely useless perks such as seeing the path to your nearest objective! Gee thanks Bethesda! It just doesn't feel like your character progresses in any meaningful way in this game.
Exploration: Remember how good Bethesda was at making interesting worlds for you to explore? Well, they failed this time around. The Commonwealth feels incredibly bland in comparison to the Capital Wasteland, even the Mojave, and especially compared to Skyrim. There's just too many "filler" locations full of raiders and ghouls, with interesting places that you actually want to explore immediately after getting the first glimpse of them being few and far between. So many areas of the map feel almost identical to each other, giving you no incentive to just head out in some random direction to see where you end up.
Story and quests: This game's story is simply mediocre. Fallout 3's story is certainly better, with New Vegas being leagues ahead. Don't even get me started about the New Vegas DLC blowing this game's story out of the water. Since the beginning of the game, your character is forced into a very specific role, removing the freedom to make absolutely any character you would like. You always have to be a parent looking for their child. The ending is simply crap. Completely unsatisfying, and does not give you a nifty slideshow like Fallout 3 and New Vegas to make you feel that the choices you made had some impact on the world. Moreover, the vast majority of quests in this game are bland "go to this place, kill everything inside (and possibly grab some item) and come back for your reward". Was Bethesda really working on this game for 5 years, or was most of the time spent modifying the engine so it wouldn't die on them, and then put the quests in at the last minute?
Customisation: Now this is one aspect of Fallout 4 I really liked. I'm a sucker for deep customisation for your weapons and other equipment, and this game certainly has a lot of that. Probably the reason why Bethesda didn't include that many weapons was because they can all be customised to different extents, allowing you to personalise them for your own gameplay style. It's certainly nice to be able to stick to your favourite weapons throughout the game by upgrading them so they are still a viable choice down the line. Some more cosmetic customisation would also have been great, but what's already in the game is pretty good.
Power armour: I love power armour. It's one of my favourite things about Fallout. Seeing these images of people wearing these indestructible mech suits, transforming them into walking tanks, is actually pretty representative of how power armour in this game feels like. This is another thing I really liked about this game. The fact that power armour is no longer just a regular outfit makes it feel much more immersive using it, and looking at a dashboard instead of your normal HUD definitely gives you the amazing feeling of being a walking tank, blasting anything in your way with a hail of gunfire from your minigun. The modifications you can make to your suits is also very cool, allowing you tailor it specifically to your playstyle. Blowing people and creatures up (or smashing their skulls in using a super sledge) never felt better! It would be the best part of Fallout 4 for me if it wasn't for one little thing. Power armour is completely ♥♥♥♥ing neutered because of how Bethesda decided to put it
. You get power armour right at the beginning of the game, and constantly bump into other suits, either abandoned at the side of the road (because if you came across power armour in a nuclear apocalypse, of course you would leave it exactly where it was, untouched), or more uncommonly used by raiders. The satisfaction you got from acquiring power armour and using it for the first time is completely gone.
Settlement building: I always enjoy being able to construct my own base and fill it with useful stuff and trophies I've acquired along the way in any game. Yes, I enjoy my occasional dose of modded Minecraft, deal with it! Settlement building in Fallout 4 though? It's something else. Firstly, it's incredibly obvious that the UI was made for consoles. It's extremely annoying to use on a PC, constantly wasting your time digging through menus to find the stuff you want. As if it wasn't for that, it only "just works" whenever the ♥♥♥♥ it wants to. I've had countless issues with stuff not snapping to each other for no apparent reason, and with not being able to place stuff where you want even though it seems perfectly reasonable. Spend some time making a house, and as soon as you start getting ambitious about your build, you slam headfirst into the build limit, because consoles. Thankfully there's mods which fix that. I can't even count the number of times I've loudly exclaimed about the stupidity of Bethesda because the pieces provided are lacking in order to build a house that doesn't look like♥♥♥♥♥♥ or other times not providing parts which would make building some stuff so much more convenient. For example, why are vaults the only structures you can build that don't require having 15 billion wires around so you can take power to where you need it?
DLC: This game's DLC is simply poop. Far Harbor and Automatron are the only ones really worth a damn. It just falls flat on its face compared to the DLC of New Vegas. Half of it could have basically been added by mods anyway.
Make no mistake, Fallout 4 is basically a first person shooter with RPG elements, and a pretty mediocre one at that. I don't know why I spent over 400 hours in this game (I probably wasn't bored to death because I enjoy FPS), but as soon as I finish Nuka World, I know that I'll never replay it like I did with New Vegas and Skyrim. I hope Bethesda have learned their lesson.

Yes, currently this game is in early access and has tons of bugs etc, etc, we've all read this before.
Let me put it this way;
If you wanna get your money's worth and if you wanna see some wicked♥♥♥♥♥♥then stick around and enjoy the bug filled ride. I say bug filled, but so far I'm only noticing some heavy balance issues. The game is brutal. Not quite "Dark Souls" level but like... "Partially Lit Souls". It just needs YOU to help the incredible developers behind this project fix it up for full release. But let me give you a proper intro to the game.
The player (Not in game, think of yourself as the commander in the background) is sent a letter from some old relative explaining what happened to his precious estate. His desires got the better of him he decides to spend his entire fortune excavating a secret portal in the dirt beneath his home. I know what you're thinking, nothing could possibly go wrong when you hear the phrase "Secret portal" lumped with "desires got the beter". Well, reader, you'd be ♥♥♥♥in-A right. So that secret portal turns out to be a portal to some deadly hellscape and all sorts of evils are let loose in his hold. He was the only one left (Go figure). So this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he sends you a letter guilt-tripping you into coming back to cleanse the estate and assorted dungeons surrounding the landscape. That's about the extent of the story so far but let me tell you, the narration is absolutely a 10/10. The writing, the voice actor, it's great. Rarely do I see a game that can tell a dark story without over selling it and becoming corny.
Now for gameplay;
You may have already seen the terms "Rogue-like" and "Dungeon Crawler" when you hear about this game and all of that is pretty accurate. You hire assorted adventureres with different classes and you deck them the ♥♥♥♥ out and you send them to their ghastly demise. The thing that makes this game a killer, though, is that they all have their own psychological profiles. So they actually go through mental torment and suffering as they fight your battles for you. I hope you can sleep at night. These different mental traits can either act as buffs or debuffs. The disorders' names can be somewhat technical but you should be able to judge just by reading them how ♥♥♥♥ed up in the head any of your group members actually is. But just in case you don't, you can just hover over and it will give you a brief rundown. The more dungeons you send your adventurers to, the more stressed out they become. Either relieve their stress mid-game with a Jester's tunes or a blessing or wait to get back and send them to the bar or the church. There is also a crude hospital you can send them to to heal them of their "Afflictions". This all can be costly but needed to make sure your company stays mentally and physically intact.
Now these are my only qualms with the game as of right now; Too much stress taken too fast. Too much damage taken too fast. Too many random moments that just plain hurt you. It's almost like the game just decides to swipe your lunch off the table without any instigation even though you've both been sitting quietly and that was literally the last cheese danish on your try.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Things like random traps, random "Eat or Starve?" prompts popping up just seconds after you eat a meal, stress while walking between rooms, etc. Like I said, this game needs YOU to help balance it out.
I will end this choppy review on some good notes. This game is well worth the $19.99 price tag. If you're looking for balance, give it a bit. I think most of these issues will be fixed shortly judging by the compassion of the team (Red Hook) involved. They've already put out about three updates and the game's just been released! They're tiny updates, but updates are always welcome nonetheless. Buy this game, you won't regret it.

Everyone has their own likes, and, of course, their own dislikes. I would definitely agree with the more-than-just-often stated fact that Fallout 4's RPG mechanics and overall story are of lackluster quality, if not directly inexistent. It's what built the franchise from the ground up, and it's honestly a shame to see what little effort was put into it.
But, if I had to state at least one single redeeming fact, it would definitely be the combat system, their beautiful animations and the overall presentation, including the dynamic smoke and, heck, even the introduction of melee shoves and quick-use grenades.
Unfortunately, all of that falls short at keeping up with what should've been the true game. Fallout: A Post-Nuclear Role Playing Game, which went from 'Role Playing Game' to 'Battlefield with Perks'. One set character, one set bunch of characteristics. You can be stronger or weaker, you can be agile or limp as a noodle, you can be a four leaf clover's worth of luck or you can be a black cat herder. But, that's about it, really. The perks that you can choose are incapable of directly defining your character as a person, as someone you'd like them to be, because it's already been done for you. The only true defining aspects are the speech choices in conversations... and, guess what. They too are lacking in terms of basically everything.
All of this might have been stated hundreds of times already, sure, but, does it really differ from the main issue at hand? I must say this now; fans of the classic games up to New Vegas might be highly disappointed, uncomfortable, unused to the feeling, or all of them at the same time. Good on you if you absolutely loved the game. It definitely has its redeeming aspects, I will admit.
In conclusion, my opinion on this game is mixed.
...that is all. I might add more later. Or not.

This is a little hollow.
I hate having 'my character' so pre-written. I hate 'my character' having a voice to somehow bolster the shortcomings of a badly, badly neutered, freedom crippling, more than often one-way dialogue system and I hate the anti-immersion of always having 4 options for what to say everytime I talk to someone. And I hate the idle animation when talking to people. Always the same slight smirk on your character, occasionally slightly darting their head to the left. Goofy as hell.
I hate that 200+ years after a nuclear war all weapons and armor are in fully woking condition and never, ever break. I hate that weapons never feel powerful, ever. Enemies scale with your level; you're going to find enemies at level 5 that take 5 body shots to kill, and at the exact same map location at level 30 you're going to find enemies that take 5 body shots with your time-consumingly and expensively upgraded arsenal. You haven't progressed your character. Why do anything when everything around just keeps up, in fact it gets worse as you level up because of how preposterously bullet-spongey enemies become. Power is always taken from your weapons for the sake of artificial difficulty, the game's balance is just abysmally lame and dry.
The Story is un-interesting. Find a relative. Just like Fallout 3, bleargh.
THE BIGGEST GRIPE I HAVE, though, is the fact that this game's art direction is so utterly god damned astounding. THE DESIGNS of everything are simply breathtaking at times. HOWEVER, the engine or some final-render design decision somewhere absolutely destroys what these models are worth. You can see so much thought in everything, but it just looks like plasticine! There's a weird grain to the surface of all people, armors and objects, never quite reflecting light properly. So much effort and it looks like it's all made out of children's clown colors modelling clay!
Man I liked Bethesda, I honestly did. But this game and all of it's consumer exploits have just proven to me that the Bethesda dev team are not themselves immersed in the Fallout universe as the fanbase is. And it's a shame that they hold the rights to the franchise. With New Vegas; people were shown what a fully 3D Fallout game looked like. And to Bethesda, that's bad for business, so we'll likely not be seeing another decent installment.

text: Imagine Terraria, with a Faster Than Light spaceship, NPC villages that you would see in an RPG, with a randomized loot system, and you have Starbound. Only in beta, and I'm loving it already.

Yes, currently this game is in early access and has tons of bugs etc, etc, we've all read this before.
Let me put it this way;
If you wanna get your money's worth and if you wanna see some wicked♥♥♥♥♥♥then stick around and enjoy the bug filled ride. I say bug filled, but so far I'm only noticing some heavy balance issues. The game is brutal. Not quite "Dark Souls" level but like... "Partially Lit Souls". It just needs YOU to help the incredible developers behind this project fix it up for full release. But let me give you a proper intro to the game.
The player (Not in game, think of yourself as the commander in the background) is sent a letter from some old relative explaining what happened to his precious estate. His desires got the better of him he decides to spend his entire fortune excavating a secret portal in the dirt beneath his home. I know what you're thinking, nothing could possibly go wrong when you hear the phrase "Secret portal" lumped with "desires got the beter". Well, reader, you'd be ♥♥♥♥in-A right. So that secret portal turns out to be a portal to some deadly hellscape and all sorts of evils are let loose in his hold. He was the only one left (Go figure). So this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he sends you a letter guilt-tripping you into coming back to cleanse the estate and assorted dungeons surrounding the landscape. That's about the extent of the story so far but let me tell you, the narration is absolutely a 10/10. The writing, the voice actor, it's great. Rarely do I see a game that can tell a dark story without over selling it and becoming corny.
Now for gameplay;
You may have already seen the terms "Rogue-like" and "Dungeon Crawler" when you hear about this game and all of that is pretty accurate. You hire assorted adventureres with different classes and you deck them the ♥♥♥♥ out and you send them to their ghastly demise. The thing that makes this game a killer, though, is that they all have their own psychological profiles. So they actually go through mental torment and suffering as they fight your battles for you. I hope you can sleep at night. These different mental traits can either act as buffs or debuffs. The disorders' names can be somewhat technical but you should be able to judge just by reading them how ♥♥♥♥ed up in the head any of your group members actually is. But just in case you don't, you can just hover over and it will give you a brief rundown. The more dungeons you send your adventurers to, the more stressed out they become. Either relieve their stress mid-game with a Jester's tunes or a blessing or wait to get back and send them to the bar or the church. There is also a crude hospital you can send them to to heal them of their "Afflictions". This all can be costly but needed to make sure your company stays mentally and physically intact.
Now these are my only qualms with the game as of right now; Too much stress taken too fast. Too much damage taken too fast. Too many random moments that just plain hurt you. It's almost like the game just decides to swipe your lunch off the table without any instigation even though you've both been sitting quietly and that was literally the last cheese danish on your try.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Things like random traps, random "Eat or Starve?" prompts popping up just seconds after you eat a meal, stress while walking between rooms, etc. Like I said, this game needs YOU to help balance it out.
I will end this choppy review on some good notes. This game is well worth the $19.99 price tag. If you're looking for balance, give it a bit. I think most of these issues will be fixed shortly judging by the compassion of the team (Red Hook) involved. They've already put out about three updates and the game's just been released! They're tiny updates, but updates are always welcome nonetheless. Buy this game, you won't regret it.

text:
Many have said that this game is essentially terraria with better graphics and space ships (which is actually a pretty good explanation.) But for the benefit of those who have never played/heard of terraria, I'll explain it in full.
Starbound is a procedurally generated, space exploration 2D sandbox RPG with eye pleasing graphics and stellar audio (despite the fact it is still in Beta). The game contains 6 distinct playable races, and tons of monsters and villans to spar with/ get murdered by. The main motif in this game is exploration: you'll find abandoned mine-shafts, avian temples, prisons, villages (complete with merchants, guards, and every day folk, all of whom speak and fight with you/against you), huts, ruins and much more to discover. There are quests to complete and loot discover. There are even in-game instruments that you can play music with, either by yourself or as a band.
Overall this is a great game, but there are some drawbacks.* For starters, the combat is pretty simple and is quite easy to master, making mobs and bosses rather easy ( a problem I felt exsisted in Terraria as well.) On top of that, mobs seem to get stuck quite often, making it VERY easy to take advantage of them ( a bug the developers have begun to address and fix.)
The bottom line is, however, that this game is stellar(get it); Its soundtrack and SFX are brilliant and stylized as is the artwork, the races are very distinctive and quite original, the random monsters and planets add alot to the immersion, and the overall amount of stuff to do and things to explore will satisfy the tastes of the greatest explorers. (And its still just a beta of the game.) This game is a must have, and its problems are mainly with combat and will likely be fixed by the developers.
*Keep in mind this is in Beta and stuff is bound to change

If you wanna get your money's worth and if you wanna see some wicked♥♥♥♥♥♥then stick around and enjoy the bug filled ride. I say bug filled, but so far I'm only noticing some heavy balance issues. The game is brutal. Not quite "Dark Souls" level but like... "Partially Lit Souls". It just needs YOU to help the incredible developers behind this project fix it up for full release. But let me give you a proper intro to the game.
The player (Not in game, think of yourself as the commander in the background) is sent a letter from some old relative explaining what happened to his precious estate. His desires got the better of him he decides to spend his entire fortune excavating a secret portal in the dirt beneath his home. I know what you're thinking, nothing could possibly go wrong when you hear the phrase "Secret portal" lumped with "desires got the beter". Well, reader, you'd be ♥♥♥♥in-A right. So that secret portal turns out to be a portal to some deadly hellscape and all sorts of evils are let loose in his hold. He was the only one left (Go figure). So this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he sends you a letter guilt-tripping you into coming back to cleanse the estate and assorted dungeons surrounding the landscape. That's about the extent of the story so far but let me tell you, the narration is absolutely a 10/10. The writing, the voice actor, it's great. Rarely do I see a game that can tell a dark story without over selling it and becoming corny.
Now for gameplay;
You may have already seen the terms "Rogue-like" and "Dungeon Crawler" when you hear about this game and all of that is pretty accurate. You hire assorted adventureres with different classes and you deck them the ♥♥♥♥ out and you send them to their ghastly demise. The thing that makes this game a killer, though, is that they all have their own psychological profiles. So they actually go through mental torment and suffering as they fight your battles for you. I hope you can sleep at night. These different mental traits can either act as buffs or debuffs. The disorders' names can be somewhat technical but you should be able to judge just by reading them how ♥♥♥♥ed up in the head any of your group members actually is. But just in case you don't, you can just hover over and it will give you a brief rundown. The more dungeons you send your adventurers to, the more stressed out they become. Either relieve their stress mid-game with a Jester's tunes or a blessing or wait to get back and send them to the bar or the church. There is also a crude hospital you can send them to to heal them of their "Afflictions". This all can be costly but needed to make sure your company stays mentally and physically intact.
Now these are my only qualms with the game as of right now; Too much stress taken too fast. Too much damage taken too fast. Too many random moments that just plain hurt you. It's almost like the game just decides to swipe your lunch off the table without any instigation even though you've both been sitting quietly and that was literally the last cheese danish on your try.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Things like random traps, random "Eat or Starve?" prompts popping up just seconds after you eat a meal, stress while walking between rooms, etc. Like I said, this game needs YOU to help balance it out.
I will end this choppy review on some good notes. This game is well worth the $19.99 price tag. If you're looking for balance, give it a bit. I think most of these issues will be fixed shortly judging by the compassion of the team (Red Hook) involved. They've already put out about three updates and the game's just been released! They're tiny updates, but updates are always welcome nonetheless. Buy this game, you won't regret it.

Alright, so Darkest Dungeon...
I like it, I've liked it since I saw it on Kickstarter (unfortunately too late to back it). The art style is amazing, the writing is fantastic and the voice overs are really well done.
The gameplay is super punishing. The game clearly states that people are going to die and there is nothing you can do about it - and I'm totally fine with that, it is what I signed up for afterall. That being said I can't help but feel that the cards are stacked in favour of a Total Party Wipe.
The things that cause stress among your party members seems to happen far more often than positive influence, and the numbers always seem to be higher for the negative. For example: One of your party has the "Selfish" negative trait, which means he basically acts like a♥♥♥♥♥♥all the time, takes credit for others accomplishments and whines a lot. Lets say one of your party lands a massive crit out of nowhere and insta-kills a big bad - awesome right? Meh not really, here is +4 to your stress level, oh wait the♥♥♥♥♥♥is here and he chimes in that your skills are clearly a result of his tutelage...that deserves -6. See what I mean about it being stacked against the player?
The other thing I haven't been able to figure out is the initiative system. Those numbers are handled behind the scenes so it can be really hard to figure out who is going to attack in what order, and god forbid that you have a negative trait that causes party members to skip turns, or act of their own volition out of turn. I guess that is there to make it more chaotic? Which I suppose makes sense, but on the other hand it kinda makes the whole "Turn Based Strategy" thing moot - well there are turns, but you aren't allowed to know what order those turns come in and we reserve the right to arbitrarily change them.
One final thing, there doesn't seem to be any non-combat healing other than food, which does next-to-nothing. So if you barely make it through one fight you, you might as well give up cause it is almost guaranteed that you won't be able to heal enough to make it through the next one.
All my ♥♥♥♥♥ing aside, when the game is fun then it is really fun. And the environments and atmosphere that the devs have created are amazing so problems aside I do wholeheartedly suggest checking out Darkest Dungeon.

Fantastic early access game--it feels pretty much complete to me, save for that whole tuning / bug-fix procedure.  There are some E.A. games that aren't playable in any sense, but Darkest Dungeon is (so far) complete and ready to go.  So don't worry about wasting dough on something meager.
How about the game?  I'll give 3 quick points to keep in mind; if any of these don't sound like your speed, I'd suggest waiting, watching videos, or giving the game a pass.
1.  It is difficult.  The actions are resolved using dice rolls, essentially, and mimic the highs and lows of tabletop games where, oftentimes, you're at the mercy of the random gods.  If you play games with "always hit" or something similar, this game will undoubtedly frustrate you to no end.
2. Part of a good "roguelike" game is losing and learning from the defeat.  I don't see how anyone can play this game and not suffer horrific losses in terms of losing characters and characters losing their mind.  Pay attention to enemy attacks, what they can do, what you're heroes can do, and start to put together some sort of tactical plan--it'll help.
3. Manage your resources carefully.  You'll collect gold and other relics used to upgrade and improve your estate buildings and, in turn, provide life-saving equipment and abilities to your heroes.  Keep an eye on what things cost and be sure to save gold for dungeon-delving supplies.  If you don't care for dealing with inventories, upgrades, and such, then stay away from the Darkest Dungeon or you'll be blighted.

Everyone has their own likes, and, of course, their own dislikes. I would definitely agree with the more-than-just-often stated fact that Fallout 4's RPG mechanics and overall story are of lackluster quality, if not directly inexistent. It's what built the franchise from the ground up, and it's honestly a shame to see what little effort was put into it.
But, if I had to state at least one single redeeming fact, it would definitely be the combat system, their beautiful animations and the overall presentation, including the dynamic smoke and, heck, even the introduction of melee shoves and quick-use grenades.
Unfortunately, all of that falls short at keeping up with what should've been the true game. Fallout: A Post-Nuclear Role Playing Game, which went from 'Role Playing Game' to 'Battlefield with Perks'. One set character, one set bunch of characteristics. You can be stronger or weaker, you can be agile or limp as a noodle, you can be a four leaf clover's worth of luck or you can be a black cat herder. But, that's about it, really. The perks that you can choose are incapable of directly defining your character as a person, as someone you'd like them to be, because it's already been done for you. The only true defining aspects are the speech choices in conversations... and, guess what. They too are lacking in terms of basically everything.
All of this might have been stated hundreds of times already, sure, but, does it really differ from the main issue at hand? I must say this now; fans of the classic games up to New Vegas might be highly disappointed, uncomfortable, unused to the feeling, or all of them at the same time. Good on you if you absolutely loved the game. It definitely has its redeeming aspects, I will admit.
In conclusion, my opinion on this game is mixed.
...that is all. I might add more later. Or not.

I hate having 'my character' so pre-written. I hate 'my character' having a voice to somehow bolster the shortcomings of a badly, badly neutered, freedom crippling, more than often one-way dialogue system and I hate the anti-immersion of always having 4 options for what to say everytime I talk to someone. And I hate the idle animation when talking to people. Always the same slight smirk on your character, occasionally slightly darting their head to the left. Goofy as hell.
I hate that 200+ years after a nuclear war all weapons and armor are in fully woking condition and never, ever break. I hate that weapons never feel powerful, ever. Enemies scale with your level; you're going to find enemies at level 5 that take 5 body shots to kill, and at the exact same map location at level 30 you're going to find enemies that take 5 body shots with your time-consumingly and expensively upgraded arsenal. You haven't progressed your character. Why do anything when everything around just keeps up, in fact it gets worse as you level up because of how preposterously bullet-spongey enemies become. Power is always taken from your weapons for the sake of artificial difficulty, the game's balance is just abysmally lame and dry.
The Story is un-interesting. Find a relative. Just like Fallout 3, bleargh.
THE BIGGEST GRIPE I HAVE, though, is the fact that this game's art direction is so utterly god damned astounding. THE DESIGNS of everything are simply breathtaking at times. HOWEVER, the engine or some final-render design decision somewhere absolutely destroys what these models are worth. You can see so much thought in everything, but it just looks like plasticine! There's a weird grain to the surface of all people, armors and objects, never quite reflecting light properly. So much effort and it looks like it's all made out of children's clown colors modelling clay!
Man I liked Bethesda, I honestly did. But this game and all of it's consumer exploits have just proven to me that the Bethesda dev team are not themselves immersed in the Fallout universe as the fanbase is. And it's a shame that they hold the rights to the franchise. With New Vegas; people were shown what a fully 3D Fallout game looked like. And to Bethesda, that's bad for business, so we'll likely not be seeing another decent installment.

Darkest Dungeon is a weird little game to look at when you've not played it.
Initial feelings on the UI is that it's mobile-friendly, for example. But people compare it to such greats as the Souls games and X-COM. (Also XCOM, but I feel the older games are more appropriate. More on that below.)
People talk about the atmosphere, but gameplay videos are underwhelming and the presentation is, at a glance, hard to read -- grim-dark? Parody of grim-dark?
The art style is billed as "crow-quill" but it's definitely taken straight from the world of comic books. People compare it to Hellboy -- personally, I'd compare it to Eduardo Risso's work on 100 Bullets and Darick Robertson's art in Transmetropolitan. Definitely comic book material, though.
So what the hell is with it?
Well, it's like this. The atmosphere of Clive Barker's Undying, the RNG-heavy difficulty and Lovecraftian overtones of X-COM: Terror of the Deep, the warped medieval world of Warhammer Fantasy, and gameplay elements akin to Rogue Legacy and Deadnaut barged into Paper Mario and wrecked the place. The spiritual successor to the late, great Tony Jay (the Elder God of Soul Reaver fame, Megabyte from ReBoot, The Transcendant One from Planescape: Torment, etc, etc...) got involved, and they decided to turn their new twisted horror show into a mobile game that could stand on its own merits on other platforms. As drawn by Eduardo Risso and Darick Robertson.
It's also captured a few inexplicable phenomena that only can be named, not described in any meaningful form. One-more-turn syndrome, the timelessness of old CRPGs (though, I must admit, not the interactivity), the grim planning of the old World of Darkness tabletop games. Most interesting to me is that it has that "flinch" reaction peculiar to horror movies. You'll wince when you get hit, you'll turn your head and try not to see the numbers. I don't think I've EVER had that happen to me in a game.
It's managed to be instantly accessible and yet have enough depth to appeal to devotees of 90s RPGs and tactical strategy games (a la X-COM, Abomination, etc).
And it isn't done yet.
Buy it, it's worth your time.

text:
Many have said that this game is essentially terraria with better graphics and space ships (which is actually a pretty good explanation.) But for the benefit of those who have never played/heard of terraria, I'll explain it in full.
Starbound is a procedurally generated, space exploration 2D sandbox RPG with eye pleasing graphics and stellar audio (despite the fact it is still in Beta). The game contains 6 distinct playable races, and tons of monsters and villans to spar with/ get murdered by. The main motif in this game is exploration: you'll find abandoned mine-shafts, avian temples, prisons, villages (complete with merchants, guards, and every day folk, all of whom speak and fight with you/against you), huts, ruins and much more to discover. There are quests to complete and loot discover. There are even in-game instruments that you can play music with, either by yourself or as a band.
Overall this is a great game, but there are some drawbacks.* For starters, the combat is pretty simple and is quite easy to master, making mobs and bosses rather easy ( a problem I felt exsisted in Terraria as well.) On top of that, mobs seem to get stuck quite often, making it VERY easy to take advantage of them ( a bug the developers have begun to address and fix.)
The bottom line is, however, that this game is stellar(get it); Its soundtrack and SFX are brilliant and stylized as is the artwork, the races are very distinctive and quite original, the random monsters and planets add alot to the immersion, and the overall amount of stuff to do and things to explore will satisfy the tastes of the greatest explorers. (And its still just a beta of the game.) This game is a must have, and its problems are mainly with combat and will likely be fixed by the developers.
*Keep in mind this is in Beta and stuff is bound to change

Everyone has their own likes, and, of course, their own dislikes. I would definitely agree with the more-than-just-often stated fact that Fallout 4's RPG mechanics and overall story are of lackluster quality, if not directly inexistent. It's what built the franchise from the ground up, and it's honestly a shame to see what little effort was put into it.
But, if I had to state at least one single redeeming fact, it would definitely be the combat system, their beautiful animations and the overall presentation, including the dynamic smoke and, heck, even the introduction of melee shoves and quick-use grenades.
Unfortunately, all of that falls short at keeping up with what should've been the true game. Fallout: A Post-Nuclear Role Playing Game, which went from 'Role Playing Game' to 'Battlefield with Perks'. One set character, one set bunch of characteristics. You can be stronger or weaker, you can be agile or limp as a noodle, you can be a four leaf clover's worth of luck or you can be a black cat herder. But, that's about it, really. The perks that you can choose are incapable of directly defining your character as a person, as someone you'd like them to be, because it's already been done for you. The only true defining aspects are the speech choices in conversations... and, guess what. They too are lacking in terms of basically everything.
All of this might have been stated hundreds of times already, sure, but, does it really differ from the main issue at hand? I must say this now; fans of the classic games up to New Vegas might be highly disappointed, uncomfortable, unused to the feeling, or all of them at the same time. Good on you if you absolutely loved the game. It definitely has its redeeming aspects, I will admit.
In conclusion, my opinion on this game is mixed.
...that is all. I might add more later. Or not.

So far, Darkest Dungeon seems to suffer from the same issues that a lot of Steam Rogue-Lite Dungeon Crawlers have. While the art direction and tone is wonderful and highly immersive, in truth, there's very little game behind it.
Once you've completed the tutorial section, you've essentially seen almost all the game has to offer. After this, you're just repeating slight variations on this narrow theme while balancing relatively uncomplex characters, stats and resources in what quickly becomes a bit of an unrewarding grind. The psyche system, while genuinely great in a lot of places, can often end up requiring you rest between 1-4 of your team between missions to heal. This means you need to maintain and level up a team of at least 8 characters to cover temporary absences in your main party, which is unfortunate as this just doubles your grind in practice.
You're endlessly recycling a very, very slight amount of gameplay, which the fantastic art style and narration can only mask for so long. The game has one great idea, which it does very, very well, but that doesn't hide the fact the game is pretty shallow beyond this unique selling point. You literally only ever walk in a completely straight line, click occasional objects to get a random buff, debuff or bit of loot, fight a turns-based battle, then repeat. It'd be more at home as an iPad game, as the controls are simple and can be played with just the mouse.
Some people enjoy this type of game, and that's fine. However, it really isn't for me, and it may not be for you either. I felt very similarly about Dungeon of the Endless, so if you've played that and liked/disliked that, you'll probably feel similarly about this game for the same reasons.
I should state to counter my negativity that there's nothing actually bad about the game. What it does, it does excellently. It just doesn't do that much, which is my problem.

Have you played Fallout 3 and NV yet?  If not, then play those first as they are amazing games and still enjoyable today.  If you've already played those and enjoyed them, then Fallout 4 is definitely worth a go.  The sheer amount of content in Fallout 4 and the attention to detail is simply mind-blowing.  Here's a rundown of my pros and cons with Fallout 4.
Pros:
Graphics - stunning environments and light effects, even on mid-range systems like mine
Content - it's loaded and you can spend an eternity in this game if you don't power through it (I never do)
Music - excellent as always and matches up perfectly with Fallout storyline
FPS Combat - outstanding and far improved over Fallout 3 which was already a fun combat system IMO
VATS - the introduction of slow motion instead of pausing in VATS keeps you immersed in the action
Weapon Crafting - incredible number of options to create the perfect weapon for your play style
Voice Acting - superb and give the characters life just like in previous Bethesda games (just not your OWN voice in game, see cons)
Middle of the Road:
PC Controls - don't get me wrong.. you'll eventually get used to them but I still find myself pressing TAB at times when needing to press ESC, etc.; Bethesda really needs to ofer better keyboard binding options for their next Fallout release on PCs
Character Models - not as bad as some pan them out to be, but some are not as well done as others (note to Bethesda - seniors shouldn't look like ghouls and babies should be .. well cute)
Building Mechanics - if you like building simulators where you create your own settlements, then this will be a solid pro for you, but I find building structures to be too time-consuming and at times frustrating for my taste
RPG Stories - I don't agree with some who say that RPG elements aren't in the game, but do agree with those who say that they aren't nearly as engaging as they were in F3 and NV
Cons:
Sluggish Start - unlike with other Fallout games, it took me longer to enjoy the immense game world and my character's actions felt more lethargic at first .. but this improved as my character progresed in level though
Your Character's Voice - this was clearly a mistake IMO as I felt more immersed in prior Fallout games when I was reading the text in my head (in my OWN voice)
Limited Decisions - fewer choices than in previous Fallout titles feels like it limits the impact your character will have, but assume Bethesda went this route to reduce decision-tree complexities while refining combat (now more FPS focused)
Don't get me wrong, this game in my opinion is an absolute must play for those who enjoyed previous Fallout titles or open world RPG/FPS games in general.  It offers enjoyable and outright addictive gameplay once you get the controls down and learn the new systems and changes introduced.  The few cons do not at all take away from the significant improvements this game offers.  My rating for this game is a 9 out of 10 (solid).

So far, Darkest Dungeon seems to suffer from the same issues that a lot of Steam Rogue-Lite Dungeon Crawlers have. While the art direction and tone is wonderful and highly immersive, in truth, there's very little game behind it.
Once you've completed the tutorial section, you've essentially seen almost all the game has to offer. After this, you're just repeating slight variations on this narrow theme while balancing relatively uncomplex characters, stats and resources in what quickly becomes a bit of an unrewarding grind. The psyche system, while genuinely great in a lot of places, can often end up requiring you rest between 1-4 of your team between missions to heal. This means you need to maintain and level up a team of at least 8 characters to cover temporary absences in your main party, which is unfortunate as this just doubles your grind in practice.
You're endlessly recycling a very, very slight amount of gameplay, which the fantastic art style and narration can only mask for so long. The game has one great idea, which it does very, very well, but that doesn't hide the fact the game is pretty shallow beyond this unique selling point. You literally only ever walk in a completely straight line, click occasional objects to get a random buff, debuff or bit of loot, fight a turns-based battle, then repeat. It'd be more at home as an iPad game, as the controls are simple and can be played with just the mouse.
Some people enjoy this type of game, and that's fine. However, it really isn't for me, and it may not be for you either. I felt very similarly about Dungeon of the Endless, so if you've played that and liked/disliked that, you'll probably feel similarly about this game for the same reasons.
I should state to counter my negativity that there's nothing actually bad about the game. What it does, it does excellently. It just doesn't do that much, which is my problem.

One of the key factors with doing even halfway decent here is finding a balance in the risk vs. reward with the different game elements, and it's something you have to learn on your own according to your play style.  I managed to log in about five hours before I finally suffered my first PC deaths, and it was mostly because I rushed in to a boss quest with an unoptimized party build because my main work horses were all out of commission healing up back in town.
There are a few tweaks I would make to help make rendering blood sacrifices to RNGesus less necessary (mostly adjustments to Accuracy), but it's not in need of a major overhaul.

Vault dwellers, Wasteland veterans, Fallout fans from day 1 ... they don't like Fallout 4. Some do, but most of them say it's dumbed down Fallout with less RPG elements and more shooting.
Do I agree? I don't know, because Fallout 4 is my first step into the Fallout universe. There, I said it ... I've never played a Fallout game before 4 and I never played a 'real RPG' either.  "OMG! How dare he?!" yeah save it, I don't care.
So how did I end up buying Fallout 4? I'm usually a 3d action / survival kinda guy who prefers story over action and tactics over fire power. Simple as that. I want something immersive. I loved the Half Life franchise, I recently played Alien: Isolation and enjoyed that a lot. And then I got into Dying Light, my first actuual  open world survival game with certain RPG elements. And I enjoyed that way too much. Over the holidays, Steam had a sale, so I purchased FarCry3 and Fallout 4 without ever playing another part of either series.
First I was floored by all the possibilities, the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, the speed & strength of the enemies and the somewhat subpar animations (Dying Light was perfect in that department, the animation there is so very lifelike). But the atmosphere, the post-nuclear landscape, the beauty of the retro-futuristic design and the free roaming got to me. I wanted to learn more, see more, explore the world and its inhabitants.
I am now 24hrs into the game (level 12) with a lot of walking around, looking at things going on. And I got into it. I'm on my way to a decent sniper built, crafting weapons & armor like crazy and I've completed a few missions here and there. And the more I play, the more fun I'm having.
Does the game live up to its predecessors? I neither know nor care! It's a very immersive, atmospheric world to discover and I quite enjoy wandering the Commenwealth, looting, meeting strange people, shooting monsters and trying not to die around every other corner.
The graphics vary between stunninly beautiful landscapes & awe-inspiring panoramas of the endtimes and glitchy animations, a bit ugly dungeons and flawed lip sync / facial animations. It's still fun to play, once you get over the fact that this game may not look nearly as great as Dying Light. It does offer a very different, immersive experience.
The gameplay isn't effing around: you're thrown into this world without any guidance or tutorial. It's kill or be killed, and the local (mutated) flora is out to get you. It's always human season in the apocalypse, it seems. But you get used to it. You get used to sneaking around. Knowing when to avoid a fight. Using the V.A.T.S. system, which is a mix of tactical dice-rolling and bullet time mode.
Right now I'm a big fan of the experience, and while I have no Fallout game to compare it to, I can say, that I enjoy this game, the gameplay and the Commenwealth very much. The possibilties to approach any given situation are plentiful, and the Perk-System is a convenient way to build a character based on your own gameplay preferences.
Wasteland Veterans may disagree, but I think Fallout 4 is a unique and entertaining experience that has to offer a lot (including weird glitches and bugs) and will take you to an alternate reality you need to experience to understand its allure.

This is basically Terraria but actually good.
I know a lot of people really liked Terraria but personally it got boring very quickly for me. This game on the other hand, is so amazing, and its only in early beta (really its alpha, since game mechanics are still being altered). It does things in a way that Terraria should have done it.
For example: In Starbound, your digging tool (pickaxe or the default thing) all more than one tile at a time. The pickaxe digs 3x3 and the default tool digs 2x2. In terraria you had to dig each block seperately, which meant that you couldn't dig straight sideways or straight down/up very easily. Another cool thing is that this game already has 5 bosses, which is almost as much as Terraria, but this is only "beta".
Other cool things include: randomly generated monsters (each monster type is generated from a random selection of parts), randomly generated planets (infinite amounts of them, I might add), a large amount of block type (more than terraria, and also planets have different colors for the same block, and that color is saved in your inventory), auto-sorting inventory (its also double the size of the terraria inventory), and in this game, ammo costs energy (since sci-fi) instead of ammo, meaning you dont have to carry 10000000 stacks of ammo. Also item stacks are 1000 per stack, which is more than Terraria. Lastly, the water and sand physics are the best I've seen in any game of this type (Minecraft, Terraria, etc).
Theres lots of other things in this game that are better than comparable things in Terraria, but if I listed them all, this review would be way longer than it already is, so I'll let you find everything cool.
TL;DR: If you didnt like Terraria, get this, you'll probably like it. If you did like Terraria, this is way better, so get this.
Also the artist is the same as the guy from Terraria, so its a similar art style. And the game is updated very often. (*cough cough* Terraria *cough cough*)
PS: There are asteroids above every planet. Also space birds. Beware of space birds.

I've got a 150 hours on PS4, this being really the only game I really ever played on this last generation of console. So I really know the game better than just three hours. I'm posting this because most of the people are being a little too hard on Bethesda. Sure, it's definitely not the exact same as New Vegas or 3, and it lost a lot of its RPG focus. But it's still a really good game. Although I feel like honestly the PC version is a port or something. It feels so much more clunky than it did when I played it on PS4. And the graphics look a lot worse. Hopefully mods can help. But overall, I thought the game was alright. It's a lot like Skyrim in ways. Except with a more survival/base building focus than Role-playing. It's definitely not the best game in the series, and it might be their worst. It is, according to many. But I rather liked it, and I liked some of the changes they made. I loved the weapon customization. I wish every game would follow suit. I would recommend it to friends and I have. I got it shortly after launch and it kind of rekindled my love for first person shooters. And if you look at it from that perspective, as an open world first person shooter with a deep story, then I really don't think it's a bad game. It's when people start comparing it to New Vegas or Fallout 3 that they get disappointed. Go into the game with the right attitude and it's still pretty fun. I still support Bethesda and although it may be true they're getting comfortable and lazy, they've brought us some of the best games ever created. The dlc was somewhat disappointing. But I didn't pay full price for the season pass on either platform, and I still ended up buying the game twice. After I gave my PS4 to my sister. She plays it and loves the game, too. I'd say the negative reviewers are just being salty, but to be honest many of them have valid points and I think Bethesda needs to start listening to its fanbase again or doom may follow them comparable to Call of Duty Infinite Warfare. We shall see, I guess. I'm hoping they learn from this, and become much more innovative. They've definitely got the character and base building down pat and done right, though. Creating things in this game is so much fun, and building shelters for settlers and maintaining these post apocalyptic villages is actually quite interesting. I hate that you can only get the badass armor schematic if you go with the Railroad though, because that makes one faction the easy best choice. If I were you and you weren't sure about this game, I'd wait until at least a 50% off sale. I think that's what I did, although I can't remember exactly what I paid it was close.
In summary it's a good game, albeit not great, getting a lot of hate for taking a survival direction that its fans didn't really want, I think. And a lot of fans from the previous games just don't like that it's becoming more mainstream first person shooter than role playing game. The skill tree (or lack there of) didn't really bother me, I play fallout games for the story. Which the first time through I didn't feel disappointed. I guessed the end, but sure that happens a lot. The end tries to be epic with the "final battle" type cliche. It was fun and I inted to play through it again over this year for the third time. Take that as a testament to how fun the game can be, with VATS being the same and combat only more fluid than ever. It's the story and role playing elements that I firmly believe have upset those dissenters. If you haven't played it, this game is worth a playthrough.. And if you get the season pass, then you're looking at 150 hours for a single playthrough I'd say. Maybe less if you don't rifle through all the containers everywhere, which to be honest inventory management is a huge part of this game for me as I collect and use everything. So I'd get it on sale, definitely, for it to really worth it if you're a penny pincher.

A living review
*EDIT* Stopped playing for a while, then came back to do a new playthrough and just unlock everything. Now that I have, enough changes have been made that I can recommend it. Will be keeping parts of my old review, but changing it up a bit.
First, the good. The art style is awesome, and I especially love the way the characters 'move' in combat, though the constant zoom in/out can be a bit much in drawn-out bouts. The atmosphere is also very well done, and you would do well to gird your loins for the best narrator since Bastion. Despite the fact it's a very 'tabletop game brought to the video game world' feel, the combat feels desperate and visceral, probably because everybody's HP doesn't go that high so losing four or five health is a bit worrisome, and you're constantly terrified of getting even the slightest hit to morale.
I like the upgrade system, the blacksmith and guilds. I liked the idea of allowing your heroes to rest to recover their morale (referred to as stress, in this game). It was pretty cool how the heroes had little tiny snippets of dialogue to express their frustrations and stress (usually mirroring yours, at the time), The stress system is very intersting, as well. In short, there are a ton of things to like about this game, most of them revolving around and aesthetic and atmosphere that's the best I've seen since Transistor, and probably won't see again unt-oh, right, Sunless Sea. Anyways. As for gameplay, well...
Now to the few bad parts that are integral to the game's design and seem to be the point of contention/love: this game relies entirely on RNG, often doesn't tell you things you need to know. and still has a few gameplay designs that I find a bit questionable.
To the first point, it's mostly a problem of the balance and more recent playing makes me suspect that the devs migth've tweaked it a bit, which I hope is true. Initially, I hated the RNG. It seems to have balanced out since I last played. The whole 'more crits in darkness' thing still doesn't seem to be making that big of an effect. I wish I could see under the hood rather than just seeing ++crit, so I'd know exactly how much chance I'll be getting.
Next: unbalanced. One huge reason the RNG can occasionally frustrating is the way the game handles its stress and health system. At one point, I figured it was just that the RNG was bad. It can still be a bit laughable (nothing like getting critted three times in a row and missing my first four attacks), but I think the real contention is that it punishes you far harder than it rewards you. So that's something to be aware of, going in.
Another problem I'm seeing in a lot of indie games these days: this game doesn't really give you a lot of insight into the complexities of its system. In a game that gives you time and space to work things out, not a problem. In a game where the tiniest slip up can result in a huge setback and a lot of time wasted, big problem. There are a dozen little features that slipped by me on my first three-hour long playthrough because they either weren't explained or mentioned. I never have a clue what the turn order is, though it seems to usually be "Everyone else before you". Then there are the stats, some of which are as clear as FF13's plot.
Now, I'm not gonna say the devs read my negative review and were like "I can see your point", but I'm still gonna pretend that's what totally happened because I'm all vain like that. The issue with useless trinkets and companions has been mostly fixed, the companions by balancing them out better and the trinkets by adjusting the stats so they weren't all rendered pointless by their drawbacks. I was actually very pleasantly surprised when I got a few trinkets that I was willing to equip on my people.
I would still like an option to sell trinkets I don't want and ESPECIALLY and option to roll unused items over to the next dungeon or automatically sell them at the exit. I'm glad that you can actually take everything with you now when you flee the dungeon, because that was a bit of a poit of contention for me.
I appreciate the devs' efforts to make the annoying chatter of freaked out companions less painful than it was, but it can still get really annoying in battle. Honestly, though, I'm not sure if there's even a fix for that without doing away with it entirely, which I wouldn't want to see.
One last thing I'd like to see changed a bit is the selection of missions. I had a pretty rough one where I was forced to go kill the Wicked Hag (I think that's her name) before I was ready to (still won through sheer luck) because it was the only dungeon that was at my level. Everything else was level 3 or 5. I'd like to see a change to that, if at all possible. Perhaps limiting the missions only to what your highest-level companion is rated at?
So at the end of the day, I can recommend it based both on the changes made and its core gameplay, but I still have to warn that it's a frustrating game. For you, hypothetical person who could be reading this review, you're gonna have to decide whether you're willing to bear this combat system.
With all this said, I will give the devs props for putting out probably the most complete and well-done Early Access I've ever seen. With all the changes that have been made and refinements, I've actually come to start appreciating the game, and may very well end up inculding this in my mental Top Ten this year.

First up: Nice job, developers! DD is a dark warhammeresque (WHFRP that is) rogue-like. As it is still in development there are some issues with savegames, crashes and balancing - but hey we all wanted it ASAP.
In DD you control a party of 4 adventurers foolish enough to help you with the restoration of the old hamlet. To gain resources dungeons have to be cleared of monsters. You will see a lot of your heroes die and only a handful will suceed. Surviving the perils of the dungeons leads to insanities which can slowly degrade your heroes to crazy babbling wrecks. You can cure them but that takes time and money. Since you often get a whole list of insane behaviours it gets harder to cure them all. There is a roster of heroes from which you will choose and you will have to make sure you have two or three working parties to have at least 4 heroes that can leave the village without dying in the first combat. Of course you can also take your insane guys down in the dungeon but their behaviour might be unpredictable and even dangerous to the mission as they follow their inner demons.
Combat
The combat system is a lot about positioning your characters and the enemies. You have 4 slots for the heroes and the same number for the foes. Some skills can only effect certain opponents/characters and your characters have to stand at the right position to do so. Combat is unforgiving and if a character has no hitpoints left he is nearly dead. All further attacks have a big chance of killing said character and since the game autosaves this hero is gone forever!
Upgrading the hamlet
Most of your hard earned treasures will be used to upgrade buidlings. The buildings have a vital role in healing insanities and giving you upgrade options for your heroes which you can use spending gold.
The pros:
- strong atmosphere (of desperation ;) )
- unique hero-classes and setting
- great Immersion
- superb art
- good sound design and voice
- interesting combat
- permadeath and high difficulty
The cons:
- still way to random (often party members are killed without you having a chance to act)
- short dungeons are without camping option so you cannot really heal your party other than in combat
- you cannot really prepare for the dungeons as you do not know what awaits you
- hunger system seems to be unpredictable
- if you are low on gold you will loose heroes due to bad provisioning which leads to low gold.
I would recommend the game to anyone who loves rogue likes, warhammer frpg, dark settings and hard games. Its still in alpha and a lot of bugs have to be killed but overall it looks and plays already fantastically.
A mix between DS1, DS2, and Bloodborne. Definitely recommended for all players who are looking for a real challange.

Darkest Dungeon is a rogue-like RPG set in a dark, gothic background. This dark atmosphere comes to life due to beautiful stylized graphics, roleplaying elements and game mechanics.
The game requires careful management of your resources in the game: the health of your adventurers, their sanity in the face of adversity and the light level, the game’s risk-reward system, in which you operate. It also features a lot of different classes, each with an ability set matching the theme of the class.
Be warned that the game can be very unforgiving. First of all it works under the ironman principle, meaning poor decisions cannot be taken back. The dungeons themselves can be brutal and relentless. Resources are not plentiful and will have to be carefully husbanded. It can be frustrating, and if this does not agree with you then the game will probably not be to your liking.
Take note:
At the moment of writing this short assessment the game is still in early release and therefore incomplete and subject to change.

The way ahead is black and grim, the caverns littered with beasts far more foul that the bandits who would initially impede your descent. The shadowy aethestic of the dungeon belies a fine tapestry of artistic quality, your actions within this world overseen by a watchful and somewhat twisted caretaker whose charistmatic voice bellows in protest of your every vain action.
No man or woman is beyond death. Every party member will have to answer deep questions during the heat of battle. Your decisions will be fraught with peril, meaningful but often in vain. Your allies and foes brings many unique and different skills to the table, and will no doubt pick up many further by dint of neccessity and cold, hard experience. Handy, in a place where neither the blade, dark alchemies, flintlock, or the works of the holy alone will see you through.
Every tool before you belies a notable polish, every door invites a new and curious terror, every chest a promise of rich conquests and, perhaps, a fresh trap to laugh in answer to your efforts. Faced with unspeakable devilry and horrors we must take a careful, appreciative approach to everything we do. But peer not too far in to the minds of your friends and enemies alike... madness waits around every corner, delighting in the chaos as your efforts descend in to anarchy, blood... and eternal rest.
Occasionally, it must be accepted, the dark horrors of crashing worlds and other multitudinous foul gremlins might rear their head... yet it would be folly to quake in fear of their looking threat for the treasures that lie ahead. The risk of a swift end awaits us all, no matter what path we take.
I only hope you will see the light before it is too late, lest perhaps there not any remaining for your journey...
Expect no quarter... and offer none in return.

The amount of content already available is quite enjoyable. It offers a unique take on the precedural generation where each coordinate of a solarsystem/planet dictates what this planet will contain, this in turn offers a massive amount of "custom" content, that is easily shared with friends and the internet. The crafting is very smooth in this game, offering the ability to intuitively design and build in your adventures. Plus the amount of blocks available is almost jaw-dropping, people who loved building in terraria and minecraft will have an absolute field day with Starbound. The music system, while at first didn't seem like a huge deal, has turned out to be the single handed best part of this game. I find myself launching the game just to fiddle about with a new song on the guitar, or any other instrument in their massive array waiting to be found in the universe. Definitely a game worth checking out if you have a few buddies to play with.
The combat is pretty cruddy and not quite fun yet, but work is being done. Massive balancing updates are being released to ensure a fun play through, as well.
I'm not a fan of the tiered approach to gear, I would much rather the game become more open and sandbox like, rather than the current approach of "Any gear on this planet, while it may look identical to the gear on *this* planet, is entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥" I suppose I'm rather biased, so if you feel that way too you may find yourself getting into what feels like a total grind after the fifth tier (due to that content not being finished, from my assessment.) As of right now the gameplay doesn't change much at all as you progress through the tiers, in all honesty the tier system is questionable and it feels just like they took the same approach as MMO's, make the gear look questionably "cooler" while jacking the, in example, armor or damage numbers up by several multitudes through the tiers.
tl;dr The game offered me many hours of intense entertainment and joy. It has a few shortfalls in terms of engaging gameplay and as a result I feel playing without a friend would be vastly less fun, but still worth a play. The current system seems that it would get old very fast, I've put about fourty hours in to the game in about a week and as a result it's getting harder and harder to find content I haven't already experienced. The music system is your friend during surface exploration.

Fallout 4 is a good game.  (I mean, I have to like it if I have over 500 hours.)  Its gunplay is spectacular and a great improvement over its predecessors.  The locations are varied and pretty interesting, from the ruined city of Boston, to the irradiated dessert that is the Glowing Sea.  The (actual) add-ons for the game are also worth the money and add great stories and gameplay.
But this isn't a "Fallout game" (nor really a RPG), it’s an open world first-person shooter.
Bethesda crafted an incredible world for this game and gave its locations some good backstories, but the game's story had much less going for it.  The characters are enjoyable but one sided.  Quests have only one "solution."  (Even when there are choices, they're just different versions of the same choice.) And half of its DLC is for the settlement building part of the game.
Don't take this wrong, as I love this game, but I'm only recommending it to those who want to explore a post-apocalyptic world.  If you're looking for a "Fallout game," just play Fallout 3 or New Vegas.

I'm mostly writing this review because I really enjoy this game and want the ratings to show it.
Despite being an Early Access Game, what has been released feels very polished and is easily as entertaining as a complete game, though it shows some areas that are planned to be added.  Overall it feels, to me, that this could be a full release game in itself.
Darkest Dungeon is a roguelike, turn-based dungeon crawler where you build a roster (a veritable army) of characters who have to fight through psychologically scarring dungeons while keeping their cool.  You compose a squad of 4 from your roster of up to over 20 heroes (once upgraded) to tackle dungeons in (currently, as of Feb. 4 2015) 3 different areas which contain differing enemies and dominant status effects that can be placed on your heroes.  Some enemies, instead of simply damaging your wards, instead inflict primarily "stress" damage; when a character reaches 100 stress they can either gain a bad (schizophrenic, masochistic, fearful, etc) or good (courageous, stalwart, others) effect, each of which can change how likely they are to listen to your orders, hurt themselves, and some other possible effects.
Additionally, when looting objects, there is a chance to spring traps or for a hero to see something psychologically scarring, which will give them a negative trait (though positive traits are also possible to obtain at the end of dungeons...with a chance of negatives as well).  These have a wide variety of effects, but can be removed by payment of some gold.
Overall, quite a good game regardless of early access status with a fair amount of content already, and more to come later.

Vault dwellers, Wasteland veterans, Fallout fans from day 1 ... they don't like Fallout 4. Some do, but most of them say it's dumbed down Fallout with less RPG elements and more shooting.
Do I agree? I don't know, because Fallout 4 is my first step into the Fallout universe. There, I said it ... I've never played a Fallout game before 4 and I never played a 'real RPG' either.  "OMG! How dare he?!" yeah save it, I don't care.
So how did I end up buying Fallout 4? I'm usually a 3d action / survival kinda guy who prefers story over action and tactics over fire power. Simple as that. I want something immersive. I loved the Half Life franchise, I recently played Alien: Isolation and enjoyed that a lot. And then I got into Dying Light, my first actuual  open world survival game with certain RPG elements. And I enjoyed that way too much. Over the holidays, Steam had a sale, so I purchased FarCry3 and Fallout 4 without ever playing another part of either series.
First I was floored by all the possibilities, the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, the speed & strength of the enemies and the somewhat subpar animations (Dying Light was perfect in that department, the animation there is so very lifelike). But the atmosphere, the post-nuclear landscape, the beauty of the retro-futuristic design and the free roaming got to me. I wanted to learn more, see more, explore the world and its inhabitants.
I am now 24hrs into the game (level 12) with a lot of walking around, looking at things going on. And I got into it. I'm on my way to a decent sniper built, crafting weapons & armor like crazy and I've completed a few missions here and there. And the more I play, the more fun I'm having.
Does the game live up to its predecessors? I neither know nor care! It's a very immersive, atmospheric world to discover and I quite enjoy wandering the Commenwealth, looting, meeting strange people, shooting monsters and trying not to die around every other corner.
The graphics vary between stunninly beautiful landscapes & awe-inspiring panoramas of the endtimes and glitchy animations, a bit ugly dungeons and flawed lip sync / facial animations. It's still fun to play, once you get over the fact that this game may not look nearly as great as Dying Light. It does offer a very different, immersive experience.
The gameplay isn't effing around: you're thrown into this world without any guidance or tutorial. It's kill or be killed, and the local (mutated) flora is out to get you. It's always human season in the apocalypse, it seems. But you get used to it. You get used to sneaking around. Knowing when to avoid a fight. Using the V.A.T.S. system, which is a mix of tactical dice-rolling and bullet time mode.
Right now I'm a big fan of the experience, and while I have no Fallout game to compare it to, I can say, that I enjoy this game, the gameplay and the Commenwealth very much. The possibilties to approach any given situation are plentiful, and the Perk-System is a convenient way to build a character based on your own gameplay preferences.
Wasteland Veterans may disagree, but I think Fallout 4 is a unique and entertaining experience that has to offer a lot (including weird glitches and bugs) and will take you to an alternate reality you need to experience to understand its allure.

Fallout 4 is a good game.  (I mean, I have to like it if I have over 500 hours.)  Its gunplay is spectacular and a great improvement over its predecessors.  The locations are varied and pretty interesting, from the ruined city of Boston, to the irradiated dessert that is the Glowing Sea.  The (actual) add-ons for the game are also worth the money and add great stories and gameplay.
But this isn't a "Fallout game" (nor really a RPG), it’s an open world first-person shooter.
Bethesda crafted an incredible world for this game and gave its locations some good backstories, but the game's story had much less going for it.  The characters are enjoyable but one sided.  Quests have only one "solution."  (Even when there are choices, they're just different versions of the same choice.) And half of its DLC is for the settlement building part of the game.
Don't take this wrong, as I love this game, but I'm only recommending it to those who want to explore a post-apocalyptic world.  If you're looking for a "Fallout game," just play Fallout 3 or New Vegas.

The amount of content already available is quite enjoyable. It offers a unique take on the precedural generation where each coordinate of a solarsystem/planet dictates what this planet will contain, this in turn offers a massive amount of "custom" content, that is easily shared with friends and the internet. The crafting is very smooth in this game, offering the ability to intuitively design and build in your adventures. Plus the amount of blocks available is almost jaw-dropping, people who loved building in terraria and minecraft will have an absolute field day with Starbound. The music system, while at first didn't seem like a huge deal, has turned out to be the single handed best part of this game. I find myself launching the game just to fiddle about with a new song on the guitar, or any other instrument in their massive array waiting to be found in the universe. Definitely a game worth checking out if you have a few buddies to play with.
The combat is pretty cruddy and not quite fun yet, but work is being done. Massive balancing updates are being released to ensure a fun play through, as well.
I'm not a fan of the tiered approach to gear, I would much rather the game become more open and sandbox like, rather than the current approach of "Any gear on this planet, while it may look identical to the gear on *this* planet, is entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥" I suppose I'm rather biased, so if you feel that way too you may find yourself getting into what feels like a total grind after the fifth tier (due to that content not being finished, from my assessment.) As of right now the gameplay doesn't change much at all as you progress through the tiers, in all honesty the tier system is questionable and it feels just like they took the same approach as MMO's, make the gear look questionably "cooler" while jacking the, in example, armor or damage numbers up by several multitudes through the tiers.
tl;dr The game offered me many hours of intense entertainment and joy. It has a few shortfalls in terms of engaging gameplay and as a result I feel playing without a friend would be vastly less fun, but still worth a play. The current system seems that it would get old very fast, I've put about fourty hours in to the game in about a week and as a result it's getting harder and harder to find content I haven't already experienced. The music system is your friend during surface exploration.
