This game is good and all, but if you want a game that doesn't take a semi-expensive rig or set up to run, but has amazing writing and a better feel than this game as a whole, then I recommend Fallout: New Vegas.
I feel like this game focuses a lot more on putting stuff into it rather than actually focusing on the content, such as writing. Also, Fallout 4 kinda sets you up with a predestined backstory, which I really didn't like. I want to make my own destiny, and not have it already predetermined. For instance, in Fallout New Vegas, you're just a courier on your merry way before you get shot, and you wake up in Goodsprings and go from there. You see what I mean? You're not a parent chasing after your kid after your spouse gets shot. Boo Hoo, where's my son.
Fallout 3 was also really good, despite the fact all you're trying to do is find your father. I know it sounds hypocritical (considering how similar the idea is), but I like it better than Fallout 4's approach, because they start you off in a vault with your dad, and you're able to get to know him as a person before having to leave. It creates a want to find him, you know? Whereas in Fallout 4 where you don't really get to know your spouse/son before the bombs drop. The empathy just isn't there as it was in Fallout 3.
I think the main selling point of this game is the graphics, the character design, the settlement building, etc. While I like this, it shouldn't be the focus. A good RPG doesn't rely on these things, it relies on writing, world-building, and the overall feel of the game.
This game IS good, don't let my review convince you otherwise. I was just let down because past games, in my opinion, have been so much better.
TLDR:
Good points: Romancing your companion, many different factions, building mechanism, interesting characters, graphics
Bad points: Writing, doesn't have a good feel, not as fluid, predetermined storyline, your son being named Shaun, lack of complex factions, the dialogue system.

For early release this game is great. Dungeon crawler/DnD/FinalFantasy (NES)...
It holds a similar aesthetic as FTL does with its clean yet complex system.
This game is not made to be easy, and things seem to be always slightly out of your control. On top of all the poison/stuns/etc, there is also a morale mechanic, where things like the dark, or being hit particularly hard by the enemy will make your teammates slowly lose their sanity. There are many interesting mechanics in this game that make it complex enough to enjoy without becoming a massive micromanagement marathon.
The art style, mood, narration, user interface, etc seems all very polished. There is a lot to enjoy, and it seems the developers are very passionate about making it (even) better.
Early experiences: 1. One out of two characters almost dying in the tutorial. 2. Party member has "kleptomania" trait, and decides randomly to keep all the loot from a chest. 3. One person gets demoralized when I had him go into a confessional booth, and as the dungeon progresses, he ends up being so negative, there's a chain reaction among the whole team becoming demoralized (which makes them reasonably harder to control in sometimes crucial ways) -- but randomly, one guy decides to become heroic and rise above it and brings up the stats of the whole team...
Lot of randomness encorporated happening here, and the best analogy would be to playing a round of Binding of Isaac where you are particularly unlucky or like in FTL where you encounter many setbacks. However, you don't just fail outright and get to start the game over quickly... so I'm not sure yet if you can end up completely stuck midgame and forced to start over from scratch.
Overall: If this was the game in its finished state, it would be worth. I've learned to cope with inflation and $20 to support a game where the devs give a damn is fine by me, especially if it's still expanding and growing. Don't pass it up when it goes on sale eventually though.
(If devs happen to read this, things I'd like added: better way to level new members mid-late game -- perhaps some sort of side dungeon that scales with your party (so difficulty isn't "way too easy/hard"), more bosses, enemies, classes (of course, always welcome), variation in the maps (perhaps roaming packs of enemies pursuing you, being attacked from behind so your parties order is reversed), better ways of demoralizing teammates (without compromising the difficulty))

*This review is based on the early access*
Pros: Excellent atmosphere, Great soundtrack and FXs, Solid core/mechanics, fantastic art design and Grim but fun story.
Cons: Poor pacing, Too intense difficulty spike, Not enough loot for effort, Lack of planning because of RNG, Lack of customization, Confusing STATS, and Unbalanced Classes.
Short review: Darkest Dungeon at this moment is a frustratingly great game that is muddled down by broken stats, poorly balanced classes, and an incredible for all the wrong reasons difficulty spike.  I recommend you wait till it's final release before purchasing!
Full Review: First of all I would like to say that I helped back this game. I absolutely loved the concept and was on board the moment I saw the combat and art style. The soundtrack is done wonderfully by Stuart Chatwood of (Prince of Persia series) fame. The art design is foreboding and dark as it should be and the small touches of dialogue from the Nameless Estate Owner's deep voice evokes fear and tension in every battle and even in respite. This game has everything going for it....until you start playing more than two hours of the game.
The start of the game is difficult and the first dungeon teaches you a very powerful lesson. "In this dark abyss, only thorough forethought and careful execution will you allow yourself to survive". It's a shame then that the game has yet to fully take it's own advice. This game wants to be Dark Souls or FTL or the Binding of Issac so bad and I do too but here's the thing about those games. They may be incredibly difficult, but they are also phenomenally well designed and balanced which is why even in death you want to try again to do better, to play smarter. I can't tell you the amount of times I've spent playing FTL over and over again. Just one more turn, one more room then I'll go to bed. This isn't one of those games; not yet at least.
Lets start with the positives, the combat. The combat is fluid and deep and each battle keeps you on edge and each victory feels great. It's such a satisfactory feeling to kill two enemies at once and have the narrator praise your strike when you were at the brink and you turned the tide of battle. It is equally heartbreaking then when an enemy kills an ally you've grown accustomed to, and like your characters your resolve breaks at the sight. That's whats great about this game what's not great is when you attack five times miss five times and the enemy kills you in one hit despite massive upgrades. For all this game does right the balancing issues comeback and take it all away. The first apprentice levels gets you accustomed to the combat but the moment you level up and move on to the next greater challenge the game slams you back HARD and destroys the flow it had been building. Yes the game is supposed to be hard I get it (comes with being a rougelike game, you know no mercy) but the sometimes sporattic RNG isn't fine tuned enough to warent an honest death. The game advices you "sometimes its better to run from a fight", I agree. However when you abandon a quest your allies never receive experience for their effort so not only do you lose money for the supplies that you can't take back you are stuck with stress and nothing to show for it. Wanna an easier level to get back on your feet after a difficult dungeon? Too bad your too strong to go back and too weak to go forward.  They want you to grind for experience and get gold and get stronger to get more skills to be prepared for the next battle. But they punish you for playing it smart and retreating or if you want to do small tasks to make back the money. The game forces your stronger companions to fight more difficult battles alienating them from the rest of your party members. So if you want to get your strongest party to fight the upcoming boss too bad that guy didn't level with the rest of them breaking up the synergy.
Speaking of party members each class is unique, you have the Crusader, the Vessel, the Bounty hunter, the Occultist, etc.. The problem is that there are classes that are clearly better than others. Why would I bring a Grave robber when I have a Highwayman? She can randomly get an item when resting, whoopee! The Highwayman has a high dodge chance and can hit three enemies for higher damage, guess which one I'm taking? Each party member gets a good quirk and bad quirk. Some make the character more unique others are diseases that need to be cured. You can get rid of the bad ones for a price but only one. Problem is between all the upgrades, the stress relievers, and the upgrades of skills there is not enough money to do what you need to survive. You can't just take a week off play it smart and weigh your options. Your forced to keep going back in. You never can do what you want efficiently and you ask yourself why you couldn't do things differently.  Why couldn't you have an upgrade where you could take away two bad quirks for a slightly increased price instead wasting an adventurer? Why can't I carry more gold like maybe 2000 per slot instead of 1500 or make this less expensive? Why can't I customize the color of an adventurers look? I know I could lose an adventurer but by the fifth bounty hunter I stopped caring about their names or quirks.
Most of the problems probably will be fixed by the time the game is finally released. Which is good but it needed to be said now. This game is still being fixed and balanced. That's why I wrote this review because I want this game to be great it clearly has the potential. I want it to be heralded as the indie Dark Souls or Resident Evil (1-4)  but it doesn't just get it handed to it because it has my money. It has to work at it like everyone else. I believe in Red Hook. It's a great team who clearly want to make a great game and I believe though that by the time it is finished I will be singing it's praises on release day. But for now I will be backing away into the dark night waiting for its foreseeable release.

Let me start by saying that I'm still pretty new to the Fallout franchise, My first game was Fallout 3 and I only played it until the end of the main story. Fallout 4 interested me due to the changes made to the core gameplay of Fallout.
The gunplay in the previous Fallout games I found very clunky, and often annoying. In Fallout 4 however, it has been improved upon, bringing it up to scratch with other FPS games. Graphics greatly improved, and lots of other core mechanics polished. The gameplay in Fallout 4 is quite more enjoyable than previous titles.
Crafting and settlement building is a feature that I personally love. Nothing better than creating that perfect settlement based on your imagination of how things showed be. However this isn't for everyone. The good thing is that it can be skipped (for the most part) if it doesn't tickle your fancy.
One of the biggest complaints about this game is the roleplaying and story telling aspect. True, the dialouge has been dumbed down from previous games, which is a bummer, as Fallout is a great roleplaying game series in general. In terms of story, I actually found it quite good. But I can understand why it wouldn't appeal to people who are die-hard fans of the series.
In general, a great game for people looking for a FPS RPG game, not so great for die-hard Fallout fans. The DLC is really good aswell.

This is one of the few early access indie titles that I didn't hesitate to purchase after doing some research and it does not dissapoint.  Although it is still early access, Darkest Dungeon is well into development, has plenty of content, and is more then worth the asking price of $20.
As for the gameplay itself, it is just as described:  A roguelike turn-based dungeon crawler rpg.  There is a good amount of depth and strategy involved, both in and out of battles.  Choosing how to spend your money and resources on upgrades and provisions, deciding which of your heroes to bring and which of their abilities to equip,  and choosing how to act during battles and other random events, etc...
The art style is absolutely gorgeous, in a gritty, atmospheric kind of way.  The art and music come together perfectly to set a dark undertone.
Oh, by the way, this game is hard.  You will always be struggling in one way or another while exploring a dungeon, and very rarely does a situation play out as planned, forcing you to change tactics and make decisions one turn at a time.  Although difficult and random (as expected from a roguelike) Darkest Dungeon never feels unfair.
Overall this game is super dank and earns 8/10 bomb nuggets.  The final product will likely be a 9 or 10.

It's still in early access but even so you can see what is to come.  The visual style is rich and coherent, not a generic retread.  The theming and atmosphere is the focus, and the mechanics the support.  Even little things like the sudden closeup sequences during attacks lends an immediecy to everything you do, to say nothing of the constant dying of the light and the need to shepherd your fragile heroes through the coils of despair and horror.
I see people harping on RNG and I don't exactly parse what they mean.  Aside from crits, which CAN be brutal.  Enemies behave in fairly predictable ways.  You can see hit percentages and damage all laid out for you.  If you're surprised by what an enemy does either you haven't fought it before, or you're not paying attention.
The stress mechanics are beautiful and for me, seem to fit a sweetspot.  I can normally shepherd my grup through a dungeon without anyone losing their mind, but a bad turn can push someone over the edge who was allready teetering and yes, once you start losing people things CAN get ugly fast.  However I must also say some of my favorite times were limping home from a mission with three people alive, one of them raving at the other two.  Hard won victories are all the sweeter.  Being able to delve, rinse, repeat without a challenge just by plugging in the 'best skillz' would turn the game into an accounting exercise and there's plenty of that sort of drivel already on the market.

This game is good and all, but if you want a game that doesn't take a semi-expensive rig or set up to run, but has amazing writing and a better feel than this game as a whole, then I recommend Fallout: New Vegas.
I feel like this game focuses a lot more on putting stuff into it rather than actually focusing on the content, such as writing. Also, Fallout 4 kinda sets you up with a predestined backstory, which I really didn't like. I want to make my own destiny, and not have it already predetermined. For instance, in Fallout New Vegas, you're just a courier on your merry way before you get shot, and you wake up in Goodsprings and go from there. You see what I mean? You're not a parent chasing after your kid after your spouse gets shot. Boo Hoo, where's my son.
Fallout 3 was also really good, despite the fact all you're trying to do is find your father. I know it sounds hypocritical (considering how similar the idea is), but I like it better than Fallout 4's approach, because they start you off in a vault with your dad, and you're able to get to know him as a person before having to leave. It creates a want to find him, you know? Whereas in Fallout 4 where you don't really get to know your spouse/son before the bombs drop. The empathy just isn't there as it was in Fallout 3.
I think the main selling point of this game is the graphics, the character design, the settlement building, etc. While I like this, it shouldn't be the focus. A good RPG doesn't rely on these things, it relies on writing, world-building, and the overall feel of the game.
This game IS good, don't let my review convince you otherwise. I was just let down because past games, in my opinion, have been so much better.
TLDR:
Good points: Romancing your companion, many different factions, building mechanism, interesting characters, graphics
Bad points: Writing, doesn't have a good feel, not as fluid, predetermined storyline, your son being named Shaun, lack of complex factions, the dialogue system.

Старбанунд - очень сырая игра, с очень малым обьемом и с очень низким качеством контента. За 10 часов дошел до последнего сектора и оделся по максимому. Встретил большую часть всех возможных встреч, нашел все технологии и 90% соцаильных айтемов. И это при том что не пользовался АБСОЛЮТНО никакими гайдами и вики. Только вечером сравнил с итогом и был неприятно удивлен. В Террарии контента гораздо больше. Это "творение" я прошел за один выходной. Случайный генератор вещей в игре - фигня. Все равно бегать будете с тем что сами сваяли, ибо это всегда лучше. В Террарии было что выбивать из боссов, из мобов, что искать, уникальных монстров за лут мутузить.Тут этого нет. Боссы в Старбаунде на 1 раз, убил скрафтил доступ в новый тир и забыл. Боевка убога. В Террарии были тринкеты от которых было много пользы и которые разнообразили тактики. Тут тактики нет априори. Да прикольно что есть много разных локаций, но толку от них если ничего там не спрятано, из мобов ничего не падает. Тут смысл игры - забуриться поглубже, так что бы мобы не прикапывались и накопать руды на доспехи.Планеты разные? Фигу - все одно и тоже, мобы перекрашены, трава перекрашена, пара других текстурок, а один фиг в одной и той же земле ковыряться и уникальности никакой нет. В Террарии есть привязка существ к биомам. В разных биомах разные вещи. Тут же - нигде ничего не найти, кроме руды - которая везде одинаковая. Тут 10 тиров то есть фактически 10 планет, все и то они различаются только рудой и силой монстров.Повторюсь осилил весь контент примерно за 10 часов. и отстаньте от Террарии, нельзя ее с этим хламом сравнивать.

I played Fallout 3 and New Vegas on console. Several times each, in fact. I never finished Fallout 4. Maybe that's all you need to know. If it isn't, let me continue.
I didn't get into the Fallout franchise until the release of Fallout 3. I played it whenever I could at my local college common area, and eventually got it at home.  When New Vegas came out, I got it immediately. I picked up a legacy collection that included Fallout 1, 2, and Brotherhood of Steel. All of these, save the last, were interesting RPGs, with plenty of meaningful choice.
Meaningful choice in Fallout 4 was apparently not part of the design document. Or, if it was, it was cut out. Skills are gone, and so is the branching storyline. You can be a good guy, a good guy who behaves like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, or a good guy who asks questions. Apparently this was good enough for Bethesda following after a game where you could have any one of several factions, including yourself, take control of an area, and all sorts of faction interplay. Factions return in Fallout 4, but all of them are happy to appoint you grand poobah regardless of your behavior.
The gunplay is... I suppose improved over Fallout 3/New Vegas. The crafting system, even with a few features like ammo crafting removed, is pretty robust. The settlement system seems misguided to me, but if you want to make a stronghold out of scrap, this will let you do it.

I havent played alot yet, but beleive me I INTEND to. I tend to ramble, an bounce around so ill leave the summary at the top.
TL:DR: This game is fantastic in the most grim, DIRE way imaginable.
Story: If your interested in Lovecraftian stories, tales of hopeless all-consuming darkness, then you've found the right game. The setup is pretty simple, and i havent really played far enough to see if it evolves any further in the grand canon. HOWEVER, there is undeniably a facinating story to be found in the moment to moment gameplay.
Examples: (In maybe my 2nd or 3rd quest one party member developed the "masochistic" trait. Later on, she is mortally wounded in a fight, when this happens you have a chance to heal them, but the next time they take damage theyre done. Before my healer gets a turn to bring her back around she cries "I welcome the hangmans noose!" and killed herself. im not even exaggeratting.) (Then there was the timei had completed the quest, but could see on the map another section to explore, we werent to bad off, and it was just one section so what could go wrong? 1 teammate died, the rest went insane and had to spend the next week drinking, praying, and fornicating respectivley. I FELT like such a greedy fool, the game didnt have to tell me in a cutscene.
Combat: Turn based RPGs arent my forte, so its hard for me to coment on this part. I tend to get frustrated when i miss, or sustain a critical hit as it feels like i couldnt have really dont anything about it. Ill give this game a pass on that solely because it fits really well with the aesthetic and tone. That being said, no huge insta-gib moves that ive seen so its not particularly offensive, but still the randomness is strong. Enemeis are distinct and varied, your character classes are fun and interesting. Game doesnt hide information from you, tells you your chance, how much dmg the hit might do, all the enemies resistances, its rlly nice. OH one key difference, POSITIONING! All moves have a required position in the party line up, and a required position for the enemy to be in (Denoted by a series of yellow and red dots respectivley). which makes assembling your party all the more interesting.
Systems: The sanity meter doesnt really feel as impactfull as id hoped, but some people may prefer that. Improving your town requires special recources, which is nice. Most stuff however is bought with gold, character improvements, recouperation, and most importantly supplies. supplies that vary from essential food and torches, to cure type items, and multiple "key" type items. There is visible depth even from the begining, and alot of hard choices on what to level and how to spend your resources.
Aesthetic: 11/10 the art is what initially grabbed me on the project, finally seeing more I must say it continues to impress. The systems also strengthen the tone of general madness, like with the second story example. Finally, and most importantly...THAT NARRATOR! Wayde June absolutley kills it with his performance, and all the lines are perfect. Every line had me smiling the widest cheshire cat grin, its just so satisfying.

If you are reading this the chances are you wanna know if you should buy this game. And in my opinion, when you get it on sale (the last one gave 66% off) without any DLCs, you get an
amount of value for a beautiful and immersive open-world FPS/RPG. As someone who likes immersion, crafting, time-unlimited exploring and creating personal bonds with custom weapons, this game was a 100% hit for me, although my final grade isn't 10/10. If you wanna know why, read on (zero spoilers, but with an extra "spoiler section" at the bottom).
I haven't played any earlier Fallout games, but from what I understand this game wouldn't deserve the "choices matter" tag as its predecessors do, so that's where RPG might not apply either in the eyes of some. But the skill development tree (the existence of which actually has an explanation, which I loved), individual relationship building with great voice acting and *sufficient* dialogue variety with complex emotions to consider and potential penalties make it very much an RPG in my view. Just...don't let the negative reviews ruin this experience for you if you're into the genre. These are people who had pre-conceived expectations.
This is a highly polished and graphically fairly well optimized game, which already qualifies it as an "AAA game". There is however some googling around and editing you might need to do (read: most likely) in the setting files to truly get the best and smoothest FPS for your machine, so obviously that's a minus. There are
of in-game mechanics, some of which have their flaws and will lead to frustration, but it's like when a pretty kitten blinks at you, what are you gonna do, say no? So this game is as pretty as a blue-eyed kitten, accept it and ignore that other thing you should be doing IRL.
(I wouldn't really weight them against the pros, they are just negatives worth mentioning):
A world of awesome things to do.

And finally, I'd just like to say I hope we're nearing an era where enemy respawning feels perfectly natural/there's a story-driven explanation for it. This game hit close, but we're not quite there. Just a dream of mine.

Another buffer....ok. Inventory is so badly managed. While there are some innovations on the matter, most of handling the inventory feels like typing in a fatality command on Mortal Kombat, and then you get that weapons spec you needed, have to exit, wait for an animation or two, then type in another another fatality. For an early access release, the game is also extremely fleshed out. Implemented systems work very well, which is crucial given the game being based around the psychological ramifications of what your dungeon-going party witnesses, and the stress accrued from fighting eldritch horrors.
All in all, this is highly recommended!

Pros
+Awesome Atmosphere: Everything from the art to the narration and sound design really sells the world this game takes place in. And by that I mean crushingly dark and oppressive but that makes each hard earned victory that much more worthwhile
+Huge Variety: There are a great amount of classes each with their own sets of abilities you can mix and match, plenty of horrifying monters that require different stragies (so far I have only seen one palette swap too) items that change how your characters play and of course all the inflictions your hero's get. These really change things up and make it interesting as you have to adapt and can create some silly emergent stories like my priest who was banned from the brothel and only like to gamble or my highwayman compelled to pray but was also a kleptomaniac. You never know what you're gonna get
+Satisfying and Thoughtful Combat: Hits feel really impactful and setting up a chain of abilities just right makes you feel like a tactial genius. The cool party order system makes you really consider how to set up the heros to get the most out of each one while also letting you mess with enemies by say pulling their mage to the front to be slaughtered by your barbarian
+Did I mention the absolutely gorgeous art?: Well I'm mentioning it again anyway. Seriously this style is perfect for the game and very impressive.
+So Much Replayability: All the gameplay aspects I mentioned above are randomly generated meaning you can keep going back and discovering new things.
Cons
-Its Hard: If you don't like punishing games this probably isn't for you. This game doesn't pull any punches and will do its best to brutally murder you. I personally don't mind but just a fair warning.
-Confusing At First: While the tutorials are very helpful not everything in the dungeon is explained thoroughly. It took me a couple runs to figure out how scouting worked (its automatic, I thought it was a button press I did accidentally and couldn't find it again) and some symbols on the map aren't explained so you kinda have to guess.
Those are really the only problems I had with this game and I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good turn based RPG and likes a challenge. Or anyone who enjoys a quality made game.

Darkest Dungeon casts a very XCOM-shaped shadow due to its high stakes, stressful gameplay, and combat-on-top-of-base-building structure. However, Darkest Dungeon keeps the concepts fresh and engaging thanks to its stylish emphasis on horror and desperation, and it's incredible looking art. Maybe you opted not to heal a party member during a turn when they were on death's door, or you neglected to bring a spade to shovel aside a massive pile of corpses. Darkest Dungeon uses RNG in the best way possible; to leave you fist pumping in relief one moment while second-guessing every choice you make right after.
I have experienced a couple of sudden crashes, but the frequent saving kept me from losing progress. Aside from some other potential balance issues and only a handful of classes to play as (a few more would be nice), there's very little here to indicate its "Early Access" moniker.

I havent played alot yet, but beleive me I INTEND to. I tend to ramble, an bounce around so ill leave the summary at the top.
TL:DR: This game is fantastic in the most grim, DIRE way imaginable.
Story: If your interested in Lovecraftian stories, tales of hopeless all-consuming darkness, then you've found the right game. The setup is pretty simple, and i havent really played far enough to see if it evolves any further in the grand canon. HOWEVER, there is undeniably a facinating story to be found in the moment to moment gameplay.
Examples: (In maybe my 2nd or 3rd quest one party member developed the "masochistic" trait. Later on, she is mortally wounded in a fight, when this happens you have a chance to heal them, but the next time they take damage theyre done. Before my healer gets a turn to bring her back around she cries "I welcome the hangmans noose!" and killed herself. im not even exaggeratting.) (Then there was the timei had completed the quest, but could see on the map another section to explore, we werent to bad off, and it was just one section so what could go wrong? 1 teammate died, the rest went insane and had to spend the next week drinking, praying, and fornicating respectivley. I FELT like such a greedy fool, the game didnt have to tell me in a cutscene.
Combat: Turn based RPGs arent my forte, so its hard for me to coment on this part. I tend to get frustrated when i miss, or sustain a critical hit as it feels like i couldnt have really dont anything about it. Ill give this game a pass on that solely because it fits really well with the aesthetic and tone. That being said, no huge insta-gib moves that ive seen so its not particularly offensive, but still the randomness is strong. Enemeis are distinct and varied, your character classes are fun and interesting. Game doesnt hide information from you, tells you your chance, how much dmg the hit might do, all the enemies resistances, its rlly nice. OH one key difference, POSITIONING! All moves have a required position in the party line up, and a required position for the enemy to be in (Denoted by a series of yellow and red dots respectivley). which makes assembling your party all the more interesting.
Systems: The sanity meter doesnt really feel as impactfull as id hoped, but some people may prefer that. Improving your town requires special recources, which is nice. Most stuff however is bought with gold, character improvements, recouperation, and most importantly supplies. supplies that vary from essential food and torches, to cure type items, and multiple "key" type items. There is visible depth even from the begining, and alot of hard choices on what to level and how to spend your resources.
Aesthetic: 11/10 the art is what initially grabbed me on the project, finally seeing more I must say it continues to impress. The systems also strengthen the tone of general madness, like with the second story example. Finally, and most importantly...THAT NARRATOR! Wayde June absolutley kills it with his performance, and all the lines are perfect. Every line had me smiling the widest cheshire cat grin, its just so satisfying.

Darkest Dungeon is a Roguelike Turn-based RPG. You must guide your team of heroes through the depths of your ancestral estate and combat the horrors the dwell within.
In it's current state, DD is a fun game. I enjoyed it so far. It's unforgiving though and a few things are, I feel, underexplained. That does lend to the depressing reality of the game. People will die.
The game features Health and Stress as the two major things you must manage. Health is self explainitory. You take damage, you lose it. You eat food, you recover it. Stress is more fluid though. What stresses each person out is different. Some heroes are stout and not very afraid and thus gain resistance to stress, others may be afraid of the dark and need you to keep the torches well lit while they're underground. Critical hits or overkill damage on enemies will rally your troops and give them a reduction of stress. Enemy attacks (more so for Criticals) will demoralize the receiver and even the party. The death of a party member will greatly effect the group too. Stuck underground with no food? Health loss and major stress. Prepare accordingly.
The game's battle system takes place on a 2D screen. Character's positions define what abilites they have available or what they can be hit with. Some characters are better suited to the front and some to the back but no where is safe. Combat is quick and brutal (often to you) with relevant stats displayed on the bottom half of the screen.
The art work and sound, narration in particular, is wonderful. The only slightly negative thing I can say is that the narrator talks A LOT but it's not overly annoying. I just hope that he doesn't run out of things to say five battles later.
Full Disclosure: I am a backer on Kickstater so that may skew my views.

Darkest Dungeon is a Roguelike Turn-based RPG. You must guide your team of heroes through the depths of your ancestral estate and combat the horrors the dwell within.
In it's current state, DD is a fun game. I enjoyed it so far. It's unforgiving though and a few things are, I feel, underexplained. That does lend to the depressing reality of the game. People will die.
The game features Health and Stress as the two major things you must manage. Health is self explainitory. You take damage, you lose it. You eat food, you recover it. Stress is more fluid though. What stresses each person out is different. Some heroes are stout and not very afraid and thus gain resistance to stress, others may be afraid of the dark and need you to keep the torches well lit while they're underground. Critical hits or overkill damage on enemies will rally your troops and give them a reduction of stress. Enemy attacks (more so for Criticals) will demoralize the receiver and even the party. The death of a party member will greatly effect the group too. Stuck underground with no food? Health loss and major stress. Prepare accordingly.
The game's battle system takes place on a 2D screen. Character's positions define what abilites they have available or what they can be hit with. Some characters are better suited to the front and some to the back but no where is safe. Combat is quick and brutal (often to you) with relevant stats displayed on the bottom half of the screen.
The art work and sound, narration in particular, is wonderful. The only slightly negative thing I can say is that the narrator talks A LOT but it's not overly annoying. I just hope that he doesn't run out of things to say five battles later.
Full Disclosure: I am a backer on Kickstater so that may skew my views.

Do enjoy playing games that make you so STRESSED OUT to the point where you’ll go INSANE? Well, you can revel in your misery and pain on the pile of your dead adventurer corpses.
Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based roguelike that offers an immersive experience not suited for the weak-hearted. You control and manage a roster of adventurers seeking to find gold and glory in the depths of the Darkest Estate. But your adventurers are not your special type of heroes. No, they are mere humans: having a mortal body and a fragile mind. Their mental state is constantly tested as they battle against unspeakable horrors that threaten to end their existence. If left too stressed, their resolve is tested to see whether they are courageous and continue to fight with full strength, or become fearful and cower behind the backs of their allies.
WARNING: There is a very strong RNG element to this game
This game is does a fantastic job in immersing you into the world. From the soundtrack, to the artwork, and especially the narrator, you can feel the effects of every decision you make. There is a high difficulty curve and is extremely brutal to the player. You WILL lose someone, you WILL fail a quest, and your party WILL go insane. This is a game where you mustn’t lose heart in the face of a hopeless situation. The level of difficulty is very in-tune with the theme of the game. Learning to recognize a hopeless situation is key to your success.
The soundtrack is great. It fully immerses you in the town, the dungeon, and in combat. Every battle theme generates a form of intensity that really stresses how hard the encounters can be. The artwork is amazing contains little details that make the monsters look even more horrific. And the narrator quotes really adds a lot of flavor in every aspect of the game from describing each building to getting crit from a monster.
HIGHLY RECOMMEND 10/10

Fallout 4 is not a good RPG. It's not a good "Fallout" game. It is, however, a good "Kill things and look at cool places" game.
Fallout 4 feels more like Far Cry 3 with dungeons than it does Fallout New Vegas, but when you view it as a game that meant to do that it's actually pretty great in a lot of ways. Instead of just clearing out base after base with a silenced sniper rifle from half a mile away, you explore interesting buildings and areas that have (ever so slightly) more enemy types than just guys with guns and interesting stories to make them feel like real places. The story kind of sucks and all of the quests, both main and side quests, are pretty underwhelming and only realy serve to make you go find a place and kill the things in it. If thats what you're expecting, though, it's not all that bad.
If I want to play an interesting RPG experience I'll sink a few more weeks of my life into Pillars of Eternity or The Witcher 3 or Neverwinter Nights or Baulders Gate or Fallout 1 / 2, but I'm happy messing around in Fallout 4 as it is. Honestly, why would you even expect an in-depth RPG from Bethesda at this point anyways? Bethesda games are basically their own genre at this point, and if you don't like Bethesda games you probably won't like Fallout 4. Fallout 4 is a game for filthy casuals and that's totally fine by me.

I'm pretty pleased with this game, and I'm glad I helped Kickstart it. So far, the environments and atmosphere are everything the developer promised: Dark, tense dungeons; edgy and unusual character classes, including unique spins on archetypal fantasy jobs like the paladin and cleric; a great soundtrack that enhances the eerie feel; and uncompromising, challenging gameplay.
I can say that this is the first "roguelike" I've genuinely gotten into. Normally, I'm a professional sore loser; I get attached to my characters (even nameless grunts in huge armies) and hate when they meet with misfortune. Darkest Dungeon gets that out of the way early on by telling you, straight up, "Here is a giant graveyard for the pile of dead adventurers you will slowly accrue." No words are minced regarding the survivability of the party, and you're subtly encouraged to become emotionally invested in the story, as opposed to the somewhat disposable "heroes." In another game, I might call this a flaw, but Darkest Dungeon sells it.
The anxious, disheartened narrator follows you throughout the opening cinematics and into the dungeons, themselves, commentating upon your party's performance in a way that makes your failures seem important and your victories exceptional. The way his voice lifts slightly in response to describing a critical hit or a moment of particularly heroic resilience is a small detail, but one that serves to simultaneously remind you that this is a dark story, where flashes of light are precious, few, and often crucial to success. The banter and asides by the actual characters are pretty good, too, as they succumb to stress or act out their virtues and flaws.
Darkest Dungeon is a tough and demanding game with unforgiving combat, but that's what it's supposed to be. It plays very smoothly compared to a lot of early access games I've tested, and most of the crticisms I would express are minimal and restricted to balancing issues, rather than complaints about flavor or performance. On the hardware side of things, I DID have to go into my Nvidia control panel and force the game to run using my Nvidia GPU rather than the on-board Intel processor, even after I updated to the latest drivers, because it kept hanging up on the intro screen and crashing back to the desktop. Since I did that, however, it's run without a hitch.
I'm not 100% happy with the plague doctor hero, as the class abilities seem dismally weak in light of how tactical they are. It's also hard to get used to how crappy healing is (you can't use abilities outside of combat, so it's eating precious food, camping, or nothing) with an eye on how easy it is for characters to die, but that's a feature, not a bug; it just takes time for players like me to get into the right mindset. The only genuine bone I have to pick is that the virtues and flaws your characters develop at the end of a mission don't properly reflect the challenges they faced in the dungeon, and in fact seem kind of disappointingly random.
The spontaneous traits they can pick up as a result of on-the-spot exposure to dangers (or as a positive consequence of rallying against the odds) are a good fit, and accurately portray the circumstances: Suffering too many critical hits from undead foes, for instance, might cause a character to develop a phobia of the undead that reduces their accuracy against such enemies and causes their stress to increase more rapidly when battling against them. That's fine; but then, upon completing a quest, heroes might acquire traits like "kleptomaniac" or "beast slayer" that have absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with anything that happened during said quest. It makes the overall mechanic seem cheap and significantly less meaningful than it should be, considering that's a big part of how the game was advertised and a big part of what it was built on.
Overall, Darkest Dungeon is a great casual game that's fun to play alone or with the lights off. It has a few bugs to work out, but it's got a lot of promise, and it's already a game worth sinking a few hours into, even if it isn't perfect, yet.

** Review of game subject to change because it is early access. ** (1/30/2015)
The idea of Darkest Dungeon is genius, which is why I backed it on Kickstarter. You have a bunch of heroes going through random dungeons which tear them down both physically and mentally. The art is grim and dark, very much like Mike Mignola's work on Hellboy. The different classes are fun (Grave Robber, Jester, Leper, Crusader, etc.) are a nice change from your general wizard, rogue, knight (though they'll fill the same sort of roles). And the traits are pretty interesting. I don't remember all the names but I had one hero who loved dead bodies, another that talked to unheard voices in various lanugaged (including coding), and another who decided they didn't want to fight anymore and would pass every time it was their turn.
The game plays very well, especially being early access and I definitely think is worth youre money BUT not before some major balancing. And I'm really hoping the people at Red Hook make some changes because this game has so much potential for stealing hours of my life.
SHORT VERSION:
- game is poorly balanced
- too much grinding
- some unintuitive design choices
IN DEPTH
- The upgrade system is much like Rogue Legacy. You bring back money from your dungeon raids. However everything is far too expensive making a lot of your characters useless. More on that later
- You have to bring items with you into the dungeon. Food and torches are a must. However for the minimum amount, you're looking at about 1500 gold per run. And if you run into some bad luck, you're gonna be screwed for awhile on your next trip.
- stats system is never explained and is not very intuitive.
- While there are a lot of classes, there really isn't that big a difference between them. They all have ranged and melee attacks. Some have buffs, some have debuffs, but they all feel rather similiar, which is a shame.
- You can get new "heroes" after every dungeon. However by the end of their first dungeon, more than likely they will be riddled with either mental or physical ailments. Now this is part of the fun but to it costs about 1500 gold to heal someone of a single ailment or to bring their stress down. Early in the game you aren't going to have any money for that.
- A couple of upgrades don't actually do anything. At least the stats say they don't. I also had a skill up reduce the damage my hero did, but bring the damage window (possibility of lowest and highest amount of damage) just 1 closer. So not really worth it because of the huge gap
- There are ways to buff your heroes sanity, but your heroes will be losing sanity at such a constant rate, it's not worth it at all. We're talking you buff for 4 on a character (using that heroes turn) only to have an enemy land a hit and cause a hero to lose 28 sanity, and 14 to those around them. And that's one attack
- You don't know the turn order of attacking. So less strategy
- The heroes talk all the time, adding some flavor text, which is fun. HOWEVER, the game stops when they do. So you're walking, you have to stop and listen. You're fighting, you have to stop and listen. And they are REALLY chatty. It ends up getting pretty frustrating because it breaks up the flow way too much, especially with all the grinding you'll be doing.
- When trying to pick heroes from the wagon, their speech bubbles will block the hero above them, making it impossible to pick the hero you wanted for a short while
- Various dungeons you can enter open and close for no forseeable reason. Want to play the randomly generated version of the first dungeon? Maybe you can, maybe you can't.
- The game is too much about grinding. It sells itself as being really hard. And it is but for all the wrong reasons. The Dark Souls games are hard but because they're very well designed to slow down the player and play cautiously, using your head. Darkest Dungeon right now is hard because all the numbers are off. Stuff is too expensive, damage is too varied, and stats might as well be in brale. (I had a hero who I think had an 80% accuracy but would hit maybe 30% of the time, with no debuffs). The game quickly feels like you're grinding through the dungeons (often without much success) to give yourself a better shot later off with very little payoff.
Again, I think the game at its core is great. But there needs to be some major balancing and a few design fixes to get it back on the right track of being an awesome game of seeing a group of heroes unravel and try to recover from the horrors they've seen in the dark below.
I look forward to seeing this game grow.

This used to be a positive review.  I've left the original review at the bottom.
I put about 55 hours into the game back when Early Access was initially released, last February and March.  The game was a lot of fun then, with a lot of room for improvement.
I left it alone for a number of months, and when I saw the recent Inhuman Bondage patch, I decided to check the game out again.  This is what I discovered:
Every ounce of fun and terror that was initially in this game has been wrung out, and replaced with tedium and more tedium.
"Tedious" is pretty much the only adjective I can come up with to describe the game, now.  It's too frustrating to be simply boring; it's too infuriating to be simply frustrating; and it's too boring to be simply infuriating.  A vicious cycle.
Many other reviewers have gone on and on about the particulars of the game's failings.  Let me just say that they are correct.  The words you'll find below, in my original review, are no longer true, which makes me very sad.
Don't buy this game.  Please.  Hopefully someone else will come along and make what this game should have been.
****ORIGINAL REVIEW*****
The Darkest Dungeon is an absolute success.
The game places the player in the position of managing an ever-growing (and occasionally shrinking) team of adventurers tasked with clearing out the player's ancestal estate of bandits, cultists, the undead, monsters, and eldritch horrors.  A wide array of classes are represented, each fulfilling a unique and useful role.  On top of managing the battles and dungeon exploration, the player must see to the emotional/psychological needs of his or her roster of adventurers.
As your adventuring parties explore and accomplish quests, additional quests are opened, as are opportunities to improve the estate's town, where adventurers can be upgraded, trained, and given treatments for the stresses of having come face to face with their own mortality, not to mention the unspeakable terrors that ever await them below.
The game does a fantastic job of representing all of the above, and is balanced to perfection.  It's rare that a quest is accomplished with ease -- the game walks a fine line of making it seem as though failure is always a hairsbreadth away.  Similarly -- and crucially -- victories are typically earned by the skin of one's teeth.
The most important praise I think I can give to the game is that while some failures are almost inevitable, in no way is there a danger of spiraling into a an inescapable cycle of loss after loss, as one might find in a game like Xcom:  Enemy Unknown.  The game is hard, but it's never unwinnable.
I recommend The Darkest Dungeon without reservation.

Bethesda has pretty much ruined modding with the Creation Club. How you might ask. It's quite simple. For those who use mods from the Nexus, many of those mods rely on F4SE (Fallout 4 Script Extender) to run. However, each time some new Creation Club content comes around the game has to be updated. This in turn screws up F4SE and makes it impossible to run properly. It can also lead to some mods breaking your game because it doesn't work right. If you already own Fallout 4 and it never recieved the first Creation Club update, do not let the game update. Just use the script extender to launch the game whether you're doing a modded playthrough or not and set the game to only update when you try to play it. If you're using the script extender to launch the game, it shouldn't update.

The immersion of this game is friggin' fantastic.
Everything in this game fits together so well: the music, the atmosphere, the action... It all works together. That cinematic trailer for Darkest Dungeon? It really captures exactly how the game feels.
In combat, the music is tense, and the camera zooms into attacks for effect. It's very quick, so no time is wasted, but it makes every attack feel exciting and apprehensive. There is a narrator that really pumps up the excitement as well, commending a crit or a kill... or a loss. When your stress limit hits 100%, the hero's resolve is tested... and there's a brief pause... will he become Courageous and rally his comrades? Or will he become Hopeless and become the doom of everyone?
Town mechanics are pretty neat too. You upgrade the town facilities using these items you collect from your adventures, but you upgrade/fix your heroes using the gold you have accrued. This separation of resources is nice, because it lets you focus your gold on party management.
Party management is pretty nifty but simple. Between adventures in dungeons, you can put various party members in the tavern or abbey to relieve the stress they have added up through adventuring. You can also slowly eliminate negative afflictions that your heroes have.
The game's main gimmick is "Stress". As your heroes fight in the dungeons, they will become stressed after witnessing unsettling things or taking critical hits or being debuffed by the enemy. The higher one hero's stress is, the more susceptible he/she is to the enemy's attacks. This can also trigger the hero's quirks (ex. Stress > 50: -2 Speed). At 100% stress, "The Hero's Resolve Will Be Tested". When this happens, RNG will happen to see if your hero can overcome this or not. It's quite epic to see your hero get a perk out of it and display his/her heroism. It also feels incredibly hope-shattering to see them become 'Hopeless' or 'Abusive'.
In addition to "Stress", there are also "Quirks". Each hero can have good quirks (perks) and bad quirks (afflictions). These are permanent attributes to a hero, and there are ALOT! There are several ways that a hero can earn a quirk. At the end of a dungeon, there is a chance for a hero to earn one. During a dungeon the hero may learn something from a book or an altar. Quirks include things like "Slugger", "Evasive", "Slayer of Eldritch" or "Syphilis", "Creeping Cough", "Deviant Tastes". You can even get quirks in town!. For example, your hero enjoyed meditation so much that they gain the "Meditator" perk which makes meditating more effective. Or perhaps they went to the bar to relieve stress but earned the affliction of "Tippler", making alcohol their only method of stress relief. There is a building in town that lets the player pay gold to rid afflictions one at a time, but it will cost gold and put the hero out of commission for one adventure.
The last gimmick of the game is the in the Dungeons. There is a light meter that continually drains as you make progress in the dungeon. The darker the dungeon is, the more dangerous and stressful it becomes (but more rewarding as well!). Before you enter the dungeon, you will buy and bring provisions with you such as food (to heal or feed your party when they get hungry) or torches (to increase the light meter as you consume them) or other misc items like shovels and bandages.
As of this review, the game has a few bugs, some more noticable than others. Notably there are bugs regarding gold and text. It's relatively stable in my experience. I had two crashes on Day One but have not had one since. There are a few questionable balance decisions that are being pointed out in the forums, and hopefully they will be weighed and addressed. Definitely feels like it's in beta, but it's very playable in it's current state and it's lots of fun. I can only imagine how this game will look once it leaves Early Access. I have high hopes here!
There's also this thing that people are butthurt about, and it's a kickstarter exclusive class. Though I am a kickstarter, I was not in the donation level to get it. I have no idea what it is and I totally forgot there was one. The game as-is is awesome, and the lack of one class was not detrimental to my experience. Might be the principle of the matter I guess, but I can say at least that this game is not broken without it.

This game is utterly fantastic, and I am super happy that I backed it when it came out. Let me start off by saying the devs are extremely responsive and constantly show up in the forums. Which is a huge plus, especially for an early access game. They listen to our feedback, and are quick to fix issues within the game. Just wanted throw a kudos to Red Hook. Y'all are awesome.
On to the game now. The game is extremely high risk/high reward. Your team is low, but you've got one room left and you'll finish the quest. Do you risk it and attempt to see if the room is clear/fight the battle, or do you haul it back to town with your team in-tact and the treasure you've collected so far? There are interactable objects that can also save your run, or set you back which adds a lot to do while crawling through the dungeons. The game is extremely difficult, but in the best possible way.
Starting off you're going to die, a lot. Until you learn the mechanics, learn how to build a balanced team for each dungeon. Learn how the abilities work and function. You will die, but that's ok. In Darkest Dungeon every death is a new lesson. The variety of heroes we've been given is pretty vast so far including the Grave Robber, Vestal, Occultist, Crusader, Highwayman, Hellion, Jester, and Leper. All of them work differentlky and do their jobs well.
A tag you won't see on this game that is a major part of it is, Puzzle. Every fight is a puzzle of sorts, especially boss fights. They all have weaknesses and different attacks/combinations that mess up the enemies momentum and attacks. Got a dude sniping you from the back? Use Eldritch Pull to yank him to the front and knock him out. Got a Plague Doctor? Use Flash Powder to stun the back line while you eat their beefy front line leaving them open.
There is so many to go through a dungeon and it's just an all-around fantastic game. The community is very helpful and we're all learning and helping each out. If you're into difficult, but rewarding games with a dark atmosphere, and Cthulhu/Eldritch creatures, then Darkest Dungeon is the game for you.

What is Darkest Dungeon ?
Its like XCOM meets the Roguelike genre in a Lovecraftian setting, low fantasy with a very Gothic and dark wibe in it,
you are in control of a small town under the shadow of a grim mansion built above the ruins of a portal linked to the universe of everything that is awful and unspeakable.
Everything is out for blood and wants to kill you, so you will soon recruit some Mercenaries and use them to reclaim your Estate, but here's the fun part :
What happens when your "heroes" stop being what they are and freak out ? this game does a goob job narrating how pricy the psychological toll is on your adventurers, the "Affliction" system present in the game will give your characters a personality which is always on the verge of instability, that mutates to a full fledged psychosis that refuses to answer your orders and direction.
You'll get to explore 5 different dungeons with multiple themed monsters, objects to interact with, Bosses and Quests which will grant you huge reward at the expense of your Soldiers life, which are irreversible because of the Permadeath system.
This game is mad fun.

This game is very clearly unfinished, but it shows a lot of potential. My biggest gripe at the moment is that, after 8 hours of gameplay with two people working toward common goals, my friend and I are still fighting with bows and swords, wearing medieval plate-mail, and gathering resources with pickaxes. That's not to say it isn't fun, but it doesn't really feel like science fiction. Replace the spaceship with a giant eagle and you might as well be in Middle Earth. I feel it would be greatly improved by giving you acces to futuristic technology much sooner. The NPCs all have laser rifles and power armor, so why can't I? Even if I can't craft it (which is reasonable, given the circumstances), at least let me loot some of it off them so I get an inkling of the fact that I'm playing a space game.
Now that that's over with, let me just say that the rest of the game is spectacular. The way each planet has its own randomly-generated biome colors and alien species makes it really feel like you're in a different world every time. The hunger mechanic is nothing new, but the addition of warmth into the mix adds an extra level of difficulty. The building control is much more intuitive than Terraria's, as it's simply left click to build in the foreground and right click for the background, instead of having to convert them by crafting. The music is excellent, and there's enough of it that you don't get stuck with the same track over and over. The semi-pixellated art style is interesting in the way the background has a higher resolution than the foreground, but it's not unattractive.
Overall, it's a very promising game, but it needs some work. Were it a full release, I'd be pretty annoyed about the slow start. SInce it's in beta, however, I'll withhold my judgement in the hopes that the problems get ironed out.

Bethesda has pretty much ruined modding with the Creation Club. How you might ask. It's quite simple. For those who use mods from the Nexus, many of those mods rely on F4SE (Fallout 4 Script Extender) to run. However, each time some new Creation Club content comes around the game has to be updated. This in turn screws up F4SE and makes it impossible to run properly. It can also lead to some mods breaking your game because it doesn't work right. If you already own Fallout 4 and it never recieved the first Creation Club update, do not let the game update. Just use the script extender to launch the game whether you're doing a modded playthrough or not and set the game to only update when you try to play it. If you're using the script extender to launch the game, it shouldn't update.
For those who don't care about mods that rely on F4SE:
Honestly if you liked Fallout 3 even remotely, then you'll like this one. It's better than 3, though not by much. Unless you like building up settlements that aren't all that useful or meaningful. Howver if what I've said isn't enough for you to want to play it, then you can pass this game up. Mods have certainly made this game a whole lot better, but if you're not going to play with mods, this game has a pretty lack luster story and most of the dlcs are like expansion packs for the settlement system. Combat in this game is certainly faster than Fallout 3 and is one of its good points. However, it's still pretty slow paced, especially when using vats. Also if you have played Fallout 3 on at least hard difficulty, then I suggest stepping the difficulty to Very Hard or Survival if you truly want to have a challenge. Though I will admit that Very hard is really easy. Survival difficulty felt more like a chore despite the improvements made to it. Still if you loved Fallout 3, then Fallout 4 is a great game. It just has a bad story, but it is full of fun quests to do. Weapon crafting could've been better and the AI really needed some improvements. And if you're the explorer type, don't worry. There's plenty to explore. And if you add mods into the mix, it's even better. Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone who has played Fallout 3. Otherwise if you haven't, then play it for a little while or watch videos on YouTube. It's definitely the type of game that appeals to people who hardly care about the story and care more about the whacky gameplay.

Legitimate review. For my first fallout game it was pretty good. If people tell you New Vegas is better they aren't saying that FO4 is bad, its just not what they perceive as best.
-As an RPG the game does a♥♥♥♥♥♥job at storytelling, the player just answers yes in an assortment of ways and little choice is actually given. Perks aren't well explained at the beginning when choosing initial stats but are uncapped so  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯. Most Quests are "radiant" or whatever and are just snowclones of "Go to X and help Y by killing Z", there are a good number of properly written quest lines however. Another issue I have is that the sole survivor can join rivaling factions of the commonwealth (i.e. The Brotherhood & The Railroad) and none have any issues with siding with the enemy.
-As an FPS fallout 4 has great gun mechanics and diversity (barring nade spam from NPCs). My only beef is the scarcity of ammo as it requires the player use 5+ guns or rely a bit on melee(granted perks alleviate this and this increases diversity in fights).
-As a sandbox game the settlement system is pretty good and fits into the game nicely(should considering a good 30% of the base game revolves around settlements). If you played Hearthfire in Skyrim you can definetly see improvement from Bethesda.
I still had (and having) loads of fun building settlements and gibbing Raiders.
For me , the best game of 2016. :D

My biggest gripe at the moment is that, after 8 hours of gameplay with two people working toward common goals, my friend and I are still fighting with bows and swords, wearing medieval plate-mail, and gathering resources with pickaxes. That's not to say it isn't fun, but it doesn't really feel like science fiction. Replace the spaceship with a giant eagle and you might as well be in Middle Earth. I feel it would be greatly improved by giving you acces to futuristic technology much sooner. The NPCs all have laser rifles and power armor, so why can't I? Even if I can't craft it (which is reasonable, given the circumstances), at least let me loot some of it off them so I get an inkling of the fact that I'm playing a space game.
Now that that's over with, let me just say that the rest of the game is spectacular. The way each planet has its own randomly-generated biome colors and alien species makes it really feel like you're in a different world every time. The hunger mechanic is nothing new, but the addition of warmth into the mix adds an extra level of difficulty. The building control is much more intuitive than Terraria's, as it's simply left click to build in the foreground and right click for the background, instead of having to convert them by crafting. The music is excellent, and there's enough of it that you don't get stuck with the same track over and over. The semi-pixellated art style is interesting in the way the background has a higher resolution than the foreground, but it's not unattractive.
Overall, it's a very promising game, but it needs some work. Were it a full release, I'd be pretty annoyed about the slow start. SInce it's in beta, however, I'll withhold my judgement in the hopes that the problems get ironed out.

Solid, incredibly hard, but not unfair, and very addicting. Combat is rarely a cakewalk, and you need to be calculating in your choice of classes, their positions, their moves, and targeting. The current classes are pretty varied, but ultimately boil down to melee DPS/tanks, ranged, and support/healer classes that you are used to. The classes are all very good in their own right, but their does definitely need to be some balancing done between them imo, as some classes are objectively better than others.
Currently melee classes like Leper, Bounty Hunter, and Crusader are far better than the others. They have high HP+DEF
do far more damage than any other class, so if it weren't for the fact most of their skills can only be used if they are in the first two positions, you'd just want to fill your ranks with them. Ranged DPS sucks for the most part, and the support classes really onli have very weak buffs/debuff, very low damage attacks, and/or very weak healing spells.
I don't think the melee should be nerfed entirely, but tanks shouldn't have high dmg output, and vice versa: DPS shouldn't be invincible. Ranged should have low DEF/HP, high damage instead of low HP/DEF and low damage, and support classes should have higher stats on their buffs, and at the very least, do better healing. Healing skills tend to be less than 50% of what a single enemy attack does, so there is almost never a point to using them atm. There are no HP potions, and food doesn't heal for♥♥♥♥♥♥ so something is definitely needed to allow some reasonable degree of healing without removing the games difficulty. Classes like Plague Doctor and Jester are currently not worth the slot they occupy atm, unless you have no other options for those back two slots.
That said, the framework and skills of the classes, even the ones I'm complaining about are honestly pretty wonderful, it's just a matter of changing some numbers around slightly, which I do hope happens. It is an Early Access game after all, so these kinds of things are to be expected, and expected to change over time as the final product takes shape. The gameplay tons of fun of even now, it's just frustrating sometimes when you're stuck with one or more party members that can't pull their weight at all.

Already there are many hours of content. I'm ten hours in and have barely scratched the surface. (A few bosses down, chars still lowish level, etc.). This is partially do to the game's difficulty, slow pace,high-ish (but not necessarily steep) learning curve, rate of progression, and the fairly large variety of classes and missions already available. The game (currently) definitely requires plenty of grinding, but that's pretty par for the course in the genre.
Characters very level slowly (if you can keep them alive in the first place). Upgrades (two kinds - overworld upgrades ala Rogue Legacy, and character skill/gear upgrades through gold) aren't terribly expensive, but much of your gold will be spent de-stressing characters and buying consumables before each dungeon so their isn't much left to spend on character skills/gear, and overworld upgrades are earned pretty slowly through completing dungeons.
You can also find random loot items in dungeons, or as a reward for completing certain dungeons. However, of the dozens of items I've found so far I've equipped exactly zero of them. Every item has a benefit (like +dmg) with a cost (-HP, for example), which is good, but currently it seems like every item I've found has, at best, marginally more COST than benefit, and more often than not, is more of a gimp than anything. These items definitely need some balancing as well imo to provide at least somewhat of a net benefit. The idea is already implemented and cool, it just needs some tweaking.
This game has lots of cool mechanics, however the two that make it unique are the stress mechanic and the light mechanic.
The stress mechanic is awesome and definitely makes sets the game apart, but it might be a little heavy. For most games, you will be lucky to get your characters through a single dungeon without at least one hitting 100% stress ("afflicted"). They then have to be relaxed in the overworld, which takes them out of rotation for a whole dungeon, and costs a significant amount of gold. Even if they don't hit 100% in the first one, you can almost never take them through a second dungeon back to back without relaxing them first, or they will quickly get to 100% in your next run, stressing out your other characters in the process, and often dooming the whole run.
This brings me to the light mechanic, which is really cool by itself. The higher the light, the better the chance to scout ahead between rooms, and the higher the chance to 'surprise' any enemies, causing them to skip their attack phase during the first round. Light is based on consumable torches. The light bar decreases as you progress, and you can use torches to replenish it. If you let light fade, you increase your stress levels, but also increase the loot. Sounds cool, and it can be. However, because you get sooooo much stress in dungeons as it is right now, it's almost never wise to not just keep the light topped off, just to delay hitting that inevitable 100% stress level, so you don't really get to use it much.
You get stress walking (full light or not) you get stress from mob attacks (like 15+ stress per hit), traps, items, damage, and your other characters. If one char gets crit, HP down to "1", or hits 100% stress, guess what? The rest get tons of stress too. It adds up quick really quick, and a few bad hits in an early encounter in a dungeon can send the whole thing snowballing down quickly to the point you have no option but to retreat, abandon the dungeon, and lose any items/gold you had earned, plus now you'll have to send all 4 characters to 'relax' and pay thousands of gold for it. If stress were nerfed just a little bit, even in one area (like not getting random stress when walking at 100% light), then the light mechanic could be utilized a lot more.
That said, if it sounds like I'm bashing these mechanics or the game, I'm definitely not. I like them, and I'd definitely recommend the game to anyone who likes the genre, there's just some minor numbers that need to be changed for balance here and there. Or hell, maybe I'm just really bad and just need to L2P. Either way, I wouldn't change a single thing about the functionality of the mechanics or game itself, just tweak the balance a bit

I originally wrote a preview of this game, since it just hit early access, but it could easily serve as a review of sorts for now, so here is a shortened version of it:
Fear, stress and darkness is what Darkest Dungeon is all about. This dungeon crawling RPG throws you at a gothic world filled with lovecraftian horrors, human-made abominations, and an encroaching darkness that seeks to rip the glow out of your perishable heroes. Heroes that are molded by eldritch horrors, the scolding or praise of their allies, and the struggles of each adventure.
Camping image:
Like the hardest of RPGs, Darkest Dungeon seeks to defeat you at every turn in several very challenging, and punishing, ways. However, it is done in a way that makes a successful run feel so much sweeter and satisfying. Much like the Souls series, Darkest Dungeon’s difficulty level slaps the confidence out of you and throws you into the dirt as your heroes scream insults at each other instead of focusing on the crazed cultist who calls upon dark incantations or the bloodthirsty monstrosity that reaches out to rend them asunder, but rewards you greatly as you learn how to manage each demoralizing event or the most ruthless of battles. Your knowledge will grow as your heroes’ resolve (level) will mold them into fearsome adventurers.
At the start all you have is two measly two heroes, a crusader and a scoundrel, who come to a decrepit hamlet that has but one building standing and a travelling stage coach that provides fresh adventurers. The crusader, seemingly, was called there to restore and save his family's town, and their estate, which was lost to cultist’s, monsters and unfathomable entities that do not belong in the world. As you take the party from two heroes to over a dozen you also restore the hamlet to its former glory, which will continually provide more and more useful services to your heroes, and all of that is done by sending your heroes on randomized and dangerous adventures of varying length, difficulty, objectives and environments.
Plague doctor character sheet:
Each dungeon run consists of you taking four party members through a number of questionably perilous rooms, which you know nothing about at the start, and the unfriendly corridors in between them. As you travel between each room you might find loot, a group of enemies, traps, obstacles, or a wide variety of unique objects, like an alchemy table that might make your crusader fearful but could inspire your Occultist or even teach him something new. Your heroes can be torn down slowly by damage over time effects, like blight or bleeding, and it will whittle down their health, but more importantly they constantly fight against stress.
One of the most important, and challenging, aspects of Darkest Dungeon is stress. Each hero can only take one hundred points of stress and then their resolve will be tested, which will usually give them an affliction (which can only be removed at the hamlet) or if you are very lucky a boon. Afflictions create a lovely snowballing effect that will possibly make you mutter obscenities under your breath. Each affliction is different, but they are all terrible in their own ways. For instance, masochism, one of the weirder ones, will make a hero yearn to be hit by enemies and when he or she is hit, they will then make comments about it that will stress out the other party members. Furthermore, any affliction, on top of it causing unspeakable amounts of stress to other party members, can also make that party member disobey your commands and act on their own, especially with afflictions like selfish or fearful.
Critical hit gif:
Imagine you’re having a tough fight with a group of monsters or cultists and it’s been a bit rough so far just because the enemies are doing more damage than you are dishing out or healing, and then an enemy gets a critical hit on your jester, who then freaks out, becomes selfish and decides to yell at any other party member whenever they hit anyone he wants to hit or whenever they miss an enemy. Having a full party of stressed out of heroes at max stress with afflictions is just so wonderfully frustrating that it makes you try so very hard to never let that happen again. It makes you scared to push your party further when they are so close to breaking or it makes you choose actions that might prioritize lowering stress instead of healing, even though a character with low health can be permanently killed if they drop to zero and are hit again afterwards (before being healed). It’s a lovely and unique system that punishes you in cruel ways that are entirely avoidable and manage-able, but still very tough to deal with.
At its best, Darkest Dungeon feels like a seemingly abusive parent who seems cruel and uncaring, but in reality cares greatly about you and wants to mold you into someone formidable, knowledgeable and confident enough to come out on top of nearly any situation. Even in its unfinished early access state this RPG feels polished, deep and endearing. It is also filled with content, after ten hours of gameplay I’ve managed to take down two bosses, out of seven, and upgraded maybe thirty percent of the hamlet. The art is also lovingly designed to fit this bleak, dark and cruel world, and it really brings to life this lovecraftian setting.
Boss image:
Despite being so dark and harrowing, Darkest Dungeon is also charming and captivating, with characters that respond to most situations, whether it is an ally being hit by a trap, the torch fizzling out, or stories being told around a campfire, it all gives your heroes character and humanity, even when they act out in fear, anger or delusions. This is one of those games where just doing one more dungeon run will always be on your mind, especially after you get past the incredibly rough first dozen runs or so, and start to really learn how to endure, succeed and prosper. The voice of the haunted narrator will always be calling you back for just one more try.
