Massive open world to explore with alot of rich lore and detail to soak up!
Fallout 4 is another in a line of very fun wasteland exploration games and it certainly ranks as one of the best.
New players to the series may be a little overwhelmed by the possibilities in the game but once you break the ice and look into how things work and explore the wasteland the fun can be overwelming. Gameplay involves a first or third person view from/of your character, you can swap between this using once of the keys (all of my keys are custom bound so I wont get into them unless I am sure they are the default binding). Within this wasteland many weapons are availible to you and combining this with V.A.T.S. (a special targetting system) even those with bad aim can be skilled enough to survive. Using VATS you can slow down time and select a target on an enemy and attempt to kill them, of course depending on your skills and abilities you may miss but its alot more sure fire then just randomly firing off and hoping to hit. The weapons range from devistating Mini Nuke launchers (highly dangerous if you dont know how to use it) to assault rifles to shanks! The variety of weapons is glorious in matching your prefered play style. Speaking of which, Fallout 4 is very much a RPG as you can pick the role of wasteland saviour or apocolyptic killer and anywhere in between. Thus being an RPG you can build your character into what ever you like and match your armor and weapons to your build. The amount of items within this game is massive, letting your explore and collect alot of gear. Once you have a character set up, you can then start to build settlements with a new feature to the series. Settlement building is not manditory, you can play the game without doing any building besides very basic and vital things for some quests. These settlements can serve as player homes, trading hubs, or farms for materials/items. This layer of settlement building really adds more aspects to the game as you can start to build your legacy as a wasteland saviour! If you choose to do so of course.
I could go on and add alot more to my review however this may start to drag on and on so I will stop going to deep. Fallout 4 is a great exploration RPG with FPS elements within it. If your a skilled shooter, you will enjoy playing the game without ever using the VATS mechanic, if your not so accurate with your aim, VATS is there to help you! If you want to build towns and help settlers survive the wasteland, go ahead and build settlements! If you enjoy games with rich lore and alot of stuff to do! Then Fallout 4 is right for you!
I highly recommend it based off of the large amount of quests, items, weapons, armor, and much more to do, collect, and see. Im at 285 hours played on Fallout 4 and thats only on the PC, I have this game on the PS4 and cant get enough of it! And before I finish my review I must mention that on the PC edition you can mod your game with a large assortment of mods further adding more gameplay and abilities!
Pick this game up for your collection, you should not be dissapointed, but of course look at some videos and decide for yourself.

Kickstarter backer, have killed my weekend playing this since I got an early copy. If it looks at all interesting to you, it will be. If these guys don't win a few awards this year for coming up with an original machanic that adds a ton of stressful fun to the classic party based dungeon crawl then I quit the Internet!
Tips from someone who is just barely doing OK after a few hours in:
-Your party is going to break and go insane. It WILL happen, especially in the early stages of the game. Don't sweat it, roll with it. After a few runs you'll be able to unlock a few ways for them to calm down and remove negative traits in town, and until then you can hire a few fresh rookies who have no idea what they're in for and let the maniacs rest a bit.
-First thing you'll want to start upgrading is the carriage that brings new folks to town. You're going to lose people, and the ones who come back will need a break. Having a larger selection of folks in reserve and more coming in at a time is a huge benefit.
-If you're struggling in a dungeon and can't seem to keep the party alive, consider running from battles and ending the mission early. Sure, you'll only take back a small portion of the loot, but your people will still gain some experience, and will live to go insane another day.
-The game recomends 8 food and 5 torches early on. Screw that. Bring extra food and at least 1 more torch then you think you'll use, especially with an inexperienced party. Starving is no fun, you can use any spare food to bring people back from "Death's Door", and the worst feeling is having 3 more rooms to go with a barely scraping by party in total darkness because you wanted to save 150 gold.
-Stuns are the most powerful moves to have going for you. Especially when so many moves can stun AND cause damage.
-The most dangerous enemies are probably in the back rows, with crazy full party shotgun blasts or super stress-inducing goblets of wine to toss. Use a bounty hunter to pull them to the front, or some long-range attaks to take them out ASAP. The big beefy guys in front are usually not so hot at causing actual damage and take a long time to kill.

Never before have I loved a game that hated me so much.  You can check out my impression/gameplay in video form below or read on!
Darkest Dungeon is that will very likely be described as a 2D, turn-based, Dark Souls and that description isn't entirely inaccurate, albeit cliché.  Darkest Dungeon is a game that asks a lot of you and very specifically warns you of this before you start playing.  Without going into too many details, the backdrop for the game seems to take inspiration from Lovecraftian horror and that is a strong focus on how the game plays out.
There are two main aspects of the game: Dungeon exploration with combat and Party management.  Managing your party becomes as important, if not more important, than your performance in combat.
Your estate is comprised of a number of buildings that unlock as you progress through the game.  All of these buildings can be upgraded and perform variation functions: Recruiting new party members, relieving party member stress, upgrading equipment, training skills, and so on.  The money and loot you receive from dungeon exploring can be applied directly into upgrading these buildings and building up your party.
Dungeon crawling takes place in randomly generated dungeons in one of four major locations.  Each dungeon comes with an overall objective for success, though you're able to leave at anytime (though at the cost of party stress).  Before entering a dungeon you choose a party of 4 and purchase supplies, then it's off into the madness.
Dungeons are explored on a 2D plane, room by room, hallway by hallway.  Along the way you'll find combat, treasure, and objects to interact with.  Each of these will affect your party in a variety of ways.
The real meat of the game comes in managing your party both in and out of combat.  Characters are allowed to take 4 active skills into combat (up to 7 total which can be switched out anytime outside of combat), each skill has positional requirements for both party placement and targeting.  Additionally, all characters have a set of quirks and traits that they acquire as they grow, with positive and negative effects.  As characters engage in combat and explore the dungeon they become further and further stressed out.  Once their stress reaches a max level  they have a chance to either rise to the occasion, or essentially go insane ('Afflicted' as the game calls it).  These effects can range from bolstering performance and encouraging party members, to acting on their own and causing other party members to follow them down the path of insanity.  Oh and characters can all be renamed, adding a little more of personalization to your doomed heroes.
All of these systems work together to create a wonderfully atmospheric and engaging experience.  Luck is rarely on your side, but careful management of resources will lead to success.  Knowing when to run and when to press on, what sacrifices to make, and how to manage the lingering insanity leads to challenging gameplay that is incredibly rewarding!

This is a very solid turn-based dungeon crawler with rogue-lite elements that keeps you coming back for more.

Solid, incredibly hard, but not unfair, and very addicting. Combat is rarely a cakewalk, and you need to be calculating in your choice of classes, their positions, their moves, and targeting. The current classes are pretty varied, but ultimately boil down to melee DPS/tanks, ranged, and support/healer classes that you are used to. The classes are all very good in their own right, but their does definitely need to be some balancing done between them imo, as some classes are objectively better than others.
Currently melee classes like Leper, Bounty Hunter, and Crusader are far better than the others. They have high HP+DEF
do far more damage than any other class, so if it weren't for the fact most of their skills can only be used if they are in the first two positions, you'd just want to fill your ranks with them. Ranged DPS sucks for the most part, and the support classes really onli have very weak buffs/debuff, very low damage attacks, and/or very weak healing spells.
I don't think the melee should be nerfed entirely, but tanks shouldn't have high dmg output, and vice versa: DPS shouldn't be invincible. Ranged should have low DEF/HP, high damage instead of low HP/DEF and low damage, and support classes should have higher stats on their buffs, and at the very least, do better healing. Healing skills tend to be less than 50% of what a single enemy attack does, so there is almost never a point to using them atm. There are no HP potions, and food doesn't heal for♥♥♥♥♥♥ so something is definitely needed to allow some reasonable degree of healing without removing the games difficulty. Classes like Plague Doctor and Jester are currently not worth the slot they occupy atm, unless you have no other options for those back two slots.
That said, the framework and skills of the classes, even the ones I'm complaining about are honestly pretty wonderful, it's just a matter of changing some numbers around slightly, which I do hope happens. It is an Early Access game after all, so these kinds of things are to be expected, and expected to change over time as the final product takes shape. The gameplay tons of fun of even now, it's just frustrating sometimes when you're stuck with one or more party members that can't pull their weight at all.

Already there are many hours of content. I'm ten hours in and have barely scratched the surface. (A few bosses down, chars still lowish level, etc.). This is partially do to the game's difficulty, slow pace,high-ish (but not necessarily steep) learning curve, rate of progression, and the fairly large variety of classes and missions already available. The game (currently) definitely requires plenty of grinding, but that's pretty par for the course in the genre.
Characters very level slowly (if you can keep them alive in the first place). Upgrades (two kinds - overworld upgrades ala Rogue Legacy, and character skill/gear upgrades through gold) aren't terribly expensive, but much of your gold will be spent de-stressing characters and buying consumables before each dungeon so their isn't much left to spend on character skills/gear, and overworld upgrades are earned pretty slowly through completing dungeons.
You can also find random loot items in dungeons, or as a reward for completing certain dungeons. However, of the dozens of items I've found so far I've equipped exactly zero of them. Every item has a benefit (like +dmg) with a cost (-HP, for example), which is good, but currently it seems like every item I've found has, at best, marginally more COST than benefit, and more often than not, is more of a gimp than anything. These items definitely need some balancing as well imo to provide at least somewhat of a net benefit. The idea is already implemented and cool, it just needs some tweaking.
This game has lots of cool mechanics, however the two that make it unique are the stress mechanic and the light mechanic.
The stress mechanic is awesome and definitely makes sets the game apart, but it might be a little heavy. For most games, you will be lucky to get your characters through a single dungeon without at least one hitting 100% stress ("afflicted"). They then have to be relaxed in the overworld, which takes them out of rotation for a whole dungeon, and costs a significant amount of gold. Even if they don't hit 100% in the first one, you can almost never take them through a second dungeon back to back without relaxing them first, or they will quickly get to 100% in your next run, stressing out your other characters in the process, and often dooming the whole run.
This brings me to the light mechanic, which is really cool by itself. The higher the light, the better the chance to scout ahead between rooms, and the higher the chance to 'surprise' any enemies, causing them to skip their attack phase during the first round. Light is based on consumable torches. The light bar decreases as you progress, and you can use torches to replenish it. If you let light fade, you increase your stress levels, but also increase the loot. Sounds cool, and it can be. However, because you get sooooo much stress in dungeons as it is right now, it's almost never wise to not just keep the light topped off, just to delay hitting that inevitable 100% stress level, so you don't really get to use it much.
You get stress walking (full light or not) you get stress from mob attacks (like 15+ stress per hit), traps, items, damage, and your other characters. If one char gets crit, HP down to "1", or hits 100% stress, guess what? The rest get tons of stress too. It adds up quick really quick, and a few bad hits in an early encounter in a dungeon can send the whole thing snowballing down quickly to the point you have no option but to retreat, abandon the dungeon, and lose any items/gold you had earned, plus now you'll have to send all 4 characters to 'relax' and pay thousands of gold for it. If stress were nerfed just a little bit, even in one area (like not getting random stress when walking at 100% light), then the light mechanic could be utilized a lot more.
That said, if it sounds like I'm bashing these mechanics or the game, I'm definitely not. I like them, and I'd definitely recommend the game to anyone who likes the genre, there's just some minor numbers that need to be changed for balance here and there. Or hell, maybe I'm just really bad and just need to L2P. Either way, I wouldn't change a single thing about the functionality of the mechanics or game itself, just tweak the balance a bit

I originally wrote a preview of this game, since it just hit early access, but it could easily serve as a review of sorts for now, so here is a shortened version of it:
Fear, stress and darkness is what Darkest Dungeon is all about. This dungeon crawling RPG throws you at a gothic world filled with lovecraftian horrors, human-made abominations, and an encroaching darkness that seeks to rip the glow out of your perishable heroes. Heroes that are molded by eldritch horrors, the scolding or praise of their allies, and the struggles of each adventure.
Camping image:
Like the hardest of RPGs, Darkest Dungeon seeks to defeat you at every turn in several very challenging, and punishing, ways. However, it is done in a way that makes a successful run feel so much sweeter and satisfying. Much like the Souls series, Darkest Dungeon’s difficulty level slaps the confidence out of you and throws you into the dirt as your heroes scream insults at each other instead of focusing on the crazed cultist who calls upon dark incantations or the bloodthirsty monstrosity that reaches out to rend them asunder, but rewards you greatly as you learn how to manage each demoralizing event or the most ruthless of battles. Your knowledge will grow as your heroes’ resolve (level) will mold them into fearsome adventurers.
At the start all you have is two measly two heroes, a crusader and a scoundrel, who come to a decrepit hamlet that has but one building standing and a travelling stage coach that provides fresh adventurers. The crusader, seemingly, was called there to restore and save his family's town, and their estate, which was lost to cultist’s, monsters and unfathomable entities that do not belong in the world. As you take the party from two heroes to over a dozen you also restore the hamlet to its former glory, which will continually provide more and more useful services to your heroes, and all of that is done by sending your heroes on randomized and dangerous adventures of varying length, difficulty, objectives and environments.
Plague doctor character sheet:
Each dungeon run consists of you taking four party members through a number of questionably perilous rooms, which you know nothing about at the start, and the unfriendly corridors in between them. As you travel between each room you might find loot, a group of enemies, traps, obstacles, or a wide variety of unique objects, like an alchemy table that might make your crusader fearful but could inspire your Occultist or even teach him something new. Your heroes can be torn down slowly by damage over time effects, like blight or bleeding, and it will whittle down their health, but more importantly they constantly fight against stress.
One of the most important, and challenging, aspects of Darkest Dungeon is stress. Each hero can only take one hundred points of stress and then their resolve will be tested, which will usually give them an affliction (which can only be removed at the hamlet) or if you are very lucky a boon. Afflictions create a lovely snowballing effect that will possibly make you mutter obscenities under your breath. Each affliction is different, but they are all terrible in their own ways. For instance, masochism, one of the weirder ones, will make a hero yearn to be hit by enemies and when he or she is hit, they will then make comments about it that will stress out the other party members. Furthermore, any affliction, on top of it causing unspeakable amounts of stress to other party members, can also make that party member disobey your commands and act on their own, especially with afflictions like selfish or fearful.
Critical hit gif:
Imagine you’re having a tough fight with a group of monsters or cultists and it’s been a bit rough so far just because the enemies are doing more damage than you are dishing out or healing, and then an enemy gets a critical hit on your jester, who then freaks out, becomes selfish and decides to yell at any other party member whenever they hit anyone he wants to hit or whenever they miss an enemy. Having a full party of stressed out of heroes at max stress with afflictions is just so wonderfully frustrating that it makes you try so very hard to never let that happen again. It makes you scared to push your party further when they are so close to breaking or it makes you choose actions that might prioritize lowering stress instead of healing, even though a character with low health can be permanently killed if they drop to zero and are hit again afterwards (before being healed). It’s a lovely and unique system that punishes you in cruel ways that are entirely avoidable and manage-able, but still very tough to deal with.
At its best, Darkest Dungeon feels like a seemingly abusive parent who seems cruel and uncaring, but in reality cares greatly about you and wants to mold you into someone formidable, knowledgeable and confident enough to come out on top of nearly any situation. Even in its unfinished early access state this RPG feels polished, deep and endearing. It is also filled with content, after ten hours of gameplay I’ve managed to take down two bosses, out of seven, and upgraded maybe thirty percent of the hamlet. The art is also lovingly designed to fit this bleak, dark and cruel world, and it really brings to life this lovecraftian setting.
Boss image:
Despite being so dark and harrowing, Darkest Dungeon is also charming and captivating, with characters that respond to most situations, whether it is an ally being hit by a trap, the torch fizzling out, or stories being told around a campfire, it all gives your heroes character and humanity, even when they act out in fear, anger or delusions. This is one of those games where just doing one more dungeon run will always be on your mind, especially after you get past the incredibly rough first dozen runs or so, and start to really learn how to endure, succeed and prosper. The voice of the haunted narrator will always be calling you back for just one more try.

Massive open world to explore with alot of rich lore and detail to soak up!
Fallout 4 is another in a line of very fun wasteland exploration games and it certainly ranks as one of the best.
New players to the series may be a little overwhelmed by the possibilities in the game but once you break the ice and look into how things work and explore the wasteland the fun can be overwelming. Gameplay involves a first or third person view from/of your character, you can swap between this using once of the keys (all of my keys are custom bound so I wont get into them unless I am sure they are the default binding). Within this wasteland many weapons are availible to you and combining this with V.A.T.S. (a special targetting system) even those with bad aim can be skilled enough to survive. Using VATS you can slow down time and select a target on an enemy and attempt to kill them, of course depending on your skills and abilities you may miss but its alot more sure fire then just randomly firing off and hoping to hit. The weapons range from devistating Mini Nuke launchers (highly dangerous if you dont know how to use it) to assault rifles to shanks! The variety of weapons is glorious in matching your prefered play style. Speaking of which, Fallout 4 is very much a RPG as you can pick the role of wasteland saviour or apocolyptic killer and anywhere in between. Thus being an RPG you can build your character into what ever you like and match your armor and weapons to your build. The amount of items within this game is massive, letting your explore and collect alot of gear. Once you have a character set up, you can then start to build settlements with a new feature to the series. Settlement building is not manditory, you can play the game without doing any building besides very basic and vital things for some quests. These settlements can serve as player homes, trading hubs, or farms for materials/items. This layer of settlement building really adds more aspects to the game as you can start to build your legacy as a wasteland saviour! If you choose to do so of course.
I could go on and add alot more to my review however this may start to drag on and on so I will stop going to deep. Fallout 4 is a great exploration RPG with FPS elements within it. If your a skilled shooter, you will enjoy playing the game without ever using the VATS mechanic, if your not so accurate with your aim, VATS is there to help you! If you want to build towns and help settlers survive the wasteland, go ahead and build settlements! If you enjoy games with rich lore and alot of stuff to do! Then Fallout 4 is right for you!
I highly recommend it based off of the large amount of quests, items, weapons, armor, and much more to do, collect, and see. Im at 285 hours played on Fallout 4 and thats only on the PC, I have this game on the PS4 and cant get enough of it! And before I finish my review I must mention that on the PC edition you can mod your game with a large assortment of mods further adding more gameplay and abilities!
Pick this game up for your collection, you should not be dissapointed, but of course look at some videos and decide for yourself.

Each dungeon run consists of you taking four party members through a number of questionably perilous rooms, which you know nothing about at the start, and the unfriendly corridors in between them. As you travel between each room you might find loot, a group of enemies, traps, obstacles, or a wide variety of unique objects, like an alchemy table that might make your crusader fearful but could inspire your Occultist or even teach him something new. Your heroes can be torn down slowly by damage over time effects, like blight or bleeding, and it will whittle down their health, but more importantly they constantly fight against stress.
One of the most important, and challenging, aspects of Darkest Dungeon is stress. Each hero can only take one hundred points of stress and then their resolve will be tested, which will usually give them an affliction (which can only be removed at the hamlet) or if you are very lucky a boon. Afflictions create a lovely snowballing effect that will possibly make you mutter obscenities under your breath. Each affliction is different, but they are all terrible in their own ways. For instance, masochism, one of the weirder ones, will make a hero yearn to be hit by enemies and when he or she is hit, they will then make comments about it that will stress out the other party members. Furthermore, any affliction, on top of it causing unspeakable amounts of stress to other party members, can also make that party member disobey your commands and act on their own, especially with afflictions like selfish or fearful.
Critical hit gif:
Imagine you’re having a tough fight with a group of monsters or cultists and it’s been a bit rough so far just because the enemies are doing more damage than you are dishing out or healing, and then an enemy gets a critical hit on your jester, who then freaks out, becomes selfish and decides to yell at any other party member whenever they hit anyone he wants to hit or whenever they miss an enemy. Having a full party of stressed out of heroes at max stress with afflictions is just so wonderfully frustrating that it makes you try so very hard to never let that happen again. It makes you scared to push your party further when they are so close to breaking or it makes you choose actions that might prioritize lowering stress instead of healing, even though a character with low health can be permanently killed if they drop to zero and are hit again afterwards (before being healed). It’s a lovely and unique system that punishes you in cruel ways that are entirely avoidable and manage-able, but still very tough to deal with.
At its best, Darkest Dungeon feels like a seemingly abusive parent who seems cruel and uncaring, but in reality cares greatly about you and wants to mold you into someone formidable, knowledgeable and confident enough to come out on top of nearly any situation. Even in its unfinished early access state this RPG feels polished, deep and endearing. It is also filled with content, after ten hours of gameplay I’ve managed to take down two bosses, out of seven, and upgraded maybe thirty percent of the hamlet. The art is also lovingly designed to fit this bleak, dark and cruel world, and it really brings to life this lovecraftian setting.
Boss image:
Despite being so dark and harrowing, Darkest Dungeon is also charming and captivating, with characters that respond to most situations, whether it is an ally being hit by a trap, the torch fizzling out, or stories being told around a campfire, it all gives your heroes character and humanity, even when they act out in fear, anger or delusions. This is one of those games where just doing one more dungeon run will always be on your mind, especially after you get past the incredibly rough first dozen runs or so, and start to really learn how to endure, succeed and prosper. The voice of the haunted narrator will always be calling you back for just one more try.

Those days will be remembered all throughout my adulthood and thats why this franchise means so much to me.
THE FALLOUT 4 CRAZE
Years follow after the release of Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas and there is no future Fallout game to be seen in sight, but then a website gets created generating tons of buzz on gaming news channels about the "countdown" of a new Fallout game, which was essentialy a plain black website with a vault tec symbol ontop of a countdown timer. though I didn't bye it, it did intriuge me and ignited my imagination on what a new Fallout game could actually be, "it could have better writing, cutting edge graphics and more options to tackle your problems", it truly pains me to say this but the final product sadly didn't acomplish my expectations.

After viewing the teaser and first gameplay trailer, I will admit I was foaming with anticipation and excitment. "The STORY,
the GAMEPLAY and the VISUALS!" I yell in shock, then the protagaonist speaks....."umm ok thats new to Fallout, but its new and adds to the game right....right.......". At that point I honestly didn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥if they gave dog meat a voice actor, all I said in my own mind was "Pre-order now, pre-order now, pre-order now", I was hypnotised by the hype and praise of this brand spanking new fallout game,just as the voices in my head demanded me to, I pre-ordered it on steam (Pipboy edition ran out)
THE MONTHS OF HYPE AND FANBOYISM
It was finally here, the game to beat all other games, forged by the godly high elf known as Todd Howard in the peak of mount dew.

I just want to say that I have had thousands of pleasant experiences with Bethesda and especially Fallout (New Vegas in particular if I have to specify it), there's a reason I've put hundreds of hours into these games. But I've had it with their policy of "Make something, hope it works as intended, release, wait for modders to fix the bugs for us" that their games have had for so many years.
Fallout 4 is an open-world, post-apocalyptic first/third-person shooter with RPG elements. You assume the role of your customizable Sole Survivor, the name being derived from the events of the prologue, searching through the ruins Commonwealth of Massachusetts (now known as just "The Commonwealth") for your missing son Shaun.
Throughout the game you visit a large variety of locations, from small farms to large abandoned military bases, making allies, killing enemies and gathering items and equipment to build an arsenal to fit your playstyle.
Pros:
Cons:
Now, I want to address the elephant in the room, the main reason why I decided to write this review: The previously mentioned bugs and glitches, as well as the poorly implemented settlement system.
To put it simply; If something has a chance to go wrong, it most likely will. Many imporant NPCs (such as Trader Rylee or other level 4 merchants) can bug out at the most inopportune times, locking you out of their services or unique rewards. This problem has been apparent in other games as well, such as Skyrim, Fallout 3, Oblivion. The last two have the excuse of being old games, but what's Skyrim and FO4's excuse?
And now the settlement system... Probably going to recieve a lot of hate for this one, but here goes: It is an amazing idea on paper, but it has been executed HORRIBLY.
The basic idea goes like this: You build a settlement, slowly but surely gathering your desired population, while making sure their needs (food, water, defense and happiness) are fullfiled.
Two problems: Happiness is very difficult to get above the 80 mark without serious micro-managing and research into the mechanics about it, my least favorite example is making sure all beds are under shelter from rain (only problem is that the game never specifies what counts as a roof and what doesn't).
The second problem is that defense does basically nothing. You'd think having a fortified base would allow the settlement to defend itself without needing your assistance? Well no, when a settlement gets attacked, the game just flips a coin to see if the settlement wins or loses. It doesn't account for walls you've built, it doesn't account for population of armed settlers, and it
.
I know I've gone on a bit of a rant, but I had to get this whole thing written to vent my frustrations with the game.
I want to like the game, but the bugs and poorly implemented mechanics keep me from doing so. Final score: 5/10, I suggest spending your money on something else.

Simply dripping with atmosphere and tough as nails Darkest Dungeon is a journey into the little explored aspects of dungeon crawling, namely the immense psychological pressures involved.

The art is to die for, the music is splendid and Wayne June’s narration is right on point. Together they transport you into a world filled with Lovecraftian horror which has never before seemed so charming.
Though it’s early access the game is solid. There’s some balancing issues and some mechanics need a bit more development. There are two more dungeons to come and at least 2 or 3 more hero classes but if this was released as is it could pass as an excellent game just in need of a bit of bug fixing.

So onwards friends, into the abyss that awaits but be warned, everyone has a breaking point and in the dark where the howls of beasts and the chants of dread ritual scream through ancient and forgotten halls you and your heroes may, no, will find theirs.

I don't typically bother writing reviews, but this one has dragged me out of seclusion just to do so.
For a game toting the "Early Access" flag, it feels more polished and complete of an experience than most release PC titles I played last year.  The game is stunning not only visually but also in terms of atmosphere and audio design.  Production values are fantastic across the board.
The game play is solid, tactical, and unrelentingly difficult.  While a heavy dose of the game revolves around RNG, it never feels like the RNG is straight-up screwing you in quite the same way that XCOM does.  Even the most horrific of situations can often be salvaged with a lot of thought and a little luck.
This is not a game for the weak of heart.  The challenge level is high and the possibility of winding up in a state where you are basically doomed to failure is very real.  Forethought and planning are required in order to keep the dungeon-ball rolling safely.
If you have a taste for rogue-likes, an interest in the unique, and the idea of a 2D crossbreed of Dark Souls and XCOM sounds magical to you, then you may have just found your game.
May your torches be ever bright.  Try not to die too fast.

The story of the wasteland now shifts to the "Commonwealth", to the northeast of the Capital Wasteland. Again, you rose up from a vault and roam the world around you. You can craft all sorts of things, from the most powerful weapon mods to the most impressive settlement objects. This alone is the greatest breakthrough in the entire Fallout series.
But, something's amiss. It's not there, not anymore. And I am treading some mighty thin ice here. I loved New Vegas for both of its gameplay and its story. The weapon system in NV was expansive, varied and at the same time balanced. It was also lore-friendly and "American". The combat mechanics successfully merged previous FO elements with FO3 elements. The story was long and deep, especially if you peak Honest Hearts an Lonesome Roads, some of the best quest chains and game world out there.
By contrast, while I have invested up to 1000 hours in FO4, I at last made peace with it. By dropping the whole game until a time where modding could renew the game to match its potential. The game for me was streamlined and simplified to such a degree that it felt lackluster. The weapon and armor system was simplified; no longer could you find armor piercing rounds or damage threshold. Instead you have "legendary" weapons which are literally in every corner of the game. The game allows you to extensively modify weapons now, but at the cost of a much less varied weaponry. And not to mention the un-lore-friendliness of its weapons. But, what got me disappointed the most was the feeling of the game lacking in the story and role-playing department. I roamed the wasteland so many times that now I realize that I have not found much impressive and memorable people and places. Quests are brief and bland and lackluster. Characters are not rounded and unrealistic at worst. Even the new affinity system for companions, which is clearly taken from Mass Effect, could not save it. Eventually, I do not feel that I have much influence on how the course of the game would take, how different the Commonwealth would be if I choose a different chain of choices. Eventually, the only thing I feel like doing was mindlessly shooting and building stuffs. Even Skyrim has more to offer.
This might sound like elitist talking, and indeed I am all for role-playing games, but if you are a RPG fan like me, you may find FO4 somewhat... off. I am a shooter fan too, but that is not what I want from FO4. In my opinion, at the end of the day, FO4 failed both ways. It is not as good as a shooter game, like Battlefield or Call of Duty, nor is it comparable to role-playing title like Mass Effect or even earlier FO titles like FONV. It is something inferior to both, and I could play dedicated FPS and RPG games instead of FO4 any day. If you like this sort of combination the FO4 is presenting, you got it. But, as a person who believed and expected a great 2015 game and bought the season pass at the first sign of it, I do not recommend you to play this game, if you are a RPG fan like me. I do not wholly regret buying the game, but you should consider other titles, such as earlier FO3 or FONV or any other game, than FO4.

Judged in a vacuum Fallout 4 is a well made game with fairly solid mechanics even if rather casualized and senselessly grindy. However judged as the latest entry in the Fallout series and in particular when judged against the previous installment New Vegas it's extremely disappointing.
This is a series that's known at least up till now anyway for it's very deep lore, worldbuilding and roleplaying elements. Fallout 4 is however pretty much just a simplistic open world shooter whose only real additions to the mechanics are a deeply flawed crafting and settlement building system plus what is to be fair probably the best take on power armor to date. More has been stripped out of the experience than added and while there's a cool character here and a neat story twist the factions are all pretty one dimensional and most of the characters a bit cartoonish or shmaltzy in all the wrong ways.

For a lot of people, Darkest Dungeon is going to feel like the game they've been waiting for. The team behind it has done a great job.

It's impossible to discuss Darkest Dungeon without praising the beautifully stark art direction; it channels the deep shadows of Mike Mignola (of "Hellboy") perfectly, and the colors shift and suppurate everywhere from the doomed hamlet at the foot of the Darkest Dungeon to the deepest and most Godforsaken pit you'll chuck adventurers into like a wood chipper. The music deftly changes between ominous, somber, and stirring as the situation demands, and the narrator keeps the tone set wonderfully, commenting (though not annoyingly so) on every turn of fate in a Tony Jay timbre.

Even putting aside the excellent and cohesive creative vision on display, the core mechanics of Darkest Dungeon are brutally satisfying. You'll begin the game tentatively sending small, untested and largely unfamiliar adventurers (I really suggest you not bother naming the poor souls yet) on short jaunts through nightmarish corridors -- keep the torch brightly lit in these beginning forays! -- in the hopes that some of them will back come out the other end with cash and relics to upgrade your town, relax and medicate your mercenaries, and keep the gears (the pulping, threshing gears) of your little dungeon-centric industry going.

The dungeons themselves are hesitant strolls punctuated by combat where every single point of health and stress counts. Darkest Dungeon keeps its numbers small: it'll be exciting when the Leper smacks a bandit for 11 damage, whether or not the Crusader heals for 4 points will be a matter or life and death, and the first time the Bounty Hunter gets a critical hit on a Marked target with Collect Bounty, 40 damage will seem miraculous. The first three-digit enemy will be more than a little worrisome. The RNG is still as fickle as ever though, so be prepared for even the best-laid plans to get ruined by bad luck.

Those tools at your disposal -- the mercenaries -- are a really great puzzle in themselves, too. Where should each fighter stand? What skills can even be used where they're standing? Is it too risky to have a mercenary who's useless if he's knocked out of position by a spell or an ambush? Is having a mercenary who can act in every position going to leave him spread thin? If you put two skills on an adventurer that can only be used in the very back row, what happens if someone in the party dies and there IS no back row? Should you send a very stressed Occultist with a fresh group of mercenaries and risk him driving them ALL mad? Is it safe to send a half-useless and untested Jester with three experienced pigstickers if it means his death will ruin their morale?

This decision-making only gets worse (better) as the game goes on, and opens you up to a really great obligation to constantly shift, rearrange, retrain and reassess your bands of brethren. Missions will get longer, necessitating that your heroes stop to camp and comfort each other with incense, mockery, medicine, or prayer. As you start to get a few of your hires to a higher level of skill and bravery, sometimes so high that they'll refuse some missions as being beneath their abilities, the management of the town transforms from a largely between-dungeons concern to a much greater part of the metagame.

You'll swap afflicted but useful madmen in and out of the sanitarium and make decisions on whether it's more pertinent to cure your Bounty Hunter's accuracy-ruining case of The Yips or purge him of Deviant Tastes apparently so unspeakable he's not allowed at the brothel.

You'll wish a million painful deaths on the Caretaker because he took the last seat at the bar and your Hellion who's psychologically coming apart at the seams -- the Hellion that you NEED for the next outing -- can't relax with anything but a tall tankard.

You'll stare at the weekly report that tells you than your Crusader, who you sent to meditate his cares away, decided to leave the hamlet on a vision quest and take his holy wrath with him when otherwise your whole 'A-team' skeleton demolition crew is ready to go.

The town influences your quests into the subterranean meat grinders and vice versa. Parties that before seemed perfect will be split up because the Grave Digger needs her Rabies cured and the Plague Doctor's medicines seem more appealing when faced with the Blight-dripping porcine residents of the Warrens. It keeps the player out of complacency in a really satisfying way; fans of X-COM or other high-stakes strategy will love the feeling of having to scramble in the face of disaster or cut their losses and tell the veteran Vestal and Leper to abandon the quest as well as the bodies of their compatriots.

Darkest Dungeons is a satisfying, strategic game about risk, reward, and reanimation. The dungeon crawls revitalize a task that's otherwise become almost a joke; there's no hazardous smashing through pinata baddies filled with loot here, and each time you hit 'Embark' you'll never really be sure what will be left of your party, if anything at all. The town management is a compelling game of its own, echoing "worker placement" board games and charming you as you hone blades, upgrade skills, and wrangle holy alcoholics into their barstools.

There's still some rough edges from Early Access here and there. Placeholder dialogue pops up occasionally and the central story has been held off until it's done, but even unfinished and in a mostly sandbox state both halves of Darkest Dungeon interact with other in a way that'll have you coming back for more. More, and more, and more, until in the folly of your hubris, the keening susurrations within the deepest abominable chambers beneath your lineage's empty-eyed manse ring out across the blighted land in an unendurable cacophony of gibbering and most terrible doom.

As a person who has Kickstarted (45$ Backer) this game. All I can say is that I'm very, very happy how this has come out.
The graphics are gorgeous, and the music is wonderful put it. From the forboding hyms in town, to the death-defying drumbeats in mortal combat. The Heroes are also very fun to use and play as and are unique in their very own way and can shift even the worse battles in your vary if used correctly.
This is a Roguelike game though, and if you have been living under a rock and don't know what those types of games are then I'll explain:
Roguelikes are games designed to be tough for the player, and usually have such things as perma-death where when your hero dies, he, or she, is gone for good. You'll need to be good at preparing your party and planning ahead as this game auto-saves your every decision no matter what you do.
Pros:
-Roguelike with wonderful graphics, sound, and music.
-Great, unique Heroes which you can freely custimize, upgrade, and  choose their skills. Each one brings their own unique feel to the fight.
-The Town you're in can be upgraded by finding trinkets and baubels while doing expeditions.
-Old Man talking in the background adds some great atmosphere to game.
-Deadly, and terrifying enemies that're unique in their areas and always bring something you'll be afraid no matter what party build you bring.
-Solid game mechanics which has you regularly experiment with what you have, and the stress/affliction system brings a whole new level of fear and strategy.
Cons:
-Min/Max Hero Parties: Building a certain party with certain heroes brings along a ♥♥♥♥ing hard-to-kill♥♥♥♥♥♥train-of-pain and Darkness that makes me wonder why monsters don't suffer a whole new level of insanity when they go against these guys. I won't tell you what that party is; I'll leave that to you guys to find out what it is.
-Powerful (but too powerful) monsters: Lets face it. You like games like these, right? Well you do know about that ONE monster that makes you want to cry and curl up into a fetal position and weep girly tears? Well Darkest Dungeon has that, but it's ♥♥♥♥ing all of them. All the monsters, even the weakest ones, are capable of utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥kicking your ill-prepared party if the RNG Gods dictate it so. And that can happen. A lot.
-No "skip week" button: Having some more control over when your party can leave for an expendition or choose to skip out a week to recover would be nice. But then again: this is Early Access, so it could be out at a later date.
And that's all I have for Cons so far.
FINAL VERDICT & SUMMARY:
Since this is still early access, I'll refrain from giving this game a rating till its full release.
Darkest Dungeon is a solid game that delivers what (I personally believe) a large community of Roguelike fans have been waiting for. This game is unique, tactical, and very fun. And It's Call of Cthululu, H.P. Lovecraft design is wonderfully implemented. The Combat is solid and forever changing based on the situation of your party, light/darkness, and the enemies you're facing. And the heroes themselves are fun and unique who deliver their own dialogue based on the situation they're facing. From testing their resolve in battle to relaxing at the brothol.
You can't go wrong with buying this game.

“What, you'd like to know my story?  There's not much to tell, I'm sorry to say. I came here, same reason as you – for glory, for gold. And not one man can fault me with cupidity, no. I tempted good friends, capable friends, spewing that very promise, HA, and don't let them tell you, CONVINCE YOU, that their hands were forced. They came willingly, yes.
“Like pigs to the slaughter.
“The first month was uneventful at the estate. Harried heroes came and went, but my friends and I were heartier fare. We spent what treasures we pilfered on libation, often causing a ruckus in the tavern. New adventurers would swagger in, ♥♥♥♥♥ure, and we'd put them right in place. We'd usually frighten the greener ones off... the rest would perish, often crying out – for God, for their mother, for the sweet release of death. Fools.
“My friends and I, we don't adventure anymore. We tend the estate, greet would-be heroes such as yourself, to give fair warning. All your skills, all your learning, all your experiences past mean nothing here. You will die, likely alone and raving in the dark. Death is all that you can count on. Death is all you will know.
“What, my necklace? No, these are no ordinary charms, child. These are my friends, you see. I carry them with me still, even after death. They quiet my mind, when the dark comes, you see. It was the least I could do; their bodies gave me sustenance – their bodies give me sustenance, HA, and don't let them tell you, CONVINCE YOU, that their hands were forced. They came willingly, yes.
“And so will you.”
Darkest Dungeon is an RPG turn-based roguelite dungeon crawler – and yes, I've written this phrase so much it autocorrects genres without prompting. I've named my dog “RPG turn-based roguelite dungeon crawler” and he hates me. But I digress. Story is that your wealthy relative has died, not before sending you a letter, urging you to come to the ancestral♥♥♥♥♥♥hole to spruce things up and purge the ancient, unknowable evil that lurks, broods, and taints up the place like an unruly teenager. The game starts off with a neat little tutorial, explaining some of the nuances of gameplay: tactical placement of characters, attacks, effects, etc. These are all standards we've come to know and love in the genre, nothing out of the ordinary. But there are a few twists that set Darkest Dungeon apart.
When you set out on a journey you'll select your adventurers, and there are a lot to choose from. Some are tanks, some are roguish, some are healers, and some suck (stupid damn plague doctor I HATE YOU SO MUCH). You can select your character order as well, and right clicking on a portrait provides insight into their ideal placement. Different heroes provide different bonuses, like scouting ahead to spot traps and treasure. After you pick your team you'll need provisions, a risk and reward proposition...  are you detecting a pattern? You'll need food for characters, particularly on the longer treks (there's even a camping/survival mechanic to replenish health and stress for such undertakings), or they're liable to starve. You'll need torches  to light the way and keep characters from intermittently having nervous breakdowns. And you'll need various health items to keep bleed and blight effects in check. Does this sound like a lot to juggle? Because I am not doing the death-defying, chainsaw spinning, greased up, foot juggling spectacle justice, I assure you. There aren't enough words. After your quest these provisions don't carry on to the next journey, unfortunately. So do you risk spending too much, or spending too little? Both carry consequence.
But there's more.
Every hero and heroine has a stress bar beneath their health. With each enemy encounter, trap, and the act of WALKING, the adventurers will accrue stress. This is countered by killing blows, critical hits, and some support abilities. Inevitably someone will reach their breaking point after one too many knock knock jokes and one of two things will happen: they'll rally courageously, lowering their stress and everyone elses, or become afflicted. This affliction, whether it be cowardice, masochism, irrationality (and more!), means you won't always be in control of that hero, often to their detriment and the team's.
After you clear (or flee) a dungeon you return to the estate, a hub where your weary adventurers can get some much needed R&R. Mirroring the core gameplay, your decisions in the hub world are deeply tactical. Some characters are religious, and will only be willing to visit the abbey to relieve stress. Others will happily drink and gamble their sorrows away. And as less savory quirks develop (buffs and debuffs gained through adventuring and R&R, separate from affliction), you can send them to the sanitarium, where presumably all the fun is. All of this is costly in time and money, and you'll have to manage carefully. Fresh heroes and heroines are wheeled into town after every adventure, but they are newbly in nature. With each subsequent successful quest, estate properties unlock, providing you the ability to upgrade abilities, armor and weapons, survivor traits, and more (you can upgrade your town's buildings to improve their respective output). Expect to spend a lot of booty.
After enough victories more procedural dungeon locales unlock, bosses become available to fight, and the game gets tougher. I'm not joking when I suggest that YOU, the player, will experience every quirk, affliction, and solace your characters do. I was paranoid. I was stalwart. I was masochistic. I was even hagiophobic (the last time a game introduced me to such cool vocabulary was Eternal Darkness). That is an accomplishment. And it was all worth it, every second of crawling, creeping madness, to play this game.
It's only February 2015 and this will easily be a contender for GOTY, of that I have no doubt. The art direction is spectacular; beautiful and visceral at the same time, like an old, dusty, medieval anatomy book. The turn-based attacks are so cool, so varied. The enemies are bizarre, terrifying, and menacing. The heroes and heroines are flawed, heroic, almost real. The dungeon crawling is rewarding, the victories are often bittersweet, and the office cooler conversation potential of this game is off the charts with so many variables. But the narration, sweet tap dancing Allfather, Allmother, and every Allrelative in between, the narration is amazing. It's omnipresent, in the hub and dungeons, raising hopes and dashing them in dulcet tones. It's like Vincent Price and Paul Frees' (Disney's Haunted Mansion) voices got married and Cthulhu officiated.
I have a few teeny, tiny criticisms. The game can be unrelentingly punishing at times, unfair even. And while there is no fail state per se, things can get so bad that you'll want to just restart. I'd like the option to play a game in which I can save. XCOM has a save mode AND  an Ironman mode, and I'd prefer that option here as well. There are also little technical glitches here and there, grammatical and spelling errors occasionally. That's about it. That's the sum of my complaints. I'd like to be able to save and there are a few little errors. And this title is in Early Access, which means we can anticipate lots of fine tuning and HOPEFULLY some cool additions as well. But what's already here, what's already been done, is spectacular.
It would be a grave crime against the Elder Gods to pass this up, and madness will surely follow.

You can read my full hands-on of Darkest Dungeon here:
In a nutshell, Darkest Dungeon is a brutal and unforgiving rogue-like RPG that will test the stress tolerance of both you and your heroes. You will curse and you will get frustrated. Your heroes will die and be replaced with other heroes that will also die. Defeat comes swiftly and often, and you will undoubtedly find yourself thinking more than once that the game is unfair.
But when victory comes, fleeting though it may be, it is oh so sweet and feels like a real accomplishment. Plus the artistic style and sounds effects are simply outstanding and really lend themselves to the dark and foreboding mood of the game.
Combat is turn-based like the classic video game RPGs, and for much of it you will be at the mercy of the random number generator for hitting, dodging, critical strikes, healing and the like. Your hero stats help with this, put for many battles victory is not assured. You really need to think about your turn carefully and what abilities you will use and how you will position your party. Proper positioning is vital in Darkest Dungeon because every ability in the game has required positioning for both your hero and the enemy target (and not being able to do anything because a hero is out of position happens all too often).
And then there is the stress system, which is difficult to manage and can take a good situation from good to very bad in an instant. Stressed out heroes can refuse to follow orders, refuse healing, and cause panic in the rest of the party. It is an interesting mechanic that definitely adds another layer of difficulty, although currently the stress system is quite harsh and I think misses the mark somewhat on being a creative push and pull during combat (i.e. you can’t stress out your foes in the same manner).
Overall though I enjoy the higher difficulty of the game. If you like challenging RPGs and can handle a bit of frustration then I highly recommend Darkest Dungeon. But keep in mind it is not for the gaming faint of heart.
Personally, I love it so far.

This is a brilliant game, one of the best all-time games ever. It's a huge world. The choices you make are often permanent and effect the overall world, but it eases you into most of the big choices so that you have more context before committing to support or oppose the 4 very interesting factions in the game.
The game is designed brilliantly. You can wander the world randomly and find all kinds of cool stuff, and almost never interfere with the main storyline. Either you'll just already earn an item that unlocks a later quest, or you'll have to storm the same location later when a new group of bad guys has taken it over.
You get to build fantastic settelements with populations and defenses, and even cook up some drugs heh!
In terms of the negatives, here's two: bugs and crashes. In a complex game where u can join any of 4 (mostly opposing factions), some story bugs are inevitable. With how much they tried to do in this game, sometimes it's inevitable that you do something in the story where the quest has trouble advancing. I've yet to encounter any that can't be solved by searching the Fallout 4 wiki and entering a console command, but still this does come up enough to be an annoyance. However, with how huge this game is, and the fact that you're making choices with real consequences in any number of interactions, this was inevitable.
A differnt kind of issue that's not inevitable are the frequent crashes I experienced. Often, when switching between two locations, the loading screen holds forever and u have to exit with Alt+F4. However, that also doesn't actually close the game due to a design flaw, so you have to load up the task manager and stop the program still running. Then the game re-syncs and can be replayed successfully. That may be my system, but it's a significant problem. I often have to restart the game 3 times during a normal 2-3 hour play session... which gets pretty frustrating. Lately, I've experienced a second error where the game is crashing my system (this may be related to my graphics card but no other new games like Assassin's Creed series etc. cause this issue), and frankly I get sick of developer's being like "Sure that's within our required specs but the problem is still your fault" so I leave it here anyway.

War may never change, but Fallout sure as hell did.
Fallout is one of the best RPG franchises known to man. The originals by Interplay are some of the most highly-regarded turn-based role playing games in history and then there's Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas which are also regarded as some of the best RPGs ever made.
So, what seemed like a simple task to make yet another great sequel has taken a turn... for the worst.
In short; Fallout 4 is by far the worst game in the franchise. In addition, as a game, it is both objectively and subjectively bad and after packing 300+ hours away underneath my belt and with nearly every quest complete; I'm going to try and explain why.
--- ISSUE #1: Plot, Dialogue and the Writing. ----
First and foremost, my biggest issue with the game lies with the dialogue, plot and writing. It is by far this game’s biggest issue, without question nor shadow of doubt. In comparison to its predecessors; it is downright insulting.
---- SPOILER WARNING ----
It’s bad as an outline, but it’s made truly horrible thanks to the awful, amatureish writing.
It actually makes me cringe whenever I even think about the writing in this game. Compared to New Vegas’ writing; it is an insult to the franchise. There is almost nothing redeeming about it. It's extraordinarily bland and there are even spelling errors in places! The writing is sub-amature at best and it’s completely unacceptable in a big-budget game.
None of the NPCs in the game are developed because of the writing and they’re all completely throwaway because of it. I’d be very hard-pressed, even after 300+ hours, to even remember any NPC’s name.  Most of the followers are just as under-developed and are largely forgettable (with the exception of Nick Valentine (though that’s only because of the Far Harbor DLC) and Dogmeat (because he’s a dog).
All the dialogue choices for your character are also uninteresting and poorly-written and even the sarcastic options (which are the best-written player dialogue pieces in the game, aside from the dialogue bits in Far Harbor) are poor and the sarcasm/jokes are largely unfunny.
There is the Far Harbor DLC, as mentioned before and that does have acceptable writing, but that’s just a crutch for the otherwise writing-crippled game.
---- ISSUE #2: Voiced Character ----
When the trailer for this game first came out, I was actually optimistic about the voiced protagonist. I didn’t really buy into the whole “having a voiced protagonist removes the player’s attachment to the character” argument. Now that I’ve put 300+ hours into this game however… My tune has changed.
It does remove the player’s attachment to the character completely. No longer are you the mysterious and fabled Lone Wanderer. Instead you’re playing as some military veteran guy or some lawyer gal. It completely removes the feeling of “I did that” and instead replaces it with “I helped my character do that”. Fallout 4 is more open-world, post-apocalyptic action game now, rather than the post-apocalyptic, role-playing game that made the franchise famous.
I remember when Todd Howard stated that having a voiced protagonist was supposed to make the story more “personal” and or “believable” before the game launched. What a load of garbage that was. If anything; it only made the story worse and less believable.
One second; you’re frantically looking for your kidnapped, infant son with concern and anguish written on your character’s face and audible in your character’s voice. The next; you’re making sarcastic prostate exam jokes and gallivanting off to help one of the seemingly-endless settlements that are incapable of defending themselves without you. Does that sound more personal and more believable?
Thought not...
The time and energy they spent on writing for and voicing the main character could and should have been spent on coming up with a better story and then refining said story. They spread their time and resources too thin and everything suffered because of it.
And don’t bother trying to lecture me about how mods can fix this. All the dialogue in the game was designed around a voiced protagonist and it’s evident when you get a mod to mute the character. The dialogue feels off and awfully thinned-out in every area of the game with such a mod installed.
---- ISSUE #3: Perks and Balancing ----
This game’s perk system and balancing is beyond horrble.
No longer do your perk and trait choices mold you, your character and your playstyle. Instead, you don’t even get traits anymore! Because of this new system that Bethesda adopted, it allows for “master of all trades” characters to be built. While fun at first, your character becomes incredibly overpowered very early on in the game. It’s not like you can avoid it too, as there are certain perks that are required for certain parts of the game. It therefore doesn’t take long for the game’s initially-decent balancing to become ruined.
I want a challenge, darn it! I want to mold my character differently with each playthrough. I don’t want to become a god of the wasteland! I want to fear Deathclaws like I did back in New Vegas and not get mildly annoyed by them and then kill them with the same amount of ease as killing a wolf in Skyrim!
I know they made this choice to make the game more “accessible” for new players, but at the cost of the fun, challenging gameplay that Fallout is known for!
---- ISSUE #4: Business Practices ----
The Season Pass for Fallout 4 cost $50. The Season Pass for Witcher 3 cost half that. With Fallout 4’s Season Pass, we got one decent story DLC, two horrid excuses for story DLCs and then three useless cash-grab settlement add-ons whose content was inferior versions of stuff that had already been made by the modding community.
Witcher 3’s expansion pass came with two incredible story expansions. There was also a plethora of free DLC and game updates that only added more stuff to do in that game.
Witcher 3’s Season Pass is the bar I set for Season Passes. Fallout 4’s Season Pass falls so short of that bar; it’s pitiful. I feel ripped off having bought the Season Pass. There is no value to be had in purchasing it.
At least I know now not to buy their Season Passes anymore.

For a lot of people, Darkest Dungeon is going to feel like the game they've been waiting for. The team behind it has done a great job.

It's impossible to discuss Darkest Dungeon without praising the beautifully stark art direction; it channels the deep shadows of Mike Mignola (of "Hellboy") perfectly, and the colors shift and suppurate everywhere from the doomed hamlet at the foot of the Darkest Dungeon to the deepest and most Godforsaken pit you'll chuck adventurers into like a wood chipper. The music deftly changes between ominous, somber, and stirring as the situation demands, and the narrator keeps the tone set wonderfully, commenting (though not annoyingly so) on every turn of fate in a Tony Jay timbre.

Even putting aside the excellent and cohesive creative vision on display, the core mechanics of Darkest Dungeon are brutally satisfying. You'll begin the game tentatively sending small, untested and largely unfamiliar adventurers (I really suggest you not bother naming the poor souls yet) on short jaunts through nightmarish corridors -- keep the torch brightly lit in these beginning forays! -- in the hopes that some of them will back come out the other end with cash and relics to upgrade your town, relax and medicate your mercenaries, and keep the gears (the pulping, threshing gears) of your little dungeon-centric industry going.

The dungeons themselves are hesitant strolls punctuated by combat where every single point of health and stress counts. Darkest Dungeon keeps its numbers small: it'll be exciting when the Leper smacks a bandit for 11 damage, whether or not the Crusader heals for 4 points will be a matter or life and death, and the first time the Bounty Hunter gets a critical hit on a Marked target with Collect Bounty, 40 damage will seem miraculous. The first three-digit enemy will be more than a little worrisome. The RNG is still as fickle as ever though, so be prepared for even the best-laid plans to get ruined by bad luck.

Those tools at your disposal -- the mercenaries -- are a really great puzzle in themselves, too. Where should each fighter stand? What skills can even be used where they're standing? Is it too risky to have a mercenary who's useless if he's knocked out of position by a spell or an ambush? Is having a mercenary who can act in every position going to leave him spread thin? If you put two skills on an adventurer that can only be used in the very back row, what happens if someone in the party dies and there IS no back row? Should you send a very stressed Occultist with a fresh group of mercenaries and risk him driving them ALL mad? Is it safe to send a half-useless and untested Jester with three experienced pigstickers if it means his death will ruin their morale?

This decision-making only gets worse (better) as the game goes on, and opens you up to a really great obligation to constantly shift, rearrange, retrain and reassess your bands of brethren. Missions will get longer, necessitating that your heroes stop to camp and comfort each other with incense, mockery, medicine, or prayer. As you start to get a few of your hires to a higher level of skill and bravery, sometimes so high that they'll refuse some missions as being beneath their abilities, the management of the town transforms from a largely between-dungeons concern to a much greater part of the metagame.

You'll swap afflicted but useful madmen in and out of the sanitarium and make decisions on whether it's more pertinent to cure your Bounty Hunter's accuracy-ruining case of The Yips or purge him of Deviant Tastes apparently so unspeakable he's not allowed at the brothel.

You'll wish a million painful deaths on the Caretaker because he took the last seat at the bar and your Hellion who's psychologically coming apart at the seams -- the Hellion that you NEED for the next outing -- can't relax with anything but a tall tankard.

You'll stare at the weekly report that tells you than your Crusader, who you sent to meditate his cares away, decided to leave the hamlet on a vision quest and take his holy wrath with him when otherwise your whole 'A-team' skeleton demolition crew is ready to go.

The town influences your quests into the subterranean meat grinders and vice versa. Parties that before seemed perfect will be split up because the Grave Digger needs her Rabies cured and the Plague Doctor's medicines seem more appealing when faced with the Blight-dripping porcine residents of the Warrens. It keeps the player out of complacency in a really satisfying way; fans of X-COM or other high-stakes strategy will love the feeling of having to scramble in the face of disaster or cut their losses and tell the veteran Vestal and Leper to abandon the quest as well as the bodies of their compatriots.

Darkest Dungeons is a satisfying, strategic game about risk, reward, and reanimation. The dungeon crawls revitalize a task that's otherwise become almost a joke; there's no hazardous smashing through pinata baddies filled with loot here, and each time you hit 'Embark' you'll never really be sure what will be left of your party, if anything at all. The town management is a compelling game of its own, echoing "worker placement" board games and charming you as you hone blades, upgrade skills, and wrangle holy alcoholics into their barstools.

There's still some rough edges from Early Access here and there. Placeholder dialogue pops up occasionally and the central story has been held off until it's done, but even unfinished and in a mostly sandbox state both halves of Darkest Dungeon interact with other in a way that'll have you coming back for more. More, and more, and more, until in the folly of your hubris, the keening susurrations within the deepest abominable chambers beneath your lineage's empty-eyed manse ring out across the blighted land in an unendurable cacophony of gibbering and most terrible doom.

As a person who has Kickstarted (45$ Backer) this game. All I can say is that I'm very, very happy how this has come out.
The graphics are gorgeous, and the music is wonderful put it. From the forboding hyms in town, to the death-defying drumbeats in mortal combat. The Heroes are also very fun to use and play as and are unique in their very own way and can shift even the worse battles in your vary if used correctly.
This is a Roguelike game though, and if you have been living under a rock and don't know what those types of games are then I'll explain:
Roguelikes are games designed to be tough for the player, and usually have such things as perma-death where when your hero dies, he, or she, is gone for good. You'll need to be good at preparing your party and planning ahead as this game auto-saves your every decision no matter what you do.
Pros:
-Roguelike with wonderful graphics, sound, and music.
-Great, unique Heroes which you can freely custimize, upgrade, and  choose their skills. Each one brings their own unique feel to the fight.
-The Town you're in can be upgraded by finding trinkets and baubels while doing expeditions.
-Old Man talking in the background adds some great atmosphere to game.
-Deadly, and terrifying enemies that're unique in their areas and always bring something you'll be afraid no matter what party build you bring.
-Solid game mechanics which has you regularly experiment with what you have, and the stress/affliction system brings a whole new level of fear and strategy.
Cons:
-Min/Max Hero Parties: Building a certain party with certain heroes brings along a ♥♥♥♥ing hard-to-kill♥♥♥♥♥♥train-of-pain and Darkness that makes me wonder why monsters don't suffer a whole new level of insanity when they go against these guys. I won't tell you what that party is; I'll leave that to you guys to find out what it is.
-Powerful (but too powerful) monsters: Lets face it. You like games like these, right? Well you do know about that ONE monster that makes you want to cry and curl up into a fetal position and weep girly tears? Well Darkest Dungeon has that, but it's ♥♥♥♥ing all of them. All the monsters, even the weakest ones, are capable of utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥kicking your ill-prepared party if the RNG Gods dictate it so. And that can happen. A lot.
-No "skip week" button: Having some more control over when your party can leave for an expendition or choose to skip out a week to recover would be nice. But then again: this is Early Access, so it could be out at a later date.
And that's all I have for Cons so far.
FINAL VERDICT & SUMMARY:
Since this is still early access, I'll refrain from giving this game a rating till its full release.
Darkest Dungeon is a solid game that delivers what (I personally believe) a large community of Roguelike fans have been waiting for. This game is unique, tactical, and very fun. And It's Call of Cthululu, H.P. Lovecraft design is wonderfully implemented. The Combat is solid and forever changing based on the situation of your party, light/darkness, and the enemies you're facing. And the heroes themselves are fun and unique who deliver their own dialogue based on the situation they're facing. From testing their resolve in battle to relaxing at the brothol.
You can't go wrong with buying this game.

I have no idea what I'm supposed to do in this game, and not in the good way. The map, while graphically interesting is shallow and lacks anything unique. In all my time playing the game I couldn't find a single out of the ordinary location. Everywhere in the game is just bandits and ghouls, and the occasional super mutant. No interesting quests or NPCs for the most part. I feel like I am missing all the interesting content.
The worst offences of the game are not how bad the world is though - that goes to the removal of being an evil character, the addition of the voiced protagonist, and the 4 choice dialogue system. I could go on for hours on how the dialogue alone is enough to make this game absolute gutter trash, but I'll save you the time and just say "yes" "no(usually yes, or just rejects quest)" "sarcasm(yes)" and "info(reroutes to same options)" is not compelling dialogue. It would have been better for the game at this point to have no dialogue at all, because the way it's structured is so blatantly transparent it just feels like a roadblock to go back to shooting things. It's an insult to former fallout games' branching questlines and interesting characters.
In addition, the 4 choice structure of dialogue does not permit you to be an evil character. At best you can try to take the money from some unimportant NPCs with charisma, and shoot some unimportant civilians (not like they had any meaningful dialogue anyways) and try to pretend the game actually cares that you performed any of these action in the vain attempt of trying to play this game as a role playing game (like every other main game + NV in the series is).
Of course, all of the problems in the dialogue are symptom of the brand new voice protagonist literally no one wanted or asked for, yet here it is. Outside of the issues stated above, the voiced protagonist further removes you from the role playing aspect of the game (implying there is any at all), as the voice, at least for me, is not the one I think of my character speaking in. Eventually I just picked up a mod to make the idiot shut his mouth (permanently), and the game was mildly more enjoyable as a result.
Other problems include the game running horribly (comparable to Assassin's Creed Unity in some areas), and being terribly balanced. This includes most early armors being utterly useless straight out of the vault, survival difficulty practically forcing you to play a gun stealth role if you don't want to die from a single bullet (also makes endurance a joke), and ammo being stupidly rare to the point I needed to download a crafting mod to get more
Things I don't like that aren't certainly problems in everyone's eyes are: The removal of weapon conditions, VATS is real time, gun customization is boring and I hate collecting everything like this is minecraft (I'd rather just have more unique guns than finding the same pipe pistol variant 50 billion times), the map starts you in a corner rather than the center (less replayability, only one real direction to go), I think settlement building is a waste of time and is poorly implemented (and I spent loads of time with it)
The few things I think were positive changes on former fallout titles: The combat is much more punchy and feels good, I love the new skill system (which is funny considering how many people I see disliking it; let me ask you - when is the last time you made any character in FO3 and NV that didn't have 6 or more intelligence and either lots of agility or strength? FO4's skill system is a lot more replayable in my eyes; I can think up dozens of different types of builds with completely different S.P.E.C.I.A.L. and perk sets that are interesting)
