“What, you'd like to know my story?  There's not much to tell, I'm sorry to say. I came here, same reason as you – for glory, for gold. And not one man can fault me with cupidity, no. I tempted good friends, capable friends, spewing that very promise, HA, and don't let them tell you, CONVINCE YOU, that their hands were forced. They came willingly, yes.
“Like pigs to the slaughter.
“The first month was uneventful at the estate. Harried heroes came and went, but my friends and I were heartier fare. We spent what treasures we pilfered on libation, often causing a ruckus in the tavern. New adventurers would swagger in, ♥♥♥♥♥ure, and we'd put them right in place. We'd usually frighten the greener ones off... the rest would perish, often crying out – for God, for their mother, for the sweet release of death. Fools.
“My friends and I, we don't adventure anymore. We tend the estate, greet would-be heroes such as yourself, to give fair warning. All your skills, all your learning, all your experiences past mean nothing here. You will die, likely alone and raving in the dark. Death is all that you can count on. Death is all you will know.
“What, my necklace? No, these are no ordinary charms, child. These are my friends, you see. I carry them with me still, even after death. They quiet my mind, when the dark comes, you see. It was the least I could do; their bodies gave me sustenance – their bodies give me sustenance, HA, and don't let them tell you, CONVINCE YOU, that their hands were forced. They came willingly, yes.
“And so will you.”
Darkest Dungeon is an RPG turn-based roguelite dungeon crawler – and yes, I've written this phrase so much it autocorrects genres without prompting. I've named my dog “RPG turn-based roguelite dungeon crawler” and he hates me. But I digress. Story is that your wealthy relative has died, not before sending you a letter, urging you to come to the ancestral♥♥♥♥♥♥hole to spruce things up and purge the ancient, unknowable evil that lurks, broods, and taints up the place like an unruly teenager. The game starts off with a neat little tutorial, explaining some of the nuances of gameplay: tactical placement of characters, attacks, effects, etc. These are all standards we've come to know and love in the genre, nothing out of the ordinary. But there are a few twists that set Darkest Dungeon apart.
When you set out on a journey you'll select your adventurers, and there are a lot to choose from. Some are tanks, some are roguish, some are healers, and some suck (stupid damn plague doctor I HATE YOU SO MUCH). You can select your character order as well, and right clicking on a portrait provides insight into their ideal placement. Different heroes provide different bonuses, like scouting ahead to spot traps and treasure. After you pick your team you'll need provisions, a risk and reward proposition...  are you detecting a pattern? You'll need food for characters, particularly on the longer treks (there's even a camping/survival mechanic to replenish health and stress for such undertakings), or they're liable to starve. You'll need torches  to light the way and keep characters from intermittently having nervous breakdowns. And you'll need various health items to keep bleed and blight effects in check. Does this sound like a lot to juggle? Because I am not doing the death-defying, chainsaw spinning, greased up, foot juggling spectacle justice, I assure you. There aren't enough words. After your quest these provisions don't carry on to the next journey, unfortunately. So do you risk spending too much, or spending too little? Both carry consequence.
But there's more.
Every hero and heroine has a stress bar beneath their health. With each enemy encounter, trap, and the act of WALKING, the adventurers will accrue stress. This is countered by killing blows, critical hits, and some support abilities. Inevitably someone will reach their breaking point after one too many knock knock jokes and one of two things will happen: they'll rally courageously, lowering their stress and everyone elses, or become afflicted. This affliction, whether it be cowardice, masochism, irrationality (and more!), means you won't always be in control of that hero, often to their detriment and the team's.
After you clear (or flee) a dungeon you return to the estate, a hub where your weary adventurers can get some much needed R&R. Mirroring the core gameplay, your decisions in the hub world are deeply tactical. Some characters are religious, and will only be willing to visit the abbey to relieve stress. Others will happily drink and gamble their sorrows away. And as less savory quirks develop (buffs and debuffs gained through adventuring and R&R, separate from affliction), you can send them to the sanitarium, where presumably all the fun is. All of this is costly in time and money, and you'll have to manage carefully. Fresh heroes and heroines are wheeled into town after every adventure, but they are newbly in nature. With each subsequent successful quest, estate properties unlock, providing you the ability to upgrade abilities, armor and weapons, survivor traits, and more (you can upgrade your town's buildings to improve their respective output). Expect to spend a lot of booty.
After enough victories more procedural dungeon locales unlock, bosses become available to fight, and the game gets tougher. I'm not joking when I suggest that YOU, the player, will experience every quirk, affliction, and solace your characters do. I was paranoid. I was stalwart. I was masochistic. I was even hagiophobic (the last time a game introduced me to such cool vocabulary was Eternal Darkness). That is an accomplishment. And it was all worth it, every second of crawling, creeping madness, to play this game.
It's only February 2015 and this will easily be a contender for GOTY, of that I have no doubt. The art direction is spectacular; beautiful and visceral at the same time, like an old, dusty, medieval anatomy book. The turn-based attacks are so cool, so varied. The enemies are bizarre, terrifying, and menacing. The heroes and heroines are flawed, heroic, almost real. The dungeon crawling is rewarding, the victories are often bittersweet, and the office cooler conversation potential of this game is off the charts with so many variables. But the narration, sweet tap dancing Allfather, Allmother, and every Allrelative in between, the narration is amazing. It's omnipresent, in the hub and dungeons, raising hopes and dashing them in dulcet tones. It's like Vincent Price and Paul Frees' (Disney's Haunted Mansion) voices got married and Cthulhu officiated.
I have a few teeny, tiny criticisms. The game can be unrelentingly punishing at times, unfair even. And while there is no fail state per se, things can get so bad that you'll want to just restart. I'd like the option to play a game in which I can save. XCOM has a save mode AND  an Ironman mode, and I'd prefer that option here as well. There are also little technical glitches here and there, grammatical and spelling errors occasionally. That's about it. That's the sum of my complaints. I'd like to be able to save and there are a few little errors. And this title is in Early Access, which means we can anticipate lots of fine tuning and HOPEFULLY some cool additions as well. But what's already here, what's already been done, is spectacular.
It would be a grave crime against the Elder Gods to pass this up, and madness will surely follow.

You can read my full hands-on of Darkest Dungeon here:
In a nutshell, Darkest Dungeon is a brutal and unforgiving rogue-like RPG that will test the stress tolerance of both you and your heroes. You will curse and you will get frustrated. Your heroes will die and be replaced with other heroes that will also die. Defeat comes swiftly and often, and you will undoubtedly find yourself thinking more than once that the game is unfair.
But when victory comes, fleeting though it may be, it is oh so sweet and feels like a real accomplishment. Plus the artistic style and sounds effects are simply outstanding and really lend themselves to the dark and foreboding mood of the game.
Combat is turn-based like the classic video game RPGs, and for much of it you will be at the mercy of the random number generator for hitting, dodging, critical strikes, healing and the like. Your hero stats help with this, put for many battles victory is not assured. You really need to think about your turn carefully and what abilities you will use and how you will position your party. Proper positioning is vital in Darkest Dungeon because every ability in the game has required positioning for both your hero and the enemy target (and not being able to do anything because a hero is out of position happens all too often).
And then there is the stress system, which is difficult to manage and can take a good situation from good to very bad in an instant. Stressed out heroes can refuse to follow orders, refuse healing, and cause panic in the rest of the party. It is an interesting mechanic that definitely adds another layer of difficulty, although currently the stress system is quite harsh and I think misses the mark somewhat on being a creative push and pull during combat (i.e. you can’t stress out your foes in the same manner).
Overall though I enjoy the higher difficulty of the game. If you like challenging RPGs and can handle a bit of frustration then I highly recommend Darkest Dungeon. But keep in mind it is not for the gaming faint of heart.

Story
Shortly after signing up to be part of the local fallout shelter Vault 111, a local news broadcast informs viewers of impending nuclear attacks. After rushing to the Vault entrance, you barely escape the destructive wave of a nuclear bomb that detonated off in the distance. You, your spouse, and infant son Shaun are talked into entering a cryogenic tubes to be frozen. After an unknown amount of time you are awakened to find strangers have opened your spouses tube. After kidnapping your child the leader of the bunch shoots your spouse and re-initiates your tube, leaving you to drift into unconsciousness and awaken sometime in the future.
When the life support system fails you wake up, unaware of how long you've been under and make your way to the surface. What was once a beautiful world teeming with life is now a barren wastleland plagued with mutated beings and no sign of environmental growth. Determined to find your missing son Shaun you venture into this new world, gathering resources to aid in your mission, allying with remaining locals, and hunting down those responsible.
Gameplay
Fallout 4 is an open world action RPG that has a great deal to offer in terms of content and scale. Base-building and crafting, weapon and armor customization, and a large amount of playstyle options. Controls and movement are responsive and fluid while combat is engaging and challenging. Where Fallout 4 falls short is in its story-telling, with little to offer in terms of quest varieties you find yourself replaying the same formula of a quest you did twenty minutes ago. "Get this, get that" and "Kill target, get this." The side quests however proved to be enjoyable as they weren't pertinent to the story itself but shed new light on a bleak radiated world. With interesting characters along the way and remnants of how life used to be, the side quests help make up for a predictable and cliché story.
To survive in this harsh new world you must rely heavily on resource gathering and crafting. I found that resources were rare enough that exploration was required but not overly abundant making for easy upgrades. Settlement building, while very enjoyable and capable of some pretty creative designs, is clunky in function and the snapping of selected items isn't always ideal.
The world of Fallout 4 is quite massive and surprisingly detailed in terms of items, creatures and humans, as well as interesting structures and landmarks worth exploring. Rarely do you find yourself running into copy-pasted buildings though the layouts might appear similar. The game offers a handful of difficulties including a Survival mode where hunger, thirst, and stamina all play a role in how you go about your roaming. The playing field is almost even in terms of damage and makes for a very tense play-through, saving your progress relies on finding a suitable bed to sleep in and afflictions must be treated sooner rather than later.
Overall the gameplay is significantly improved on from its predecessors however the engine itself had little noticeable benefits. Objects, enemies, and player interaction can be buggy, nothing game breaking (from my experience) but definitely a nuisance.
Sound
About what you would expect after playing a game from the Fallout or Elder Scrolls series. Dialogue is quite bland and lifeless, little emotion or enthusiasm outside of the subtle cut-scene style conversations. Primarily noticeable in the lack of emotion from the protagonist, seeing as, well, his son was kidnapped and his wife shot before his eyes. Despite the lackluster dialogue, sound effects are on par with its triple A quality and the music is fitting for the setting and tone of the game.
Graphics
Visually appealing but leave much to be desired in the optimization aspect. In one area you may be sitting at on average 70fps and twenty feet later 35fps, granted this is most common in large cities. Despite the choppiness in condensed urban areas, it runs smooth enough to be enjoyable. Lighting is a significant improvement from previous games in the series and textures have made a noticeable stride for the better. Animations feel mechanical and clipping is minor issue while movement feels like your on a multi-directional treadmill (in 3rd person at least). Overall the graphics are pretty but the game's immersion breaking flaws pull you out of the atmosphere and setting frequently.
Replay Value
The breadth of content is impressive and gives Fallout 4 a great deal of replay value. The main quest can be completed in a decent amount of time but at around 80 hours of playtime I feel that I've only skimmed the surface in terms of exploration and side quests available.
Wrapping Up
Fallout 4 delivers a wonderful experience as a whole. It's story is rather shallow and the AI leaves much to be desired, but it's a worthwhile purchase for any RPG fan. I myself typically complete a game before installing mods so my second play-through was much more enjoyable as there is a great deal of community created content available that fine tunes your experience to your liking. Regardless, Fallout 4 meets expectations in terms of a quality Open World RPG and offers a great deal of playstyles, all wrapped in a beautifully crafted dangerous wasteland.

The game has some grind in it, so you'll be spending a lot of your time underground. The first planet I spawned on had next to no iron, leading to a lot of frustration. When I realised I could hop on to another planet provided I had enough coal, things got a lot better. I still find myself grinding for a particular resource every now and then, though. I'd imagine this wouldn't be as bad if you played multiplayer, but since I haven't tried it yet, I'm not sure.
Unlike Terraria and Minecraft (which are closest comparisons to Starbound), this game does have a tutorial of sorts in form of quests. Unfortunately, they still seem to need a lot of fixing, and the confusion I mentioned before is partially because of this. After getting started, the game is quite easy to get into. I look up some things on the wiki every now and then, but most of the stuff probably can be discovered if you just craft everything interesting looking and try it out.
If you like Terraria, it's a safe bet to say that you will like this also. If you didn't, you might still like it. Starbound controls very much like Terraria, but is more complex, varied and has a more refined feel to it. And it is in space. For me, I find Starbound much more enjoyble of the two. Let's see... a review for Starbound. Keep in mind it's currently still Beta so things can and will change.
To get the first point out of the way, if you have played or experienced Terraria, then you basically already know the gist of this game. You are set loose into a world which you can sculpt and alter with pick and axe. There are also lots of things that want to cut your life short. So lets talk about what is different than Terraria. First of all you have different races at your disposal. Each with their own history and maybe eventually even different story arcs. These different races also come with various different racial armors and weapons. Which is neat in my opinion. Especially when you make a game of it to hunt the recipes from the other races. Which so far isn't fully implemented. At least I haven't seen peaceful settlements for some species yet.
Anyway I digress. Now comes the important part where it's different. Your starship. Your home away from home. Probably the only constant in this procedually generated game. WIth it you can easily bugger off into a new star system in case the one you're in currently isn't to your liking. And as you progress through the material tiers, you will most likely be doing a lot of planet hopping. Which is sadly a big downturn too, as it gives little incentive to actually build and create a marvellous fortress for yourself. Since by god the starmap is horrible so far and good luck finding some system again after leaving it.
In it's current shape the game also has some pretty hefty balancing problems, especially in the higher tiers where monsters easily one shot you while having atrocious amounts of health.
Um... so yeah, before I blunder on more here.
If you liked Terraria and want to try something new, get this. If you like exploration games with procedually generated content, get this. If you want a game that totally gives you a red thread to follow in order to find adventure. Don't get this.
As it currently stands, it's all about the exploration.

In general the game is just OK.  The previous release was a lot better in terms of story, gameplay, and entertainment value.  There are a lot of cool added aspects that make it a bit more interesting than the Las Vegas version, like being able breakdown junk to get specific resources to building things and the means of upping one's skills set is an improvement.  However, while it looked like it was going to be a very good storyline, much of the game seems to be very redundant where you are going out to find something, or clear the mutants, raiders, or whatever, out of some location.  It gets old pretty quick.  There are also a few glitches in this version.  There are short load periods when switching from exterior to interior locations that too often cause a crash of the game.  That it is, it leaves and never comes back.  Also, for some quests you are sent to locations that don’t’ seem to have the persistent problem of not being ‘findable.’  That is, for most locations, when you approach them for the first time the game identifies the location and places it on your map.  Barring that, if you have never been there but are being directed to the location for the quest, it places it on your map at that point.  For at least a couple (e.g., USAF Olivia Satellite Station, and Hub 360), that doesn’t happen so you cannot get credit for completing the task…small, but annoying little glitches.  Anyways, given that this game is still priced at $60, I’d suggest there are much better options out there for that kind of money.

First of all, beta is beta. If you are looking for a completed game, this is not for you. A lot of essential things are missing, which caused a lot of confusion for me before I gave up and opened the wiki on my other screen. Also, the early beta means that your character can be wiped, and you'll have to start over.
However, if you don't mind the early beta phase, this game is awesome. The attention to detail in this is amazing - each of the races have their own respawn animations, armor sets, and even different descriptions if you examine an item. Each of the planets I have visited so far has been different; different colors, different biomes, different mobs. And the soundtrack is awesome.
The game has some grind in it, so you'll be spending a lot of your time underground. The first planet I spawned on had next to no iron, leading to a lot of frustration. When I realised I could hop on to another planet provided I had enough coal, things got a lot better. I still find myself grinding for a particular resource every now and then, though. I'd imagine this wouldn't be as bad if you played multiplayer, but since I haven't tried it yet, I'm not sure.
Unlike Terraria and Minecraft (which are closest comparisons to Starbound), this game does have a tutorial of sorts in form of quests. Unfortunately, they still seem to need a lot of fixing, and the confusion I mentioned before is partially because of this. After getting started, the game is quite easy to get into. I look up some things on the wiki every now and then, but most of the stuff probably can be discovered if you just craft everything interesting looking and try it out.
If you like Terraria, it's a safe bet to say that you will like this also. If you didn't, you might still like it. Starbound controls very much like Terraria, but is more complex, varied and has a more refined feel to it. And it is in space. For me, I find Starbound much more enjoyble of the two. Definitely worth the low price point.

Story
Shortly after signing up to be part of the local fallout shelter Vault 111, a local news broadcast informs viewers of impending nuclear attacks. After rushing to the Vault entrance, you barely escape the destructive wave of a nuclear bomb that detonated off in the distance. You, your spouse, and infant son Shaun are talked into entering a cryogenic tubes to be frozen. After an unknown amount of time you are awakened to find strangers have opened your spouses tube. After kidnapping your child the leader of the bunch shoots your spouse and re-initiates your tube, leaving you to drift into unconsciousness and awaken sometime in the future.
When the life support system fails you wake up, unaware of how long you've been under and make your way to the surface. What was once a beautiful world teeming with life is now a barren wastleland plagued with mutated beings and no sign of environmental growth. Determined to find your missing son Shaun you venture into this new world, gathering resources to aid in your mission, allying with remaining locals, and hunting down those responsible.
Gameplay
Fallout 4 is an open world action RPG that has a great deal to offer in terms of content and scale. Base-building and crafting, weapon and armor customization, and a large amount of playstyle options. Controls and movement are responsive and fluid while combat is engaging and challenging. Where Fallout 4 falls short is in its story-telling, with little to offer in terms of quest varieties you find yourself replaying the same formula of a quest you did twenty minutes ago. "Get this, get that" and "Kill target, get this." The side quests however proved to be enjoyable as they weren't pertinent to the story itself but shed new light on a bleak radiated world. With interesting characters along the way and remnants of how life used to be, the side quests help make up for a predictable and cliché story.
To survive in this harsh new world you must rely heavily on resource gathering and crafting. I found that resources were rare enough that exploration was required but not overly abundant making for easy upgrades. Settlement building, while very enjoyable and capable of some pretty creative designs, is clunky in function and the snapping of selected items isn't always ideal.
The world of Fallout 4 is quite massive and surprisingly detailed in terms of items, creatures and humans, as well as interesting structures and landmarks worth exploring. Rarely do you find yourself running into copy-pasted buildings though the layouts might appear similar. The game offers a handful of difficulties including a Survival mode where hunger, thirst, and stamina all play a role in how you go about your roaming. The playing field is almost even in terms of damage and makes for a very tense play-through, saving your progress relies on finding a suitable bed to sleep in and afflictions must be treated sooner rather than later.
Overall the gameplay is significantly improved on from its predecessors however the engine itself had little noticeable benefits. Objects, enemies, and player interaction can be buggy, nothing game breaking (from my experience) but definitely a nuisance.
Sound
About what you would expect after playing a game from the Fallout or Elder Scrolls series. Dialogue is quite bland and lifeless, little emotion or enthusiasm outside of the subtle cut-scene style conversations. Primarily noticeable in the lack of emotion from the protagonist, seeing as, well, his son was kidnapped and his wife shot before his eyes. Despite the lackluster dialogue, sound effects are on par with its triple A quality and the music is fitting for the setting and tone of the game.
Graphics
Visually appealing but leave much to be desired in the optimization aspect. In one area you may be sitting at on average 70fps and twenty feet later 35fps, granted this is most common in large cities. Despite the choppiness in condensed urban areas, it runs smooth enough to be enjoyable. Lighting is a significant improvement from previous games in the series and textures have made a noticeable stride for the better. Animations feel mechanical and clipping is minor issue while movement feels like your on a multi-directional treadmill (in 3rd person at least). Overall the graphics are pretty but the game's immersion breaking flaws pull you out of the atmosphere and setting frequently.
Replay Value
The breadth of content is impressive and gives Fallout 4 a great deal of replay value. The main quest can be completed in a decent amount of time but at around 80 hours of playtime I feel that I've only skimmed the surface in terms of exploration and side quests available.
Wrapping Up
Fallout 4 delivers a wonderful experience as a whole. It's story is rather shallow and the AI leaves much to be desired, but it's a worthwhile purchase for any RPG fan. I myself typically complete a game before installing mods so my second play-through was much more enjoyable as there is a great deal of community created content available that fine tunes your experience to your liking. Regardless, Fallout 4 meets expectations in terms of a quality Open World RPG and offers a great deal of playstyles, all wrapped in a beautifully crafted dangerous wasteland.

That it is, it leaves and never comes back.  Also, for some quests you are sent to locations that don’t’ seem to have the persistent problem of not being ‘findable.’  That is, for most locations, when you approach them for the first time the game identifies the location and places it on your map.  Barring that, if you have never been there but are being directed to the location for the quest, it places it on your map at that point.  For at least a couple (e.g., USAF Olivia Satellite Station, and Hub 360), that doesn’t happen so you cannot get credit for completing the task…small, but annoying little glitches.  Anyways, given that this game is still priced at $60, I’d suggest there are much better options out there for that kind of money.

Absolutely hate it, and it really pains me to say that after how excited I was for the launch after that amazing E3 presentation. I have no idea what I'm supposed to do in this game, and not in the good way. The map, while graphically interesting is shallow and lacks anything unique. In all my time playing the game I couldn't find a single out of the ordinary location. Everywhere in the game is just bandits and ghouls, and the occasional super mutant. No interesting quests or NPCs for the most part. I feel like I am missing all the interesting content.
The worst offences of the game are not how bad the world is though - that goes to the removal of being an evil character, the addition of the voiced protagonist, and the 4 choice dialogue system. I could go on for hours on how the dialogue alone is enough to make this game absolute gutter trash, but I'll save you the time and just say "yes" "no(usually yes, or just rejects quest)" "sarcasm(yes)" and "info(reroutes to same options)" is not compelling dialogue. It would have been better for the game at this point to have no dialogue at all, because the way it's structured is so blatantly transparent it just feels like a roadblock to go back to shooting things. It's an insult to former fallout games' branching questlines and interesting characters.
In addition, the 4 choice structure of dialogue does not permit you to be an evil character. At best you can try to take the money from some unimportant NPCs with charisma, and shoot some unimportant civilians (not like they had any meaningful dialogue anyways) and try to pretend the game actually cares that you performed any of these action in the vain attempt of trying to play this game as a role playing game (like every other main game + NV in the series is).
Of course, all of the problems in the dialogue are symptom of the brand new voice protagonist literally no one wanted or asked for, yet here it is. Outside of the issues stated above, the voiced protagonist further removes you from the role playing aspect of the game (implying there is any at all), as the voice, at least for me, is not the one I think of my character speaking in. Eventually I just picked up a mod to make the idiot shut his mouth (permanently), and the game was mildly more enjoyable as a result.
Other problems include the game running horribly (comparable to Assassin's Creed Unity in some areas), and being terribly balanced. This includes most early armors being utterly useless straight out of the vault, survival difficulty practically forcing you to play a gun stealth role if you don't want to die from a single bullet (also makes endurance a joke), and ammo being stupidly rare to the point I needed to download a crafting mod to get more
Things I don't like that aren't certainly problems in everyone's eyes are: The removal of weapon conditions, VATS is real time, gun customization is boring and I hate collecting everything like this is minecraft (I'd rather just have more unique guns than finding the same pipe pistol variant 50 billion times), the map starts you in a corner rather than the center (less replayability, only one real direction to go), I think settlement building is a waste of time and is poorly implemented (and I spent loads of time with it)
The few things I think were positive changes on former fallout titles: The combat is much more punchy and feels good, I love the new skill system (which is funny considering how many people I see disliking it; let me ask you - when is the last time you made any character in FO3 and NV that didn't have 6 or more intelligence and either lots of agility or strength? FO4's skill system is a lot more replayable in my eyes; I can think up dozens of different types of builds with completely different S.P.E.C.I.A.L. and perk sets that are interesting)
tl;dr: I'd rather play bad rats

Let's see... a review for Starbound. Keep in mind it's currently still Beta so things can and will change.
To get the first point out of the way, if you have played or experienced Terraria, then you basically already know the gist of this game. You are set loose into a world which you can sculpt and alter with pick and axe. There are also lots of things that want to cut your life short. So lets talk about what is different than Terraria. First of all you have different races at your disposal. Each with their own history and maybe eventually even different story arcs. These different races also come with various different racial armors and weapons. Which is neat in my opinion. Especially when you make a game of it to hunt the recipes from the other races. Which so far isn't fully implemented. At least I haven't seen peaceful settlements for some species yet.
Anyway I digress. Now comes the important part where it's different. Your starship. Your home away from home. Probably the only constant in this procedually generated game. WIth it you can easily bugger off into a new star system in case the one you're in currently isn't to your liking. And as you progress through the material tiers, you will most likely be doing a lot of planet hopping. Which is sadly a big downturn too, as it gives little incentive to actually build and create a marvellous fortress for yourself. Since by god the starmap is horrible so far and good luck finding some system again after leaving it.
In it's current shape the game also has some pretty hefty balancing problems, especially in the higher tiers where monsters easily one shot you while having atrocious amounts of health.
Um... so yeah, before I blunder on more here.
If you liked Terraria and want to try something new, get this. If you like exploration games with procedually generated content, get this. If you want a game that totally gives you a red thread to follow in order to find adventure. Don't get this.
As it currently stands, it's all about the exploration.

TLDR at bottom.
It's incredibly fashionable to wail on Fallout 4 and I do understand why. It's not as good as FNV, it's not as good as Fallout 3 and it's unrecognisable from the classic isometric epics. The principal reason for this is that world is vast but is also lifeless in places and much of the expansive wasteland is unused in terms of lore and plot. It's also taken another step from dark and forboding to kitschy and quaint.
Ironically, despite the swathes of empty terrain, I'd actually say there's too much "content" in the game. A lot of the missions are repetitive, radial fetch quests or characterless kill quests with little soul that the game could have done without. As a result, I'm currently sitting at some 138.9 hours for a game I bought at steam-sale prices. To the people complaining about Bethesda's business practices (mostly, I suppose, because the DLC was somewhat rubbish) I would say that's incredibly good value for money. Most triple-A games won't come close to that and whilst there's a question of quality versus quantity, nobody put a gun to my head and made me (or anyone else) play and the game is a tidy timesink.
I should add that whilst my version of FO4 is modded extensively (which I'd put as another mark in the "buy" column,) the modded content has not added quests/missions/land as such should have little impact on my playtime.
I've read reviews of people claiming to be on their fourth or fifth playthrough or whom have put in a thousand odd hours and yet they're telling people they wouldn't recommend the game. This brings me back to my initial point, it's popular to lay in to FO4 but, lets be honest, if you can sink a thousand hours in to a title then you've clearly had your money's worth and you obviously didn't hate it all that much.
Is FO4 the best in the franchise? No. Is it probably the worst? Sadly so. But is it still a game with a lot of enjoyable content that'll quite comfortably justify it's cost by the time you've finished? I'd say so.
TLDR: buy it accepting it's not as good as it's predecessors and you won't be let down. It's still good fun and still worth playing, it just could have been more.

The Bad

- 3 Factions that seek to be exclusive winners

- Radiant quests that are used as XP filler
- Respawning of opponents nearly everywhere detracting from accomplishing anything

- Main story is quickly exhausted for interest, lacks depth

The Ugly
- Factional play does not recognize nor respect protagonist if taking up a faction leader position
- Factions unable to be diverted or see sense when interests align for cooperative work
- Factions not well integrated into DLC content
- The good concept of a pre-war protagonist is wasted on simplistic plot
- Protagonist background and life experience is tossed away and actually ignored by and large
- Skills and Perks rolled into simplified Perk Tree removing hard RPG based decisions
- Retroactive Continuity changes that make no damned sense
- Simplistic main quest
- Use of 'future seeing' NPC that covers many main quest situations indicating lack of freedom of choices for RPG play
- No indication of what Perks and base Stats are influencing decisions leading to heavy use of Charisma based clothing
- Settlements that do not follow the prior game template or historical concept of what a settlement actually is
- Frustrating settlement build system becomes a requirement for parts of main quest
- No DIY main quest options to forego all factions which limits replay interest for main quest
- Really poor AI for companions
- Respawning detracts from immersion and makes little damned sense
- No Karma system
I truly do like Fallout 4 and think it is a decent part of the franchise and well worth buying as a bundle with all its DLCs.  With that said the glaring simplistic main story with its rails that have few decision points and ruthless nature of the main factions towards other factions quickly exhausts that main quest for interesting features.  Coming from a functioning past should have major ramifications for the Fallout universe, and is squandered to the point where any wastelander with a similar problem and drive could fill the protagonist slot due to the nature of the faction driving the quest line.  Having a voiced protagonist limits depth of story as all choice branches would require voice acting and that can get expensive.  These choice limitations make the main story simplistic, rigid and that requires factions to be so rigid in their outlook that they would prefer dying for their cause than to actually interact and negotiate with each other.
As an RPG, Fallout 4 is a pretty good First Person Shooter.  As an FPS, it is a pretty good RPG.  As a Factional game, it lacks faction interplay, removes negotiation and makes crafting interesting RPG stories nearly impossible.  Becoming a Faction leader opens up no opportuinities for guiding that faction, no budgeting, no assignment of NPCs to duties and even has one NPC that can be found tha actually understands how the faction leader of a militia actually works.  This has been a problem with Bethesda and Faction leadership for a long, long time: for all the faction interplay, the logistics end that is the meat and potatos of being a faction head is never granted to the player.  All of this is done with the intention of getting a wider audience and player base for the game and increase revenue, but also points at a lack of understanding of just how sophisticated the average gamer or even the casual gamer is in the modern world.
Thus for smooth game play, stability and very interesting side quests, and a well crafted open world, Fallout 4 is recommended.  As part of the Fallout franchise, it falls behind Fallout New Vegas, Fallout 3 and even the older Fallout and Fallout 2 for lore, continuity of background which is broken by many retcons with little to no back story to them.  Working with prior established limitations in alt-history is a challenge to anyone crafting a game with such prior background and should be utilized and built upon even when it causes troubles since that is an opportunity for enhanced story telling and game play via depth of that background.  Tossing out hard to use background on the altar of smooth game play indicates lack of respect for that background and lack of ingenuity on the part of the game designers.  Fans of a game can be satisfied and challenging game play retained while still making the experience smoother with better physics engines, rendering engines and scripting engines.  Bethesda acquired the Fallout franchise, built on it and that is something that they should respect as a company for their own work that has gone into it, if nothing else.
The elements for a truly great, very deep story line with quests are present but not put into a coherent form to be a part of the main quest.  Thus elements which should naturally fit together, don't.  Interactions with NPCs is frustrating beyond words for the extremely limited options made available to the PC.  For all the voice acting the PC has very little to say in the game.  Coupling these items then makes for RPG frustration as this is the center of RPG play: finding and knitting together options that game designers put into the game to allow for a wide array of choices.
As a player the concept of 'Radiant Quests' and respawning areas make no damned sense at all.  Missions have objectives, objective completion has ramifications, and clearing out a place means it is finally cleared for a good, long time.  In a wasteland with few people, it is impossible to reconcile all the respawning of individuals with the overall low population of the wasteland.  Ditto creatures, come to think of it.  This is filler content put in to cover over lack of meaningful XP rewards and depth of world game play. If there were more and more interesting things to do in the game world, then the concept of Radiant Quests could go away completely.  Tasks that are difficult, that can be done and then offer non-monetary rewards (such as faction reputation) which used to be a part of the prior two installments is removed, which means managing reputation is also removed.
Fallout 4 is a missed opportunity to make a truly great RPG.  For all the misses, frustration with story, and lack of diverse game play it is still on my recommend list for the parts that are right with it, and the general entertainment of being in an interesting open world.  Do all the side quests, do the DLCs and explore to your heart's content and you will not be disappointed.  The engrossing content of Far Harbor, the fun or Automotron or understanding just how Raiders semi-function and why they are irritating as all hell in Nuka World, all will give a great gaming experience.  Try to keep the main story as background, the missions taken up as ones to get some equipment or unlock upgrades, and then bail out on it and just have fun in the game world.  All of the non-main story stuff indicates that Bethesda does know how to create great content if they put their minds to it, and that is worth the price of discounted admission to all the attractions.

At first, Starbound was a quiet, little gem of a building sidescroller, with limited hints of adventure. It was still thrilling enough to keep me immersed. Then the devs began adding more and more features, events, and more content. Naturally, the character wipes were annoying, but I endured. I had to endure. A little more blah blah, a little more rinse and repeat, and we find ourselves at the current form the game's taken.
From humble beginnings to an absolutely enjoyable sidescrolling masterpiece, there's almost a limitless amount of things to do, from general omnicide, to a bit of ye olde farming. Swing a hoe at some dirt, or just swing at a ho. I've sunk over 700 hours into this game and in all likelihood, with the way the devs keep things updated, I'll be sinking even more into it. Goodbye, life, I'm venturing into the realm of the unknown, courtesy of Starbound.
As usual, I'll list what I consider to be both pros and cons:
Pros:
- A seemingly infinite universe.
- Enough content in the unmodded game itself, to keep players immersed.
- A decent storyline.
- Simple controls, easy to pick up once you know what you're doing.
- The ability to upgrade your doofy poop-shuttle into a battleship!
- Brand spankin' new SPACE STATIONS. Deep space nine, eat your heart out!
- A generous amount of discoverable cosmetics, because your beginner clothes warrant a slap to the face.
- Easy wiring system, you don't have to be an engineer to understand how to wire things in Starbound!
- A game you can play with others, or by yourself. Both are enjoyable.
Cons:
- After pumping 700+ hours into Starbound, I've realized that it seems way more interesting than my life at present.
- That pet you get in your ship at the start, you can't get rid of it without a mod. This is probably the only real con I can think of.
In closing, this is a fantastic game, and if you're not a fan of the genre, at least consider Starbound, it may very well change your mind. It's worth the dosh!

Fallout 4. It's a good game, not great but certainly good and in true Bathesda style it is now and likely forever will be plagued with technical issues.
Storywise it's very restrictive in terms of personal character. In modern fallout games you've always had a semi-forced starting persona. In Fallout 3 you were the vault dweller looking for a lost family member, In Fallout: NV you were the betrayed courier out for revenge and in Fallout 4 it's sort of a call back to three where you're a vault dweller (I use that term very loosely) out looking for a lost family member so a forced starting persona isn't really new or the main issue here, it's how you go about spending your time in the wasteland that counts and here, the choice to be a bad guy just feels....wrong. that's the issue.
If you wish you can go out in to the wasteland and act like the worst person in the world to anybody and everybody, make bad choices etc.. etc.. but at the end of the day the way they set your character up for you it just feels wrong. Going out and looking out for number one feels stupid as you're told you have to care about your son being abudcted and your husband (or wife) being murdered (Which would naturally be the case). Walking around acting like the most feared and brutal being in the wasteland falls flat when you get in to a conversation where you start blubbering about your missing family.
Gameplay wise there are some huge improvements over the previous titles. The gunplay feels great, they clearly put a lot of work in to this new system but as a result the game is a lot more action oriented that the previous titles and that may not be a good fit for some people. Navigating your way around the wasteland as a smooth talking passifist or a stealthy ghost who avoids engaging enemies is no longer a possibility, you have to fight, you don't have a choice in the matter.
You can now build settlements in Fallout and while the concept is great, the execution is just downright poor. It's too limited (A lot of the problems with settlements are overcome with mods but this review is being written for the base game, no mods as not all people like to use mods) You'll get constantly annoyed with how you can't place this thing here because the terain isn't level and there's not a damn thing you can do about it without your settlement having random, ugly looking concrete foundations in the middle of it.
Your settlers should just get replaced with feral ghouls because at least they'd have more life in them. They are like dead-eyed zombies that more often than not will have trouble navigating their way around the settlement you've built. All settlements will fly under the "Minute Men" banner which makes sense logistically speaking but each settlement feels independant from the other rather than a living, breathing community that co-exists with the other allied settlements. You can set up supply lines between settlements but all that does is let you use your collective materials in each settlement so you don't have to grind for each settlement to have building materials.
You can also put stores in your settlements which apart from getting a few measily caps (Which you most certainly will not need by the time you even get to build stores) do nothing. I expected to build a shop and for my settlers to buy things there, maybe outfit themselves with new gear etc.. but no, nobody except you will use them. Settlements are fun to build but pretty much pointless.
If you want your settlers to have better gear, you have to equip each settler individually and if you've got multiple settlements that have their population maxed out (max of 21 per settlement) you'll soon just let them rot with their raggedy clothes and weak pipe weapons. Seriously, if they're too stupid to outfit themselves with better stuff then they deserve their fate. C'mon Bethesda...less dead-eyed zombie AI please..
The world you inhabit is pretty huge, there is plenty to do and there are even quests that just do not end (Granted they get real boring real fast) There are plenty of places to explore, plenty of factions to learn about and plenty of interesting characters to meet and while the game isn't exactly on the cutting edge graphically, it still looks pretty damn beautiful....if you can ignore the unfixable and horrid rainbow textures that appear after it's been raining.
I reccomend getting this game but know just like most Bathesda games you are going to have to put up with this game giving you some serious abuse in terms of bugs and stability. Maybe wait for a price drop or a sale.

TLDR at bottom.
It's incredibly fashionable to wail on Fallout 4 and I do understand why. It's not as good as FNV, it's not as good as Fallout 3 and it's unrecognisable from the classic isometric epics. The principal reason for this is that world is vast but is also lifeless in places and much of the expansive wasteland is unused in terms of lore and plot. It's also taken another step from dark and forboding to kitschy and quaint.
Ironically, despite the swathes of empty terrain, I'd actually say there's too much "content" in the game. A lot of the missions are repetitive, radial fetch quests or characterless kill quests with little soul that the game could have done without. As a result, I'm currently sitting at some 138.9 hours for a game I bought at steam-sale prices. To the people complaining about Bethesda's business practices (mostly, I suppose, because the DLC was somewhat rubbish) I would say that's incredibly good value for money. Most triple-A games won't come close to that and whilst there's a question of quality versus quantity, nobody put a gun to my head and made me (or anyone else) play and the game is a tidy timesink.
I should add that whilst my version of FO4 is modded extensively (which I'd put as another mark in the "buy" column,) the modded content has not added quests/missions/land as such should have little impact on my playtime.
I've read reviews of people claiming to be on their fourth or fifth playthrough or whom have put in a thousand odd hours and yet they're telling people they wouldn't recommend the game. This brings me back to my initial point, it's popular to lay in to FO4 but, lets be honest, if you can sink a thousand hours in to a title then you've clearly had your money's worth and you obviously didn't hate it all that much.
Is FO4 the best in the franchise? No. Is it probably the worst? Sadly so. But is it still a game with a lot of enjoyable content that'll quite comfortably justify it's cost by the time you've finished? I'd say so.
TLDR: buy it accepting it's not as good as it's predecessors and you won't be let down. It's still good fun and still worth playing, it just could have been more.

Fallout 4 - The Good
- Smooth game play mechanics
- Stability, low crash rate
- Weapon and armor modification system
- Sidequests that are very interesting and worth the price of admission
- 3 DLCs worth getting as a bundle: Automotron, Far Harbor, Nuka World
- Scrapping and building system at workstation and settlements
- Cross-platform MOD availability
- Open world that is fun to explore, always offering more to see on repeat playthroughs
- Good foreshadowing in main quest
- VATS now slows down time, making combat more imminent for game play
The Bad
- 3 DLCs that are workshop oriented, not story driven
- 3 Factions that seek to be exclusive winners
- Choices for story driven by voiced protagonist, which detracts from RPG immersion
- Radiant quests that are used as XP filler
- Respawning of opponents nearly everywhere detracting from accomplishing anything
- Very few unique weapons
- Legendary system for special weapon and equipment, coupled with respawning leads to farming for equipment
- Main story is quickly exhausted for interest, lacks depth
- Lack of variety in weapons and armor
- Companions while interesting still get in the way during combat, often stepping in front of player when firing
The Ugly
- Factional play does not recognize nor respect protagonist if taking up a faction leader position
- Factions unable to be diverted or see sense when interests align for cooperative work
- Factions not well integrated into DLC content
- The good concept of a pre-war protagonist is wasted on simplistic plot
- Protagonist background and life experience is tossed away and actually ignored by and large
- Skills and Perks rolled into simplified Perk Tree removing hard RPG based decisions
- Retroactive Continuity changes that make no damned sense
- Simplistic main quest
- Use of 'future seeing' NPC that covers many main quest situations indicating lack of freedom of choices for RPG play
- No indication of what Perks and base Stats are influencing decisions leading to heavy use of Charisma based clothing
- Settlements that do not follow the prior game template or historical concept of what a settlement actually is
- Frustrating settlement build system becomes a requirement for parts of main quest
- No DIY main quest options to forego all factions which limits replay interest for main quest
- Really poor AI for companions
- Respawning detracts from immersion and makes little damned sense
- No Karma system
I truly do like Fallout 4 and think it is a decent part of the franchise and well worth buying as a bundle with all its DLCs.  With that said the glaring simplistic main story with its rails that have few decision points and ruthless nature of the main factions towards other factions quickly exhausts that main quest for interesting features.  Coming from a functioning past should have major ramifications for the Fallout universe, and is squandered to the point where any wastelander with a similar problem and drive could fill the protagonist slot due to the nature of the faction driving the quest line.  Having a voiced protagonist limits depth of story as all choice branches would require voice acting and that can get expensive.  These choice limitations make the main story simplistic, rigid and that requires factions to be so rigid in their outlook that they would prefer dying for their cause than to actually interact and negotiate with each other.
As an RPG, Fallout 4 is a pretty good First Person Shooter.  As an FPS, it is a pretty good RPG.  As a Factional game, it lacks faction interplay, removes negotiation and makes crafting interesting RPG stories nearly impossible.  Becoming a Faction leader opens up no opportuinities for guiding that faction, no budgeting, no assignment of NPCs to duties and even has one NPC that can be found tha actually understands how the faction leader of a militia actually works.  This has been a problem with Bethesda and Faction leadership for a long, long time: for all the faction interplay, the logistics end that is the meat and potatos of being a faction head is never granted to the player.  All of this is done with the intention of getting a wider audience and player base for the game and increase revenue, but also points at a lack of understanding of just how sophisticated the average gamer or even the casual gamer is in the modern world.
Thus for smooth game play, stability and very interesting side quests, and a well crafted open world, Fallout 4 is recommended.  As part of the Fallout franchise, it falls behind Fallout New Vegas, Fallout 3 and even the older Fallout and Fallout 2 for lore, continuity of background which is broken by many retcons with little to no back story to them.  Working with prior established limitations in alt-history is a challenge to anyone crafting a game with such prior background and should be utilized and built upon even when it causes troubles since that is an opportunity for enhanced story telling and game play via depth of that background.  Tossing out hard to use background on the altar of smooth game play indicates lack of respect for that background and lack of ingenuity on the part of the game designers.  Fans of a game can be satisfied and challenging game play retained while still making the experience smoother with better physics engines, rendering engines and scripting engines.  Bethesda acquired the Fallout franchise, built on it and that is something that they should respect as a company for their own work that has gone into it, if nothing else.
The elements for a truly great, very deep story line with quests are present but not put into a coherent form to be a part of the main quest.  Thus elements which should naturally fit together, don't.  Interactions with NPCs is frustrating beyond words for the extremely limited options made available to the PC.  For all the voice acting the PC has very little to say in the game.  Coupling these items then makes for RPG frustration as this is the center of RPG play: finding and knitting together options that game designers put into the game to allow for a wide array of choices.
As a player the concept of 'Radiant Quests' and respawning areas make no damned sense at all.  Missions have objectives, objective completion has ramifications, and clearing out a place means it is finally cleared for a good, long time.  In a wasteland with few people, it is impossible to reconcile all the respawning of individuals with the overall low population of the wasteland.  Ditto creatures, come to think of it.  This is filler content put in to cover over lack of meaningful XP rewards and depth of world game play. If there were more and more interesting things to do in the game world, then the concept of Radiant Quests could go away completely.  Tasks that are difficult, that can be done and then offer non-monetary rewards (such as faction reputation) which used to be a part of the prior two installments is removed, which means managing reputation is also removed.
Fallout 4 is a missed opportunity to make a truly great RPG.  For all the misses, frustration with story, and lack of diverse game play it is still on my recommend list for the parts that are right with it, and the general entertainment of being in an interesting open world.  Do all the side quests, do the DLCs and explore to your heart's content and you will not be disappointed.  The engrossing content of Far Harbor, the fun or Automotron or understanding just how Raiders semi-function and why they are irritating as all hell in Nuka World, all will give a great gaming experience.  Try to keep the main story as background, the missions taken up as ones to get some equipment or unlock upgrades, and then bail out on it and just have fun in the game world.  All of the non-main story stuff indicates that Bethesda does know how to create great content if they put their minds to it, and that is worth the price of discounted admission to all the attractions.

Firstly, my review is only a no because of this:
This is not a true Fallout game. Regardless of characters, setting, and the works. This is not a Fallout game.
Fallout is supposed to be an open-ended experience where you discover the world through your own eyes, in retrospect, Fallout 4 had none of these qualities. While the very definition of open-ended is true to this game, it is a very linear experience. I couldn't finish this games story, I was so bored by the premise. Haven't we had enough revenge plots? Fallout has never been about revenge, it's been about redemption, or moral ambiguity and emancipation.
Let's talk about the base-building. While I agree, this is awesome fun, but there is too much of a focus put around it. I found myself building settlements and caring more about Goodfeels the drug-tripping robot than Shawn, and that is a sign that you are not doing Fallout right. Fallout 3 was a far cry from 1 and 2, but it was welcomed with open arms, people loved it. I remember seeing Fallout 3 on EP Daily on G4TV and thinking "Holy crap, that game looks awesome!" and a year later I got my first X-Box 360 and played hundreds of hours of Vanilla Fallout 3. And then picking it up and playing on my old POS laptop at 27 FPS for another few hundred of hours on disc. And then got it again when I retrieved this account from the dusty remnants of a family PC.
I love this game, but because it is a fun game to play. It is, in my heart, not a true sequel and will never be one. If Bethesda can redeem themselves with the next installation, then I will be happy, but as someone who spent days playing Fallout 1, 2, 3 and New Vegas (Which I might add was a more complete Fallout game), I am dissapointed in Todd Howard & Co. for producing a shell of what Fallout is meant to be.

Allow me to get straight to the business, the most note wordy  addition to this game are the weapon arts.While they are a nice addition, I have found myself forgetting about It's existence.
Everything else is standard gameplay that we all know and love so don't expect much innovation.
If you didn't like the other games i don't see any reason why you should pick this one up.

+ Gunplay is vastly improved, no longer do you feel like you are aiming down a brick... or firing one.
- Game is optimized like said bricks. (Well at least the shadows and certain parts are, set shadows to minimum if you need a MAJOR framerate boost)
+ Although game is surprisingly stable, very rarely had crashes in my first 100 hours up until I finally finished the main quest. (Then my save file eventually got huge and crashes became more common)
+ Magazines are more useful and shiny, there are also Pip-Boy minigames. You can loot containers and enemies in realtime, or choose to loot the old fashioned way with a paused menu.
- They removed skillpoints, merged it with perks, equipment is indestructable, you can no longer shoot weapons out of enemy's hands, and they dumbed down a bunch of other stuff.
+ You can customize weapons for maximum death, power armor actually feels like power armor, that actually needs power, and not just some bulky heavy armor you need some obligatory training to use, and VATS is even more useful now with guaranteed crits you charge up with successful hits in VATS.
- Karma is no longer a thing, you are now Neutral Mcgee, forced to pick between 3 factions by the end which are also more or less neutral themselves.
+ People no longer talk to you with a fixed gaze of death like you're about to pick their pockets, which is probably true, because you usually do.
/ Voiced protaganist is... alright. Could be better, and also maybe give us multiple voice actors for the player character, kind of like Saints Row did.
- Dialogue options are shortened and somewhat vague at times
+ Junk items now infinitely more useful, and you can build and manage settlements as a home base with shops and farming.
Overall it's still a pretty fun game, definitely worth it on a good sale. Although it seems like most of the DLC is bricks, time to play the waiting game again...

As my first Souls experience, I can't say a bad word about this game. I enjoyed it from the very beginning to the very end; the atmosphere is just great, awesome level design and many beautiful sceneries. The enemies (quite a lot of them, at least) are tough, and especially the wonderfully designed bosses sometimes require a great deal of patience, precision and memorizing their moves. As a player of average skill, I've seen the iconic "YOU DIED" many times on some of them, but it's simply fun to learn how to overcome obstacles in form of various difficult enemies. Plus the soundtrack of this great game is one of the best I've ever heard, making the bossfights even more epic. Lore of this dark world is really hard to understand, but the more you learn, the more interesting it gets.
About the first DLC, Ashes of Ariandel, in my opinion it adds to the game one of the best, if not the best, areas we've got. Some say it's short, however, the high quality of its content is undisputable and that's what matters. Also, it adds the best, most epic a probably hardest bossfight in all Dark Souls III. Worth every cent, I would say.
Dark Souls is especially known for its difficulty, but I can definitely say that it excels in many more ways. I went through it five times already and I'm still looking forward for my next adventure with a new character, new ways to play, and, of course, a lot of red "YOU DIED" texts all over my screen...
PS: Don't listen to those who say, that you can't enjoy the game with mouse & keyboard. You definitely can.

Okay so first off as i write this review the game is still in beta and is not complete, so with that in mind this review is reviewing the game as such and not as a finished product: Are you at all a fan of sandbox-based games with building elements, similar to terarria or minecraft? Are you in the mood for something just a tad different than those? Well that's what starbound is. It's a relatively simple idea, based mostly around the setup of Terarria (one of the heads of this game worked on Terarria as well, and this is now his baby). It's a sidescrolling sandbox builder game. However, it is far more in-depth than Terarria, with a lot of features that give you more to do besides just randomly dig or walk around. I mean, you still do those things mostly, but random 'dungeons' and buildings spawn along with villages, and some of these buildings  are fairly large and pretty much become an adventure in themselves, jumping over electrified floors or avoiding blade traps, platforming and fighting the inhabitants. The towns have shops with buyable goods of different types. There are a multitude of weapons of many types, from axes, swords, spears and daggers to guns. You can dual wield your 1 handed weapons, or take one and a shield. You can keep your default outfit for looks, and put on better armors under it. Each planet only really has 1 or 2 biome types for the most part, but thankfully that's why you have a space ship. Get some coal, throw it in the feul tank and jump around the galaxy. So many random places to explore, you shouldn't get bored any time in the next milennia. Character creation is a bit more in-depth than terarria, with many clothing options, a few different races, and a 'default pose' option. The soundtrack is very well-done, especially when using headphones (a lot of what's in there is quite subtle and ambient, so headphones really help you catch a lot more of it). The music also changes in different ways depending on the situation, such as becoming 'muffled' when you go underwater, or something like a monster becoming hostile towards you changing it entirely. The backgrounds are miraculously beautiful. You can see the planets or moons near you setting and rising in different ways depending on the rotation, and there are layers upon layers to the backgrounds themselves to help set a very large amount of visual ambience that blows you off your feet when you realize just how much there is to it. This game is totally the pinnacle of sidescrolling sandbox games. I honestly don't even want to talk about the few downsides there are because they don't really detract from the game much... but the only thing I should mention is that you have a heat meter and if there's no sun or you're not near a fire, you will potentially slowly freeze to death, but throw down a torch or two and crouch, and you're all set in a few minutes. As for the beta status of the game don't let that fool you. The game is very far along already and very, very functional. What little you'll notice in terms of bugs and the like, you won't even notice after you really get going. I honestly can't think of any REAL bugs at this point, I have to say. There were a few small ones when I first got the game on launch day, but they have been remedied and anything anyone notices gets reported and the team fixes it as soon as they can. Also the game is going to be fully mod-capable similar to minecraft, which is awesome, and then they are also making it possible to make your own quests as well (oh, yeah, there's actually a small amount of storyline attached to the game to give you minor incentive to actually progress in your explorations). If you're still not convinced, maybe you should watch a few videos. I can't picture anyone disliking this game besides those who hate sidescrolling (i dont care for it much), or those who absolutely need an engrossing story.

As my first Souls experience, I can't say a bad word about this game. I enjoyed it from the very beginning to the very end; the atmosphere is just great, awesome level design and many beautiful sceneries. The enemies (quite a lot of them, at least) are tough, and especially the wonderfully designed bosses sometimes require a great deal of patience, precision and memorizing their moves. As a player of average skill, I've seen the iconic "YOU DIED" many times on some of them, but it's simply fun to learn how to overcome obstacles in form of various difficult enemies. Plus the soundtrack of this great game is one of the best I've ever heard, making the bossfights even more epic. Lore of this dark world is really hard to understand, but the more you learn, the more interesting it gets.
About the first DLC, Ashes of Ariandel, in my opinion it adds to the game one of the best, if not the best, areas we've got. Some say it's short, however, the high quality of its content is undisputable and that's what matters. Also, it adds the best, most epic a probably hardest bossfight in all Dark Souls III. Worth every cent, I would say.
Dark Souls is especially known for its difficulty, but I can definitely say that it excels in many more ways. I went through it five times already and I'm still looking forward for my next adventure with a new character, new ways to play, and, of course, a lot of red "YOU DIED" texts all over my screen...
PS: Don't listen to those who say, that you can't enjoy the game with mouse & keyboard. You definitely can.

Original Review: I wish steam had a 'kinda' rating when I recommend a game like this. If you're low on cash and desperately want something to play, skip this title and get Skyrim or Fallout: New Vegas. If you've got both of those then get an older title in both franchises, if you've got all that then get this, although I'd recommend skipping all the DLC except for Far Harbor.
Why? You might be asking yourself. Because this game is mediocre at best. The main quest is meh, the characters are pretty dull, there's not much in the way of interesting things to do aside from a few side quests and occasionally shooting up a town for no good reason. If you're interested in the settlement building system there are games out there that probably do it better. The settlers you have are all useless and the list of things you can create it pretty small.
While you're likely to spend quite a few hours playing this game, and enjoying them, it's not exactly something that'll blow you away unless you're new to open world games.
Typically when Bethesda brings out a meh game like this the modding community props it up, but they delayed the release of the creation kit (the tool used to make mods) until this game was able to get modding for consoles. As a result the modding community quickly lost interest and went back to Skyrim and New Vegas. These days there's little more than cheat mods and skimpy armor mods being released. Although there are a few things of minor interest dotted around the Fallout 4 Nexus (Don't waste your time on Bethesda's official modding platform,
.
As for the DLC, like I said, only Far Harbor is worth it. All the other DLC's are for the settlment system save for one: Nuka World. Whatever you do don't waste time on Nuka World, it's got grindy hide and seek fetch quests and grinds that would put most B-rate MMO's to shame. If, for some reason, you got the season pass like me then you should simply shoot your way through the DLC and leave it behind as soon as you can, It's just plain awful.
TL;DR: GET SKYRIM OR FALLOUT NEW VEGAS. FALLOUT 4 IS A MEH TITLE, EVEN IF THE BASE GAME IS WORTH THE COST IN TERMS OF HOURS FOR YOUR MONEY!

OR

Fallout 4 is visually striking game that launches you straight into the irradiated wasteland that is post nuclear fallout of America. I've always been a huge fan of the fallout series, from the old 2D RPG to the amazing fallout 3 and New Vegas. There was always something special about this game series, the story was there but you yourself can decide how the game will be played. The same goes for Fallout 4. There is a huge amount of independence in this game, you can explore the every nook and cranny or goes straight to each destination in a linear fashion, it's your decision to make. However there are some instances that are a little annoying, such as the wait feature in the previous games. Need to travel a long distance but are afraid of the dark? Well you have the option to "wait" until sunrise, just click a button and boom, it's a beautiful sunny day in the wasteland! Not anymore. You have to be lucky enough to run into a bench or a stool or an upside down spackle bucket to wait, they completely yanked that feature which is a little upsetting but not a huge deal for most players who don't like to nit pick. Another feature which is less than stellar is the loot ability. Instead of the simple press of a button to open and close the loot screen, it now happens automatically. Sounds great, right? Well if your set in your ways you'll end up hitting that close screen button which instead will bring up your pip boy and trust me, it'll happen every time. Now to the major reason why this game is gonna be game of the year is simple, just one word. Dogmeat. This dog will keep you company in the lonely wasteland and also defend you from the terrifying mutants and farrel ghouls, he'll even find you supplies and loot you might have missed in your frantic searching. Dogmeat is truly a hero of our times. All in all Fallout 4 is a bit different, which is good but it'll take a while to adjust, it is the closest you'll be to experiencing the terror an joy of a post apocalyptic wasteland. I would recommend to anyone who enjoys dogs and killing mutants.

Okay so first off as i write this review the game is still in beta and is not complete, so with that in mind this review is reviewing the game as such and not as a finished product: Are you at all a fan of sandbox-based games with building elements, similar to terarria or minecraft? Are you in the mood for something just a tad different than those? Well that's what starbound is. It's a relatively simple idea, based mostly around the setup of Terarria (one of the heads of this game worked on Terarria as well, and this is now his baby). It's a sidescrolling sandbox builder game. However, it is far more in-depth than Terarria, with a lot of features that give you more to do besides just randomly dig or walk around. I mean, you still do those things mostly, but random 'dungeons' and buildings spawn along with villages, and some of these buildings  are fairly large and pretty much become an adventure in themselves, jumping over electrified floors or avoiding blade traps, platforming and fighting the inhabitants. The towns have shops with buyable goods of different types. There are a multitude of weapons of many types, from axes, swords, spears and daggers to guns. You can dual wield your 1 handed weapons, or take one and a shield. You can keep your default outfit for looks, and put on better armors under it. Each planet only really has 1 or 2 biome types for the most part, but thankfully that's why you have a space ship. Get some coal, throw it in the feul tank and jump around the galaxy. So many random places to explore, you shouldn't get bored any time in the next milennia. Character creation is a bit more in-depth than terarria, with many clothing options, a few different races, and a 'default pose' option. The soundtrack is very well-done, especially when using headphones (a lot of what's in there is quite subtle and ambient, so headphones really help you catch a lot more of it). The music also changes in different ways depending on the situation, such as becoming 'muffled' when you go underwater, or something like a monster becoming hostile towards you changing it entirely. The backgrounds are miraculously beautiful. You can see the planets or moons near you setting and rising in different ways depending on the rotation, and there are layers upon layers to the backgrounds themselves to help set a very large amount of visual ambience that blows you off your feet when you realize just how much there is to it. This game is totally the pinnacle of sidescrolling sandbox games. I honestly don't even want to talk about the few downsides there are because they don't really detract from the game much... but the only thing I should mention is that you have a heat meter and if there's no sun or you're not near a fire, you will potentially slowly freeze to death, but throw down a torch or two and crouch, and you're all set in a few minutes. As for the beta status of the game don't let that fool you. The game is very far along already and very, very functional. What little you'll notice in terms of bugs and the like, you won't even notice after you really get going. I honestly can't think of any REAL bugs at this point, I have to say. There were a few small ones when I first got the game on launch day, but they have been remedied and anything anyone notices gets reported and the team fixes it as soon as they can. Also the game is going to be fully mod-capable similar to minecraft, which is awesome, and then they are also making it possible to make your own quests as well (oh, yeah, there's actually a small amount of storyline attached to the game to give you minor incentive to actually progress in your explorations). If you're still not convinced, maybe you should watch a few videos. I can't picture anyone disliking this game besides those who hate sidescrolling (i dont care for it much), or those who absolutely need an engrossing story.

This game is by far in my opinion the best of the Souls series. The combat is smooth and satisfying. The story is, as always, in the background waiting to be uncovered. The entire world looks absolutely gorgeous.
For those of you who haven't played a Souls game before here is the basis that you need to know before buying
1: This game is rutheless
This game will kill you time and time again however if you stick to it and learn the mechanics it can be the most satisfying game you will ever play
2: The story is not directly told
This game tells its backstory by not doing it at all. Every piece of backstory is found through items and dialog throughout the game.
3: The gameplay is primarily skill based
Sure you can get a super upgraded weapon and one shot everything up to the boss but that boss will then put you in your place as you then have to learn mechanics of how to best combat it.
4: Git gud
Ask any veteran Souls player on how to play this game and this will be their response. Mostly because that is the only way to play it. By getting better and better until you start to subconciously start to learn attack patterns and strategies.
Overall if you want a satisfying game that will give you a satisfying challenge while also subtly giving the backstory to the world then I would highly recommend this game
