I didn't expect to like Fallout 4 much. I knew the systems had been simplified, the UI designed even more for consoles this time, and the full voice acting would mean less dialogue. These were the reasons I disliked Skyrim and Morrowind remains my favorite of that series.
Why I ended up really enjoying Fallout 4, then, I don't know, because of all of that was true. And if anything, Fallout 4 strays even more from the roots I love than the Elder Scrolls has - the original Fallout being just a tad different. Maybe it's that one already had to consider Fallout 3 and New Vegas so differently than the original two that made me not mind the simplification so much. That made me already consider it primarily a shooter, rather than an RPG.
And as a... role-playing open world shooter, it excels. The storyline is good, if possessed of that typical Bethesda bugginess and random immersion-breaking oversights, depending on the order you do things. And not that that should be glossed over, but you do expect it from games so big and open.
And yes, the systems have been simplified, but I actually think it's for the better, despite hating the similar simplifications in Skyrim. That being first and foremost an RPG and this being first and foremost a shooter, and also being based on a... more archaic ruleset (a term I used because it was originally designed as much as a pen and paper RPG as a CRPG, which did hurt it, arguably). I kinda miss skills but the expanded perks actually replace them quite well, and not having to worry so much about a character build lets you just... play. It was exactly what I wanted, as I finally broke down and got it at a time I just wanted action and stealthy violence.
It's not an RPG anymore, and I do wish Bethesda would give Obsidian rights to make isometric Fallout RPGs (though New Vegas was better than 3 as not-that, so maybe just give them everything) and let Bethesda go full-on shooter. But it's a good game.
The interface is more clunky than it needs to be for mouse and keyboard for sure, and that's a flaw, but not a dealbreaker.
On the neutralish side is the settlement-building system. It's pretty bad. You'd think a big studio could do it better than the early access survival crafting games, but nope, it's worse than those. Getting things to snap together properly can be a huge hassle and there's so many oversights in terms of features and building pieces. And a large part of the problems come from needing to make the system simple enough to work with controllers. If not for that, it'd be a lot less frustrating to get things set up right and to get to the pieces you need without a thousand awkward button presses. But all that said, I'm still glad it's there. I'm a sucker for settlement-building. It's fun.
My main complaints, in regard to continuity errors and in other regards, is with the DLC. Playing Far Harbor (which, mind you, you're not prompted to do, I just stumbled upon it) before a certain point in the main quest denies you a lot and makes some things make no sense at all later. So, yeah, have a chat with Nick first.
And most of the smaller DLC is tat. It's almost horse armor. The Vault-Tec Workshop I don't regret getting because it has significantly more content than the others and I have a thing for bunkers, but for the rest I wish I'd just bought them individually instead of bundled. They're garbage. Astoundingly so. Even if there weren't mods that do what they do far, far better, they'd be pathetic. To charge $5 for them is ridiculous. As for the big DLC though, Far Harbor's very very good. Nuka-World is okay but presents a role-playing/characterization problem of it gives your character no good reason to get involved and not just kill everyone immediately. So I'm gonna try a less "good guy" playthrough and then maybe it'll make more sense to (SPOILER!) be dealing with and ruling raiders.
And, as an update, Creation Club is now a thing. Paid mods that totally aren't paid mods but are actually paid mods. And they're garbage; worse versions of things available for free. And the creators get a horrible deal for their efforts. It's a stupid program. But it doesn't really hurt your experience. Okay, there have been a couple updates there otherwise wouldn't have been that have required not-crap, free mods to update. Which sucks, and is a bit of a hassle. It's definitely a negative thing, but not enough to make the game not enjoyable - as the mods that make it great still work, once their wonderful authors update them. And there's no evidence Bethesda is doing this deliberately to mess up free mods, at least that I know of.
So yeah, fudge the Creation Club, but it's really not something that matters much; just choose not to use it. There's even mods to disable it in your game so it's not shoving ads at you. Bottom line: Bethesda are greedy jerks; the game is good anyway.

This is not a terrible game. That's the best that I can say for Fallout 4. It's adequate. No more, no less. It's like Bethesda assumed that the gaming world has been sat around twiddling their collective thumbs since FNV, therefore releasing a game that doesn't greatly improve upon the previous games in the series would be okay. However, war may not change, but gaming expectations certainly do.
I put plenty of hours into Fallout 4, and it's been an okay experience. However, few memorable moments come to mind. Certainly, there's nothing memorable about the story writing. It chugs along, but never creates any emotional impact. The lazy "this is your son therefore you must care" trope didn't grab me at all. I enjoyed shooting things, so I stayed with it, but i never gave a damn about the story from beginning to end. There's the illusion of choice, but all paths lead to the same end with only a few cosmetic variations. Bethesda have churned out a decent action shooter, but at the expense of any discernible roleplaying experience.
This brings me to another problem. NPCs in Fallout 4 are the kind of lifeless RPG mannequins that must surely be unacceptable in modern RPGs, especially when set against the NPCs found in games like Witcher 3. I enjoyed killing the NPCs in Fallout 4, but I never enjoyed a single conversation with any of them. Once again, they're adequate but nothing more. Worse than this , the companion choice is dreadful. The approval/disapproval system is bizarre and illogical and the constant repetition of the few lines of dialogue given to each companion is maddening. Companions in Fallout 4 are a bland, poorly executed, tick box addition. Each companion's simplistic motivation is driven home with all the subtlety of a stake driven through a vampire's heart, and their behaviour in battle is often insane, operating as a bullet shield for the enemy as they weave back and forth in front of you, soaking up your bullets. Take my advice and solo the game.
I actually enjoyed the settlement building aspect. It's badly thought out, poorly executed and ultimately has little discernible pay off. However, I enjoy settlement building games, so i overlooked the bad points in favour of building things. My impression though, is that Bethesda introduced the settlement building element with the best of intentions, but like so many aspects of Fallout 4, they checked out when it got too complicated and left a half built, buggy mechanic that doesn't really go anywhere.
DLC isn't up to much, lacking quantity (given the price of the Season Pass) and quality. Again, much of it is adequate but nothing more than that. If you never had any of it, you wouldn't be any worse for its absence. It's just more of the same, really.
As an open world shooter, Fallout 4 is a decent enough game. There's plenty of opportunity to shoot a reasonable varity of enemies in different places. If you're not big on RPG elements, then I can guarantee that you won't find many anyway, so all well and good.
I didn't finish my first play through, but when i returned to the game a few months later, I treated it as an average shooter rather than a profoundly disappointing RPG, and enjoyed it a bit more, managing to finish it. However, finishing games like DAI, Witcher 3 and the Mass Effect games left me with a void in my gaming that took a while to fill. I had no trouble moving on from Fallout 4, and that's disappointing.
If Bethesda are intent on continuing to churn out bland cash cows, then I don't think i'll be purchasing any more of their titles. There's nothing in Fallout 4 that indicates a creator wanting to dazzle the gaming community. Instead it's a game that smacks of a Bethesda team that knew it could get away with churning out an average game, because gamers would still purchase it anyway. Shame on them and shame on us for going along with it. Sadly, I don't expect to see a change in their next title, as they seem happy to cede the quality ground to other producers in return for creating bland, forgettable profit makers.
Fallout 4 is a decent shooter and I never got bored with shooting things. As an RPG though, it's a throwback to games that have long been surpassed. Years ago, Bethesda could get away with a by the numbers story and a world full of bland NPCs. All the other games back then were pretty much the same, anyway. Nowadays though, RPG gamers are feasting on games like Witcher 3 and in comparison, as an RPG Fallout 4 is an outdated, clunky and banal disappointment. It's a thumbs down from me, because I wanted a great RPG and instead I got an average shooter with a big price tag attached.

Fallout 4 is visually striking game that launches you straight into the irradiated wasteland that is post nuclear fallout of America. I've always been a huge fan of the fallout series, from the old 2D RPG to the amazing fallout 3 and New Vegas. There was always something special about this game series, the story was there but you yourself can decide how the game will be played. The same goes for Fallout 4. There is a huge amount of independence in this game, you can explore the every nook and cranny or goes straight to each destination in a linear fashion, it's your decision to make. However there are some instances that are a little annoying, such as the wait feature in the previous games. Need to travel a long distance but are afraid of the dark? Well you have the option to "wait" until sunrise, just click a button and boom, it's a beautiful sunny day in the wasteland! Not anymore. You have to be lucky enough to run into a bench or a stool or an upside down spackle bucket to wait, they completely yanked that feature which is a little upsetting but not a huge deal for most players who don't like to nit pick. Another feature which is less than stellar is the loot ability. Instead of the simple press of a button to open and close the loot screen, it now happens automatically. Sounds great, right? Well if your set in your ways you'll end up hitting that close screen button which instead will bring up your pip boy and trust me, it'll happen every time. Now to the major reason why this game is gonna be game of the year is simple, just one word. Dogmeat. This dog will keep you company in the lonely wasteland and also defend you from the terrifying mutants and farrel ghouls, he'll even find you supplies and loot you might have missed in your frantic searching. Dogmeat is truly a hero of our times. All in all Fallout 4 is a bit different, which is good but it'll take a while to adjust, it is the closest you'll be to experiencing the terror an joy of a post apocalyptic wasteland. I would recommend to anyone who enjoys dogs and killing mutants.

Ok so after reading some negative reviews given to this game lately, I decided to make one my self.  The amount of hours played you see above are hours ACTUALLY played, not idle.
I absolutely loved this game.  From graphics, to game play, to story, and side quests.  Its fantastic.  Honestly one of my top 5 favorate RPGs I've ever played.
Story: Many reviewers claim the story to be boring, but I didn't find this to be true.  The trick to enjoying the story is to    allow yourself to get distracted by the sidequests that naturally are encountered as you proceed with your main story.  This is one of those things I really enjoyed about this game.  There are many gray areas in the way the story unfolds.  I believe that the developers meant for this.  Many times you will find that the best decision isn't the perfect decision you wish existed.  There are some repetitive quests that seem to go on forever. These are tied directly to each faction and require some fetching and killing.
Gameplay:  The game can be played both in 3rd person and first person point of view, and over all the gameplay feels more like an action game than an RPG.  I played the game in survival so this is more true in my case.  You either kill fast or are killed fast.
Graphics:  Fantastic! Considering this game is a sandbox, the graphics are neat, stable, with good art style.  Comparing the graphics of this game to a modern first person shooter may not really be appropriate due to the fact that this game is a huge sandbox, not a static piece of land with nothing to interact with.
DLCs
So far I've only played and finished Far Harbor and Automatron, on these add-ons I probably played more than 60 hours combined.  The Far Harbor story line follows the same concept as the main story line, where the best ending isn't the 'perfect' ending.
There were some things I didn't enjoy as much.
Story:
As mentioned above, the story has too many gray areas.  I found myself reloading many times to choose different dialogs in order to see which decision gave the better outcome.  It just isn't obvious which decisions are the absolute BEST.  I believe this was intended, I just wish it was more clear which choice is the 'good' or 'evil'.
Gameplay:
I wish the game was more 'dangerous' than what it is.  I find myself walking for long distances without encountering any enemies or danger zones, even in survival.
Overall I absolutely recommend this game to anyone.

Three hundred plus hours and I'm still feeling conflicted. I played through on Survival mode until that was patched into something very different, then played on Very Hard after that. I never used fast travel, though I did use teleportation and vertibirds when they were respectively available.
The core of the gameplay I enjoy from Fallout is still here. Exploration, discovery, varying quests to go on, but... at the same time, things are more modular than before. The radiant quests quickly become cookie-cutter affairs with nothing to offer - I literally visited the same school three or four times after getitng a quest to wipe out ghouls there. After the first time, I'd just march through the school, and there literally would be one ghoul who'd stand up to obligingly provide a target. I'd kill that ghoul, then return to collect my reward when I felt like it.
Still, there are marked improvements. The game looks fantastic compared to its predecessors, though animations are as janky as ever - right now, I have a survivor whose hands clip into her pouches if she goes into idle stance. When certain robots were given the ability to run, they weren't given a running animation. Instead, they walk super-fast in an animation that would go along well with Yakety Sax. Having conversations modeled after Mass Effect with full voice is a welcome improvement to me - it at least gives an excuse to look at my painstakingly modelled character.
Companions are vastly better than Fallout 3, though they tend to be a mixed bag, with some having genuinely great writing while others flounder in bizarre, self-contradictory ways. Like the one companion motivated solely by family that then chastises you for saving a child at your own (modest) personal cost. Increasing one's relationships is an obtuse and unclear system that at times will require you to consult a game guide to make heads or tails of. One time I made best friends with somebody by robbing a totally abandoned house. This impressed him, somehow.
Settlement creation is a lot of fun, when the clunky lego-style construction system isn't frustrating with its unexplained quirks. Building large buildings to the sky was my favorite part, but ultimately it doesn't matter too much. By making it entirely optional, there's no profound rewards after making two dozen or so havens of humanity. I mean, I feel a little better after bothering, but that was a lot of time spent on something the game fundamentally doesn't reward. Of course, playing without fast travel made them more personally useful for me as waystations and crafting zone, but if you're playing the game as designed, there's less of a point.
Enemies are improved with better animations and more variety, though only modestly so. Instead of just having "guy with gun that shoots at you" and "creature that charges to bite or claw" you also have some tunneling monsters, ghouls will zig-zag and lunge, deathclaws will throw stones at you when out of range... but the improvements are slight. Mostly it's still guns and biting. Still, effort was made. Some enemies are "legendary", a stupid way of saying they're damage soaks that contain a random item. These are a big deal until you've settled on a loadout of rare items, after which point they become pinatas with more saleable loot.
Perks are now plentiful and can be leveled up, but generally don't vastly change things. Some are still, annoying, just gating mechanisms (crafting, hacking, lockpicking) while others specialize you with numeric bonuses. Some enable more serious changes (like trade routes, which become essential if you're into building) but they're in the minority. In general, the idea of a "build" is dampened a bit as you'll often be just getting into the gating perks right off the bat and not getting to specialize until dozens of levels in.
The story is the biggest weakness. While you have unparalleled choice in many of the system elements, the story requires you to settle on some degree of moral compromise (unless you pick the boring guys) with no ability to change the beliefs or policies of the faction you're with. The factions are there to change you, not the other way around, and all you can do is just settle the score under whatever flag you choose, even if it's a way you never wanted to do it for a faction you likely feel distasteful. Though Bethesda likely thought having this kind of forced moral ambiguity was more "deep" narratively, it mostly just makes you feel like a prisoner of the script.
After all this, why did I put in 300+ hours and give this a thumbs up? Because despite all that, this is still one of the top open-world exploration games out there. Its most exciting moments are unplanned, like that time I was trapped in a house early on in a deathclaw, afraid to step out to get slaughtered. Building my power armor museum over the river. Beating a super-mutant boss with my sword, too close for him to wind-up his miniguns. Hell, I haven't even started up on mods, which will likely improve my experience massively as that community grows and develops.
So it's flawed, but its ambition makes it consistently compelling nonetheless. Though I've finished my survivor's story, I'll be coming back with mods maybe a year down the road... and maybe another 300 hours. We'll see.

Starbound is a Terraria Clone, I said to myself when I was still young and ignorant to the world - five days ago.
I vastly prefer Starbound over Terraria. I'll give Terraria credit with being an early, mainstream, 2D, "True Sandbox" though. A lot of people saw it as Minecraft2D, basically, and that's mostly because it's part of the same genre. Resource gathering and base making.
I think the devs of Starbound looked at Terraria and said, "Okay, here's what's good about the game, and here's what's bad. How can we remove the bad and make the good better?" I think they really did achieve that goal, even with the early beta access, and I have high trust in the future of the game.
Minecraft really did start that whole "True Sandbox" thing - at least as far as I'm aware. It was very basic at the time, though. A lot of people tried to piggyback on to it by making Minecraft clones, but they rarely changed anything up. None of them really seemed to come into the mainstream and stick.
Terraria comes along and changes the game by putting in a 2 dimensional world that was more focused on action gameplay, rather than resource gathering, even though the gathering and building was still part of the core gameplay. Like Minecraft, Terraria was (to my knowledge) the first game of its kind - but it was still basic. The combat didn't feel like it had much variety, there are some balancing issues in the game, and the monsters were very generic.
Enter Starbound.
Starbound has implemented something that both Minecraft and Terraria neglected - a plot. While it narrows the scope for interpretation, it also creates a very subtle narrative and provides a "why" for the "what". Now when I play the game, I'm not just playing for the sake of building and and expanding. I'm playing to figure out what's going on. I want to learn the lore of the different races and explore the motivation of my character. I want to walk into a village and get an idea of what the people are like through the books they keep, the things they say, and the things in the environment. On a superficial level, Starbound really does look like a Terraria clone, but once again it has changed something. It added a story. It makes me actually feel for what's happening in game. I feel like I'm motivated to do the things I do, rather than to just do them.
Starbound gives me hope for the continuation of the True Sandbox genre, as I like to call it. The manipulation of the world is great, stories are present now, and we have a great deal of ways to express ourselves in game. In my opinion, the next step is to create combat that feels satisfying. I want to play a game like Minecraft with a Z-targeting fighting style like seen in Legend of Zelda. If not that, then give me a game like Terraria or Starbound with a fighting system like Dust: An Elysian Tail.
There's just SO much room for growth in this genre, and I'm super excited to see where the future takes it. Starbound is definitely another step in furthering this genre, and if you enjoyed games such as Minecraft or Terraria, you will absolutely love Starbound.

People have demonstrated consistently since Fallout 4's release how dangerous expectations can be. To expect great things from the game, and to be disappointed when those expectations are not met, is quite normal. When judgement is rendered solely on the result of those expectations, the fatal mistake is made. It in turn leads to a propensity for jumping to conclusions, and from that point it's a rapid descent into ignorance.
Back when Fallout 4 was released, most of the Steam reviews consisted of incoherent, furious ranting that tarnished the whole title after only a few hours worth of gameplay. After being shocked by the overwhelming amount of negativity, I decided to make my own and openly condemned the bad reviews for what they were: baseless and devoid of perspective. It was quite obvious the authors made that fatal mistake, which is unfair to the many developers who put their soul and passion into creating the game.
In the end, Fallout fans will almost assuredly find disappointments with Fallout 4, as did I. But if the ignorance of the older reviews and reception of previous games ought to teach one thing, it's that those disappointments are no excuse for blind judgement or jumping to conclusions. If an opinion is to be rendered of this game in the form of review, let it be guided by reason and supported by logic. It is in the pursuit of that fairness and clarity that I chose to write this review.
----------------------------------------
Fallout 4 is a deeply enjoyable and well-crafted game. However, it definitely has its issues. Bethesda tried new things in this title, some more ambitious than others, and not all of them were successful.
It's true that dialogue has been watered down as the devs chose to forgo text conversation choices in favor of a voiced and much more simplified dialogue wheel, which is further hampered by boring choices and weak voice work. Character advancements have been combined into a single perk/SPECIAL sheet. Settlement building, while certainly fun, is mostly aesthetic filler that has little impact on the game world. Side quests far too often amount to just killing some mandatory enemies, particularly with the Minutemen (who are supposed to be the "good guys" of this installment), and can become repetitive.
My most prominent grievance with Fallout 4 is the dialogue overhaul and removal of the karma system, which was completely unnecessary and not desired by a single player in existence. Unlike the previous flaws, this thoroughly irks me. I realized that this ties in to the primary weakness of Fallout 4: its lack of meaningful dialogue in comparison to most Bethesda titles. Far too often, your dialogue choices are short, shallow, meaningless, or all three.
The only choices that have any outcome are blatantly outlined as persuasion options, a lot of which only help you get some extra caps. It's not that you should be making major decisions all the time; the problem is that you, as a speaking character, now have a voice that carries no power. What you decide to say is almost always inconsequential. The dialogue system is highly reminiscent of Mass Effect except watered down; the reason it doesn't work in Fallout is that the two games have totally different approaches to conversation. The previous Fallout games had much better dialogue options because they meant something. Sometimes, your choice of words just made someone hate you, allowed you to entice or inspire others, or developed your reputation through the karma system. Now that karma is gone, your choices are just that much more pointless.
The bottom line is that Bethesda sacrificed a tremendous amount of RPG dialogue elements to accommodate full voice-work. While it was an ambitious attempt, it was an all-around mistake and it sticks out like a sore if you're a fan of Bethesda games or RPG's in general. The dialogue wheel system could have worked out just fine, but Bethesda carried it out in the wrong way.
----------------------------------------
All the aforementioned flaws are some of the most central complaints naysayers have about Fallout 4 and yet not a single one of them has been horrific enough to ruin my experience or let me down. Despite the few bugs I've come across, despite the certain questionable and sometimes idiotic design choices Bethesda made here, this game is still extremely well done. I still feel that incomparable thrill that only Fallout can bring.
Even though Fallout 4 falls extremely short on dialogue and all aspects associated with it, it's still an improvement over its predecessors in almost every other way imaginable. The game suffers some graphical issues like muddy textures and poor lighting at times, like any good Bethesda game, but it's still astoundingly beautiful and even breathtaking at times. Movement, melee, gunplay, and physics are better and smoother than they've ever been.
People were quick to judge the Commonwealth map based on its size and I was prepared to be disappointed as well, but it's surprisingly the best one Bethesda has whipped up thus far. The suburban locations are more organically dispersed and things become more compressed as you near the cities. Streets are narrow, buildings are tall, and locations are absolutely jam-packed alongside a ton of unmarked ruins and buildings you can enter. There are hardly any copy-pasted environments and they all show great attention to detail.
I was also worried that granting access to power armor and a minigun within the first thirty minutes of the game would be a huge balancing issue as well, but it really isn’t. Power armor relies on uncommon fusion cores for power and you’re not an unstoppable god while wearing the suit, especially not at higher difficulties or levels. You can acquire some strong weapons like the minigun or Fatman relatively early but finding sufficient ammo is another matter entirely.
----------------------------------------
Skyrim was a simplification of the Oblivion formula, but it was still a fantastic game. In much the same way, Fallout 4 is a simplification of the Fallout 3/New Vegas formula and is still extremely good. Even in light of its issues, this game has not been a disappointment at all. RPG elements can be enhanced through the wonderful modding community and will eventually make up for some of the game's weaker points, a perk of the PC version. Bethesda has, however, been on a recent trend of simplifying their games too much and I hope they change course.
Truthfully, the negative Steam reviews had me partly worried that I’d be disappointed but I chose to disregard them and arrive at my own opinion. I’ve learned that nearly every point of contention was blown out of context. The few issues that haven’t been redeemed in my eyes still pale in the face of the tremendous work that was done to bring this new and beautiful Fallout world to life. I have no doubt that the naysayers worked up their expectations to heights beyond reason, and it’s therefore no mystery that they hit the ground so hard afterwards. I chose to see Fallout 4 for what it is rather than what I expected or imagined it to be: a lovingly crafted game that, despite being marred by some of its shortcomings, has that same engaging splendor that far supercedes its flaws.
I highly recommend you try the game and approach it with a neutral and reasonable demeanor, and you won’t be disappointed.
----------------------------------------

I hope that my review has given you some useful perspective, either good or bad.

You're automatically a male infantry army veteran or a female law major with a certain voice that might not match your personal vision of this character at all, with a son, not a daughter, that you've spent little to no time at all with and are expected to search for simply on the basis of it allegedly being your child. (Which I have doubts of myself when my family is blonde and white and my son looks African -_- ) #NateIsACuckConfirmed
You are to do this despite the best efforts of the entire world's petty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that they could solve themselves, by walking virtually halfway across the map to a city where you are presented with more of other peoples' problems. Now of course, you don't have to do any of these, I understand that. But many of these problems such as kidnappings, stolen items, etc. realistically carry a certain agency to them that in real life I just wouldn't simply ignore for a month or two or forever.
Then when it comes to factions, every single one, save for the Minutemen (which in order to progress in you have to do all those petty quests I mentioned a second ago) is extremely stubborn about their ideology and provides no potential way to interfere with this in any significant manner. Once you're finished with the Institute play-through, people treat you like garbage and question you and Ad Hominem you based on issues with the Institute you could have changed if the choices were broadened, such as halting the kidnapping of Commonwealth citizens and an incredibly high speech check to treat Synths more respectfully. Overall, it felt like I was nothing more than a tool for each faction's agenda.
Unique weapons and gear, while at first being somewhat useful, don't really look all that unique in comparison to earlier games. The effects they provide are very repetitious and the actual Uniques are eventually watered down by Legendary pickups of potentially greater effect. I prefer having no Legendary drops and unique weapons of demonstrable long-term value that I can't simply one-up 5 levels later.
For some reason, everything in this game is ridiculously heavy! 28 pound assault rifles? Really? What the hell are these things made of, were soldiers injected with Steroids regularly? 45 pound hammers? Come on!
Then the power armor disappointed me pretty hard in a couple ways. For starters the fact that you literally can get it as soon as 5 minutes after leaving the Vault with no barriers saddened me. Whatever happened to specialized training? Why do I see just about every raider stronghold there is with guys in power armor? Next, there's the fact that they require 15 minute fuel sticks called Fusion Cores. What?! No, no, no. Power armor, at least the T-51, is powered by fuel cells that last 100 years. A hundred years! If fusion cores were supposed to be those fuel cells, you should have only required one per PA frame. Third, Power Armor is supposed to be a man-portable tank. Tanks don't fall apart when shot 30 times with pipe guns. Not even in the exact same spot. The only things that could have potentially done real damage to power armor were high explosives, which again, are far too common, you literally can acquire a Fat Man some 3 miles away from Sanctuary Hills, and MAYBE anti-material weapons such as the .50 caliber sniper, which was laughably impotent after discovering the Overseer's Guardian which has MUCH more common ammunition, and the Gauss rifle.
The graphics, while praised by many, were too cartoonish, low-detailed, and way too happy and colorful for my tastes. The slow movement and the headbob combined with the non in-game adjustable LOW FOV gave me motion sickness after a few hours unless I sat 8 feet away and played with a controller. For the last time, headbob is NOT realistic. Your brain literally compensates for head bob when you walk to give as smooth of a transition as possible. Bobbing arms are more than enough to show that you're moving, and if you can't tell when you're sprinting or walking, something is wrong with the game's speed. Nuff said.
The optimization on my beyond recommended spec PC was as poor as boiled peasant♥♥♥♥♥♥to drink, with crippling frame dips on my FX-8350 4.5 GHz and R9 380X 1100MHz with 16 GB of 1866 RAM, and the loading times were abysmal on my Crucial SSD with specifically separate installation from my OS. To me, having consistently smooth framerate at common resolutions is more important than graphics and story combined, because if I get nausea trying to discover a plot, I'm better off reading a book.
And there's no reputation, OR Karma system! No consequences for being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not enough options TO be a♥♥♥♥♥♥
The dialogue was atrocious and copied Bioware RPGs. More skill checks and perk references!
The world Bethesda built was incredible, but I feel like there should have been more of it. And the small stories found via terminals and holotapes were fun.
The leveling system is a joke. Please, go to New Vegas' system and give us the option to cap our levels so we don't become masters of everything. Better yet, why not do an Oblivion style level system, where you have main skills, secondary skills, class presets, traits in the place of birthsigns, and what you aren't good at, you don't advance in nearly as fast as your talents.
The lore, as per the usual with a Bethesda game post-2002, contradicts the ♥♥♥♥ out of itself.
And no more level scaling!
Rant over.

The game is pretty fun. Though, unfortunately, it needs mods to really be a great game.
The base game just feels a bit hollow and lifeless. The story was actually pretty good, I personally don't care about your character being voiced. I wish they were a little more original with your overarching goal. F3 "Where's my dad?" F4 "Where's my son? A bit lazy and the dialogue can be annoying.
Settlements! I love the idea of settlements. I absolutely loved the RTS (Real Time Settlement Mods) from Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas. And the concept behind making a settlement is something I always wanted and just love. The problem, is pretty huge though. Settlements are fun to build in - and that is about it.
Settlers are completely devoid of life. They focused way to much on the building part and no where near enough on making settlers themselves interesting. It is lackluster. Scavenger settlers don't really do much besides wander to a few points - would be amazing if they actually wandered out a ways into the world looking for actual scrap. Farmers just farm for all eternity and don't really do anything else. Vendors/shops that you open just sit there.. waiting for you - because no one else will ever visit or use them.
You can't tell settlers to follow you around, they don't have names, they don't have anything that would make you feel connected to them - they are just a number to your settlement. Settlers are immortal without mods which removes any suspense there might be in being raided.
I could almost forgive them for this if they didn't champion this has some great feature they added. It just feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and misses half the importance of a settlement - it isn't just minecraft building it is also about the settlers and feeling some sort of investment in them. But it is lifeless and not immersive. And several DLC focus entirely on expanding settlements! But they only expand what you can build.
DLC: Far Harbor is great. Automatron is pretty cool. I haven't bought the others yet because, honestly, after much research into them they just don't seem worth the full price. Nuka World allows a new type of settlement - raider settlements! Except.. it is just as lifeless as all the others.
It should be noted that Vault-Tec DLC appears to add some life through the couple of items that they add - the "experiments" can essentially function as recreational items - allowing your settlers to do something besides sit around all day. They really should of added a ton more of these.
Big complaints:
The terrible trend of dumbing down PC games in order to make it easier/cheaper to port them to consoles is a big negative here. I have nothing against consoles but it is clear this was the case. Example #1: YOUR BASH KEY AND STRONG ATTACK ARE ALSO THE SAME KEY AS THROW GRENADES. The most horrific thing to be added into a game in a long time. Whoever thought of this should be fired. Trying to power attack or bash an enemy? Oh, you got caught up in that intense fight and held that key for .1 seconds too long - well enjoy your own molotov nuking your face off.
Dialogue. Not a fan of how they dumbed it down and were lazy about it. I suppose they thought they could cut corners with a voice actor and just make every option "yes, no, sarcastic, leave". No idea what your character will actually say. Really lame.
Combat and graphics are good, no real complaints.
The World: The world, is great. It is smaller than previous titles - but there is so much detail and life in it that I find it acceptable. I still find myself discovering new things in the city that I never saw or noticed before. Amazing world building, for sure.
Why a negative review? I do think the game is worth full price and it is very fun and you will most likely get your money's worth. But negative review because they should of done so much better. I want this franchise to grow in a positive way. And I don't feel that Fallout 4 was a great leap forward from New Vegas or Fallout 3. It was just kind of a side step. It got better graphics but lost out on so much more - worse writting, less immersive, etc. And a lot of the DLC felt like they didn't know what direction to go with - it just feels impromptu - just so they could push out DLC.
TL;DR:
Settlements feel lifeless. Buy all the DLC only on sale - except Far Harbor, that one is really worth full price.

People have demonstrated consistently since Fallout 4's release how dangerous expectations can be. To expect great things from the game, and to be disappointed when those expectations are not met, is quite normal. When judgement is rendered solely on the result of those expectations, the fatal mistake is made. It in turn leads to a propensity for jumping to conclusions, and from that point it's a rapid descent into ignorance.
Back when Fallout 4 was released, most of the Steam reviews consisted of incoherent, furious ranting that tarnished the whole title after only a few hours worth of gameplay. After being shocked by the overwhelming amount of negativity, I decided to make my own and openly condemned the bad reviews for what they were: baseless and devoid of perspective. It was quite obvious the authors made that fatal mistake, which is unfair to the many developers who put their soul and passion into creating the game.
In the end, Fallout fans will almost assuredly find disappointments with Fallout 4, as did I. But if the ignorance of the older reviews and reception of previous games ought to teach one thing, it's that those disappointments are no excuse for blind judgement or jumping to conclusions. If an opinion is to be rendered of this game in the form of review, let it be guided by reason and supported by logic. It is in the pursuit of that fairness and clarity that I chose to write this review.
----------------------------------------
Fallout 4 is a deeply enjoyable and well-crafted game. However, it definitely has its issues. Bethesda tried new things in this title, some more ambitious than others, and not all of them were successful.
It's true that dialogue has been watered down as the devs chose to forgo text conversation choices in favor of a voiced and much more simplified dialogue wheel, which is further hampered by boring choices and weak voice work. Character advancements have been combined into a single perk/SPECIAL sheet. Settlement building, while certainly fun, is mostly aesthetic filler that has little impact on the game world. Side quests far too often amount to just killing some mandatory enemies, particularly with the Minutemen (who are supposed to be the "good guys" of this installment), and can become repetitive.
My most prominent grievance with Fallout 4 is the dialogue overhaul and removal of the karma system, which was completely unnecessary and not desired by a single player in existence. Unlike the previous flaws, this thoroughly irks me. I realized that this ties in to the primary weakness of Fallout 4: its lack of meaningful dialogue in comparison to most Bethesda titles. Far too often, your dialogue choices are short, shallow, meaningless, or all three.
The only choices that have any outcome are blatantly outlined as persuasion options, a lot of which only help you get some extra caps. It's not that you should be making major decisions all the time; the problem is that you, as a speaking character, now have a voice that carries no power. What you decide to say is almost always inconsequential. The dialogue system is highly reminiscent of Mass Effect except watered down; the reason it doesn't work in Fallout is that the two games have totally different approaches to conversation. The previous Fallout games had much better dialogue options because they meant something. Sometimes, your choice of words just made someone hate you, allowed you to entice or inspire others, or developed your reputation through the karma system. Now that karma is gone, your choices are just that much more pointless.
The bottom line is that Bethesda sacrificed a tremendous amount of RPG dialogue elements to accommodate full voice-work. While it was an ambitious attempt, it was an all-around mistake and it sticks out like a sore if you're a fan of Bethesda games or RPG's in general. The dialogue wheel system could have worked out just fine, but Bethesda carried it out in the wrong way.
----------------------------------------
All the aforementioned flaws are some of the most central complaints naysayers have about Fallout 4 and yet not a single one of them has been horrific enough to ruin my experience or let me down. Despite the few bugs I've come across, despite the certain questionable and sometimes idiotic design choices Bethesda made here, this game is still extremely well done. I still feel that incomparable thrill that only Fallout can bring.
Even though Fallout 4 falls extremely short on dialogue and all aspects associated with it, it's still an improvement over its predecessors in almost every other way imaginable. The game suffers some graphical issues like muddy textures and poor lighting at times, like any good Bethesda game, but it's still astoundingly beautiful and even breathtaking at times. Movement, melee, gunplay, and physics are better and smoother than they've ever been.
People were quick to judge the Commonwealth map based on its size and I was prepared to be disappointed as well, but it's surprisingly the best one Bethesda has whipped up thus far. The suburban locations are more organically dispersed and things become more compressed as you near the cities. Streets are narrow, buildings are tall, and locations are absolutely jam-packed alongside a ton of unmarked ruins and buildings you can enter. There are hardly any copy-pasted environments and they all show great attention to detail.
I was also worried that granting access to power armor and a minigun within the first thirty minutes of the game would be a huge balancing issue as well, but it really isn’t. Power armor relies on uncommon fusion cores for power and you’re not an unstoppable god while wearing the suit, especially not at higher difficulties or levels. You can acquire some strong weapons like the minigun or Fatman relatively early but finding sufficient ammo is another matter entirely.
----------------------------------------
Skyrim was a simplification of the Oblivion formula, but it was still a fantastic game. In much the same way, Fallout 4 is a simplification of the Fallout 3/New Vegas formula and is still extremely good. Even in light of its issues, this game has not been a disappointment at all. RPG elements can be enhanced through the wonderful modding community and will eventually make up for some of the game's weaker points, a perk of the PC version. Bethesda has, however, been on a recent trend of simplifying their games too much and I hope they change course.
Truthfully, the negative Steam reviews had me partly worried that I’d be disappointed but I chose to disregard them and arrive at my own opinion. I’ve learned that nearly every point of contention was blown out of context. The few issues that haven’t been redeemed in my eyes still pale in the face of the tremendous work that was done to bring this new and beautiful Fallout world to life. I have no doubt that the naysayers worked up their expectations to heights beyond reason, and it’s therefore no mystery that they hit the ground so hard afterwards. I chose to see Fallout 4 for what it is rather than what I expected or imagined it to be: a lovingly crafted game that, despite being marred by some of its shortcomings, has that same engaging splendor that far supercedes its flaws.
I highly recommend you try the game and approach it with a neutral and reasonable demeanor, and you won’t be disappointed.
----------------------------------------

Starbound is a Terraria Clone, I said to myself when I was still young and ignorant to the world - five days ago.
I vastly prefer Starbound over Terraria. I'll give Terraria credit with being an early, mainstream, 2D, "True Sandbox" though. A lot of people saw it as Minecraft2D, basically, and that's mostly because it's part of the same genre. Resource gathering and base making.
I think the devs of Starbound looked at Terraria and said, "Okay, here's what's good about the game, and here's what's bad. How can we remove the bad and make the good better?" I think they really did achieve that goal, even with the early beta access, and I have high trust in the future of the game.
Minecraft really did start that whole "True Sandbox" thing - at least as far as I'm aware. It was very basic at the time, though. A lot of people tried to piggyback on to it by making Minecraft clones, but they rarely changed anything up. None of them really seemed to come into the mainstream and stick.
Terraria comes along and changes the game by putting in a 2 dimensional world that was more focused on action gameplay, rather than resource gathering, even though the gathering and building was still part of the core gameplay. Like Minecraft, Terraria was (to my knowledge) the first game of its kind - but it was still basic. The combat didn't feel like it had much variety, there are some balancing issues in the game, and the monsters were very generic.
Enter Starbound.
Starbound has implemented something that both Minecraft and Terraria neglected - a plot. While it narrows the scope for interpretation, it also creates a very subtle narrative and provides a "why" for the "what". Now when I play the game, I'm not just playing for the sake of building and and expanding. I'm playing to figure out what's going on. I want to learn the lore of the different races and explore the motivation of my character. I want to walk into a village and get an idea of what the people are like through the books they keep, the things they say, and the things in the environment. On a superficial level, Starbound really does look like a Terraria clone, but once again it has changed something. It added a story. It makes me actually feel for what's happening in game. I feel like I'm motivated to do the things I do, rather than to just do them.
Starbound gives me hope for the continuation of the True Sandbox genre, as I like to call it. The manipulation of the world is great, stories are present now, and we have a great deal of ways to express ourselves in game. In my opinion, the next step is to create combat that feels satisfying. I want to play a game like Minecraft with a Z-targeting fighting style like seen in Legend of Zelda. If not that, then give me a game like Terraria or Starbound with a fighting system like Dust: An Elysian Tail.
There's just SO much room for growth in this genre, and I'm super excited to see where the future takes it. Starbound is definitely another step in furthering this genre, and if you enjoyed games such as Minecraft or Terraria, you will absolutely love Starbound.

This game was absolutely incredible. Easily one of the best in the fallout series and I'm honestly kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off I waited so long on buying this game based on the negative reviews. I could not put this game down from the moment I started playing it. The story is great as well as the plethora of sidemissions which are everywhere to be found.
Normally I would get incredibly bored by the massive number of side missions which had no depth or story whatsoever. This game was different. I actually WANTED to explore the many different areas of the game because every building and area has it's own story or interesting things to discover.
The settlement building was great once I got the hang of how the building system works. Building defensive structures and massive multi-story buildings to house your settlers in as well as planting gardens was great. TLDR - If you've been holding off on buying this game and been on the fence about it because of some of the reviews, don't be! The next time it goes on sale, BUY IT. You won't regret it.

The game is pretty fun. Though, unfortunately, it needs mods to really be a great game.
The base game just feels a bit hollow and lifeless. The story was actually pretty good, I personally don't care about your character being voiced. I wish they were a little more original with your overarching goal. F3 "Where's my dad?" F4 "Where's my son? A bit lazy and the dialogue can be annoying.
Settlements! I love the idea of settlements. I absolutely loved the RTS (Real Time Settlement Mods) from Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas. And the concept behind making a settlement is something I always wanted and just love. The problem, is pretty huge though. Settlements are fun to build in - and that is about it.
Settlers are completely devoid of life. They focused way to much on the building part and no where near enough on making settlers themselves interesting. It is lackluster. Scavenger settlers don't really do much besides wander to a few points - would be amazing if they actually wandered out a ways into the world looking for actual scrap. Farmers just farm for all eternity and don't really do anything else. Vendors/shops that you open just sit there.. waiting for you - because no one else will ever visit or use them.
You can't tell settlers to follow you around, they don't have names, they don't have anything that would make you feel connected to them - they are just a number to your settlement. Settlers are immortal without mods which removes any suspense there might be in being raided.
I could almost forgive them for this if they didn't champion this has some great feature they added. It just feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and misses half the importance of a settlement - it isn't just minecraft building it is also about the settlers and feeling some sort of investment in them. But it is lifeless and not immersive. And several DLC focus entirely on expanding settlements! But they only expand what you can build.
DLC: Far Harbor is great. Automatron is pretty cool. I haven't bought the others yet because, honestly, after much research into them they just don't seem worth the full price. Nuka World allows a new type of settlement - raider settlements! Except.. it is just as lifeless as all the others.
It should be noted that Vault-Tec DLC appears to add some life through the couple of items that they add - the "experiments" can essentially function as recreational items - allowing your settlers to do something besides sit around all day. They really should of added a ton more of these.
Big complaints:
The terrible trend of dumbing down PC games in order to make it easier/cheaper to port them to consoles is a big negative here. I have nothing against consoles but it is clear this was the case. Example #1: YOUR BASH KEY AND STRONG ATTACK ARE ALSO THE SAME KEY AS THROW GRENADES. The most horrific thing to be added into a game in a long time. Whoever thought of this should be fired. Trying to power attack or bash an enemy? Oh, you got caught up in that intense fight and held that key for .1 seconds too long - well enjoy your own molotov nuking your face off.
Dialogue. Not a fan of how they dumbed it down and were lazy about it. I suppose they thought they could cut corners with a voice actor and just make every option "yes, no, sarcastic, leave". No idea what your character will actually say. Really lame.
Combat and graphics are good, no real complaints.
The World: The world, is great. It is smaller than previous titles - but there is so much detail and life in it that I find it acceptable. I still find myself discovering new things in the city that I never saw or noticed before. Amazing world building, for sure.
Why a negative review? I do think the game is worth full price and it is very fun and you will most likely get your money's worth. But negative review because they should of done so much better. I want this franchise to grow in a positive way. And I don't feel that Fallout 4 was a great leap forward from New Vegas or Fallout 3. It was just kind of a side step. It got better graphics but lost out on so much more - worse writting, less immersive, etc. And a lot of the DLC felt like they didn't know what direction to go with - it just feels impromptu - just so they could push out DLC.
TL;DR:
Settlements feel lifeless. Buy all the DLC only on sale - except Far Harbor, that one is really worth full price.

Let's get something straight out: if you ever buy this game, and do hope you do it while it's on special, don't buy it for the story, it's a Bethesada game after all. And please be aware that there are numerous bugs, some small and some... quite bothersome. Even problematic as far as game progress is concern. As I already said, this is a Bethesda game.
Some of the good points: the engine does a good job at rendering the post-apocalyptic retrofuturism 50's world. If you have the machine with the stomach to digest the highest settings of course. Getting a power armor, and you do so early in the game, makes you feel like you're wearing a power armor and the NPC's react to it. You also have lots to explore but don't expect something different than the two previous games. Although it's an open world every building that you enter is a instance on its own. The voice acting is better than before, thanks to Bethesda having hired more than two voice actors. You can personalize your character to your heart's content, wheter it's male or female. You have a lot of quests and side-quests to complete. And let's no forget mods.
Now, for the less shiny parts. Like I said, there are many quests and side quests but unfortunately, during the course of the game, many interactions with NPC's can simply shut down. Sometimes it happens because you took a wrong path in the conversation tree and at some other times NPC's become non-responsive for no reason at all. When this happens this unfortunately forces you to roll back to a previous save, thus erasing any progress you've made. Also aforementioned, the size of the map. Yes, it's big but in order to keep you from going in a certain direction, Bethesda opted to use the very old and dated "You Cannot Go In That Direction". No obstacle and no natural barrier other than a perfectly invisible wall. If you can customize your character you cannot, quite unfortunately choose your own adventure as the game sets you into a prefabricated role ready to fit into a very bland storyline. You have no choice in the matter. If I said that you can play with mods don't get your hopes on too high. In fact, not at all, at least if you want to unlock achievements because playing with mods actually does just that: it locks you out of achievements even if you just want a mod that makes the grass a bit greener. So to unlock the different achievements you have to play plain vanilla Fallout 4.
On a final note, I initially didn't recommend this game but ultimately decided to recommend for one reason: the Nexus. Although you can download and activate mods in-game, it's really at the Nexus that Fallout 4 can truly shine because of the sheer amount of high quality mods you can download and thanks to the Nexus Mod Manager, mods can be installed fast and easy. Some of these mods can even turn Fallout into a totally different experience, like the Pilgrim mod which I can't recommend enough along with the Conifer Redux mod. You'll thank me later.

People have demonstrated consistently since Fallout 4's release how dangerous expectations can be. To expect great things from the game, and to be disappointed when those expectations are not met, is quite normal. When judgement is rendered solely on the result of those expectations, the fatal mistake is made. It in turn leads to a propensity for jumping to conclusions, and from that point it's a rapid descent into ignorance.
Back when Fallout 4 was released, most of the Steam reviews consisted of incoherent, furious ranting that tarnished the whole title after only a few hours worth of gameplay. After being shocked by the overwhelming amount of negativity, I decided to make my own and openly condemned the bad reviews for what they were: baseless and devoid of perspective. It was quite obvious the authors made that fatal mistake, which is unfair to the many developers who put their soul and passion into creating the game.
In the end, Fallout fans will almost assuredly find disappointments with Fallout 4, as did I. But if the ignorance of the older reviews and reception of previous games ought to teach one thing, it's that those disappointments are no excuse for blind judgement or jumping to conclusions. If an opinion is to be rendered of this game in the form of review, let it be guided by reason and supported by logic. It is in the pursuit of that fairness and clarity that I chose to write this review.
----------------------------------------
Fallout 4 is a deeply enjoyable and well-crafted game. However, it definitely has its issues. Bethesda tried new things in this title, some more ambitious than others, and not all of them were successful.
It's true that dialogue has been watered down as the devs chose to forgo text conversation choices in favor of a voiced and much more simplified dialogue wheel, which is further hampered by boring choices and weak voice work. Character advancements have been combined into a single perk/SPECIAL sheet. Settlement building, while certainly fun, is mostly aesthetic filler that has little impact on the game world. Side quests far too often amount to just killing some mandatory enemies, particularly with the Minutemen (who are supposed to be the "good guys" of this installment), and can become repetitive.
My most prominent grievance with Fallout 4 is the dialogue overhaul and removal of the karma system, which was completely unnecessary and not desired by a single player in existence. Unlike the previous flaws, this thoroughly irks me. I realized that this ties in to the primary weakness of Fallout 4: its lack of meaningful dialogue in comparison to most Bethesda titles. Far too often, your dialogue choices are short, shallow, meaningless, or all three.
The only choices that have any outcome are blatantly outlined as persuasion options, a lot of which only help you get some extra caps. It's not that you should be making major decisions all the time; the problem is that you, as a speaking character, now have a voice that carries no power. What you decide to say is almost always inconsequential. The dialogue system is highly reminiscent of Mass Effect except watered down; the reason it doesn't work in Fallout is that the two games have totally different approaches to conversation. The previous Fallout games had much better dialogue options because they meant something. Sometimes, your choice of words just made someone hate you, allowed you to entice or inspire others, or developed your reputation through the karma system. Now that karma is gone, your choices are just that much more pointless.
The bottom line is that Bethesda sacrificed a tremendous amount of RPG dialogue elements to accommodate full voice-work. While it was an ambitious attempt, it was an all-around mistake and it sticks out like a sore if you're a fan of Bethesda games or RPG's in general. The dialogue wheel system could have worked out just fine, but Bethesda carried it out in the wrong way.
----------------------------------------
All the aforementioned flaws are some of the most central complaints naysayers have about Fallout 4 and yet not a single one of them has been horrific enough to ruin my experience or let me down. Despite the few bugs I've come across, despite the certain questionable and sometimes idiotic design choices Bethesda made here, this game is still extremely well done. I still feel that incomparable thrill that only Fallout can bring.
Even though Fallout 4 falls extremely short on dialogue and all aspects associated with it, it's still an improvement over its predecessors in almost every other way imaginable. The game suffers some graphical issues like muddy textures and poor lighting at times, like any good Bethesda game, but it's still astoundingly beautiful and even breathtaking at times. Movement, melee, gunplay, and physics are better and smoother than they've ever been.
People were quick to judge the Commonwealth map based on its size and I was prepared to be disappointed as well, but it's surprisingly the best one Bethesda has whipped up thus far. The suburban locations are more organically dispersed and things become more compressed as you near the cities. Streets are narrow, buildings are tall, and locations are absolutely jam-packed alongside a ton of unmarked ruins and buildings you can enter. There are hardly any copy-pasted environments and they all show great attention to detail.
I was also worried that granting access to power armor and a minigun within the first thirty minutes of the game would be a huge balancing issue as well, but it really isn’t. Power armor relies on uncommon fusion cores for power and you’re not an unstoppable god while wearing the suit, especially not at higher difficulties or levels. You can acquire some strong weapons like the minigun or Fatman relatively early but finding sufficient ammo is another matter entirely.
----------------------------------------
Skyrim was a simplification of the Oblivion formula, but it was still a fantastic game. In much the same way, Fallout 4 is a simplification of the Fallout 3/New Vegas formula and is still extremely good. Even in light of its issues, this game has not been a disappointment at all. RPG elements can be enhanced through the wonderful modding community and will eventually make up for some of the game's weaker points, a perk of the PC version. Bethesda has, however, been on a recent trend of simplifying their games too much and I hope they change course.
Truthfully, the negative Steam reviews had me partly worried that I’d be disappointed but I chose to disregard them and arrive at my own opinion. I’ve learned that nearly every point of contention was blown out of context. The few issues that haven’t been redeemed in my eyes still pale in the face of the tremendous work that was done to bring this new and beautiful Fallout world to life. I have no doubt that the naysayers worked up their expectations to heights beyond reason, and it’s therefore no mystery that they hit the ground so hard afterwards. I chose to see Fallout 4 for what it is rather than what I expected or imagined it to be: a lovingly crafted game that, despite being marred by some of its shortcomings, has that same engaging splendor that far supercedes its flaws.
I highly recommend you try the game and approach it with a neutral and reasonable demeanor, and you won’t be disappointed.

Oh man... What can i say about Dark souls 3 that wasn't said already.
Ok... This game... I can't decide, if this is either the best, or the worst of the series. There are many variables.
Let's start with why i think this is the best
-The atmosphere
I think this game surpasses even Dark souls 1 in atmosphere and in that narrative style where part the lore is told trough imagery rather than words. This game took what Dark souls 1 did and improves it a notch.
-Graphics. WEll it's a current gen game, and it shows. It shows way better than Dark souls 2, that was a game that couldn't either belong to the previous gen or the current one.
- Difficulty curve Of all the Souls games, this one is possibly the one with the best difficulty curve, Dark souls 1 starts out easy , becomes REALLY hard until Ornstein and Smough, and then mellows a little. Dark souls 2 starts BALLS TO THE WALL hard, but once you level up enough it loses any challenge. Dark souls 3 has an almost perfect difficulty curve, There are some exceptions, like Yhorm, but most of the game feels increasingly difficult, wich makes the game progression feel more fluid
-Maps design. All the maps are brilliant in this game. They feel organic, There is a really cool navigation in the maps. The same can't be said about the cohesion between maps
-The combat mechanic is possibly the most refined, most weapons one as strong and capable as the other.
It's the worst because
- Lack of color doesn't mean atmosphere, While the game wins in atmosphere because of the level design , sound design, monsters, and the overall thematic of the game. It has no color. Remember brown and bloom? This is grey and black. Most of the game is either grey or desaturized, and it feels dead inside.
- Gimmicky bosses.Every souls game has atleast one boss with gimmicks to defeat it... It's alright to have one. Sometimes it's even an option, and not a really obvious, like making the giant fall or the ceaseless discharge fall. But The White dragon and  Yhorm... It's too much, One gimmicky boss was enough. And the problem is, if you don't use the intended strategy, the battle can last forever. I beat the white dragon without the plunge. It took like 15 minutes, Im not lying.
-Map Cohesion. Now, don't worry. The maps are more connected than in Dark souls 2. But the game can't decide if they wanted you to have teleports from the beginning of the game or not. There are unnecessary shortcuts everywhere.
-Bonfires everywhere. The game is full of them. Why there is a bonfire before farron swamp, before the gate, before the farron wolf... Finding a bonfire was a relief. Now there are so many bonfires there isn't even a point. The game is even more full of them than Dark souls 2.
- The game plays it too safe Dark souls 2 was an experiment phase. It had lots of wins and lots of loses. Dark souls 3, instead of improving from there, mostly backpedaled.
-The replacement for poise isn't as effective as the poise from Dark souls 2. It's just bigger tolerance to hits while swinging.
-Creative Stagnation. Bringing back familiar places is one thing. Filling the game with references to previous one isn't. It fills the place that could be filled with an expanded universe. The universe in this game isn't really expanded a lot.
-The netcode isn't as good as Dark souls 2
So. I Think this game is only good if you liked Dark souls 1 but didn't want it to improve a lot at anything and made more accesible for the mainstream public
If you wanted to go beyond what DS2 did and see an improved series of mechanics... you won't find a lot of that here. If you want some Dark soul 1 you should definitely play this game.

I held off buying this game for a long time because I saw a lot of negative reviews and reviews saying this was a shooting game and had practically no rpg elements to the game at all. This game was absolutely incredible. Easily one of the best in the fallout series and I'm honestly kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off I waited so long on buying this game based on the negative reviews. I could not put this game down from the moment I started playing it. The story is great as well as the plethora of sidemissions which are everywhere to be found.
Normally I would get incredibly bored by the massive number of side missions which had no depth or story whatsoever. This game was different. I actually WANTED to explore the many different areas of the game because every building and area has it's own story or interesting things to discover.
The settlement building was great once I got the hang of how the building system works. Building defensive structures and massive multi-story buildings to house your settlers in as well as planting gardens was great. Making sure they have enough purified water as well as building generators and running electricity to all the structues and lighting everything up. I spent hours upon hours doing nothing but playing with the settler building system and had a blast doing it.
The weapon/armor modding system was also a nice addition. I will say that it could have been better but still really cool as-is. My main gripe was not being able to actually wear the armor/outfit that I wanted to. You're pretty much forced into wearing the dumbest looking outfits ever if you want to be the most protected. There is however a downloadable mod that fixes this problem and will enable you to wear what you want without sacrificing armor.
TLDR - If you've been holding off on buying this game and been on the fence about it because of some of the reviews, don't be! The next time it goes on sale, BUY IT. You won't regret it.

Starbound Review based on length of play time:
So far during my time playing Starbound, I have had plenty of different experiences that have made this both a really fun game and an annoying one - but simply this is down to the current state of the game. I have played Starbound solo and with friends and both present there own benefits which can help you play the game, but down to the actual review.
As the game is in beta, most of the things i am about to talk about may and possibly will change before the official release so please keep that in mind.
Starbound is a mash-up of different types of games and take big factors of games such as Minecraft and Terraria which are games that have both done well since they were released. The game is much better to play with friends due to the fact of being able to progress faster and be able to chat about the game and have a bit of banter while playing.
The game itself has many different variations of things to do including role-playing, adventuring across stars and the multiple planets you encounter, and within each planet they are jobs such as mining, combat and building to be done. The game has lots of little mini extras that make the game a little quirky - instruments can be found while adventuring which then can be played to lighten the mood.
The graphical aspect of the game is a part of the game that is hard to talk about as it is unlikely to change much or even at all due to the style of the game, but looking at it as a future games developer, the genre of the game and the style that has been set forth has been done to a very high quality.
If i was looking at this game as someone that hasn't bought it yet or hasn't tried some similiar games then i would suggest you only buy this if you have others to play it with, as i found playing solo, i could only be bothered to play 1-3 hours at the most a day but that was upscaled when playing with my friends.
Overall, I would give this game ( in its current state ) a good 7.5/10 possible a 8/10 on  a good day, the developing team are bring lots of updates very frequently so keep up-to-date with it to see how it goes :)

I held off buying this game for a long time because I saw a lot of negative reviews and reviews saying this was a shooting game and had practically no rpg elements to the game at all. I didn't want to buy a dud after having enjoyed the fallout series so far up to this point and I didn't want to be disappointed by a bad game. This game was absolutely incredible. Easily one of the best in the fallout series and I'm honestly kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off I waited so long on buying this game based on the negative reviews. I could not put this game down from the moment I started playing it. The story is great as well as the plethora of sidemissions which are everywhere to be found.
Normally I would get incredibly bored by the massive number of side missions which had no depth or story whatsoever. This game was different. I actually WANTED to explore the many different areas of the game because every building and area has it's own story or interesting things to discover.
The settlement building was great once I got the hang of how the building system works. Building defensive structures and massive multi-story buildings to house your settlers in as well as planting gardens was great. Making sure they have enough purified water as well as building generators and running electricity to all the structues and lighting everything up. I spent hours upon hours doing nothing but playing with the settler building system and had a blast doing it.
The weapon/armor modding system was also a nice addition. I will say that it could have been better but still really cool as-is. My main gripe was not being able to actually wear the armor/outfit that I wanted to. You're pretty much forced into wearing the dumbest looking outfits ever if you want to be the most protected. There is however a downloadable mod that fixes this problem and will enable you to wear what you want without sacrificing armor.
TLDR - If you've been holding off on buying this game and been on the fence about it because of some of the reviews, don't be! The next time it goes on sale, BUY IT. You won't regret it.

Update 7/22/2017 - Updated to an EVGA GTX 1060 6GB and game runs just fine on highest settings on both my 1600x900 monitor and 1080 television screen. Avg FPS according to GeForce experience is sitting at about 58 FPS, no notable dips.
You know what, I love this game. It's not quite the same love felt in New Vegas however. A bit more restrained, the choke chain is a bit longer and doesn't yank back as often to remind you your in an unforgiving apocalytpic radiated world. Though there are plenty of memorable characters, few in the Fallout world will ever come across with as much gravity as The Boomers, Uylsses, Craig Boone, Frank Weathers and a slew of other characters. Yes, Fallout 4 does achieve this to some extent with companions, but when it comes the NPCs you slowly come to know through your travels in and out of hubs such as Diamond City, many don't come across a personalities you'll remember a couple dozen hours down the road.
As for gameplay, it feels more polished over the previous games and more streamlined, but almost streamlined to a fault. Removing things like weapon repairs but adding a delicious pile of weapon modifications. The same goes for armor. Power armor is a much bigger focus, coming with it's own pack of modifications. But when it comes to how deadly the wasteland is, something feels missing. Radiation is always an issue of course, but it never feels like it puts you into a serious bind of helplessness. Even in the Glowing Sea, a place packed with rads is easily survived through only a handful of rad-x and rad-away packs.
Combat can sometimes feel like it took to many cues from games like Borderlands with unique and randomized weapon variations being dropped from unique enemies and personally. A major disapointment is the total absence of a moral system. You can't strive to become a wasteland messiah or muck everyone in your path over by being comically evil. You're forced into a somewhat contrived story where you're more or less forced to become "the good guy" but even then, there aren't any real effects from your actions that aren't felt immediately rather than a choice coming back to haunt you hours later with no warning. The surprise the story you as the vault dweller choose to create falls flat in almost every circumstance.
As for base building, it's fairly straightforward and can be a fun timesink when the mechanics actually work properly and happiness of a settlement actually coincides with their quality of life, rather than arbitrarily fluctuating between 90% and 50%. It becomes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you've spent hours building up these virtual peoples lives only to be hampered by either bad AI or in-game mechanics which aren't functioning as they should.
Oh and quick note on the technical side, as I really haven't had many issues. I do feel the game could be better optimized, but I've only had one single crash to desktop and a fair handful of frame drops which forced me to alt-F4 out of the game. Otherwise, things are pretty tight on that end in my case. I'll put my PC specs on the bottom of the review for personal comparison.
Update 10/23/17-
Alright, so this Creation Club thing, I'm sure we can all agree on, is fairly stupid. However, from a company perspective and when it comes to content that is much more stable than your typical mods from the Nexus, or whever you source your mods, it is practical on paper. But put into practice, it can appear to be little more than a cash grab and that's really what it is. I can understand the desire to create an extra revenue stream, but it doesn't mean I approve of it. Along with that, what almost seems like a lack of expansions or dlc is rather disappointing. The previous title, New Vegas, had extra content coming out of every creative hole Obsidian could find. Fallout 4 on the other hand feels a bit hollow in the end. Though it's two main expansions, Far Harbour and Nuka-World were fairly decent and added to the world, their impact is short lived and there isn't much more to say to that.
Pros:
