-Like other Bethesda open world games, you're pretty free to progress as you like

Cons:

-The main story is mediocre

Ugh could Bethesda f* up this wonderful series any more?? Look, i'm ok with Skyrim and all that, but leave Fallout alone, Bethesda, you make it worse and worse every time you touch it.
I had ok expectations at first because friends said it was "ok", although i'm pretty sure every single one of them got bored and never finished this game.
Then i started running into more and more issues, and i decided to start a list of all those, and i was going to wait till the list is complete to write a review - but i seriously cannot force myself to play this thing anymore. Ugh i went back to World of Warcraft because it felt LESS farmy than this game (how bad is that??).
Anyway, here's a list of all the bad things i've gathered so far:
1. There is no more skills system (remember how you used to have a ton of skills i.e. lockpicking or rifles that you could put points in to improve your chances of success? yeah there is none of that now. They only left the "perks").
2. You can no longer target limbs with stimpacks.
3. Targeting in VATs is all sorts of messed up: if limbs overlap slightly - the program keeps snapping back and forth between the two, and it's really annoying to select one.
4. VATs accuracy is even worse than before. Remember how everyone always complains that "you miss 3 times in a row with 95% chance hit"? Well there is that still, and IN ADDITION to that, VATs is not frozen in time and enemies keep moving slowly. This means that when you target something at 95% chance, if after after you shoot the enemy goes behind cover - after you already shot - your accuracy goes down to 0%. So it's 95% when you pull the trigger, but it's 0% when the bullet actually hits them. This was really frustrating every fight. What the hell is the point of VATs then? I might as well play the game like a regular fps and not bother with VATs.
5. I constantly got stuck hacking terminals. After you leave the hacking screen your character gets stuck and you can't move, the only way around is to reload.
6. You also get stuck on other environment at lot.
7. There was no good walkthrough for settlement management, i had to keep looking stuff up online.
8. Idiotic interface - they have different commands using the same button (depending on how long you press it), so you constantly have to re-press until you  get the right outcome. Wtf, you have a whole damn keyboard at your disposal - could you not have used different keys, Bethesda??
9. And all the farming, oh my god. All you do is drag scrap to your settlement from far away places just so you can build one more turret. I was told it only gets worse the more you play - because you start having several settlements and they get attacked constantly so all you do is run around try to help them.
Way too many frustrating things with this game. I actually went in with an open mind, because last Fallout game i played was New Vegas and that was acceptable. But this one - it's unifnished, unpolished, buggy, horrible. The only good thing about it is that the environment is more interesting and better looking than in Fallout 3. But then again if you want pretty environment - go play Skyrim instead.

Now building settlements is something I LOVE in this game even tho it is pretty wonky and again feels rushed and the settlements should have a waay bigger build limit, It makes the game still fun after you beat it. Then came the workshop DLCs. Oh how that screwed up my opinion of the game. It was essentially horse armor 2.0 and I lost quite a bit of respect for Bethesda over it. Then came Far Harbour, which I thought was a pretty solid expansion with a genuinely compelling story and interesting setting. Then came more workshop DLCs. See where I am going with this? Fallout 4 is a great game with extremely annoying blemishes such as some of the DLC and a drift away from the RPG mechaincs that popularised the series. I fully reccomend the game to those looking for an adventure in a well crafted world with an in-depth lore. I do not reccomend it  to those looking for a solid RPG experience with seamlessly integrated mechanics to enrich the players experience.

I wouldnt recommend this game to people like myself. People who loved the roleplay, the lore, and everything what made
Fallout 1, 2 and New Vegas great.
Fallout 4 isnt a rpg anymore it is a shooter with rpg elements. Its the exact opposite to the older games (rpg with shooter elements) . The story is totally linear in Fallout 4. Yes there are different endings but still the way to get there is like driving on rails. You dont have a choice other than choosing the end what you want to have at the end of the game. In New Vegas you had the choice to complete the quest in the way you wanted. In FO4 every dialogue option leads to the same conclusion and every mission will be played very similar. In FO1 and 2 you could get shot when you said the wrong thing to the wrong person. These games were real rpgs.
Another point is that I for myself dont find much to do in the commonwealth other than to mess around with mods etc.
In older Fallouts you had tons of side quests and a lot of lore around that. In Fallout 4 there is no depth in side quests.
Fallout 4 also has very few mentionable side quests and these are often more like go there, shoot the enemy, come back and you are done.
At last I want to mention the greed from Bethesda with their DLC/Addon policy. I for myself cant judge on the big expansions like Far Harbor but I can say something about the little workshop dlcs and automatron. These little DLCs are not that expensive but a lot of that stuff could be found on nexus. A lot of the stuff you can do in Vault Tec workshop you could do in a mod that was made before the DLC.
At last all I can say is that for people who search a rpg this isnt something you should look for. For these people I would recommend older Fallout game like 1, 2 and NV.
For people who search for a open world survival shooter with story elements, this could be your game. Just keep in mind that you play a game that totally screwed the original concept of Fallout.
BTW! this is only an explanation why I wouldnt recommend this game. I left out the positive things of Fallout 4 which surprisingly exist.

Bear in mind that I am only about 3 gameplay hours into Starbound, let me give you my initial opinion of the game!
First of all, my laptop is an old beater. It won't even play very simple side-scrollers at anything about the average graphic level, but Starbound runs on it almost perfectly! It lags on occasion, but I'm willing to let that bypass my complaint list.
The environment is very Terraria-esque, which is to be expected, but it could almost be considered a Terraria 2.0! The world seems to run a lot smoother and you can get a lot more accomplished before sundown. The enemies make the overworld interesting. Some are aggressive, some are calm, but you won't figure that out until you're a few feet away and the charge music kicks in. It adds a bit of suspense. The overworld has a ton of surprises. I found a random anchor attached to a chain and promptly stole it for a decoration haha. The addition of a questing feature gives you a greater sense of purpose as well. When I had the opportunity to play Terraria, I just felt like I was wandering aimlessly, looking for something to do or see. Aside from the boss fights, there wasn't much to offer. This game gives you goals, but allows you to take them at your own comfortable place.
I have yet to explore the underworld yet as I am still trying to find a simple way to survive above ground!
Overall, from what I've seen, this game is a gem in the making and you should most definitely pick it up! Don't let the Terraria look deter you, this is a game all its own.

Different than the dark depressing tone of the other Fallout game(s) such as Fallout 3, where the nocturne of nuclear war remains, this game is not meant to be the same.
This game is meant to give you hope and the opportunity to re-establish what other Fallout games couldn't have done by your choices: By building upon those choices, not doing the choices.
Character development is somewhat lacking for the very reason: Your character is a family member, driven by the kidnapping of his/her son and will do what's necessary. In the end, you have built upon the choices you have made.
That is the game.
--

Nuclear detonations are confirmed in multiple locations as you evacuate to the local vault, Vault 111. Your gutsy is left behind as your partner brings young Shaun, your baby boy to the Vault. A nuclear detonation happens South-West of your current location, the mushroom cloud forming as a wave of radiation and debris overturn the Commonwealth as you descend the Vault.
You prepare for a new life.
A life you never wanted but ready for.

There's been lots of flak about Fallout since it's release. I was skeptical myself, but after almost 300 hours of playing the game to full completion, it'd be hard for me to actually say this game is bad, because it really isn't.
Now. I'll review this based on a whole general perspective, not clouded in bias from just one aspect of the game *cough* *cough*. So here's a run-down of the thingst:

Some say the beginning premise of the game is too atypical, unoriginal. Whereas FO3 is about you looking for your dad, FO4 is about you looking for your son. But that's about it. The story is nothing the same as FO3 from there. The intro begins in a new fasion of actually letting the player experience the fallout from the very beginning: when the nukes dropped. The main theme present throughout the game is on the rise of Synths created by the Institute, a shadowy organisation that is never revealed until the end. This blurs the line between who is human and who is not. Should synths even be treated as human? Who is a synth and who isn't, comes the philosophy behind it. As far as story goes, the structure seems to fall in the second half of the questline with endings just..lacking in much needed substance.
I must say, for a wasteland setting, FO4 delivers quite well in a its world. The Commonwealth is the setting of the game and basically, it is Boston.. if it got hit by a nuke. Environment is well varied enough, from the grassy wilderness, to many abandoned small towns, the dense city of Boston full of tall-rise buildings to explore, to some muddy swamps to the brilliantly bleak Glowing Sea.
There are plenty of locations to discover and many have their own stories to be told (which can usually be uncovered further through terminal entries, not that I bothered reading). Level design is impressively well done and almost every location feels unique in its own way.
I was initially skeptical about the settlement-building aspect of the game so touted about. It's largely optional and can be ignored if you don't care but it is quite a shove-in-your-face kind of feature. But still to say,getting to build your own houses is quite a satisfying experience.
Settlement-building is a nice way to give players more freedom, creativity in what they can do but it just falls short when there's too limited building offered. For instance, there's only 2 types of structures you can build in the game, and you're pretty much forced to stick with these sh**tty wooden houses. You can't repair all the broken settlement roofs, walls or anything which is a big shame. There isn't much help info given on settlements either, with the game only informing you of the very basics, the rest being quite a complicated mess to figure out at first.
This is by far the most overlooked and underrated aspect of FO4. The follower system in FO4 is truly the most refined and improved upon part of the game and of the entire Bethesda games. Followers actually feel like people worth caring for this time, not silent zombies that just follow behind your footsteps that past games were so muddled in. There are hundreds of voice lines for each follower recorded, allowing them to comment on almost literally everything you do in the game, from quests, to discovering locations, lockpicking, hacking, killing enemies and most importantly, making moral decisions. Most of the followers have their own quests which further flesh out their character and their social standing with you. This is known as 'affinity' which is what has replaced the karma system in FO3/NV. After all, how can you be judged for actions no one notices like stealing? With followers with you, they now observe your actions and are the ones to judge you for it. What you do could end in the follower either looking up to you admirably or leaving you for good.
Oh yes, another dumb complaint people have about FO4 so I'll just clarify here. Almost every side mission I have done (and by that I mean all side quests) has some choice in the end that yes, actually matters. If talking about dialogue conversation choices instead, that's another story. The only con I find here is that there seems to be TOO FEW side quests. But where you do find one, it's often one to be greatly enjoyed.
It's good to see Bethesda at least taking key notes of what some of their past games lacked in, even from New Vegas. Unlike FO3 where you had minimal choices in the questline, FO4 offers more flexibility in what you can do.
There's four main factions you can choose (and have choose) to side with and there's not so much of a clear-cut good or bad ending for each one.
The main questline eventually converges at some points, regardless of factions. Is it too much of the same? I'd say, not really. Especially if you don't join all factions in one playthrough, there is alot to experience.
The dialogue in FO4 is changed a little and no doubt for the worst. Bethesda tries to copy Mass Effect's way of playing conversations and apparently they think the game needs to be even more simpler than it already is by completely removing the traditional dialogue choice menu for a pathetic dialogue wheel instead, that only offers FOUR options, with a few words of hint of what your chaaracter might actually say. It's like Bethesda thinks just reading a few lines of words is too much for players to do. What are they...selling to 10-year olds?
This is personally one of the biggest gripes I have about the game. The fallout games aren't known to have crafting, instead gear, guns and armor need to be found and looted throughout the world. Higher level gear would usually be found in more higher level areas and so on.
But apparently, Bethesda now thinks it's a better idea to just toss most of the unique gear including many OP weapons and armor onto vendors who appear in your face and makes themselves available as early as the very start of the game. Yes, unique gear on vendors normally costs lots of caps and this could have been fair, except the gear are NOT scaled in value based on their quality.
By the first few hours of the game, I could already afford the Overseer's Rifle, arguably the 2nd most powerful rifle in the game. Meanwhile, a crap armor piece like the leather Mantis gear can cost over four times that amount. JUST WHY? It makes absoluutely no sense whatsoever and only disrupts the balance of the loot distribution tremondously.
This is another complaint many have, although I honestly...don't really see much issues with it. Bethesda has removed the Skills stats from FO4, now leaving only SPECIAL and perks. The benefits of skills arent excluded but instead integrated into the perks system, so now therés more perks to choose. The only shortcoming I feel, is how magazines feel less substiantial, each offering more minor effects. The level cap has also been remoeved, a good decision, which encourages more progress through the game. Enemies will scale with you but weapons damage and armor are limited by crafting. So level up too absurdly high and you'll eventually regret it or enjoy the increasingly high challenge.
Overall to say, apart from some balancing issues and bad game design, FO4 doesnt disappoint me. Even without owning the DLCs, I got more than I bargained for with its hefty price tag. Is it a bad game? By far it's not. If you liked FO3, FO4 is an improvement in almost every way, from gun combat to enemy AI. If you liked FNV, the story and characters might feel significantly flat and bad in comparison as atypical of Bethesda's generic writing. But if you're playing more for the gameplay and exploration itself, you won't regret it. FO4 still holds up in its own way as a remarkable open-world RPG, offering a great deal to experience.

I've just finish 100% this game. It has been a task to complete a dark souls game since I got my hands on Dark Souls 1. I feel as though this plus my playtime garners a full review, so that it may help others experience the good and bad as I have taken part in it all.
Dark souls 3 offers a complex storytelling experience with a fantastic combat system that offers deep and inviting gameplay. If you are familiar with the more general 'skyrim-like' combat system and not much else, this will be a very new experience. Each weapon having individual movesets and combos creates infinite combat scenarios. PvP not once has felt stale, and the PvE content can be grueling. I mean, come on. Its a Souls game, I'm sure you're aware of the memes. / Picking up this game will deliver an unforgettable experience, helped along by great visuals and theming as well as a fantastic score to boot.. Every area feels distinct and the enemies are very memorable. You will most likely have 'that one enemy' that you want to kill at the mention of its name, or runaway in fear. The bosses are also challenging and exciting in their own right. Besides a few technical errors, the game runs great, and I have not experienced a single crash across multiple systems. The game is great with any gamepad, and a little awkward with a keyboard.
Dark Souls 3 offers one of my favorite singleplayer experiences of all time. The areas are impeccable and the challenges you will come across are unexpected and, well, sometimes a bit BS. I missed a few entire areas my first playthrough because one, i walked in, said, "Nope." and walked out. I never needed to return so it never was completed. Two, because i completely missed any hint around the area, and constantly wondered what those things i saw in the distance were. The way you dynamically build a character and try out newer and newer weapons as you grasp hold of the game is such a good time, i wish i could wipe my memory and play a souls game for the first time again. The PvE content will last you about 25-50 hours depending on playstyle and pace. (For reference, my first run i missed three areas and completed in 35 hours, second runthrough, i completed the entire game in 35 hours, including all the new areas.) On top of that, NG+ and beyond are viable options if you wish to continue the seeking of the flame.
A big part of the game is covenents, these little organizations you can align with in game that give you certain tasks for rewards. Covenents play a big part of the game, trust me, i have all of them at their highest level. Some will randomly summon you to an area where you must kill the tresspasser, which is another player just trying to progress as you have. Others will have you summon to fight by these players, and some are all about madness and being a wild card. The way that people interact in the Souls games is unlike any other. On one side, you'll summon someone (they join your game to help fight) and they will take you all the way to the boss and help you beat it. On the other side, you'll be invaded (someone will join your game with the intention to kill you.) and they will not stop trying to get their reward (by killing you of course). This has create for me, some of my favorite experiences in gaming, and has led to making some great fiends. Later in the game, you'll discover new ways to interact with your fellow players, by joining in jolly cooperation, and fighting agianst one another in the arena. The developers have shown they support the PvP scene with new content patches and weapon balancing. They even put in an arena with the new DLC so getting to fight is now stremlined. (look up DS fight clubs if you're interested) A  ton of builds can be made in Dark Souls, and PvP will always have a META of what is considered 'good', but always play to what you find fun!
I give Dark Souls 3 a 9.5/10, for continously being the game i can return to and shove all of my time into it.
Previous Souls game players: Go for it, this offers a much faster pace game that its precessors (look up info about the poise system)
The guy looking for something new: Take a shot, this will at least let you understand some of the references, right? In all seriousness, if you look at gameplay and are not fully sold, see if you have the funds during a sale.
Just browsing what Steam has to offer: Don't pass this one up because of the goofy halloween trailer! check out some videos online, or gameplay. This could offer you something new and interesting!
Anyone else: Again take a harder look and decide for yourself. Sales come around and the price will drop, maybe stick it onto your wishlist.

Fallout 4, although containing a few bugs and glitches, is still an overall fun game. I've never been a masochist in my life until I play this.

If you're looking for a story with twists and epicness, this game is for you.
Unlike the other Fallout 4 games, you take a role on a character that has a limited mind and wants to piece his/her family back together, instead of choosing your own character and making up your own story. Different than the dark depressing tone of the other Fallout game(s) such as Fallout 3, where the nocturne of nuclear war remains, this game is not meant to be the same.
This game is meant to give you hope and the opportunity to re-establish what other Fallout games couldn't have done by your choices: By building upon those choices, not doing the choices.
Character development is somewhat lacking for the very reason: Your character is a family member, driven by the kidnapping of his/her son and will do what's necessary. In the end, you have built upon the choices you have made.
That is the game.
--
You start out as a male/female in a house at Sanctuary Hills, planning to go to the Veteran's Hall. Nuclear detonations are confirmed in multiple locations as you evacuate to the local vault, Vault 111. Your gutsy is left behind as your partner brings young Shaun, your baby boy to the Vault. A nuclear detonation happens South-West of your current location, the mushroom cloud forming as a wave of radiation and debris overturn the Commonwealth as you descend the Vault.
You prepare for a new life.
A life you never wanted but ready for.

So, what is this game? It's a 2D old school rpg with that lets you travel to randomized planets.
The negatives:
1. Its very unbalanced at the moment regarding loot and enemy progression. There is no progressional loot that you can find by killing hostile npc. Quite literally 99% of the time you never find an item uprade for your character, instead you just craft the stuff yourself through mining before you even get to the "next level" of planets, essentially starting with the best gear as you start on higher tier planets and weapons that drop are NEVER better than what you've already crafted. Armor items do not even drop, you can only craft them other than back-piece items.
2. The space-aspect of the game is lacking, considering that's the biggest feature of this game. Guns for the most part are useless compared to melee weapons and you can't make your own guns even though you own and fly a space ship. You can only find guns by killing enemies, and the damage on them is usually 40% lower than melee weapon damage making them useless for the most part.
3. The ship you start with cannot be expanded upon or improved.
4. Traveling to planets becomes stale, most of the civilizations you encounter do not sell you anything of value in regards to weapons or armor (they will never sell you anything better than you can craft before you even enter a higher-tier of planets), the only armor in the game that you can find is crafted yourself, making merchants that you can potentially find on planets completely worthless regarding armor and guns, its meaningless. There is no trading or cargo delivery missions or anything like in regards to any sort of questing/missions aspect in the game at all, and in-game money (pixels) is way too easy to get. There are no missions or quests you can randomly find on planets is what I'm trying to say.
5. The bosses are way too easy, enemies are way too easy to exploit regarding using the matter manipulator (just build some strategic dirt walkways and the boss will never even get a chance to hit you).
6. Building your own house/base on a planet is absolutely pointless. There is no advantage or gain in doing so, there is no benefit. There is no trading, or the ability to set up trading ports that you build. You cannot build space stations, you cannot expand your ship but even if you could there would be no point in doing so. Being able to build in-general is meaningless and pointless in this game.
7. Mining ore becomes tedious, as it takes up 80% of your time in the game until you reach end-game armors and weapons that you can craft through your time spent mining. After that you can finally enjoy the game by exploring, but once you do you realize there's nothing to do. Crafting your weapons and armor is better than anything you can find regarding weapons/armors as you progress through the content. You basically just mine ore, craft your next melee weapon and armor set, then go into the next level of planets already starting with the best gear. It makes progressing boring because you start out with the best armors and weapons every time and can't actually FIND anything better than what you craft yourself. There is no sense of loot progression whatsoever. It's completely unbalanced. There basically is no loot at all in a sense.
8. There are a variety of biomes, (tentacle, magma, grasslands, deserts, ice) but all of them are exactly the same in the end, they all have merchants that sell absolute crap items that are worthless, have no quests or missions to complete on them whatsoever. Basically the only reason you travel to different planets is to mine different ores, THAT'S IT!
9. There are no missions you can find on planets, No trading missions, no cargo missions, No quests, no missions, No nothing, no loot progression. The only point in traveling to higher tier planets is to find better ore types, but once you reach the end-game that too becomes pointless.
Overall, it's a bad and unbalanced game. It could be absolutely fantastic with about 5 or 10 more content patches but right now its just an empty unbalanced shell of a 2D game that has a lot of potential but right now that potential is nonexistent. It's basically a mining simulator, but a bad one, this game has nothing to do with space or technology at all in its current form.

Exlaimer!  Since this is a review, it will most likely have some spoilers but I will keep them to a minimum.
I began the Fallout series with Fallout 3.  I really loved the story of FO3 as it drew me in.  I was able to get an attachment to the various NPCs I interacted with as they all had personalities that felt real enough.  This goes especially for the father, who is a part of your "life" as you grow up in the vault (part character creation, part tutorial).
So with that said, when it comes to FO4, I'm searching for my son instead of my father.  There is a problem though, and that is I never really got to interact wth my son in any real, meaningful, way.  Rather than have the opposing parent shot and the infant son taken, it would've been better had the character creation / tutorial part of the game span over a period of ~15 years or so, with time jumps much like growing up in FO3.  Giving you choices on how you interact with your son, allowing you to develop a bond, and even having those choices have an impact on the story down the line.  For example, you neglect him and at the end he sees the bad guy as his "father" instead of you.
So to stay on topic of developing attachments to characters, the game does well with the various NPCs you come across.  Not only can you develop attachments as the player but there is even a system in game to determine how various NPCs like you.
Next I'll move onto the factions.  This game has a number of different factions you can get involved with.  Some of which are at odds with each other.  Unfortunately the game doesn't have the system found in FO:NV.  This should be a staple in future FO games and should include the "bad guys" and not just the "good guys".  While some are inherently good (minutemen), and some inherently bad (raiders), others should be inherently neutral (gunners).  The gunners, from my understanding, are guns for hire.  They should be neutral unless you do things to get on their bad side.  You should also be able to join them, as well as the raiders (provided you can get on their good side since they are hostile by default), and even the supermutents.  Getting good with one faction should likely mean opposing another.  Hell, imagine having the option of helping the hurt alien and joining an alian faction whose base of operation is in orbit?
There is also an imbalance with how the factions are presented.  With the minutemen, it is thrown in your face at the beginning of the game.  Meanwhile, other factions, like the underground railroad, require you to overhear a conversation and then you go on a wild goose chase.  Now I'm not saying that they should be introduced the same way, just that the different ways should come with equal opportunity.  Hell, rather than just Concord, Codsworth should randomly pick one of several locations you should try first (several = number of factions), resulting in an equal opportunity that the first faction you join is any of the ones available.  This would also increase the games replayability factor.
Now for controls.  The controls are responsive and smooth but they haven't really changed at all from game to game.  Modern FPS games have made improvements and yet, despite FO being part FPS, they haven't adopted those improvements.  The NPCs have more control and movement options than the player with their pressing up against cover, peeking around corners, shooting from cover, etc.  The advantage the player has over the enemy is being able to freely jump.  Why is it so hard for AI to jump?
Keeping controls in mind, I want to talk about the stealth mechanic which also hasn't changed and is the same in the Elderscrolls series (since Morrowind).  Sneaking shouldn't be something you "activate".  It should simply be something that is passive/active.  After all, if you see an enemy walking in the distance and they are not aware of you, you shouldn't have to "activate sneak" to get the sneak attack.  A shot from standing should also work.  So by removing crouching from sneaking, you can then introduce three position options often seen in FPS games.  Stand, crouch, and prone.
So with stealth a more passive system, it wouldn't be without it's active elements.  Lighting and sticking to the shadows, weight of your gear, how fast you move, lower profile (so crouched simply reduces detection while prone reduces it further), line of sight, etc.  Sound detection should be in contrast to ambient sounds.  An enemy in a generator room shouldn't be able to hear me running down the hall.  Also with objects like bushes, even though you can pass through them freely, should still impact line of sight for detection purposes.
Now for mods.  Mods have always been a wonderful addition to both the ES and FO games.  As single player games, mods allow players to individually cator the game to their wants.  Being able to get mods and install them via the title menu within the game is what I would call another staple that should be seen from here on.  With that said, any mod made via the creation kit and made available in game should be "approved" mods.  What I mean is, non "cheat" mods or otherwise mods that would warrent turning off achievements.  They should also be mods that have been tested to be bug free with incompatabilities kept to a minimum.  With that said, the ingame mod feature really needs a bug/incompatability reporting system and not just a reporting system for "inappropriate content".  While on that topic, I should be able to prove my age to gain access to 'age appropriate content'.  As a 34 yo I like, not only an ultra realistic game, but a more mature game.
The developers need to get serious with in-house play testing prior to release.  This is actually benefitial to both the player and developing studio alike.  If you consider the manhours (and associated cost) put into fixing bugs post release, if these bugs were identified and fixed mid-production, the customers would be happier with a higher quality product (which means more revenue) and the developers would've spent lest money on in-house play testers finding bugs that could've been fixed by the devs as they were already working on the game, than on those same devs fixing the bugs on a finished product when those manhours could be better spent on revenue content like DLCs and expansions.
As it stands with Bethesda, I do not recomment pre-odering.  I don't even recommend buying on the day it releases.  My recommendation, wait one year then buy it.  This is so that the bigger bugs will be fixed, post-production production (O.o) is finished, mods have been releases, and more honest reviews have been made.  Since you're waiting, wait for a sale and save some money.  Remember that waiting for a sale isn't some statement that means anything to Bethesda.  Retail sales don't impact producer revenue.  It's just a matter of 'why spend money you don't have to?'.  It's the refusal to pre-order and the delay in buying that sends a message.  In the business world, money talks, and so it is better to let your wallets do the talking when dealing with developer transgression.
I'll conclude with a general consensus.  Despite the room for improvement, and despite the bugs that persist to this day, the game is all-in-all really good.  It's visually appealing, with 100s of hours of content that is quite enjoyable.  Mods really make this game worth getting, and some of the bugs can even be fixed easily with a little online searching as others have found either a solution or a work-a-round.  There are even some mods that fix bugs.  It's for this reason that I say "yes" to recommending the game but emphasize on not pre-ordering and even waiting a year before buying future Bethesda games as a means of sending a message to Bethesda that they are getting slack with their products.

The Fallout series is one of my favorite game series that I have played, and I would highly recommend for anyone who enjoys story-driven, lore rich games, and first person shooter action in newer titles like Fallout 3, New Vegas, and 4. While some believe 4 to be a lesser to the critically acclaimed New Vegas, and in some aspects like choices and lore New Vegas does better, but Fallout 4 is still an incredibly solid entry into the Fallout franchise. The game, from a veteran of the franchise's perspective, may feel a bit linear compared to its predecessors, but in terms of combat and role-playing elements, it retains that Fallout feel that many love. Side quests and various main questlines are incredibly entertaining and full of dark humor that defines the franchise. The new modding feature allows you to customize everything from your weapons, armor, and power armor sets, allowing for many diverse playstyles and looks to your builds. Settlements are a new edition that allow your charecter to set up living places throughout the Commonwealth, serving as both bases and homes to the many followers and settlers you meet on your adventure. The new and revamped "survival mode" does excatly what it says, make every day a struggle to keep yourself from dying. Harder enemies, mangement of your charecters food, water, and sleep levels, along with diseases that can hinder your charecters overall health. This keeps the game fresh, especially after beating it a few times on normal diffuculties, its rejuvenates the fun that this game offers. There are also plenty of dlc, 3 of which, Automatron, Far Harbor, and Nuka World, offering new locations, enemies, weapons, and stories/lore. For those who like building, there are also the Wasteland Workshop and Vault-Tec dlc's, which offer more placeable items and a new location for building, and even a unique questline involving a incomplete Vault. In closing, Fallout 4 is a great game, and a must have for anyone who enjoys being emersed in a post-apocolyptic setting with deadly monsters, radiation, stories, and plently of weapons and armor to help you survive the nuclear winter that is Fallout.

Exlaimer!  Since this is a review, it will most likely have some spoilers but I will keep them to a minimum.
I began the Fallout series with Fallout 3.  I really loved the story of FO3 as it drew me in.  I was able to get an attachment to the various NPCs I interacted with as they all had personalities that felt real enough.  This goes especially for the father, who is a part of your "life" as you grow up in the vault (part character creation, part tutorial).
So with that said, when it comes to FO4, I'm searching for my son instead of my father.  There is a problem though, and that is I never really got to interact wth my son in any real, meaningful, way.  Rather than have the opposing parent shot and the infant son taken, it would've been better had the character creation / tutorial part of the game span over a period of ~15 years or so, with time jumps much like growing up in FO3.  Giving you choices on how you interact with your son, allowing you to develop a bond, and even having those choices have an impact on the story down the line.  For example, you neglect him and at the end he sees the bad guy as his "father" instead of you.
So to stay on topic of developing attachments to characters, the game does well with the various NPCs you come across.  Not only can you develop attachments as the player but there is even a system in game to determine how various NPCs like you.
Next I'll move onto the factions.  This game has a number of different factions you can get involved with.  Some of which are at odds with each other.  Unfortunately the game doesn't have the system found in FO:NV.  This should be a staple in future FO games and should include the "bad guys" and not just the "good guys".  While some are inherently good (minutemen), and some inherently bad (raiders), others should be inherently neutral (gunners).  The gunners, from my understanding, are guns for hire.  They should be neutral unless you do things to get on their bad side.  You should also be able to join them, as well as the raiders (provided you can get on their good side since they are hostile by default), and even the supermutents.  Getting good with one faction should likely mean opposing another.  Hell, imagine having the option of helping the hurt alien and joining an alian faction whose base of operation is in orbit?
There is also an imbalance with how the factions are presented.  With the minutemen, it is thrown in your face at the beginning of the game.  Meanwhile, other factions, like the underground railroad, require you to overhear a conversation and then you go on a wild goose chase.  Now I'm not saying that they should be introduced the same way, just that the different ways should come with equal opportunity.  Hell, rather than just Concord, Codsworth should randomly pick one of several locations you should try first (several = number of factions), resulting in an equal opportunity that the first faction you join is any of the ones available.  This would also increase the games replayability factor.
Now for controls.  The controls are responsive and smooth but they haven't really changed at all from game to game.  Modern FPS games have made improvements and yet, despite FO being part FPS, they haven't adopted those improvements.  The NPCs have more control and movement options than the player with their pressing up against cover, peeking around corners, shooting from cover, etc.  The advantage the player has over the enemy is being able to freely jump.  Why is it so hard for AI to jump?
Keeping controls in mind, I want to talk about the stealth mechanic which also hasn't changed and is the same in the Elderscrolls series (since Morrowind).  Sneaking shouldn't be something you "activate".  It should simply be something that is passive/active.  After all, if you see an enemy walking in the distance and they are not aware of you, you shouldn't have to "activate sneak" to get the sneak attack.  A shot from standing should also work.  So by removing crouching from sneaking, you can then introduce three position options often seen in FPS games.  Stand, crouch, and prone.
So with stealth a more passive system, it wouldn't be without it's active elements.  Lighting and sticking to the shadows, weight of your gear, how fast you move, lower profile (so crouched simply reduces detection while prone reduces it further), line of sight, etc.  Sound detection should be in contrast to ambient sounds.  An enemy in a generator room shouldn't be able to hear me running down the hall.  Also with objects like bushes, even though you can pass through them freely, should still impact line of sight for detection purposes.
Now for mods.  Mods have always been a wonderful addition to both the ES and FO games.  As single player games, mods allow players to individually cator the game to their wants.  Being able to get mods and install them via the title menu within the game is what I would call another staple that should be seen from here on.  With that said, any mod made via the creation kit and made available in game should be "approved" mods.  What I mean is, non "cheat" mods or otherwise mods that would warrent turning off achievements.  They should also be mods that have been tested to be bug free with incompatabilities kept to a minimum.  With that said, the ingame mod feature really needs a bug/incompatability reporting system and not just a reporting system for "inappropriate content".  While on that topic, I should be able to prove my age to gain access to 'age appropriate content'.  As a 34 yo I like, not only an ultra realistic game, but a more mature game.
The developers need to get serious with in-house play testing prior to release.  This is actually benefitial to both the player and developing studio alike.  If you consider the manhours (and associated cost) put into fixing bugs post release, if these bugs were identified and fixed mid-production, the customers would be happier with a higher quality product (which means more revenue) and the developers would've spent lest money on in-house play testers finding bugs that could've been fixed by the devs as they were already working on the game, than on those same devs fixing the bugs on a finished product when those manhours could be better spent on revenue content like DLCs and expansions.
As it stands with Bethesda, I do not recomment pre-odering.  I don't even recommend buying on the day it releases.  My recommendation, wait one year then buy it.  This is so that the bigger bugs will be fixed, post-production production (O.o) is finished, mods have been releases, and more honest reviews have been made.  Since you're waiting, wait for a sale and save some money.  Remember that waiting for a sale isn't some statement that means anything to Bethesda.  Retail sales don't impact producer revenue.  It's just a matter of 'why spend money you don't have to?'.  It's the refusal to pre-order and the delay in buying that sends a message.  In the business world, money talks, and so it is better to let your wallets do the talking when dealing with developer transgression.
I'll conclude with a general consensus.  Despite the room for improvement, and despite the bugs that persist to this day, the game is all-in-all really good.  It's visually appealing, with 100s of hours of content that is quite enjoyable.  Mods really make this game worth getting, and some of the bugs can even be fixed easily with a little online searching as others have found either a solution or a work-a-round.  There are even some mods that fix bugs.  It's for this reason that I say "yes" to recommending the game but emphasize on not pre-ordering and even waiting a year before buying future Bethesda games as a means of sending a message to Bethesda that they are getting slack with their products.

So, what is this game? It's a 2D old school rpg with that lets you travel to randomized planets.
The negatives:
1. Its very unbalanced at the moment regarding loot and enemy progression. There is no progressional loot that you can find by killing hostile npc. Quite literally 99% of the time you never find an item uprade for your character, instead you just craft the stuff yourself through mining before you even get to the "next level" of planets, essentially starting with the best gear as you start on higher tier planets and weapons that drop are NEVER better than what you've already crafted. Armor items do not even drop, you can only craft them other than back-piece items.
2. The space-aspect of the game is lacking, considering that's the biggest feature of this game. Guns for the most part are useless compared to melee weapons and you can't make your own guns even though you own and fly a space ship. You can only find guns by killing enemies, and the damage on them is usually 40% lower than melee weapon damage making them useless for the most part.
3. The ship you start with cannot be expanded upon or improved.
4. Traveling to planets becomes stale, most of the civilizations you encounter do not sell you anything of value in regards to weapons or armor (they will never sell you anything better than you can craft before you even enter a higher-tier of planets), the only armor in the game that you can find is crafted yourself, making merchants that you can potentially find on planets completely worthless regarding armor and guns, its meaningless. There is no trading or cargo delivery missions or anything like in regards to any sort of questing/missions aspect in the game at all, and in-game money (pixels) is way too easy to get. There are no missions or quests you can randomly find on planets is what I'm trying to say.
5. The bosses are way too easy, enemies are way too easy to exploit regarding using the matter manipulator (just build some strategic dirt walkways and the boss will never even get a chance to hit you).
6. Building your own house/base on a planet is absolutely pointless. There is no advantage or gain in doing so, there is no benefit. There is no trading, or the ability to set up trading ports that you build. You cannot build space stations, you cannot expand your ship but even if you could there would be no point in doing so. Being able to build in-general is meaningless and pointless in this game.
7. Mining ore becomes tedious, as it takes up 80% of your time in the game until you reach end-game armors and weapons that you can craft through your time spent mining. After that you can finally enjoy the game by exploring, but once you do you realize there's nothing to do. Crafting your weapons and armor is better than anything you can find regarding weapons/armors as you progress through the content. You basically just mine ore, craft your next melee weapon and armor set, then go into the next level of planets already starting with the best gear. It makes progressing boring because you start out with the best armors and weapons every time and can't actually FIND anything better than what you craft yourself. There is no sense of loot progression whatsoever. It's completely unbalanced. There basically is no loot at all in a sense.
8. There are a variety of biomes, (tentacle, magma, grasslands, deserts, ice) but all of them are exactly the same in the end, they all have merchants that sell absolute crap items that are worthless, have no quests or missions to complete on them whatsoever. Basically the only reason you travel to different planets is to mine different ores, THAT'S IT!
9. There are no missions you can find on planets, No trading missions, no cargo missions, No quests, no missions, No nothing, no loot progression. The only point in traveling to higher tier planets is to find better ore types, but once you reach the end-game that too becomes pointless.
Overall, it's a bad and unbalanced game. It could be absolutely fantastic with about 5 or 10 more content patches but right now its just an empty unbalanced shell of a 2D game that has a lot of potential but right now that potential is nonexistent. It's basically a mining simulator, but a bad one, this game has nothing to do with space or technology at all in its current form.

The Fallout series is one of my favorite game series that I have played, and I would highly recommend for anyone who enjoys story-driven, lore rich games, and first person shooter action in newer titles like Fallout 3, New Vegas, and 4. While some believe 4 to be a lesser to the critically acclaimed New Vegas, and in some aspects like choices and lore New Vegas does better, but Fallout 4 is still an incredibly solid entry into the Fallout franchise. The game, from a veteran of the franchise's perspective, may feel a bit linear compared to its predecessors, but in terms of combat and role-playing elements, it retains that Fallout feel that many love. Side quests and various main questlines are incredibly entertaining and full of dark humor that defines the franchise. The new modding feature allows you to customize everything from your weapons, armor, and power armor sets, allowing for many diverse playstyles and looks to your builds. Settlements are a new edition that allow your charecter to set up living places throughout the Commonwealth, serving as both bases and homes to the many followers and settlers you meet on your adventure. The new and revamped "survival mode" does excatly what it says, make every day a struggle to keep yourself from dying. Harder enemies, mangement of your charecters food, water, and sleep levels, along with diseases that can hinder your charecters overall health. This keeps the game fresh, especially after beating it a few times on normal diffuculties, its rejuvenates the fun that this game offers. There are also plenty of dlc, 3 of which, Automatron, Far Harbor, and Nuka World, offering new locations, enemies, weapons, and stories/lore. For those who like building, there are also the Wasteland Workshop and Vault-Tec dlc's, which offer more placeable items and a new location for building, and even a unique questline involving a incomplete Vault. In closing, Fallout 4 is a great game, and a must have for anyone who enjoys being emersed in a post-apocolyptic setting with deadly monsters, radiation, stories, and plently of weapons and armor to help you survive the nuclear winter that is Fallout.

TLDR: Get a refund and buy New Vegas instead along with the DLC's.
- There is no level cap
- Grinding is unbelievably easy. I've played 43 hrs so far and I'm already level 39.
- Amount of XP required to level up is small
- The skill system is entirely different from any previous installment. You get a single skill point for every level and that point can be placed into perks or any of the S.P.E.C.I.A.L skills. Since there's no level cap you can max all of these out, hence making a unique character is not possible unless you purposefully withhold skill points.
- There's no karma system
- Very few factions
- You can't be a part of multiple factions. You become a part of one faction the others just become your enemy.
- Can't enslave people.
- You can't make peace between factions
- A voiced protagonist means you aren't playing as yourself but instead you're just controlling a puppet
- No Enclave
- No weird random crap that made fallout so amazing ( like the sex robot in New Vegas or the Dunwich building in 3 )
- No unique weapons. Sure you can find weapons with names but you can just end up building those anyways.
- No unique armor. Again yeah you can find named ones but you can always just build that same one or a better one.
- Power armor requires fusion cells for some reason
- Armor system went back to the basic like in 3 instead of something more complex like in New Vegas ( I mean that there is no Damage Threshold, and no condition bar so armor can't break with the exception of Power Armor )
- Power armor is too OP and makes the game child's play ( I restricted my use of the Armor for more of a challenge )
- No extensive dialogue trees like before. Instead you get a system similar to the one used in Mass Effect. Every option is just a vague decription of what your character will say, which is a horrible idea. I want to know exactly what I'm saying so I don't♥♥♥♥♥♥off the NPC and get locked out of a quest or get fired on or accidently become enemies.
- Enemies are so weak, yes even the Deathclaws. So to make up for it you have fight them in hordes which just becomes a boring grindfest that just drags on forever. Takes the joy out of killing.
- Landmines E V E R Y W H E R E and they spawn in randomly. I wouldn't mind this if it weren't for the fact that they are everywhere.
- The stupid animation when using stimpaks prevents you from running or aiming. I've died to landmines and other crap because of this.
- Radiation reduces over all health as opposed to mutating you or reducing your S.P.E.C.I.A.L skills like previously. Keep in mind this is a game taking place in a post-nuclear war os radiation is everywhere. Stack up on Radaway.
- You can't have more than one companion
- Companions are boring.
- So many meaningless fetch quests. The Preston settlement quests get old quick, same with the technical documents, viable samples, etc. These bear no effect on the story.
- The story is short and extremely linear. I finished the damn thing in less that two days and this was me avoiding doing the main quest.
- The game was just a mash up of previous installments. Most obvious ripoff being Liberty Prime, it was the same scenario as it was in Fallout 3.
- Finally getting to meet your son was about as emotionally cathartic as opening a New York Peppermint Patty on a Tuesday.
- The settlements are just there as a time waster. They provide no contributions to the story.
- The settlement building system is meh at best and just another time waster.
- You can't buy hookers
- "RPG"..............................................................................................................Undertale was more of an rpg

- Fighting is just such a chore. Like "Yeah I can go fight that Legendary Mirelurk King no problem ezpz, but nah too boring"
- Very little satisfaction gained from fightin enemies or doing quests.

(This review was written a long time ago, there has been a HUGE content update since then.)
Since Christian wrote KIND OF a one sided review I'm going to tell you all you need to know about this game before you buy it.
(it sure seems for everyone of these pros I need to put an asterisk by it.)
First the Pros.
For a game that's not nearly finished there is sure a lot of content and a lot to do.
The artstyle is great and colorful for the most part, everything's distinct, you're not gonna get confused or overwhelmed.
The space travel has potential and early on you'll be having fun with it.
The music is wonderful, it's like if Halo and TES: Oblivion's composers got together on this because some of the music sure reminds me of those games.
If you want difficulty, you're sure going to be dying a bunch early on in this game because there's a lot of things to contribute towards death; hunger, heat, creatures and whatnot.
-The difficulty isn't forced and if you die you felt like it's your fault.
Now for the cons.
While early on you'll be having a blast, it soon gets repetitive once you've played enough, every planet feels the same and it bores you. I really do savor the moments when I find something interesting, like a military prison that has been overrun by its prisoners or a temple full of angry florans.
But finding these things takes chance and by 15 hrs in the game you're on the wiki looking for cool places to visit.
The music feels off. The game is very sci-fi-esque and they've got the music set to a fantasy world.
It can fit in the right planets but most of the time it feels like you're playing death metal while frolicking in the flowers.
Tediousness. The game feels like you're just grinding way too much.
Scouring the land in search of coal JUST to fuel your ship just feels like busy-work
Having to create a beacon for a boss fight JUST to die and have to create it AGAIN.
It's infuriating and certaintly takes away from the experience.
It's unfinished. Now mind you I know this is early access but this review is for someone who is wanting to PURCHASE the game.
No It's not riddled with bugs.
Yes if you play it enough it gets dull.
I've heard they are adding new things like space combat.
But if you are wanting a FULL game stacked to the top with content then, you may or may not want to hold your cash.
So that's my review, it's a good game, not the greatest albeit I did enjoy this game a lot more than Terraria.
I'm really hopeful in the future of this game.

Fallout 4 is my second game in the Fallout franchise. I have previously only played Fallout 3. I love adventure/action games that have huge worlds to explore and Fallout 4 fufills that criteria. I knew i would like this game even before i started and i was not disapointed.
There's a lot of quests and the main story is very engaging, at least in the beginning. I usually dont like replaying games i have finished but i guess the replay value would be good since there are a lot of quests and you will probably miss many of the side quests if you're not a questaholic. You can also play in any style you want, stealth/sneaking, gung-ho warrior or whatever suits you.
The slow-motion mode in combat is cool, but also slows down the pace of the action somewhat.
The feel of movement and use of weapons are very good and flows well. The enemies are also interesting and well voice-acted, but as in many of these games, after a while you begin to hear the same phrases by the enemies, which is fine.
The crafting and building mechanics are also a cool addition to the franchise and it is a good system where you can build some very fancy creations. It is however a bit limited in where you can place items and building-parts. There are methods and glitches you can make use of to get around this limitation. Search youtube :)
After a while and if you have freed many settlements you can get kind of bored with these types of quests, and there are many settlements. I mean, how many settlements can you build and upgrade before it gets a bit repetetive. So unless you're a crafting fanatic who love spending hours upon hours bulding houses and detailing your bases, which can be very trying due to the placing limitations mentioned earlier, this will probably not be your favourite part of the game.
All in all however i highly recomend this game if you like first person adventure/action/RPG type of games.

I have played a lot of FO4. A LOT. I bought it on PS4 originally because I wanted to take away the urge to cheat or mod it, I just wanted to experience the game. And that was great, for a time. You reach a point where you're just glitching things to make them work the way they should, you're reaching limits that don't make sense and getting bored with the available vanilla content. So I bought it on PC and modded it to death and I mean that because my game got broken a few times due to mods not liking Bethesdas updates. Yes, I mean that Bethesda broke the mods by updating their own game, they kept trying to fix things within the game without telling the community that was modding the game without any help from Bethesda because the CK was released soooooo late, I think in part because the game was so buggy.
So the developer ruined my gaming experience and the game was buggy? Yep. So I obviously hate the game then? Nope. I love the game but I really think it could have had more love from the developer. The story is a little shallow, a lot of the decisions you make don't really have any effective repercussions and I think there were a lot of game mechanics dropped from the finished game to make it more console friendly. The limits on settlement size are not there for PC players benefit, it's solely for console players but I exceeded the vanilla limits on PS4 many times over with very little issue. One of the things I didn't like was that the building of settlements didn't really have any impact on the story or the world and didn't encourage people to build or reward those that did, I think this was a bit of a copout on Bethesdas part. The DLC is another matter, other than Far Harbour and Nuka World the other DLC should have been included at launch, there was no reason for it to be an extra cost and the assets were already in the game. It's the kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that causes bad blood within the gaming community. The console modding controversy and Bethesdas handling of it also caused further animosity but I'm not going to get into that.
Would I recommend this game though? HELL YES! It's a good game, there are parts of the game that annoy me beyond belief and others that just need more attention (that the modding community have sorted) but it's a fun game and I enjoy settlement building. I think that if you just want a game to play and don't want to build up settlements in the world and roleplay then this game may not be for you but if you enjoy those elements and are prepared to mod your game (because modding helps to fix a number of issues/annoyances with the game) then you should buy it (and you probably already have).

This is gonna be a review of Fallout 4 without any of the DLC, so I've only got that to go off.
Fallout 4 is a bad roleplaying game but a decent timekiller, which is awful considering the price of the game, as well as how much time went into developing it in the first place. Fallout 4 forces you to play as the same character with a predetermined backstory, destroying any opportunity you have of creating a truly customizable character. It also completely mutilates the old dialogue system implemented by the previous 2 Fallout games (as well as the older isometric games) by replacing the dialogue window's multiple, detailed options for each choice and replacing it with a discount Bioware dialogue wheel, with even less choices (4), and with the information of each option available to the player being so low, it may as well be considered a mini puzzle game just figuring out what each one means.
Fallout 4 does do a lot of really good stuff for the series, though all of it is overshadowed by all of the other fundamental roleplaying flaws. There are REALLY good ideas in this game, the power armor system, the weapon custimizaton (to a degree), and the overall feel of the gunplay is a huge improvement for the Fallout series. Unfortunately for Fallout 4 one of its other premiere features, settlement building, feels like a shallow addition to the game that forces several areas of it to be empty (as well as Bethesda putting an insane amount of importance in this system, at least for a few factions.
Overall I'd say Fallout 4 is a decent timesink, but I wouldn't put it anywhere near the same league as New Vegas or even Fallout 3 in terms of depth and replayability. It's fun to explore the wastes and shoot stuff with your companions for a few hours. If you just want a game that does exploration well, then go ahead and buy this, try to wait for a sale first though as Fallout 4 is still quite pricey. If you want a genuine roleplay experience then I suggest doing a bit more research before deciding whether or not you should buy the game, as while genuinely bad in this regard, some of its issues can be lessend through the use of mods.

Fallout 4 is my second game in the Fallout franchise. I have previously only played Fallout 3. I love adventure/action games that have huge worlds to explore and Fallout 4 fufills that criteria. I knew i would like this game even before i started and i was not disapointed.
There's a lot of quests and the main story is very engaging, at least in the beginning. I usually dont like replaying games i have finished but i guess the replay value would be good since there are a lot of quests and you will probably miss many of the side quests if you're not a questaholic. You can also play in any style you want, stealth/sneaking, gung-ho warrior or whatever suits you.
The slow-motion mode in combat is cool, but also slows down the pace of the action somewhat.
The feel of movement and use of weapons are very good and flows well. The enemies are also interesting and well voice-acted, but as in many of these games, after a while you begin to hear the same phrases by the enemies, which is fine.
The crafting and building mechanics are also a cool addition to the franchise and it is a good system where you can build some very fancy creations. It is however a bit limited in where you can place items and building-parts. There are methods and glitches you can make use of to get around this limitation. Search youtube :)
After a while and if you have freed many settlements you can get kind of bored with these types of quests, and there are many settlements. I mean, how many settlements can you build and upgrade before it gets a bit repetetive. So unless you're a crafting fanatic who love spending hours upon hours bulding houses and detailing your bases, which can be very trying due to the placing limitations mentioned earlier, this will probably not be your favourite part of the game.
All in all however i highly recomend this game if you like first person adventure/action/RPG type of games.

I have played a lot of FO4. A LOT. I bought it on PS4 originally because I wanted to take away the urge to cheat or mod it, I just wanted to experience the game. And that was great, for a time. You reach a point where you're just glitching things to make them work the way they should, you're reaching limits that don't make sense and getting bored with the available vanilla content. So I bought it on PC and modded it to death and I mean that because my game got broken a few times due to mods not liking Bethesdas updates. Yes, I mean that Bethesda broke the mods by updating their own game, they kept trying to fix things within the game without telling the community that was modding the game without any help from Bethesda because the CK was released soooooo late, I think in part because the game was so buggy.
So the developer ruined my gaming experience and the game was buggy? Yep. So I obviously hate the game then? Nope. I love the game but I really think it could have had more love from the developer. The story is a little shallow, a lot of the decisions you make don't really have any effective repercussions and I think there were a lot of game mechanics dropped from the finished game to make it more console friendly. The limits on settlement size are not there for PC players benefit, it's solely for console players but I exceeded the vanilla limits on PS4 many times over with very little issue. One of the things I didn't like was that the building of settlements didn't really have any impact on the story or the world and didn't encourage people to build or reward those that did, I think this was a bit of a copout on Bethesdas part. The DLC is another matter, other than Far Harbour and Nuka World the other DLC should have been included at launch, there was no reason for it to be an extra cost and the assets were already in the game. It's the kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that causes bad blood within the gaming community. The console modding controversy and Bethesdas handling of it also caused further animosity but I'm not going to get into that.
Would I recommend this game though? HELL YES! It's a good game, there are parts of the game that annoy me beyond belief and others that just need more attention (that the modding community have sorted) but it's a fun game and I enjoy settlement building. I think that if you just want a game to play and don't want to build up settlements in the world and roleplay then this game may not be for you but if you enjoy those elements and are prepared to mod your game (because modding helps to fix a number of issues/annoyances with the game) then you should buy it (and you probably already have).

(This review was written a long time ago, there has been a HUGE content update since then.)
Since Christian wrote KIND OF a one sided review I'm going to tell you all you need to know about this game before you buy it.
(it sure seems for everyone of these pros I need to put an asterisk by it.)
First the Pros.
For a game that's not nearly finished there is sure a lot of content and a lot to do.
The artstyle is great and colorful for the most part, everything's distinct, you're not gonna get confused or overwhelmed.
The space travel has potential and early on you'll be having fun with it.
The music is wonderful, it's like if Halo and TES: Oblivion's composers got together on this because some of the music sure reminds me of those games.
If you want difficulty, you're sure going to be dying a bunch early on in this game because there's a lot of things to contribute towards death; hunger, heat, creatures and whatnot.
-The difficulty isn't forced and if you die you felt like it's your fault.
Now for the cons.
While early on you'll be having a blast, it soon gets repetitive once you've played enough, every planet feels the same and it bores you. I really do savor the moments when I find something interesting, like a military prison that has been overrun by its prisoners or a temple full of angry florans.
But finding these things takes chance and by 15 hrs in the game you're on the wiki looking for cool places to visit.
The music feels off. The game is very sci-fi-esque and they've got the music set to a fantasy world.
It can fit in the right planets but most of the time it feels like you're playing death metal while frolicking in the flowers.
Tediousness. The game feels like you're just grinding way too much.
Scouring the land in search of coal JUST to fuel your ship just feels like busy-work
Having to create a beacon for a boss fight JUST to die and have to create it AGAIN.
It's infuriating and certaintly takes away from the experience.
It's unfinished. Now mind you I know this is early access but this review is for someone who is wanting to PURCHASE the game.
No It's not riddled with bugs.
Yes if you play it enough it gets dull.
I've heard they are adding new things like space combat.
But if you are wanting a FULL game stacked to the top with content then, you may or may not want to hold your cash.
So that's my review, it's a good game, not the greatest albeit I did enjoy this game a lot more than Terraria.
I'm really hopeful in the future of this game.

While it may look essentially like Terraria but in space, it is actually.......Terraria but in space. But wait, there's more!. Starbound is 10x better than Terraria in every aspect (well apart from the combat, but that's being addressed even as I write this), what with the ability to create entire towns and even a civilization, completely under your control.
You have complete freedom to explore right from the get go (provided you acquire enough resources from your starting planet) and see a massive plethora of worlds(around 200 billion worlds added so far), each a part of one giant sector and each sector a part of one gigantic universe, that is constantly expanding with each update.
And if that doesn't excite you, the game is completely moddifiable, right down to the base code allowing even the most brain dead of gamers who haven't a single clue how to even edit a simple text file, to implement whatever their hearts desire (tired of your spaceship?, want to fly around in the USS Enterprise or a Star Destroyer?, just design it in an image editing software, follow an in depth guide from the starbound forums so you can implement it and there we go!).
And this is all just in the early access beta phase and at a reasonable price of £11.99. You honestly can't go wrong with buying this, it's not only very fun to play alone but extremely enjoyable when with others, and thanks to the game being so similar to Terraria it is very simple to set up your own home made server for all your friends to join.
Overall I highly recommend acquiring this game, it is one of the best games out there and is one of the most popular on steam at this moment, so hurry up and get this game right now!.

Fallout 4 is my second game in the Fallout franchise. I have previously only played Fallout 3. I love adventure/action games that have huge worlds to explore and Fallout 4 fufills that criteria. I knew i would like this game even before i started and i was not disapointed.
There's a lot of quests and the main story is very engaging, at least in the beginning. I usually dont like replaying games i have finished but i guess the replay value would be good since there are a lot of quests and you will probably miss many of the side quests if you're not a questaholic. You can also play in any style you want, stealth/sneaking, gung-ho warrior or whatever suits you.
The slow-motion mode in combat is cool, but also slows down the pace of the action somewhat.
The feel of movement and use of weapons are very good and flows well. The enemies are also interesting and well voice-acted, but as in many of these games, after a while you begin to hear the same phrases by the enemies, which is fine.
The crafting and building mechanics are also a cool addition to the franchise and it is a good system where you can build some very fancy creations. It is however a bit limited in where you can place items and building-parts. There are methods and glitches you can make use of to get around this limitation. Search youtube :)
After a while and if you have freed many settlements you can get kind of bored with these types of quests, and there are many settlements. I mean, how many settlements can you build and upgrade before it gets a bit repetetive. So unless you're a crafting fanatic who love spending hours upon hours bulding houses and detailing your bases, which can be very trying due to the placing limitations mentioned earlier, this will probably not be your favourite part of the game.
All in all however i highly recomend this game if you like first person adventure/action/RPG type of games.
