I have played a lot of FO4. A LOT. I bought it on PS4 originally because I wanted to take away the urge to cheat or mod it, I just wanted to experience the game. And that was great, for a time. You reach a point where you're just glitching things to make them work the way they should, you're reaching limits that don't make sense and getting bored with the available vanilla content. So I bought it on PC and modded it to death and I mean that because my game got broken a few times due to mods not liking Bethesdas updates. Yes, I mean that Bethesda broke the mods by updating their own game, they kept trying to fix things within the game without telling the community that was modding the game without any help from Bethesda because the CK was released soooooo late, I think in part because the game was so buggy.
So the developer ruined my gaming experience and the game was buggy? Yep. So I obviously hate the game then? Nope. I love the game but I really think it could have had more love from the developer. The story is a little shallow, a lot of the decisions you make don't really have any effective repercussions and I think there were a lot of game mechanics dropped from the finished game to make it more console friendly. The limits on settlement size are not there for PC players benefit, it's solely for console players but I exceeded the vanilla limits on PS4 many times over with very little issue. One of the things I didn't like was that the building of settlements didn't really have any impact on the story or the world and didn't encourage people to build or reward those that did, I think this was a bit of a copout on Bethesdas part. The DLC is another matter, other than Far Harbour and Nuka World the other DLC should have been included at launch, there was no reason for it to be an extra cost and the assets were already in the game. It's the kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that causes bad blood within the gaming community. The console modding controversy and Bethesdas handling of it also caused further animosity but I'm not going to get into that.
Would I recommend this game though? HELL YES! It's a good game, there are parts of the game that annoy me beyond belief and others that just need more attention (that the modding community have sorted) but it's a fun game and I enjoy settlement building. I think that if you just want a game to play and don't want to build up settlements in the world and roleplay then this game may not be for you but if you enjoy those elements and are prepared to mod your game (because modding helps to fix a number of issues/annoyances with the game) then you should buy it (and you probably already have).

I can't in good conscience recommend this game in its current state.  I think this game has great potential, but right now, it's just not fun.  I feel like I'm playing a game where gaining the best furniture is the greatest feat.  Terraria was great, and this game is definetly similar in ways, but it's missing something, and I can't put my finger on it.  For one, it's utterly boring and tedious to play in single player.  Everyone seems to be strung up on the space exploration and new proceduraly generated worlds that are everywhere, but what they don't realize is Terraria did this too.  The only difference is that in Terraria, you have to leave the game and create a new procedurally generated world through the menus screens.  In this game, they give the illusion that these "worlds" are simply out there and waiting for you by bypassing the "create new world" process and putting you in a space ship to travel to these already "existing worlds".  I'm sorry, but why don't people see this?  It's nothing new!
I also can't come to terms with the "random" creature generation process.  Every 50 feet, you come across a new enemy, which coincidentily is paired with another creature of the same make.  This isn't new and innovative, it's hardcoded, select a random creature based on the world, and spawn 2 of them every 50 feet.  It hurts my soul how deep people are getting sucked up by this.
Now, to say this game is bad would be silly.  There are definetly good aspects of this game (in it's current state), but I think they just don't fit yet, being as it is still in an alpha or beta build.  The crafting and upgrading to new tiers by killing a new boss or collecting a rare item is kind of cool, I guess, but meh, I'm not over the top in love with it.  I also think progress is a bit slow, but that's just me.  One thing I particullarly like is the random weapon generation functionality (kind of).  It's a cool concept, but at the time being, I am hard pressed to find an upgrade to my current weapon without a crazy amount of farming.
I've got high hopes for this game once it's finished, but for now, I'd say stay away unless you'd like to be involved in the alpha/beta process.  However, if you have 2+ friends to play this with at the moment, then by all means I'd say jump in.  Just don't be surprised to get bored quickly if you choose to play alone.

I can't in good conscience recommend this game in its current state.  I think this game has great potential, but right now, it's just not fun.  I feel like I'm playing a game where gaining the best furniture is the greatest feat.  Terraria was great, and this game is definetly similar in ways, but it's missing something, and I can't put my finger on it.  For one, it's utterly boring and tedious to play in single player.  Everyone seems to be strung up on the space exploration and new proceduraly generated worlds that are everywhere, but what they don't realize is Terraria did this too.  The only difference is that in Terraria, you have to leave the game and create a new procedurally generated world through the menus screens.  In this game, they give the illusion that these "worlds" are simply out there and waiting for you by bypassing the "create new world" process and putting you in a space ship to travel to these already "existing worlds".  I'm sorry, but why don't people see this?  It's nothing new!
I also can't come to terms with the "random" creature generation process.  Every 50 feet, you come across a new enemy, which coincidentily is paired with another creature of the same make.  This isn't new and innovative, it's hardcoded, select a random creature based on the world, and spawn 2 of them every 50 feet.  It hurts my soul how deep people are getting sucked up by this.
Now, to say this game is bad would be silly.  There are definetly good aspects of this game (in it's current state), but I think they just don't fit yet, being as it is still in an alpha or beta build.  The crafting and upgrading to new tiers by killing a new boss or collecting a rare item is kind of cool, I guess, but meh, I'm not over the top in love with it.  I also think progress is a bit slow, but that's just me.  One thing I particullarly like is the random weapon generation functionality (kind of).  It's a cool concept, but at the time being, I am hard pressed to find an upgrade to my current weapon without a crazy amount of farming.
I've got high hopes for this game once it's finished, but for now, I'd say stay away unless you'd like to be involved in the alpha/beta process.  However, if you have 2+ friends to play this with at the moment, then by all means I'd say jump in.  Just don't be surprised to get bored quickly if you choose to play alone.

Excellent game!
This is a fantastic game and I recommend it to everyone. Here are some of the good parts:
1. The Story. The story is great. It has twists and places where you have to make irreversible decisions. All the while, there are chances to backstab your allies. Also, the decisions you have to make are never black and white. There are pros and cons to each.
2. Sheer content. It took me 80 hours to clear this game. At the end, I felt like I was rushing just to get to the end. It was one of those games that I liked so much, it was consuming me. I felt like I just needed to finish, but still took 80 hours! I have no doubt that there is over 200 hours worth of content in this game.
3. Weapons and crafting. The weapons in this game are really cool. Legendary weapons add extra bonuses to weapons you already like. Then, you can mod them. Be sure to save ALL your junk, because modding weapons is so good. To give you an example, the Fat boy shoots a mini nuke. Devestating damge. The legendary form I found shoots two projectiles (while still only using one ammo per shot). When you mod it, it makes the mini nuke split into 8 mini-nukes. So for the final battle, I had a gun that could launch 16 mini nukes...KABOOM!
4. Perks. The perk tree in this game is excellent. There's a ton of variety in how you build your character and plenty of perks that overlap, so you never really feel like theres no room to expand. I personally built a melee weilding, drug pumping maniac. When I got in a pinch, I took a drug that makes time slow down. So I'd sprint around the room in slow mo, absolutley wrecking face with my supersledge hammer.
5. Replayability. I can see myself coming back and playing the game several times. There are 4 factions to choose which i'm sure create dramatically different endings. I also want to try a different build next time. Probably something stealthy, since I was a "run in all drugged up and smash face" build.
6. Base building. Base building is fun, but not required. I like that. The things you build are also useful. Like, if you build your perks properly, you can build vendors in your bases. Makes it really easy to get all the supplies you need. But if that's not your thing, you'll have a bunch of perks you can use for damage dealing and survival.
7. Quality. This game is well made. There's a big attention to detail and a million little easter eggs you can find. For example, if you find an overdue book, you can drop in the library return box for rewards. There's countless little things that keep the game interesting and will help me replay it over and over.
Cons:
I enjoyed this too much and neglected my wife.
Some features are not explained well in game. A throw back to older games. Just google stuff and you'll be fine.
It could feel like there's too much to do. At one point, I had over 20 quests. It was hard to tell which ones moved the story forward.
Some of the character interactions are awkward. Preston kept telling me how much he trusted me and how he'd never say these things to someone else.
If you build your perks poorly, you'll suffer. I recommend playing an hour or two to get a feel for things, then reset.

I have been following and supporting this game since development of it began, and I have to say I am mostly disappointed with it.
I constantly suffer from fatal crashes when trying to play. The game hangs at startup 60% of the time, if I try to jump to another planet the game crashes or suddenly becomes very zoomed in, if I warp to my ship and back down to a planet too quickly the game crashes. And then there are these times when the game seems to be running perfectly fine, and it suddenly freezes. I agree that beta is beta, but even most indie devs have their game properly optimized by the time they bring it to open beta.
When I actually do manage to get the game running, however, I run into even more problems, namely the sheer lack of content the game has to offer. And what it does have to offer, Terraria does better. Yes, for the most parts, in beta there is often still a lot of content to be added to the game and tweaks to be made. However,  this game feels like it is still in alpha. The mob and npc AI is terrible, most npcs camping out in the wilderness die to mobs before I even get to see them on the screen, you can't even properly interact with npcs at the moment, mining for resources feels horrendously tedious, crafting progression is very slow, the UI is pretty poor and fiddly, and the combat is basic at best and feels quite boring.
As for the randomly generated animals and worlds it all feels rather superficial as all worlds have the same resources available (albeit in different amounts), the monsters all act in the same predictable way, and there aren't all that many different body parts for the different monsters so once you see all of the randomly generated body parts any new monsters you see quickly loose their novelty. The only unique and interesting things that new worlds have to offer are the dungeons, and even then, once you encounter all the dungeon types they are no longer exciting or enjoyable to explore.
I can't help but feel that this genre of game has been exhausted. I was hoping that Starbound would rejuvenate it and bring some interesting and new ideas to the table, but it is just the same thing over and over again. Now, I'm not saying at all that Starbound is a bad game. I bought this game with full knowledge that it isn't finished yet. Terraria, their previous game, took a very long time to flesh out and become what it is today. Given a couple of years, this game has the potential to be even more enjoyable and vast in content as Terraria is. But for now it's a solid avoid for me.

Exploration feels hollow because, despite planets having different flora, fauna, and terrain, these procedurally generated elements seem repetitive after a while. The universe does not feel alive, it feels constructed. It seems like procedural generation is less impressive than a fixed universe with real planet names, real people and places and events.
The crafting system requires use of "pixels", a currency which is used not only to purchase items from npcs but also to pay in part for the items you craft. i.e. you can't build things out of the materials you spent time mining unless you have enough money to buy it. Although this is not the case for simpler items (like bandages, torches, rope), any items of higher caliber require it. The 3D printer is a nice idea, but I'd much rather be able to simply find these items and craft them myself than have to print them.
One of my biggest gripes is that the ship cannot be changed. Maybe with mods, but I tend not to count those as part of the actual game, any more than I would count DLC as part of a base game. I wouldn't mind being able to add rooms to my vessel, or new technology, weapons, color. I know I can change the walls and hang pictures or whatever, but that's immaterial compared to being able to add more space to store my belongings.
Overall, Starbound seems to lack the focus of Terraria. It incorporates some of the best elements of that game and some of the worst. And there is a certain lack of logic to the game which I find unnerving: Why am I using medieval craftware if I arrived on a spaceship? Why does my ship burn coal to travel to other star systems? Why am I finding the same elements on every single planet? Why do robots need to eat or breathe? How do all of these planets have life forms on them?
I think adding a logical scifi-esque element would give the game a little more focus, just as a magical questing element lent direction to Terraria.
When Chucklefish finishes the game, it may be worth its cost. Until then, wait for it to go on sale.

Please understand that the game is still in development and when the game is updated the information in this review may be obsolete. When the development surpasses Beta [Indignant Koala 12/11/2013] you may be able to use this review to compare how the game has changed over development.
While the game progresses in development, it may also /invalidate/ your universe, ship and/or character. This can happen without warning due to it being in beta and not being the release candidate. If you are turned off by the possibly losing progress, consider something else until after the beta cycle.
--------------
Introduction
--------------
Starbound is a mixture of Sandbox, nonlinear game play, RPG and Exploring. That currently evolves around traveling the vast reaches of space to see wonders, slaughter masses and horde items within a pixel art format. The following will be a short break down of the different genre this game falls into.
Sandbox (Open World Concept) games are games which allow the player have many freedoms in the approach of how to play.  These types of games normally have a freeform type of play and are limited by the player’s interest over time or by the developer’s intent or overall content to explore.
Role playing games normally follow a format where the player plays in a type or role is able to identify with the lead role they take on. There are normally some types of multifaceted stats related to the role they take on, character development, story-telling and narrative elements. There are normally complexity to the features related to these games including character actions, experience, levels, inventory, combat and immersion.
Exploring is a hybrid of a platform game due to the graphics style.
If you are turned off by sandbox games, or open ended games you may want to do more research or look for something else entirely.
----------------------------
Concept / Features
----------------------------
Good amounts of the game is generated using a procedural format; so the planets will not be exactly the same, it may still have the same feeling however.
While you explore space, or really planets the player will spent a good deal of time using their spaceship. The spaceship can be used to house chests, items, tools, etc. The ship itself is also used as a means of travel between planets and sectors.
Building and crafting can be a bit tedious, since it is required for space progression, going to harder planets for better stuff. When starting the game, the game is limited to one sector and you must progress up the teir tree by facing 'bosses' to move to the next sector. Building is not limited to you can only build 'some things', the space ship has a Pixel Printer on it to duplicate items you've found while exploring. Thus you can keep producing things as long as you have pixels to do so.
Special abilities are introduced also; however the player is limited to using only one at a time currently. That is after actually finding the blueprint for a special ability on a planet.
Character wise, there is light customization at the start with selection of race, gender, color and clothes. When you progress in the game you are able to change your clothes select using a vanity option.
Being able to host individual servers is a nice touch, allows for customization, collaborative play and changes overall games experience.
--------------
Atmosphere
--------------
Atmosphere is a mixture of space; alien races which follow themes. Aliens you run into can be a hostile, non aggressive or crazy ape scientists; this changes per planet for the most part. There are also the 'animal' like alien life forms per planet which change also.
The ambiance the music creates is alright, the music can be customized by using the abc formatted music into the systems music related folder.
Graphics follow a somewhat fluid pixel art format, and most of the concepts and items follow theme and fit nicely together.
--------------
Stability
--------------
Starbound is still in beta; however it does have a large chunk of stability problems. Patches and updates have been present and there was a patch provided on launch day, so the development teams are working to solve the technical issues.
There are error dumps and other problems which can be off putting times however you should make sure to submit your problem so the developers are able to utilities the generated reports to fix problems.
Starbound has a large and growing community that the development staff uses as a platform to communicate with their customers. Their community platform is also used for reporting of bugs.
The current stability problems I still noticed that may not be changed over the span of this first beta is that the client side when run by itself has a resource hogging problem. Resources were not that problematic for the client computer when it was playing via a decent server. If you are fine with server only play this is fine, for individuals that want to play solo there is a problem.
I found from personal use just by running a personal server to connect to for myself that resource drain were greatly improved and it was more stable. However this would require the player to have two different computers that meet the minimal requirements if they wanted to play completely solo.
If you are using an older computer which has a single core and the rest meets the requirements you will find that it will have resource problems, even if it comparable to the dual core in speed. You may also need to disable the steam overlay while playing.
--------------
Conclusion
--------------
I would currently recommend this to someone who is /interested and willing/ to try a sandbox space exploration game combined building. This game will have a very interesting development, including they take a great deal of information, suggestions and concepts from the community. Chucklefish has a very interesting child here.

Welcome To My Review Of Fallout 4, I Was Really Excited To Play This Game, I Had Already Played Fallout 3 And Fallout New Vegas And Spent Over 500 Hours In Them. And Had Very High Expectations.
Graphics - The Graphics Look Amazing Compared To Fallout 3 And New Vegas, However Games Like The Witcher 3 Have Better Graphics.
Gameplay - It Is Great, A Huge Improvement In The Fallout Franchise.
Story - The Main Story Is Not The Best, I Would Say Decent, After You Find Your Son It Becomes A Lot Less Interesting, But The Small Stories Which You Will Find Through Doing Hundred Of Quests, They Are More Then Amazing!
The World - Its Huge, Its Looks Great, They Are Thousands Of Places To Explore And Loot Everywhere! What Do You Want Else?
Dialogue - It Is Worser Then In Fallout 3 And New Vegas, No Question There, Howerer Its Not As Bad Most People Say There Is Still A Lot Of Talking In The Game.
Loot - It Is Amazing, I Always Loved To Collect Every Item In Every Game I Played, And Fallout 4 Is Like A Dream For A Collector. Unique Armor,Weapons,Magazines,''Action Figures'' And Of Course Junk For Building Objects.
Settlement Mode - I Love It, Building Is Addicting As Hell, It Gives Junk A Purpose And A Bunch Of Playtime, Hovewer I Didnt Like The Fact That They Did 3 DLCS Only For The Settlement Mode.
DLC - It Has One Of The Best Season Passes Ever, You Can Buy It For Only 30Euros On Steam Key Websites. Even 50Euros Would Be Justified For It, The 3 Workshop DLCS Are Nice, But Not Amazing. But Nuka World,Far Harbor And Automatron Could Be Games On Their Own, So Much New Stuff! 2 New Worlds,Hundreds Of Quests,Weapons And Junk Of Course.
Achievements - The Design Is Amazing And 84 Achievements (With DLC) Is More Then Enough, But There Is 1 Thing Missing, And That Is Grinding Achievements, For Example Reach Max Level Or Collect All The Unique Weapons And Have Them In Your Inventory, Something Like That.
Play Time - You Can Play It Atleast For 500Hours, Reaching Max Level, Discovering All Locations, Getting All Unique Weapons, Completing All The Quests Propably Is Going To Take You About 1000Hours
Overall - Its Amazing, In My Opinion Its Better Then Fallout New Vegas But Not Better Then Fallout 3

A very good addition to the Fallout sequel. Not perfect, but it does some new things very well. If you've played Skyrim and purchased every home in every hold or if you really enjoyed Hearthfire, I would absolutely recommend this game. For me personally, the addition of the base building element probably doubled my enjoyment of the entire game.


I think as far as set-backs, the game doesn't feel like it has quite the depth as Fallout 3 seemed to have. There aren't quite as many of those tiny, story-like side quests and it felt as though there were a few too many of the repetitive, "endless" quests that perhaps drained a bit of realism away.


But, even with those faults, I would still absolutely recommend this game. I would recommend to someone who liked the past Fallout games, Skyrim, or any sort of adventuring and exploring RPG. It does not out-shine past Fallout or Elder Scroll games, but it's a solid addition to the library and it brings in some successful and interesting new elements.

I will give this game a thumbs-up again as soon as they justify this shaky development process with a more polished interface and more content.
The game is not unenjoyable really. I did find an underground high-tech warren of autonomous robots who look like they're straight out of 1960's scifi, so cheers! But that is about the only npc encounter I've had besides the random one-man hut with a person in it who has one line to say. Exploration feels hollow because, despite planets having different flora, fauna, and terrain, these procedurally generated elements seem repetitive after a while. The universe does not feel alive, it feels constructed. It seems like procedural generation is less impressive than a fixed universe with real planet names, real people and places and events.
The crafting system requires use of "pixels", a currency which is used not only to purchase items from npcs but also to pay in part for the items you craft. i.e. you can't build things out of the materials you spent time mining unless you have enough money to buy it. Although this is not the case for simpler items (like bandages, torches, rope), any items of higher caliber require it. The 3D printer is a nice idea, but I'd much rather be able to simply find these items and craft them myself than have to print them.
One of my biggest gripes is that the ship cannot be changed. Maybe with mods, but I tend not to count those as part of the actual game, any more than I would count DLC as part of a base game. I wouldn't mind being able to add rooms to my vessel, or new technology, weapons, color. I know I can change the walls and hang pictures or whatever, but that's immaterial compared to being able to add more space to store my belongings.
Overall, Starbound seems to lack the focus of Terraria. It incorporates some of the best elements of that game and some of the worst. And there is a certain lack of logic to the game which I find unnerving: Why am I using medieval craftware if I arrived on a spaceship? Why does my ship burn coal to travel to other star systems? Why am I finding the same elements on every single planet? Why do robots need to eat or breathe? How do all of these planets have life forms on them?
I think adding a logical scifi-esque element would give the game a little more focus, just as a magical questing element lent direction to Terraria.
When Chucklefish finishes the game, it may be worth its cost. Until then, wait for it to go on sale.

Summary:
-Tries to be Terraria but tries to be different by poorly implementing mechanics from Minecraft.
-Character control feels more heavy and burdened like a 3D game, making 2D control difficult.
-Crafting is tedius.
-The attempt at a directed narrative falls flat when trying to pair it with co-op and super-sandbox mechanics.
-The animations are sparse, most are motion tweens, drawn animations are very choppy, feels like lego men movement.
-The Arbitrary unit "pixels" used as currency and crafting catalyst feels out of place and annoying.
If you're looking for Terraria in space, look elsewhere.
Expanded explaination:
This game takes the things I loved about terraria and replaces them with things I hated or just disliked from minecraft. The crafting system is far more cumbersome and slow than terraria, the music is more akin to minecraft's docet ambience than terraria's "listen anywhere anytime" soundtrack, most imporantly, the game feels much worse than terraria. For example, the jumping has roughly the same vertical height as terraria's, standard for 2d games where up and down replace the spectrum of movement available in 3D, however this jumping has the same physics and momentum of a 3D game specifically minecraft. In a combat centric game, having a floaty jump with very little horizontal control is beyond frustrating. This is amplified by having randomly generated caverns that have no cohesion with the scale of fall damage in the game, falling 1.5 "screens" (viewable vertical distance) is an instant kill. Terraria also had instant fall damage but it was more of a slap on the wrist for poor decision making and very rarely punished you for exploring while in starbound I often found myself dying from fall damage unexpectedly and quite often. The slow crafting in minecraft fits the survival realism motif, in starbound, waiting forever for ore to smelt just feels incredibly tedius, even more so than minecraft.

7.5/10 Keep up the good work. BETA is amazing already. Cant wait for more content to be added over time. Some issues still need to be resolved but its still early stages and Im sure theyll get ironed in time. Similarities to Terraria is obvious but it was expected. Starbound is alot more appealing to me personally though. The massive amount of content already and the huge galaxies to explore, allows for hundreds of hours of gameplay and replayability as well.
Will keep updating as more content is added.

The biggest issue for Fallout 4 lies in the fact that this game catered to the zealous horde of Bethesda fans who jumped on the Fallout station wagon after Fallout 3 came out, not the original long-time Fallout fans who've been around as early as Wasteland. Now I understand that Bethesda doesn't have to necessarily shape their game in the exact style of Fallout 2. When a game changes hands, the new developers have different ideas for the series. However, there's a sizable difference between a post-apocalyptic RPG and an action post-apocalyptic game with RPG elements. You can guess which one Fallout 4 falls under.
I won't deny that I've logged 200+ hours in this game, it is an exhilirating experience. On the contrary, when you look at the insipid storyline, the heavily flawed factions (Bethesda makes an isolationist faction like the BoS into a fascist suporpower piloting a zeppelin), the numerous plot holes, the lack of Wasteland charm, severe lack of character development (save some of the companions), the pestering Minutemen side quests, and the abhorrent Nuka-World DLC, you see through the superficiality of Fallout 4, and how it pales in comparison to the classic Fallout pieces.
Bethesda somehow managed to strip away a good story formula, a desolate almost horror-like aspect, and amazing lore capacity from the Fallout franchise, put it in a blender with Far Cry 3 and Elder Scrolls, and feed it to the zombified masses that is commercial video game fanatics. Well done, Bethesda.

TL:DR Good game, bad Fallout game.
So today, I was browsing games by tags today, and I saw this little disapointment within, and I thought, "Hey, why don't I review that game?"
Fallout 4 saddens me when I look at it. I had tapped into the Fallout series only two years before, and was AMAZED. New Vegas brought joy to my heart with it's art syle, tone, and story.
But fallout 4...well.
Firstly, the fact that I found this game in "story rich" is ridiculous. Maybe before it become "pick one of the boring factions for the boring arc" but other than that, the story is lackluster. Characters make Skyrim's look deep, and it does not surprise you in any way. It lacks any moral grips from previous games(Far Harbor actually has pretty decent story that is MUCH better though).
RPG aspects? Yup, I'm still looking for those as well. No perks or stats because screw actual rpg menchanics.
Gunplay and combat? Meh, with the immolation of the RPG systems, my choices of perks makes the combat not as personally craftable. But, with the new graphics, it is alot better to observe than in previous games.
Crafting and Settlement building? The crafting is exceedingly better, but I comes at the cost of some gun variety. Being a strategy game fan, I personally love the settlement building (with mods). Its not bad.
Graphics? Good.
Now I don't know where I completely stand on this game. I had fun, but not as much fun as I had in previous Fallout games. So, this game is good. But as a Fallout game, I just can't reccomend it.

Dark Souls 3 is the perfect coda to the Dark Souls trilogy, full of the brutal difficulty fans expect as well as the dreamlike world, labyrinthine dungeons and memorable characters. Full of references to the prior games (fans of the PS3 predecessor, Demon's Souls, will be pleased to see quite a few callbacks as well) and retaining tight combat controls as well as a huge diversity of viable character builds, it's instantly familiar to anyone who's played one of the previous games. Newcomers may be a bit put off by the lack of direction (even for games as notoriously undirected as the Souls series) and the high difficulty curve, but the game is not much less accessible than its predecessors.
The only change I am sorry to see to the formula of Dark Souls 2 is the dual-wielding "power stance", which has been replaced by a set of special moves available to all weapons. It's acceptable, but I liked dual wielding in DS2 a lot more than I like the new moves.
Another masterpiece from From Software, easily a 9/10. Buy!

Dark Souls 3 is a pretty good, but certainly not great ending to the Souls series. Playing this game I never did got the same great vibe I got from Dark Souls 1 & 2. Some of the bosses on the game or nothing short of disappointing, the questlines to some characters have little payoff (though some are great), and the game leans very heavily on past nostalgia from Dark Souls 1, with improved combat mechanics.
Buuut.. Did I hate this game? Oh no. I loved it. It is a Souls game still, true and true. The lore is amazing, and still found through gameplay and not cutscenes. Combat is faster than ever, there are even more amazing boss weapons, and some areas are larger than before.  But there are aspects of it that will frustrate you.
Pros:
-Faster combat, and maneuverability
-Some areas are definitely longer...
-Still has the good old Souls feel
-Lore is given to the interested players through very optional ways
-PvP funner than ever
-Co-op with friends is easier, with a password that allows you to summon only those with the same password
Cons:
-Wether the new weapon skill system was neccessary, is subjective.
-Some areas are definitely longer... but there are fewer of them and some are very very annoying.
-Summoning is sometimes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ as it fails if you summon more than 1 phantom simultaneously.
-End bosses are mostly disappointing..
-A lot of unwarranted nostalgia from DS1 holds this game up
-Seems a little too easy for some.

Fallout 4 from a world building perspective is one of the best in the series. The game is also being the least buggy of all the Bethesda made games to date. However, there are some legit concerns on where the series is headed with the game, which was especially apparent with the DLCs.
People play and love Fallout 4 because of the world, the story, the quests, the lore. However, with the 4th game, Bethesda went on a completely different direction. They tried to make the game about base building and crafting. At first it felt like it was a nice change of pace, however with the coming DLCs (which Bethesda charged its users dearly) it hammered done on settlements and only settlements. This is not why people love Fallout, heck there are much better games out there already which does settlement a lot better. The idea of Fallout is to explore, discover and leave. With this game, Bethesda wants you to oddly settle down on the same spot. It is a severe clash of game designs both trying to undo each other's effort. Really shame as the world in Fallout 4 is beautifully realized with half the game telling you to stop exploring and settle down.
The story was good, but not great. The quest design felt really weak and simple, nothing outrageous and Fallout-like except a couple of them. The gameplay took 2 steps forward and 3 steps back: The shooting felt much more natural. At times it felt like a shooter which was great. However, the RPG aspects was dumbed down to the point it didn't feel like an RPG like the way you progressed throughout the game. One major reason the entire RPG system broke is because your character can be jack of all trades. There is no reward whatsoever to specialize as there is no point. You can basically be good at everything. This hurts the gameplay a lot. Great power is worthless without great limitations.
Overall, I recommend this game on the sale price of $20 because it is a great game in this price bracket. However, if you are a fan and expect a true Fallout game, you will be disappointed. At least the base game is more Fallout than the DLCs...

tl;dr Replay Fallout 3 and NV with content mods to make a new game instead.  FO3 has a better main plot and NV has better companions, and mass murder is optional in both games.
tl:dr 2: If you are going to play Fallout 4, use mods.  Frost turns it into an entirely different - and challenging - game.
tl:dr 3: After completing the game in just under 100 hours, doing all the misc/side quests and finishing two of the four factions in hopes of getting a different cutscene ending (you don't), I can say that the Pink Power Armor was the best part, followed by learning how the Wasteland got Super Mutants.  Everything else, half-marks.
Long version.
I'm only 20 hours in and am so bored I looked up how to get all the achievements in order to finish the game quickly so I can mod it heavily in order to get some sort of enjoyment from it.  It's nothing like FO3 or NV, even though it should be.  Here's what I'm finding wrong:
1.  No brightness/gamma adjust availability.  At all.  Anywhere.  So you get a white out that's super white during the day and those of us who have trouble with night in games being too dark sans flashlight are stuck having to find a bed to fastforward time for half the game.
2.  The wasteland is empty.  Like, really empty.  In FO3 and NV, I would run into animals and mutants and raiders consistently, giving you the feel that going out into the wasteland is a dangerous idea.  Not so here.  In the 20 hours I've played, I've mapped out the entire NW quadrant of the map and have run into one pack of ghouls, two sets of bloatflies, one set of minelurkers, a handful of dogs, two yaois, and three raiders.  The wasteland is a waste of land.  (ETA: Far south seems to have a lot more of random encounters, especially in the radioactive zones.)
3.  The buildings you can enter have no mobs in them.  I've been to several landmarked places that are ghost buildings, or have a small handful of occupants.  Some of the buildings are triggered events rather than having a static population, so unless you happen to create the trigger, it's an empty building in which to pick up junk.
4.  No explanation for pretty much anything.  FO3 and NV were both intuitive and you had people/materials in game you could read to help you along.  Every play session I've had in 4, I've had to Alt-Tab out and look something up on the wikia as to how it works/what its purpose is.  The popups that explain don't really do that good of a job.  Settlements, Power Armor modification, how to use the Perk Chart - none of these come with adequate enough hand-holding to help you understand them.
5.  The main plot is dumb.  Fallout 4 is really about the Settlements and that should be what the main story is focused around.  Instead, you are looking for your son, who should not be alive anyway based on the events in Vault 111 and that Cogsgrove tells you the amount of time that has passed.   I knew from the start that this was the plot and it was dumb, but I didn't realize it would be inconsistent with the information we're given in the beginning of the game.  [ETA, having finished the game, it still ends up being dumb even when you're given more information.]
6.  The factions are not explained very well, if at all.  So far I've met a Minuteman and the Brotherhood of Steel.  All I know about the Minutemen is that they'd like to go back to how things were - helping people - and the Brotherhood is made up of pompous a**es.  However, I didn't know that these guys were factions that, if you help one, you end up screwing the other.  The Brotherhood is presented as a faction you join.  The Minutemen are not; Preston has Side Quest Giver written all over him.     I've learned through Google that in only one faction's quest do you get a warning that you're at a point of no return.  The rest are sneaky.  As someone who likes to do all the quests in a game, up to points of no return, that really stinks.  [ETA: I met the Railroad and synths from the Institute.  The Railroad are a bunch of robot-savers and the Institute apparently kidnaps people and replaces them with robots.  No hard choices to make as to who to join if you are playing a goodie heroic Sole Survivor.]
7.  Being stupid doesn't do anything.  Unlike FO3 and NV, if you choose to have low intelligence, it nets you no fun dialogue.  Idiot Savant is a nice perk at low int, but there has been stats now done that you can max out int and max the perk and get lots of xp.
8.  Mods disable achievements.  I know this is a dumb quibble for most people, but I play PC games because they can be modded.  There are so many glitches even after a year that the Unofficial FO4 Patch a modder has made would be wonderful to have, but I can't if I want to get the achievements.
[ETA 9.  You fail quests in your journal that you don't actually fail or don't even start other than picking it up (no notification that it's timed). This pisses me off.  Even if you complete the task but don't turn it in it fails.  And every time you're near Preston, he gives you annother quest that you need to drop everything else you want to do and complete it before the unknown amount of time is up.  This is a FAIL on Bethesda's part, big time.  Also, radiant quests FTL.]
I don't recommend this game for those who like the Fallout series, unless you plan to mod it to death to bring some life into it.  I'm planning to race to the end to get the achievements and then mod the F out of it.   Or go back and play the more enjoyable Fallouts.
ETA: I did enjoy the side quest with the USS Constitution and the robots at roughly 30 hours in.  A spark of wit and fun in a surprisngly lifeless game.  I wished I could go with them.

Dark Souls 3 is a pretty good, but certainly not great ending to the Souls series. Playing this game I never did got the same great vibe I got from Dark Souls 1 & 2. Buuut.. Did I hate this game? Oh no. I loved it. It is a Souls game still, true and true. The lore is amazing, and still found through gameplay and not cutscenes. Combat is faster than ever, there are even more amazing boss weapons, and some areas are larger than before.  But there are aspects of it that will frustrate you.
Pros:
-Faster combat, and maneuverability
-Some areas are definitely longer...
-Still has the good old Souls feel
-Lore is given to the interested players through very optional ways
-PvP funner than ever
-Co-op with friends is easier, with a password that allows you to summon only those with the same password
Cons:
-Wether the new weapon skill system was neccessary, is subjective.
-Some areas are definitely longer... but there are fewer of them and some are very very annoying.
-Summoning is sometimes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ as it fails if you summon more than 1 phantom simultaneously.
-End bosses are mostly disappointing..
-A lot of unwarranted nostalgia from DS1 holds this game up
-Seems a little too easy for some.

The only time I've ever invest so much time into a game was back when Maplestory was still extremely hard, Mabinogi still had pay-to-rebirth, or when Runescape in-browser graphics were revolutionary for its time. This is the FIRST week the game has come out and I've invest nearly two full 24-hour days into the game and its still in Beta.
Let's talk about the actual game now. 2D Sandbox Platformer in space, with the ability to become a huge randomly generated MMORPG. That's the potential it has and it's pretty much what I love. Combat is done fairly well, but it could use fine-tuning (remember, BETA). The building and finding a home planet that you like will take awhile (Still in BETA). Ship expansion isn't possible yet but could be added. The "techs" are essentially special skills centered primarily around movement with only one being active at a time (BETA). Much of the items you find on the planets found in villages or towns cannot be crafted unless you obtain the blueprint or take it, scan it, and 3D-printed. The game is still being balanced, many of the planned features are still being added, but even then, the game is amazingly fantastic.
In a nut-shell, if you like platforming, sandboxing, and a large exploration system, this game is for you. I recommend this.

TL:DR Good game, bad Fallout game.
So today, I was browsing games by tags today, and I saw this little disapointment within, and I thought, "Hey, why don't I review that game?"
Fallout 4 saddens me when I look at it. I had tapped into the Fallout series only two years before, and was AMAZED. New Vegas brought joy to my heart with it's art syle, tone, and story.
But fallout 4...well.
Firstly, the fact that I found this game in "story rich" is ridiculous. Maybe before it become "pick one of the boring factions for the boring arc" but other than that, the story is lackluster. Characters make Skyrim's look deep, and it does not surprise you in any way. It lacks any moral grips from previous games(Far Harbor actually has pretty decent story that is MUCH better though).
RPG aspects? Yup, I'm still looking for those as well. No perks or stats because screw actual rpg menchanics.
Gunplay and combat? Meh, with the immolation of the RPG systems, my choices of perks makes the combat not as personally craftable. But, with the new graphics, it is alot better to observe than in previous games.
Crafting and Settlement building? The crafting is exceedingly better, but I comes at the cost of some gun variety. Being a strategy game fan, I personally love the settlement building (with mods). Its not bad.
Graphics? Good.
Now I don't know where I completely stand on this game. I had fun, but not as much fun as I had in previous Fallout games. So, this game is good. But as a Fallout game, I just can't reccomend it.

The only time I've ever invest so much time into a game was back when Maplestory was still extremely hard, Mabinogi still had pay-to-rebirth, or when Runescape in-browser graphics were revolutionary for its time. This is the FIRST week the game has come out and I've invest nearly two full 24-hour days into the game and its still in Beta.
Let's talk about the actual game now. 2D Sandbox Platformer in space, with the ability to become a huge randomly generated MMORPG. That's the potential it has and it's pretty much what I love. Combat is done fairly well, but it could use fine-tuning (remember, BETA). The building and finding a home planet that you like will take awhile (Still in BETA). Ship expansion isn't possible yet but could be added. The "techs" are essentially special skills centered primarily around movement with only one being active at a time (BETA). Much of the items you find on the planets found in villages or towns cannot be crafted unless you obtain the blueprint or take it, scan it, and 3D-printed. The game is still being balanced, many of the planned features are still being added, but even then, the game is amazingly fantastic.
In a nut-shell, if you like platforming, sandboxing, and a large exploration system, this game is for you. I recommend this.

Fallout 4 is a GOOD game. Great even and it is absolutely worth playing if you are interested in open world post apocalyptic games.  Bethesda doesnt make "bad" games. Or even really "mediocre" games.  That being said, yes, Fallout 4 in many ways is the studio's weakest title yet. It makes a fantastic first impression, and for a good while(for the amount of time and even longer than many other games last in their entirety) you will be throughly enjoying yourself. Bethesda are masters of how to makes games addicting, and Fallout 4 is no exception. The world is huge and immersive. The gunplay is great(like REALLY good in my honest opinion). The story starts off pretty interesting and theree are a few strong moments scattered here and there, nut ultimately its pretty bland and forgettable. Also kind of boring tbh. Bethesda definitely needs to hire new writers. Great idea, but poorly executed. Side quests are another issue(and this unfortunately has been a growing trend amongst RPGs and open world games lately). There are few decent ones and I few that I quite liked, but the majority of them are simple generic fetch quests or "go here and kill stuff". Todd Howard actually brought that up in an interview. So at least they are addressing some of the problems. A lot of these things probably won't dosappoint you much if you have never played a Bethesda game before and if you dont go in with "too" high expectations. But if you are comparing this to a lot of Bethesda's past work, it definitely takes some steps in the wrong direction I think. Then there is of course the whole "RPG mechanics or lack there of" controversy. People like to throw around the word "streamlined" a lot and that Bethesda is "dumbing it down for filthy casuals", which I partly agree with. Ya they totally revamped the Skills and SPECIAL system and the dialog options or lack there of aren't great. A lot of people saw this coming when they played Skyrim which some people felt was too "streamlined"(personally I thought they were overeacting). Unfortunately they were right. However I still maintain hope taht Bethesda can change and go back to their roots while also making as many people happy as possible. As I said before, todd Howard has addressed some of the complaints that people hav had with Fallout 4 and it sounds like has realized that they made some mistakes. The fact that our voices have been heard can even be seen in game with additions like the Survival Mode. And then you have the Far Harbor expansion which was pretty solid. They definitely put more effort into the dialog and the story was much less linear. So I still have faith. Either way, Fallout 4 is certainly enjoyable and you WILL get your money's worth. But if its amazing story telling you are looking for, go buy The Witcher 3 instead

If I could, I would give this game TWO thumbs up.
Some people criticize Fallout 4 for a lack of immersion or freedom of choice, especially in comparison to former instalments of this series. I did not find this to be the case, I played several very different playthroughs and felt immensely immersed.
For example, you often read that the skill and perk system had been "dumbed down". Actually, they have been merged into an intricate and nicely presented table of perks that you unlock while levelling up, essentially having the same impact on the gameplay as perks and skills had separately in former games. In addition to that, you get attribute buffs from clothing you can find or power armor paints as well as other permanent perks at completion of certain questlines, especially those your long-term companions give you, and items you can collect, namely vault-boy bobbleheads and magazines. The latter makes a lot more sense than the temporary skill buffs you got from magazines in FO3 or FONV, because in real life, you don't just forget what you learned after a few minutes. My point is: The merged perk-skill-system is still multilayered, it is just more specifically connected to playing the game and exploring the world.
Furthermore, I do not miss the old Karma system at all. It was a dubious concept to begin with, as it practically gave telepathic abilities to NPCs who could not possibly know what kind of person you were. Reputation with factions whose members communicate with each other is a different matter and of course more realistic and immersive, but faction reputation was monitored independently of Karma in the older games. It did not make sense, and FO4 is by no means worse for getting rid of it.
Also, weapon deterioration is gone, which is a good thing in my opinion, as I do not feel excited by abstract bars going down and repeating the same maintenance processes over and over... Without that, I can concentrate on activities that are actually interesting, which makes me feel more like a hero and less like a mechanic.
One other example often complained about is the new dialogue system, that limits your options to four answers at each point. I have to say that I prefer the new way that presents you with short summaries of your answers, giving you a very good idea what you are going to say without holding the flow of the scene for too long. More importantly, you do not only have four options at important points in the story, because additional options or questions are hidden behind statements like "I want to ask you something else", which opens four extra choices. The Witcher-3-style voice acting of the protagonist is OK with me, especially when it is executed as well as here.
As for the flexibility missed by some: There is indeed a great variety of characters you can play! Yes, an important part of the background story is fixed: You are a military man or woman (a plausible explanation why you can pick up any weapon and armour in the wasteland knowing how to use it) with a family, and your son is abducted (the initial motivation to start out). That being said, you can still play a lot of diverse roles.
What kind of military personnel were you? A grunt, a NCO or an officer? A power-armour infantryman, a sniper, a paratrooper commando, a medic, a scientist in a military lab or a military intelligence operative? All that can influence your role-friendly distribution of attribute points and choice of perks.
Have you served proudly until the Great War, have you left service because of an injury, a drug addiction, or have you left on grounds of conscience? This part of your background might determine how you relate to the militaristic Brotherhood of Steel, the subversive Railroad and other groups and NPCs.
Do you go on the quest to find and rescue your son with guns blazing like a modern avenging angel, do you start more cautiously by making friends and building an army before you take on your enemies, or are you a depressed and desperate character who just mourns the loss of his family and gives up on finding Shaun, avoiding the main quest and making a living for himself in the New World Dis-Order?
Thus, I found many possibilities to flesh out my character, with diverse combinations of attributes, perks and equipment as well as choices in the storyline (join different factions, choose different companions, make a different kind of home, not to mention the major decisions in the main quest) to express myself!
With that undeserved criticism out of the way, I come to the undisputable goodies: The combat is a dream, more specifially: an addicting, exciting apocalyptic nightmare that makes you come for more for hundreds of hours! Compared to earlier FO games, your weapons and how you handle them, how their impact feels has improved significantly. The companion AI is still annoying at times ("Out of the line of fire, Dogmeat!"), but then, you don't have to take a follower with you, there is even a perk for lone wanderers. The deep crafting system for weapons and armours, that by the way gives a new purpose to looting junk and breaking it down for useful materials, adds a lot to the immersion: You customize your character, and you see and feel the different results in action.
This effect of immersion by having a visible impact on the world is even stronger with the new settlement building system. I always enjoy housing in an RPG, but this here goes far beyond what Skyrim Hearthfire once offered. You can literally build little towns with houses, shops and defence mechanisms from scratch with a lot of creative freedom. There are a few limitations and glitches here, but that is to be expected in such a complex feature. Overall, it is fun to make certain places in the world your own this way.
Even without that, the open game world is a wonder to behold. So many diverse places to explore, so many different NPCs to relate to, so many items and quests to find, all while listening to the stylish playlist of hits from the Fifties... When I encounter minor animation or clipping glitches in such a vast, but incredibly detailed world, I am willing to forgive that. "It is Bethesda after all" is not an excuse, but at bottom line, there is no excuse needed: Bethesda delivered a great game well worth its price. I hope they will develope a new, modern engine with improved AI next time, but as for now, they deserve respect for what they did with the old one.

Fallout 4 from a world building perspective is one of the best in the series. The game is also being the least buggy of all the Bethesda made games to date. However, there are some legit concerns on where the series is headed with the game, which was especially apparent with the DLCs.
People play and love Fallout 4 because of the world, the story, the quests, the lore. However, with the 4th game, Bethesda went on a completely different direction. They tried to make the game about base building and crafting. At first it felt like it was a nice change of pace, however with the coming DLCs (which Bethesda charged its users dearly) it hammered done on settlements and only settlements. This is not why people love Fallout, heck there are much better games out there already which does settlement a lot better. The idea of Fallout is to explore, discover and leave. With this game, Bethesda wants you to oddly settle down on the same spot. It is a severe clash of game designs both trying to undo each other's effort. Really shame as the world in Fallout 4 is beautifully realized with half the game telling you to stop exploring and settle down.
The story was good, but not great. The quest design felt really weak and simple, nothing outrageous and Fallout-like except a couple of them. The gameplay took 2 steps forward and 3 steps back: The shooting felt much more natural. At times it felt like a shooter which was great. However, the RPG aspects was dumbed down to the point it didn't feel like an RPG like the way you progressed throughout the game. One major reason the entire RPG system broke is because your character can be jack of all trades. There is no reward whatsoever to specialize as there is no point. You can basically be good at everything. This hurts the gameplay a lot. Great power is worthless without great limitations.
Overall, I recommend this game on the sale price of $20 because it is a great game in this price bracket. However, if you are a fan and expect a true Fallout game, you will be disappointed. At least the base game is more Fallout than the DLCs...

tl;dr Replay Fallout 3 and NV with content mods to make a new game instead.  FO3 has a better main plot and NV has better companions, and mass murder is optional in both games.
tl:dr 2: If you are going to play Fallout 4, use mods.  Frost turns it into an entirely different - and challenging - game.
tl:dr 3: After completing the game in just under 100 hours, doing all the misc/side quests and finishing two of the four factions in hopes of getting a different cutscene ending (you don't), I can say that the Pink Power Armor was the best part, followed by learning how the Wasteland got Super Mutants.  Everything else, half-marks.
Long version.
I'm only 20 hours in and am so bored I looked up how to get all the achievements in order to finish the game quickly so I can mod it heavily in order to get some sort of enjoyment from it.  It's nothing like FO3 or NV, even though it should be.  Here's what I'm finding wrong:
1.  No brightness/gamma adjust availability.  At all.  Anywhere.  So you get a white out that's super white during the day and those of us who have trouble with night in games being too dark sans flashlight are stuck having to find a bed to fastforward time for half the game.
2.  The wasteland is empty.  Like, really empty.  In FO3 and NV, I would run into animals and mutants and raiders consistently, giving you the feel that going out into the wasteland is a dangerous idea.  Not so here.  In the 20 hours I've played, I've mapped out the entire NW quadrant of the map and have run into one pack of ghouls, two sets of bloatflies, one set of minelurkers, a handful of dogs, two yaois, and three raiders.  The wasteland is a waste of land.  (ETA: Far south seems to have a lot more of random encounters, especially in the radioactive zones.)
3.  The buildings you can enter have no mobs in them.  I've been to several landmarked places that are ghost buildings, or have a small handful of occupants.  Some of the buildings are triggered events rather than having a static population, so unless you happen to create the trigger, it's an empty building in which to pick up junk.
4.  No explanation for pretty much anything.  FO3 and NV were both intuitive and you had people/materials in game you could read to help you along.  Every play session I've had in 4, I've had to Alt-Tab out and look something up on the wikia as to how it works/what its purpose is.  The popups that explain don't really do that good of a job.  Settlements, Power Armor modification, how to use the Perk Chart - none of these come with adequate enough hand-holding to help you understand them.
5.  The main plot is dumb.  Fallout 4 is really about the Settlements and that should be what the main story is focused around.  Instead, you are looking for your son, who should not be alive anyway based on the events in Vault 111 and that Cogsgrove tells you the amount of time that has passed.   I knew from the start that this was the plot and it was dumb, but I didn't realize it would be inconsistent with the information we're given in the beginning of the game.  [ETA, having finished the game, it still ends up being dumb even when you're given more information.]
6.  The factions are not explained very well, if at all.  So far I've met a Minuteman and the Brotherhood of Steel.  All I know about the Minutemen is that they'd like to go back to how things were - helping people - and the Brotherhood is made up of pompous a**es.  However, I didn't know that these guys were factions that, if you help one, you end up screwing the other.  The Brotherhood is presented as a faction you join.  The Minutemen are not; Preston has Side Quest Giver written all over him.     I've learned through Google that in only one faction's quest do you get a warning that you're at a point of no return.  The rest are sneaky.  As someone who likes to do all the quests in a game, up to points of no return, that really stinks.  [ETA: I met the Railroad and synths from the Institute.  The Railroad are a bunch of robot-savers and the Institute apparently kidnaps people and replaces them with robots.  No hard choices to make as to who to join if you are playing a goodie heroic Sole Survivor.]
7.  Being stupid doesn't do anything.  Unlike FO3 and NV, if you choose to have low intelligence, it nets you no fun dialogue.  Idiot Savant is a nice perk at low int, but there has been stats now done that you can max out int and max the perk and get lots of xp.
8.  Mods disable achievements.  I know this is a dumb quibble for most people, but I play PC games because they can be modded.  There are so many glitches even after a year that the Unofficial FO4 Patch a modder has made would be wonderful to have, but I can't if I want to get the achievements.
[ETA 9.  You fail quests in your journal that you don't actually fail or don't even start other than picking it up (no notification that it's timed). This pisses me off.  Even if you complete the task but don't turn it in it fails.  And every time you're near Preston, he gives you annother quest that you need to drop everything else you want to do and complete it before the unknown amount of time is up.  This is a FAIL on Bethesda's part, big time.  Also, radiant quests FTL.]
I don't recommend this game for those who like the Fallout series, unless you plan to mod it to death to bring some life into it.  I'm planning to race to the end to get the achievements and then mod the F out of it.   Or go back and play the more enjoyable Fallouts.
ETA: I did enjoy the side quest with the USS Constitution and the robots at roughly 30 hours in.  A spark of wit and fun in a surprisngly lifeless game.  I wished I could go with them.

Well, what can I say? To me, this is the best Fallout game ever.
The streamlining of the character stats saves a lot of time and makes character advancement more fun than that bunch of stats we used to have. I keep hearing people whining that it's been dumbed down, but it's not. Streamlined is the adjective. And actually the weapons perks make a lot more sense now than they used to.
It's also nice to see a Fallout game that is nearly bug free from beginning to end. It's no small endeavour considering the sheer size of the game.
And now we get to the parts that interested me most.
First and easiest to describe: power armours. They have never been so fun and so cool to play with. They make you feel like you're in a vehicle more than an armour, and that's just splendid to me. Entering my armor always gives me that little glee.
Second, the settlements! I frowned when I first knew about this subsystem of the game, as I've never been a fan of that sort of resource management in an rpg: I was afraid it'd distract me from enjoying the story. Far from it, it enhanced the story, giving me a tangible feel that my character's actions are actually changing the world. The theme of rebuilding from the ashes of the apocalypse is really strong and well implemented. In a word, I loved settlement building.
And last and most important. Best. Storyline. Ever. Every faction you choose, every choice you make is grey morality. Choosing is HARD. Every faction except the Minutemen has a bright side and a very dark side. Side quests are fun! So few fetch quests and so much to discover and interact with.
All in all, great story, great NPCs and great quests. It's the best I can ask to an rpg. Compared to games like Dragon's  Dogma which are made of boring NPCs and fetch quests which do nothing to keep me interested in a game despite the good gameplay, I much prefer this. I think I played every possible sidequest and explored every inch of the Commonwealth, driven by curiosity and never disappointed when I found new locations.
One of the best rpgs of all time if you ask me.

Although I had a ton of fun with this game and do recommend it, this Fallout game does not leave me wanting to come back and play it. It didn't have the charm that 3 or New Vegas had that led me to play those games for about 250 hours each across various systems. I spend a very fun 80 hours on my first play through, and the rest trying to pick up the survival mode and starting other play throughs but I just can't seem to get interested in doing it all again. I think that my problems stem from how they did away with the skill system and simplified the dialogue. The combat (compared to the other Fallout games) is where this game shines, as it got a much needed update, but when it comes down to it now there are other games that do dialogue better, combat better, and have a more complex and deep skill systems. I hope to see them take a step back in time and see what made 3 and NV so great and incorporate those into Fallout 5 (or Fallout New Vancouver or whatever they decide) rather than further simplification of an already simple system.
Some credit should also be given to the base building mechanic and the really involved crafting system. I never played Fallout to build a home but experience a story so it wasn't really my thing. The crafting system was really cool on my first playthough, but coming back to it it felt like a chore to scavenge adhesive and aluminum from every corner of this game. In 3 crafting was something reserved for a select few weapons and in NV it hit a very good middle ground where you could craft ammo and some other miscellaneous items but by no means everything. In 4 it feels like a necessity to craft every damn sight and grip and barrel to get that slight edge in combat. It's not very nuanced is the problem, it's just collecting X adhesives and metals in order to make Y part, it involves no skill, no real thinking other than just looking for a certain number of items, and isn't unique in any way.
All things aside I still had a very fun 80 hour play though. Very few games outside of the Witcher 3 can say that it took 80+ hours to complete, however Bethesda (the developer) may have spread their resources too thin between the shallow crafting system, the pretty ok base/home building system, and the simplified skill system (compared to previous Fallout games). However, the combat has never been better, the story still stands strong, pure exploration has never been this fun, and I would reccomend it to anyone interested in RPGs.

Although I had a ton of fun with this game and do recommend it, this Fallout game does not leave me wanting to come back and play it. It didn't have the charm that 3 or New Vegas had that led me to play those games for about 250 hours each across various systems. I spend a very fun 80 hours on my first play through, and the rest trying to pick up the survival mode and starting other play throughs but I just can't seem to get interested in doing it all again. I think that my problems stem from how they did away with the skill system and simplified the dialogue. The combat (compared to the other Fallout games) is where this game shines, as it got a much needed update, but when it comes down to it now there are other games that do dialogue better, combat better, and have a more complex and deep skill systems. I hope to see them take a step back in time and see what made 3 and NV so great and incorporate those into Fallout 5 (or Fallout New Vancouver or whatever they decide) rather than further simplification of an already simple system.
Some credit should also be given to the base building mechanic and the really involved crafting system. I never played Fallout to build a home but experience a story so it wasn't really my thing. The crafting system was really cool on my first playthough, but coming back to it it felt like a chore to scavenge adhesive and aluminum from every corner of this game. In 3 crafting was something reserved for a select few weapons and in NV it hit a very good middle ground where you could craft ammo and some other miscellaneous items but by no means everything. In 4 it feels like a necessity to craft every damn sight and grip and barrel to get that slight edge in combat. It's not very nuanced is the problem, it's just collecting X adhesives and metals in order to make Y part, it involves no skill, no real thinking other than just looking for a certain number of items, and isn't unique in any way.
All things aside I still had a very fun 80 hour play though. Very few games outside of the Witcher 3 can say that it took 80+ hours to complete, however Bethesda (the developer) may have spread their resources too thin between the shallow crafting system, the pretty ok base/home building system, and the simplified skill system (compared to previous Fallout games). However, the combat has never been better, the story still stands strong, pure exploration has never been this fun, and I would reccomend it to anyone interested in RPGs.

Okay, here's a quick run-down of the pros and cons:
PROS:
- Nice graphics.
- Combat system is fun, melee system in particular is an improvement on #3 and New Vegas.
- The ability to create and expand settlements is a great idea.
- Some interesting and unique locations to visit, and the map is huge.
- Lots of crafting options.
- Almost every item in the game is useful in some way.
- Survival mode is a nice addition for hardcore gamers.
- Good range of challenging enemies to fight.
- Character creation is fun.
CONS:
- The factions you can join aren't particularly interesting.
- Storyline isn't particularly original, and it's not that interesting.  There is a twist in the story, but it's heavily hinted at throughout the game, and you'll probably figure it out before the big reveal.
- Companions have about as much personality as a brick, with the exception of Piper.
- Companions can be as much a hindrance as a help, especially that bloody dog.
- The characters in general have about as much personality as a brick.
- Radiant quests get annoying very quickly (stop what you're doing and go help the settlement being attacked by raiders before the time runs out)
- Dialogue system is♥♥♥♥♥♥
- While you can do bad things, you can't really choose to play as a bad guy.
CONCLUSION:
It's not a bad game, but it feels like there's something missing, and that's not just because I don't have the DLC.  If you like shooters, you'll love this, but if you're looking for a decent plot and interesting characters think again.

Although I had a ton of fun with this game and do recommend it, this Fallout game does not leave me wanting to come back and play it. It didn't have the charm that 3 or New Vegas had that led me to play those games for about 250 hours each across various systems. I spend a very fun 80 hours on my first play through, and the rest trying to pick up the survival mode and starting other play throughs but I just can't seem to get interested in doing it all again. I think that my problems stem from how they did away with the skill system and simplified the dialogue. The combat (compared to the other Fallout games) is where this game shines, as it got a much needed update, but when it comes down to it now there are other games that do dialogue better, combat better, and have a more complex and deep skill systems. I hope to see them take a step back in time and see what made 3 and NV so great and incorporate those into Fallout 5 (or Fallout New Vancouver or whatever they decide) rather than further simplification of an already simple system.
Some credit should also be given to the base building mechanic and the really involved crafting system. I never played Fallout to build a home but experience a story so it wasn't really my thing. The crafting system was really cool on my first playthough, but coming back to it it felt like a chore to scavenge adhesive and aluminum from every corner of this game. In 3 crafting was something reserved for a select few weapons and in NV it hit a very good middle ground where you could craft ammo and some other miscellaneous items but by no means everything. In 4 it feels like a necessity to craft every damn sight and grip and barrel to get that slight edge in combat. It's not very nuanced is the problem, it's just collecting X adhesives and metals in order to make Y part, it involves no skill, no real thinking other than just looking for a certain number of items, and isn't unique in any way.
All things aside I still had a very fun 80 hour play though. Very few games outside of the Witcher 3 can say that it took 80+ hours to complete, however Bethesda (the developer) may have spread their resources too thin between the shallow crafting system, the pretty ok base/home building system, and the simplified skill system (compared to previous Fallout games). However, the combat has never been better, the story still stands strong, pure exploration has never been this fun, and I would reccomend it to anyone interested in RPGs.

I believe that a major point has been missed in many of the negative reviews here, and elsewhere on the web.  While Fallout 4 does have it's flaws compared to what could be considered the ideal medium of Fallout New Vegas(Lets face it, aiming down the sights should have been standard from the get go in Fallout 3!), but we also live in a changing world where many individuals have never had to play a game on a device that required more than one pointer finger to operate, or two little thumbsticks to manipulate your world.
I grew up in the golden age of Computer Gaming.  Lets face it, when it came to gaming platforms, the Computer made consoles look like pacman machines from the 80's until after the new millenium. Control options, content size, expandability/mod-ability, and graphics were the computer's biggest selling points. Now, with multiple consoles sharing the limelight, but still falling short of the dedicated gaming PC in my opinion, most producers are making games to fit the simplistic, mass produced, ease of use, and dumbed down plug and play console system so that the same game can be marketed accross all platforms.  This means simplification to limit the ammount of glitches caused by crossover in coding.
So where does Fallout 4 win in spades? First and foremost, Fallout 4 is an exploring game. Bethesda has always gone to great lengths in its franchise series games to create a completely immersive Lore/backstory behind the game. From the books in the Eldar Scrolls, to the human interactions you find in emails once you have successfully hacked a Terminal in Fallout 4, slowly piecing together a little of what happened on that fateful day the bombs fell.  That is what the Fallout Franchise has been about since Fallout 3 when I picked up the title for my first console that was purchased for multiple players when I had friends over. Lets face it, only one person can Dogfight in a world war two piston engined fighter at a time, or conquer the globe as a roman emperor in a conquest of total war.  To me, the shooter aspect of the Fallout series has always been secondary, with emphasis on exploration and crafting first and foremost.  Fallout 4 continues in that tradition nicely, giving up a little more than may be liked in terms of full out character customization, but still acceptable none the less.
If you look at Fallout 4 in that frame of mind and accept it for the merit within, it is a decent game worth your time, but something you may want to rotate around in your gaming/relaxation schedule. For those who had trouble with black screen no starts upon install.... Update your drivers like crazy!! Drivers must be updated and properly configured for Fallout 4 to run, especially on a fresh install.  With that in mind, good luck, and enjoy your portable Nuclear Catapult.

First of all, let me state that this game is really, really good, fun to play, and I've enjoyed most of my time with it.
I would absolutely recommend it if it weren't for one little thing: It is not made clear enough that automatic save wipes are common with updates.
As a hobbyist game developer I can understand that it takes a lot of effort to ensure that old files are compatible with newer versions, especially in an early state like this where massive changes to balancing and game systems are common. I have no problem with that. However, I don't think that a customer should expect this to happen in an early access game, especially not when some people will invest dozens of hours of playtime in one character. In other early released games I played developers usually invested the time to make sure save files were compatible to newer versions, or at least discouraged the average player from buying the game early (Prison Architect).
TL;DR:
Please inform potential buyers about this before they buy your game, I know you are not actively hiding anything and communicate future save wipes etc. on your website and through other means, but I think it's important to mention this on the store page to prevent drama.
