I'm going to review two things here - the game itself, and their use of the term beta.
Firstly, their use of "beta". I've always internally defined "beta" like this: "The game runs for longer than 20 minutes without crashing, and the bulk of its initial featureset is implemented, however don't expect completeness or stability". While the first part of this definition interestingly disqualifies certain Skyrim patches, Starbound fits the definition perfectly - I can run the game for hours on end, with no crashes, and I do get the odd bug here and there (also it doesn't seem like Chucklefish has figured out balance yet at the time of this writing). If you buy in early, be prepared for character wipes - they seem to be rare currently, but
Now onto the game itself. Essentially, the game is "Terraria in Space". This isn't a bad thing. In fact, Starbound improves on many concepts Terraria introduced (e.g. player manipulated background tiles - no need to convert your stone blocks into "stone walls", just select your cobblestone and right click), as well as adding brand new things such as FTL travel to other planets. Getting bored of your starting planet? Drop some fuel into your ship and take off, you never know what you're going to find! Heck, the new planet may already have people and civilization there!
All in all, I give this game ten Florans out of a wood table (positive marks).

If you are looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
1/2 cup butter,
softened 1/2 cup peanut butter
1 cup packed brown sugar
1/2 cup white sugar
2 eggs
2 tablespoons light corn syrup
2 tablespoons water
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 cups chopped semisweet chocolate
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
In a large bowl, cream together the butter, peanut butter, brown sugar, and white sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the corn syrup, water, and vanilla. Combine the flour, baking soda, and salt; stir into the peanut butter mixture. Fold in chocolate chunks. Drop by 1/4 cupfuls 3 inches apart onto ungreased baking sheets.
Bake for 12 to 14 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are golden. Allow cookies to cool for 1 minute on the cookie sheet before removing to wire racks to cool completely.

Starbound. Hoo boy, here we go. Yes, I would recommend Starbound. Personally, because I got it while it was still in early access, the gameplay feels kind of stale, but I believe that's at least partially due to having to start over many many times from the wiping of saves they did while this game was still in development. However, the explorer and collector in me are both still very pleased with this game, even if the adventurer in me is not. Between cute 2D graphics, a variety of races to try, (Floran and Novakid are definitely my favourites) a literally never-ending procedurally generated universe to explore, a charming soundtrack that gives the game such an innocent feel and a pretty good story, this game is great. My only real complaint is that it starts to feel repetitive after a while. But even then, that's only after several hundred hours playing it. This game is definitely a worthwhile purchase for the price. Go, shoo, hop to it.

Fallout 4:
(I'm gonna keep this breif)
Story: Eh? It's a basic Fallout plot we've come to expect. Someone is missing go and find them. It's the same for 3 and maybe New Vegas except you want to kill the person instead of help them.
Gameplay: Improved! Instead of cheating the game by pausing in V.A.T.S you must make your decisions while the world is still slowly moving. However, this does take away many Role Playing mechanics. One of the biggest complaints is that the gunplay has changed so much it's practically an FPS but you WILL still use V.A.T.S when approaching a combat schenario instead of shooting your way through manually.
Graphics: Better. Instead of having the entire game painted brown like previous Fallout games the world is vivid and there are actual colours (yes I spell *colour* like that, I'm British). However, don't expect graphics rivaling the Crysis games or any of the new COD games coming out. It has a cartoonish smooting on everything that adds to Fallout's themes and the cartoonish Vault logos and advertising.
Roleplay elements: This is where they really screwed up. The dialogue system is bad, but bareable however, the thing that everyone hates about this is the fact that the character has a voice and speaks which removes all roleplaying elements. On the plus side, there are now new base building mechanics. If you enjoy base building in games like Minecraft then you will enjoy this but I found it very clunky ESPECIALLY on a slow computer. Consequently, it's still an amazing feature.
Overall, Fallout 4 is a great Bethesda game, as long as you don't mind leaving behind a few roleplaying mechanics for smoother, overall gameplay.

Well, Dark Souls 3... not my favourite, nor my least favourite of the souls series. I'd place Dark Souls 3 above Dark Souls 1 and below Dark Souls 2.
PvE:
The PvE is pretty alright, the bosses are fun and the areas are pretty interesting and well designed. There are some pretty boring, stupid, or just plain easy and a waste of time, tedious bosses, such as the tree boss, but there's also a good mix of good areas and bosses between those. I like the areas much more than Dark Souls 2's level design, and of course it's a lot more smooth and the bosses seem to be more complex, which just comes with time and technological advancements and whatnot I suppose. Either way, the PvE in Dark Souls 3 is pretty well rounded out. While overall I still preferred Dark Souls 2 PvE because it was more difficult and the bosses were more plentiful and fun for me, I still enjoy Dark Souls 3 PvE, especially with certain bosses such as Friede or the lightning guy.
PvP:
The PvP is... interesting. Some improvements from other games, some things which should not have been added. Compared to Dark Soul 1, the PvP is still a massive improvement. It requires somewhat more skill and work and isn't just a backstab or hacking fest. While there are still a decent amount of hackers, there's really not that many compared to what you could have found previously in the other games. Now, compared to Dark Souls 2... the PvP is really lacking here. Dark Souls 2 featured a LOT more variety and viable builds, and while *technically* anything COULD be viable, that's not really an argument that I'm using here because, really, it's stupid. Dark Souls 3 has a *HUGE* problem when it comes to metas and people simply using the most OP weapons in the game at the time, which shifts as adjustments are made to weapons and weapon classes. Unfortunately, there are entire weapon classes in the game which simply become useless due to balancing issues and whatnot, such as greathammers. While they're usable, there's no point in using them aside from a challenge... the only good one in the game is the gargoyle one. If you want to win 90% of your PvP matches, there's a good set of armour, weapons, and rings readily available to make you extremely OP, especially with the introduction of the DLC weapons, which are absolutely ridiculously strong. Now, something that's not specific to weapons but the base game itself is stamina... the rate at which it is consumed is MUCH too small, and the rate at which it recovers is WAY too high, even without any stamina recovery boosting items. This, however, is a base game component, used in PvE and PvP, and unfortunately isn't really something that could be changed to more resemble Dark Souls 2's stamina, as it would require pretty much a complete rework.
Overall, I'd give it a good 7/10. It could use some improvements, which may or may not come over time, but the game is still very fun to play, especially with friends, and even though there are some major problems with balancing and quite a few hackers still, it's still a very fun and enjoyable game imo.

First off, the good parts. Gunplay is greatly improved; the scopes and shots feel smooth and action - packed, and the enemies are more challenging in their new behaviours such as leaning from behind walls and jumping you, especially in Survival mode. The companions were good; so was the optional romance component, which is slightly more developed than Skyrim's, in that romance actually has dialogue and development beforehand. Each companion usually has their own quest to earn their loyalty, which I didn't mind as I ended up liking most of these NPCs anyway. Weapon and armor customization is more extensive and welcomed - especially in the range of mods you can apply to guns to make even a pistol operate life a rifle.
Music and visuals were fine, though I wonder if some of the music on the radio was recycled from previous games.
Minor gripes included performance - despite my decent rig, I was getting pretty bad FPS in quite a few areas, and cells would not always load before I got there, including quite a few blotchy textures and inoperable doors.
My biggest gripe, though, is the general direction in which this franchise is going. It's also in how the game feels; Bethesda's ridiculous amount of merchandise for this game and advertising rubs me the wrong way in what their focus has become.
This isn't an RPG. This wasn't apparent much of the time, but most of the game involves exploring, killing and looting. However, it's obvious that not as much effort was put into this, even though the amount of content isn't lacking. There weren't many unique locations. Any story a location had felt like I was observing it rather than experiencing it. The limited dialogue tree isn't too important most of the time, but some situations call for more than 4 responses, especially when many different quests are involved with the same NPC. I played this game with a few mods from the very start; the notion that I couldn't even tell what I was going to say in dialogue is so backwards I couldn't play the game without a mod to fix it.
There are many, many frustrations that arise from Bethesda's laziness, too. Instant death by touching a car. Walking on water for no reason. NPCs breaking dialogue and breaking quests if you talk to them out in the open. Various bugs that still haven't been patched, even though I was using the unofficial patch. They also barely learned or utilised any feedback from New Vegas; and when they did, they mishandled it.
The biggest, most important problem, is how I felt during quests that I was supposed to be invested in, especially in the end game. While there are four factions you can join, in the end, I didn't feel invested or caring about any of them. The main quest boils down to one factions beating the others, and Bethesda somehow expects that to be emotionally investing. What's the point, when the character I played always had to do something that they would never do? He couldn't even try to solve things peacefully in the end, always killing innocent people (which are conveniently hostile) - and that's not how my character would have done it. Sure, he could fail, and end up being enemies with all the factions, but in previous Fallout games, he could at least try. And in previous Fallout games, if played right, he could succeed, and leave me fulfilled and satisfied with my journey in the world, rather than being disgusted and angry at what has happened to this franchise.
I only recommend this game because I got my money's worth, and it's better to spend your money here than with most other trash coming out recently. But I was terribly disappointed, even disheartened at what's happened to Fallout and Bethesda. It's become obvious that I'll never get a Fallout end game as emotionally investing as Fallout 2; nor an awesome RPG experience like New Vegas, or even a game like Fallout 3 in which a developer's attention and love for the game comes out. This game may not be a bad game, but I've lost hope due to this game, more than any other I've played. I doubt I'll ever play this game again, nor buy any Fallout game again.

The game mechanics may stem a bit from Terraria, but there have been major changes from that game into this one. For instance, you now have a hunger, warmth/cold meter, as well as an energy meter instead of a finite ammo system for guns and whatnot.

Another thing I like about this game is that the world seeds can mostly be shared between friends, and their friends. So that, if you find an airship that sells guns, you can tweet it or send it to the community forums without it being different (usually) for others. (As a note though, there IS a "Universe Seed" but it doesn't always make a severe difference.)
I seriously recommend this game if you like sandboxes. (Oh and, you can full-circle planets, unlike Terraria!)
A couple things that I found helpful while playing the game: Holding CTRL makes your camera pan toward your mouse cursor's location. Pressing ALT shows your hunger bar on-demand. You can use Middle-Click (Middle Mouse Button / Scroll Wheel Click) to use items rather than having to press E all the time.

I'm going to review two things here - the game itself, and their use of the term beta.
Firstly, their use of "beta". I've always internally defined "beta" like this: "The game runs for longer than 20 minutes without crashing, and the bulk of its initial featureset is implemented, however don't expect completeness or stability". While the first part of this definition interestingly disqualifies certain Skyrim patches, Starbound fits the definition perfectly - I can run the game for hours on end, with no crashes, and I do get the odd bug here and there (also it doesn't seem like Chucklefish has figured out balance yet at the time of this writing). If you buy in early, be prepared for character wipes - they seem to be rare currently, but
Now onto the game itself. Essentially, the game is "Terraria in Space". This isn't a bad thing. In fact, Starbound improves on many concepts Terraria introduced (e.g. player manipulated background tiles - no need to convert your stone blocks into "stone walls", just select your cobblestone and right click), as well as adding brand new things such as FTL travel to other planets. Getting bored of your starting planet? Drop some fuel into your ship and take off, you never know what you're going to find! Heck, the new planet may already have people and civilization there!
All in all, I give this game ten Florans out of a wood table (positive marks).

If you are looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
1/2 cup butter,
softened 1/2 cup peanut butter
1 cup packed brown sugar
1/2 cup white sugar
2 eggs
2 tablespoons light corn syrup
2 tablespoons water
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 cups chopped semisweet chocolate
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
In a large bowl, cream together the butter, peanut butter, brown sugar, and white sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the corn syrup, water, and vanilla. Combine the flour, baking soda, and salt; stir into the peanut butter mixture. Fold in chocolate chunks. Drop by 1/4 cupfuls 3 inches apart onto ungreased baking sheets.
Bake for 12 to 14 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are golden. Allow cookies to cool for 1 minute on the cookie sheet before removing to wire racks to cool completely.

However, the explorer and collector in me are both still very pleased with this game, even if the adventurer in me is not. Between cute 2D graphics, a variety of races to try, (Floran and Novakid are definitely my favourites) a literally never-ending procedurally generated universe to explore, a charming soundtrack that gives the game such an innocent feel and a pretty good story, this game is great. This game is definitely a worthwhile purchase for the price. Go, shoo, hop to it.

Well, if you played Terraria, then you won't need to read this to fall in love with this game, now, if you haven't, I'll explain you why it's sooo awesome.
Just like Terraria, Starbound is an Indie Game that creates random adventures with lots of monsters, items and all sort of things. It generates random worlds for you to explore, and each one is different from the other, so there you go, infinite gameplay! But that's not all it has to offer, there are tons of items, wich will aid you on your journey. There are weapons, armors, craftables, furniture and a badass SpaceShip that will blow your mind! Each Planet has a different Biome, wich you'll have to adapt, from regular forests filled with evil aliens to frosty hellish planets that will chill you to death!
But hey, you're not alone here! You have a multiplayer mode, so just go on and call your friends to help you!
When you start, you'll get to a random planet and will have to find some fuel to your Ship, well, don't go expecting to fly around everywhere without fuel. You'll have to face fearsome creatures along the way, but at some point you'll find shelter, or well, you could build one! Yes, you can create AND fully decorate your own house! You can get materials from underground or in the surface, with wood from trees, water, minerals and so on...
For Terraria players, you'll feel like it's the same game, but at the same time a very weird and awesome game! It's like a Spacial Upgrade to your favourite game.
For new players, well, feel home, or far away from it in this beautifully made game! You still haven't seen nothing, cadet!
But be warned, this game is very adictive!!!!

Yes, it is like Terraria, but what Terraria has, Starbound lacks.
(Opinion is subject to change, since this game is still in beta.)
Did you like taking multiple items obtained through a series of; exploration, scrounging, monster slaying, and hard labor in the caves for days, then combining them to make a very awesome item(s) in Terraria?
Did you like taking those items and combining them to make an even better one?
Well if you did, then tough luck, because this game literally has none of that.
The game is fun, but it is not worth the 15$ as it is.
the combination of exploration, item progression, item combinations, and challenging bossess were what made Terraria a great and fun game.
Starbound on the other hand, lacks alot of those at the moment.
Exploration is unnecessary since alot of the required ores to progress can be found on the surface,
bosses can not move through blocks, so you can easily exploit it by trapping them in dirt cages and shooting them to hell,
items cannot be combined into better items (Master ninja gear, Terra Blade, etc...), you dont need higher tier tools to obtain higher tier ores (high tier pickaxe to mine Chlorophyte, adamantine, etc...), and do you like to run left or right? because that is what you'll be doing 90% of the game once you understand it.
there is a hunger meter, but that is completely irrelevant, since dieing refills your hunger, and food is abundant in the many worlds you'll be going to. add that to a slow hunger decline, and you'll be stockpiling food instead of anxiously looking for them.
Overall, Starbound is fun, but if you liked terraria for the things that i've listed, then you'll probably find it unsatisfying. For someone new to this kind of game though, it'll undoubtedly be a great experience.
And dont forget the Starbound OST. probably the best music i've heard in a game that i bought.
if not the game, go and buy the soundtrack. actually, screw the game, just buy the soundtrack.
Love it, mods make this game 10x better though.

If you are looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
1/2 cup butter,
softened 1/2 cup peanut butter
1 cup packed brown sugar
1/2 cup white sugar
2 eggs
2 tablespoons light corn syrup
2 tablespoons water
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 cups chopped semisweet chocolate
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
In a large bowl, cream together the butter, peanut butter, brown sugar, and white sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the corn syrup, water, and vanilla. Combine the flour, baking soda, and salt; stir into the peanut butter mixture. Fold in chocolate chunks. Drop by 1/4 cupfuls 3 inches apart onto ungreased baking sheets.
Bake for 12 to 14 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are golden. Allow cookies to cool for 1 minute on the cookie sheet before removing to wire racks to cool completely.

Well, Dark Souls 3... not my favourite, nor my least favourite of the souls series. I'd place Dark Souls 3 above Dark Souls 1 and below Dark Souls 2.
PvE:
The PvE is pretty alright, the bosses are fun and the areas are pretty interesting and well designed. There are some pretty boring, stupid, or just plain easy and a waste of time, tedious bosses, such as the tree boss, but there's also a good mix of good areas and bosses between those. I like the areas much more than Dark Souls 2's level design, and of course it's a lot more smooth and the bosses seem to be more complex, which just comes with time and technological advancements and whatnot I suppose. Either way, the PvE in Dark Souls 3 is pretty well rounded out. While overall I still preferred Dark Souls 2 PvE because it was more difficult and the bosses were more plentiful and fun for me, I still enjoy Dark Souls 3 PvE, especially with certain bosses such as Friede or the lightning guy.
PvP:
The PvP is... interesting. Some improvements from other games, some things which should not have been added. Compared to Dark Soul 1, the PvP is still a massive improvement. It requires somewhat more skill and work and isn't just a backstab or hacking fest. While there are still a decent amount of hackers, there's really not that many compared to what you could have found previously in the other games. Now, compared to Dark Souls 2... the PvP is really lacking here. Dark Souls 2 featured a LOT more variety and viable builds, and while *technically* anything COULD be viable, that's not really an argument that I'm using here because, really, it's stupid. Dark Souls 3 has a *HUGE* problem when it comes to metas and people simply using the most OP weapons in the game at the time, which shifts as adjustments are made to weapons and weapon classes. Unfortunately, there are entire weapon classes in the game which simply become useless due to balancing issues and whatnot, such as greathammers. While they're usable, there's no point in using them aside from a challenge... the only good one in the game is the gargoyle one. If you want to win 90% of your PvP matches, there's a good set of armour, weapons, and rings readily available to make you extremely OP, especially with the introduction of the DLC weapons, which are absolutely ridiculously strong. Now, something that's not specific to weapons but the base game itself is stamina... the rate at which it is consumed is MUCH too small, and the rate at which it recovers is WAY too high, even without any stamina recovery boosting items. This, however, is a base game component, used in PvE and PvP, and unfortunately isn't really something that could be changed to more resemble Dark Souls 2's stamina, as it would require pretty much a complete rework.
Overall, I'd give it a good 7/10. It could use some improvements, which may or may not come over time, but the game is still very fun to play, especially with friends, and even though there are some major problems with balancing and quite a few hackers still, it's still a very fun and enjoyable game imo.

Fallout 4 - Bethesda magic on screen.
It's a game I find myself constantly coming back to, whether it's to have a little fun modding or explore the wasteland to find new parts of the game/Easter eggs or locations I haven't visited.
The story itself is quite linear, there doesn't seem to be much variation for the choices you make.
However, to counter that argument I always felt engrossed in Bethesda's story progression. Just like Skyrim, Fallout 3/New Vegas and many more. The story is quite self contained and the main/only reason you're alive is to find your stolen son Shaun.
There are lot's of side quests/stories (obviously) that still keeps me busy even after 100+ hours of gameplay.
The AI interaction menu received quite a handful of criticism, I don't really agree with the popular opinion that having only 4 dialogue options wasn't enough. Each answer you quote pick is expanded on and they seem to take the words out your mouth; whether it's sarcasm, threaten or trying your luck. A fine example on how I'm trying to explain this is the posh woman with blonde hair in Diamond City insults you and you can return with a swift B of the itch and those were the first words that came out of my head before I got the option.
You have to remember in Fallout 4 having low intelligence to high intelligence makes no difference to their dialogue: It's a different story with Fallout 3's lone wanderer and New Vegas's Brainless man. The S.P.E.C.I.A.L Perks in Fallout 4 are more like an addition rather than a hindrance on the other Fallout Titles.
You really need to give yourself a 5/10 hours of gameplay before you put your verdict on this game honestly. There's so much to explore in this game and you're just kicking yourself in the behind if you're just concerned for the story
The story is gripping the first time you play, but very tedious a second time round so I wouldn't advise rushing the story. You can make 10 hours 100 hours of gameplay if you actively quest and take side stories whilst on your goal to get your son back.
I hope this cleared some potential Q/A's BYB (Before you buy) Enjoy this game, I love it.

Do you play Terraria, but prefer sci-fi to fantasy? Well, then Starbound is for you. I have only played it for a short time, but I already prefer it to Terraria. The menus and crafting are obviously slightly different, but I prefer them to Terraria, and where Terraria gives you a world to explore, with multiple eco systems and enemies, Starbound gives you MANY worlds, each different and as diverse as Terraria’s one world.
The object of the game seems to be to search for the perfect new world to replace Earth (recently lost in some tragedy) whilst keeping your ship fuelled, and making little bases on each world to explore from and create and discover new technology and weapons.
There is one problem however, this is one of the less stable early-access games I have played, it took 2 attempts to open it, and it spammed some pretty unfriendly errors at me when I closed it (im still not entirely sure it saved, I am yet to check) The game also comes with a warning that it may crash, bug-out or delete your characters at random, so maybe don’t get too invested in it yet, but get it all the same, because it’s definitely worth a try (even if it is pretty rough around the edges) and always remember the greatest part of early-access games, you can suggest improvements, and you actually stand the slightest chance of being listened to.

This is a great game, but not one without flaws.
It sets up an interesting and complex game world with engaging factions and NPCs. Companion interaction is much improved in this version of the game, as your sidekicks chime in with relevant comments and react to your choices with regularity. There are a lot of quests and things to do within the game - almost a staggering number. Indications on the map when you have cleared enemies out of an area saves time. The removal of a level cap means that you can keep playing for a while and still enjoy character advancement, which is especially nice in the later game, particularly since there are far more perks to choose from than one could ever collect.  Weapon and armor crafting is interesting and it's nice that the random junk that you find lying around has a purpose beyond selling for caps (of which you have somewhat more expensive special weapons and armor to spend them on in this game). Removal of the silly karma metric is a plus, though not replacing it with anything (including the lack of faction relationship metrics) makes everything feel slightly empty.
It's a long game if you want to experience all of the content. A decision to emphasize quality over quantity here would have been appreciated. In New Vegas, they kept all of the locations relatively small and short and got to the point. FO4, like in FO3, has a bunch of large buildings that simply prolong the experience without enhancing it. I'm okay with the choices available to the character, though they tend to devolve into choosing who to murder more often than not. Inventory management remains clunky as heck and quest items get stuck in there often, even with the recent version of the game. Anything to do with the workshop is unpleasant at best and actually pulled me out of the moment when I realized that I was essentially participating in a level designer in game. It was a very poor choice for inclusion in this type of game. Managing settlements should have been fun, but didn't really result in much and ended up being a chore as they would regularly need help, drawing you out of what you were engaged in doing. The ending is barebones sparse and doesn't reflect basically anything that you chose to do in the world, so you have to appreciate the changes that you see in game.
It was fun and worth playing, in my opinion. If you liked Fallout 3 and aren't tired of the mechanics, then you'll enjoy this one. It doesn't really bring anything new to the table, however, and shows that Bethesda can't deliver on the Fallout experience as well as Obsidian. If you haven't played New Vegas yet, choose that one first.
It also teaches you to value glue, tape, and any adhesive you can find. Enough so that while walking around in daily life, I had to resist the urge to swipe any tape I spotted for weeks!

TL;DR: Fallout 4 is only worth it if you are into a walking simulator set in a post apocalyptic setting, it is basically Call of Duty but with an inventory system. If you're into that, then it might be worth it, but even then, only when it is on sale.
Pros
Great Shooter elements
Crafting systems (Guns, armour, settlements) add replayability
Great atmosphere; Bethesda excels at atmospheric storytelling. There will be many times you will stumble upon locations and wonder what the hell happened here? It is eerie and the ambient soundtrack going with it, is an amazing combo.
Great sidequests and exploration. This was my favourite element of the game that basically saved it for me, I spent most of my time in this game exploring the map and doing the sidequests (which there are plenty and some are great, but some are pretty stupid).
Survival Mode. Need I say more? This may be the best aspect of this game. The survival mode makes it where your character needs to drink water, eat food, sleep (in a comfortable enough bed), and also fight infections, parasites and illnesses, it's very immersive and might give you an incentive to have a 2nd playthrough.
Cons
Streamlined RPG elements; the S.P.E.C.I.A.L stats mean nothing when you're Level 15-20+ as you can at that point, have 10 points in each stat, in addition to the removal of "Skills" you can no longer specialize at a certain attribute and this leads to all of your playthroughs feeling the same (this ties into the disappointing story decisions).
Story can feel very boring as your character is very one-dimensional and most decisions seem to operate on a black and white basis. You are only allowed to say "Yes" or "No" in most situations.
Factions are hypocritical and the story forces you to make allegiences, there is no wildcard option here and if you wanted to feel that your decisions actually made an impact on the Commonwealth, you are mistaken. The world remains the same after the ending.
All of the endings feel the same and they suck. Just my personal opinion, but the endings did not feel as impactful as they should have.
Dialogue system sucks. For most of the game your only options of dialogue will be "YES." "NO." "SARCASTIC." "QUESTION". Which all essentially lead to you saying either "YES." or "SARCASTIC." If not, you will not progress the game.
Performance
Running this game with an i5 and a GTX 1060, with the optimized settings from the nvidia panel the game ran at a constant 60fps for most of the time. There are very noticeable stutters where the game freezes for half a second (as all Bethesda games do..). In terms of game bugs, I did not encounter many, but that can be attirbuted to the unofficial Fallout 4 patch that I downloaded. BUT expect there to be some bugs that will hinder you to advance some quest objects and where you might need to backtrack to a previous save file.
The Last Word: With some great gameplay and exploration to be had, this game offers a very visually appealing, dark and gritty post-apocalyptic experience. Apart from that, this game does not offer much in terms of meaningful, impactful and a morally ambigious story. The story and  character building (RPG elements, dialogue system, allegiences with factions, choices) are quite♥♥♥♥♥♥as they are streamlined, for example, each faction will accept you as one of their own with no background check or give you any meaningful responsibilities that can hinder your other allegiences, the very existence of factions is annoying as at one point you can work for all of them at the same time despite all of them hating each other. Bethesda were definitely not thinking logically when coming up with the story of this game. Worth it under $20 and if you like mindless shooters.
My Rating: In retrospective, this game really disappointed me and even though I've had 150+ hours across the PS4 & PC those 150 hours probably only had around 20-30 quality hours that were decent. Most of the other time was spent grinding and in search of the other "quality hours" as this game did have some glimpses of greatness, but they did not last long. Overall I give it a 5.5/10. This game is barely above average because of its gorgeous looking scenery, art style, sidequests and Far Harbor DLC.

Well. With the new Steam Awards Nominations I have finally decided to put forward my own review of this game. While I still haven't played the first Dark Souls game(not sure if I ever will due to the poor PC port, don't judge me console peasents), I've been absolutely attached to this series since Dark Souls 2, and I couldn't have waited for more action. The third game in the installment is mostly the same in idea and genre as the previous ones, however Dark Souls 3, tries to bring back more memories by being rather closer to Dark Souls 1 in style and execution. The fast paced combat and intense bosses, put you in nail biting conditions as you struggle to succed. Enemies that are made progressively difficult as you move forward, and traps everywhere, that can be avoided by always looking carefully at your souroundings. This game is an absolute masterpiece of the RPG, action style. With multiple endings, and hundreads of items and collectibles this game will make you go for it again... and you will discover things you haven't seen before(unless you already watched everything on Youtube). The story will also leave you filled with all kinds of emotions, but most of them will probably be of sadness and hopelessness, in a world consumed by darkness. My only negative points are related to the multiplayer system(although that has been improved a bit with the most recend DLC), and the weird and unnexpected change to the "poise" system. The game has also been made to be slightly easier, and thus more accessible to new players. For some reason, I still prefer the style of Dark Souls 2, but maybe that's because it's the first Souls game I've played(and it's a true bond that forms as you play this kind of game).
And as with other games I have made an full mostly blind Playthrough of this game on Youtube and it has been an absolute blast to play it, and you can check it for yourself here:
Once again, a fantastic game and I'd recommend it with a 9/10 score to everyone I know.

Dark Souls is a series that took me by surprise. When I first started playing Dark Souls 1, I didn't think much of it. It was ok for me. As time went by, and as I understood the concept of "git gud", I started falling more and more for this series. Eventually, it would become my favorite. Nothing could top that, not even the "sequel" that Miyazaki wasn't a part of... until Dark Souls 3 came by.
Just like with Dark Souls 1, I didn't think much of this game at first. It felt like Dark Souls 1 on steroids. Then it dawned on me: this IS Dark Souls 1 on steroids. Good Steroids. Everything about this game is smoother compared to DS1, for better or worse. The game is a lot more forgiving than DS1 in some aspects, and in some others it's as ruthless as it can be.
I'm too lazy to finish this review right now, so I'll skip to my final words right away: this game became my favorite game of all time, and I've beaten it at least 50 times, and I'm still not tired of it. If you're an RPG purist, skip this series, but if you're in for a game that will not hold your hand in any way, don't think twice about getting this game.

I find so many of the negative reviews about this game hysterical. Do yourself a favor if you're looking through the reviews. Look at the hours played then measure that against the review. Many of them have over 200, 300 even over 400 hours played. But they give it a negative review. To put that in perspective, the average full time job requires you to work around 160 hours a month. If you play a game for more time than you spend working in a month, you like that game. If you played the game for for even fifty hours, you like it.
You can tell by my hours played, I love this game. I'll quickly tick off why.
1) combat works. It's that simple. You can cripple, decapitate, sever limbs and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up.
2)settlements. A great feature to add. Is it perfect? No, but it's hardly broken. Everything works fine and every settlement ends up looking different.
3)Stories. The main story is nothing special, but it's not bad. A parent hunting for their kid.  People's main complaint is that is lacks the depth of previous games and they want more choices but for me the choices are enough. I've gone through four full playthroughs and each time my story moved differently. Seems fine to me.
4)Sub-stories. There are plenty of cool little side tales and gems for you to fine and the nice thing is they aren't full or complete. They exist as if you are an outsider coming in and stumbling upon something. From bodies to notes to chain letters you find between characters in different locations, a network of life stories come out that make the bodies you leave behind characters, not just corpses.
5)Mods. Bethesda's greatest strength is their acceptence and promotion of mods and the modding community for Fallout4 have done amazing work. From simple cosmetic changes to full combat overhauls and enemy AI retooling, the modding community turned this game into one of the top two I've ever played in terms of overall experience.
6) Character. This game has great atmosphere and character. Boston feels like Boston. The people feel worn out and with the settlement system you are able to see actual change and impact on the environment that you are directly in control of and responsible for, and you can constantly change it. For me that trumps a momentary satisfaction that you get with having six conversation choices instead of four.

Despite it is not a classic 'Fallout' game, Fallout 4 is a great successor of its series.
Here are some pros and cons for the game (In my opinion, and I could go on and on...):
Pros:
- Settlement system
- Weapon modifications
- Fully voiced player characters
- Better combat system (It feels better than in previous titles)
- Good level progression system
- No level cap (You may encounter some problems, if you reach level 65535 or above :) )
- If you follow the main story, the game is awesome (There are some heavy decisions to make)
- Easy mod support (Mods can fix minor flaws of the game)
- etc...
Cons:
- A UI designed to fit consoles (can be changed with mods)
- Besides the main story, there isn't much left of a game
- You can't really play a bad/badass character, like in the previous titles (This option is more or less available in the DLCs)
- (sadly) etc...
I know mods can fix minor to major problems of a game, but they shouldn't. They should be an extension to the game, not a patch, without the game would be unplayable. But that's not the case here.
So in an overall conclusion I can only recommend the game and I won't ever regret buying it.

This is an excellent game, plain and simple. It is not a completely free form, choose your own adventure type game however. There is a strong central plot that guides you along most of the way, and it's something that constantly is motivating your characters actions, even if you don't neccessarily care at all. So that's probably the biggest issue a lot of people have; you are playing your version of a certain character, not a character of your own invention.
That being said, if you think of this game more like Mass Effect, it's just phenomenal. You have to resign yourself to the fact that you're always going to have to do certain things, but everything around that is open to exploration in any order or fashion you see fit. Also much like Mass Effect, a great deal of the enjoyment in this game comes from your companion characters. The potential companions are all radically different and you'll quickly develop strong feelings towards them. Not that they change the gameplay that much, they all essentially serve as distractions while you reign down terror like a force of nature, but their personalities and backstories are varied and universally interesting.
And speaking of stories, this game is packed with them. This is something that New Vegas and Fallout 3 both excelled at, and this is no different. Around every corner are small dramas unfolding, and you can take as much or as little interest in them as you would like. Taking the time to read terminals and notes, and listen to holotapes often reveals vivid details chronicalling someones final moments. You sometimes forget you're playing a game set in a post apocalypse because you're so used to the setting, but then you'll find a home with two skeletons lying in bed with a gun next to them, and the reality sets back in. It's the kind of world building that makes a place really feel alive, and even menial tasks like clearing an area of ghouls or super mutants can be suprisignly rewarding if you look around and learn the story of the place.
I love this game. Some people have an idea in their head of what Fallout is "supposed" to be, and this might not be it. But taken at face value, it's one of the most vivid, engaging, interesting, and fun games I've ever played.

It's been over a year and I finally feel like I should put up one final review for this entry in the series. Here it goes:
I spent months fine tuning my original character; gathering all the magazines, "unique" items, maxing all the companion affections, building up my settlements, collecting 1 of each base weapon (at least), and reading all the scraps of the old world I could find. That being said, the best I can say is that the folks at Bethesda have either finally played, or have hired people who played the first two fallout games. This one has more of the aesthetics and architecture of the original games, and genuinely feels like it belongs in the same world in that regard. There are a few lore slip-ups here and there that somewhat irk me- such as Jet being mentioned in vault 95's pre-war entries- but these aren't exactly deal breakers. There is a lot of feeling to this one that it could actually connect to just Fallout 3 (in more than just a reference) if they did fix these lore issues, dependent upon which ending becomes canonical.
The lack of the Karma system feels wrong or simply off, as does the lack of real reputation, and it is sad to see gone from the series as part of the effort to stream line the game for a broader audience. The near castration of the dialogue system is really the biggest drawback however. Before where there was a larger varieties to choose from, it has been boiled down to four base options, with two situational choices being; 1)the simple yes, 2) sarcastic yes, 3) hesitant yes, 4) rude yes, 5) more info, but yes, and 6) persuasive yes. Of course for saying no you still have the classic option of killing them as long as they don't happen to be one of the "essential" NPCs. I believe them when they say they wrote more dialogue for this one than any other, but it just does not feel that way while you are playing. Perhaps the worst part is that the quests seem to blur into borderlands-y murder fetch-quests after a time, instead of just stumbling into trouble while exploring and having to fight your way out.
The ability to built your own settlement is nice, but the areas you get to built in are restricted and in some cases very poorly laid out with immovable obstructions meant to give them "flavour". The workshop is also rather sparse in items for customization despite three of the six DLC being solely for the workshop, and while there are mods out there that fix this, the developers have left it up to the community to do the thing they did not feel like doing despite the $110 dollar price tag for the full experience. Much of the workshop ire I have is from the items that the game lacks implemented in workshop are in other parts of the game, meaning that it would be easier for the devs to add them in free patches or have simply included them. There is also a distinct lack of armour and weapons carried over from other games, and especially Fallout 3 when you consider that this entry has many characters, and a major faction who are from Fallout 3.
Where this game has more polish is in the larger DLC, such as Far Harbor and Nuka world. For example the Granchester Mystery Mansion is both a nice nod to a side quest in the Den from Fallout 2 (and a reference to the real world Winchester Mansion), and brings back some of the super natural undertones the series has always had. The environments in both aforementioned DLCs really shine, and each has some really good world building put into it.
I really enjoyed this game until a month or so after the last DLC came out. Now every time I play it makes me want to play the older games, and makes me want and updates and more refined version of them (I really do miss being able to sprint while playing NV these days). This game is good. It just lacks the staying power or draw of the older games to me, in part due to the lack of the role playing part of this supposed RPG. Would I recommend it? Yes, whole heartedly. Would I recommend it over the older games? I honestly don't know.
It definitely provides a good amount of content, and is a good investment if you want a lot of game for less money, even if the heart and soul of a great Fallout experience is missing.

SInce the days of Terraria, Minecraft and other open-world sandboxes released over the recent five years, we've had the opportunity to explore vast lands, deep undergrounds, and unbelievable structures, acquiring the riches and fighting off the evils that reside. Within Starbound, you get to do just that... all across the universe.
Starbound is the second game released by popular developer Redigit, and acts much alike their previous title. As your ship's fuel depot finally depletes over a foreign alien planet, you must go down to find a source of fuel, essentually crafting, building, and fighting your way to victory.
In the last week alone, it has already preoccupied more time than Terraria did in it's first week for me. Notable differences are the introduction of a psuedo-storyline based on your race, a much more intensive interaction that hints much more highly at the term of survival, and a series of solar systems that truly make the game feel alive, all incorporated with an amazing soundtrack and dialogue that jumps all over the emotional pallette.
As of far, the game is still very much a beta-class game, but is updated every day by a very dedicated team, which results in bugs and difficulty curves being managed both quickly and efficently. A definite recommendation to anyone who had just as much fun with alike games, and wants to make the whole of space their own.

I find so many of the negative reviews about this game hysterical. Do yourself a favor if you're looking through the reviews. Look at the hours played then measure that against the review. Many of them have over 200, 300 even over 400 hours played. But they give it a negative review. To put that in perspective, the average full time job requires you to work around 160 hours a month. If you play a game for more time than you spend working in a month, you like that game. If you played the game for for even fifty hours, you like it.
You can tell by my hours played, I love this game. I'll quickly tick off why.
1) combat works. It's that simple. You can cripple, decapitate, sever limbs and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up.
2)settlements. A great feature to add. Is it perfect? No, but it's hardly broken. Everything works fine and every settlement ends up looking different.
3)Stories. The main story is nothing special, but it's not bad. A parent hunting for their kid.  People's main complaint is that is lacks the depth of previous games and they want more choices but for me the choices are enough. I've gone through four full playthroughs and each time my story moved differently. Seems fine to me.
4)Sub-stories. There are plenty of cool little side tales and gems for you to fine and the nice thing is they aren't full or complete. They exist as if you are an outsider coming in and stumbling upon something. From bodies to notes to chain letters you find between characters in different locations, a network of life stories come out that make the bodies you leave behind characters, not just corpses.
5)Mods. Bethesda's greatest strength is their acceptence and promotion of mods and the modding community for Fallout4 have done amazing work. From simple cosmetic changes to full combat overhauls and enemy AI retooling, the modding community turned this game into one of the top two I've ever played in terms of overall experience.
6) Character. This game has great atmosphere and character. Boston feels like Boston. The people feel worn out and with the settlement system you are able to see actual change and impact on the environment that you are directly in control of and responsible for, and you can constantly change it. For me that trumps a momentary satisfaction that you get with having six conversation choices instead of four.
This is a great game. Period. And the price it's at while I'm writing this is an absolute steal. 67% off? You serious? Get it already!

This game is a SPIRITUAL successor to Terraria with a greater emphasis on sci-fi elements. With that in mind, you go around in an open-box world gathering an assortment of materials to unlock new crafts to make yourself better and if you so choose, a base as well. However, there's more focus on exploration as opposed to base building since you have a ship that allows travel to countless star systems, all with numerous worlds to explore.
It should be noted however that this is an early BETA. Updates, some of them major, are being implemented almost on a day-to-day basis. Please check out the Starbound website to inform yourself of what this entails. Currently the BETA is in PHASE 1 which means CHARACTER/WORLD WIPES ARE TO BE EXPECTED. If you don't mind building up a character only to have it wiped out due to an update, go ahead and start playing and enjoying. Otherwise, it would be better for you to wait until PHASE 3 when wipes will no longer be done. An enjoyable game and with the speedy updates, continues to be interesting despite the resets in progress. Recommended!

I loved this game. I put hundreds of hours into it on the Xbox before buying a PC that could actually run it, and put hundreds of hours into it once again. I got over a hundred mods, went through multiple playthroughs, and thoroughly enjoyed this game, and gave it a positive review. I just want to make it clear that this is a great game, while not a great Fallout game, or RPG, it's an excellent open world, beautifully made, fantastic stories to be found in the world, great companions, and gameplay unrivalled by the past few Fallouts in terms of gunplay, movement, and general gameplay. Gameplay wise, this is probably my favourite in the series. The game has controversial voice acting of the player character, which is well done, but takes away almost all of the role playing in the game. However it's hard to see the same story being done without the voice acting, as it's a very personal story (another flaw; too much backstory also kills roleplaying). There are around 300 locations in the Commonwealth without any add-ons, and what seemed like hardly any side quests compared to the past Fallouts. The 15/16 (13 in base game, 1 in Nuka World, 1 in Far Harbor, and kinda 1 in Automatron) companions are well made with nice backstories and individual quests that give more insight to their pasts. The weapon and armour customization is fantastic, but there doesn't seem to be enough weapons late game. The settlement mode is actually really well made and I do really enjoy building in it, but the inclusion of it to the level that it was implemented in the game eliminated the need for actual towns and cities made by other survivors. Locations from Fallout 3 and New Vegas like Goodsprings, Megaton, Rivet City, Arefu, Republic of Dave, Big Town, New Vegas itself, The Fort, and so many more only truly have two or three counterparts in this game: Diamond City, Vault 88 (arguable), and Goodneighbor. That's it, no more cities or settlements other than those few in the base game. Now for the DLC.
The first set of DLC included Automatron, Wasteland Workshop, and Far Harbor. Automatron was a well crafted short side questline involving robots "invading" the Commonwealth. It introduces a new companion, a robot named Ada, and pits you against the Mechanist. While I enjoyed this addon, it was not at all balanced, so be prepared for many deaths, no matter what level you are or what difficulty you play on. It also adds a new robot crafting system, which is enjoyable and lets you make as many companions as you please. Wasteland Workshop was a small addon that added more items and functionality to the settlement mode that should have been in the base game. That's it really. Last but not least, Far Harbor is an absolutely incredible expansion, truly showing that with the right amount of effort, Fallout 4 could be made into a true role playing experience. This DLC added a new landmass, a couple dozen locations, a companion, Old Longfellow, new enemies, new weapons and armour, and a main questline that actually made me question the indentity of the character I was playing as, and made me choose between many grey morality choices. This DLC is one of the best in the franchise, up there with Old World Blues and Lonesome Road in my opinion.
The second set of DLC had Contraptions Workshop, Vault-Tec Workshop, and Nuka World. Like the previous workshop DLC, these next two just added what seemed to be things that could have easily been in the base game, Contraptions especially. But Vault-Tec Workshop was different in that it gives you multiple quests to complete, and the ability to build and run your very own vault. I really enjoyed this DLC, spending hours going through the various caves in the incomplete vault, clearing them out, and making the vault one of my favourite settlements to go to. However the quests aren't too deep and mostly just revolve around clearing caves and doing experiments. Finally, Nuka World, one of the most painful things I've had to endure. I couldn't get through this DLC on the Xbox, and I forced myself through it after purchasing on PC. It has an interesting premise, a theme park taken over by raiders, but executes this poorly, as it is simply a shooting gallery for the majority of it. There are a few memorable locations and moments, like the time spent in the wild west themed part of the park, but for the most part, this DLC is just a new worldspace with more enemies to shoot.
Overall, this is a game that I enjoy a lot, but is drawn back by it's lack of roleplaying elements, lacking side quests, overusage of shooting and killing to solve problems and go through locations, simplification of levelling up, and the amount of focus put on the settlement building in the game. This is a good game, but not a good Fallout game or a good RPG. Therefore I do recommend it. But there is something new, something sinister and truly ridiculous and outragious that's forcing me to not recommend this game.
Let me introduce Creation Club: a microtransaction system for mods already installed onto your computer, which none of the profit goes towards the modders. Let me explain. The other day, Fallout 4 got a 2GB update, and had changed to version 1.10. So I launched the script extender to launch the game, and I got an instant crash to desktop. After updating F4SE, same issue, and same thing after updating mods using F4SE. I'm starting to get frustrated at this point, and start to deactivate some mods, texture mods, model changes, UI changes, pretty much everything I can sort of do without. Still, crash to desktop. I do some research and find out that I am far from the only one to be dealing with this issue. But the biggest thing that boggles my mind about this is the fact that the 2GB update was the mods. To be clear I was not at all going to use the Creation Club, unless there were massive quests or additional worldspaces being released here. But instead they released Pipboy reskins, and weapons and armours that have better mod equivalents already. This is absolutely ridiculous: I lost the ability to play this game because of a paid mod system that I had no intention of using downloading mods onto my system, screwing up my current mods and game files, and ultimately ruining how I view one of my favourite games and developers. This really ruined Bethesda Game Studios for me, and I'll be hard pressed to find a reason to support them after they pulled this move, and that just kills me. I love Skyrim, Fallout 3, and this game. But I just can't be expected to support a company that ruins my experience of a game with a single 2GB update.
I love Fallout 4, but don't support Bethesda's sick excuse for a "premium mod system".

Fallout 4 is a hard game to critique since it has to live up to its predecessors which are regarded as some of the finest games ever created. With that being said, the game on its own is a competent shooter with a distinctive dystopian setting which is elevated by the lore from the Fallout universe. As with most of the game, the story could have been executed much better. There is a serious lack of an emotional connect for your spouse or child in this game which is a shame since it reduces the game to a shallow mindless shooter at many times. The game does, however, present adequate arguments for and against ai rights via factions like the Railroad and the Brotherhood of Steel. The gameplay in terms of gun play is much improved from previous Fallouts which is both a boon and a bane since more fluid gunslinging reduces the need for vats. Lastly, the graphics of the game are dated and the amount of horse power required for this game is ridiculous; there is a clear lack of optimisation. The main setting which seems to cause fps drops is Shadowdistance; this set to ultra drops my I5 4660/ 970 rig to 40-38 fps in some places and my I7 6700/ 1070 rig to 50-40 fps in some areas. Overall, the game is satisfactory not the magnum opus which many were hoping for.

One of my all time favorite games. Is it perfect? No. No game is. Many fallout fans and bethesda fans in general seemed upset by certain aspects of the game. but the fact is there are easily 100+ hours of gameplay in the main game and another 50+ with the DLCs. I have put 300+ hours on it, almost all of those hours on my first character in one playthrough. the world is incredible, the story starts incredible but as it continues it gets bogged down by the fact that Bethesda wanted to make this game have choices that change the ending while still all culminating in the single final Act.
I've pretty much beaten every quest and explored the Commonwealth, and I have to say it was a wild ride and one of my favorite gameworlds. This game is worth the asking price, but since it is a Single Player game, I would suggest grabbing it with all the DLC on sale to maximise your value. I bought the game pre-order because I'm a huge Fallout fan and bethesda fan in general, and I also bought the DLC season pass when it was cheaper, around $30 for all. So I paid $90 and got every cent back in entertainment.
As for DLC, Far Harbor might be the best DLC for any of the newer gen Fallout games. The Far Harbor story is even better than the main Fallout 4 story to many fans. incredible DLC. Automatron is a short questline DLC but it adds robot companions and it really adds to the lore of the game and fleshes out the world, with the new enemy faction. Nuka World is a great expansion that is not as big as Far Harbor, but definitely fun and adds the ability to become a raider boss if you like to go the evil route.
The settlement building is great for those who enjoy that sort of thing, but it is unnecessary for those who would rather just run and gun through post-apocalyptic Boston. At first I found it tedious but as I got more resources and learned how to use it I became engrossed in building up all the settlements. If you like the building aspects, buy the DLC "Vault-Tec" so you can make your very own Vault!!! even if you don't like the building as much, the Vault-Tec has some missions you can enjoy, although I wouldn't recommend buying it if you absolutely hate building.

Fallout 4 is a hard game to critique since it has to live up to its predecessors which are regarded as some of the finest games ever created. With that being said, the game on its own is a competent shooter with a distinctive dystopian setting which is elevated by the lore from the Fallout universe. As with most of the game, the story could have been executed much better. There is a serious lack of an emotional connect for your spouse or child in this game which is a shame since it reduces the game to a shallow mindless shooter at many times. The game does, however, present adequate arguments for and against ai rights via factions like the Railroad and the Brotherhood of Steel. The gameplay in terms of gun play is much improved from previous Fallouts which is both a boon and a bane since more fluid gunslinging reduces the need for vats. Lastly, the graphics of the game are dated and the amount of horse power required for this game is ridiculous; there is a clear lack of optimisation. The main setting which seems to cause fps drops is Shadowdistance; this set to ultra drops my I5 4660/ 970 rig to 40-38 fps in some places and my I7 6700/ 1070 rig to 50-40 fps in some areas. Overall, the game is satisfactory not the magnum opus which many were hoping for.

First off, Dark Souls isn't for everyone. It's pretty different from your modern RPG (Witcher 3, Skyrim, etc.). You probably already know this, but Dark Souls is known for it's diffculty. In fact, that might be what keeps you from picking up this title. But I encourage you to give it a chance, especially since you can refund it as long as you have less than 2 hours.
Just to make it clear, if you are looking at this game for a fleshed out story then this probably isn't for you. The story is practically buried "under hundreds of layers of cement." Small pieces of dialogue and item descriptions basically make up all the lore. It's often pretty mysterious, vague, and confusing.
In my opinion, one of the greatest things of Dark Souls is it's difficulty. I'm not the kind of person that likes putting himself through pain or frustration. In fact, the reason I enjoy the difficulty so much is the feeling of accomplishment. This feeling is backed up by the game design. Everytime you die in this game, most of the time it's because of a mistake
made. You have to be patient, aware, and think about what you are doing carefully. Maybe I should try luring out the enemy to this location. Maybe I should try out a weapon or use a ranged weapon. I could use an ember to increase my health for this life, but I could be invaded. These are all thoughts that most if not all experienced players with this game have had. But once you get past that tough spot, you feel like you are on top of the world. That is until you die again. In case you also are not aware, you don't level up by "experience." Everytime you kill an enemy, you get souls. These souls can later in turn be exchanged for levels or items. But everytime you die, you will drop them (a green orb). You have to go back to where you died and pick them up, but if you die before that happens you will lose them forever.
The PVP system is alright, though it's not my cup of tea. The PVP system allows you to invade other people's worlds and basically screw them up. If you use embers a LOT, this will happen to you a lot. You have to be careful though as when I've played it there is this slight sense of latency. Often hits don't feel like they connect but somehow they do (at least for me). It feels just a little delayed, so if you don't mind that you should still enjoy it.
You can also play co-op with friends. There is a summoning system where players can put down a "sign" on the ground and the other player wanting to play with them can summon them to their world. You might be thinking it's gonna be hard to just see his sign and not the rest. Thankfully, Dark Souls 3 has a password system (though honestly I don't think password is really the best name for it). You essentially put in whatever text you want and it filters out everyone who doesn't have that text in the password blank. I personally have only played it with one friend before, so I don't have much of a grasp on my opinion of it.
In the end, I think it's a fantastic game and worth a try if you like a challenge.

First off, Dark Souls isn't for everyone. It's pretty different from your modern RPG (Witcher 3, Skyrim, etc.). You probably already know this, but Dark Souls is known for it's diffculty. In fact, that might be what keeps you from picking up this title. But I encourage you to give it a chance, especially since you can refund it as long as you have less than 2 hours.
Just to make it clear, if you are looking at this game for a fleshed out story then this probably isn't for you. The story is practically buried "under hundreds of layers of cement." Small pieces of dialogue and item descriptions basically make up all the lore. It's often pretty mysterious, vague, and confusing.
In my opinion, one of the greatest things of Dark Souls is it's difficulty. I'm not the kind of person that likes putting himself through pain or frustration. In fact, the reason I enjoy the difficulty so much is the feeling of accomplishment. This feeling is backed up by the game design. Everytime you die in this game, most of the time it's because of a mistake
made. You have to be patient, aware, and think about what you are doing carefully. Maybe I should try luring out the enemy to this location. Maybe I should try out a weapon or use a ranged weapon. I could use an ember to increase my health for this life, but I could be invaded. These are all thoughts that most if not all experienced players with this game have had. But once you get past that tough spot, you feel like you are on top of the world. That is until you die again. In case you also are not aware, you don't level up by "experience." Everytime you kill an enemy, you get souls. These souls can later in turn be exchanged for levels or items. But everytime you die, you will drop them (a green orb). You have to go back to where you died and pick them up, but if you die before that happens you will lose them forever.
The PVP system is alright, though it's not my cup of tea. The PVP system allows you to invade other people's worlds and basically screw them up. If you use embers a LOT, this will happen to you a lot. You have to be careful though as when I've played it there is this slight sense of latency. Often hits don't feel like they connect but somehow they do (at least for me). It feels just a little delayed, so if you don't mind that you should still enjoy it.
You can also play co-op with friends. There is a summoning system where players can put down a "sign" on the ground and the other player wanting to play with them can summon them to their world. You might be thinking it's gonna be hard to just see his sign and not the rest. Thankfully, Dark Souls 3 has a password system (though honestly I don't think password is really the best name for it). You essentially put in whatever text you want and it filters out everyone who doesn't have that text in the password blank. I personally have only played it with one friend before, so I don't have much of a grasp on my opinion of it.
In the end, I think it's a fantastic game and worth a try if you like a challenge.

Crafting weapons and such is very nice and I liked turning a laser pistol into a rifle, or a machine gun! Very Cool!

As an avid player of both Terraria and Minecraft, it's a pleasant surprise to see the amount of resources available for in-game architects. NPC interaction, while bare at the moment, holds a lot of promise as further quests and side-quests are created.
I am looking forward to all the great work these devs will put forward in the coming weeks and months (and maybe years?) and would reccomend this to anyone that has played a game in the past 10 years. This game is Terraria with more random.
Having played Terraria and beaten the 7 bosses, though I'm not sure how many there are at the time of this review, it is a fun game with potential for limitless hours of fun. However the problems Terraria has Starbound solves. What do you do in Terraria when you've mined what you want and done all there is to really do? You regenerate a new world and start the arduous process of moving all your favorite things from one world to the new one. What do you do in Starbound? Feed your ship some trees and fly to a new planet. What will you find when you get there? The scanner tells you the threat level and biome of the planet and the size of the planet determines how large the level is but besides that you don't know what enemies you will face. The creatures have randomly spawning heads, body, tail, abilities, and evolutions, in that as you go further down you will encounter slightly larger and different creatures resembling those on the surface. There are bosses which are also generated rather than predetermined, such as the Eye of Cthulu. The creatures are not all hostile either, besides the bunnies, birds, and npcs' everything else in Terraria will try to kill you. In Starbound you may encounter creatures that attack on proximity, but there are also those that don't attack unless attacked. There are settlements both good and bad that the player can encounter and some in the middle in that they want to attack you and are just waiting for you to give them a reason.
In playing Starbound I have encountered a lot that I liked and few that I did not. The game has a bit of a harsh difficulty at first and to date there is no way to increase your maximum health, so your best and only option is to increase your armor from copper to iron and so on. Of the things I've liked I'd have to say my favorite has been in NPC Interactions and settlements. I chose to play as an Avian, because why play a human when we do that already, and I encountered three different Avians settlements so far. One was a tribe of Egyptian-esc Avians who worship a god named Kleox and attack on sight as you are "unworthy", another was a large town of all Avians on a moon who while they all said only one thing there were several merchants who sold many different things that the player cannot create themselves so they have great use. The guards even warned me that equipping a weapon in the city would end badly and I dared not question that as I wanted to see what the town had to offer. There was even an Avian who once I spoke to admitted their worship of Kleox who the guards quickly dispatched and left me in awe. The third was when I was on a planet and encountered an anchor and a chain leading up. A quick stack of dirt and I found myself on a ship of pirate Avians who constantly reminded me that they were watching me and I better not do anything sketchy, but their Quartermaster was willing to sell me guns and no one attacked me so it all ended well. Avian aside I also encountered an alien prison of Floreans, or flower people, who had many prisoners that when I pressed the control panel at the top of the room they ignored me and attacked the guards and then each other until the last came for me. I also encountered on two separate planets a large medieval castle filled with robotic knights who insisted I not enter but my sword insisted harder that I do. I also encountered a high tech science lab that was populated of a species I can’t recall but claimed that I couldn’t survive having seen their technology and my sword also silenced them. All of this was simply amazing to me. Seeing how the NPCs' interacted with me and each other was a very pleasant surprise from what I expected.
My encounter with planets has also gone very well. Having dug to the bottom of several planets and encountered the magma core at the center of each planet, and I’m hoping to encounter one with a robot factory or some sort for some unexpected fun, I found plenty of some resources but not others which adds to the randomization of the worlds. Before I begin, I started playing the Fallout franchise from New Vegas and on. I have so far sunk 600+ hours into Fallout 4. I will do the typical pros and cons that you see in other reviews but I'll also put in my own person take and feel about the game.
From the beginning, you have choices you can make but until you get in the vault, you're pretty much forced to do certain things (ie accept membership into the vault and then go to the vault after the news report of the bombs dropping happens). After escaping the vault though, the options are endless. Don't want to do the main storyline quests? Then don't. Want to explore? Do it! There are certain limitations such as being a low level character in the glowing sea, where radiation and more powerful creatures not only roam around, but nest and infest certain areas.
Now, I'm not some person who goes, "Z0MG!!!! Best Game Evur! Nothing will ever beat it!" It does have its downfalls. The VATS system needs some work. What I mean by that is if you can see the monster and when you fire and you get the view from the enemies side of you firing at them and you can see the gun is over an item by a bit but your shot hits the object directly in front of you even though it shouldn't. There is no "good and evil/bad" karma type system, which would affect how people view and talk to you. Your companions do have an affection level but that's it. Then there's Preston Garvey. If you've ever had a friend that's "I need this." "Can you do this for me?" "I need help with this." Then you've met someone who's about 1/100th as annoying as he is. I was sent to one settlement 4 times for 4 different quests from him, 3 times the same person was kidnapped. The fourth time they were being threatened by some group.
Now for the controversial part, settlements. The original settlement building ability is okay at best. You need to scrap a lot of stuff in a settlement in order to really start building and scrapping most or everything in a settlement can be a massive pain in places like sanctuary where there's a lot of land to cover and a lot of trees and random crap to scrap. The workshops added on more things to build. If you also get mods, you can download a lot, which will give more items to make and build with, mods to increase the amount you can build and more. So with the workshops and mods, it goes from a pain and not really worth it to a fun experience in my opinion.
Now for the pros and cons section:
Pros:
-Graphics are amazing
-Massive Open World (This only increases with Far Harbor and Nuka-World)
-Lots of fun quests (not talking about the hell that Preston Garvey puts you though)
-The companions each have their own storylines and will give quests once you reach a certain level of friendliness with them
-Lots of final end game choices (Institute, Minuteman, Railroad, Brotherhood)
-Far Harbor and Nuka-World are pretty fun
-Settlements are fun with mods
-You don't have to follow the main storyline and can go off and do what you want.
-Exploring can be pretty fun with the random people, enemies and other that you can encounter
Cons:
-Settlements without the workshops and mods is meh
-Preston Garvey is so bad that he got his own meme
-The game tries to give a sense of urgency in order to save the main character's child but does little in the way of actually trying to push people to follow it. "I need to save my son! OH! A baseball field turned into a city!" *78 hours later after quests from Diamond City are done, exploring various areas, and doing more quests from other people along the way* "My Son! I need to find my son!"
-VATS's firing system needs a little work so that shots that should hit, do.
-No karma system except for with companions and even then it's really easy to gain good rep with them.
-Deathclaws are laughable, especially if the character is a higher level.
All in all, I would recommend this game as I have had a lot of fun in the game. Mods can make things more interesting. I've been running around in deadpool's bodysuit. Mod makers have made some fun and interesting quests and have made more areas accessible for exploration.
I hope this review is helpful for at least someone. Now if you all excuse me, both the Minuteman Radio and Preston Garvey are saying that some settlement is in dire need of help. I think I'll start dragging him around with me, not like it will help keep him from saying that another one needs help.
