Stunning: Fallout 4- A masterclass in game design.
The world design is rich and varied, the city sprawling out so naturally as to feel genuine while the commonwealth as a whole is a joy to explore, and sometimes completely unexpected. I've stumbled on satanic swords, jazz listening 'cool cats' and a hippie-cult just to name a few. It trounces Skyrim in terms of the physical wolrd design, BUT the world isn't as quite immersive, the random events not being as common or varied, with a few shout-outs though.
The major reason this gets negative reviews is because it isn't the same as New Vegas. New Vegas is a great game, and the moral choices are somewhat lacking in Fallout 4, but I believe thats intentional. If you need the game to give you a meter telling you how good or bad you are then you are playing the system not the game. The moral choices here are down to the player's own moral judgement- it's freakin' genius!
The gunplay is also exceptional. Really good. I want to try every gun I find because it feels so good to unload them into a raider's stupid face. The loot system is really well tied in as well. It gives meaning to all the clutter lying around and actually makes you feel like you're rebuilding the world one step at a time. People don't like the building, which is kinda clucky and broken, which is fine, but there is also the gun modding, armour modding ect. It just feels so well thought through.
I'm not saying it's perfect. It isn't. It can get repetive, the main story is hit-or-miss (I like some bits though- more than others), and it does have other problems, but it doesn't matter to me. The game is so solid and forward thinking in stream-lining itself in all the right areas that it makes it great. I think I this is bethesdas best RPG, despite a love of Skyrim, and is pretty under-rated.
So to conclude:
Pros:
+ One of the best worlds in gaming at the moment
+ Great gunplay and systems that reward players through exploration and play
+ Wonderful side-quests (the best has to be a superhero themed one i'm not going to spoil)
+ A moral system that requires the player to think and actually role-play
Cons:
- Weak main story
- At points grindy
- The wolrd isn't as alive as other RPGs such as the Witcher 3
- Some wonky controls, especially in building
It is a solid 8.5/10 and with DLC you can bump that up by 1

If you like open-world RPGs with story hidden under every dead body you find, this game will mostly satisfy.
If you like an intense storyline filled with cool set-pieces and moral dilemmas, this game will mostly satisfy.
If you like balls to the wall action with a large variety of weapons to wield, this game will mostly satisfy.
To me, Bethesda games are always a rock solid 8/10. They always give you the foundation of an amazing experience, that may very well happen with just the base game. The writing is good and reliable, with characters that you'll likely learn to enjoy the company of.
Fallout 4 in particular is a real time-vampire. If you're not watching the clock, you can have half the open wasteland mapped out and it'll be 4 hours past your bedtime or more. It draws you in very well to say the least... And as for that part about being "mostly satisfying" I say it because the modding community for this game, is what puts it up over any downfalls it may have.
If you find a glitch, or a bug, or a low quality texture it can be modded out.
If you find a very hard group of bandits to kill, you can mod in a jetpack and minigun that fires nuclear bombs.
If you find a companion whose face you particulary don't like, you can mod in a replacement for it with makeup, a new haircut, and maybe even a fancy new walking animation that makes them sway from side to side as they go along sort of like a showgirl.
I'd recommend Fallout 4 to anyone, any gamer, because of how good the starting game is, and even more so, how good you can make it with mods.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I don't know how anybody could give this game a thumbs down. Its not perfect but the amount of content is amazing. I don't play alot of these types of games so not a 3d FPS type person, but having said that, if you got a new gaming PC and want to find something graphically immersive this could do it for you.
First, the city scape of Boston is amazing, and its an open environment. Its something to see when you climb the fire escape of a tall building and look across the bay at the buildings, sky scrapers, boats and bridges. And then you can actualy walk out to those locations. Combat along the way. And combat is fun, not tedious. Its not a tactical game exactly I would like to go prone or lean on corners but no, the most you can do is crouch, stand, run , walk, zoom with scopes and sights, and hold your breath for a steady shot. That works for me.
Its not mission scripted. And I felt like I could walk away from some of the tedium and still progress the plot forward. There are main quests that need to lead to the next plot line. But you have choices.  I'm not into constructing a settlement and have not had any problem by not persuing that requirement. I do F5 alot, quick save is fast and easy. I have not had to replay the same battle over and over, and thats what I like, if you get over your head, just escape and come back later to settle the score.
The environment does a good job of being dynamic. The first time I saw brotherhood gun ships strafing Mutants I sat back and watched as a spectator. The next time I saw a gunship hover nearby I couldn't resist the temptation and sniped the door gunner from a distance, he fell out, I then went and looked for his body and looted it. Hmmm, you can actually do stuff like that. The environment also changes its weather with rad storms, rain, fog, day, night dusk, all that.
Oh I could go on with all the cool stuff. But there are some cons. The way what you scrounge is sorted and organized is tedious. Example, you want to pass some weapons to an NPC because you are max loaded. You have to surf through a list that could contain a hundred different things just to find the sighted composite lazer pistol you picked up. Sure its alphabetical but you forgot it was a "sighted" composited laser pistol. Then you have to look for that other weapon that is weighing you down what was it called again? Do this over and over you really hate to pick up weapons and armor.
Anyways its overwhelmingly a great game and i'm going to finish it as I'm not bored yet.
Oh, and the AI combat teams, such as raiders you bump into are not just camping, sometimes they pull off some decent ambushes and flanking tactics.

+ Amazing graphics, fast-paced action game with several cool moments
+ Awesome modding community & resources
+ Settlement building could be fun, rewarding time-sink
- More of an action game than the traditional Bethesda/Fallout RPG gameplay
- Extremely bad script, storyline and plot; seriously watered down lore and backstory (or lack thereof) from previous FO series
- Poor dialogue choices; generic options disguised as different phrases that lead to identical outcomes
- Your actions have no tangible long-lasting effect in the game; no sense of achievement for clearing out an area of enemies
- Overuse of boring, repetitive radiant quests that serves no purpose other than adding flavour to a dying game, and also highlights the laziness and poor attitude of the developers
- It's as if Bethesda doesn't care anymore
On DLCs:
++ Far Harbor is REALLY GOOD and brings the series back closer to its FO roots and gameplay, with Bethesda bringing back the rich Fallout atmosphere and lore that were severely lacking in vanilla FO4.
+ Nuka World adds a new playground for high level characters but none of Far Harbor's ingenious lore, atmosphere and storyline. New challenges, trinkets to collect, and some changes to settlement gameplay for those looking forward to build their own raider gang.
- Automaton & Wasteland Workshop are flavour DLCs that add little to no improvements to the core gameplay, unless you are into settlement building.
Verdict:
Be awed for the first hour of gameplay, but keep a low expectation for what's coming next. The fun dies down real quick.

I have to admit that I have played far too many hours on this game already.  I love the atmosphere that the game presents.  Its the 50's nostalglia meets science fiction fusion that I find engaging.  It is a wonderfuo blend of 50's technology with futuristic enhancements.  The game itself is wonderfully open ended and really rewards one for simply wandering about and exploring the countryside to see what is out there.  The bleak countyside with small encampents of population really gives a post-apocalyptic feel to the game.  I found many of the quests to be enjoyable as well as many of them had a small story to tell rather than being the typical "go kill 18 mutants and bring me their toes".
The companion system was enjoyable as well, though some of them were annoyingly difficult to gain affinity (that silly super mutant who gets upset because one picks a lock was particularily annoying for me).  I do wish that there was more character development with the companions once they gained affinity or were romanced.  It would be fun from a role playing perspective if there was more depth to them, particularily with the romance option.  There is almost no dialogue with them, and no story lines, once affinity/romance is gained.
The perk system seems to work fairly well and allows for fun customization of one's character.
The crafting game is fun as well, though I wish there was a better mechanism for hauling back the mountains of scrap that one needs in order to build towns, items, etc.  Even just a brahmin to haul stuff around would be useful.
I found the town building to be quite fun as it felt liks one is trrying to rebuild society.  I do wish the system went further and had more story line with respect to the Minutemen.  I would have liked to rebuild trade routes, a militia some form of government, etc.  There is a bit of a trade route system in terms of making some supplies avaiable at a town, but it is difficult to manage and I would have liked to see more.  But even without that, I have spent many, many hours building up towns at every possible construction site.
The Far Harbor DLC was quite atmospheric as well.  My parents live near there and it was really quite fun to see how it was rendered in the game.
The time I have spent playing the game is testimony to how much I have enjoyed it.  My only complaint is that I would have liked more depth on the various faction lines an companion lines - primarily so that I could continue the immersive experience that the game provided.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

As I am writing this review I would like to mention beforehand that I have not played Demon Souls, DS1 nor DS2.
Before I bought DS3, I was rather sceptical about it- about wether I would even like it or not, and worrying that it might become a game I would end up disliking completely and never finish it.
And in the beginning, I actually came close to that moment. To the moment, where I felt like I wanted to give up. To the moment, where I became tired of fighting the first boss over and over again, only to be stomped into the ground and die. Over and over again.
Thankfully, I kept trying. After some practice, enough attempts and luck I was able to beat the first boss. From that point onwards I discovered the Firelink Shrine, the comfortable home-base, and all it's features. I started to like the game more and more. The level-design, the large variety of enemies and bosses, with a lot of them bearing new challenging tactics, movesets and combos,  the architecture, the different environments you get to discover...and so on.
As of now, while I am writing this review, I have over 200 hours in this game. I'm on NG+.
Short summary:
Positive:
+Gameplay Tutorial
+Design
+Epic Fights
+Interesting enemies and bosses
+Interesting lore and backgrounds to discover
+Lots of weapons and armor (and magic)
+Higher difficulty than in most RPG's
+Co-Op
+PvP
Negative:
-Discovering/Completing all questlines can require more than one playthrough
-Questlines and possible outcomes sometimes hard and nearly impossible to foresee
-No endless load of quests like you might be used to after playing other RPG's

After scaring the hell out of their player base with the release of Dark Souls 2 (vanilla and DLC) there was a lot of thought that this game was gonna suck. There were probably people who wanted it to suck. I can't blame them, I waited a long time to get this game because of that debaucle and what I thought was a mistake in releasing the game again under the subtitle title Scholar of the First Sin.
Dark Souls 3, however, delivers. Not on everything, but enough to be a hell of a game and a game to keep installed. Combat learned a few things from Bloodborne in its pacing, keeping things fluid and moving as opposed to the general feeling of clunk that 2 and Scholar brought. It makes for a fun, though not objectively awesome gameplay. Spell variety is up there, but slightly lacking compared to Scholar of the First sin.
What does this game have then? Polish. Everything feels like it should be in this game, from the maps you traverse, dodging and winding through willowy foes and dancing around the left behind fat, festering creatures and sluggish yet still dangerous anachronisms of ages long past. You feel like you stand between the final days of two leaderless armies facing off for the right of being the last one to welcome the coming end that is so evident that it even drips from the sun and piles far off in lands filled with things that no one wishes to remember. From the first moment you take step, you realize this is a world that has gone cold and begun to shrivel, from the faces of your enemies to the face that lies beneath your skin alongside true power, this world is not dying, its dead. This world has died, and the only thing left to do is to decide what to do with the body, a hotly contested battle that has been raging since before history was first spoken between those with the ability to listen to the voice of another.
And like many before you, you stand at this precipice, seeing options to the world with no real idea of what they truly will mean. There isn't a good and evil end in this game. There's only the one you believe is good, and the one you believe is evil.

Its hard to deny that Dark Souls 3 is a good game. I had fun with it, and it did a lot of things well. However, there are still some massive flaws that kill the experience in a lot of ways for me. And shockingly, one of my main gripes is with lack of difficulty in many cases, something I've never thought I'd ever say when talking about this series. It is an objectively good game, but in terms of the Dark Souls series as a whole it is somewhat lacking. This review will focus on PvE, since enough people have burned the PvP in this game.
FromSoftware did a lot of thing right, and they do deserve praise for those. First, humanity is finally well balanced. They changed the name to ember, and the only difference there is that being hollow is now optional; you retain your human appearence while not embered. Plus, being embered gives a 30% health boost, which gives reason to using it aside from multiplayer.
Most of the bosses in the game are amazing. There's a lot more consistancy compared to Dark Souls II, with the really good ones being completely original bosses. Abyss Watchers is still one of my favorites, Pontiff Sulyvahn and the dancer are well designed and hard, and the tutorial boss is one of my favorites yet. The secret final boss has great design, breaking the trend of getting under the legs to win. The final boss is not as original, but its still such a good fight I honestly don't mind.
Miyazaki is a genius when it comes to level design; almost everything in the PvE portion of the game is great. However, there's a few large problems I have with it. My main problem, and a rather game breaking problem at that, is that the enemies will almost never be in your way. Unless you need the time to look around and explore for items, or are doing co-op, it is almost always disadvantageous to fight. Sure if you mess up you will get ganked and probably die, but not many enemies will be able to keep up with you while sprinting. From what I've found, its usually only the dogs or the pontiff knights you have to worry about. Almost every area in the game follows a pattern of putting a lot of elite enemies right at the start of a level, most of which will aggro in groups unless you lure one at a time with a ranged weapon, and after the first bonfire they're spread out evenly. The idea is clear; you're just supposed to lose your ember at the start, and since you often don't have enough time to light and rest at a bonfire, that's often a suicide run, and that strategy gets repetitive and boring.
From when I found this strategy late game to ng+ to my second character, just running will allow you to skip most of the difficult sections throughout the entire game. I still have trouble beating the winged knight at the start of the game, but I never had to learn because the first time I could just safely kill him with a bow and he couldn't fight back, and the second I just ran past him and made some return suicide runs to get all the nearby items. The iframes on animations means you never have to clear out a room to move on, so you never have to git gud until a boss.
Second, levels never loop back into a previous level. If you go one direction, you will often be going down a linear path to either the next objective or a piece of loot. It lacks Dark Souls's interconnected levels, which made all of them feel more memorable. Dark Souls III has II's overworld map, but with each location being as well designed as the first. Its better than II, but the first is a lot more interesting.
Also, its missing, as Yahtzee put it, Metriodvania level progression. You only really have two directions you can go at any given point, and both of them are mandatory. There's a way to get into the final area of the game in the first level, but since its blocked by a late game boss its more for new game + players than anything. Even then you have to go the normal direction eventually, so its not a good speedrunning tactic, and you can't suicide run a high leve area to get some good loot early on. Ignoring that example, at every point in the game it goes linear, then you get to a point where there's exactly 2 path to take, before going back to being linear.
For those of you who have played the game / don't care about being spoiled,
You can't even do your first optional area until you're at the final level, and all but one of the optional bosses are in those areas. Simply put, I want the option to sequence break / skip certain bosses and areas, and do them in a seperate order. Even if they won't be used often, or if I'll have to go back anyways, its always nice to at least have the option. I like being able to skip to the final section of the game right at the start, but there's simply not enough of that throughout the game.
While the tutorial is good, and gives the basics, the things it leaves out are vital to know. First, they kept the Dark Souls II two handing of pressing or holding to chose which hand to use, something I didn't understand coming from Dark Souls and the simple message of "press y" didn't make me understand there was a second version, until I tried Dark Souls II and learnt it there. Second, the iframes on rolls. This is a huge one, since many bosses require that you roll through attacks. The huge amount of iframes made me realize I was basically untouchable if I could time my roll to the boss's attack. Then, there's poise. I understand having things be cryptic from a lore perspective, but hiding a mechanic is too much
There's naturally a fair share of bad bosses along with the great bosses. The dragon boss is an asylum demon copy (the first level copy of running away and coming back for a plunging attack, only now its a 1hko), the deacons mob boss is boring and easy, and Wolnir is a dps test, who can be impossible to kill if you don't do enough damage and the rng has him spamming fog.
Co-op breaks the bosses. Bosses are at Bloodborne's speed, and having anyone to take the aggro off you means you can alternate free heals. Plus everyone gets a ton of estus to spam, so you only lose if you die in a combo or trekked the entire level beforehand.
One of the changes I personally love, however, is the shortened run back to a boss. It might be a grueling trip to the boss the first time if you stop to kill all the enemies along the way, but usually after reaching it once you can unlock a shortcut that skips all the enemies. Sometimes I feel they go a little overkill with it though; my prime examples are in the last area, where the two bosses have a short gauntlet of foes before the boss, which should create a scenario forcing the player to take risks. The option should be fighting all the enemies, costing precious estus, or ember before the run to drop a quick summon, risking losing it to the enemies or getting a summon failed after entering the boss fog. However, there's a lift before both fights, right after unlocking a shortcut right before it. The final and hidden final bosses don't even have a run of any sort; there's a bonfire right before the boss. The only one without this is
. I view this as a positive change, since with most of the bosses being well balanced, it will probably take most players a few tries to learn the pattern.
I disliked this game because I beat it easily, and never had to git gud. There's no penalty for using the optimal strategies I did, and co-op is overpowered. Phantom estus needs a nerf, and enemies should block your path more often.

As I am writing this review I would like to mention beforehand that I have not played Demon Souls, DS1 nor DS2.
Before I bought DS3, I was rather sceptical about it- about wether I would even like it or not, and worrying that it might become a game I would end up disliking completely and never finish it.
And in the beginning, I actually came close to that moment. To the moment, where I felt like I wanted to give up. To the moment, where I became tired of fighting the first boss over and over again, only to be stomped into the ground and die. Over and over again.
Thankfully, I kept trying. After some practice, enough attempts and luck I was able to beat the first boss. From that point onwards I discovered the Firelink Shrine, the comfortable home-base, and all it's features. I started to like the game more and more. The level-design, the large variety of enemies and bosses, with a lot of them bearing new challenging tactics, movesets and combos,  the architecture, the different environments you get to discover...and so on.
As of now, while I am writing this review, I have over 200 hours in this game. I'm on NG+.
Short summary:
Positive:
+Gameplay Tutorial
+Design
+Epic Fights
+Interesting enemies and bosses
+Interesting lore and backgrounds to discover
+Lots of weapons and armor (and magic)
+Higher difficulty than in most RPG's
+Co-Op
+PvP
Negative:
-Discovering/Completing all questlines can require more than one playthrough
-Questlines and possible outcomes sometimes hard and nearly impossible to foresee
-No endless load of quests like you might be used to after playing other RPG's

After scaring the hell out of their player base with the release of Dark Souls 2 (vanilla and DLC) there was a lot of thought that this game was gonna suck. There were probably people who wanted it to suck. I can't blame them, I waited a long time to get this game because of that debaucle and what I thought was a mistake in releasing the game again under the subtitle title Scholar of the First Sin.
Dark Souls 3, however, delivers. Not on everything, but enough to be a hell of a game and a game to keep installed. Combat learned a few things from Bloodborne in its pacing, keeping things fluid and moving as opposed to the general feeling of clunk that 2 and Scholar brought. It makes for a fun, though not objectively awesome gameplay. Spell variety is up there, but slightly lacking compared to Scholar of the First sin.
What does this game have then? Polish. Everything feels like it should be in this game, from the maps you traverse, dodging and winding through willowy foes and dancing around the left behind fat, festering creatures and sluggish yet still dangerous anachronisms of ages long past. You feel like you stand between the final days of two leaderless armies facing off for the right of being the last one to welcome the coming end that is so evident that it even drips from the sun and piles far off in lands filled with things that no one wishes to remember. From the first moment you take step, you realize this is a world that has gone cold and begun to shrivel, from the faces of your enemies to the face that lies beneath your skin alongside true power, this world is not dying, its dead. This world has died, and the only thing left to do is to decide what to do with the body, a hotly contested battle that has been raging since before history was first spoken between those with the ability to listen to the voice of another.
And like many before you, you stand at this precipice, seeing options to the world with no real idea of what they truly will mean. There isn't a good and evil end in this game. There's only the one you believe is good, and the one you believe is evil.

Starbound is basicly a new twist on one of my old favorites, Terraria. But there is a catch....This game has A LOT more to do and it also A LOT harder. Although in beta, id for sure get this game if you get a chance.

Lately I have been playing a good amount of video games, and I've started to ponder to myself, "What makes a video game good?". After dwelling on this subject for a time, I came across Starbound. And everything that I think makes a game good is in Starbound. Granted, it is not perfect, but it is still in Beta, so I cannot be too harsh on it.
You start out with a standard character costumization screen, with races, appearances and such. Yet I found that the lore and appearances of the races made it slightly more unique in this case. After you are done with the character, they give you a brief explanation of why you are alone in space, which I thought was quite nice. Then you go onto your own planet that you start on, and begin your unique journey.
Now, one of the problems I came across is that the game does not explain itself as well as I'd like. I had to ask around just to find out how to craft something. The first boss was much too strong, but I heard it was just a placeholder, so I'm fine with it for now.
The random weapon combinations and the armor assisting your players in more ways than just "defence" was brilliant, I thought. It allowed lots of excitement when finding/crafting your items. The vast size of the universe I also thought was a great part of the game. It always feels great when you land on a new planet and have a new experience, and that makes me keep coming back again and again.
Overall - This game is only in beta, yet it is such an enjoyable experience for myself. I have high expectations for this game, and I hope it keeps on growing for years to come.

For a beta, it is brimming with content as it is. It reminds one of Minecraft and Terraria, For good reason too, it brings the exploration of minecraft, the boss battles, of Terraria, and brings exciting stuff of its own! The Developers of Starbound are attentive and listen to what their fans have to say. Games rarely make me sit down and play it non stop for several days, but Starbound acheives that effortlessly. When i want to stop, It looks at me with big eyes and says, one more planet?

Plenty of other people have had their chance to rant so I'll just keep mine quick and simple.
Fallout 4 is barely an RPG and more of an open world shooter with really dumbed down gameplay mechanics compared to the previously released Fallout titles. Just can't shake the feeling that Bethesda made a game that would sell better rather than a game the fans would love (and I'd wager money that they planned to the let the modding community do the real work for them).
Got this title and the season pass on sale and I'd recommend you do the same if your a hardcore RPG fan.
Update:
Decided to give this game a second shot and check what the modders cooked up (I've also been in need of more games I can play offline). Some mods have helped address a lot of complaints I have with this game and I've began to enjoy it more, but I still stand by my earlier assesment. This title does a lot of things right and not so much in other cataglories. In terms of gameplay, this game either threw out or altered gameplay mechanics (karma, weapon variety, equipment maintenance, ammo types, perks, etc.) to the point that the game just felt kinda shallow at times.
Some of the season pass content was also a let down. Far Harbor was great, Nuka World would either be good or really short depending on your moral standards, Automatron left me feeling more could have been done with it, and everything else just amounted to optional gameplay addons that focused on settlements.
I'm still not a huge fan on the settlements feature so it didn't help that Vault-Tec, Contraptions, and Wasteland Workshop ended being useless to me.
While this isn't the type of game that made me fall in love with the franchise or hoped for when it was announced it's still a good game as its own thing, but if Bethesda keeps going the direction they went with Fallout 4, then it's just going to seperate itself from what made Fallout stand out from other titles.
There are other complaints I have, but I really don't feel like ranting much longer.
If your looking for an open world shooter with light rpg elements, then this is a great title. If you wanted an open world rpg shooter, then look somewhere else unless you haven't played Fallout 3 or New Vegas.

Alright, at this point I think I'm biased. I've played and loved the previous two Dark Souls games, I don't think I have a clear or fresh perspective on Dark Souls III. I am in there praising the sun while I get tossed around like a dog toy by whatever the latest monstrosity is.
Here's how you know if this series has taken you. It's not the immense satisfaction of finally overcoming a difficult boss fight or when you find yourself being drawn into the world or even when you're playing Fashion Souls and spend way too much time on the "look" of your character. No, you'll know you've been bitten when some total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t happens to you and you still think "Well, Dark Souls is a
game, that was my fault clearly".
OK, so what's good about this installment? Well for me DS3 has the best boss fights, they all feel unique and interesting and the build up to them is generally well done.
Like in Dark Souls 2, you gain the teleport between bonfires ability at the start of the game. But the world of Dark Souls 3 feels much more connected than in 2, which was something I felt was lacking from that game. It really helps when you can look around at certain points of the game and see where you've been, and where you're going.
The combat is your typical Dark Souls, you run around in weird armor smashing monsters and players with oversized weapons. Or if you're mad you only level Intelligence so that magic is actually useful. Or if you're downright insane you try to use Faith spells.
The downside to this game is that there's this one enemy type called the Jailer that drains your health when it looks at you and it also pokes you with a stick and stun locks you. The downside is that they're only in one area, they should be everywhere. Also there's no romance options what kind of RPG is this I want to date little Lord Ludleth.

I really don't want to write this review. I really really want to give this game the ol' thumbs up. But I just can't
Dark Souls 3 is, suprisingly enough, the third game in From Soft's Dark Souls series. It takes the dark fantasy themes from the pervious games and puts them into a whole new world, with the callbacks to the past you would expect after Dark Souls 2.
Interestingly enough, this is the first Dark Souls game I finished without taking a break. I stll haven't completed Dark Souls 1, and only finished Dark Souls 2 after taking a long multi month break. I find the gameplay in the Souls series to get dull fast, where each fight breaks down to roll-parry-hit-repeat. I do love the visuals, sound, and story of the games, which keep drawing me back. Dark Souls 3 is by far the prettiest of the 3, being the most recent. I can spend time just walking around, trying on different armors to see how they look. The music is as great as I have come to expect from a From Soft game, and the sounds of the swords and spells are the familiar ones from the pervious games.
The areas are also well designed, a mixture of seemingly realistic architecture mixed with challenging gameplay. In particular, the Cathedral of the Deep was exceedingly well done, reminging me of the Undead Burg from Dark Souls 1. Enemies are placed intelligently, as if they actually live in and defend their areas, and you can often use the terrain to our advantage if you stop to look and think about it, which is a boon to a filthy casual like myself.
Unfortunantly, beyond aesthetics, Dark Souls 3 left me dissapointed. I won't rant about the poor balance or the lack of poise, others have talked about that at length. Magic is still bad and bleed is insane, frostbite is impossible to afflict and worthless. These are all problems with the game. I want to talk about something different, because you can read about those anywhere. Dark Souls 3 felt very repetitive to me. Every area seemed to break down into a normal enemy, a ranged enemy, a caster enemy, a tank enemy, and some sort of miniboss enemy. Outside of bosses, each area felt like a reskin with the difficulty amped up. Now I know that thats not exactly true, but its extremely close. I never had to vary to tactics to the enemy or switch my resistances; I also never had to use the status resist or purge items. There were a few very small areas that were different - the Consumed King's Garden comes to mind - but they were very small and easilly missed. The sheer power of some weapons relative to others also stagnated my build (I beat the game as a pure faith caster spamming the upgraded Gnaw spell) to the point where I never upgraded my equipment beyond cosmetic changes after I was about halfway through.
Bosses are the highlight of the Souls series, and Dark Souls 3 did not dissapoint. Each boss looks and sounded amazing, boss areas were well done and bonfires were placed close enough that nothing felt like a slog. Unfortunantly, after discovering the strategy to each boss, the fights were trivialized. I never felt that my ability to execute a strategy was being tested, and high health bars only slowed the process down. By the time I reached the final boss, he couldn't even reach me to land a hit before my extremely high damage brought him down.
The true nail in this game's coffin to me is From Soft themselves. I am going to put in a link to the official path notes for an update.
Yeah. This is inexcusable. This patch came out when the majority of the community was complaing about the dark sword and the estoc, but neither of those weapons were touched. From Soft has repeatedly shown that they do not listen to the community and do not know how to balance this game. I wanted to like it so bad, but From has ruined any joy I could get from this game by my knowing that they made it. I do not own, and do not intend to own, the Ashes of Ariandel DLC content for this game. Please watch a playthough of the DLC if you plan to purchase it. After months of work, it takes only 2-3 hours to finish. I don't want to discuss the DLC more, because this review is not about the DLC. I mention it only to show that From Soft is not the developer I used to love. I would not reccomend purchasing this game if for no other reason then to show that you do not support the direction they are going. I personally will not be buying another From Soft game.
Overall, I rate this game one thumb down. Dark Souls 3 is an ok game tied down by poor design and even poorer support.

The only positive I actually care for in this game is the smoother animations and combat - something that should not come at the expense of the core foundation of the game which is, again, role-playing. Ok now I will go over the biggest Pro and Con to the game:
This game reallt felt like the final entry, it had many memorable and climactic moments! Many boss fights were memorable, unlike previous entry Dark Souls 2. The final boss was wonderful!
All in all this game dramatic and delivered the feeling of finality that it needed to!
The community for this game series over the years has become quite toxic, people are impossing their own rules on others, and they are very aggressive about it. Even expressing your criticism for certain mechanics can get you a major outrage from the community and it is a shame for that. Many people in the PVP community treat the game more like a religion than a game and it's sad, so don't expect a warm welcome from these "souls fans" because they're very few kind hearted ones, I speak from experience I've been in the community since the begining.
After all these valid criticisms I do still love the game, it is a wonderful job by Fromsofware, but I know they can do better and I hope they will in the future. 8/10

Mixed opinions on this game, I'm weighing in. Just saying I'm a long time fallout player, not new. Started on Ps3 wih F03 years ago.
NO SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW! NO SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW!
TL;DR (Too long, didn't read)
DIALOGUE: Poorly executed. Dialogue options too vague, aquired perks in the game don't get you unique dialogue and always having 4 options to choose from is a problem.
ENVIRONMENT: Great environment it feels unique, just too many "kill the enemies and leave" or "settlement" locations, although settlement mode is a nice touch. Both problems are fairly small.
STORY: Good until you meet the people that kidnapped your son, writing gets sloppy after that, and the decisions you make HARDLY impacts the ending, with the exception of two sentences being about what you did.
PERFORMANCE: Decent, except the "Shadow distance" setting can lower fps, yet not increas the looks of the graphics.
CHARACTER PROGRESSION: Other fallout games did it much better.
SIDE QUESTS: Too many side quests are just fetch quests/kill enemies quests, other fallouts had many sidequests, and all seemed interesting and engaging, fallout 4 is too much of fetch quests and kill enemies at *insert location here*.
REMEMBER! This was the TL;DR, the rest of the review elaborates on this.
The Dialogue System:
Had potential, poorly executed. When speaking in dialogue you ALWAYS have from 4 choices of dialogue to choose from, this creates problems if you want their to be options for more or less than4 dialogue options, meaning a yes or no question will have 2 Yes answers, and Two no answers, EG: Yes, No, Maybe, I'll think about it could be dialogue options, and between the "Maybe," and "I'll think about it" you have no way of telling which is the yes or no, therefor you have to steer clear of any vague dialogue... Which brings me too my next point. The dialogue is WAY too vague, such as the infamous to fallout 4; "Sarcastic" dialogue option. Sometimes it will offend people, sometimes they'll laugh, sometimes is hardly even sarcastic in the slightest way. This brings the problem of when you dont know what your saying, you may have to go back to a save because you messed up the conversation you were having. Also, the fact that speech is now a dice roll, and the perks/skills you have no longer bring you unique dialogue choices is frustrating. About the voiced protagonist... I dont really mind. Seems fine to me.
The Environment:
Amazing, I loved the environment in fallout 4, from the unique glowing sea, to the city of boston, its great. I really liked how the environment is based on levels, so the game isnt easy all the way through like fallout 3, the map is divided by different areas wuth different leveled enemies, which is a great touch to the game. Also, compared to the other fallout's Brown/Yellow colour pallette, this one is nice and colorful, but doesn't break the post-apocalyptic theme. I always love that enemies will use the environment in combat to hide behind, take cover or peek over to shoot at you. This was brilliant! I can't praise the enviornment enough, however I had 2 problems with it. An annoying thing was that most places you find in fallout 4 are just for shooting up, kill a few enemies and never visit again unless you wanna travel to a place that's nearby the area, so you would fast travel to the cleared location to get there faster... I just feel that at the least 5+ more unique locations that have have people that you can talk to in it would be great. However, I do love that for these locations, sometimes you can find a backstory behind them, that makes the place seem depressing, interesting or horryfing. The backstories to some places in fallout 4 or great, and I would definately reccomend keeping an eye out for holotapes and terminals in fallout 4, at those locations. The other problem I had was that there are too many settlements, and as such you drain all your recources trying to build at least a few things at a few settlements. The Settlement system would've been MUCH more enjoyable system if there were only 2-4 settlements in the game, also I would like to add that I did quite enjoy the settlement system. Both of these problems were quite small and insignificant.
STORY Don't worry, no spoilers in this review. Being as vague as possible with the story when neccesary.
At the start, I thought the story was great, it captures your attention, and sends you searching across the unforgiving land of the post-nuclear-war massachusetts. You meet a few interesting characters, including a synth detective, Nick Valentine, a synthetic, fake human. (This detail plays out into his back-story quest later). You find the man who kidnapped your son, and from that you get a lead to the people he worked with... Here's where the story gets fishy, and bad. Whatever you do to these people, they don't hate you, unless you kill some of them. You can align with their enemy factions and they wont care, until something happens the leader of them, something that has no relevance to your enemy factions. You can't even mention that in the upstairs area their are a bunch of turrets that kill on sight, that they could be evil, you cant tell him about it. Their enemy factions don't ask about what you've seen in the place, nor can you tell them, until they ask... Which is one time per each faction... The story writing got really sloppy when you meet the people who are working with the man who kidnapped your son. And the ending, in of vague of terms as possible, depending on what faction you sided with, you get one line that's relevant your ending, and then it goes on about "How war never changes." It doesn't tell you about the decisions you've made in the game or how you helped or didn't help certain groups... Although LITERALLY every other fallout made has a multitude of good or bad endings. It's like your stripped of your choices for the story, albeit there are more faction choices and diversity than fallout 3, but there's not a detailed ending, unlike fallout 3
Performance:
Here's a tip, if you're suffering framerate drops in places like the city, but you got a decent pc like mine, next time you launch the game, go into the advanced graphics options and put "Shadow distance" onto Medium. It makes NO difference to graphics, but on max settings, you should always be getting 60 fps now, granted, if your pc is good enough. Other than that easily fixable issue, performance is good. Not really great, but its good. It works fine but not flawlessly.
Character progression:
Its good that enemies and side quests give you enough XP to actually level up once you get past level 30, but the way you spend your points when you level isn't good anymore. This part is hard to explain without images, but to put it in simple terms fallout 3& New Vegas had a better system in which you level up, where you choose what skills to invest your level up points in, buyt fallout 4 just gives you 1 point per level up, and you choose one skill to level up. Different skills in fallout 4 have different ammounts of levels to invest into leveling up (For some reason).
Side quests:
I just didn't feel like there were enough side quests, let alone good uniqye ones that arent fetch quests, such as "Hey, go over to *insert random place here*  and get this technology for me. The only unique quests on the top of my head are: The kid in the fridge, Human error, Long time coming (Only because it reveals interesting information about a companion character) The secret of the cabot house, and Last voyage of the USS consitution. All the other side quests I've done feel really uninspired and lackluster. However, keep in mind there are quite a few nmore quests I've read about that seem great, but I haven't done. The side quests feel more "Quantity over quality"
Heck this took long too write haha hope this helped! Overall, I reccomend the game, it has its negatives but the positives certainly outweigh them!

Lately I have been playing a good amount of video games, and I've started to ponder to myself, "What makes a video game good?". After dwelling on this subject for a time, I came across Starbound. And everything that I think makes a game good is in Starbound. Granted, it is not perfect, but it is still in Beta, so I cannot be too harsh on it.
You start out with a standard character costumization screen, with races, appearances and such. Yet I found that the lore and appearances of the races made it slightly more unique in this case. After you are done with the character, they give you a brief explanation of why you are alone in space, which I thought was quite nice. Then you go onto your own planet that you start on, and begin your unique journey.
Now, one of the problems I came across is that the game does not explain itself as well as I'd like. I had to ask around just to find out how to craft something. The first boss was much too strong, but I heard it was just a placeholder, so I'm fine with it for now.
The random weapon combinations and the armor assisting your players in more ways than just "defence" was brilliant, I thought. It allowed lots of excitement when finding/crafting your items. The vast size of the universe I also thought was a great part of the game. It always feels great when you land on a new planet and have a new experience, and that makes me keep coming back again and again.
Overall - This game is only in beta, yet it is such an enjoyable experience for myself. I have high expectations for this game, and I hope it keeps on growing for years to come.

First Fallout game I ever played. TL;DR - between 5/10 and 7/10. Maybe. RPG needs more RP.
In terms of game mechanics, the VATS system and shooting is probably the best of all 3 of the newer Fallout games. Settlement building is good fun for people who enjoy playing The Sims: Apocalypse, though the radiant quests will be as annoying as they were in Skyrim.
The world itself is more colourful than the previous 2, but does feel empty. Bethesda tends to create lots of types of things and use that to fill your world rather than create lots of storylines branching out that fill your world. As an example, there are 5 different variants of each enemy, at least, but don't expect huge amounts of depth to any of them. They're there to be shot.
There's no karma system, which means that your nasty actions have no effect unless you've got a morally good companion with you. This is probably what is the cause of some of the shallow story. Your actions don't matter, whereas in order to inject some realism and actual investment in the story, your character needs to feel the trouble they might start or enjoy the worship they receive by being Wasteland Jesus.
Also, height scaling? Lots of people are the same height. Not great.
Now onto the story.
It's not as deep as it could be. Pretty straight-forward - you play the avenging Mother/Father of a kidnapped son and a murdered spouse, recently freed from a cryo facility where you've been on ice for 210 years, ever since the bombs dropped on October 22nd, 2077. You hunt down your son and join 4 different factions, but the end result is mostly the same regardless of who you choose.
SPOILERS BELOW
The death of your spouse and your relationship with your son feels very ham-fisted, and you're not given an opportunity to really care about either of them.
3 of the four factions end up with the same result - Institute is destroyed, there's a big ol' radioactive chunk of Boston close to where people, oh, I dunno, *actually live* (which in terms of in-game consequences is never mentioned or considered to be an issue - 'why's everyone turning into ghouls Maureen?' asks one resident of Diamond City. 'Oh well they nuked the Institute so now we just have to deal with the nuclear fallout Jessie, no big deal,' her friend replies.)
FACTIONS
Institute - your typical amoral science nerds in a shiny chrome bunker who think they're saving the world. They make synths, synthetic humans, whom they treat like nonhuman robots. Very clearly set up to be the bad guys you end up nuking. Would have liked to see more reasons to spare them, perhaps more ways in which they genuinely believe they're helping the surface world. Basically, my son runs these guys, that's my son, y'know, the main drive of the Sole Survivor. Brian Delaney and Courtenay Taylor are excellent voice actors and deliver their emotional lines with great punch, but it feels hollow without giving the gamer a proper chance to bond. 5/10.
Railroad - cool spies who help out their robot buddies. Actually quite enjoyable and in fact written as slightly more ambiguous and morally grey than maybe they were planned? Particularly Desdemona's staunch refusal to work with you after a certain point until you're competely in with them and swear to forego using the other factions to take out the Institute. Could still use more bonding time with them, though. Particularly after the Nuclear Option, where they mention dead characters - would've been nice to see them honouring people more. 8/10.
Brotherhood of Steel - they're the East Coast but they're not Lyons' East Coast, though they're less conservative than the West Coast. Picture a mix of the two. Still mostly filled with giant bags of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though the lil' squires are quite sweet and if you get attached to kids, makes it difficult to blow their flying ship out of the air. Led by Arthur Maxson (phwoar - excuse me,) they're great for a free set of T-60 and a vertibird for flying in style. Hostile as ever to ghouls and super mutants, and now synths. Personally had many idealogical conflicts with them but (as I said, RPG needs more RP) conflicting with them won't get you punished or at the most extreme kicked out of the Brotherhood. You gotta go full Institute/Railroad for that. 6/10, but bump it up to 7/10 just because they wear these form-fittign jumpsuits that are really nice around the butt. (Maxson, rawr.)
Minutemen - generally considered the good guys, join the Minutemen if you want endless radiant quests of 'DEFEND X SETTLEMENT'. My favourite faction simply because I have mods that stop settlement attacks, they're not as xenophobic as the BOS or as synth-mad as the Railroad. Also, Preston Garvey is a literal angel despite the constant radiant quest-giving, can be romanced, interesting back-story and always happy to help people, 10/10 loveliest NPC ever.
DLCs
Fallout 4 has 6 DLCs, two and a half have an actual plotline, the other 3.5 are alllllll about the settlements, people. I personally rate 8/10 because I like building, but as content goes, 6/10 just because of how little extra story we get.
Automatron - You hunt down the Mechanist, get a sweet new robot buddy, and can build robots. 6/10 because the RobCo sales and service centre provides more interesting 'Pre War government was AWFUL' material, and the main villain has a twist, but other than that it's mostly just modifying robots.
Far Harbour - Probably the best of them all. Bethesda seems to like DLCs where you end up on a mysterious island (see Bloodmoon, Shivering Isles, Dragonborn.) Whole place is covered in fog, and there are 3 factions again. Some of your choices matter here, but still not enough to feel like your character is actually part of this world. You've got the synths, the town of Far Harbour, and the Children of Atom. The synths are actually one of the better written factions - they seem at first glance to be a haven for synthetics, but their leader is more neutral good/neutral and 'end justifies the means'. The Children of Atom are quite nutty, but have some enjoyable quests. Far Harbor is pretty much 'everyone in this town is drunk and probably stinks of fish.' Not horrible people, but certainly hardened. 7/10-8/10 but Bethesda copies an entire quest from a New Vegas mod.
Wasteland Workshops - just adds♥♥♥♥♥♥to build with. Useful. Not really able to rate because I like building and I'm biased.
Vault-Tec - you too can be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ living in your own Vault experimenting on your dwellers. 4/10, lots of stuff to build but can only do so in one location, also there's a ♥♥♥♥ing Mirelurk Queen in this cave, bruh.
Nuka-World - had lots of promise but sadly very, very shallow. You turn up at Nuka World, there's now like a billion variants of Nuka Cola, everyone's awful, you're the boss now. And even if you choose to murder every raider in the park, it's left completely empty and you can't do anything with it. 6/10, interesting location and some new enemies, but doesn't really offer anything and it's like, covered in trash and gore. You can't clean it up either.

Played it and finished every major quest and side quest I cam across.  Was thoroughly disappointed when comparing it to Fallout: New Vegas and even Fallout 3. RPG elements are stripped back to a bare minimum, allows for next to no min-maxing and very little general customisation.  The "characters" you meet are almost all 2 dimensional or just not really characters at all with one or two exceptions. Graphically it looks fairly terrible with everything maxed out in terms of both texture quality and aesthetic. The colour palette is boring and drab but it lacks some of the interesting landmark features included in 3 and NV which make those games at least a little interesting visually. The story was boring and predictable. It actually has a couple of interesting story beats near the beginning with Nick Valentine but quickly goes downhill with no sign of stopping.  They seemingly went for a similar story climax/choice as New Vegas which elected to essentially let you choose between different political ideologies, none of them being particularly "evil" or "good" depending on your perspective, but Fallout 4 misses the point completeley and has 2 obviously "evil" choices and 2 obviously "good" choices with very little incetive to choose any of them over the other aside from if you want to be a boogie man or a saint.  It's also full of bugs, I repeatedly experienced crashes on the lengthy loading screens and had NPC pathing and textures completely bug out.  The radient quests and side quests are boring busywork that are worth doing once to see what they are (usually go to a location and kill some raiders/mutants) and then they just repeat in different locations displaying a stunning lack of good quest design.  The settlement system and base building is clunky, poorly implemented and completely superfluous. Again it amounts to little more than busywork to soak up time doing essentially nothing of value from a gameplay/story standpoint.
The gunplay is somewhat better than the prior games though so I guess there's that.

the only step up fallout 4 took from 3/new vegas is the combat but honestly i'd have preferred it if it got better at literally. anything else.
your ability to RP is severely restricted, since you're given a pre-established backstory right off the bat which is a significant step down from new vegas. the player should be able to create their main character, or if not, have a well-developed one to use (which fallout should still not have), and (to no one's surprise) bethesda can't do that properly. there's a massive disconnect between you and your character, because your character cares about a spouse and kid you saw for 5 minutes and don't give one solitary ♥♥♥♥ about.
dialogue options are severely limited. the strict 4-panel thing does not work in a series like fallout. you can't tell what you're saying and there's no opportunity to rp like you could in 1/2/3/NV with your wide range of dialogue choices. it's truly mind-boggling that someone at bethesda thought this was a good idea -- they've publicly said now that it 'didn't work as intended'.
the """"renovated"""" perk/skill chart is also a horrific idea. all it did was force bethesda to put all the skills from the other games into the perk chart, which makes the perk chart boring because half the time you're taking perks that skill points would have taken care of and it's just number increases. number increases are not exciting. nobody cares, and you're not taking them to further your rp purposes like you might in fnv taking something like sneering imperialist. you're taking them so you can kill things with your chosen weapon and you're going to take the same things for every character for that reason.
tied into this, the elimination of skills eliminates skill checks, which are practically integral to fallout. your character could be really good at one thing, and really horrific at another, and it would show when you interacted with someone. now it's just charisma. you just have to have good charisma nothing else matters. it just contributes to making every one of your characters feel the exact same.
radiant quests just exist to pad game length and are an exercise in pointlessness, particularly since they make up such a large percentage of available quests. everything that isn't a main quest (and hell, some things that are main quests) are incredibly linear -- there's no branching paths to any of them, just go there, shoot/collect that, and come back. even with this desperate focus on charisma there's no option to talk enemies down like you could do with lanius, ulysses, and dr. klein in new vegas -- if they were in fo4 you'd just have to kill them.
next to the improved combat, the only good thing i can say about this game is that the companions were written a hell of a lot better than fo3's. i loved a lot of them. but that doesn't make up for the tire fire that is the rest of it.

Despite a collection of flaws, Fallout 4 manages to live up to its predecessors in terms of content quality, adictiveness and gameplay length, making it well worth a purchase for fans of the genre.
Fallout 4's weaknesses largely stem from Bethesda's unwavering habit of using an aging engine and failing to address glaring performance issues/bugs. These choices are intentional, glarlingly financially motivated and - where older gaming hardware was able to cover up in the past - has well outworn its welcome.
However, the team's talents for creating compelling quests, storylines and an unrivaled immersive world are still able to overcome the majority of shortcomings. In short, what's good about Fallout 4 is worth experience enough to power through performance frustrations or otherwise.
Additionally, the modding potential and thriving community make it well worth the cost.

Dark Souls III is another great entry in the Souls series, the PvE is great and the PvP, while broken in some aspects, is still fun. It's the same idea of third person dodging and exploring simulator as Dark Souls and Dark Souls II but it's smoother and bigger. The game is slightly easier compared to Dark Souls II but on the same level of difficulty as the original Dark Souls. There are a great number of weapons and spells for your character and it's a blast to go through the levels with your favorite weapon and overcoming the bosses. The game does go hard on returning characters/locations of previous games, and playing Dark Souls and Dark Souls II before Dark Souls III will definitely make your experience better. The game does stand just fine on its own however.
All in all a great game, personal GOTY 2016.
P.S. The Boss music is absolutely phenomenal in Dark Souls III, it deserves a special mention.

Krispy Kreme sued for fraud in federal court over doughnut ingredients
Krispy Kreme is facing a class-action lawsuit filed in Los Angeles federal court Wednesday by a former customer who says the doughnut chain is guilty of false advertising and fraud because some of its supposed fruit-filled and maple-glazed products are made with “nutritionally inferior ingredients.”
Krispy Kreme has conducted “false and misleading business practices” because products like its “Glazed Raspberry Filled,” “Glazed Blueberry Cake” and “Maple Iced Glazed” doughnut and doughnut-holes aren’t actually made with real fruit or maple, the lawsuit alleges.
Instead, Krispy Kreme uses sugar, corn syrup, gums and artificial food coloring to “mimic the texture, shape and color” of these “Premium Ingredients,” as they’re called in the complaint, in lieu of naturally occurring products with proven health benefits, according to the court filing.
Attorneys at the L.A. office of Faruqi & Faruqi are now seeking class-action status for their claim as well as upwards of $5 million in damages from the North Carolina-based doughnut chain because of the absence of these “Premium Ingredients.”

The mantra of the Krispy Kreme Challenge epitomizes the test of physical fitness and gastrointestinal fortitude. What started as a challenge among ten friends has transformed into a nationally publicized charity race, and the number one tradition to complete before graduating from North Carolina State University.
The competition, which began a dozen years ago, is organized by scholars at North Carolina State University to raise money for the University of North Carolina Children’s Hospital, according to the News & Observer. The race begins at the N.C. State Bell Tower and ends at the Krispy Kreme in downtown Raleigh, where runners eat a dozen doughnuts each before heading back to campus, according to the newspaper.

A very satisfying and content filled open world action game with base RPG elements. If you want an RPG, start with Fallout: New Vegas instead of 4. 4 does a very good job of capturing a setting, an atmosphere, and an ambience very much like other open world action games such as S.T.A.L.K.E.R., where choice and dialog are a factor in the gameplay - but serve more as a storytelling medium than an actual RPG where you feel more in control, and like your decisions matter. Not that the decisions you make in this game don't matter- there are a lot, actually. And they have dramatic effects on the gameplay and world as well. Characters and you have relationships. But they don't feel the same as in a well written, purpose built RPG like New Vegas that puts story/RPG elements first, and gameplay/content second. Fallout 4 does the opposite. But nonetheless- I have only spent 400 or so hours on one character, one playthrough. I could do it all again, and completely different, and spend another 400 hours discovering new things. It really is a lot. This game honestly goes toe to toe with Skyrim in terms of content and replayability.

TL;DR (Too long, didn't read)
DIALOGUE: Poorly executed. Dialogue options too vague, aquired perks in the game don't get you unique dialogue and always having 4 options to choose from is a problem.
ENVIRONMENT: Great environment it feels unique, just too many "kill the enemies and leave" or "settlement" locations, although settlement mode is a nice touch. Both problems are fairly small.
STORY: Good until you meet the people that kidnapped your son, writing gets sloppy after that, and the decisions you make HARDLY impacts the ending, with the exception of two sentences being about what you did.
PERFORMANCE: Decent, except the "Shadow distance" setting can lower fps, yet not increas the looks of the graphics.
CHARACTER PROGRESSION: Other fallout games did it much better.
SIDE QUESTS: Too many side quests are just fetch quests/kill enemies quests, other fallouts had many sidequests, and all seemed interesting and engaging, fallout 4 is too much of fetch quests and kill enemies at *insert location here*.
REMEMBER! This was the TL;DR, the rest of the review elaborates on this.
The Dialogue System:
Had potential, poorly executed. When speaking in dialogue you ALWAYS have from 4 choices of dialogue to choose from, this creates problems if you want their to be options for more or less than4 dialogue options, meaning a yes or no question will have 2 Yes answers, and Two no answers, EG: Yes, No, Maybe, I'll think about it could be dialogue options, and between the "Maybe," and "I'll think about it" you have no way of telling which is the yes or no, therefor you have to steer clear of any vague dialogue... Which brings me too my next point. The dialogue is WAY too vague, such as the infamous to fallout 4; "Sarcastic" dialogue option. Sometimes it will offend people, sometimes they'll laugh, sometimes is hardly even sarcastic in the slightest way. This brings the problem of when you dont know what your saying, you may have to go back to a save because you messed up the conversation you were having. Also, the fact that speech is now a dice roll, and the perks/skills you have no longer bring you unique dialogue choices is frustrating. About the voiced protagonist... I dont really mind. Seems fine to me.
The Environment:
Amazing, I loved the environment in fallout 4, from the unique glowing sea, to the city of boston, its great. I really liked how the environment is based on levels, so the game isnt easy all the way through like fallout 3, the map is divided by different areas wuth different leveled enemies, which is a great touch to the game. Also, compared to the other fallout's Brown/Yellow colour pallette, this one is nice and colorful, but doesn't break the post-apocalyptic theme. I always love that enemies will use the environment in combat to hide behind, take cover or peek over to shoot at you. This was brilliant! I can't praise the enviornment enough, however I had 2 problems with it. An annoying thing was that most places you find in fallout 4 are just for shooting up, kill a few enemies and never visit again unless you wanna travel to a place that's nearby the area, so you would fast travel to the cleared location to get there faster... I just feel that at the least 5+ more unique locations that have have people that you can talk to in it would be great. However, I do love that for these locations, sometimes you can find a backstory behind them, that makes the place seem depressing, interesting or horryfing. The backstories to some places in fallout 4 or great, and I would definately reccomend keeping an eye out for holotapes and terminals in fallout 4, at those locations. The other problem I had was that there are too many settlements, and as such you drain all your recources trying to build at least a few things at a few settlements. The Settlement system would've been MUCH more enjoyable system if there were only 2-4 settlements in the game, also I would like to add that I did quite enjoy the settlement system. Both of these problems were quite small and insignificant.
STORY Don't worry, no spoilers in this review. Being as vague as possible with the story when neccesary.
At the start, I thought the story was great, it captures your attention, and sends you searching across the unforgiving land of the post-nuclear-war massachusetts. You meet a few interesting characters, including a synth detective, Nick Valentine, a synthetic, fake human. (This detail plays out into his back-story quest later). You find the man who kidnapped your son, and from that you get a lead to the people he worked with... Here's where the story gets fishy, and bad. Whatever you do to these people, they don't hate you, unless you kill some of them. You can align with their enemy factions and they wont care, until something happens the leader of them, something that has no relevance to your enemy factions. You can't even mention that in the upstairs area their are a bunch of turrets that kill on sight, that they could be evil, you cant tell him about it. Their enemy factions don't ask about what you've seen in the place, nor can you tell them, until they ask... Which is one time per each faction... The story writing got really sloppy when you meet the people who are working with the man who kidnapped your son. And the ending, in of vague of terms as possible, depending on what faction you sided with, you get one line that's relevant your ending, and then it goes on about "How war never changes." It doesn't tell you about the decisions you've made in the game or how you helped or didn't help certain groups... Although LITERALLY every other fallout made has a multitude of good or bad endings. It's like your stripped of your choices for the story, albeit there are more faction choices and diversity than fallout 3, but there's not a detailed ending, unlike fallout 3
Performance:
Here's a tip, if you're suffering framerate drops in places like the city, but you got a decent pc like mine, next time you launch the game, go into the advanced graphics options and put "Shadow distance" onto Medium. It makes NO difference to graphics, but on max settings, you should always be getting 60 fps now, granted, if your pc is good enough. Other than that easily fixable issue, performance is good. Not really great, but its good. It works fine but not flawlessly.
Character progression:
Its good that enemies and side quests give you enough XP to actually level up once you get past level 30, but the way you spend your points when you level isn't good anymore. This part is hard to explain without images, but to put it in simple terms fallout 3& New Vegas had a better system in which you level up, where you choose what skills to invest your level up points in, buyt fallout 4 just gives you 1 point per level up, and you choose one skill to level up. Different skills in fallout 4 have different ammounts of levels to invest into leveling up (For some reason).
Side quests:
I just didn't feel like there were enough side quests, let alone good uniqye ones that arent fetch quests, such as "Hey, go over to *insert random place here*  and get this technology for me. The only unique quests on the top of my head are: The kid in the fridge, Human error, Long time coming (Only because it reveals interesting information about a companion character) The secret of the cabot house, and Last voyage of the USS consitution. All the other side quests I've done feel really uninspired and lackluster. However, keep in mind there are quite a few nmore quests I've read about that seem great, but I haven't done. The side quests feel more "Quantity over quality"
