First Fallout game I ever played. TL;DR - between 5/10 and 7/10. Maybe. RPG needs more RP.
In terms of game mechanics, the VATS system and shooting is probably the best of all 3 of the newer Fallout games. Settlement building is good fun for people who enjoy playing The Sims: Apocalypse, though the radiant quests will be as annoying as they were in Skyrim.
The world itself is more colourful than the previous 2, but does feel empty. Bethesda tends to create lots of types of things and use that to fill your world rather than create lots of storylines branching out that fill your world. As an example, there are 5 different variants of each enemy, at least, but don't expect huge amounts of depth to any of them. They're there to be shot.
There's no karma system, which means that your nasty actions have no effect unless you've got a morally good companion with you. This is probably what is the cause of some of the shallow story. Your actions don't matter, whereas in order to inject some realism and actual investment in the story, your character needs to feel the trouble they might start or enjoy the worship they receive by being Wasteland Jesus.
Also, height scaling? Lots of people are the same height. Not great.
Now onto the story.
It's not as deep as it could be. Pretty straight-forward - you play the avenging Mother/Father of a kidnapped son and a murdered spouse, recently freed from a cryo facility where you've been on ice for 210 years, ever since the bombs dropped on October 22nd, 2077. You hunt down your son and join 4 different factions, but the end result is mostly the same regardless of who you choose.
SPOILERS BELOW
The death of your spouse and your relationship with your son feels very ham-fisted, and you're not given an opportunity to really care about either of them.
3 of the four factions end up with the same result - Institute is destroyed, there's a big ol' radioactive chunk of Boston close to where people, oh, I dunno, *actually live* (which in terms of in-game consequences is never mentioned or considered to be an issue - 'why's everyone turning into ghouls Maureen?' asks one resident of Diamond City. 'Oh well they nuked the Institute so now we just have to deal with the nuclear fallout Jessie, no big deal,' her friend replies.)
FACTIONS
Institute - your typical amoral science nerds in a shiny chrome bunker who think they're saving the world. They make synths, synthetic humans, whom they treat like nonhuman robots. Very clearly set up to be the bad guys you end up nuking. Would have liked to see more reasons to spare them, perhaps more ways in which they genuinely believe they're helping the surface world. Basically, my son runs these guys, that's my son, y'know, the main drive of the Sole Survivor. Brian Delaney and Courtenay Taylor are excellent voice actors and deliver their emotional lines with great punch, but it feels hollow without giving the gamer a proper chance to bond. 5/10.
Railroad - cool spies who help out their robot buddies. Actually quite enjoyable and in fact written as slightly more ambiguous and morally grey than maybe they were planned? Particularly Desdemona's staunch refusal to work with you after a certain point until you're competely in with them and swear to forego using the other factions to take out the Institute. Could still use more bonding time with them, though. Particularly after the Nuclear Option, where they mention dead characters - would've been nice to see them honouring people more. 8/10.
Brotherhood of Steel - they're the East Coast but they're not Lyons' East Coast, though they're less conservative than the West Coast. Picture a mix of the two. Still mostly filled with giant bags of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though the lil' squires are quite sweet and if you get attached to kids, makes it difficult to blow their flying ship out of the air. Led by Arthur Maxson (phwoar - excuse me,) they're great for a free set of T-60 and a vertibird for flying in style. Hostile as ever to ghouls and super mutants, and now synths. Personally had many idealogical conflicts with them but (as I said, RPG needs more RP) conflicting with them won't get you punished or at the most extreme kicked out of the Brotherhood. You gotta go full Institute/Railroad for that. 6/10, but bump it up to 7/10 just because they wear these form-fittign jumpsuits that are really nice around the butt. (Maxson, rawr.)
Minutemen - generally considered the good guys, join the Minutemen if you want endless radiant quests of 'DEFEND X SETTLEMENT'. My favourite faction simply because I have mods that stop settlement attacks, they're not as xenophobic as the BOS or as synth-mad as the Railroad. Also, Preston Garvey is a literal angel despite the constant radiant quest-giving, can be romanced, interesting back-story and always happy to help people, 10/10 loveliest NPC ever.
DLCs
Fallout 4 has 6 DLCs, two and a half have an actual plotline, the other 3.5 are alllllll about the settlements, people. I personally rate 8/10 because I like building, but as content goes, 6/10 just because of how little extra story we get.
Automatron - You hunt down the Mechanist, get a sweet new robot buddy, and can build robots. 6/10 because the RobCo sales and service centre provides more interesting 'Pre War government was AWFUL' material, and the main villain has a twist, but other than that it's mostly just modifying robots.
Far Harbour - Probably the best of them all. Bethesda seems to like DLCs where you end up on a mysterious island (see Bloodmoon, Shivering Isles, Dragonborn.) Whole place is covered in fog, and there are 3 factions again. Some of your choices matter here, but still not enough to feel like your character is actually part of this world. You've got the synths, the town of Far Harbour, and the Children of Atom. The synths are actually one of the better written factions - they seem at first glance to be a haven for synthetics, but their leader is more neutral good/neutral and 'end justifies the means'. The Children of Atom are quite nutty, but have some enjoyable quests. Far Harbor is pretty much 'everyone in this town is drunk and probably stinks of fish.' Not horrible people, but certainly hardened. 7/10-8/10 but Bethesda copies an entire quest from a New Vegas mod.
Wasteland Workshops - just adds♥♥♥♥♥♥to build with. Useful. Not really able to rate because I like building and I'm biased.
Vault-Tec - you too can be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ living in your own Vault experimenting on your dwellers. 4/10, lots of stuff to build but can only do so in one location, also there's a ♥♥♥♥ing Mirelurk Queen in this cave, bruh.
Nuka-World - had lots of promise but sadly very, very shallow. You turn up at Nuka World, there's now like a billion variants of Nuka Cola, everyone's awful, you're the boss now. And even if you choose to murder every raider in the park, it's left completely empty and you can't do anything with it. 6/10, interesting location and some new enemies, but doesn't really offer anything and it's like, covered in trash and gore. You can't clean it up either.

Played it and finished every major quest and side quest I cam across.  Was thoroughly disappointed when comparing it to Fallout: New Vegas and even Fallout 3. RPG elements are stripped back to a bare minimum, allows for next to no min-maxing and very little general customisation.  The "characters" you meet are almost all 2 dimensional or just not really characters at all with one or two exceptions. Graphically it looks fairly terrible with everything maxed out in terms of both texture quality and aesthetic. The colour palette is boring and drab but it lacks some of the interesting landmark features included in 3 and NV which make those games at least a little interesting visually. The story was boring and predictable. It actually has a couple of interesting story beats near the beginning with Nick Valentine but quickly goes downhill with no sign of stopping.  They seemingly went for a similar story climax/choice as New Vegas which elected to essentially let you choose between different political ideologies, none of them being particularly "evil" or "good" depending on your perspective, but Fallout 4 misses the point completeley and has 2 obviously "evil" choices and 2 obviously "good" choices with very little incetive to choose any of them over the other aside from if you want to be a boogie man or a saint.  It's also full of bugs, I repeatedly experienced crashes on the lengthy loading screens and had NPC pathing and textures completely bug out.  The radient quests and side quests are boring busywork that are worth doing once to see what they are (usually go to a location and kill some raiders/mutants) and then they just repeat in different locations displaying a stunning lack of good quest design.  The settlement system and base building is clunky, poorly implemented and completely superfluous. Again it amounts to little more than busywork to soak up time doing essentially nothing of value from a gameplay/story standpoint.
The gunplay is somewhat better than the prior games though so I guess there's that.

With Fallout 4, comes a myriad of changes, improvements and disappointments. You can now build and improvement settlements. (Which is further expanded upon by the Wasteland, Contraptions and Vault Tec Workshop DLCs.) The combat system has been greatly improved since Fallout 3. With weapon mods in-game, weapons can be improved further with different aspects. You can even build your own robot companions with the Automatron DLC.
The RPG aspect of the franchise has been further diminished. Do not expect Obsidian's Entertainment's approach to Fallout: New Vegas. Your choices have been even more inconsequential and characters more forgettable. Companions are a burden in combat(especially when you're playing a stealth character) and the game does not give you any reason to care about them.
However, that does not make this game any less fun. You'll often find yourself spending far too much time decorating your settlements or experimenting with your settlers. Ultimately, Fallout 4 is definitely a far better game than Fallout 3 and you'll have fun with it.
So yes, I recommend this game(with the DLCs).

A very satisfying and content filled open world action game with base RPG elements. If you want an RPG, start with Fallout: New Vegas instead of 4. 4 does a very good job of capturing a setting, an atmosphere, and an ambience very much like other open world action games such as S.T.A.L.K.E.R., where choice and dialog are a factor in the gameplay - but serve more as a storytelling medium than an actual RPG where you feel more in control, and like your decisions matter. Not that the decisions you make in this game don't matter- there are a lot, actually. And they have dramatic effects on the gameplay and world as well. Characters and you have relationships. But they don't feel the same as in a well written, purpose built RPG like New Vegas that puts story/RPG elements first, and gameplay/content second. Fallout 4 does the opposite. But nonetheless- I have only spent 400 or so hours on one character, one playthrough. I could do it all again, and completely different, and spend another 400 hours discovering new things. It really is a lot. This game honestly goes toe to toe with Skyrim in terms of content and replayability.

Dark Souls 3 is very much like previous entries of the Dark Souls series. The graphics are beautiful leaving me in awe on the first minutes of the game. While the game had some performance problems the first weeks they were later alleviated with patches making the performance on this game fantastic. The combat is fluid, the design of everything is breathtaking and the music is fantastic. There are a lot of weapons to use, diverse builds that you can create to change your playstyle, stat and resetting for trying something different. There is of course as every other Dark Souls game also multiplayer. You can read messages left by other players to aid you on your quest, you can coop with two or three other players and you can invade or be invaded by other players for player versus player.
As for the cons. The lack of covenant variety is sad and some covenants plain don't work correctly. There could had been some great stuff that could had been included on the covenants but given what is in the game the only ones who get constant activity are the pvp invasion covenants and the coop covenants. The covenants that rely on being summoned into a faction area almost never work and for some reason some players get summoned more than other players.
While PvP Arenas are finally in the game via it's first dlc I believe it's something that should had been on the base game. Regardless even with it's cons the game is still fantastic and I would greatly recommend it.

Fallout 4 is not the perfect Fallout game many hardcore Fallout fans such as myself expected. However it is not the awful game I believe so many are making it out to be. The games story was pretty good but it could of been improved upon. Outside of the main story there is not many sidequests, and the few side quests there are, are very similar. Most of the side quests are just go here, clear out all the enemies, come back to me and recieve a reward. The side quests are still enjoyable but few have RPG elements that Fallout is known for. Things like the perk system, the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, and the voiced protagonist take away some of the beloved RPG mechanics in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. For what Fallout 4 didn't do as well as the previous games, it fixed a lot of other problems that Fallout 3 and New Vegas had. The core gameplay is very smooth and feels really nice and easy to use. Another thing that this game does phenomenally well is the atmosphere. Bethesda nailed it when it came to making you feel as if you were in post nuclear Boston. Overall the game is a great game that has its flaws. I would recommend this to any Fallout fan, or just to anyone who wants a great Action/Adventure game. Fallout 4 is just not the greatest RPG and is a big divergent from the previous 2 games. But it still stands as good game on it's own.

If you like Terraria, an endless(almost) universe, building, boss fights, space and exploration all in 2d pixel art, this game might be for you.

I'm not exactly sure how to describe Starbound. The simplest way would be to say Terraria in Space, but that just doesn't do it justice. First let me say that Starbound is good, I just want to clarify that. However it may be the kind of game that takes a bit of getting used to and really learning how the mechanics work before really being able to play. Don't let that scare you off though, it's not that hard, It's just that I can see some people getting stuck at certain parts. My best advice would be, Follow the quests, and check the outpost whenever you don't have a quest.
Pros:
- Runs fairly well (with minor exceptions here or there)
- Similar in style and feel to Terraria
- Intersting characters/story/lore
- Lots of item variety
- Lots of decorative items
- Very fair game balancing
- Procedurally generated universe/weapons/creatures
Cons:
- Occasional hiccup in performance
- Potentially confusing at times for new players
- Sort of linear in terms of questing
I certainly feel that Starbound is well worth the money, however I can imagine certain people not enjoying the game as it's a little bit of an acquired taste. Again, not to say it's bad in any way shape or form, it's just... unique in a lot of ways that some players simply might not be used to. My point is, Yes, buy the game, just do it. JUST, DO IT.

I want to say, I dont really give this game a negative. Its just another case of Steam needing a "Maybe" or "In-Between Button".
I am a massive Fallout fan. Hell, the Complete Fallout Collection was the second thing I ever bought on Steam. Fallout 1, 2, and New Vegas are some of the best games Ive ever played. I thought 3 was a good game, it just wasnt my taste. We dont talk about the Brotherhood games, okay?
Anyway, point is, Fallout is my jam. I was there for Survivor2299, I was there for the countdown, I was there yadda yadda. I just...cant feel this is a good Fallout game. Its a fun game, the gunplay is awesome, the world feels fairly lived in, the balance is pretty good. The settlement mechanics were alright, could be better but I enjoy stuff like that. Power armor was cool, a mechanic I think they should keep in later Fallout games.
But at the same time, I feel spoiled by Fallout NV. Oh yeah, yeah, dismiss it as NV wank, but I truly feel NV is the best Fallout. Thats a discussion for another time, however. New Vegas had consequences. Thats what really lacked in Fallout 4. Your actions meant nothing unless it directly affected you, i.e giving you new armor or a companion. In NV, there were actual consequences on the world. That brings me to my second point: your character. I dont mind the voiced protagonist, except for the fact it destroyed any semblance of RPG dialogue. Bethesda either didnt care enough, or was forced to, only have 4 ♥♥♥♥ing dialogue options.
Oh boy, the dialogue. It can be:
-Yes (Accept Quest)
-No (Accept Quest)
-Later (Accept Quest Later)
-Sarcastic (50/50 Chance to Accept Quest)
The dialogue is nothing more than "I accept the quests." Theres no conversation. Theres nothing but quest dialogue. In every Fallout before this (Brotherhood games are not fallout!) you could talk to NPCs. Many didnt even give quests: they were simply there to talk. That was the beauty of it. Thats what made it feel alive. There wasnt just "One quest giver plus 2 generic NPCs." The one exception I would like to point out is Companions. Companions in this game are ♥♥♥♥ing great, but many feel Fallout is a companion-less experience (I disagree though).
This really went on too long. I just..I just feel cheated a bit. Ive always supported Bethesda, and Ive always loved Fallout. It just that they removed the RP from my RPG.

Not that the decisions you make in this game don't matter- there are a lot, actually. And they have dramatic effects on the gameplay and world as well. Characters and you have relationships. For the third and final Dark Souls game, there are some really worrying issues. I still love DSIII but will start off with the problems cos there are so many.
- Enemies have a tendency to sometimes get stuck inside the architecture, fall through floors/ceilings, and if you rotate the camera, some enemies will teleport or have their animations cancelled. Dogs and Silver Knights are the best examples but it happens with other mobs too.
- Walls don't seem to be as solid as they appear, since there are times where I have been shot with arrows/bolts through the bricks and buildings I was using as cover. One enemy type just shoots pyro's
buildings.
- It is possible to kill enemies that spawn only once which have a guaranteed drop of a ring or some such item, only to get summoned to someone else's world at the exact moment of killing it. When returning after the summon, the item is not there and the non-respawning enemy is nowhere to be seen. In essence it is possible to lose items in a playthrough and have to go to the next cycle to obtain it.
- It's possible to get cornered by an enemy and try to roll out of the corner through what appears to be empty space, yet the enemy's hitbox prevents you from rolling out. Since every mob in the game has chain-attacks of up to 5 or 6 with minimal cooldown this is really frustrating as once you are trapped by an invisible barrier, you quickly get stunlocked to death.
- I died a few seconds before a cutscene, but the cutscene played anyway, and warped me to an at the time unfamiliar location (since it was my first playthrough) and that location was where the game decided I actually died. But I respawned at my previous bonfire with no way of knowing where to go to recover my souls...
- My souls have dropped in places that should be impossible (in the Nameless King boss arena).
- Desync in co-op/pvp is a fairly big issue. As a phantom I can't traverse the boss fog to help the host at least 15% of the time, character models of other players frequently get frozen and they just glide along stuck in a pose, and sometimes it takes a minute or two for invaders to sync to the host.
They've had almost a year to patch things up and the game still feels like it lacks polish in many areas.
In terms of how the game's combat plays out, it feels like DS1 - which is to say it feels like a bit of a step backwards compared to DS2.
Attack cancelling should have been kept considering how much faster paced the enemy and boss encounters are. Left hand movesets are back to DS1's days of being less functional than they should be - which really makes you wonder why From expects everyone to play as a right-handed character.
Weapon upgrade restrictions mean that if you do low SL runs with high-upgraded weapons, your character won't be able to co-op with other randoms. Password system means that if people weren't twinking in DS1 or 2, they probably are now.
In many of ways almost feels like a re-imagining of, and a love-letter to the first game. The atmosphere is amazingly tense throughout and the sense of achievement when you fell a difficult boss is tremendous.
Boss movesets are significantly more complex than the bosses of old, leaving few openings to attack and attacking much more aggressively than ever before.
The various mobs are fearsome - some even horrifying, and each different environment you travel to feels like even your surrounds are out to get you.
Oh, and the world is just stunning to look at. Lothric is a place of decaying beauty and it's easy to get lost in the majestic vistas you will journey through. From a decaying castle with towering cathedrals, to an icy city of cathedrals, to a deep, epicly huge chapel, and... yea there's lots of cathedrals but it's all total eye candy.
The length of the campaign is perfect. Not too overlong, but it's by no means something you'll knock off in 20 or even 30 hours on your first blind playthrough.

Ok, so with a little over 10 hours of game play I thought I'll give this game a review. Please take this review from a person that has no prior experience with Terraria or any other sandbox adventure game. I come from a long history of first person shooters and got this game just to try something different. And boy am I glad I did! I really liked the game right from the start. But it was not until a few hours of game play, that I fell in love with this game. This game is incredibly well made and the amount of content that it currently has is just out of proportion. From a price stand point, you really get your money's worth and much much more. The music is so beautiful and unbelievably relaxing that I keep finding myself falling asleep when I play the game. Not because is boring, is just because I am able to relax to the point where my body just wants to give in. I highly recommend the Starbound soundtrack as well. It has 60 songs!
It is important to note that Starbound is a gem still in the making. However, the amount of content currently in game is well over what many other early access games out there have to offer. You can literally dig yourself into great discoveries. You can build, you can farm, you can craft, you can hunt, you can literally do anything you want. Don't really like the planet you are in? No problem! In Starbound you can collect fuel for your mighty spaceship, fire up the engines and just head to the next moon or planet available. The game mechanics are great, the graphics are stunning, and there is a interesting storyline to follow.
I value games for what they have to offer, but I value them even more for the amount of hours I can get out of them. If you go out and pay over $20 to watch a movie for 2-3 hours of entertainment, then 14.99 doesn't seem so bad considering the well over 100 hours you can easily get from this early accesses game. That's what I call valuable entertainment.
In conclusion, if you are looking for something different like me and you want to make sure that you get your money's worth, get this game! See you in the Starbound Universe ;)

Ok, so with a little over 10 hours of game play I thought I'll give this game a review. Please take this review from a person that has no prior experience with Terraria or any other sandbox adventure game. I come from a long history of first person shooters and got this game just to try something different. And boy am I glad I did! I really liked the game right from the start. But it was not until a few hours of game play, that I fell in love with this game. This game is incredibly well made and the amount of content that it currently has is just out of proportion. From a price stand point, you really get your money's worth and much much more. The music is so beautiful and unbelievably relaxing that I keep finding myself falling asleep when I play the game. Not because is boring, is just because I am able to relax to the point where my body just wants to give in. I highly recommend the Starbound soundtrack as well. It has 60 songs!
It is important to note that Starbound is a gem still in the making. However, the amount of content currently in game is well over what many other early access games out there have to offer. You can literally dig yourself into great discoveries. You can build, you can farm, you can craft, you can hunt, you can literally do anything you want. Don't really like the planet you are in? No problem! In Starbound you can collect fuel for your mighty spaceship, fire up the engines and just head to the next moon or planet available. The game mechanics are great, the graphics are stunning, and there is a interesting storyline to follow.
I value games for what they have to offer, but I value them even more for the amount of hours I can get out of them. If you go out and pay over $20 to watch a movie for 2-3 hours of entertainment, then 14.99 doesn't seem so bad considering the well over 100 hours you can easily get from this early accesses game. That's what I call valuable entertainment.
In conclusion, if you are looking for something different like me and you want to make sure that you get your money's worth, get this game! See you in the Starbound Universe ;)

As the final episode in the Dark Souls series (if not the Souls franchise), this game may have had some shortcomings, but was otherwise a satisfying piece of art that enticed me in the world throughout the hours of bittersweet adventure that felt all too reminiscent to its predecessors.
While staying true to its notorious combat mechanics, it implemented weapon arts unique to each class of weapon, as well as having variants within the classes. The weapon arts provided great utility in both PvE and PvP in addition to a visually appealing approach to defeat formidable enemies. The arsenal of weapons and spells available in each class was fairly abundant, which also included notable weapons from previous games that emphasised on the connection between this world and the one we once trod. This made experimenting with unique builds a lot more fruitful - along with silly cosplays. The amount of spells that can be used per bonfire run was replaced by a Focus bar, which in my opinion was an excellent change for mage builds.
The world design was impeccable at the fact that it reflected on the exponentially decaying nature of the exhausted realm and the fading Fire with great precision. Attention to both subtle and intricate details, coupled with the prolific graphics of the engine together did an amazing job in portraying a dying world with such vibrant appeal. Certain aspects of locations - be it landscape, architecture, NPCs, loot or even the location as a whole - have been borrowed from the previous games, among which Anor Londo seemed to be the most obvious. While it was annoying to notice how particular compartments damaged in previous games looked good as new (one ought to wonder who would fix that broken window with the Dragon Greatbow loot from Dark Souls while not giving a second thought to the desecrated hall beneath Gwynevere's bedchamber), and the repetation may have become mundane at one point, reliving the moments alone was an astounding experience. Often times, discovering particular elements that would reflect upon the events of the first game in said location would be all the more rewarding throughout the exploration.
Knowing Souls games, they never tell you the entire story. Instead, they let you figure things out through flavour texts, use your own imagination to analyse and come to a conclusion. That is what makes the franchise a pinnacle of storytelling in video games. Hidetaka Miyazaki did not fail to surprise yet again with the grotesque and abominable boss designs, and their places in the game's complex lore. The thematic soundtracks made each bossfight feel all the more exhilarating. Needless to say, the game still held its reputation for difficulty throughout majority of the runs and bossfights. The constant invasions and abundant co-op opportunities, along with the covenant interactions, amplified the experience further when playing online.
Even so, the game had its share of shortcomings. Not all weapon classes were shown justice. While some lacked versatality or simply failed to scale properly at later stages of the game, others were overpowered and downright silly. As was the case in previous games, bows still required more attention. Hexes were removed and instead merged with Sorceries, Pyromancies and Miracles bit by bit. Despite the vast choice of weapons and spells, some would dominate well above the others, restricting the PvP meta to a very short set of gear and magic.
When it comes to wearable equipment, heavy armour was drastically undermined. The seemingly useless poise mechanic, coupled with the insignificance of high absorption, limited the choice of armour to the lighter tier. This made investing points in Vitality almost completely fruitless. The absence of poise resulted in the shorter, faster weapons winning over tanks with mere pokes. While this approach to combat prevented the advent of giantdads, it tipped the scales a bit too much to the lighter class. That said, wearing lighter gear did not reward one with any unique bonuses either - the lack of versatility of armour mechanics, coupled with discrimination to the heavy tier, brewed a disaster in the game's PvP meta (RIP Havelyns though).
Covenant interactions seemed creative on paper, but the way these mechanics complemented themselves as a whole caused Covenant preferences to converge, limiting to a handful. One would have to wait several minutes to even hours of queue time before being summoned as a Watchdog of Farron, Blue Sentinel or Darkmoon Blade, whereas it would take seconds or minutes at most to be summoned as an Aldrich Faithful.
The verdict: A fruitful piece of art, albeit imperfect, worth every dollar and hour spent with a promising 2000+ hours of gameplay content. Minor changes in gameplay mechanics relative to previous installments may feel underwhelming, but the added content is bound to compensate for that. Dark Souls III is a game worth playing to have one last taste of the brutal yet nostalgic world of Souls before transcending to what Miyazaki envisions to be a "vital turning point" in the series.

Dark souls 3 is a perfect game for anyone who's up for a challenge. A real challenge.
Other games hold your hand through them and guides you, what dark souls does is something else. They give you some♥♥♥♥♥♥ throw you in a pithole and then leave you there to handle things on your own.
Dark souls have always had varying and beatiful environment and this game nails it. The lightning is good, the surroundings look good, the sounds are amazing! And the soundtrack. The soundtrack is fkn amazing!
Many different weapons, all kinds of weird♥♥♥♥♥♥like dual-wielding two hammers who's bigger than yourself. All the weapons are incredibly good designed and looks astonishing! The animations are really smooth and look very real.
The PvE in this game is amazing! The bosses are really cool and some are really REALLY hard and some are actually dissapointingly easy. They are all very different frome one another. The amount of bosses isn't that much, Dark souls 2 have MUCH more bosses, but dark souls 3 is more like quality over quantity which I prefer.
The voice acting is good. It's nothing impressive but they keep to the dark theme which just fits perfectly.
And then there's PvP... I love it. PvP is the only thing I do now in the game now that I've completed the game two times. PvP has its ups and downs. What makes pvp slightly bad in this game is not the pvp itself, but the players. The constant ganking. When I invade a world I'm aware that it should be a hard time for me to beat the host, but not like this. When 4 people just hide and wait for an invader to invade and then gank the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him, that destroys the purpose to invade. Thanks to this I never ever invade anymore since it's hopeless 'cause the game priorities the hosts with friends so there will almost allways be 2v1, 3v1, 4v1. In some very few cases I invaded a lone host which turned out to be really fun, but that only happened 3-4 times under my entire experience with ds3. But, there's an amazing side to the PvP, and that is the fight clubs. In some areas it's very popular to set up fightclubs, where the host watches and summons people to the fightclub where you fight other players in a duel. Duels have community-made rules which I love! This is what makes PvP viable! Even if I suck at PvP, I cant stop playing it!
And if you have the new DLC, there is a matchmaking system for the PvP which is amazing! You can search for duels, 2v2, 3v3, 2 player brawl, 4 player brawl or 6 player brawl! This makes PvP even more fun! The sad thing is, that there is no rewards, not even some souls. But it still is the most fun I have in this game!
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Without a doubt, yes. This game will offer you something very unique unlike any other game you've played before.

Fallout 4 is not the perfect Fallout game many hardcore Fallout fans such as myself expected. However it is not the awful game I believe so many are making it out to be. The games story was pretty good but it could of been improved upon. Outside of the main story there is not many sidequests, and the few side quests there are, are very similar. Most of the side quests are just go here, clear out all the enemies, come back to me and recieve a reward. The side quests are still enjoyable but few have RPG elements that Fallout is known for. Things like the perk system, the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, and the voiced protagonist take away some of the beloved RPG mechanics in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. For what Fallout 4 didn't do as well as the previous games, it fixed a lot of other problems that Fallout 3 and New Vegas had. The core gameplay is very smooth and feels really nice and easy to use. Another thing that this game does phenomenally well is the atmosphere. Bethesda nailed it when it came to making you feel as if you were in post nuclear Boston. Overall the game is a great game that has its flaws. I would recommend this to any Fallout fan, or just to anyone who wants a great Action/Adventure game. Fallout 4 is just not the greatest RPG and is a big divergent from the previous 2 games. But it still stands as good game on it's own.

Often times, discovering particular elements that would reflect upon the events of the first game in said location would be all the more rewarding throughout the exploration.
Knowing Souls games, they never tell you the entire story. Instead, they let you figure things out through flavour texts, use your own imagination to analyse and come to a conclusion. That is what makes the franchise a pinnacle of storytelling in video games. Hidetaka Miyazaki did not fail to surprise yet again with the grotesque and abominable boss designs, and their places in the game's complex lore. The thematic soundtracks made each bossfight feel all the more exhilarating. Needless to say, the game still held its reputation for difficulty throughout majority of the runs and bossfights. The constant invasions and abundant co-op opportunities, along with the covenant interactions, amplified the experience further when playing online.
Even so, the game had its share of shortcomings. Not all weapon classes were shown justice. While some lacked versatality or simply failed to scale properly at later stages of the game, others were overpowered and downright silly. As was the case in previous games, bows still required more attention. Hexes were removed and instead merged with Sorceries, Pyromancies and Miracles bit by bit. Despite the vast choice of weapons and spells, some would dominate well above the others, restricting the PvP meta to a very short set of gear and magic.
When it comes to wearable equipment, heavy armour was drastically undermined. The seemingly useless poise mechanic, coupled with the insignificance of high absorption, limited the choice of armour to the lighter tier. This made investing points in Vitality almost completely fruitless. The absence of poise resulted in the shorter, faster weapons winning over tanks with mere pokes. While this approach to combat prevented the advent of giantdads, it tipped the scales a bit too much to the lighter class. That said, wearing lighter gear did not reward one with any unique bonuses either - the lack of versatility of armour mechanics, coupled with discrimination to the heavy tier, brewed a disaster in the game's PvP meta (RIP Havelyns though).
Covenant interactions seemed creative on paper, but the way these mechanics complemented themselves as a whole caused Covenant preferences to converge, limiting to a handful. One would have to wait several minutes to even hours of queue time before being summoned as a Watchdog of Farron, Blue Sentinel or Darkmoon Blade, whereas it would take seconds or minutes at most to be summoned as an Aldrich Faithful.
The verdict: A fruitful piece of art, albeit imperfect, worth every dollar and hour spent with a promising 2000+ hours of gameplay content. Minor changes in gameplay mechanics relative to previous installments may feel underwhelming, but the added content is bound to compensate for that. Dark Souls III is a game worth playing to have one last taste of the brutal yet nostalgic world of Souls before transcending to what Miyazaki envisions to be a "vital turning point" in the series.

For the third and final Dark Souls game, there are some really worrying issues. I still love DSIII but will start off with the problems cos there are so many.
- Enemies have a tendency to sometimes get stuck inside the architecture, fall through floors/ceilings, and if you rotate the camera, some enemies will teleport or have their animations cancelled. Dogs and Silver Knights are the best examples but it happens with other mobs too.
- Walls don't seem to be as solid as they appear, since there are times where I have been shot with arrows/bolts through the bricks and buildings I was using as cover. One enemy type just shoots pyro's
buildings.
- It is possible to kill enemies that spawn only once which have a guaranteed drop of a ring or some such item, only to get summoned to someone else's world at the exact moment of killing it. When returning after the summon, the item is not there and the non-respawning enemy is nowhere to be seen. In essence it is possible to lose items in a playthrough and have to go to the next cycle to obtain it.
- It's possible to get cornered by an enemy and try to roll out of the corner through what appears to be empty space, yet the enemy's hitbox prevents you from rolling out. Since every mob in the game has chain-attacks of up to 5 or 6 with minimal cooldown this is really frustrating as once you are trapped by an invisible barrier, you quickly get stunlocked to death.
- I died a few seconds before a cutscene, but the cutscene played anyway, and warped me to an at the time unfamiliar location (since it was my first playthrough) and that location was where the game decided I actually died. But I respawned at my previous bonfire with no way of knowing where to go to recover my souls...
- My souls have dropped in places that should be impossible (in the Nameless King boss arena).
- Desync in co-op/pvp is a fairly big issue. As a phantom I can't traverse the boss fog to help the host at least 15% of the time, character models of other players frequently get frozen and they just glide along stuck in a pose, and sometimes it takes a minute or two for invaders to sync to the host.
They've had almost a year to patch things up and the game still feels like it lacks polish in many areas.
In terms of how the game's combat plays out, it feels like DS1 - which is to say it feels like a bit of a step backwards compared to DS2.
Attack cancelling should have been kept considering how much faster paced the enemy and boss encounters are. Left hand movesets are back to DS1's days of being less functional than they should be - which really makes you wonder why From expects everyone to play as a right-handed character.
Weapon upgrade restrictions mean that if you do low SL runs with high-upgraded weapons, your character won't be able to co-op with other randoms. Password system means that if people weren't twinking in DS1 or 2, they probably are now.
In many of ways almost feels like a re-imagining of, and a love-letter to the first game. The atmosphere is amazingly tense throughout and the sense of achievement when you fell a difficult boss is tremendous.
Boss movesets are significantly more complex than the bosses of old, leaving few openings to attack and attacking much more aggressively than ever before.
The various mobs are fearsome - some even horrifying, and each different environment you travel to feels like even your surrounds are out to get you.
Oh, and the world is just stunning to look at. Lothric is a place of decaying beauty and it's easy to get lost in the majestic vistas you will journey through. From a decaying castle with towering cathedrals, to an icy city of cathedrals, to a deep, epicly huge chapel, and... yea there's lots of cathedrals but it's all total eye candy.
The length of the campaign is perfect. Not too overlong, but it's by no means something you'll knock off in 20 or even 30 hours on your first blind playthrough.

I've spent about 30 hours playing this game the last few weeks, and I'm finding myself incredibly addicted.  Here are a few pros/cons:
Pros:
-If you liked the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, game play is really similar in the regard of completing various quests while avoiding dangerous mutants and situations while collecting and upgrading weapons and clothes/armor.  Where Fallout 4 surpasses STALKER is in the sheer size of the environment (no surprise since it's a much newer game), and you have the ability to create things by scrapping out the junk that you find in your quests.
-The amount of armor and weapon combinations and customizations is enormous.
-You can choose to play as someone who wants to help others, or you can play only for yourself...it's your call, and there's no right or wrong way to play.
-Through the perk system, you have the ability to improve your personal capabilities (lock picking ability, strength, etc.) as you level-up.
Cons:
-As of December of 2016, the price of Fallout 4 is still $59.99.  You can buy this game much cheaper elsewhere.  That being said, having the game part of your Steam library affords you the ability to download the software rather than keep disks around.
-You will be spending many, many hours playing this game.  You'll be trying to spend more and more time improving your armor, collecting gear, and finishing quests.  If you don't have a significant other who is cool with that, you're going to have a problem.  My wife has mentioned how much I've been playing, but she's been pretty cool about it so far.
-There are almost too many quests and deviations.  You'll be trying to complete a quest, and you'll end up with two or three more things on your list.  If you're a "cross it off your list" person, it will drive you nuts.
Overall, two thumbs up.  I just hope I can finish the game before my wife serves me divorce papers!

Let me start off by saying that the PvE in this game was excellent.  It was a significant improvement over Dark Souls 2 and I enjoyed most of it.  My issue with the game comes from the fact that poise does not function as it did in either of the last two games.  This wasn't much of a problem in the PvE (except for the small enemy gank/spam fests that seem to occur, especially with rats) but it really hurts the PvP aspect of the game.  If you don't really care about PvP then you can stop reading here but if you do care about the PvP you might want to keep reading.
I feel like a good 70% of my issues with PvP could be solved by making poise work like it did in Dark Souls 1 and 2 (though maybe to a greater/lesser extent depending on balancing).  My experience was that most people just spam R1 with things like Estoc or Dark Sword.  Bleed builds are also pretty annoying.  These two things in particular wouldn't be so bad if you could poise through it.  I primarily played on a quality build.  I tried to use several weapons but would default to the Profaned Greatsword a lot of the time for the hyper armor and because the 2H R1 can't be parried.
A couple other things that didn't bother me too much but might bother others a lot:
1) If you invade someone you almost always end up fighting 2 or more people
2) Casters are harder to play as because the stat and gear investment is pretty high.  I don't see too many in PvP and I think it's because of one of those reasons.

I jumped into this straight from Dark Souls 1 because I heard that it has a lot more to do with that than 2.
I haven't played 2 or Bloodborne even, but if 2's supposed to have more artificial difficulty and if Bloodborne is much faster & more dodge-focused then 3 sounds like a cakewalk in comparison. Bloodborne isn't technically a Souls game but looking at the gameplay it really may as well be with just a few different mechanics and name changes.
Playing with a KB+M is very possible but the game's interface is very heavily designed towards playing with a controller as usual. You can at least play with both KB+M and a controller simultaneously if you feel the desire to switch it up.
The plot's straightforward; slay the mentioned names and link the fire, again, at least if you want to. The lore's big and learned through reading item descriptions as usual and of course you can piece together certain events that have happened by reading the lore and following some things you see in the environment.
The scenery in the series has always been neat to look at. A lot of areas you see in the distance tend to be places you've just walked on or will walk on which is always a neat way to show how sizable the world is. Unlike Dark Souls 1 though the world's a lot more linear and fewer maps are connected to one another. From beginning to end it feels more like I'm walking through a tunnel with only a few side-paths here and there. The level designs are pretty alright & can get clever as well as the shortcuts & contraptions. Because of linearity however the shortcuts are only really useful for the current area which is basically until you beat the area boss. By then you've already moved on to the next map so the only good reasons usually to go back to a particular map is to invade, be summoned for co-op, and look for possibly missed loot.
I also think that there are way too many bonfires this time around, especially when bosses always spawn a bonfire after they've been defeated, too. It could be that it only looks that way to me due to how linear this game started to look. Some bonfire placements hardly make any sense. An example of this is where late in the game you beat a certain boss, it spawns the obligatory bonfire, but moving forward 20 steps or so there's another bonfire with not even an enemy in between making the one you took 20 steps for practically pointless.
Only a little after the very first boss fight of the game you end up in a new Firelink Shrine which is now Demon's-Souls-esque hub of sorts where practically all the NPCS you meet in your journey end up if you allow them. I personally don't find most of the NPCs interesting and only a few really have any actual quests on 'em. Some of the NPC's quests are so specific that you'll most likely need a wiki or guide to complete them properly. It doesn't help either that some quests can abruptly end another without notice.
Instead of the mechanic being a reward for going through a tough journey, you gain the ability to warp between bonfires practically as soon as you light the bonfire in Firelink. It makes the game look a lot smaller than it is but it's at least convenient.
The gameplay's more focused on speed when it comes to attacking and avoiding damage even though the mechanics don't exactly suggest that.
The game has a habit of throwing hordes of enemies at you and a lot of 'em can do frantic combos too making encounters like that more annoying than difficult, almost encouraging you to cheese through some areas through unconventional means. The beefier 1-on-1 focused mob enemies are a lot less stressful to try to beat. They can be crazy tough and tend to have an attack for almost wherever you go but they're a lot more fair to try and deal with so long as no other force joins in to harm you. The same goes for the bosses (save for 1 or 2 where a clone-esque enemy spawns).
Mechanically I think practically all the bosses are designed pretty well, at least when faced alone. Plenty of them are considerably easier in co-op because every boss can be easily distracted just by doing a bit of damage to 'em. Practically all bosses attack fast and do combos & attacks for all angles so you really have to pay attention to what they do. Dodging in panic can be punishing & the same goes for badly timed heals which they tend to notice if you try to heal up and by then they'll usually try to interrupt that by having some kind of gap-closing attack.
You find a weapon that best suits you, or use the right one that's best for the situation, or both.
There's a hefty variety of equipment to customize yourself with based on your current build and/or personal preference. Each weapon now has a "Weapon Art" and depending on the weapon in hand it's either going to be a self-buff or a fancy attack with some more useful than another. Weapon Art uses the new Focus Point mechanic, which can be restored via Ashen Estus Flask, which is acquired at the start of the game. For melee weapons, you need enough FP to make a Weapon Art attack effective. For self-buffs & spells, it's best to just think of FP basically as "mana".
In the games I've played in this series the only weapons I ever get truly accustomed with are large swords/greatswords, which aren't too slow and doesn't deflect from big shields when two-handed. I don't know much about other melee weapons, spells, & even the new FP mechanic as I barely use 'em.  I've also got very little experience with shield-usage or even "heavy" builds as I usually just try to dodge-roll from everything with light/semi-light armor so I don't know what to say about all that and this popular "poise" issue.
Instead of Humanity now there's Ember, which boosts your max HP by 30% and allows the usual online play of summoning someone and being invaded though you don't need an Ember yourself to be summoned.
Hollowing is a progressive matter and you can't turn hollow in this game anymore unless you go through specific actions and then die a lot. Hollowing doesn't prevent you from anything now and reversing it requires more specific actions, a little more to permanently remove the ability to be hollowed. Even then you're only able to have the ability to be hollowed once per playthrough and the only good reason for doing it is for reaching an ending.
Online play can get interesting but it can also be an absolute mess because some people's connections can be bad enough where it starts to look like they're running in place.
There's a password system but its only purpose is to match you up with others who are using the same password so you can only be summoned by them and vice versa. Normally the game matches you up with people who are in the same level range as well as have a weapon with similar upgrade ranks, regardless whether or not they're the same type, but the password system disregards all that. Whoever is summoned in that manner though will have their stats match the host's, though I'm not exactly sure how. You can still be invaded regardless whether or not a password's been set.
You can summon up to 2 co-op phantoms and be invaded by one dark phantom. With a certain item it's 3 co-op phantoms and 2 invaders. From my experience most of the people I've invaded have a phantom or two with them, making me think that the the majority of people that play this game are either bad enough to always want a partner with them and/or they've got friends to play with. Still, co-op with someone up to the boss and trying to screw someone over through invasions can be pretty fun. People complain about being interrupted from invasions but I'm pretty sure that's the point of it.
There are a lot more things I feel like saying about this game and there are likely things I missed despite 4 playthroughs.
It's not the best Souls game I think but it's still a decent one.

There is no video game without sin. I think many reviewers are forgetting that when reviewing this product. The game has it's problems but it doesn't make it a bad game. Let's sytematically anylise the goods and bads, I wouldn't want to waste your time and I certainly wouldn't want to waste mine.
Pros.
• Amazing new weapon mechaninics. Every gun, to bat, to launcher feels satisfying to shoot and swing.
• The map: It's big yet not too big. There is verity in landscapes (swamps, cities). A thing we didn't see much of in F3 and FNV.
• Some people (me included) Rather enjoy the expansiveness of the settlement feature.
• It's runs well and loading screens are non-existant (if you have an SSD.)
• The followers are deverse, interesting and all unique.
• The brotherhood are pretty neat
• Legendary items and enemies would always fill me with excitement when I came across one.
• I actually rather enjoyed a voiced protagonist.
Cons.
• Holy hell. Roleplaying and infamy is non-existant. We're forced to be a good guy. You can do bad things. But you always only get remembered as a good guy. (With the exeption to Nuka World DLC content). For instance. Imagine if you could join the raiders attacking preston and the minutemen. It's not entirely out of possibility
• There is no Karma, a roleplay game needs karma systems and reactions for your negative ations.
• The story is... Meh, forgettable. Especially the endings!
• Marcy Long.
• Preston Gar- another settlement needs your help.
• Not enough GOOD side quests. Skyrim and Fallout NV were filled with them. There are some cool sidequests in Fallout 4, for instance the Museum of Witchcraft and the USS Constitution. Almost any other sidequest are just "Hey, raiders called us mean names go and kill them."
• Too much shooting. Not enough roleplay. This point comes down to younger audiences (With smaller attention spams- not an insult, its science. The human race is getting stupider and we have smaller attention spams.) People dont want to sit in dialong conversations for minutes at a time. Atleast, not new players of the franchise.
• The Dialog wheel. I know, yes there is a mod that changes it and thank god for it. But we still had to deal with it for a few weeks at launch so yeah. It sucked. Shorter options and less of them really break roleplay and immersion.
In conclusion. Fallout 4 is a masterpiece that consumed my attention for a good four months last Christmas. And I've began replaying this year around purely because of how influensial this game was to me. I have so many fond memories. In my break. Several DLC's have arrived as has the creation kit so great mods will really keep this game alive for me. I strongly suggest that everyone should play this game.

First of all, I really enjoyed this game for a long time, that's why I'm recommending it.
I really like the map with all it's hidden locations and I sure liked the storyline. The weapon crafting system seems great.
But once again, bethesda is struggling with npcs, especially companions. That super mutant just didn't want to get into that elevator and I had to reload a couple of times, losing a couple of hours when I realized I need him for a quest.
Fallout 4 has such a wide variety of features, but that's also one of it's problems. Sometimes, more is less and less is more.
I'm not really happy with the limited dialogue options we're offered here.
I would have really liked to have more individual speech checks instead of 4 things you can say to a character, almost the same for every character. Sometimes those "2 word sentences" trigger a very different result than you would expect.
Also, I don't like helping (the same) settlements over and over again. Settlers are armed to the teeth and there's plenty of turrets in all the settlements. I'm asked to help quite frequently, sometimes 3 settlements are under attack simultaneously. When I get there, the settlers and turrets get the job done rather quickly, but not when I decide to go somewhere else because I think they'll be alright anyway, they get kidnapped.
And well, basebuilding mechanics pretty much suck in this game, although we again have a wide variety of cool building parts, the menu is annoying after a while and scrapping for hours is required to really build anything. And when you just thought "ima build a nice tower right there" the game will tell you that you have built too much, blocking any further basebuilding.
The difficulty... (is a casual game after all)
"Normal" is very easy.
"Hard" is Normal
"Very hard" feels like hard should feel
"Survival" is fun, but companions go down too fast, doge was eating all my stimpaks and random deaths by incoming mini nukes - I still liked it and after reaching level 30 I think there is no alternative to survival mode, because very hard will still be very easy if you are level 30.
The biggest of all cons within this game is how legendary loot is generated. The narrow variety of stats and the lack of actual unique items like in fallout 3 is disappointing. Legendary guns have very little variation in damage amount or type, I've got up to 4 pieces of the exact same legendary gun, collecting over 100 in total. Sometimes you'll get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ armor with great stats and vice versa, even at level 50+ you get level 5 armor pieces from legendary opponents.

The final entry (? Armored Core pls From Software) in the Souls trilogy (not including Demon's Souls and Bloodborne obviously because console exclusives), and boy, it is definitely as hard as always.
Though it may pander to the fans of previous titles especially the first Dark Souls, the game can still be accessible to newcomers after a trial by fire which is accompanied by the words 'YOU DIED', which may appear from a few dozen to a few thousand times according to your skill level.
Enemies are much more varied now than the typical large men with large swords in heavy armor of Dark Souls II, and their movesets are quite more complicated now. I did not try PVP extensively because of slow internet, but there are still NPCs which can invade you or be summoned to help you. (though I hear mage builds are less viable now)
Soundtrack is epic as always, and the sound design can be very atmospheric (hint: turn up the volume when you reach Irithyll Dungeon).
Story-wise, the game doesn't explicitly tell it to you in your face, but the background lore can be gleaned from tidbits in dialogue and item description so that you yourself can connect the dots.
If you like a challenge, get this game.

Fallout 4 is a game that has a great amount of value but does have some drawbacks.  As i know most have already played this game or have at least reviewed it, I'll be brief:
+ Hundreds of hours of gameplay potential
+ If you like games like Oblivion, Skyrim, this game will feel similar (albeit too similar)
+ The game settings convey an apocalyptic world very well
+ The base of friends/allies throughout the game is engaging
+ The ability to create weapons, make certain types of choices, alignment, creates a significant amount of choice/value/risk scenarios
+ Innovative gun-play style and character rpg elements
- The grey overtone of the world can become dreary and removes some of the "fun" of the overall game
- It has been a while since I have played Oblivion, Skyrim, Fallout 3 but even with that, the game still seemed very familiar.  I'd say to the point that the models and the text conversation felt recycled/repetitive.
- Some story arcs were too simplistic
- Lack of ability to do full turn-based gun-play
All said and done, this game delivered on its promises and I have spent a significant # of hours playing this game.  I still have more to do as it seems the game (plus the expansions) add significant # of hours for side quests ad main quests.  The story arcs are a bit predictable but still fun.  I'd recommend this game  if you are fan of the other Fallouts or Skyrim/Oblivion.  if you are new to the world of Fallout or the game type, I'd highly recommend playing it.
Overall:  7.9/10 (very good value with hours and hours of gameplay)

I've spent about 30 hours playing this game the last few weeks, and I'm finding myself incredibly addicted.  Here are a few pros/cons:
Pros:
-If you liked the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, game play is really similar in the regard of completing various quests while avoiding dangerous mutants and situations while collecting and upgrading weapons and clothes/armor.  Where Fallout 4 surpasses STALKER is in the sheer size of the environment (no surprise since it's a much newer game), and you have the ability to create things by scrapping out the junk that you find in your quests.
-The amount of armor and weapon combinations and customizations is enormous.
-You can choose to play as someone who wants to help others, or you can play only for yourself...it's your call, and there's no right or wrong way to play.
-Through the perk system, you have the ability to improve your personal capabilities (lock picking ability, strength, etc.) as you level-up.
Cons:
-As of December of 2016, the price of Fallout 4 is still $59.99.  You can buy this game much cheaper elsewhere.  That being said, having the game part of your Steam library affords you the ability to download the software rather than keep disks around.
-You will be spending many, many hours playing this game.  You'll be trying to spend more and more time improving your armor, collecting gear, and finishing quests.  If you don't have a significant other who is cool with that, you're going to have a problem.  My wife has mentioned how much I've been playing, but she's been pretty cool about it so far.
-There are almost too many quests and deviations.  You'll be trying to complete a quest, and you'll end up with two or three more things on your list.  If you're a "cross it off your list" person, it will drive you nuts.
Overall, two thumbs up.  I just hope I can finish the game before my wife serves me divorce papers!

There is no video game without sin. I think many reviewers are forgetting that when reviewing this product. The game has it's problems but it doesn't make it a bad game. Let's sytematically anylise the goods and bads, I wouldn't want to waste your time and I certainly wouldn't want to waste mine.
Pros.
• Amazing new weapon mechaninics. Every gun, to bat, to launcher feels satisfying to shoot and swing.
• The map: It's big yet not too big. There is verity in landscapes (swamps, cities). A thing we didn't see much of in F3 and FNV.
• Some people (me included) Rather enjoy the expansiveness of the settlement feature.
• It's runs well and loading screens are non-existant (if you have an SSD.)
• The followers are deverse, interesting and all unique.
• The brotherhood are pretty neat
• Legendary items and enemies would always fill me with excitement when I came across one.
• I actually rather enjoyed a voiced protagonist.
Cons.
• Holy hell. Roleplaying and infamy is non-existant. We're forced to be a good guy. You can do bad things. But you always only get remembered as a good guy. (With the exeption to Nuka World DLC content). For instance. Imagine if you could join the raiders attacking preston and the minutemen. It's not entirely out of possibility
• There is no Karma, a roleplay game needs karma systems and reactions for your negative ations.
• The story is... Meh, forgettable. Especially the endings!
• Marcy Long.
• Preston Gar- another settlement needs your help.
• Not enough GOOD side quests. Skyrim and Fallout NV were filled with them. There are some cool sidequests in Fallout 4, for instance the Museum of Witchcraft and the USS Constitution. Almost any other sidequest are just "Hey, raiders called us mean names go and kill them."
• Too much shooting. Not enough roleplay. This point comes down to younger audiences (With smaller attention spams- not an insult, its science. The human race is getting stupider and we have smaller attention spams.) People dont want to sit in dialong conversations for minutes at a time. Atleast, not new players of the franchise.
• The Dialog wheel. I know, yes there is a mod that changes it and thank god for it. But we still had to deal with it for a few weeks at launch so yeah. It sucked. Shorter options and less of them really break roleplay and immersion.
In conclusion. Fallout 4 is a masterpiece that consumed my attention for a good four months last Christmas. And I've began replaying this year around purely because of how influensial this game was to me. I have so many fond memories. In my break. Several DLC's have arrived as has the creation kit so great mods will really keep this game alive for me. I strongly suggest that everyone should play this game.

Let me start off by saying that the PvE in this game was excellent.  It was a significant improvement over Dark Souls 2 and I enjoyed most of it.  My issue with the game comes from the fact that poise does not function as it did in either of the last two games.  This wasn't much of a problem in the PvE (except for the small enemy gank/spam fests that seem to occur, especially with rats) but it really hurts the PvP aspect of the game.  If you don't really care about PvP then you can stop reading here but if you do care about the PvP you might want to keep reading.
I feel like a good 70% of my issues with PvP could be solved by making poise work like it did in Dark Souls 1 and 2 (though maybe to a greater/lesser extent depending on balancing).  My experience was that most people just spam R1 with things like Estoc or Dark Sword.  Bleed builds are also pretty annoying.  These two things in particular wouldn't be so bad if you could poise through it.  I primarily played on a quality build.  I tried to use several weapons but would default to the Profaned Greatsword a lot of the time for the hyper armor and because the 2H R1 can't be parried.
A couple other things that didn't bother me too much but might bother others a lot:
1) If you invade someone you almost always end up fighting 2 or more people
2) Casters are harder to play as because the stat and gear investment is pretty high.  I don't see too many in PvP and I think it's because of one of those reasons.

First of all, I really enjoyed this game for a long time, that's why I'm recommending it.
I really like the map with all it's hidden locations and I sure liked the storyline. The weapon crafting system seems great.
But once again, bethesda is struggling with npcs, especially companions. That super mutant just didn't want to get into that elevator and I had to reload a couple of times, losing a couple of hours when I realized I need him for a quest.
Fallout 4 has such a wide variety of features, but that's also one of it's problems. Sometimes, more is less and less is more.
I'm not really happy with the limited dialogue options we're offered here.
I would have really liked to have more individual speech checks instead of 4 things you can say to a character, almost the same for every character. Sometimes those "2 word sentences" trigger a very different result than you would expect.
Also, I don't like helping (the same) settlements over and over again. Settlers are armed to the teeth and there's plenty of turrets in all the settlements. I'm asked to help quite frequently, sometimes 3 settlements are under attack simultaneously. When I get there, the settlers and turrets get the job done rather quickly, but not when I decide to go somewhere else because I think they'll be alright anyway, they get kidnapped.
And well, basebuilding mechanics pretty much suck in this game, although we again have a wide variety of cool building parts, the menu is annoying after a while and scrapping for hours is required to really build anything. And when you just thought "ima build a nice tower right there" the game will tell you that you have built too much, blocking any further basebuilding.
The difficulty... (is a casual game after all)
"Normal" is very easy.
"Hard" is Normal
"Very hard" feels like hard should feel
"Survival" is fun, but companions go down too fast, doge was eating all my stimpaks and random deaths by incoming mini nukes - I still liked it and after reaching level 30 I think there is no alternative to survival mode, because very hard will still be very easy if you are level 30.
The biggest of all cons within this game is how legendary loot is generated. The narrow variety of stats and the lack of actual unique items like in fallout 3 is disappointing. Legendary guns have very little variation in damage amount or type, I've got up to 4 pieces of the exact same legendary gun, collecting over 100 in total. Sometimes you'll get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ armor with great stats and vice versa, even at level 50+ you get level 5 armor pieces from legendary opponents.

The final entry (? Armored Core pls From Software) in the Souls trilogy (not including Demon's Souls and Bloodborne obviously because console exclusives), and boy, it is definitely as hard as always.
Though it may pander to the fans of previous titles especially the first Dark Souls, the game can still be accessible to newcomers after a trial by fire which is accompanied by the words 'YOU DIED', which may appear from a few dozen to a few thousand times according to your skill level.
Enemies are much more varied now than the typical large men with large swords in heavy armor of Dark Souls II, and their movesets are quite more complicated now. I did not try PVP extensively because of slow internet, but there are still NPCs which can invade you or be summoned to help you. (though I hear mage builds are less viable now)
Soundtrack is epic as always, and the sound design can be very atmospheric (hint: turn up the volume when you reach Irithyll Dungeon).
Story-wise, the game doesn't explicitly tell it to you in your face, but the background lore can be gleaned from tidbits in dialogue and item description so that you yourself can connect the dots.
If you like a challenge, get this game.

This is a difficult game for me to review. I'm nearly 150 hours in, and I have not finished the main story line yet. I should be saying that this game is amazing. But there is a difference between an effective time sink and an actual, good game that one truly enjoys playing. From a technical perspective and from a writing perspective, there are many bizarre, incongruous choices that smack of laziness, of not caring to think out the full consequences of a decision and instead slapping a bow on it and calling it good. Here are the main problems I have that keep me from being fully engrossed in this game.
First off, it's too easy, in the wrong way (increasing difficulty just makes the game slower-paced and ridiculous, not challenging). In every Fallout game, it is entirely possibly to become a demi-god in combat prowess, this is true; in this game, I stopped feeling challenged very, very early on. The rare times I feel like I'm taking any appreciable amount of damage, it never feels epic; because of how armor works, I'm not scared of the enemy firing missles at me, I'm not afraid of huge, muscular behemoth trying to smush me, but I AM cautious around full-auto weapons of even the smallest caliber, because THAT hurts more. Gangs of raiders with rifles and auto-pistols are a bigger threat than deathclaws. The leveling system, which has been so altered that it's difficult to summarize succintly, along with the diminished returns on armor, make it both easy and necessary to become a terror dealing massive damage to foes in the shortest period of time. The equipment modification system further enhances your ability to devestate entire rooms of enemies in seconds, with both mods and perks giving you gargantuan boosts in damage output. Combat is arguably improved, but it also feels like a fairly average shooter and not RPG-like.
Speaking of equipment modification, this has been a huge change, and is good in some ways. But, basically, it makes exploration boring. No more does equipment break down (so you have no need to find and horde duplicates), and for the most part, looking for unique, extra-powerful gear is a waste of time. Nope, just take regular old guns off the ground and modify them with generic "junk" items to become your instrument of pain. In fact, shopping is almost absent from this game; sure, you might buy some stims or ammo, but no longer are you trying to save up and buy something awesome, like a .50 cal, you don't even bother to sell anything. All you care about, want, NEED, 99% of the time, is literal junk; old tools, aluminum cans, duct tape, etc. Yup, you need it to modify and build about a million things, and that's the game's focus. Found a super-duper experimental prototype laser rifle? Pfft, too heavy, I need to carry these old desk fans and some glue, I don't have room for that. So...why care? You rarely find anything good or exciting; for the most part, you go through one location after another, collecting literally tons of scrap and garbage, and then take it home to store it for future projects. It's all the same, beginning, middle, and end. Even if you do find something better, it's so slight of an increase that you don't care.
Writing-wise...yes, they botched lore terribly, even stuff from Fallout 3. Let's just make that clear from the start, these people don't give a hoot about previous titles. The factions are poorly fleshed out, the companions are so lazy and boring that they may as well not exist (one of them puts their entire life on hold to travel with you, potentially orphaning a young child she is raising, because you do her a small favor for literally 5 minutes that barely helps her), and the overall plot, while a decent idea, has no engagement because we never get to have those arguments, those conflicts of ideology, it's just "Pick your favorite jerk and win!" You don't get the slightest bit of probing, of depth, to any one. And just to add insult to injury, they included the radiant quest system. The characters for two entire factions don't even say the words, they just say "Go to the place with the thing" and your quest log tells you what place that is, and what your goal is. Incredibly lazy and completely devoid of even the tiniest shred of emotional attachments. There is a total lack of internal logic as well, of course.
There you have it. I could go on, but basically, while I put in alot of time, what I've realized is I'm mostly just doing it for novelty, to see what's there. It's not consistent, or rational, or emotional, and I have long since acquired the greatest gear possible, and the companions are just cannon-fodder, and hell, even the dialogue system is broken, where long, extended  conversations with questions are eliminated for short, quick convos where details are skipped over and possible quest resolutions are missed just because you asked for clarification or something mundate. This is an exploration game with a light SIMS element, that's it. It's not an RPG. It's nowhere near as awesome as New Vegas, and I don't even know if it is as good as Fallout 3, which at least had a clear and understandable plot.

Summary of review:
For those of you who play for the PvE in this series, get this game. However for those who play the game for the PvP, to put it frankly, it's a waste of time.
If you have never played a souls game before or love the PvE in this series then definitely buy the game and it's DLC. However with that said I cannot recommend this to PvP players. Let’s get to the meat of the review.
The PvP in this game is the worst of every single souls game. Invasions are awful, it’s just invaders getting ganked by 4 people 90% of the time. Which is how PvP invasions are intended to be in this iteration. Which is a very strange decision since invaders are at a disadvantage, I think you can figure out how this ♥♥♥♥s up PvP yourself. Sorcery and miracles are completely useless in PvP. They never hit , they have insanely slow casting speeds, and require a HUGE level investment to make even slightly viable. with pyromancy being the exception. Also the dark magic class of spells, added in DS2 which many people liked,  isn't an actual class of spells there are just spells that do dark damage, like in DS1. Furthermore the only weapons you will see used in this game are the paired weapons or ultra greatswords/axes/curved greatswords, with nothing else being viable, except for possibly long swords. I mentioned paired weapons earlier, this brings up another thing people liked in DS2 that was removed. Duel wield stances for weapons. I understand why they might remove this for balance reasons, but it removes a ton of depth from the game's combat.
