I originally reviewed Dark Souls 3 when it first came out, but I'd like to revisit my review after 150+ hours of gameplay to help you, the buyer, make a more detailed decision.
For the first timers, Dark Souls 3 is the latest in the DS trilogy that takes action RPGs to a pure, combat heavy level. Gameplay is fairly simple, but difficult to master. Every player has the option to specialise in any role they choose, use any weapon they wish (provided they have the stats), and change their playstyle on the fly based on desire. Enemies are designed like small puzzles to solve, often requiring you to have a gameplan before each encounter. Light puzzle elements, platforming, and exploration give the series a feeling of old school adventure often lost in the more rigid, textbook RPGs.
Set in the ruined kingdom of Lothric, Dark Souls 3 immediately sets the pace of a faster, slimmer souls game. Taking queues from Bloodborne, DSIII has given the series a major stream lining in gameplay. Healing no longer stops you dead in your tracks, weapons no longer break (for good or bad based on your opinion of challenge), enemies are way more aggressive, and animations are much faster. This may through off some of you, but IMO it's a change for the better.
Level design is back to a mastercraft level, providing the most cohesive experience of all 3 DS games. Highlights include a dilapidated village, an enormous church and surrounding grounds, a moon lit city, and an enormous library shrouded in dark. While some areas are not as well developed as others, with a particular zone midgame, overall quality is way more consistent that previous entries. The fine models, textures, and world design is second to none. The environmental detail is astounding, often telling a story of its own. Bosses, the highlight of any souls game, make a triumphant return after the poor showing in DS2. You can expect some very interesting fights this time around, as well as some neat encounters never experienced before.
However, DSIII is not without its flaws. If you are a returning veteran, DSIII may be the easiest game in the series. The reduced stamina cost of rolling, lower health pools of bosses, and forgiving iframes allow you to get away with more risks than ever before. Sorcery and faith based builds have been nerfed from previous entries. Poise is gone, replaced by a hyperarmor system that is tied to weapons, armor, and frame data with swings. Invasions are much harder as coop has been given a major boost in stability and length, often leading you to gank squads of estus chugging try hards that will mock you when you lose their 3v1 game. And, while it's an engaging experience, DSIII is on the short side. You can expect an average playthrough of 30 hours, give or take how much gimping you do yourself and assuming you don't get help from other players.
DSIII will test your patience, reward your determination, and grant you new skills. It may also ruin other ARPGs for you. This is a fantastic game that every gamer should own as it's the perfect send off to a beloved series, full of mystery and horror. See you in game, Ashen One.

Years from now, Dark Souls III is going to be known as the "Ocarina of Time" of the series. Compared to the previous Souls games: artifical difficult has been replaced by unique and skillful execution, quality of life nuisances have been remedied, and sound/visuals have been improved drastically.
In a nutshell, the biggest difference in Dark Souls III is that you aren't being tested for your patience/discipline. DS3 tests you for your skill. In DS1/2, dying was infuriating, and winning was a relief. In DS3, dying is awe-inspiring, and winning makes you feel like a lord.
I whole-heartedly recommend you get this game. As soon as I got it, I couldn't stop playing it (I put in 68 hours over 5 weeks while working full-time and going to school). It is not flawless, but it is a clear 9/10. It's quite a enjoyable and rewarding experience.
Also, in your times of struggle, remember that every death is meant to be a lesson. The game wants you to succeed.
Weapons are extremely unique and most of them are viable in PvE. You get to just pick whatever you want and feel like the badass that you want. Boss weapons are not impossible to come by and often feel the best. There are also many more choices for each weapon based on their "arte", which are more than just a guard break or a lunge forward.
The movement/dodge system is much faster and more responsive. This would be very OP in previous Dark Souls games, but enemies in previous DS titles also were hard countered by circle-backstab anyway. The rolls in this game are appropriately needed for the changes in enemy move sets. It overall just feels better just to run around and battle.
The convenants and merchants are infinitely less cumbersome than previous. Discovering a merchant relocates them to Firelink Shrine, in which all merchants and most NPCs will stay. You won't have to go traveling for 4 minutes just to get your weapon upgraded after you buy some pyromancies anymore. Convenants are also joined by being given a Sigil following discovery. You can just swap convenants by switching this slot in your inventory instead of hunting down the convenant leader again. Also, a merchant dying no longer means that you lose their products. All in all, it is much less of a chore to do small tasks like these.
The equivalent of being human is called being Embered. Unlike in previous games, this is actually useful (you get 30% extra hp). This means that more people embered overall = more PvP interaction. Also, you gain embered status for beating a boss, which means more people want to put down their summon sign to help out others with a tough boss. Summoning also has a level limit, so you don't have to be scared of getting invaded from someone light years ahead of you in levels/gear. All of these mechanics lead to greater and more meaningful player interaction throughout your time in Lothric.
You get to warp between bonfires from the get-go, and you also don't have to upgrade specific bonfires. Some have complained that this makes the world feel a bit smaller, but I disagree. The world is extremely connected save 1 or 2 exceptions, and you can see almost every other point in the game from one another. Bonfires are also a bit more on rails, meaning that it's tough to miss one. Previously, hidden bonfires (especially in
) could completely change the flow of how you play the game based on whether you stumble upon it or not. There's also a generally lower amount of arbitrary♥♥♥♥♥♥that would punish you for lack of prior knowledge.
The weapon crafting system no longer punishes you for making a choice. You can simply swap the properties of a +10 weapon instead of having to find another one and go through the full upgrade path each time. The information about each weapon is much easier to process and there are more choices for whatever nuianced build you're trying.
The menu overall is extremely good. You can finally navigate on a grid instead of a list, and you can tab between menus for your armor/weapons. You can have more rings and items equipped simultaneously. You can also view your status to see how many souls you need for a next level instead of stopping by a specific location. It is overall just much easier on the eyes, and it is optimized to provide convenient access to information.
The bosses follow suit in the weapons improvement, and (with few exceptions) they all feel varied and deep. I've fought some bosses almost 40 times and will still see some new moves. The AI is also programmed well enough to show human tendencies like getting greedy or faking out a move. You would be able to look up a guide on these most bosses and still not find the secret to beating them. In previous DS games, it felt like you would cheese all of the bosses because they'd cheese you (just walk near them and stand behind every boss). Sometimes, you'll want to intentionally separate yourself from a boss as much as possible. Some bosses have moves to punish you positioning close; other bosses have moves to punish you for rolling as a reaction to anything. DS3 bosses have several move sets that keep it fresh several times over. I never noticed how terribly annoying previous Dark Souls bosses were (from walking to each boss to the small gimmicks and lack of tactics) until realizing how good it could be when I played DS3.
Honorable mention is that the Final Boss is an absolute beast. He is
; therefore, his fight is the deepest and most "complete" that I could say I remember in a video game. He's not this way because he just "has a lot of stages" or takes 30 minutes to beat, but because he
and you will find something different each time you play him. There is also a bit of an emotional moment in which
. Sometimes you feel so emotionally connected with him, that you almost don't want to win.
The normal enemies are what you would expect, but there is fortunately a bit less mob behavior. I thought that mob behavior was a bit of a cheap excuse for difficulty, and the AI programming and enemy design has made up that difficulty in a more meaningful way in DS3.
I unfortunately don't know too much about serious PvP, but my experience with the invasions mechanics have been pleasant when fighting another player. It hasn't really felt unfair at all, yet.
Drastic performance increase. 60 fps, unlocked resolutions (I played in 1440p). The draw distance is excellent and the environments are stunning. You will find several "Oh my god" moments in which you are greeted by amazing views en route to a new area. For a little bit of preview, look up the screenshots of Irithyll of the Boreal Valley. The armor and characters are also extremely sharp, and the in-game rendered cutscenes are Blizzard quality.
The audio is overhauled. The directional sound in the game rivals Counter-Strike 1.6. The materials and general pitter-pattering is very precise and varied throughout. The sounds in the game are also overall very clear; play a bit of Dark Souls 1 and you will notice a staggering difference.
The music is the best of any in the series. Several songs feel like a perfect fit for the environment/boss, instead of just sounding like generic background tunes. Pretty much any boss theme is great, but Abyss Watchers, Soul of Cinder, Pontiff Sulyvahn, Father Ariandel and Sister Friede (from the DLC), Twin Princes, and Oceiros get honorable mentions for great music. The Main Menu theme is pretty damn good, too.

This is a difficult game for me to review. I'm nearly 150 hours in, and I have not finished the main story line yet. I should be saying that this game is amazing. But there is a difference between an effective time sink and an actual, good game that one truly enjoys playing. From a technical perspective and from a writing perspective, there are many bizarre, incongruous choices that smack of laziness, of not caring to think out the full consequences of a decision and instead slapping a bow on it and calling it good. Here are the main problems I have that keep me from being fully engrossed in this game.
First off, it's too easy, in the wrong way (increasing difficulty just makes the game slower-paced and ridiculous, not challenging). In every Fallout game, it is entirely possibly to become a demi-god in combat prowess, this is true; in this game, I stopped feeling challenged very, very early on. The rare times I feel like I'm taking any appreciable amount of damage, it never feels epic; because of how armor works, I'm not scared of the enemy firing missles at me, I'm not afraid of huge, muscular behemoth trying to smush me, but I AM cautious around full-auto weapons of even the smallest caliber, because THAT hurts more. Gangs of raiders with rifles and auto-pistols are a bigger threat than deathclaws. The leveling system, which has been so altered that it's difficult to summarize succintly, along with the diminished returns on armor, make it both easy and necessary to become a terror dealing massive damage to foes in the shortest period of time. The equipment modification system further enhances your ability to devestate entire rooms of enemies in seconds, with both mods and perks giving you gargantuan boosts in damage output. Combat is arguably improved, but it also feels like a fairly average shooter and not RPG-like.
Speaking of equipment modification, this has been a huge change, and is good in some ways. But, basically, it makes exploration boring. No more does equipment break down (so you have no need to find and horde duplicates), and for the most part, looking for unique, extra-powerful gear is a waste of time. Nope, just take regular old guns off the ground and modify them with generic "junk" items to become your instrument of pain. In fact, shopping is almost absent from this game; sure, you might buy some stims or ammo, but no longer are you trying to save up and buy something awesome, like a .50 cal, you don't even bother to sell anything. All you care about, want, NEED, 99% of the time, is literal junk; old tools, aluminum cans, duct tape, etc. Yup, you need it to modify and build about a million things, and that's the game's focus. Found a super-duper experimental prototype laser rifle? Pfft, too heavy, I need to carry these old desk fans and some glue, I don't have room for that. So...why care? You rarely find anything good or exciting; for the most part, you go through one location after another, collecting literally tons of scrap and garbage, and then take it home to store it for future projects. It's all the same, beginning, middle, and end. Even if you do find something better, it's so slight of an increase that you don't care.
Writing-wise...yes, they botched lore terribly, even stuff from Fallout 3. Let's just make that clear from the start, these people don't give a hoot about previous titles. The factions are poorly fleshed out, the companions are so lazy and boring that they may as well not exist (one of them puts their entire life on hold to travel with you, potentially orphaning a young child she is raising, because you do her a small favor for literally 5 minutes that barely helps her), and the overall plot, while a decent idea, has no engagement because we never get to have those arguments, those conflicts of ideology, it's just "Pick your favorite jerk and win!" You don't get the slightest bit of probing, of depth, to any one. And just to add insult to injury, they included the radiant quest system. The characters for two entire factions don't even say the words, they just say "Go to the place with the thing" and your quest log tells you what place that is, and what your goal is. Incredibly lazy and completely devoid of even the tiniest shred of emotional attachments. There is a total lack of internal logic as well, of course.
There you have it. I could go on, but basically, while I put in alot of time, what I've realized is I'm mostly just doing it for novelty, to see what's there. It's not consistent, or rational, or emotional, and I have long since acquired the greatest gear possible, and the companions are just cannon-fodder, and hell, even the dialogue system is broken, where long, extended  conversations with questions are eliminated for short, quick convos where details are skipped over and possible quest resolutions are missed just because you asked for clarification or something mundate. This is an exploration game with a light SIMS element, that's it. It's not an RPG. It's nowhere near as awesome as New Vegas, and I don't even know if it is as good as Fallout 3, which at least had a clear and understandable plot.

Unfortunately, there is a major learning curve for people who are unfamiliar with serious RPGs.

Summary of review:
For those of you who play for the PvE in this series, get this game. However for those who play the game for the PvP, to put it frankly, it's a waste of time.
If you have never played a souls game before or love the PvE in this series then definitely buy the game and it's DLC. However with that said I cannot recommend this to PvP players. Let’s get to the meat of the review.
The PvP in this game is the worst of every single souls game. Invasions are awful, it’s just invaders getting ganked by 4 people 90% of the time. Which is how PvP invasions are intended to be in this iteration. Which is a very strange decision since invaders are at a disadvantage, I think you can figure out how this ♥♥♥♥s up PvP yourself. Sorcery and miracles are completely useless in PvP. They never hit , they have insanely slow casting speeds, and require a HUGE level investment to make even slightly viable. with pyromancy being the exception. Also the dark magic class of spells, added in DS2 which many people liked,  isn't an actual class of spells there are just spells that do dark damage, like in DS1. Furthermore the only weapons you will see used in this game are the paired weapons or ultra greatswords/axes/curved greatswords, with nothing else being viable, except for possibly long swords. I mentioned paired weapons earlier, this brings up another thing people liked in DS2 that was removed. Duel wield stances for weapons. I understand why they might remove this for balance reasons, but it removes a ton of depth from the game's combat. On top of all of that the PvP community seems to be full of asshats that can’t do basic math because the PvP level meta is the same as DS1's or lower making for incredibly restricted builds, especially considering there is one more attribute and the major changes to other attributes. There are also duels, but they have their own issues on top of the ones I mentioned earlier. And That's all I have to say about PvP so let's move on.
With all of that said let's move on to the PvE. It's amazing. The level design is fantastic, the bosses are varied and difficult, and the trash mobs tend to be difficult too. The first thing I'd like to talk about are trash mobs. They are generally varied and fun to fight(Except dogs, ♥♥♥♥ them) There are some issues with trash mobs though, the major one being they are insanely aggressive, making them just not fun to fight. Some mobs also just don't telegraph attack well enough. That's all I have to say about trash mobs(Insert trash joke here). I mentioned the boss fights briefly earlier and to build on that, they are amazing and probably the best in the series. It seems that the devs finally realized dudes in armour, while cool, are not exactly very interesting to fight after the tenth one. Another thing fairly new to the Souls series is boss phases which are interesting and very well executed. One example (spoilers AHOY!) is the first bossfight. The dude in armour explodes into a puss monster(end of spoilers). So yeah PvE is amazing and fun.
And, finally, DLC. It's okay I guess not to much to say about it except it's got more cool bosses, and a whole lot more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

I originally reviewed Dark Souls 3 when it first came out, but I'd like to revisit my review after 150+ hours of gameplay to help you, the buyer, make a more detailed decision.
For the first timers, Dark Souls 3 is the latest in the DS trilogy that takes action RPGs to a pure, combat heavy level. Gameplay is fairly simple, but difficult to master. Every player has the option to specialise in any role they choose, use any weapon they wish (provided they have the stats), and change their playstyle on the fly based on desire. Enemies are designed like small puzzles to solve, often requiring you to have a gameplan before each encounter. Light puzzle elements, platforming, and exploration give the series a feeling of old school adventure often lost in the more rigid, textbook RPGs.
Set in the ruined kingdom of Lothric, Dark Souls 3 immediately sets the pace of a faster, slimmer souls game. Taking queues from Bloodborne, DSIII has given the series a major stream lining in gameplay. Healing no longer stops you dead in your tracks, weapons no longer break (for good or bad based on your opinion of challenge), enemies are way more aggressive, and animations are much faster. This may through off some of you, but IMO it's a change for the better.
Level design is back to a mastercraft level, providing the most cohesive experience of all 3 DS games. Highlights include a dilapidated village, an enormous church and surrounding grounds, a moon lit city, and an enormous library shrouded in dark. While some areas are not as well developed as others, with a particular zone midgame, overall quality is way more consistent that previous entries. The fine models, textures, and world design is second to none. The environmental detail is astounding, often telling a story of its own. Bosses, the highlight of any souls game, make a triumphant return after the poor showing in DS2. You can expect some very interesting fights this time around, as well as some neat encounters never experienced before.
However, DSIII is not without its flaws. If you are a returning veteran, DSIII may be the easiest game in the series. The reduced stamina cost of rolling, lower health pools of bosses, and forgiving iframes allow you to get away with more risks than ever before. Sorcery and faith based builds have been nerfed from previous entries. Poise is gone, replaced by a hyperarmor system that is tied to weapons, armor, and frame data with swings. Invasions are much harder as coop has been given a major boost in stability and length, often leading you to gank squads of estus chugging try hards that will mock you when you lose their 3v1 game. And, while it's an engaging experience, DSIII is on the short side. You can expect an average playthrough of 30 hours, give or take how much gimping you do yourself and assuming you don't get help from other players.
DSIII will test your patience, reward your determination, and grant you new skills. It may also ruin other ARPGs for you. This is a fantastic game that every gamer should own as it's the perfect send off to a beloved series, full of mystery and horror. See you in game, Ashen One.

Into the Deep End
As a Dark Souls newbie, this game was extremely punishing at first and tested my patience to the next level. Never have I been forced to realize how bad I am at combat. True, unadulterated, combat. The kind where it is your fault for going in too deep when the enemy was preparing an attack. Where slowing down and observing is just important as attacking. Death after death, and then some more for good measure, I finally managed to take down Iudex (the starting boss)…down to his second phase. Of course he had to have a second phase, I mean, it’s only been 5 minutes since I created my character and this guy is more difficult than most games’ final bosses. Alright fine, let’s try it again….and naturally, the stupid skeleton guarding the boss entrance chunked me for half of my health. This obnoxious heathen never managed to hit me in my previous 16 runs, but now its eyes gained some sort of holy enchantment to make every arrow land on my back. This is the type of game DARK SOULS III is. One without mercy, care, or pity. It took me approximately 2 hours to beat Iudex as a starting Mercenary, but the thrill and adrenaline post-battle was truly something no other game offered. Who knew I could come to love a game that wanted to kill me so badly.
Ashes, Cinders, and Bonfires
As I fought my way through the story, I began to become immersed with the lore and progression system. Every single item’s description, name, and method of acquisition imparts just a tiny bit of knowledge or history onto the player. At first, most of this information is useless at worst, or intriguing at best. These little puzzle pieces manage to eventually paint a very vivid and dark image about the world of Lothric and its inhabitants. Ashes and unique equipment often detail the previous owners’ qualities; a gift to fans of previous games in the series. Although DS III is fairly disconnected with any of the other SOULS games, certain NPCs and discoveries will tie up loose ends and provide closure for particular aspects of the first DARK SOULS game.
Unlike the previous games, bonfires are placed just when you truly need them, and most important of all, teleportation between bonfires are available from the get-go. Firelink Shrine, the base of operations of sorts, serves as the location for player stat upgrades, weapon upgrades/infusions, Estus flask upgrades, and bonfire upgrades (increases healing per flask). Similar to Humanity or Human Effigies from the previous games, Ember heals the player and boosts max health in exchange for allowing human and NPC invasions.
Although the world design is fairly spectacular, it was mostly linear/bi-linear (city with a dungeon below it) with moderate exploration required for completionists. The traditionally grand map comprised of interconnecting smaller maps through shortcuts is replaced with a more direct route, however, the world is still HUGE. In fact, without proper investigation, it is extremely easy to completely miss 4 optional areas with their own bosses. In total, there are 19 bosses that will do their best to make sure life in Lothric is a living Hell, along with several other mini-bosses in between. The grunt and fluff type enemies are never too difficult – just strong enough to warrant consistent player attention. The extremely well planned level and boss design (excluding a couple) easily makes DS III one of the most memorable games I have ever played. I can clearly recount most of the paths in every area along with every bosses’ movesets and shenanigans. From clones and body doubles, to massive variances in combat range and aggressiveness, the boss fights and surrounding environements are truly, and remarkably, unforgettable.
The Art in Killing
One of the most noticeable changes to the tried-and-true combat involves the introduction of weapon arts. Think of it as a special skill move belonging to certain weapon types. Hacking and slashing is always fun, but turning that long sword into a propeller of death is even more so. Special and boss type weapons are often imbued with properties of their wielder, including a unique weapon art that can be so hauntingly beautiful to perform. Lance thrusts with bursts of electricity, sword strikes covered in fire, and duel-wielded weapons moving in an artistic dance are only some of what you will see. Unfortunately, most of these arts require the use of FP (focus points), and once out, they won’t be usable until replenished.
Issues & Updates
DS III launched with quite a few minor grievances, mostly sporadic FPS drops, but all of them have been fixed. The only major issue at the moment is regarding softbanning due to “Data Inconsistencies” which may occur due to advancing in the game offline (de-syncing with the server) or from online hackers. Continuous patches have been applied since the posting of this review in order to keep up to date with the demanding pvp balance and bug encounters.
Verdict
I can’t stress enough how much I really enjoyed playing DS III. This game is one of my personal contenders for 2016 GOTY. I really regret never playing the earlier two during their heyday, but at least it gives me something to do while i lament the end of this great journey – at least, until the Season Pass content gets released. For those that want to continue into New Game +, DS III fortunately provides 3 other endings with vastly different consequences to uncover, increasing replayability immensely. One of those endings also requires an extremely strict quest-line progression, ultimately leading to one of the most shocking moments in the game!

First off, this game is great. It has an absolutely absurd amount of content available. All the planets are procedurally generated, plus all the monsters on each planet are generated randomly from bits and pieces of various other monsters. Basically, each planet actually feels like you are visiting an aliens world. Out of the 31 hours that i have played, i haven't ran into any 2 monsters alike on different planets. Which is really really cool considering there are all these planets that you can explore. It generally feels great that each planet is unique to its' own species.
Secondly, the difficulty is great. At the beginning you generally feel like you have nothing. You really have to push forward to get some good gear at the start. Which is nice because it really makes you kinda strive for survival. Surely, you can just die, get recloned, and beam back down from your ship. But if you really wanna stay alive, survive, and try not to die; it isn't easy, at least until you get better gear.
Third, the games depth is incredible. My friend showed me how to exit the solar system that you start on. So i went into my ship, navigated to the captain's seat and right clicked to see the planets around me. I right clicked again, and i saw our solar system. I right clicked once more to see a HUGE amount of other various stars that each had their own solar systems filled with 4-5 planets each. I could have scrolled through all the stars, that you could visit, in the universe for about an hour just counting all of the different planets. Not to mention, after you defeat the first boss you can craft a piece that expands your sector. Meaning an ENTIRELY new array of thousands of planets that you can visit. All procedurally generated with their own monsters and threats.
In conclusion, if you liked Terraria. Get this game. If not, get this game.It is a great building kind of game, but it also has a nice balance of exploration tied into building. I find myself flying around other various planets more than i find myself building things. Most of my stuff is in my ship, and the only resources i really ensure i farm are ores and wood for fuel to get to the next place. There are some things you need to collect in order to get the good equips. But sometimes you may end up visiting a planet that just so happens to have friendly shopkeepers and NPCs. There are a few things that can be worked on, some more expansions that i would like to see. Such as a better matter manipulator upgrade that way you don't have to keep on carrying around a million different tools. So far though, i can't really think of much more. It is a great game with very few flaws, as far as i can see.
Would i recommend this game? Absolutely. The devs are bringing frequent patches and they have promised that they will continue to do so even in the future. They have promised to keep everyone working on it for about a year, then a smaller team would continue to work on it afterwards. So far, it looks very promising. And even though there may be a few character wipes due to early beta, i am still very compelled to keep playing. Its also coming to Vita and PS4 so what's not to love.

Starbound contains both quests and story driven missions, buried inside its vast sandbox universe.
The space station in Starbound is sprawling and full of potential. Throughout your travels you'll find ways to upgrade and repair it, restoring it to its former glory. You'll need to find a crew, conduct research, catch rare creatures, and unlock its multitude of facilities. From a factory capable of producing mechs to labs where captured enemies can be studied and trained, the space station contains everything you need to explore the universe.

That name used to mean something less than a year ago. It wasn't a game, back then. It was an ideal, a game that existed only because we wanted it to. The world would be better with it's presence, we thought. Gaming would never be the same if it appeared; like an atom bomb, it would change the way we looked at things forever.
It has now been over a year since that name was brought from shadow, to spotlight, and now discussion. What do we have now, six DLCs down the road and plenty of time to sink in hour upon hour?
: While New Vegas might have been in a dusty desert, brown in excess is never a good thing. Fallout 4 finally gives us some richer colors to stare at. Metal foundries turned Raider Strongholds have fiery hues to inflame our anger towards injustice. The countryside has pleasantly clean skies and lush vegitation in the remains of old highways and parks. Rad storms and the poisoned Glowing Sea cast a harsh green glow onto the landscape, flashes of lightning jolting us from our idle stares into the maelstrom above.
: At long last, 3D Fallout shoots like it should. We can sprint for the first time, quickly moving from cover to play that deadly game of bullet ping-pong. Recoil feels right, and moving guns with a controller isn't linear and stiff, but fluid and responsive, allowing for quick manuvers of sight-hip-repeat. Grenades can be tossed with your rifle out, allowing you to coax opponents out of cover and into your waiting line-of-sight. These tenets of design may be standard on other shooters, but they were lacking in Fallout. And now, it's here and (almost) perfect.
: Cigarettes, electronics, and chemicals won't be the only things you pick up anymore. Bethesda has put purpose behind every coffee cup, every discarded glass, and more. To let your creative desires flow in your canvases of guns and housing, you'll need the right materials. Every peice of junk you come across has little salvagable components within themselves that you can then use to make useful things. Want to construct a wonderful bungalow for your character out of a gas station? You'll need steel and wood-and both of things exist in clipboards and tin cans. With the exception of folders, you'll find yourself reaching for whatever isn't welded to the floor.
: Previously, every raider has the same rifle as a soldier. Fallout 4's crafting system allows for what New Vegas tried to do: mods that made your gun yours. Enemies can have weapons creatively-tuned or plain as paper; one raider's ramshackle rifle has a tuned receiver or a hair-trigger, while another's Pipe Pistol is just a tool for the job. But with the right perks and parts, you can make very special armor and weapons for yourself. Why have a Standard Laser Rifle when you can tweak it to scatter beams or incinerate to disintigrate? Why have just a Leather Chestpeice when you can shadow it to sneak and stab? Your character can be as unique as your tools.
: Fallout 3 and NV had only three slots: Face, Hat, and Body. Skyrim got closer, segmenting the body into Greaves, Boots, Torso, and with Necklaces and Rings to boot. Now we have something magical: from top to bottom, Hat, Eyes, Face, Left arm, Torso, Right arm, Left leg, and Right leg, and a new "underarmor" slot for close-skin clothing that can be worn underneath your armor. Mix and match for effectiveness or looks, but regardless, it's diverse.
The game will go as long as you let it. No DLCs required to expand the level cap-it's already cranked up to infinity. Build the most impossibly powerful individual for as long as you keep playing. And when the ending hits, your survivor keeps walking to mop up leftover quest and locked perks.
: Past games had their share of good pals to support the sadness of the wastes, and this game keeps that bar high. Each companion has their own stories, likes, dislikes, dreams and hopes. They routinely make subtle movements and little dialogue quirks that bring real people out of virtual constructs. And with their perks being unlocks rather than presence-based, you're welcome to try them all.
: Bethesda's past ventures often had small crews of common voices, but they've done something with this one that prevents dialogue from going stale audio-wise. I can't quite put my finger on it...bigger cast? Similar voices? Regardless, it's better here.
: The character creator in this game's absolutely phenomenal. Dials and numbers become a stretch-and-pull plethora of wonderful options of any face and body shape you can think of. Channing Tatum or horrible scar-rack? Your choice.
: Truth be told, it's not that bad. It has about one good twist, but that's it. Granted, the main story wasn't the spotlight in these games.
: Alright, the Minutemen are a great way of discovering workshoops and places to build settlements. This is ruined by the fact you have to babysit your territory while the okay-companion Preston is forced to become a pez-dispenser of "do this' quest. Trimming down the quest he gives or the amount of workshops you can have and use would easily make this better to bear, but presently it's a pain that hinders your desire to build in different places.
: In addition to canonicly making no sense at all, the Power Armor system, while cool and interesting, isn't extrememly needed or even utilized. You can mix and match peices onto a frame, and there's an alright system in place for making your own extreme exosuit, but your parts can take damage and break off of you, requiring more scrap to fix. You're also slower in it and using it will require Fusion Cores, a costly fuel source that makes constant use an impossibliity. By the time you have plenty of gas, your player will often be stronger apart than with Power Armor.
: New songs sit in the radio-about two of them. The rest are re-used from older games, leading to a quickly-annoying earworm generator that's even more grating than the previous titles. AI still gets stuck in places and onto things, animations are still not flawless (but better.) This is the only Fallout game I had where I actually completed every quest in one run, leaving nothing to do. The Armor system doesn't allow you to wear EVERYTHING (would it kill to make all common clothes underarmor?) And of course, bugs on bugs.
: In an attempt to trim dialogue, Bethesda made every encounter have four dialogue options. This wouldn't be as bad as it is if every option you choose is described in two words or less, so you'll never know exactly what you'll say. The biggest gripe is the "sarcastic" option. It's never described as "yes" or "no", just "sarcastic." It's ridiculous.
APPROVED-Worth a buy.
A year later, this game is still giving. Still, I find new things to do, new contraptions to build, and new adventures even after plenty of hours more than my friends. Though all in all, I have to say this is a weaker RPG for Bethesda. It's a greater shooter, no doubt, but it's no RPG, and for some people, that's all Fallout was. I understand that frustration.
But in all of the bad, remember this: this game almost went the route of No Man's Sky. Hype infatuated so high, hopes set to an unreachble bar, that when the product finally dropped, the flaws that were there clashed so intensly with our impossible ideal. Now, UNLIKE No Man's Sky, this game actually did meet many of it's promises, thankfully. But make no mistake, this is not the game you see in the Announcement Trailer.
At least, not without Far Harbor.

This review is for buyers who are new to the souls series.
To be brief, this game is like a challenging completion quest. I think of it as a distant evolution of a platformer. You are meant to beat the level and get the bosses soul, which are like the stars in Mario or bananas in DK. It is a great atmospheric game and I recommend it to anyone looking for a rewarding challenge.
I would not recommend this game to anyone looking for an RPG as it does not contain some of the key RPG elements. For example, Its story is lacking heavily (slightly better than Destiny). Also, loot like weapons or armor has a big impact on gameplay, but is not a draw of this game. You have a lot of freedom as far as skills, weapons, and armor, but as a first time player you will need to use a sword and shield. I tried to become an archer, but the bosses were not designed to be taken down with arrows. In that way it lacks the classes of typical RPGs, such as caster, tank, rogue. Instead Dark Souls shows you through trial and error what is fun and effective to play.
Unfortunately, I did not beat the game and I do not intend to. I just do not have a reason to beat the next boss. I am not someone who plays to complete a game or likes to get achievements, so this game is not for me.
PvP is a seperate beast and is definitely a reason I would get back into this game. First time players will not be able to compete online for awhile, but getting crushed by other players shows you what skills you need. The online players are the true bosses in Dark Souls.

If you are fan of the series. And you are mainly singleplayer player. Buy this game. Singleplayer experience is far better than in Dark souls 2. Bosses are well designed and locations are beautiful.
Gameplay
Game is overall much faster than any other in the series. From Software probably got inspired by Bloodborne and decided to make it much faster. The thing i don't like are the insta hitting attacks from some bosses/enemy. But yea, maybe i'm just bad. Anyway, bosses are probably as good as in Dark souls 1, so on that part From Software did a great job. Feeling and enjoyableness is pretty good.
The thing i don't like is that this game doesn't have as much of a replay value as Dark souls 2 had. I finished Dark souls 2 many times for 2 reasons. New enemies, PvP. And this Dark souls, didn't do any of it well.  In Dark souls 2 you had on NG+ new enemies and you just wanted to get more content, so you enjoyed it. But there, you will just play NG+ for new rings. Even the difficulty on NG+ is almost same as it is on NG.
Multiplayer/PvP
Horrible. PvP in Dark souls 3 is nowhere as good as it was in Dark souls 2. What you do in Dark souls 3, if you get hit? You just simply heal with your estus. Is it worth? Yes, because healing with estus is worth even if you get hit for it, because healing animation cannot be canceled at some point. This turned Invading into total♥♥♥♥♥♥and actually made me quit PvP, which was the main reason why i was playing DS2 for so long.
Next thing. Poise. I feel like it doesn't matter how much poise you have. You always get staggered even if you are wearing some kind of heavy armor with high poise. This applies to PvE too. Do you want tank boss like you could in Dark souls 1? Yea, FeelsBadMan. You can't.
The worst thing. Lagging/ping or whatever it is. Imagine yourself starting backstabbing animation. You will start it and the enemy player just rolls and you end up being stuck in animation for 2 seconds and not doing any dmg.
Or you can just enjoy not doing any dmg despite hearing yourself hitting the enemy player. this happens A LOT. I feel like PvP is unplayable and it actually killed my motivation to play this game over and over again for new builds etc...
Overall, PvP is unplayable and i don't see it fixed even after so many time. So it will most likely stay as bad as it is right now.
Story

As a Fallout fan this was my most anticipated game of 2015. So when I got the game I was very curious if it was a fantastic game like Fallout 3 and New vegas.:
Info about my save:
I currently played this game over 190 hours on the time that I’m writing this review, so I really played it. I completed all quests and all dlc’s. Was it worth it? Yes but if I restart the game, everything will be te same. This is a big con. The main reason I buy Bethesda games is that I can replay the game at least 2 time and having 2 different stories. This one failed on this. Yet my first/current save was better than other Fallouts. The reason it does not have that replayabilty is that there are almost no RPG elements in the game anymore, Bethesda wanted that we would see everything in one playthrough. This is not in Skyrim. The graphics are amazing for a Fallout. I mean, the graphics are not on The Witcher 3 level but they are decent. Some addition that I liked is the volumetric lightning also known as god rays.
The gameplay is awesome, in this long road I never questioned myself if I liked the fast paced action that this Fallout contains. Bethesda really focused on the gunplay aspect. You got customization on all weapons. The FOV is good. (some people complained about it)
The story is better than the other Fallouts, it has more emotion and sometimes those little sounds make the change. Fallout 4 is about a parent (You) finding his/her son.
The building in Fallout 4 was something I wanted a long time since I installed a mod in fallout 3 and new vegas. It works very nice. The only downside from these settlements was that I had to defend them in the middle of a quest that I was playing.
The ingame mod system is very handy form people that are new to installing mods. Personally I still prefer Nexus, but that can be hard.
I own the season pass so I have all dlc’s. I’ll start about the workshop dlc’s. Unfortunately 3 out of the 6 were workshop dlc’s. I am disapointed because I expected 6 story dlc’s like Nuka world and Far Harbor. The workshop dlc’s added some extra building stuff, it feels like a microtransaction for extra furniture on a sims game.
Luckily there are 3 good Dlc’s, I start with Automatron. It was a short story dlc. It costed me 3 hours to complete, beware that I’m someone that wants to see everything before leaving a building. The ending was suprising, I didn’t expect that this was the outcome of Automatron. (This is a pro) I go further with my favourite Fallout dlc ever: Far Harbor. When I saw the trailer for this I thought that it was just a Point Lookout copy but it wasn’t. (For people that don’t know, Point Lookout is a Dlc in Fallout 3) Bethesda showed everyone they could still make an awesome RPG. Far Harbor has replayability. It has a very fun story and much choices. And last but not least Nuka World. This was a very fun Dlc. I’m a real Nuka Cola fan so this was my most anticipated Dlc for this game. It didn’t disapoint me. It was what I thought it was going to be. It has some secrets in the park so it is very fun to explore. A con was that you could only play as a bad guy.
This game was worth my money, the season pass too. Yes the roleplaying elements are almost gone but it still reached my level of expectation. In total I spend €70 for this game with Dlc. Everyone else seems to think that DS1 is the best in the series, but I'm not one of those people. Let me explain.
First of all, let's be honest, Dark Souls 1's graphics have definetly not aged well, especially considering it came out in 2011. Dark Souls 3 has beautiful landscapes, and areas with great atmosphere. In one area, you can see the ghosts of those who used to live there, and they aren't hostile or anything like that, but you actually find them throughout the game, and it gives you this sense of what someone (who I will not spoil) has done to them. In another place, you're in a dungeon, and you pass by cells filled with hollows, like the undead asylum, but better.
The combat seems to have taken a lesson from bloodborne, and feels a lot smoother than its' two predecessors. You're always on your toes, constantly dodging attacks and looking for openings to strike. There are rarely those akward DS2 moments when the boss would just kinda wait around to give you an estus window. The hitboxes feel much more refined, I was even able to dodge a bosses' attack once because my character's model is lowered during the attack animation. Although, in PVP, I couldn't help but notice that a lot of people buff around 2 times before each fight, and a lot of the time you'll just be strafing around each other. So watch out for that, I guess.
And the bosses. My god, the bosses in this game are so good. They seemed to have learned their lesson from the last two games, and I'm happy to say that although there are only 19 bosses in the base game, only one of them is a re-hashed boss from earlier in the game, but (spoiler alert) it's kinda like fighting the giant lord, except the boss is several times better, and the boss it's "based on" was already great to begin with. Out of the 19 bosses, there are only two or three that I would consider forgettable, even some of the easier ones. For example, do any of these bosses come to mind when you think of as being "memorable":
Centipede Demon
Taurus Demon
Iron Golen
Ceasless Discharge
Both of the Asylum Demon clones
Guardian Dragon
Flexile Sentry
Mytha
Oh yeah, and in case you couldn't tell, none of those were gank bosses, or from the DLC.
On the topic of gank bosses, although one of the worst bosses in DS3 is a gank boss, there is only one other main game gank boss, which is done amazingly. (oh yeah, and for you O&S fanboys, there's a boss pretty close to that in the DLC, and I'm not talking anything like the ruin sentinels.)
The main complaint against the game is it being easier than the other two games in the series, but for me, this is easy to overlook. No, this does not have to do with how bad I am, it actually has to do with the lack of BS areas and bosses. (although I must admit, the game could do without some of the shortcuts and bonfires.) For example, did you go through the depths thinking, "wow, this is a great area, I can't wait to go through this place again! I love the atmosphere!"? The answer is no, no you did not. How about, "Nito is such a fun boss! I really like how you get ganked by respawning skeletons!"? No? Okay then.
In Dark Souls 3, there was only one area that I didn't like. You'll know it when you find it. However, I can almost garuntee that unless you're underleveled or something, every boss will feel like a fair challange that relies on your skills as a player.
Overall, great game, have played through many times, will do again many more.

What's there to say? It's the 4th game in a venerated series. You're either a long-time fan that's played every game in the series and don't need a reason to buy this game, or you're new to the series and have probably already heard of how brutally difficult- yet rewarding- these games can be.
To start, the game is kind of easy compared to previous Souls games. Not that it's 'easy' in the conventional sense by any means, but there are very few bosses in this game that veterans would describe as 'hard'. Maybe this is the skewed perspective of long-time players, maybe not, all I know is that I had few difficulties with most of the bosses on my first playthrough.
But still, I highly recommend this game to new players and veterans alike. The combat has its flaws, but definitely shows improvements implemented from the years of experience that FromSoft has gained with designing these games. The graphics are pretty good for a game built for a console, with many beautiful scenic locations and a wide variety of arms and armor. And if there's one thing you should've heard about Souls games is that the boss music is beyond fantastic. Some people complain that there's no zone music, but that only serves to enhance the epicness of the boss themes.
The only downside to this game is that it should really be called "Dark Souls III: The Dark Soulsiest". I say that in jest, but the mind-numbing amount of references and fan service in this game is a double-edged sword. Either you've played every game and enjoy the references... up until the point where you're like "Miyazaki pls stop, pls, it's starting to get forced". Or, you're new and don't get them at all!
As a final word, and to thoroughly date this review, I just finished playing The Ashes of Ariandel DLC released today, which was in-part the thing that made me want to write a review. I'm an avid PvPer (500 hours of PvP in Dark Souls II can attest to that), but when I started playing this game on day 1, the PvP was... pretty bad. Broken weapons, cheesy builds and R1 spammers abounded. After my experience with the Bloodborne PvP (a laggy mess), I immediately gave up on this game's PvP in disgust.
Now, however, I'm happy to say that FromSoft has done a lot of balancing to improve the PvP... and more to the point, with the release of The Ashes of Ariandel DLC, they've added in an arena system that is extremely easy and convenient to access (albeit you have to do the DLC to get it). This new arena is the best thing to happen to a Souls game in a long time, and has reignited my love for Dark Souls PvP.
This game is definitely a must-buy, whether you're new to the series, or a long-time fan that's on the fence.

I have now played all Dark Souls titles (excluding Demon Souls & Bloodborne),  and I got to say: although this one holds your hand the most (in terms of fast travels to bonfires, loot, insanely OP weapon skills, etc), it ALSO challenges you the most.
Unlike DS1 and 2, I thoroughly felt invested each time I made a character to see them succeed, no matter the cost. And so far I have done so. With now over 300 hours into the game, I cannot say I don't recommend it. You need to buy this game and experience a Dark Souls journey.
And as for the DLC: Though Ashes of Ariendal was shorter than Ringed City, I still suggest getting both: as both DLC offer a huge learning curve in boss battles, AI enemies that'll wreck your sh*t m8, fantastic loot and more.
Although I have done just about everything in this game, I still find myself returning to Lothric to begin anew, again, and endure the death, mischieve, and thrill of Dark Souls 3.
Pros:
- Great graphics, even on the lowest settings! (I tried it even with low texture detail, still looks amazing)
- With lowest settings, playable for just about any PC with a half-decent, bottom-end GPU (albeit: a GTX 870, etc. etc.)
- Amazing combat system, with stances and skills assigned to each weapon (some recycled, but others suprisingly different/unique to anything else)
- Awesome boss fights (progressively get better as you progress the game)
- Skeletons
- Dragons
- Smooth AF attack schemes and combos from enemy AIs (can be considered a Con too, but this is seen as a pro because the other DS titles never really had enemies that performed attacks every so smoothly as in DS3)
- PVP is challengingly fun (sometimes frustrating, but not always)
- Huge and expansive levels (Unlike DS1 and 2).
- TONS of different AI's (some repeated later, but most regions have a wide variety of enemies)
- Best Dark Souls to start from (NOT easiest, but BEST)
(DLC)
- Great loot
- Arena Mode (YUSSSSSS!)
- INSANELY CHALLENGING BOSSES (after your +2 journey)
Cons:
- HItboxes can be dumb at times (which is fair, cuz its Dark Souls; more nitpicking really)
- BAD CONNECTIONS TO/FROM INVADERS = GANKED/INVINCIBILITY/HAX
- Minor bugs every now and then (warped through walls and die under the map when hitting an illusion wall)
- Does not cooperate with some software graphical settings (NVIDIA, AMD, etc.), such as Crossfire or FreeSync. (Mine used to work with crossfire on, which was fine, but now it drops FPS like crazy. Thankfully, my GPU can handle 2K Resolution @ 60fps with Crossfire disabled)

As a Fallout fan this was my most anticipated game of 2015. So when I got the game I was very curious if it was a fantastic game like Fallout 3 and New vegas.:
Info about my save:
I currently played this game over 190 hours on the time that I’m writing this review, so I really played it. I completed all quests and all dlc’s. Was it worth it? Yes but if I restart the game, everything will be te same. This is a big con. The main reason I buy Bethesda games is that I can replay the game at least 2 time and having 2 different stories. This one failed on this. Yet my first/current save was better than other Fallouts. The reason it does not have that replayabilty is that there are almost no RPG elements in the game anymore, Bethesda wanted that we would see everything in one playthrough. This is not in Skyrim. I’m playing Skyrim and I still see things that I have never seen.
The graphics are amazing for a Fallout. I mean, the graphics are not on The Witcher 3 level but they are decent. Some addition that I liked is the volumetric lightning also known as god rays.
The gameplay is awesome, in this long road I never questioned myself if I liked the fast paced action that this Fallout contains. Bethesda really focused on the gunplay aspect. You got customization on all weapons. The FOV is good. (some people complained about it)
The story is better than the other Fallouts, it has more emotion and sometimes those little sounds make the change. Fallout 4 is about a parent (You) finding his/her son.
The building in Fallout 4 was something I wanted a long time since I installed a mod in fallout 3 and new vegas. It works very nice. The only downside from these settlements was that I had to defend them in the middle of a quest that I was playing.
The ingame mod system is very handy form people that are new to installing mods. Personally I still prefer Nexus, but that can be hard.
I own the season pass so I have all dlc’s. I’ll start about the workshop dlc’s. Unfortunately 3 out of the 6 were workshop dlc’s. I am disapointed because I expected 6 story dlc’s like Nuka world and Far Harbor. The workshop dlc’s added some extra building stuff, it feels like a microtransaction for extra furniture on a sims game.
Luckily there are 3 good Dlc’s, I start with Automatron. It was a short story dlc. It costed me 3 hours to complete, beware that I’m someone that wants to see everything before leaving a building. The ending was suprising, I didn’t expect that this was the outcome of Automatron. (This is a pro) I go further with my favourite Fallout dlc ever: Far Harbor. When I saw the trailer for this I thought that it was just a Point Lookout copy but it wasn’t. (For people that don’t know, Point Lookout is a Dlc in Fallout 3) Bethesda showed everyone they could still make an awesome RPG. Far Harbor has replayability. It has a very fun story and much choices. And last but not least Nuka World. This was a very fun Dlc. I’m a real Nuka Cola fan so this was my most anticipated Dlc for this game. It didn’t disapoint me. It was what I thought it was going to be. It has some secrets in the park so it is very fun to explore. A con was that you could only play as a bad guy.
This game was worth my money, the season pass too. Yes the roleplaying elements are almost gone but it still reached my level of expectation. In total I spend €70 for this game with Dlc. This was the best adventure I have ever had. This a very good Fallout and it will be a gem to some people and some people will say that it is a flop because of the lack of RPG.
My rating: 10/10

I know the Dark Souls series is notious for "insane diffiuclty" and "frustratingly impossible enemies"  but i am here to tell you the truth about DS3.
As someone who only did one run through of DS2, and who cried in a corner the moment i even touched Bloodborne, I can honestly say that I have a pretty decent background with From Software's beloved series.
DS3 really does feel a bit impossible at first if you are a mediocre gamer (like me) or new to the series.  The tutorial boss easily felt like a near impossible hurdle for me when I first booted the game up.  I think I clocked nearly 20 deaths before I finally beat him.  Five characters and 250 hours later I can easily say that I laugh at that boss now.
I tell this story because it is easily the best way to describe the Dark Souls experience.... IT GETS BETTER.... Or should I say; YOU get better.
Playing with others, even randoms, makes the game that much more bearable and this third installment does a better job that is predecessors at balancing frustration and reward.
If you're on the fence about this title, all I can really say is give it a shot.  YES it can be difficult, but its not the "impossible to beat super niche" game that I think the Souls community sometimes tries to make them out to be.

The gunplay is nice. The crafting and armors and weapons are all nice. The world is neat to explore.
But damned if I don't have a laundry list of problems with this game.
The protagonist and main story is kind of boring, all the dialogue options are severely limited to the point of making conversation in this game irrelevant, theres very few interesting, non-generated world quests. After a while, the game just starts to feel boring and repetitive.
Maybe that wouldn't even be a problem if it wasn't supposed to be a Fallout game. In most previous interations of the series, it stressed being able to approach situations a variety of ways and playing the game in different ways. But it doesn't really feel like theres a need to do that in this game since all the conversation options feel basically arbitrary all most quest are randomly generated "go and shoot these guys".
Even the new perks system feels boring and unvaried. It feels like very few things in it actually alter the way you play the game.
Maybe if I wanted to play a game about going and shooting dudes that would be okay, but not what I wanted out of a Fallout game.
TL:DR
Pros: Exploration, Gunplay
Cons: Uninteresting dialogue, meaningless choices, eventually repetitive gameplay, perk system not fun.
"Go Play New Vegas Instead" out of Ten.
EDIT!:
This edit is occuring a few months after the initial review.
Perhaps at the time I was being unfair to Fallout 4. Do I enjoy the game? Not as much as I'd like, but I still think I should give a stronger points in its favor for fairness.
While you are hit with procedurely generated quest pretty early in the game, not all of the quests are like this. In fact, a lot of the world still has the quirky humor that the Fallout series is loved for, with things such as the Silver Shroud or USS Constitution quests. And some features in the game are improvements from previous interations, such as the power armor, crafting or armor systems in the game.
Don't get me wrong, I love the Fallout series and I do appreciate some of the steps this game was trying to take, I just think some of the things worked out better than others. I just think some of the things Bethesda tried to accomplish resulted in a game that didn't quite feel Fallout to me.
Also:
A lot of people have pointed out that I haven't played enough of the game to really get a full grasp of what I'm talking about.
I do sympathize with your point: I should be willing to explore more aspects of a game before writting it off.
But at the same time, if I'm 20 hours into a game and still think my over all impression is moderate enjoyment at best, then that probably has more to do with my personal tastes in games.

Draft #1 for Review.
*SPOILERS*
Fallout 4 is a masterpiece of ideological storytelling, a wonderfully-crafted open world game, a great shooter, a watered down AAA RPG, and the worst FALLOUT game since Brotherhood of Steel...allegedly.
Ideologic Storytelling:

Fallout 4 begins its Introduction with the repeated phrase, "War Never Changes." Throughout the game we encounter Individuals, Groups, and Factions that are all at war with something.
-The Minutemen are at war with threats to the Commonwealth's common man.
-Covenant is at war with The Institute
-The Brotherhood is at war with threats to pure-humans (Hck* Enclave *Hck)
-Piper is at war with deception
-Hancock and Nick Valentine and Kasumi and Danse and ect. Are at war with their Identity
-The Railroad is at war with INSTITUTIONALIZED *haha* Racism
-The Institute is at war with everyone.

Now the wars that are waged are hardly the interesting points of contingency. What makes the peoples of the Commonwealth so interesting is the Why(s), the How(s), and how this in-turn relates to the player character in terms of the story; Man/Woman looking for child, or, how it relates to you in terms of your personal beliefs and thoughts. You may have found yourself genuinely compelled by the downtrodden survivors of Quincy, or the boots on the ground soldiers of the Brotherhood, or the freedom fighters of the Railroad, or even the institute's belief in human transcendence.
Constantly the game engages you with encounters that either challenge, or reaffirm your current beliefs on the major philosophic arguments the game tries to make, directly or indirectly:
-What Constitutes as a Automaton, or a Person?
-Is Humanity strictly superior to other forms of life?
-What is the role of leadership, and the individual?
-Do the ends justify the means?
-Who is indisputably the most important person in Vault 101: He who shelters us from the harshness of the atomic wasteland, and to whom we owe everything we have, including our lives?
Where you fall on these topics will push you toward furthering the goals of these Factions and Characters, and if you're anything like me, you will finish the games multiple times without feeling truly satisfied with your decisions.. but it keeps me playing, and it keeps me thinking... 10/10
The Open World:

If you've played a Bethesda Game Studios game, you know how much environmental storytelling exists. Fallout 4 continues this tradition, and arguably out-does the precursors to this title. I remember soberly, exploring Warwicks Homestead on my 2nd-3rd playthrough. At this point I was aware that Daddy Warwick was indeed a replacement, but I did not expect what I saw; Behind the sewage machinery, you can find children's toys. There were 3 letter blocks... reading the blocks "BYE" was written.. and I teared up.
I think this method of storytelling is one of the most compelling things in this game, and it allows you to see something you've seen 20 times in a different light. It's very cool, Tunnel Snakes rule.
It's in the Game:
The moment-to-moment combat is utterly satisfying.
You shoot a guy/gal in the head, where did their head go?
You smoke some scooby-snacks, everyone slows to a crawl as you Barry Allen your way through 10 Raiders.
You want to be Solid Snake? Get some Shadowed Leather Armor and put guns to the back of Genome Soliders.
You don't like the way that MURDERING, KIDNAPPING, PSYCHOPATH stole your son shaun.. Shoot him with a Fat-man.
Gunplay feels great, VATS is still OP, Weapon mods and legendary effects lead to shenannigans*. Enemy AI, while still very exploitable, has become much more responsive to your fighting tactics. A pack of ghouls running at you can be genuinely terrifying. A raider taking cover, and then charging you when you reload. There are many possiblities in combat for very engaging, frustrating, glorious, and hilarious moments.
I like it.
I am not Commander Sheppard:
Alright, this is where everything goes downhill. The Voiced-Protaganist does a good job. The Dialog wheel works as intended. Never do this again Todd Howard. Within the first 30 minutes of Fallout: 3 the other day, I had:
-Told a bully his mother was fat
-Told a bully he was a coward, and let his mom get eaten in front of him
-Told my best friend that I was glad I slaughtered her father, and that she was next if she got in my way.
-asked a ex-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if she still offered her services
-Told a Sheriff he looked stupid
-Screamed at a ghoul
-Slept with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
-Told a Beggar i'd give him water, then said "Just kidding"
-Detonated a Nuclear Bomb.
Every single one of those dialogs and choices were optional, and did not further the main plot. Fallout 4 pours so much energy into tying everything into the plot, that the world is devoid of interesting, and possibly inconsequencial choices to enhance the roleplaying. Fallout 4 tries to make you be the character "The Sole Survivor", Just as you were "The Dovahkiin" in skyrim. An overly important character is overly strung along character.
In Oblivion, you were not, "The Last son of the Septim Empire". You were a lucky prisoner who found yourself tied into the intrigue of the kingdom. This allowed you to be whoever you wanted to be, "Live Another Life in Another World". Fallout 4 Suffers as an RPG because it tries too hard to be an Action Adventure game.
I don't like it.
Fallout, more like... Post-Appocolypse Shooter #42:
Final Point, this game is hardly Fallout.
Fallout: 1 is a game about the Necessity of Water , and the inhabitants of the wasteland
Fallout: 2 is a game about Civilization rebuilding, and the different Factions
Fallout: 3 is a game about The Necessity of Water, and the inhabitants of the wasteland

Now, a important parallel that makes Fallout:4 like Fallout:3 is the Concept of Family, American History, and the Father and the Son. (Mother/son, Father/Daughter)... The important distinction, however, is that Fallout:3, as well as all preceding Fallout games... are completely bonkers.

The biggest upside?  There is no real end to the game, just the main story line—something I wished the previous games had included.  Another big upside?  The number of companions you can choose from, and thereby change the way you play the game.  Let’s face it, you play differently with Nick the detective than you do with Piper the reporter or Dogmeat.  Another upside? Originally, I was intimidated by the dark souls series. From the "git gud" culture, to the add campaigns which make note of the games difficulty.
It is not that bad. If you persist, and are willing to die a few (or more) times, the game can be overcome by any average player. Dark souls 3 tends to reward observation and experimentation. The game tries to go out of its way to give you hints. For example, in the preceding level, you will often find items that buff your weapon with the element that the boss is weak to. Worse comes to worse, you can always summon.
So, if we ignore difficulty, why should you play? It is one of the best action rpgs to date. The game will constantly present new challenges, keeping you engaged. Due to the amount of depth to the combat system, this can continue to hold you over multiple replays of the game. And while the leveling system will be underwhelming at first, you will eventually enjoy the flexibility offered by it.
And of course there is the rush you get from taking down a boss for the first time. Because sometimes that boss can be pretty damn hard.

Dark Souls 3 is another great entry into the souls series. While I enjoyed Dark Souls 2, this game brings a lot from the first game back and I really love that they did that.
Postitves:
+ Beautiful world with great level design to go with them
+ Tough and unique bosses (if you're experienced in Dark Souls, the first few may feel easy, but they get tougher fast)
+ It's faster paced than usual, but not Bloodborne fast. It allows for a balance of defence and offence play styles
+ All the challenge that the souls games are known for is still here and it's amazing
Mixed:
+- The PC port has few technical issues. It runs at 60 most of the time but does suffer from stuttering in some places
Negatives:
- Don't know why they would keep the whole teleport to hub to level up from DS2. It's annoying
- Because the world isn't interconnected anymore, the early game progression is very linear compared to previous games
- Can't upgrade armors anymore. So now it's a battle between fashion and stats and I hate that
- They went back to DS1's NG+ where enemies have more health and do more damage instead of how DS2 added new enemies and enemy placements and overall making the game feel different with each playthrough
Overall, this is a great Dark Souls game. If you are a fan of the souls series, I strongly recommend this game. If you are new, it's still a great place to start although you might be lost when learning about the lore.

Dark Souls 3- Pre DLC- Post Axe/Hammer/GS update.
Coming up to my 100 hour mark, I wanted to make a review before the DLC was pushed out. Dark Souls 3 is one of my favorite games in the series, and one of my favorite games of all time.
Positive Things
The PVE is very well made, every enemy seems unique and can be hard until you learn them, and there are tons and tons of enemies. From knights, to giant crabs, to ninja skeletons throwing knives everywhere, the enemies are far from the same. Every area feels unique and interesting, we have castles, swamps, fiery lakes, mountain peaks, and many more. There are TONS of different weapons to choose from, and almost every class of weapons is completely unique and awesome. I can say there are only 3 weapon classes you would never in your right mind use, and around 15-20 more. Now for the mechanics. DS3 does not have the traditional "poise" system of the last 2 installments. Poise, for you newcomers, is a mechanic in DS1 and 2 that made it so the heavier armor you wear, the more hits you can take before getting staggered. This made heavy armors a little too strong, and was removed. Now, poise is only activated when you swing your weapon. Depending on the size of your weapon, you will get more or less poise from the swing. What this does is promote really fast-paced risky playstyles, and discourages the tank heavy builds. Some like it, some hate it, but it more or less doesn't change the game all that much. You can still use heavy armor, but it will rely on a heavy weapon for poise now. Now for the bosses. Most of the bosses in this game are humanoid looking, but they all have different fighting styles. Some weird gigantic halberds, some dual wield greatswords, some switch weapons every 20 seconds to keep you on your toes. I really like the bosses in DS3, and think that they are pretty close to the difficulty of the DS1 bosses save for a couple.
The music in this game is utterly breathtaking, every boss's theme makes it feel like an awesome showdown against a great being of power, it enhancing the experience quite a bit.
Now for things I dislike in DS3. This game is a straight line from start to finish. There is a total of 2 times you can do one or two areas early, but that's it. The game is stupidly linear compared to past installments. Faster weapons are very powerful, and can stunlock people if they haven't practiced fighting them, making spam attacking very common in this game. The covenants in the game are very shallow and don't offer much difference to gameplay at all. There are 3 hidden areas, which is nothing compared to past games. Pretty much every weapon is good on the same "quality" build (40 STR 40 DEX) and there is little variety when it comes to builds because of this. The PVP called invasions is utterly horrendous compared to past versions. The person invading has around 16 disadvantages and has the smallest chance in the world if they don't use one of 3 solid invasion builds. Auto Summon covenants are ok except for one, which you have a better chance to get struck by lightning then to get summoned with. Shields are also complete crap in this game, they can block 1-2 hits before exposing you to a critical riposte attack which against other players is generally an instant kill. The only Shield that can block a good amount of hits is the Greatshield of Glory found in the Profaned Capital. Only problem with this shield? It weighs more than most everything else in the game by far. Also, you can roll 20-30 times in a row, which may not be negative if you want to be Sonic the Hedgehog.
Regardless of its many flaws, I love Dark Souls 3, and will continue to play it for years to come. It is probably the easiest starting point for new arrivals as well, I completely recommend it if you are new to the series. I'll see you on the field of battle my fellow Ashen Ones!!!
Overall, I give the game an 8.5/10

I know the Dark Souls series is notious for "insane diffiuclty" and "frustratingly impossible enemies"  but i am here to tell you the truth about DS3.
As someone who only did one run through of DS2, and who cried in a corner the moment i even touched Bloodborne, I can honestly say that I have a pretty decent background with From Software's beloved series.
DS3 really does feel a bit impossible at first if you are a mediocre gamer (like me) or new to the series.  The tutorial boss easily felt like a near impossible hurdle for me when I first booted the game up.  I think I clocked nearly 20 deaths before I finally beat him.  Five characters and 250 hours later I can easily say that I laugh at that boss now.
I tell this story because it is easily the best way to describe the Dark Souls experience.... IT GETS BETTER.... Or should I say; YOU get better.
Playing with others, even randoms, makes the game that much more bearable and this third installment does a better job that is predecessors at balancing frustration and reward.
If you're on the fence about this title, all I can really say is give it a shot.  YES it can be difficult, but its not the "impossible to beat super niche" game that I think the Souls community sometimes tries to make them out to be.

Originally, I was intimidated by the dark souls series. From the "git gud" culture, to the add campaigns which make note of the games difficulty.
It is not that bad. If you persist, and are willing to die a few (or more) times, the game can be overcome by any average player. Dark souls 3 tends to reward observation and experimentation. The game tries to go out of its way to give you hints. For example, in the preceding level, you will often find items that buff your weapon with the element that the boss is weak to. Worse comes to worse, you can always summon.
So, if we ignore difficulty, why should you play? It is one of the best action rpgs to date. The game will constantly present new challenges, keeping you engaged. Due to the amount of depth to the combat system, this can continue to hold you over multiple replays of the game. And while the leveling system will be underwhelming at first, you will eventually enjoy the flexibility offered by it.
And of course there is the rush you get from taking down a boss for the first time. Because sometimes that boss can be pretty damn hard.

While still a reasonable game, Fallout 4 was a letdown compared to Fallout 3. As somebody who loved 3 and has played it over and over for several years, 4 alters the formula in a way that will only appeal to certain gamers. Some of the most notable differences include: No weapon maintenance. In 4, weapons have magically become eternally non-maintenance. You never have to repair weapons, armor, anything. Instead, you get to mod stuff. This might be fun for those that like such things, but I'm not one.
Next, there are no level caps. While on the surface this might seem like a good thing, it leads to "lazy gaming". You don't have consider very hard where you spend your level up points, because if you play long enough, you'll get everything.
Worst of all is the Sim-City-esque need build and maintain establishments. As somebody who has never been a fan of Sim-type games, this is as tedious as it gets. "Quests" include saving the same sorry establishments from the same threats over and over and over.
In short, this is a game that tried to add elements that don't improve the enormous, yet still tightly constructed game that 3 was. Get this game on sale and play it through once. That's all I did, and I have no desire to go back to it.

I've played so much of this game (In F4SE, mind you) that I can't possibly say that I don't recommend it.  Sure, it isn't as "true to the franchise" as New Vegas, but in my honest opinion it is just as much fun.
Get in there, because as a wise man once said: A settlement needs your help!

Compared to Fallout 3, some important RPG elements were taken away (i.e. skills), and you simply choose a perk when you level up.
There are tons of awesome locations, but it often ends up with simply killing all the enemies there.
Having said that, I do feel that it's still a great game: there are lots of things to do, and while quests are not as deep as the ones in New Vegas, there are plenty of them. The companion characters are well thought-out and engaging. The settlement building adds a new dimension to the game. The graphics are awesome and the world by itself is pretty diverse and rewarding to explore.
So overall, I'd definitely recommend the game. 60 EUR might be a price too high though, better wait when it's discounted (30 or 40 EUR).
