The gunplay is massively improved from Fallout 3(I also picked that one up recently, so I can compare the two), I like the basebuilding, commanding my settlers, I even like the storylines.
Don't buy if you're into RPGs that are actually RPGs, don't buy it with the expectation that it'll be what Fallout used to be. If you want a decent post-apocalyptic shooter, with streamlined leveling, go for it.

I am going to share a recent experience I had with this game, which may outline my impression of it more clearly than an attempt at a concise review.
While traversing this unforgiving wasteland in the post apocalyptic future, I came across a series of portable fallout shelters with bodies scattered about. Seemingly, surviving for a period of time and finally emerging to find a nice glass food dispenser in the center, with one perfect piece of pie at the top. I imagine they were starving after hiding in those mini bunkers for what felt like a lifetime. Upon emerging, I bet they saw this pie as their salvation! But, why was the pie intact? I attempted to retrieve this tasty prize, imagining how torturous it might have been watching this slow retrieval claw delivering it to several starving people anxiously awaiting sustainance. It failed, however, ever close to the tips of their fingers. Time and time again, the little metal claw picks at the pie, only to leave it gleaming and perfect behind the glass. I imagine, given the scene, they all died in starvation, or killing each other to see who would get it first, while the pie safely watches in safety, forever preserved behind this faulty vending machine. I bet it would have been delicious, I wondered, as I walked away chewing on my iguana-on-a-stick.
I love this game.
Seriously though, I am a long-time fan of the series. I played the original fallout on a Windows 95 machine at my friends house, deeply immersed in the situation. Alone, wandering out of the vault, looking around every corner for something to attack me whiile constantly being aware of what little I have to survive. What became of this world, and what horrors await me while I try and save my people? I played each sequel over the years as they were released, eager to discover the remains of humanity, and finding ways to better prepare myself to survive it.
This feeling remains intact in Fallout 4, deeply immersing you in a rich, almost endless world to explore. I have played this game through, from character creation to each alternate ending, coming up on 4 times now and I still find things I have not noticed from one play through to the next. A cabin in the woods, an encounter in an alley while scouring the remains of a city, a secret cache of supplies underneath a once bustling boardwalk.
There are attractions for many kinds of players here, yet my favorite feature is managing the settlements. Even if the primary narrative was not present, I would still enjoy this game as a "post apolacyptic settlement survival simulator". I thorougly enjoyed unlocking each settlement, scoping out the possibilities of defense and resource generation. Overcoming the obstacles each location provides, and picking my favorites out to spend hours setting up every detail.
One of my favorite projects was setting up a proper pool table in my shopping center I created in my hometown of Sanctuary. I had a jukebox playing, a bar set up with scavenged booze carefully placed on the shelf behind the bartender. I had a pool table set up on the opposite side with pool cues, and a complete set of pool balls I scoured the wasteland for, finally completing my collection after looting many, many establishments over my adventures. (though, I did later find a full intact set in a preserved location you may have discovered as well). I looked forward to each return trip home, appreciating my little respite from the horrors outside.
Beyond that, this is a great shooter, and a fantastic RPG.
Many will argue it is not perfect (Oh gee, tell me more problems a settlement has Preston. I just came back to grab my Power Armor, leave me alone!), but many works of art are not about perfection. It's about a vision and an experience than an artist, or several artists in the case, has toiled over for your enjoyment. I noticed the extreme level of detail and dedication to immerse the player in this rich world, and this game remains among my favorite of all 30+ years I have been a gamer. While not for everyone, this game does have much to offer many kinds of players, if you buckle in, turn the lights low, and breathe in the radiation while you enjoy adventuring through the wasteland that is the commonwealth.
Edit: I originally purchased on the PS4, and only recently bought this on sale on the PC. I did not have a proper gaming system at the time, thoroughly enjoying my 4th playthrough. Dude. Aiming with a mouse is way easier, and it was nice cranking up the graphics.

Certainly the most disappointing of all the fallout games. Gameplay itself is still fun, and the UI will be familiar to anyone who's played the previous games, but the story is insultingly bad. Where New Vegas gave you the freedom to be whatever kind of person you wanted to play, and the story supported that, #4 railroads you from the very beginning to be a specific type of person doing one utterly unambiguous job. Your only choices are which group you ally with to accomplish that job, and the amount of attitude in your responses while you are railroaded along a linear path regardless of how ridiculous the available responses would be for a person in that situation, even if you chose to play the one type of character that they force you to be. Yes, it's even worse than Fallout 3 ever was.
Their token addition of base-building and the massive expansion of crafting in the game adds very little value to actual play, and the utter lack of agency in the "settlers" that populate your bases means that you spend more time caring for them like disabled infants than doing any actual adventuring or pursuing the poorly conceived plot. The tremendous number of development hours spent implementing those features could have been better spent on competent writers and real variety of choice in play (also a substantial investment to implement).

Dark Souls III gets a huge thumbs up from me.  I just finished the game and was overall impressed and satisfied. I would say this one is better than the second and in some ways the first but it's a little unfair to really compare it with the first because the entry into the series felt so fresh and uncharted; at least to those like myself that never played Demon's Souls for PS3.
The combat is fantastic and that's the core element to the game along with exploration, finding equipment, making your way to the next bonfire (checkpoint), and of course epic boss fights.  All done nicely with a fluid 60fps. Great graphics and not too system intensive.
The level design is a big improvement over the second one. The levels seem to tie in a little more seemlessly. The game is tough but you can always summon a real life player or NPC for help.  The online system seems like it has better netcode than the previous two.  All in all, a great wrap up to the Dark Souls Trilogy.

The gunplay is massively improved from Fallout 3(I also picked that one up recently, so I can compare the two), I like the basebuilding, commanding my settlers, I even like the storylines.
Don't buy if you're into RPGs that are actually RPGs, don't buy it with the expectation that it'll be what Fallout used to be. If you want a decent post-apocalyptic shooter, with streamlined leveling, go for it.

I am going to share a recent experience I had with this game, which may outline my impression of it more clearly than an attempt at a concise review.
While traversing this unforgiving wasteland in the post apocalyptic future, I came across a series of portable fallout shelters with bodies scattered about. Seemingly, surviving for a period of time and finally emerging to find a nice glass food dispenser in the center, with one perfect piece of pie at the top. I imagine they were starving after hiding in those mini bunkers for what felt like a lifetime. Upon emerging, I bet they saw this pie as their salvation! But, why was the pie intact? I attempted to retrieve this tasty prize, imagining how torturous it might have been watching this slow retrieval claw delivering it to several starving people anxiously awaiting sustainance. It failed, however, ever close to the tips of their fingers. Time and time again, the little metal claw picks at the pie, only to leave it gleaming and perfect behind the glass. I imagine, given the scene, they all died in starvation, or killing each other to see who would get it first, while the pie safely watches in safety, forever preserved behind this faulty vending machine. I bet it would have been delicious, I wondered, as I walked away chewing on my iguana-on-a-stick.
I love this game.
Seriously though, I am a long-time fan of the series. I played the original fallout on a Windows 95 machine at my friends house, deeply immersed in the situation. Alone, wandering out of the vault, looking around every corner for something to attack me whiile constantly being aware of what little I have to survive. What became of this world, and what horrors await me while I try and save my people? I played each sequel over the years as they were released, eager to discover the remains of humanity, and finding ways to better prepare myself to survive it.
This feeling remains intact in Fallout 4, deeply immersing you in a rich, almost endless world to explore. I have played this game through, from character creation to each alternate ending, coming up on 4 times now and I still find things I have not noticed from one play through to the next. A cabin in the woods, an encounter in an alley while scouring the remains of a city, a secret cache of supplies underneath a once bustling boardwalk.
There are attractions for many kinds of players here, yet my favorite feature is managing the settlements. Even if the primary narrative was not present, I would still enjoy this game as a "post apolacyptic settlement survival simulator". I thorougly enjoyed unlocking each settlement, scoping out the possibilities of defense and resource generation. Overcoming the obstacles each location provides, and picking my favorites out to spend hours setting up every detail.
One of my favorite projects was setting up a proper pool table in my shopping center I created in my hometown of Sanctuary. I had a jukebox playing, a bar set up with scavenged booze carefully placed on the shelf behind the bartender. I had a pool table set up on the opposite side with pool cues, and a complete set of pool balls I scoured the wasteland for, finally completing my collection after looting many, many establishments over my adventures. (though, I did later find a full intact set in a preserved location you may have discovered as well). I looked forward to each return trip home, appreciating my little respite from the horrors outside.
Beyond that, this is a great shooter, and a fantastic RPG.
Many will argue it is not perfect (Oh gee, tell me more problems a settlement has Preston. I just came back to grab my Power Armor, leave me alone!), but many works of art are not about perfection. It's about a vision and an experience than an artist, or several artists in the case, has toiled over for your enjoyment. I noticed the extreme level of detail and dedication to immerse the player in this rich world, and this game remains among my favorite of all 30+ years I have been a gamer. While not for everyone, this game does have much to offer many kinds of players, if you buckle in, turn the lights low, and breathe in the radiation while you enjoy adventuring through the wasteland that is the commonwealth.
Edit: I originally purchased on the PS4, and only recently bought this on sale on the PC. I did not have a proper gaming system at the time, thoroughly enjoying my 4th playthrough. Dude. Aiming with a mouse is way easier, and it was nice cranking up the graphics.

Fallout 4 did a lot of things right, it has the best combat of any Bethesda game to date. The improvements over the previous games are numerous and substantial. Movement and attacks are that little bit more responsive.
You can build settlements, craft weapons and armor, mod weapons and armor, play in hardcord mode, the shooting is infinitely better, and power armor is the game actually feels unique, not just another armor with different stats and appearance. The companions are amazing, they generally felt unique and were not a pain to deal with. They had individual stories, often times could provide helpful advice or commentary, and are a huge step up from the companions in skryim and fallout 3.
The main problem with fallout 4 is that in a few key areas there is a lack of depth. Other gameplay mechanics or story elements like dialogue and skill checks have been removed or greatly simplified. As such, more than ever these games require good combat to remain satisfying and engaging to play, and while Fallout 4’s improvements are welcome I feel as though more are still needed.
Settlement building was clearly designed to be a huge time sink in the game because on my second playthrough I skipped all settlement building and finished the game almost 4-5 times faster. They clearly really liked the real time settler mod and it really did make sense in the fallout universe that your character might go out of their way to build or support towns. It makes even more sense given the minutemen's story and background. Building massive cities and fortifications is great and most of the DLCs added things to the settlement builder.
If that was the case you'd think that they would put a bit more effort into making sure you enjoy it. From a creativity perspective you can't share your creations with others or download things others have made. That's pretty much a standard now for games with custom buildings and designs and I wish they had incorporated it here. Settlements are also buggy. Settlers won't listen to orders, random game physics will screw up, enemies will spawn in the middle of your town, and your town will randomly not produce food, water, or happiness if you go too far away/
The other thing is how little difference building settlements ultimately makes. Turning someone into a settler actually makes them more boring. NPCs in the premade towns walking around, talk to others, interact with others, and have interesting dialogue and backstories. Once you make them a settler they gently caress plants all day, pound an perpetually broken walls, and if you built a bar they all go stand enmass near the bar. They don't sit in chairs, chat with each other, or even utilize the majority of your town. There are some mods that attempt to fix this but even with them your own towns and settlers feel... empty and lifeless. That doesn't even get into how little it impacts the world overall. You can build settlements everywhere across fallout 4. What does that get you? Some minor perks involving summoning support but in exchange you get nearly infinite requests for settlements needing your help. I can't tell you how many times I show up to a settlement under attack just to see 6 raiders get mowed down by a bunch of lasers and turrets. If you don't show up then even with max defense score your town only has a 50% chance of repelling the attack... what a joke. I can't tell you how annoying settlements are in hardcore mode.
Other than settlements there are many other things which lack depth. There are a lot of areas you visit which seemed to be... unfinished. You can tell they wanted to do more with certain areas but either ran out of time or money. An area where you recruit a certain redheaded companion comes to mind. The gun and armor system is great but there's a definite lack of diversity. There is a distinct lack of diverse enemies and areas. Most enemies are either raiders or just reflavored raiders (mercenaries, etc...). There are a lot of nice small details you can find on the map but they are really easy to miss among the endless hordes of pipe rifles, combat rifles, and laser rifles.
Overall its a fun game, I wish there was more depth but I've played the game for over 150 hours so I guess I can't complain too much. Like most Bethesda games, a lot of its problems are fixed with mods but I wish they couldn't use that as a crutch. Additionally the mods will never fix certain things like the lack of depth. This is made more difficult by the fact that your player character speaks. It was an interesting feature but it definitely makes adding more quests extremely difficult.
You get more choices and a better story than skyrim but you don't get the level of influence over the story you did in New Vegas. The smooth gameplay and overall atmosphere still make it a fun game. Its a good game, that suffers a lot of criticism largely due to high expectations but the game's detractors do have valid points.

Pros:
Survival mode is an intense experience for hardcore players.
The DLC (story DLC, anyways) is fantastic.
Balance as a whole has improved over previous Fallout titles. Granted, that's not saying much, but it's still a welcome improvement.
Fantastic armor system, in how armor is equipped, what kind of armor there is, and how damage resistance works in this game. (I'm not going to go into great detail about how damage resistance works, if you want to know all the details about it you can google it, but the basics involve having high damage values being reduced less than low damage values and having no armor level cap, similar to Fallout New Vegas and completely unlike Fallout 3 and Skyrim.)
A good amount of mods.
Cons:
Many missed opportunities, especially in the main story.
Skill checks in the base game are quite lacking in comparisson to previous fallouts.
Conclusion:
It's very different from previous Fallouts, so just because you enjoyed those doesn't necessarily mean you'll enjoy this one. It has its flaws and strengths, but given the amount of hours of entertainment this game could give you, I'd certainly encourage people to consider it.

So one thing you have to know of course is that this is a "Souls Game". A lot of the negative reviews complain about the difficulty but that's just how it is with these games. At the same time though, It's within the first tags of the game that it's difficult so these people should have known what to expect. So basically: Yes, the game is difficult but that's what a lot of players like about the game especially because it's hard in a very "fair" way. When you die, it's your fault so git gud.
With that out of the way I can say that this is a very fun game with good replay value. The graphics are good and there is a lot of content, a lot of which can be optional or hidden. The PvP is something where everyone has a different opinion. When I started playing, I didn't like it and just wanted to play the game by myself without Invasions or Co-op and so on but after playing for longer and trying it out more, I can see why they kept it and what people like about it so much.
Now there is one more thing that I want to mention and this goes especially to those who played the previous Dark Souls games. This game is a good mix between the old Dark Souls and what the developers did in their other game Bloodborne.
So what you'll notice is that this game is a lot faster and dynamic the the previous titles. Your rolls are quicker and enemies are too. Bosses also behave differently now, they are much faster and more aggresive and timing and precision is more important now.
I've played Dark Souls 1 and I do have to say that this is a very big difference but to be honest I like it a lot more. I feels better and I'm glad that From Software tried to bring something new into the series.
The old Dark Souls gameplay was ok and the quick and agile gameplay from bloodborne is really good too, this game has the best of both worlds and it's great!

UPDATE 1/20/17:
Okay, I figure I placed enough time on this game to actually give it a semi-serious review.  Lemme start with something that is stated all the time but Steam really needs a neutral reaction to reviews because ultimately that is how I feel about this game.
Why?  Well, I played the Souls games since DS1 and over the course of two sequels (and a ostracized golden child) I have found that this is quite a disappointment in comparison to the what the other Souls games have offered.
My main beef is really the level design.  Clearly you can see from the get go that this game has been designed to be straightforward as heck.  There is some alternations from the path but ultimately they still have you going back on the line to the game's story progression with most of the areas in this game being short to push that fact in your mind further (Profaned Capital anyone?).  I will also tell you that the design for most of these places are frankly just too bland and leaves a lot to be desired and out of all the souls games this probably has the least favorable level design.
That all said, for a Souls game this is probably the most polished in terms of combat mechanics.
The attacks feel so natural and not as clunky as previous games.  You can almost feel the impact of a Zwei pancaking an Estoc user so well but...yeah you get the point.
On the other side of the coin though they have (sort of) removed Poise.  Now they have it working so that it is more weapon based than armor really and that really doesn't bother me that much.  Clearly you can tell that they just adopted the same fighting style as used in BB where hitting fast is your key to winning most fights.  It makes the combat to DSIII a tad bit interesting and it made me rethink the way I should handle most fights in PvE so honestly this a YMMV situation here.
They also nailed the atmosphere in this game once again with the feeling of the end weighing you down every time you advance seeing the decrepit state of Lothric after so many have fallen to continue linking the flame.  Seeing that eclipse slowly leak the abyss onto the world really solidified it there that we are all ♥♥♥♥ed.
DSIII may leave a lot to be desired but in the end it is still a Souls game and it keeps what I love about the series: Thick atmosphere, rewarding combat, tons of items and fighting massive bosses but all in a package that is short in stature.

Visually and control-wise probably the best in the series, despite combat being heavily influenced by Bloodborne.
But the game is far from perfect, the linear approach to progression means that you have less options to explore the game's world, only a couple of areas have small side areas and those are dead ends as well. This makes the whole experience feel like it's on rails as you aren't allowed to explore some areas that you have acces to from the beginning unless you fullfil some criterias which force you to go kill 3 major bosses. This is a huge departure from DS1/2 where you had more paths open to you from the start and could bypass some encounters alltogether. Another aspect which harms the overall appeal is the heavy focus on pure fanservice, to a pont where it becomes downright silly.
The game feels like it was made with the sole purpose to please the DS1 die-hards who worship Miyazaki and shunned DS2's unique take on the formula. On this merit alone DS3 does not live up to the expectations of superseding DS1/2 in all the important areas. Other than being graphically superior, eveything else has been dumbed down.  The PvP is also a pretty obvious lowpoint for the series, from backstab teleporting in DS1 to DS2's somewhat balanced approach, DS3 completely drops the ball with some of the most laggy, edgy and gimmicky PvP the series has seen. Fast R1 spam weapon rule the meta, and poise doesn't exist outside hyper-armor for heavy weapons, but even then you have to time your attacks properly or risk getting stunlocked by a dude using a broken straight sword.
Durability and poison damage are a joke, durability is completely broken (pun intended) and serves only as a checklist feature, armor can never break and some weapons that degrade faster due to their special attacks are easily repaired, the entire "feature" is pointless in this game, and should have just been left out completely instead of having it around and make it have zero impact on gameplay.
Despite these several flaws any Souls fan who can live with the linear world design and excessive fanservice will still find plenty of enjoyment in the sometimes frantic combat. Where the game shines is its wealth of interesting characters and places one can explore. It's just a shame that the Dark Souls series had to end with a dumbed down entry that feels like a cross between DS1 and Bloodborne but without the depth and replayability those games offered.

Do I think this game is good? Yes, of course. Fallout 4 is a definitive First Person shooter with a decent story. With mods, the game gets even better, especially with Maxwell's World and the Tales of the Commonwealth.
But is it a good Fallout game? Not... really... I guess.
I clocked 224.8 hours in this game, and honestly, it's not that satisfying as Fallout: New Vegas. THAT is the Fallout game that got me into this series. I bought it on the road to Fallout 4, and that game is 10x better than this one.
Fallout 4's pros is that:
-Good FPS
-A really great character customisation
-Decent companions
-Great junk system for customising weapons
-Mod support
but it's cons are:
-Average story
-Preston f------ Garvey
-Needless DLC like the workshops that could have easily been mods
-Settlement building, because it just lacks in atmosphere. Bethesda made excellent cities in the past like Megaton, but now that they force you to build it yourself, it doesn't feel like a Fallout game
-Dumb endings. New Vegas had that system where the way you finish your quests are portrayed in the ending. This one is just... singular, for lack of a better word without spoiling.
-Lack of side quests. This is a personal point to me. Wherever you visited in New Vegas there was a buttload of side quests. The world didn't feel empty. Here, it just feels lacking.
-Did I mention Preston Garvey?
All in all, I spent 80SGD on this game, plus about 70SGD on the season pass, and I must say: I. Regret. It. Honestly, you should spent it on Fallout 3 or New Vegas. Those are great Fallout games. Hell, buy the first 2 games. They're completely different in terms of gameplay, but are still excellent in mechanics and story-telling. Hopefully, when the next Fallout game comes out, it will be fantastic and excellent compared to this.

Dark Souls 3 is very similar to DS2. The main objective in the game is exactly the same. You do trash mob after trash mob, explore a bit until you eventually get to a boss. I am a little disappointed to be honest after doing that for 40hrs in both DS1 and 2 I have to say it was a bit boring doing all the trash mobs. Having said that they have done an excellent job in level design and I did get immersed into the game and played for long periods of time.
The games port is ok just like DS2. If you play using a controller you will find the controls to be slick and smooth. You should avoid k+m as apparently they still can't get that right as the tutorial will still say things like press [Xbox b] to roll even if you're specifically using a k+m. The games art design is very nice and the monsters and bosses look scary and intimidating as ever. They've also done a great job on the soundtrack once again. Unfortunately, they haven't optimised the game very well. Playing on max and playing on low barely makes much difference to framerate so make sure you have a decent PC to run this game.
Overall the bosses in this game were a bit hit and miss. The ones nearer the end of the game seemed to be better as they had better move sets and were more challenging. However, some of the bosses are sorry excuses for bosses. One of them especially is incredibly easy to dodge and you can literally kill in 5 hits. I felt a little disappointed again as the majority of bosses were done in just a few tries and no boss really gave me great trouble aside from maybe the ending one. I think they've made the roll more lenient as well, meaning you have a bigger timing window to dodge. Sometimes you can get away with a poorly timed roll by just spamming roll afterwards.

Dark Souls III, the third and final addition to the Souls series for the forseeable future.
I will say that I jumped on the hype train for this one, and it's my very first game in the series.
I'm glad I did, as after its release I was just stunned by the beauty of each level. From Firelink Shrine all the way to
.
The enemies, especially the main bosses may seem difficult at first, but they train the player in terms of reactive play and how well you've learned from your past experiences with them.
Don't get me wrong, you'll most likely die, a lot throughout your time playing through this game, but that is just one step further towards that sweet, sweet victory message after defeating a boss, that moment where you're filled with a sense of accomplishment whether from co-oping as an incandescent sunbro, or you just 'got gud'.
Also, the lore. Even though there appears to be a lot of throwbacks to previous games in the Souls Series, theres tons of lore to be discovered and intepreted by yourself, and the community. Most of the lore may come from item descriptions, but remember the level layouts as well. These play a very important part in deciphering perhaps, why is it there? what purpose does it serve? And so on. After completing my first playthrough, I immediately spent hours upon hours of research into the lore, and every discovery I made answered a question, and asked one or more! It's marvelous what Miyazaki and FromSoftware have created. A true piece of art.
But enough about that, you just want to know if this game is worth getting or not? Let's get down to that shall we?
+ Gorgeous level design, everything looks amazing, even on low graphics settings.
+ Tons of lore to be discovered, as stated before.
+ Some of the BEST boss fights I have ever received the pleasure of going through.

+ Amazing soundtrack, really gets you into the spirit of fighting against insurmountable odds. Personal favourites include

+ A HUGE variety of weapons to choose from, even if some may deal more damage than others.
+ Of course, Fashion Souls. You'll probably spend a good amount of time dressing up your character. But hey, you'll want to be playing with style now, wont you?
+ Jolly Co-operation! It's now extremely easy to play with your friends using the password feature.
And of course, every game has its flaws.
- PvP balance in this game is, not that great I may say. Some weapons are WAY more superior than others in terms of damage and reliability.
- Magic is kind of underwhelming. You'll need to pump at least 50-60 points in either Faith/Intelligence depending on your build if you want to do reliable damage, and then you'll need to dump points into Vigor, Endurance and Dexterity for survivability and casting times. Tl:dr - Magic builds could use a lot of help.
- The game is ported over from console, and it would be appreciated if we got an optimization update in the future, as sometimes the game can lag pretty badly.
- No Poise, Heavy armour is pretty much useless in this game considering the amount of Vitality you'll need to pump in just to wear it, and the returns aren't that great.
- 2 Gimmicky Boss fights. Don't get me wrong, they were fun to figure out, but I wish that after discovering the gimmick, it didn't trivialize the fight.

- No Solaire. Where's my incandescent Sunbro From?
Overall, the game is more than worth the money you'll be paying for it, and it's extremely worth every second you'll spend mastering the game.
I will be getting both DLCs (already pre-ordered), so hopefully the 'Ashes of Ariandel' DLC (which drops on October 25th) brings along a big Optimization update and PvP balance update which will make the game run better and address some of the problems in terms of weapon choices and build variety.
Be sure to pay your respects to 'The Legend, Father of Giants'.
And may your jolly incandescent sunbro adventures treat you well throughout your time playing this game!

Do I think this game is good? Yes, of course. Fallout 4 is a definitive First Person shooter with a decent story. With mods, the game gets even better, especially with Maxwell's World and the Tales of the Commonwealth.
But is it a good Fallout game? Not... really... I guess.
I clocked 224.8 hours in this game, and honestly, it's not that satisfying as Fallout: New Vegas. THAT is the Fallout game that got me into this series. I bought it on the road to Fallout 4, and that game is 10x better than this one.
Fallout 4's pros is that:
-Good FPS
-A really great character customisation
-Decent companions
-Great junk system for customising weapons
-Mod support
but it's cons are:
-Average story
-Preston f------ Garvey
-Needless DLC like the workshops that could have easily been mods
-Settlement building, because it just lacks in atmosphere. Bethesda made excellent cities in the past like Megaton, but now that they force you to build it yourself, it doesn't feel like a Fallout game
-Dumb endings. New Vegas had that system where the way you finish your quests are portrayed in the ending. This one is just... singular, for lack of a better word without spoiling.
-Lack of side quests. This is a personal point to me. Wherever you visited in New Vegas there was a buttload of side quests. The world didn't feel empty. Here, it just feels lacking.
-Did I mention Preston Garvey?
All in all, I spent 80SGD on this game, plus about 70SGD on the season pass, and I must say: I. Regret. It. Honestly, you should spent it on Fallout 3 or New Vegas. Those are great Fallout games. Hell, buy the first 2 games. They're completely different in terms of gameplay, but are still excellent in mechanics and story-telling. Hopefully, when the next Fallout game comes out, it will be fantastic and excellent compared to this.

So one thing you have to know of course is that this is a "Souls Game". A lot of the negative reviews complain about the difficulty but that's just how it is with these games. At the same time though, It's within the first tags of the game that it's difficult so these people should have known what to expect. So basically: Yes, the game is difficult but that's what a lot of players like about the game especially because it's hard in a very "fair" way. When you die, it's your fault so git gud.
With that out of the way I can say that this is a very fun game with good replay value. The graphics are good and there is a lot of content, a lot of which can be optional or hidden. The PvP is something where everyone has a different opinion. When I started playing, I didn't like it and just wanted to play the game by myself without Invasions or Co-op and so on but after playing for longer and trying it out more, I can see why they kept it and what people like about it so much.
Now there is one more thing that I want to mention and this goes especially to those who played the previous Dark Souls games. This game is a good mix between the old Dark Souls and what the developers did in their other game Bloodborne.
So what you'll notice is that this game is a lot faster and dynamic the the previous titles. Your rolls are quicker and enemies are too. Bosses also behave differently now, they are much faster and more aggresive and timing and precision is more important now.
I've played Dark Souls 1 and I do have to say that this is a very big difference but to be honest I like it a lot more. I feels better and I'm glad that From Software tried to bring something new into the series.
The old Dark Souls gameplay was ok and the quick and agile gameplay from bloodborne is really good too, this game has the best of both worlds and it's great!

Dark Souls 3 is very similar to DS2. The main objective in the game is exactly the same. You do trash mob after trash mob, explore a bit until you eventually get to a boss. I am a little disappointed to be honest after doing that for 40hrs in both DS1 and 2 I have to say it was a bit boring doing all the trash mobs. Having said that they have done an excellent job in level design and I did get immersed into the game and played for long periods of time.
The games port is ok just like DS2. If you play using a controller you will find the controls to be slick and smooth. You should avoid k+m as apparently they still can't get that right as the tutorial will still say things like press [Xbox b] to roll even if you're specifically using a k+m. The games art design is very nice and the monsters and bosses look scary and intimidating as ever. They've also done a great job on the soundtrack once again. Unfortunately, they haven't optimised the game very well. Playing on max and playing on low barely makes much difference to framerate so make sure you have a decent PC to run this game.
Overall the bosses in this game were a bit hit and miss. The ones nearer the end of the game seemed to be better as they had better move sets and were more challenging. However, some of the bosses are sorry excuses for bosses. One of them especially is incredibly easy to dodge and you can literally kill in 5 hits. I felt a little disappointed again as the majority of bosses were done in just a few tries and no boss really gave me great trouble aside from maybe the ending one. I think they've made the roll more lenient as well, meaning you have a bigger timing window to dodge. Sometimes you can get away with a poorly timed roll by just spamming roll afterwards.
So who should buy this game? If you're a hardcore DS fan then you've already bought it anyway. If you've played through DS2 and are looking for more of the same content then you should probably buy this. If you're new to DS and you're looking for a first game then I'd highly recommend DS1.
Although an immersive experience and some enjoyable bosses, I'm going to thumbs down as it was just too much of the same as DS2.

As a Dark Souls newbie, this game was extremely punishing at first and tested my patience to the next level. Never have I been forced to realize how bad I am at combat. True, unadulterated, combat. The kind where it is your fault for going in too deep when the enemy was preparing an attack. Where slowing down and observing is just important as attacking. Death after death, and then some more for good measure, I finally managed to take down Iudex (the starting boss)…down to his second phase. Of course he had to have a second phase, I mean, it’s only been 5 minutes since I created my character and this guy is more difficult than most games’ final bosses. Alright fine, let’s try it again….and naturally, the stupid skeleton guarding the boss entrance chunked me for half of my health. This obnoxious heathen never managed to hit me in my previous 16 runs, but now its eyes gained some sort of holy enchantment to make every arrow land on my back. This is the type of game DARK SOULS III is. One without mercy, care, or pity. It took me approximately 2 hours to beat Iudex as a starting Mercenary, but the thrill and adrenaline post-battle was truly something no other game offered. Who knew I could come to love a game that wanted to kill me so badly.
As I fought my way through the story, I began to become immersed with the lore and progression system. Every single item’s description, name, and method of acquisition imparts just a tiny bit of knowledge or history onto the player. At first, most of this information is useless at worst, or intriguing at best. These little puzzle pieces manage to eventually paint a very vivid and dark image about the world of Lothric and its inhabitants. Ashes and unique equipment often detail the previous owners’ qualities; a gift to fans of previous games in the series. Although DS III is fairly disconnected with any of the other SOULS games, certain NPCs and discoveries will tie up loose ends and provide closure for particular aspects of the first DARK SOULS game.
Unlike the previous games, bonfires are placed just when you truly need them, and most important of all, teleportation between bonfires are available from the get-go. Firelink Shrine, the base of operations of sorts, serves as the location for player stat upgrades, weapon upgrades/infusions, Estus flask upgrades, and bonfire upgrades (increases healing per flask). Similar to Humanity or Human Effigies from the previous games, Ember heals the player and boosts max health in exchange for allowing human and NPC invasions.
Although the world design is fairly spectacular, it was mostly linear/bi-linear (city with a dungeon below it) with moderate exploration required for completionists. The traditionally grand map comprised of interconnecting smaller maps through shortcuts is replaced with a more direct route, however, the world is still HUGE. In fact, without proper investigation, it is extremely easy to completely miss 4 optional areas with their own bosses. In total, there are 19 bosses that will do their best to make sure life in Lothric is a living Hell, along with several other mini-bosses in between. The grunt and fluff type enemies are never too difficult – just strong enough to warrant consistent player attention. The extremely well planned level and boss design (excluding a couple) easily makes DS III one of the most memorable games I have ever played. I can clearly recount most of the paths in every area along with every bosses’ movesets and shenanigans. From clones and body doubles, to massive variances in combat range and aggressiveness, the boss fights and surrounding environements are truly, and remarkably, unforgettable.
One of the most noticeable changes to the tried-and-true combat involves the introduction of weapon arts. Think of it as a special skill move belonging to certain weapon types. Hacking and slashing is always fun, but turning that long sword into a propeller of death is even more so. Special and boss type weapons are often imbued with properties of their wielder, including a unique weapon art that can be so hauntingly beautiful to perform. Lance thrusts with bursts of electricity, sword strikes covered in fire, and duel-wielded weapons moving in an artistic dance are only some of what you will see. Unfortunately, most of these arts require the use of FP (focus points), and once out, they won’t be usable until replenished.
DS III launched with quite a few minor grievances, mostly sporadic FPS drops, but all of them have been fixed. The only major issue at the moment is regarding softbanning due to “Data Inconsistencies” which may occur due to advancing in the game offline (de-syncing with the server) or from online hackers. Continuous patches have been applied since the posting of this review in order to keep up to date with the demanding pvp balance and bug encounters.
I can’t stress enough how much I really enjoyed playing DS III. This game is one of my personal contenders for 2016 GOTY. I really regret never playing the earlier two during their heyday, but at least it gives me something to do while i lament the end of this great journey – at least, until the Season Pass content gets released. For those that want to continue into New Game +, DS III fortunately provides 3 other endings with vastly different consequences to uncover, increasing replayability immensely. One of those endings also requires an extremely strict quest-line progression, ultimately leading to one of the most shocking moments in the game!

Dark souls has always been one of those games that I sink hours and HOURS into. I first hopped on the Souls Train with Dark Souls 1, and the game has come a long way since then. For Souls Vets, this game has some new interesting mechanics to play around with, such as the MP system and Weapon Arts, that make this game rather difficult to put away.
For Series Newbies, I cannot recommend this game any higher. A couple things you need to know-
-This game has a pretty fast learning curve. You will die... a lot.
-PvP is intense, and rather difficult to avoid if you want to co op with friends, or if thats not your cup of tea.
-The Lore of the Game is rather difficult to pick up on, and if you havent played the first two games, it will be much more difficult to do so. If you are one of those people who lives for a lore filled game, I would recommend searching up the Lore on the Internet. Vaatividya is a youtuber who has dozens of videos on the Lore, and I highly recommend him if you wish to delve deeper into the story.
For Series Vets, there are also a few things you should know-
-If you played Demon Souls, you'll remember the MP bar. For people who only played Dark Souls 1 or 2, this will be a rather odd concept. Instead of the normal "Uses" for each spell in your attunement slot, you will get a blue bar under your stamina bar. this bar can be increased via spending levels in attunement, and each time you use a spell, pyromancy, or miracle, you will drain MP. Each spell has its own MP cost, so you must be careful how you use them. Fortunatley for Magic only builds, From has added a secondary estus flask that you can recharge your MP with.
-Weapon arts are also a new addition to Dark Souls 3. Each weapon in the game, excluding shields, has a special ability that can be activated in battle. Some are rather useless, such as the Perseverance ability; some are useful in certain situations, such as the Stance abilities; and some are astounding and, dare I say it, border on overpowered, such as the Dragonslayer's Swordspear's "Death from Above" and the Lothric Greatsword's Unholy "Screw your Hitbox" attack. One thing to mention, is that these abilities also drain MP.
-PvP is a bit interesting in Dark Souls 3. Invaders can now use estus in a host world, but only half of the amount of estus they would have in their world. In certain areas, such as the area after the Pontiff Sulyvahn, and with some items activated, you can have up to 8 or 9 players in a world... Most of them unfriendly.
-For people who play for the PvP and regularly engaged in Invasions in previous games, be warned... Ganking has become a bit of a problem. This issue is a rather hot one at the moment, so I wont get into it any further.
All in all, I think this game is one of Fromsoft's Best yet, and cant wait to see more of this genre develop. 10/10 "Would Die Again"

In a game where messages on the ground tell you to whack your sword at stone walls, jump off of cliffs, invaders rudely stepping into your world with the sole intent to spill your guts, and where every boss’s theme sounds like a final boss theme, it’s easy to get lost in the wonderful world of Dark Souls.
You know a video game series is getting somewhere when other games released after it are compared to the “original”. Take for example, the original DOOM from 1993, many shooters that came out after DOOM’s release, were labelled “DOOM clones”, later these games came to known as First-Person Shooters. When Minecraft received international popularity in 2011 upon its release, many games that were centered around block placing and breaking, and item crafting were labelled “Minecraft copies”, today they are known as Sandbox games. A relatively new released game, Salt and Sanctuary, has been compared to Dark Souls in terms of difficulty, and is often referred to as a “2D take on Dark Souls”, and as of recently many indie games have been released and centered upon death, and difficulty, with a heavy emphasis on bosses, games that were most likely inspired by the Souls franchise.
Don't confuse Dark Souls III with your average RPG, it's much more difficult than most can handle, and it's certainly not for the faint of heart. I've seen many people, from YouTube, on message boards, etc. stay away from the Dark Souls franchise simply because of how hard it is. Don't jump into the game expecting it to be a land full of rainbows and butterflies; because it's not. If you're not willing to get better at the game, you won't survive, it's as simple as that.
Dark Souls III manages to stand out from the crowd of modern video games, with its central theme of difficulty, demanding respect from its players, and brutally punishing those who refuse to give it that respect, something many video games are afraid to try. The game features minimal hand-holding, as the most “help” you’ll get from the developers about its mechanics is the tutorial area, which all it really does is tell you the basic controls, afterwards, players will need to do the rest of the learning process themselves; forcing its players to think, study their opponent’s move sets, time attacks precisely, and learn from their mistakes in an unrelenting arduous journey of trial and error. The game really separates those who are weak and easily broken, and those who are willing to persevere and make it through. Forget overpowered, forget one hitting bosses, forget bum rushing, there is ZERO spoon feeding. You either learn from your mistakes, or leave in a raging fit of defeat.
Since death is so heavily emphasized, it basically impossible, for new Souls players to go through an entire playthrough without dying once, (the main menu theme speaks volumes as to how much you’ll die). The game was made to be difficult so players can learn from their past attempts. Each time the player dies, you come back stronger, not by stats, but psychologically. By gathering information about your opponent on your first encounter, the game expects you to apply the knowledge in your next attempt. If you die again, learn from that and try again; it’s basically like that movie Edge of Tomorrow, every death only makes you stronger.
Because of the game’s difficulty, it ends up being the most satisfying gameplay experience no other game could ever deliver. Despite dying to that boss at least 20 times, you still managed to beat it, and boy does it feel oh-so good. You know why? Because you earned that victory, despite all those deaths, you learned from past mistakes, and applied it, and when you see those beautiful golden letters “Heir of Fire Destroyed” appear on the screen, you can’t help but give yourself a pat on the back, yell out in triumph, or just breathe out a huge sigh of relief, because you did that, and you earned that victory.
Here are some quick details to help you better grasp if the game is right for you:
- Fast and fluid gameplay. (Something reminiscent of Bloodborne)
- Amazing and unforgettable bosses (save for a select few).
- Immersive and atmospheric environments.
- Souls veterans will be greeted with much fan service, since the game features several call-backs from the first two games.
- Features multiplayer coop for those into PvE, and PvP for the competitive types.
- Something I found really neat, was the addition of password matchmaking. It basically allows exact matchmaking with anyone with same password as you, which is perfect for just playing a game with your buddies. Similar to the Name-engraved ring from Dark Souls II. Not only that, but it also removes any sort of restriction you'd otherwise recieve in normal matchmaking, so if you're Lvl 210, you can still connect with your lvl 15 friend who just got the game.
- Expansive variety of weapons, armor and spells.
- Epic boss music.
- Excellent voice acting.
- Masterful indirect story telling.
- NPC Questlines.
- Players will be put in a world knee-deep with lore, assuming players are willing to occasionally take the time to read item descriptions.
- Fair balanced difficulty—99% of deaths in PvE are because of player error; either you didn’t time your hit at the right time, you got greedy, or chose to heal at the wrong time, either way, it’s YOUR mistake that led to your death. The other 1% is the rare occurrence of some kind of glitch, which I honestly have never experienced.
- Expert enemy placement—players should be wary of grabbing items on the ground that otherwise look like a trap, you may be ambushed from the left, right, or even above you.
- Your choices matter,
, every NPC death, interaction, or anytime you ignore an NPC can dramatically alter questlines, affect the outcome of the game, affect your vendor availability, and even lead to missing many key items and materials
- Non-existence of Poise, an attribute that players from previous games should be familiar with, and another thing the game is notorious for lacking.
- Storyline can be easily missed if players don’t take the time to read item descriptions, or pay attention to character dialogue.
- Something relatively minor; 90% of character’s mouths don’t move when you talk to them, which really isn’t a big deal, but if you’re the attentive type, it might bother you.
- Game as of currently is polluted with a community of hackers, some good, some bad, and the game’s not-so-great Anti-Cheat has led to the banning of several legit players. If you want to avoid that just play offline through the in-game system settings, and stray away from anything that modifies your game’s .exe or using CE (Cheat Engine).
- For returning Souls veterans, Armor cannot be upgraded in this game, only weapons, catalysts, bows, etc. In addition, the previous upgrade cap of +15 from the first game has been reduced to +10.
- While the map isn’t 100% linear, map design is still lackluster when compared the first game.
With its array of exquisite music, large variety of weapons, armor and spells that cater to all kinds of playstyles, beautifully terrifying and memorable bosses, and breathtaking immersive environments, make this game one of the best modern games released to date, a fitting end to an amazing franchise, and a worthy contender for Game of the Year.

If you've played the other Fallout games and thought "What if everything was opposite..let's make the combat better, the dialog shallow, the choices meaningless, and the characters 0 dimensional!" then you've found the game you're looking for.

I guess it's telling that I have 160 hours of game time and, yet, the game barely makes it to a positive rating from my point of view. Fallout 4 sure is fun at first. There is so much to do and explore, so many weapons to find and a good variety of enemies to defeat. The crafting system for weapons and armor feels complementary and not latched on.
So there are a lot of positives but as the game progresses you start noticing the cracks on the game's shining surface: The game engine really isn't up to par to comparable AAA titles, the AI is limited, the main story line, though presented with great urgency and personal commitment for the hero, gets sidetracked into a list of checkboxes on the way to a lazy final decision nexus.
Then there is the base building system which is strangely unfulfilling considering that it seems to have been a development focus for this game: Housing parts don't fit together, interior design elements are either missing or useless and the base defense installations are inconsequential as you more or less stop caring about settlements after a while. Even worse, they can get annoying as heck (You learn to dread the sentence: "Another settlement needs your help!").
Then there is the DLC. Previous Fallout games were known for their great story DLC packs which really fleshed out the main character and provided additional immersion for the world around you. Bethesda sort of promised that Fallout 4 would get a similar treatment. What we got were mainly additional base building systems which added whole new dimensions of buggy content I didn't really care about because (see above) base building mostly is a useless time sink.
The "Far Harbor" DLC is great and sort of hints to what the game might have been but it comes at a very hefty price. Sadly, whatever goodwill this DLC might create will be utterly destroyed by the final "Nuka-World" DLC which sort of emphasizes this game's shortcomings: Railroaded story, the lack of R in RPG, more base building without any apparent benefit or reason.
So my advice would be: Play the main game, get Far Harbor on a discount of at least 50% and forget about the rest! Then delete the game from your hard drive because there is very little replay value if you made a smart save at the one diverging decision nexus.

As a Dark Souls newbie, this game was extremely punishing at first and tested my patience to the next level. Never have I been forced to realize how bad I am at combat. True, unadulterated, combat. The kind where it is your fault for going in too deep when the enemy was preparing an attack. Where slowing down and observing is just important as attacking. Death after death, and then some more for good measure, I finally managed to take down Iudex (the starting boss)…down to his second phase. Of course he had to have a second phase, I mean, it’s only been 5 minutes since I created my character and this guy is more difficult than most games’ final bosses. Alright fine, let’s try it again….and naturally, the stupid skeleton guarding the boss entrance chunked me for half of my health. This obnoxious heathen never managed to hit me in my previous 16 runs, but now its eyes gained some sort of holy enchantment to make every arrow land on my back. This is the type of game DARK SOULS III is. One without mercy, care, or pity. It took me approximately 2 hours to beat Iudex as a starting Mercenary, but the thrill and adrenaline post-battle was truly something no other game offered. Who knew I could come to love a game that wanted to kill me so badly.
As I fought my way through the story, I began to become immersed with the lore and progression system. Every single item’s description, name, and method of acquisition imparts just a tiny bit of knowledge or history onto the player. At first, most of this information is useless at worst, or intriguing at best. These little puzzle pieces manage to eventually paint a very vivid and dark image about the world of Lothric and its inhabitants. Ashes and unique equipment often detail the previous owners’ qualities; a gift to fans of previous games in the series. Although DS III is fairly disconnected with any of the other SOULS games, certain NPCs and discoveries will tie up loose ends and provide closure for particular aspects of the first DARK SOULS game.
Unlike the previous games, bonfires are placed just when you truly need them, and most important of all, teleportation between bonfires are available from the get-go. Firelink Shrine, the base of operations of sorts, serves as the location for player stat upgrades, weapon upgrades/infusions, Estus flask upgrades, and bonfire upgrades (increases healing per flask). Similar to Humanity or Human Effigies from the previous games, Ember heals the player and boosts max health in exchange for allowing human and NPC invasions.
Although the world design is fairly spectacular, it was mostly linear/bi-linear (city with a dungeon below it) with moderate exploration required for completionists. The traditionally grand map comprised of interconnecting smaller maps through shortcuts is replaced with a more direct route, however, the world is still HUGE. In fact, without proper investigation, it is extremely easy to completely miss 4 optional areas with their own bosses. In total, there are 19 bosses that will do their best to make sure life in Lothric is a living Hell, along with several other mini-bosses in between. The grunt and fluff type enemies are never too difficult – just strong enough to warrant consistent player attention. The extremely well planned level and boss design (excluding a couple) easily makes DS III one of the most memorable games I have ever played. I can clearly recount most of the paths in every area along with every bosses’ movesets and shenanigans. From clones and body doubles, to massive variances in combat range and aggressiveness, the boss fights and surrounding environements are truly, and remarkably, unforgettable.
One of the most noticeable changes to the tried-and-true combat involves the introduction of weapon arts. Think of it as a special skill move belonging to certain weapon types. Hacking and slashing is always fun, but turning that long sword into a propeller of death is even more so. Special and boss type weapons are often imbued with properties of their wielder, including a unique weapon art that can be so hauntingly beautiful to perform. Lance thrusts with bursts of electricity, sword strikes covered in fire, and duel-wielded weapons moving in an artistic dance are only some of what you will see. Unfortunately, most of these arts require the use of FP (focus points), and once out, they won’t be usable until replenished.
DS III launched with quite a few minor grievances, mostly sporadic FPS drops, but all of them have been fixed. The only major issue at the moment is regarding softbanning due to “Data Inconsistencies” which may occur due to advancing in the game offline (de-syncing with the server) or from online hackers. Continuous patches have been applied since the posting of this review in order to keep up to date with the demanding pvp balance and bug encounters.
I can’t stress enough how much I really enjoyed playing DS III. This game is one of my personal contenders for 2016 GOTY. I really regret never playing the earlier two during their heyday, but at least it gives me something to do while i lament the end of this great journey – at least, until the Season Pass content gets released. For those that want to continue into New Game +, DS III fortunately provides 3 other endings with vastly different consequences to uncover, increasing replayability immensely. One of those endings also requires an extremely strict quest-line progression, ultimately leading to one of the most shocking moments in the game!

If you've played the other Fallout games and thought "What if everything was opposite..let's make the combat better, the dialog shallow, the choices meaningless, and the characters 0 dimensional!" then you've found the game you're looking for.

I guess it's telling that I have 160 hours of game time and, yet, the game barely makes it to a positive rating from my point of view. Fallout 4 sure is fun at first. There is so much to do and explore, so many weapons to find and a good variety of enemies to defeat. The crafting system for weapons and armor feels complementary and not latched on.
So there are a lot of positives but as the game progresses you start noticing the cracks on the game's shining surface: The game engine really isn't up to par to comparable AAA titles, the AI is limited, the main story line, though presented with great urgency and personal commitment for the hero, gets sidetracked into a list of checkboxes on the way to a lazy final decision nexus.
Then there is the base building system which is strangely unfulfilling considering that it seems to have been a development focus for this game: Housing parts don't fit together, interior design elements are either missing or useless and the base defense installations are inconsequential as you more or less stop caring about settlements after a while. Even worse, they can get annoying as heck (You learn to dread the sentence: "Another settlement needs your help!").
Then there is the DLC. Previous Fallout games were known for their great story DLC packs which really fleshed out the main character and provided additional immersion for the world around you. Bethesda sort of promised that Fallout 4 would get a similar treatment. What we got were mainly additional base building systems which added whole new dimensions of buggy content I didn't really care about because (see above) base building mostly is a useless time sink.
The "Far Harbor" DLC is great and sort of hints to what the game might have been but it comes at a very hefty price. Sadly, whatever goodwill this DLC might create will be utterly destroyed by the final "Nuka-World" DLC which sort of emphasizes this game's shortcomings: Railroaded story, the lack of R in RPG, more base building without any apparent benefit or reason.
So my advice would be: Play the main game, get Far Harbor on a discount of at least 50% and forget about the rest! Then delete the game from your hard drive because there is very little replay value if you made a smart save at the one diverging decision nexus.

It all started with Dark Souls. The original. The unknown (to me anyway). I got it free on Xbox Live. I laughed, I cried, I loved, I died and finally I lived. Challenges that rewarded perseverance and observation.
Then came the sequel. I paid £20 for it. This is great, I thought. More of the same, but more polished. But there seem to be a lot more bonfires than in the first. And I can guess where I'm going to ambushed. Still fantastic though.
Then came this. Pre-ordered, pre-installed. £40 without a blink. Waiting, counting down for that day one patch. It's massive. The anticipation grew. And then I played it...
Dark Souls 3. What can you say? Well.
For the most part, it's a lot easier than the previous installment and considerably moreso than the inaugural game. Science tells us that this is down to two factors: either that the game was made easier or I got better. I did have a strong lean towards the first, but now think a combination of the two make it 50/50. There are definitely more bonfires (at one point you can run from one to the next in about 30 seconds) and when I would have walked blindly into a room before or past a "dead body", I now enter and roll out or shank that corpse to make sure, respectively.
The look of the game- the vistas, the enemies, the bosses - are great. They all work together to increase immersion, as does the soundtrack which I have listened to, out of game, and enjoyed.
The sense of achievement once you have killed that boss, that has been kicking seven scolars out of you, remains and, for most of the bosses, is immense. The echoes of previous bosses before hint at what is in store for the final encounter. Some are huge and looming, requiring you to become an amateur proctologist, whilst others force you to keep at a distance and wait for that perfect moment.
Weapons are varied, the different attack classes allow for different playstyles, and the armour sets look great. Infusions are more varied, meaning that you can beef your weapon with whatever powerup you want, or more precisely what the enemy doesn't like.
There are a few secrets in this game, level-design-wise, (one being considerable), but what I enjoyed was meeting friendly NPCs. They give you vague quests which you can happen to complete or fail and add variety to the main story. There are old favourites who make appearances and one who made me unbelievably focused to end their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t once and for all.
I can highly recommend this. It's an experience and created a connection I haven't felt with many games. But there, of course, some problems.
As previously stated, it feels too easy. Getting through areas isn't very tough, but the bosses are the antithesis of this.
There are minor bugs that I encountered that I found frustrating, such as not being able to massage the wyvern (warning: statement intended to be vague, not as double entendre) multiple times. Also, I would have liked a supercancel button, one that you could press (such as roll) which would cancel any animation you were performing. Chugging an estus is important but if you can see an axe bearing down on you, I would prefer to change my mind.
Thats it, aside from a few tiny points, this game is definitely recommended.

Mechanics are brutally hard to utilise, but seemingly mastered by anyone you'll come across in PvP. Except of course for any white phantoms, who will stand by and taunt you while letting you fight off two or more other invaders on your own. Nights of frustration, crying, keyboard throwing, with just enough occasional success to prevent you completely uninstalling the game. Absolutely the best game I have ever played. I have never before enjoyed being so thoroughly broken.

It all started with Dark Souls. The original. The unknown (to me anyway). I got it free on Xbox Live. I laughed, I cried, I loved, I died and finally I lived. Challenges that rewarded perseverance and observation.
Then came the sequel. I paid £20 for it. This is great, I thought. More of the same, but more polished. But there seem to be a lot more bonfires than in the first. And I can guess where I'm going to ambushed. Still fantastic though.
Then came this. Pre-ordered, pre-installed. £40 without a blink. Waiting, counting down for that day one patch. It's massive. The anticipation grew. And then I played it...
Dark Souls 3. What can you say? Well.
For the most part, it's a lot easier than the previous installment and considerably moreso than the inaugural game. Science tells us that this is down to two factors: either that the game was made easier or I got better. I did have a strong lean towards the first, but now think a combination of the two make it 50/50. There are definitely more bonfires (at one point you can run from one to the next in about 30 seconds) and when I would have walked blindly into a room before or past a "dead body", I now enter and roll out or shank that corpse to make sure, respectively.
The look of the game- the vistas, the enemies, the bosses - are great. They all work together to increase immersion, as does the soundtrack which I have listened to, out of game, and enjoyed.
The sense of achievement once you have killed that boss, that has been kicking seven scolars out of you, remains and, for most of the bosses, is immense. The echoes of previous bosses before hint at what is in store for the final encounter. Some are huge and looming, requiring you to become an amateur proctologist, whilst others force you to keep at a distance and wait for that perfect moment.
Weapons are varied, the different attack classes allow for different playstyles, and the armour sets look great. Infusions are more varied, meaning that you can beef your weapon with whatever powerup you want, or more precisely what the enemy doesn't like.
There are a few secrets in this game, level-design-wise, (one being considerable), but what I enjoyed was meeting friendly NPCs. They give you vague quests which you can happen to complete or fail and add variety to the main story. There are old favourites who make appearances and one who made me unbelievably focused to end their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t once and for all.
I can highly recommend this. It's an experience and created a connection I haven't felt with many games. But there, of course, some problems.
As previously stated, it feels too easy. Getting through areas isn't very tough, but the bosses are the antithesis of this.
There are minor bugs that I encountered that I found frustrating, such as not being able to massage the wyvern (warning: statement intended to be vague, not as double entendre) multiple times. Also, I would have liked a supercancel button, one that you could press (such as roll) which would cancel any animation you were performing. Chugging an estus is important but if you can see an axe bearing down on you, I would prefer to change my mind.
Thats it, aside from a few tiny points, this game is definitely recommended.

Single Player Review: 9/10 Such a huge improvement over DS2.
The main hub, the firelink shrine area, get soon crowded with NPCs and while intended to be a "cesspool of doddering oldfolk and degenerates", it doesnt feels like a believable place. I know it works as Demon's Soul' Nexus did, but i never playied that so i cant really compare the two.
Also, the magic of a open world, connected from top to bottom, as it was in DS1, its partially lost here; while the world design is much better than in DS2, it isnt as good as DS1. Levels are much larger, but the way they connects still miss the natural flow of the original game.
The design of enemies and bosses is generally very consistent with the environments; the style direction is well above DS2, even if some odd enemy placement can be still found.
Areas are packed with loot with steep spikes in difficulty when the player get away from the path to the area boss to adventure in completionist territory, as in some optional areas.
The fighting system is very reminiscent of that of DS2, but much faster, enriched by the weapon arts option, wich is a fancy name for the expanded weapon moveset; also the gameplay is deeper thanks to the option of juggling the estus between HP and FP, giving more options to wizards/ hybrid characters; hitboxes on enemies is generally fair, apart from some boss.
The camera and targeting system is far from perfect, presenting some problems in tight spaces packed with enemies and an even shorter locking distance than in DS1/2. A number of time you'll try to lock on to enemy while retreating, only to reset the camera...definitely ONE OF THE GAME'S LOWEST POINTS.
Graphics are good, presenting amazing sceneries most of the times, while, purely technically, the game is still reminiscent of DS2sotfs. So, artistically excellent, lacking a true "next gen" look all around. Colour palette is perfect, more vivid than DS1 but it isnt the mess DS2 presented.
The OST, sadly, is nothing special. While DS1 has some memorable tracks,(the malinconic main menu and ending theme, the terrifying asylum demon/taurus demon theme, the magnificent Ornstein/Smough theme or the final Gwyn's piano theme), DS3 tracks are truly forgettable. Not terrible, but nothing to write home about. Sounds are very good instead.
final note: works well on 360 controller as well as on M&K. Actually, camera control is soo much better with mouse! bossfight will be much easier!

Dark Souls 3 is a pretty good game. I would consider it to be a combination of Bloodborne and Dark Souls 1, not only because it runs on the Bloodborne engine.
Overall the combat is very smooth. It is faster without losing the feel of a Souls game, but once again it does also have the Bloodborne vibes to it. It's smooth, attacks are meaningful and feel good to use. Though some attacks and weapon arts are a bit disappointing.
The map design of this game delivers absolutely. There are twists and turns, ambushes, beautiful areas and they are all connected. You will see the entire world, as landmarks are visible from wherever you currently are - if you look for them. Areas you've already visited or ones coming up. Take a moment and look. Each of the areas has a unique style and appeal and stays true to its theme throughout. Since I don't want to spoil anything I will end here.
Now onto the real core of the game, the bosses:
I rate 7/10.
There are 19 bosses in the game and some of them had the potential to be something really cool. In fact, most of them are pretty cool. Some of them however will leave you pretty disappointed. There is fights that could have been pretty amazing. The setting is right, the music gets you hyped up and not to mention that you just conquered the area in front of the fog gate. But when you notice that the guy has a million HP or doesn't take much damage, you know something's up.  Three bosses have gimmicks built into their fight, two of them being required to beat the game.
That may sound like almost nothing, but I am pretty sure that you will feel a similar disappointment if you think about what those fights could have been.
Would I still recommend the game? Yes.
PVP:
There is still a good amount of invasions happening, but you probably won't get the 10 invaders per hour I got at the release.
As far as I know the PVP community is pretty active. The most active (and only?) duel spot in the game is right after the Pontiff boss fight where you will surely find many red signs to summon for a duel.
I'm not sure how active the arena is that got introduced with the DLC as I haven't tried it yet, but I am assuming that you won't have to wait forever to find something.
Just keep in mind that you may not have the best time if you face people that min max their builds while you run around with sub par weapons. You might want to work on that.

This may not be the best game in the world. It might not even be the best Fallout game in the world. It has it's faults. It's a bit buggy and glitchy in places (there, there, Bethesda. You know we still love you). The big question that any review should answer is "Did I enjoy playing the damn thing?". The answer in this case is absolutely yes.
I am currently 350+ hours into my wandering around the Commonwealth and I've enjoyed pretty much every minute of it.
Most of the faults in the game can be fixed with mods. Whether it be the annoying loop of the same commentary and songs on radio stations (eg Old World Radio Boston) or the various graphics/ENB mods out there.
Some of the faults aren't fixable with mods. I wish that your in-game decisions had more of an impact on the world you're in. Without dropping any spoilers on plot specific points, why is it that I can wipe out most of the major NPCs in a place like Diamond City and 48 hours later they've forgiven me while similar massacres many years beforehand seem to be fresh wounds?! There are other "plot progression" moments where it would make more sense to actually make consequences follow through than to implement the same things happening thus making your own decision irrelevant.
I understand that this would be vastly harder to program into a game and that it probably adds huge amounts of work to the developers but in a game of this nature that's kind of what they're taking on by creating it.
I still love this game but I am not blind to it's faults or where it could've been improved.
Overall I'd still give it a hearty recommendation purely because I've enjoyed playing it so much but that is purely on a personal level and I can equally understand how others would find that it just isn't the game for them. If you think you can live with it's flaws then go for it!

Fallout 4 was released with high expectations, and many felt left down by what has been delivered. But in the rush to criticize its shortcomings, reviewers, and players alike have overlooked some massive improvements.
Fallout 4 is less of an RPG than its predecessors, but its sense of exploration far surpass Fallout 3 or New Vegas. Its shooting mechanics are also hugely improved, and more enjoyable. The VATS system takes a back seat to real-time combat in fallout 4, and I couldn't be happier for it. The story may be muddled in places, but the choices you make feel more important, and not just part of a binary karma system.
Fallout 4 deserves your time, and will reward players with and expansive world filled with characters and places that will stay with you, inhabit your imagination, and show up in your dreams. There is no other game like it, not Skyrim, not Witcher 3, not Mass Effect. If you want a game that keeps you entranced for hour after hour you came to right place.

I have good reasons for ranking Dark Souls 3 this. Good ones. Let us go over the negatives first to get this cleared:
- The community: The community is ♥♥♥♥ing horrible. Everyone gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, gankers, negativity, agressivity, hackers, toxicity, more and more negative bs.
- The overhyped trailers: The trailers really hyped up everything about the game. Yet the reality wasn't very enticing.
- The game compared to the trailers: The graphics were downgraded to all hell. Well the graphics are far from what was promised. With the capabilities the gaming industries have, I am most certain the games could look more similar to the trailers. But no, they were downgraded for gods know why.
