- The PvP: PvP goes under the topic of community, but anyone who has even surfaced PvP will find tons of crap floating everywhere. The meta is horrible, the toxic behavior and hatemail, the gankers, the hackers? It is ♥♥♥♥ing horrible. And not just that. It is not balanced, it is far from balanced.
Don't get me wrong. I have played this game for 278.3 hours for a reason. That is because it is infact fun. Yet to a degree. Alright lets move on to the pros.
- The game got astounding boss music!
- The game areas were very scary and had me very focused onto not dying!
- The game had an interesting variety of spells. Many unique and fun to use. Yet not so efficient in PvP.
- Great cast of characters.
- Cool bosses.
And... I guess that is it really. I dunno why I actually played for as long as I did. It was just fun on those small pros that were there. Normal Dark Souls tropes I suppose.

Dark Souls lll:
Oh where do i start? As of writing the review i have 171 deaths and have completed the game 5 times to be precise. (Because i am one who writes everything important or stupid down).
Now im going to state a few things i found DS3 to be (good and bad) at.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Start: I find the tutorial area to be much more user friendly than DS1. DS2's tutorial area was much like an arena and had a nice feeling when u were doing it. In DS1 there wasn't really a tutorial area at all. They threw u right into the fray even with the small tutorial writings. DS3's tutorial area feels much easier than the first game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Combat (PVE): While the combat is satisfying when u manage to land a parry and get a riposte. I feel like the AI got slower from the last game. The hitboxes are perfectly in sync and i have never managed to miss a swing at close range on my own world that is. Other than that the PVE is excellent and manages to **** you up at every opportunity you give it.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Difficulty (and Controls): In my opinion the game feels alot easier than the first and second game. Everything is much easier to do now. Now u can perform certain actions like parrying by clicking CTRL in the corner of your keyboard. And jumping is now easier. All u have to do is hold the SPACEBAR and press it again quickly when u want to jump. In DS2 u had to hold the SPACEBAR and sprint while clicking the SCROLL button and SPACEBAR at the same time. (Like seriously who came up with that?) and i do know that u can change the keybindings for the keyboard in the menu. U can not change it for the controller however if u decide to connect one to your computer that is.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Combat (PVP): Just like in the beginning of my review i will say. Where do i start? The absurdly weird and extremely long ranges on some weapons makes me wanna puke in PVP. Yes sadly as far as i know. Every single weapon has reach longer than the weapon itself in PVP. Secondly everyone who invades will get to use estus. Yes ESTUS the one drink who we all love and hate at the same time has returned to the invaders hands. In DS1 invaders had estus and they could drink it but u could easily punish players who heal often. In DS2 invaders had no estus to drink and had to heal using other means (spells or blessings). Also in DS1 and DS2 u had to stand still to drink estus which made it easy to punish. In DS3 u don't stop when drinking but your movement gets down to crawl for a moment but it's easy to drink when out of range even with the weird weapon ranges. One thing they've done right was make it so anyone who invades or gets summoned always have HALF of their estus and not max. And one last thing players who invade or are summoned will always scale to your SOUL level if your SOUL level is below theirs. So be prepared to atleast invest a few points into Vitality so u can atleast survive a hit in PVP on higher levels. Weapons also scale to the host's maximum upgraded weapon. So keep that in mind.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall Rating: 9 / 10
The game was alot of fun. Especially if u can get a friend to play with you. Now to anyone that plans on buying this game for the first time. Prepare to smash keyboards. Alot. Im sure that by the end of this game u will have replaced atleast one or two keyboards if it is your first time playing a SOULS game. Also just give up if u feel like getting frustrated. Walk away and take a break, 30 minutes atleast and then come back to try again. First time i played DS1 i broke several keyboards and at the start of DS2 i was still mildly annoyed. Because what i learned from the first and second game was that patience is most rewarding for those who wait.

After being a longtime fan of the Fallout series; I was very excited to play Fallout 4. Initially I was completely thrown off by my lack of interest in the game on my first play-through. It wasn't that the game was bad, it was more like I was bad at playing the game. In a way, Fallout was changed dramatically with the introduction of Settlement building, and with the new dialog system. Neither of these were game breaking, but they changed so much that it threw me off. Essentially, I put the game down about midway through the storyline and walked away.
After a long hiatus from Fallout 4, my son started playing it and really enjoying everything from building structures to robots (new DLC) and even the story missions. His enjoyment was the game itself and not comparing it to the older titles in the franchise. Seeing him enjoy the game gave me a new perspective on playing the game and I haven't put it down since that point.
My advice for long time fans of the franchise is to place Fallout 1,2, Tactics, 3 & New Vegas on a "shelf" and play Fallout 4 as a new experience. It deserves its place at the table and really modernizes the RPG category in many positives ways.

Dark Souls lll:
Oh where do i start? As of writing the review i have 171 deaths and have completed the game 5 times to be precise. (Because i am one who writes everything important or stupid down).
Now im going to state a few things i found DS3 to be (good and bad) at.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Start: I find the tutorial area to be much more user friendly than DS1. DS2's tutorial area was much like an arena and had a nice feeling when u were doing it. In DS1 there wasn't really a tutorial area at all. They threw u right into the fray even with the small tutorial writings. DS3's tutorial area feels much easier than the first game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Combat (PVE): While the combat is satisfying when u manage to land a parry and get a riposte. I feel like the AI got slower from the last game. The hitboxes are perfectly in sync and i have never managed to miss a swing at close range on my own world that is. Other than that the PVE is excellent and manages to **** you up at every opportunity you give it.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Difficulty (and Controls): In my opinion the game feels alot easier than the first and second game. Everything is much easier to do now. Now u can perform certain actions like parrying by clicking CTRL in the corner of your keyboard. And jumping is now easier. All u have to do is hold the SPACEBAR and press it again quickly when u want to jump. In DS2 u had to hold the SPACEBAR and sprint while clicking the SCROLL button and SPACEBAR at the same time. (Like seriously who came up with that?) and i do know that u can change the keybindings for the keyboard in the menu. U can not change it for the controller however if u decide to connect one to your computer that is.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Combat (PVP): Just like in the beginning of my review i will say. Where do i start? The absurdly weird and extremely long ranges on some weapons makes me wanna puke in PVP. Yes sadly as far as i know. Every single weapon has reach longer than the weapon itself in PVP. Secondly everyone who invades will get to use estus. Yes ESTUS the one drink who we all love and hate at the same time has returned to the invaders hands. In DS1 invaders had estus and they could drink it but u could easily punish players who heal often. In DS2 invaders had no estus to drink and had to heal using other means (spells or blessings). Also in DS1 and DS2 u had to stand still to drink estus which made it easy to punish. In DS3 u don't stop when drinking but your movement gets down to crawl for a moment but it's easy to drink when out of range even with the weird weapon ranges. One thing they've done right was make it so anyone who invades or gets summoned always have HALF of their estus and not max. And one last thing players who invade or are summoned will always scale to your SOUL level if your SOUL level is below theirs. So be prepared to atleast invest a few points into Vitality so u can atleast survive a hit in PVP on higher levels. Weapons also scale to the host's maximum upgraded weapon. So keep that in mind.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall Rating: 9 / 10
The game was alot of fun. Especially if u can get a friend to play with you. Now to anyone that plans on buying this game for the first time. Prepare to smash keyboards. Alot. Im sure that by the end of this game u will have replaced atleast one or two keyboards if it is your first time playing a SOULS game. Also just give up if u feel like getting frustrated. Walk away and take a break, 30 minutes atleast and then come back to try again. First time i played DS1 i broke several keyboards and at the start of DS2 i was still mildly annoyed. At the beginning of DS3 i came back into a series that i had bad experiences with and remained calmed. Is this a good game? Yes.
Is it as good as any other game that From Software have made in recent years? No.
Sure, it's lore and world design are top notch (albeit with a few too many recurring themes in both) and it contends with those aspects of Dark Souls 1 quite well, however the PvP is the worst it has EVER been:
- The hitboxes are broken for a shocking number of weapons.
- Invaders are heavily punished (I invade alot, and I'd say about 90% of the invades are either two or three vs one)
- Blue sentinels/darkmoon blades hardly get any action, casters still suck for the mostpart.
- There's no actual PvP arena??? The B-Team managed this with Dark Souls 2.
- Poise is replaced with a 2-hit combo system using R1's, which means there is no point to go over a certain equip load. Furthermore, this r1 combo system heavily benefits long sword users since they can just spam R1 and fish for hits using the HUGE phantom hitboxes.
After getting so much of the multiplayer funcitonality right in Dark Souls 2, it seems like From have a habit of taking steps backwards for some reason.

Any self respecting fan of the 'Soulsborne' games should pick this up, especially those that have experienced the first Dark Souls.
Newcomers to the franchise need not worry, as the design is far more inviting yet still retaining the notorious difficulty.

Nobody is going to accuse the combat AI of being smart, either. It's pretty much keep shooting from a distance or charge directly at you.
It would be GREAT if there was an option to turn off the repetitive phases the settlers use. I don't need to hear about how Diamond City is the biggest city you ever saw over and over and over and over again.
Overall, a good time, though.

Is this a good game? Yes.
Is it as good as any other game that From Software have made in recent years? No.
Sure, it's lore and world design are top notch (albeit with a few too many recurring themes in both) and it contends with those aspects of Dark Souls 1 quite well, however the PvP is the worst it has EVER been:
- The hitboxes are broken for a shocking number of weapons.
- Invaders are heavily punished (I invade alot, and I'd say about 90% of the invades are either two or three vs one)
- Blue sentinels/darkmoon blades hardly get any action, casters still suck for the mostpart.
- There's no actual PvP arena??? The B-Team managed this with Dark Souls 2.
- Poise is replaced with a 2-hit combo system using R1's, which means there is no point to go over a certain equip load. Furthermore, this r1 combo system heavily benefits long sword users since they can just spam R1 and fish for hits using the HUGE phantom hitboxes.
After getting so much of the multiplayer funcitonality right in Dark Souls 2, it seems like From have a habit of taking steps backwards for some reason.

Any self respecting fan of the 'Soulsborne' games should pick this up, especially those that have experienced the first Dark Souls.
Newcomers to the franchise need not worry, as the design is far more inviting yet still retaining the notorious difficulty.

So... after playing Dark Souls on Old Gen, Dark Souls 2 (which was also on Old Gen) and Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin, I finally was able to play Dark Souls 3 and this was my impression:
I had a lot of fun with the old battle mechanics from Dark Souls mixed with the Engine of Bloodborne, which I couldn´t play sadly. I enjoyed the new Character Story Lines, the Weapons, the Bosses, and the PvP System! The possibility to delay attacks was a good move on the developers side. It really added some spice into it. I also played through every ending and they were great too and had their own satisfaction, even though they weren´t longer than 5 Minutes each. But if you played the other Dark Souls games, you are used to that. I also enjoyed almost all enemy types, and their unique attack patterns, which made each enemy a challenge, especially in a group.
But now for the bad parts:
- Since games like that depend on a good framerate to dodge attacks properly, I was severly disappointed in the frame
drops that happened while I was playing it. They did fix it now, but it still annoyed me pretty much.
- The game´s co-op, which has a big impact on the online experience (like the old parts), was enjoyable, but only to some
extend. For example, many coveneants which let you spawn automatically in friends or foes world, were broken and
didn´t work, or at least on very few occasions.
On top of that, the game´s community is still one of the saltiest of all games. People healing in a summoned 1v1,
gankers, hunting for invaders that want to farm their coveneant, and even hackers. Yes, I know, the Community doesn´t
anything to do with the Gameplay, but it influenced my opinion on the package alltogether.
- The Character Creation. There is a lot to customize from forehead to nose, but there where little things that annoyed me
like the incapability to make a special hair colour. You couldn´t make bright hair colours, like green or something like
that. It mostly looked bad, at least on my screen. What also annoys me is the low variety on Hair- and Beardstyles.
But with all that apart, I had a lot of fun playing this game, alone and with friends, and I am looking forward to the DLCs and more deadly surprises. I would give this game a 9/10, with the addition, that new comers to the series also can play it without thinking: What´s going on here?, because this is what Dark Souls is about. You have to figure it out by yourself, while the prequels didn´t have a huge impact on DS 3, except references and backstory wise.
WELL.
I hope this review helped you on deciding whether to buy this game or not. I´d recommend it and leave you.

What the hell will I play once I finish DS3?!?
Really tired of all the sandbox games with their side quests' broken and boring dialogues i have to click through. No time for all of that nonsense. I dreamt of sandbox RPG's when i was a kid, playing games on my C64, then Amiga. I always thought i could discover some new path or something in every game, until i was older and understood how it all works.
While sandbox games of today look like they are so big and open, there is no magic and imagination is stunted with it's precreated world. A sandbox game has to be perfect to the point of an almost perfect simulation of life and it's impossible.
Anyway, DS3 has nothing to do with sandbox, or RPG's for that matter. It's a super-satisfying dungeaon crawler/arcade/fight simulator with great combat and gameplay mechanics and a subtle story that leaves most to the imagination. No saves whenever you want, no reload of autosaves, no going back on choices you have made throughout the game, so you better take care in what you do. They nailed that part better than 'real' RPG's that claim how much your choices influence the outcome. Trust me, in this game, you will care about your every move.
Another thing they nailed better than most 'RPG's' is the continuity of the world. As you plough along, you will feel the world as one, coherent whole.
What i am trying to say is that DS beats today's RPG's, even while not trying to be one.
It beats today's shooters with the level of challenge it gives you and the sense of accomplishment when you manage to move on after getting stuck and dying countless tmes. No annoying difficulty slider you can tweak in mid-game, that so many games of today suffer from and no difficulty choice at all for that matter.
It beats all because it has a target you have to reach and doesn't distract you with uninportant fillers on your way to that target.
Speaking from the point of view of mine from my love of RPG's, again, not because the game is Role Playing, mostly because of the dark fantasy setting - If you want to wander around some 'amazing' sanbox world, talking to mentally challenged NPC's, have encounters that you can always beat by exploiting some terrain feature, or glitch that will mess with your enemy's AI mind and call that an RPG, this is not for you. Until those games have proper AI, they have nothing to offer, no matter how far you push the difficulty slider.
If you want an extremely satisfying gaming experience, in a smaller world that looks and feels great to traverse, with no silly distractions and micromanagement, with revolutionary gameplay when it comes to continuity, choices and (no)saves - try it.

I thought a long time about how to rate this game.
'Should i rate it as it's own game or in comparison to it's predecessors?'
I decided to rate it in comparison:
It still get's a thumbs up, but it's close not to, it may be a good SoulsBorne game but as a Dark Souls game i feel it is lacking something and has a few things it shouldn't.
In my opinion Dark Souls 3 has only a few new things to offer but some of them are either not really original or overshadowed by things from previous games (looking at you armour sets). The weapon arts are a nice addition but are just not useful on some weapons (like on a certain great hammer), the faster combat works well with PvP...
theoretically.
The faster fighting gives a great opportunity for interesting and adrenaline-soaking fights but sadly makes a lot of slower weapons unviable.
PvE wise the game is really great, a lot of interesting bosses, weapons and lore. Since (like in every Souls game) any weapon/build can carry you through the game there is a huge diversity between each playthrough if you want to since every fight will always play out differently (except the fact that you either win or die).
I do hope they bring back some of the Dark Souls 2 spells back though.

The enemy design is mostly put together very well except for the fact that some enemys behave as if they were in Bloodborne (fast and almost indodgeable).
All in all it's a solid title with some things they could have done better, it feels more like a well made, fanmade Dark Souls mod for Bloodborne.

The Good:
+Refreshing Combat (it's very different, more shooter like)
+Armor equipping couldn't be any more better (I can now wear individual plates on each limb separately)
+Amazing Crafting system (I can fully customize nearly every weapon available in game from stock to barrel)
+Lots of likeable followers (Followers in this game are loveable, unique and are actually nice to have around compared to the previous titles)
+Followers are more dynamic(from cutting in on your conversations to just passively doing things while you walk, they never feel like robots)
+Base Building (You will spend a TON of time doing this, it's nice to build your own setlements in the wastelands)
The Bad:
- I still CTD on startup (It's been a year already and I still can not play this game on fullscreen, and I've tried everything)
-Butchered Dialogue system (you got 4 options "QUEST", "Sarcastic Yes", "Yes", and "No")
-Mediocre story (for me the story of the game was not too interesting, I found myself wanting to build settlements, craft, and explore rather trying to continue the main storyline)
-Follower AI is stupid (It may be more dynamic as I mentioned earlier but it doesn't work well with scripted events ie in a scripted event whit skinny malone where due to my high persuasion I convinced him to give us 10 seconds to run away, my follower piper was still busy sitting around and checking crates and ended up starting a gun fight)
-Interior/Exterior (I expected bethesda to remove the need for interiors in this game for things like small houses atleast just like in the prologue, it didn't happen)
-The glitches (been a year already and I still get dialogue bugs, and mass teleporting npc's, and a bug that happens near the end of the game that just makes my character freeze up so I can't finish it even without mods)
-Less Mod friendly for Pc users, and modders
-DLC's that feel more like paid mods than official content
-Choices don't feel like they have much of an impact on the ingame world.
-It feels like a mediocre console port. (That's something you notice in the game as you play through, I have all these buttons but why can't I use them? why is the grenade button the same as melee?)
It's a fun game to play if you want to build bases, ♥♥♥♥ around, or turn your brain off and shoot things for a while but other than that I don't recommend it. (especially with the lingering bugs, in my experience as of the making of this review it's the buggiest out of all bethesda's games.)

Okay let me just get it out there I love the Souls series, and Dark Souls 3 I feel is a good step in the direction Dark souls originally set out on.
The music is a big plus here with Yuka Kitamura and Motoi Sakuraba both giving a solid performance from the sleek environmental soundtrack to the powerful boss themes that play as you strive to overcome them. I went out of my way to purchase the soundtrack after my first play through just so I could listen to tracks without raking up too many game hours or youtube bandwidth.
Thematically I believe it is stronger than Dark souls 2, it offers a far darker undertone that mimics the endless 'defeatism' of Dark Souls compared to the shattered pride theme I encountered during the second game which I truly enjoyed, each moment of beauty or awe was something that struck me and I often found myself returning to areas long cleared to just sit and look at the scenary.
Personally I felt that combat was weaker in the scene that of the current game getting high level sorcery comes really late game a huge nerf to those of us that love spells yet one that doesn't stop invaders from returning to beginning areas with said spells to wreck some peoples days. Many weapons feel 'samey' in move sets and even damage but I find myself still wanting to get them all to max level even without the 'proper' stats to use them just as a goal to enjoy.

If you're a casual gamer, avoid this as it's pretty much halo 1's "the library" on legendary for the entire game. Be prepared to memorize every enemy location, and map layout after attempting to complete a level 30 or so times.
The user interface is clunky and non-intuitive, the npc's flat and utilitarian. This is not an RPG, it's an action game. Know what you're purchasing here, I'd compare this to kingdom under fire, the circle of doom where the story was superficial to just wacking things with a new weapon; except everything can one shot if you miss a dodge or parry due to stun lock.
For those who don't care about traditional RPG elements, there's a robust weapons system as dark souls has this in spades. Be prepared to grind however as the 'side quest' system is convoluted and highly conditional per playthrough if you missed certian events. The game offers no aid in terms of where to go for level layout or how to progress. It's very hard-core in that sense that there's no hand-holding, so new players will find themselves looking at walkthroughs by others to figure out what to do.
If you enjoy the 'figure it out' and 'pure combat' aspects, then dark souls excells in that area above, and at the expense of all else. Just be prepared for the old-days punitive failing as opposed to the modern 'failing forward'. Also expect to lose hours of 'work' upon death if you can't reclaim your souls; so spend them early and often.

Two weeks into this game and I am very unlikely to play it more.
The good:
- One of the most beautiful video games out there.
The bad:
- The much vaunted challenge of this game is that you cannot save before challening places. The best speedrunners and the like get around this by copying the save file away manually and replacing it over and over again.
- Leveling trumps almost all the challenge of this game. This is typical of any and all level based games.
- Animation is KLUNKY. As pretty as the Souls world is, characters turn in jerky instantaneous shifts, and rotating the left joystick while doing anything results in an almost trademark ridiculous spin in place like a chess piece being twirled around. This is obscenely amateurish animation for 2016
- The PvP, which is what will make or break this game in terms of longevity, is broken beyond all repair for me personally. The roll mechanic is THE defensive aspect of this game, with a handful of folks mastering parries that can be rendered useless with many of the most powerful weapons when wieled with both hands. There's simply no way to make the PvP in this game interesting. The moment the player base dies back down to pre-hype levels, this game sits in your Steam collection gathering virtual dust.
Bottom Line: Ignore the Hype. Unless the artwork is enough for you (and if very nearly was for me. I had to think long and hard about whether I was going to bother reviewing this game or not because I LOVE the art work) there is no real sense buying this game.

Now, with my vast experience of every SoulsBorne game, and each of those from the Dark Souls trilogy on at least two platforms, I believe I can offer a well educated judgement of Dark Souls 3. I will be comparing it to its predecessors, naturally, but I shall also judge Dark Souls 3 as a game in its own right.
So, for those that haven't played a Souls game before, and won't understand my comparisons. Dark Souls 3 is an amazing game, but don't buy it. Go play the others, at least Dark Souls 1, or I'll come to your house and slap you until you do.
Right. For those experienced in souls, and want to know what Dark Souls 3 is like. Prepare to be both amazed and disappointed by this game.
Dark Souls 3 keeps the complex combat of the previous games, in face goes one step further by making it so complex that it makes no f***ing sense. Diminishing returns and the peculiar new 'poise' mechanic make ultra-heavy armours mostly useless, as they weigh you down. It's fine for me, because I always had 0 poise, but for those that always killed the 4 Kings by R1 spamming in Havel's.... gone are those days - but chugging is easier.
As usual, there's a hell of a lot of weapon variety. Unfortunately, only a few from each class are viable, as many weapons are wholly outclassed by others in their category. The same goes for armour, but nobody cares because fashion is what's important. Despite what some say, magic IS viable in DS3 and actually remains the most powerful thing in the game if used correctly.
Hyper Armour is a new addition. Certain weapon types now offer hyper armour during parts of their animations. This is good, since there is a lack of useful poise, but is very easily abused... and so 2-handed Hollowslayer is very powerful against someone who can't parry - not kidding, among the best weapons in the game.
The world design is similar-ish to DS2 mixed with Demon's Souls, but the individual area design is more akin to Dark Souls 1. In general, it's bloomin' good, I just wish the world as a whole was more connected. The HUB of the game works a lot like ademon's Souls and Bloodborne. Host to your very own Maiden / Doll for levelling, merchants, a blacksmith, and gathering place for various NPCs... it feels a lot like the Nexus in this regard. It is also disconnected from the main world.
The story and lore is just as expansive as its predecessors, and only more theories and secrets are coming to light as time passes. The same goes for a NPC quest lines. They are very akin to those in DS1, boasting unique encounters with NPCs and witnessing their stories unfold as yours does - take Ostrava, Siegmeyer, Solaire and Logan's quests for example. Most quests are as complex in nature, each with their own emotional and compelling story, as well as new kinds of gameplay features to improve upon the quests. Honestly, I think DS3 is host to some of the best NPC quests and characters, on par with Bloodborne and Dark Souls 1. Unfortunately, we have no Mephistopheles asking us to kill everyone, but there is one similar quest, and obvious reference.
The soundtrack is amazing, on par with that of predecessors, and accompanied by equally awesome bosses. There are slight disappointments, as with all of the games, but the majority are very good. Just be warned, bosses are more aggressive in DS3.
Finally, I'll summarise. Dark Souls 3 has its fair share of disappointments, but the are few enough not to tarnish the beauty of the game, and they are almost all mechanic based disappointments that may or may not be altered in later patches. The game, as a whole however, is fantastic and absolutely worth buying. PvP takes getting used to, because of the changes,  it is still good. And some covenants suck, but that's nothing new. However, don't let it deter you from getting yet another FromSoft masterpiece.
PS - Also... do buy that PS4 for Bloodborne, because it IS worth it.

'Ello there. I'm here because I wanted to review this game's pros and cons, and give my opinion on whether it's worth buying for almost $70.
So, speaking of issues, what kinds are there?
Well, the game certainly doesn't mind crashing every few minutes. It doesn't happen to everyone, and it only started happening to me after the 1.0.7 update that came out recently, and ironically, "fixed performance issues." Very funny. I've found the crashing can be delayed by turning settings to low and reverting your driver version back to 362.00. Reverting it further may stop it, but I have no idea and I'm too lazy to try today. I'll get back to you on that!
Other than that, the game's infusions are not very good. Not the system itself, but the infusions within.
- 4 of them (bleed, poison, fire, deep) are completely outclassed by resins.
- 3 are only useful on very specific builds (crystal, lightning, hollow).
- 2 are just passive buffs that you wouldn't put on anything but an offhand parrying tool like a Caestus (blessed, simple).
The others, Raw, Chaos, Dark, Refined, Heavy, and Sharp, are the only ones that are all-around good infusions. Raw has no scaling but great non-split damage and can be buffed; Refined is the best infusion in the game, decreasing base damage but increasing scaling for STR and DEX, can be buffed, and is useful at pretty much any amount of stat investment; Chaos and Dark give very nice scaling in FTH and INT but the damage is split between 2 types and they're unbuffable making them the worst good infusion instead of the best; Sharp increases DEX scaling a lot but lowers STR scaling and base damage, and Heavy does the opposite although it completely removes DEX scaling instead of lowering it.
Also, there are entire classes of weapons that dominate the meta. Ultra Greatswords, Katanas, and Straight Swords are the best classes of weapons in the game.
- Only FTH builds can out-trade Ultra Greatswords and their hyper armor but they're easy to dodge.
- Katanas have amazing running attacks that have great reach (especially the Washing Pole; one of the longest reaching attacks in the game), high speed, thrusting damage type, and good damage, and are good outside of said attacks as well with their great DPS and quick attacks.
- Straight Swords are Katanas with good mixup options and shorter range.
There are also plenty of individual weapons that are a little bit too good even for their weapon class.
-The Carthus Curved Sword. Think of a straight sword on steroids, crack and some sort of imaginary superdrug and you're about halfway to the CCS.
- Anri's Straight Sword, despite being nerfed, is still one of the best weapons in the game, with its amazing Luck scaling it can do absurd damage on a bleed build with Carthus Rouge.
- The Broadsword is the strongest straight sword in the game after the Dark Sword nerf, having 117 base damage, good scaling, and being available before the second boss.
- The Estoc is unarguably one of the best PvE weapons in the game, sporting absurd DPS (melts NG+6 bosses in seconds with DMB), the ability to hit around shields to prevent a well-spaced attack from hitting you after you whiff, and a surprising amount of range.
I could go on, but I won't. But I could.
But let's not talk about such depressing matters! Let's see what great things this game has to offer.
-60fps
-Graphics that fit the theme of the game (quite rare nowadays... D:)
-The most well balanced starting gifts of the series, it's not a "okay I'm going to choose this," it's a "should I choose this or this? or maybe this"
-Better PvE than Dark Souls 2, not like that's saying much
-Solid PvP
-Fairly low system requirements (I ran max settings with 100% consistency, even before the performance fix, at 60fps, using a Nvidia GeForce GTX 960, an Intel i5 6500, and 16GB RAM, pretty sure a simple laptop could run this game lol)
So overall, should you buy it? Well, really, it's up to you. If you don't care for the multiplayer, I certainly wouldn't reccomend it. If you do, you should wait for it to go on sale IMO, and test it immediately to see if you have problems with crashing so that you can refund if necessary.

'Ello there. I'm here because I wanted to review this game's pros and cons, and give my opinion on whether it's worth buying for almost $70.
So, speaking of issues, what kinds are there?
Well, the game certainly doesn't mind crashing every few minutes. It doesn't happen to everyone, and it only started happening to me after the 1.0.7 update that came out recently, and ironically, "fixed performance issues." Very funny. I've found the crashing can be delayed by turning settings to low and reverting your driver version back to 362.00. Reverting it further may stop it, but I have no idea and I'm too lazy to try today. I'll get back to you on that!
Other than that, the game's infusions are not very good. Not the system itself, but the infusions within.
- 4 of them (bleed, poison, fire, deep) are completely outclassed by resins.
- 3 are only useful on very specific builds (crystal, lightning, hollow).
- 2 are just passive buffs that you wouldn't put on anything but an offhand parrying tool like a Caestus (blessed, simple).
The others, Raw, Chaos, Dark, Refined, Heavy, and Sharp, are the only ones that are all-around good infusions. Raw has no scaling but great non-split damage and can be buffed; Refined is the best infusion in the game, decreasing base damage but increasing scaling for STR and DEX, can be buffed, and is useful at pretty much any amount of stat investment; Chaos and Dark give very nice scaling in FTH and INT but the damage is split between 2 types and they're unbuffable making them the worst good infusion instead of the best; Sharp increases DEX scaling a lot but lowers STR scaling and base damage, and Heavy does the opposite although it completely removes DEX scaling instead of lowering it.
Also, there are entire classes of weapons that dominate the meta. Ultra Greatswords, Katanas, and Straight Swords are the best classes of weapons in the game.
- Only FTH builds can out-trade Ultra Greatswords and their hyper armor but they're easy to dodge.
- Katanas have amazing running attacks that have great reach (especially the Washing Pole; one of the longest reaching attacks in the game), high speed, thrusting damage type, and good damage, and are good outside of said attacks as well with their great DPS and quick attacks.
- Straight Swords are Katanas with good mixup options and shorter range.
There are also plenty of individual weapons that are a little bit too good even for their weapon class.
-The Carthus Curved Sword. Think of a straight sword on steroids, crack and some sort of imaginary superdrug and you're about halfway to the CCS.
- Anri's Straight Sword, despite being nerfed, is still one of the best weapons in the game, with its amazing Luck scaling it can do absurd damage on a bleed build with Carthus Rouge.
- The Broadsword is the strongest straight sword in the game after the Dark Sword nerf, having 117 base damage, good scaling, and being available before the second boss.
- The Estoc is unarguably one of the best PvE weapons in the game, sporting absurd DPS (melts NG+6 bosses in seconds with DMB), the ability to hit around shields to prevent a well-spaced attack from hitting you after you whiff, and a surprising amount of range.
I could go on, but I won't. But I could.
But let's not talk about such depressing matters! Let's see what great things this game has to offer.
-60fps
-Graphics that fit the theme of the game (quite rare nowadays... D:)
-The most well balanced starting gifts of the series, it's not a "okay I'm going to choose this," it's a "should I choose this or this? or maybe this"
-Better PvE than Dark Souls 2, not like that's saying much
-Solid PvP
-Fairly low system requirements (I ran max settings with 100% consistency, even before the performance fix, at 60fps, using a Nvidia GeForce GTX 960, an Intel i5 6500, and 16GB RAM, pretty sure a simple laptop could run this game lol)
So overall, should you buy it? Well, really, it's up to you. If you don't care for the multiplayer, I certainly wouldn't reccomend it. If you do, you should wait for it to go on sale IMO, and test it immediately to see if you have problems with crashing so that you can refund if necessary.

Two weeks into this game and I am very unlikely to play it more.
The good:
- One of the most beautiful video games out there.
The bad:
- The much vaunted challenge of this game is that you cannot save before challening places. The best speedrunners and the like get around this by copying the save file away manually and replacing it over and over again.
- Leveling trumps almost all the challenge of this game. This is typical of any and all level based games.
- Animation is KLUNKY. As pretty as the Souls world is, characters turn in jerky instantaneous shifts, and rotating the left joystick while doing anything results in an almost trademark ridiculous spin in place like a chess piece being twirled around. This is obscenely amateurish animation for 2016
- The PvP, which is what will make or break this game in terms of longevity, is broken beyond all repair for me personally. The roll mechanic is THE defensive aspect of this game, with a handful of folks mastering parries that can be rendered useless with many of the most powerful weapons when wieled with both hands. There's simply no way to make the PvP in this game interesting. The moment the player base dies back down to pre-hype levels, this game sits in your Steam collection gathering virtual dust.
Bottom Line: Ignore the Hype. Unless the artwork is enough for you (and if very nearly was for me. I had to think long and hard about whether I was going to bother reviewing this game or not because I LOVE the art work) there is no real sense buying this game.

Now, with my vast experience of every SoulsBorne game, and each of those from the Dark Souls trilogy on at least two platforms, I believe I can offer a well educated judgement of Dark Souls 3. I will be comparing it to its predecessors, naturally, but I shall also judge Dark Souls 3 as a game in its own right.
So, for those that haven't played a Souls game before, and won't understand my comparisons. Dark Souls 3 is an amazing game, but don't buy it. Go play the others, at least Dark Souls 1, or I'll come to your house and slap you until you do.
Right. For those experienced in souls, and want to know what Dark Souls 3 is like. Prepare to be both amazed and disappointed by this game.
Dark Souls 3 keeps the complex combat of the previous games, in face goes one step further by making it so complex that it makes no f***ing sense. Diminishing returns and the peculiar new 'poise' mechanic make ultra-heavy armours mostly useless, as they weigh you down. It's fine for me, because I always had 0 poise, but for those that always killed the 4 Kings by R1 spamming in Havel's.... gone are those days - but chugging is easier.
As usual, there's a hell of a lot of weapon variety. Unfortunately, only a few from each class are viable, as many weapons are wholly outclassed by others in their category. The same goes for armour, but nobody cares because fashion is what's important. Despite what some say, magic IS viable in DS3 and actually remains the most powerful thing in the game if used correctly.
Hyper Armour is a new addition. Certain weapon types now offer hyper armour during parts of their animations. This is good, since there is a lack of useful poise, but is very easily abused... and so 2-handed Hollowslayer is very powerful against someone who can't parry - not kidding, among the best weapons in the game.
The world design is similar-ish to DS2 mixed with Demon's Souls, but the individual area design is more akin to Dark Souls 1. In general, it's bloomin' good, I just wish the world as a whole was more connected. The HUB of the game works a lot like ademon's Souls and Bloodborne. Host to your very own Maiden / Doll for levelling, merchants, a blacksmith, and gathering place for various NPCs... it feels a lot like the Nexus in this regard. It is also disconnected from the main world.
The story and lore is just as expansive as its predecessors, and only more theories and secrets are coming to light as time passes. The same goes for a NPC quest lines. They are very akin to those in DS1, boasting unique encounters with NPCs and witnessing their stories unfold as yours does - take Ostrava, Siegmeyer, Solaire and Logan's quests for example. Most quests are as complex in nature, each with their own emotional and compelling story, as well as new kinds of gameplay features to improve upon the quests. Honestly, I think DS3 is host to some of the best NPC quests and characters, on par with Bloodborne and Dark Souls 1. Unfortunately, we have no Mephistopheles asking us to kill everyone, but there is one similar quest, and obvious reference.
The soundtrack is amazing, on par with that of predecessors, and accompanied by equally awesome bosses. There are slight disappointments, as with all of the games, but the majority are very good. Just be warned, bosses are more aggressive in DS3.
Finally, I'll summarise. Dark Souls 3 has its fair share of disappointments, but the are few enough not to tarnish the beauty of the game, and they are almost all mechanic based disappointments that may or may not be altered in later patches. The game, as a whole however, is fantastic and absolutely worth buying. PvP takes getting used to, because of the changes,  it is still good. And some covenants suck, but that's nothing new. However, don't let it deter you from getting yet another FromSoft masterpiece.
PS - Also... do buy that PS4 for Bloodborne, because it IS worth it.

One of the themes of Dark Souls is cycles; if enough time passes certain events, people and places are likely to repeat. It is also a series about death and rebirth. If From Software is to be believed, Dark Souls III is the death of this franchise and I have to say I'm glad. Now don't get me wrong, I really like this game (not quite as much as the original) but the franchise appears to be running out of ideas (check out my in depth first impressions video for more).
The story is a continuation on the dying fire needs rekindling theme with no major additions to the lore, or explanations for why this is happening. This show, don’t tell approach worked amazingly well in the original but this is the third game in the series and some answers would be nice. Items, characters and locations also repeat with little rhyme or reason. Are they connected to the originals world and if so how much time has passed? What happened?
In its favour DS3 has the most interesting location and monster design (in terms of visuals) so far in this series and the Cathedral of the Deep is some of the best level design. Combat is a mixed bag and often leads to spamming light attack especially in pvp. The faster pace occasionally makes things more exciting but I miss poise and blocking.
This is still a good end to the series and is well worth checking out if you’re a Souls fan; just don’t expect to be blown away in the same way as you were with dark Souls.

Definitely the most accessible game in the Souls series, but still provides a challenge. The world is brilliantly designed and is my favourite of the series; not as varied as Dark Souls 2, but the level design is much more realistic and interesting. Enemies can either be harmless mooks or spiritual sub-bosses, you might get some of the super weak ones near the end of the game backed up by bulky knights that pose the real threat.
There's lots to go out and find in this game, so many secrets and surprises; it's really fun to just start playing and see where your heart takes you. I recommend going after every boss in the game, as I would consider not doing so to be not beating the game properly. Some of the bosses around the middle get quite easy, but then it definitely picks up, and especially the optional bosses will give you a run for your time and money.
Only complaint I have is to do with the graphics; overall it's a very pretty game, but all the bricks/rocks look like they're made of wax. And it's really obvious and I have no idea why no one else brings it up online. But it's a nitpick anyway.
For those looking for a challenging RPG that focuses heavily on gameplay, replayability and level design then this is a perfect game for you.

Dark Souls 3... This game is not an easy game. It challenges you to learn, failure after failure. The best part of this game is the cathartic feeling of success you get after succeeding where you previously failed. I came into the game with the previous experience of playing Dark Souls 1 and 2. Because of this it did not take me long to learn the ropes of the game. Even so, I still have trouble with certain bosses and areas. No matter how good you are you can get fatally eaten, launched off a cliff, sat on (not in the good way), stabbed from behind (also not in a good way), cursed, stomped, burned, and humiliated by naked people in pvp.
In summary, I would reccommend this game to those who are looking for a challenge. You also have to be mature enough to handle constant and utter failures. The game really isn't THAT hard though.

Dark Souls III is the final installment of the Dark Souls series, and serves as a fitting ending to a series that was intentionally vague in its story, lore and direction. It's famous for its challenging and unforgiving gameplay, but it grows on you and your victories are all the more precious and feel well earned.
The worlds and enemies are masterfully crafted, and the environments are full of personality. One of my only gripes is the absolutely abhorrent multiplayer, which I will cover in more detail later. A lot of players will mention the whole "git gud" shtick, and it's partially true, but mostly false. This generally concensus of "it's only fun if you're winning" leads to a largely negative multiplayer experience and heavy reliance on "meta" builds and weapons as opposed to "fun" ones.
ISSUE 1: Hackers.
Dark Souls III has a rather incomplete anti-hacking system, which more often punishes honest players who happen to be victims of a hacker who adds five million souls to your soul count, which prompts a ban from the game. On top of this, getting unbanned is almost always impossible, which will be covered later. In my personal experience, I was invaded by a player who used some sort of coordinate altering software to teleport my character into the air, prompting immediate death from fall damage. He did this six times in a row before my friends and I managed to rush through the area and avoid him.
ISSUE 2: Forced Multiplayer.
This is a mixed issue here. I understand that it's a classic Souls mechanic, but it still grinds my gears a little bit that you really have no control over when you are forced to engage other players in combat. You can, of course, commit suicide in-game and "un-ember" yourself to avoid being invaded, but in turn you are completely cut off from all multiplayer functions, including co-op, as well as losing a portion of your maximum health as punishment for not playing with the community. This translates as "Play with everyone or play with no one, but you're probably better off letting other players kill you."
ISSUE 3: FromSoftware itself, the developer of the Dark Souls series.
Their enormous success with their franchise has led to an equally enormous ego, and as such they do not take their fans into consideration. Most of the customer complaints go unanswered, bans from hacker interference are ignored, and next to no notice is given before server maintenance or patches. Most phone calls and emails are sent in an endless loop of customer service reps who really don't care what you have to say, and just pass you off to the next teller.
Those are my only gripes. Other than that, Dark Souls III is an amazing singleplayer experience and I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a challenge, wrapped in a vague story, coated in a sprinkle of lethal bugs(like getting stuck in a wall, unable to run away, as an enormous monster smashes you into ground beef).
For those of you who skipped to the final paragraph here, I'll recap:
(1) Hackers are rampant and unadressed,
(2) Player Versus Player Combat is out of your control unless you handicap yourself and miss out on a good portion of the game, and
(3) The Devs are egotistical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who will not provide support for unfair bans, broken games, bugs or general customer service.
(4) The game itself, however, is pretty damn awesome.

This is a game I really wanted to love. I did enjoy it for what it's worth, but it could have been so much more. I'll mostly be talking about what upset me because what there is to be loved about a Souls game is pretty much the same across the board.
I don't know why From insists on pretending that heavy builds work-as-intended when they are broken. Fine, take away the heavy str options and have everyone do quality or dex, but actually design all the builds around your new fast paced approach. From... you wanted to put Bloodborne in my game when I wanted Dark Souls. You didn't just put BB in there, you ♥♥♥♥ing JAMMED IT IN THERE and ignored all the aspects that make Dark Souls what it is.
Another thing, I didn't think it was possible for the level design to be worse than Dark Souls 2 but maybe I should have seen it coming knowing there would be a hub. This game is a disgrace to level design as far as the zone connections go. Fanboys will defend it saying there is a tiny bit of flexibility in how to go about your playthrough but they are deluded. You are following straight paths that branch off the main path, and they are dead ends. This kills the Souls. HOWEVER, Cathedral of the Deep is one of the most intricate and entertaining levels I have played in a long time and it stands alone as the shining gem within the sad mess Dark Souls 3 is.
The aesthetics are lovely, the influence of BB is apaprent but it isn't overwhelming (see: armor dudes that move like canines). Irithyll was a very cool area to explore and the creature design in that zone was also lovely with how it echoes Dancer of the Frigid Valley (or Boreal, if you are triggered by terms that may or may not refer to libido). The Deep is clearly Lovecraftian and that is a treat, though it needs a lot more elaboration, hopefully in the coming DLCs. The new firekeeper is the qtest of them all so far, but she says very few things and is devoid of any personality. RIP Gwyndolin.
I just hope From does not bring any heavy build items for the DLC so we can just make peace with going dex and have many interesting options in the type of build that actually works in this goddamn game. I'd rather have poise back with some other adjustments to combat but From is stubborn and won't admit their mistake. So let's just find the happy medium and all roll around in our fashion souls and puny swords.

Dark Souls 3 is the latest in a venerable series of games, starting with Demon's Souls.  Dark Souls has always been about risk versus reward, with challenges balanced around progress, better equipment, and growth as a character and player.  Enemy placemnent has always allowed carefully progressing players to know what's coming up ahead and plan, and in theory, even at level 1, a player could overcome these obstacles with judicious planning.
How does Dark Souls 3 stand up to these traditions?  Rather well, I'd say! You start out with next to nothing (unless you pick the Deprived class.  Then it IS nothing!) and must crawl, scrape, and fight your way past giants, demons, and the legions of mad undead to save a dying world.
Layout in the game is fairly gentle for the first few areas, with either a few aggressive enemies or a clump of passive nonhostile undead.  This changes quickly, and you learn cautious use of a bow is a requirement to peel off dangerous foes, and that any group more then two or three is a death sentence, especially early on.
Late game challenge is found not in large mobs or waves of foes, but rather strong, agile enemies that work together.  One of the hardest fights is three NPCs who fight together, flanking you, distracting you, and healing while you're dodging their allys' attacks.
Overall, I'm eagerly awaiting the launch of the DLCs, and I recommend this to anyone who wants a good game to try.  Just prepare to die at first.

Ya'll need to take off your nostalgia glasses. Dark Souls I has flaws. Dark Souls II has flaws. Dark Souls III has flaws.

I have nothing to say about the PvE aspect, which is sublime in every area of the game (Save for Irithyll Dungeon. You'll see.) and the bossfights are the best they have ever been.
Where most of Dark Souls III's flaws lie is in its PvP. Granted, this game isn't as old as the other two, and From Software is bringing out patches regularly to fix balance issues. But as it stands, PvP leaves something to be desired.
However, if you are looking for a sublime PvE experience, then Dark Souls III is sure to satisfy your needs. I personally recommend Dark Souls III to the fullest.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Dark Souls III didn't like me, and initially I didn't like it. It felt a lot like the oppressive overworked middle school teacher who would yell at you to have fun on field trips. Somewhat similar to a fascist regime I thought to myself, as I romanticized my failure to grasp the games concepts. It wasn't til later on; when I was about half way through the game when I started making that a positive link. Stating that the game would kick your teeth in and fitting them back into your gums was genuinely fun. Not quite, as that's not the greatest analogy. Hours of playtime before that I refunded it. Two minutes before I overshot the Steam refund limit.
That's right, for the first two hours I couldn't muster the capabilities to defeat my mortal enemy (at the time) Iudex Gundyr. No, his halberd far too strong for my tastes, moveset too unpredictable to the new player that I was. I admit, I went in with high expectations thinking I could pick it up and power through. Now with a 64 hour gametime and only one Journey completed my original estimate is one of ego and rumors.
At the time of refund I was using a mouse and keyboard, and would later realize that this was taking a game that should be sitting up there with Half-Life 2 and it's compatriots (Sorry Half-Life, didn't like you as much) and taking it down to a level where I was essentially trying to play Starcraft 2 on the Commodor64 without a floppy disc to actually play the game. In short, it really, really, really, didn't work out well.
After much nudging and pushing and stares aimed at the 80% positive review bar I eventually took the same refunded 60$ and got the game. Again. At full price. I also decided to be really adventurous and got the Steam Controller on whim/suggestion, as all my previous experiences with X-Box and PlayStation controllers had left me with PTSD comparable to Bastion of Overwatch.
The doors to the game (and the ones right after the Iudex bonfire) opened up and all of a sudden the game wasn't so much a grind to beat a 'level', but a functional world that didn't care if you were picking up eagle shields or invading. I was just another undead wandering around killing other undead (Pretty damn rude now that I think about it). The controller did a lot, bridging the gap between my keyboard fetish and my controller PTSD to create a working, dare I say, fun, Dark Souls III experience.
But for those who (like me at the start of this endeavor) are unfamiliar with the Souls series it's not so much instant fun as the modern day shooters that fail to impress, (That, in my opinion, barely stand up to the original Halo 1 Demo and the holy land of BloodGulch). It's a rhythmic process, akin to learning how to play an instrument. You're going to ♥♥♥♥ up, and once you accept that the world doesn't actually give a damn about you ♥♥♥♥ing up, you'll get along nicely with the plethora of surprisingly agile corpses and fauna of Lothric that inhabit it's various nooks and crannies.
Only later on did I discover the far more dynamic magical but not so magic-user friendly land of PVP. It's an interesting system to say the least. Rather than joining your buddy pals through steam or your buddy not so good pals I'd rather stab you then shake hands through a server browser you're lore bound to the world. Forced to use it's really poorly explained soapstone system that's got it's quirks but gets the job done and doesn't remove the immersion that the game so desperately strives for. The only thing that might do that would be the Estoc, but new players will figure that out pretty quickly.
But to get back on course, PVP took everything I knew about Dark Souls III and once more kicked my teeth and, but instead of telling me to have fun repeatedly learning a new area it told me to quite simply: “Git gud”. The words all those who praise the sun or otherwise take to heart when scrounging for the embers of a host.
Instead of the undead teaching me these new ways it was close friends and companions, or the ever knowledgeable land of Youtube, who through countless parry montages taught me the way of parrying (Of which I still cannot perform).
It's a mean world that you'll need to lick the boots of before understanding that those boots don't increase your hidden poise stat. The PvE is hard, and a hell of a lot easier with friends or even random summons; they can at least get you back to your souls. And the PvP is another beast entirely, something to be feared and respected. Oh, and by chance you've read this far, don't use the curved sword or the estoc. It's just rude. -Triiodine.

Dark Souls III is the final installment of the Dark Souls series, and serves as a fitting ending to a series that was intentionally vague in its story, lore and direction. It's famous for its challenging and unforgiving gameplay, but it grows on you and your victories are all the more precious and feel well earned.
The worlds and enemies are masterfully crafted, and the environments are full of personality. One of my only gripes is the absolutely abhorrent multiplayer, which I will cover in more detail later. A lot of players will mention the whole "git gud" shtick, and it's partially true, but mostly false. This generally concensus of "it's only fun if you're winning" leads to a largely negative multiplayer experience and heavy reliance on "meta" builds and weapons as opposed to "fun" ones.
ISSUE 1: Hackers.
Dark Souls III has a rather incomplete anti-hacking system, which more often punishes honest players who happen to be victims of a hacker who adds five million souls to your soul count, which prompts a ban from the game. On top of this, getting unbanned is almost always impossible, which will be covered later. In my personal experience, I was invaded by a player who used some sort of coordinate altering software to teleport my character into the air, prompting immediate death from fall damage. He did this six times in a row before my friends and I managed to rush through the area and avoid him.
ISSUE 2: Forced Multiplayer.
This is a mixed issue here. I understand that it's a classic Souls mechanic, but it still grinds my gears a little bit that you really have no control over when you are forced to engage other players in combat. You can, of course, commit suicide in-game and "un-ember" yourself to avoid being invaded, but in turn you are completely cut off from all multiplayer functions, including co-op, as well as losing a portion of your maximum health as punishment for not playing with the community. This translates as "Play with everyone or play with no one, but you're probably better off letting other players kill you."
ISSUE 3: FromSoftware itself, the developer of the Dark Souls series.
Their enormous success with their franchise has led to an equally enormous ego, and as such they do not take their fans into consideration. Most of the customer complaints go unanswered, bans from hacker interference are ignored, and next to no notice is given before server maintenance or patches. Most phone calls and emails are sent in an endless loop of customer service reps who really don't care what you have to say, and just pass you off to the next teller.
Those are my only gripes. Other than that, Dark Souls III is an amazing singleplayer experience and I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a challenge, wrapped in a vague story, coated in a sprinkle of lethal bugs(like getting stuck in a wall, unable to run away, as an enormous monster smashes you into ground beef).

This is a game I really wanted to love. I did enjoy it for what it's worth, but it could have been so much more. I'll mostly be talking about what upset me because what there is to be loved about a Souls game is pretty much the same across the board.
I don't know why From insists on pretending that heavy builds work-as-intended when they are broken. Fine, take away the heavy str options and have everyone do quality or dex, but actually design all the builds around your new fast paced approach. From... you wanted to put Bloodborne in my game when I wanted Dark Souls. You didn't just put BB in there, you ♥♥♥♥ing JAMMED IT IN THERE and ignored all the aspects that make Dark Souls what it is.
Another thing, I didn't think it was possible for the level design to be worse than Dark Souls 2 but maybe I should have seen it coming knowing there would be a hub. This game is a disgrace to level design as far as the zone connections go. Fanboys will defend it saying there is a tiny bit of flexibility in how to go about your playthrough but they are deluded. You are following straight paths that branch off the main path, and they are dead ends. This kills the Souls. HOWEVER, Cathedral of the Deep is one of the most intricate and entertaining levels I have played in a long time and it stands alone as the shining gem within the sad mess Dark Souls 3 is.
The aesthetics are lovely, the influence of BB is apaprent but it isn't overwhelming (see: armor dudes that move like canines). Irithyll was a very cool area to explore and the creature design in that zone was also lovely with how it echoes Dancer of the Frigid Valley (or Boreal, if you are triggered by terms that may or may not refer to libido). The Deep is clearly Lovecraftian and that is a treat, though it needs a lot more elaboration, hopefully in the coming DLCs. The new firekeeper is the qtest of them all so far, but she says very few things and is devoid of any personality. RIP Gwyndolin.
I just hope From does not bring any heavy build items for the DLC so we can just make peace with going dex and have many interesting options in the type of build that actually works in this goddamn game. I'd rather have poise back with some other adjustments to combat but From is stubborn and won't admit their mistake. So let's just find the happy medium and all roll around in our fashion souls and puny swords.

Revisiting my review.
Hands down the worst dark souls in the series, but still a good game.
I have 2 main complaints that give me the opinion stated above;
1. It's bloodborne, but it's also not.
The visual style, a lot of enemies and the general pacing of the game is almost straight out of bloodborne. This wouldn't be a problem if they balanced it out properly but it feels like the enemies are agressive and flurry-ish, but you're still a heavy dark souls player.
Basically if you solo this game you'll constantly find yourself just spamming dodge endlessly until you finally get a small window to attack while getting attacked by 5 of the same enemy at once.
2. It's very linear.
The thing i loved about dark souls was that you had no clear indication where to go; there were multiple paths and you would just wander into any of them, getting relentlessly beaten or fighting your way through. This also always gave you a sense of danger, because you never knew if you were walking into enemies of your level.
In dark souls 3 you just clear area after area, this coupled with the repetetive enemies makes for a bland experience after dieing in one area a couple of times, or having to clear it a couple of times.
Also it's worth noting that there's a smaller amount of unique builds you can try to make.
Basically any pvper you see will have an OP 2h weapon without any armor on, because it's worthless in this game.
Poise has been disabled but you might have heard about that, i read something about it being "re-added" into the game but you'll still feel as vulnerable in a heavy set of armor as in a light one, especially since you have to constantly roll in this game.
Combat is nice, would have liked more variety and stuff though.
For me it just doesn't feel like the enemies were designed for Dark souls 3's pacing.
Also PvP is an overglorified mess in the game, if you buy for PvP then stick with dark souls 2.
You just sprint and R1 to win.
I'm recommending this with doubts, so if you're a big dark souls fan you might be disappointed by the changes here.

Revisiting my review.
Hands down the worst dark souls in the series, but still a good game.
I have 2 main complaints that give me the opinion stated above;
1. It's bloodborne, but it's also not.
The visual style, a lot of enemies and the general pacing of the game is almost straight out of bloodborne. This wouldn't be a problem if they balanced it out properly but it feels like the enemies are agressive and flurry-ish, but you're still a heavy dark souls player.
Basically if you solo this game you'll constantly find yourself just spamming dodge endlessly until you finally get a small window to attack while getting attacked by 5 of the same enemy at once.
2. It's very linear.
The thing i loved about dark souls was that you had no clear indication where to go; there were multiple paths and you would just wander into any of them, getting relentlessly beaten or fighting your way through. This also always gave you a sense of danger, because you never knew if you were walking into enemies of your level.
In dark souls 3 you just clear area after area, this coupled with the repetetive enemies makes for a bland experience after dieing in one area a couple of times, or having to clear it a couple of times.
Also it's worth noting that there's a smaller amount of unique builds you can try to make.
Basically any pvper you see will have an OP 2h weapon without any armor on, because it's worthless in this game.
Poise has been disabled but you might have heard about that, i read something about it being "re-added" into the game but you'll still feel as vulnerable in a heavy set of armor as in a light one, especially since you have to constantly roll in this game.
Combat is nice, would have liked more variety and stuff though.
For me it just doesn't feel like the enemies were designed for Dark souls 3's pacing.
Also PvP is an overglorified mess in the game, if you buy for PvP then stick with dark souls 2.
You just sprint and R1 to win.
I'm recommending this with doubts, so if you're a big dark souls fan you might be disappointed by the changes here.
Buy it for base building. otherwise the RPG story elements will let you down.

F4 is beyond awesome. Veterans to the series may complain that the early power items in this iteration made the game more of a walk through shooting gallery than a survival game, but as a true to form RPG, it's honestly how you play.
Part 1: The "Bro" Version. Part 2: The Great Wall of Text
1. The "Bro" Review
"Hey, bro, so, like this game, I was walkin' around this cool lookin' wasteland with this crazy lookin' rifle that shoots partcles 'n schtuff and this giant green hermit crab pops outta the ground and I'm like 'whaaa' then I shot it till it's head popped off. It was sweet. Then I found some meat on it, cooked it and ate it to get my health back. Then I found this chick who was like 'where's my son?' and I was like 'wanna help' and she was like 'sure' and we went and killed these robot dudes at this house-thing, and she turned out to be their leader and it was like a trap and like yeah. Yeah bro, it was sick."
2. The Great Wall of Text Review
Bethesda gives you more "dungeons", random encounters, customizability, and sheer map size than anything I've seen in their other games. You can use this however you'd like to, but the real fun and challenge comes in crafting a character that uniquely suits your playstyle. Stealth-oriented players can sneak up on enemies for massive damage multipliers and tanky minigun toting power armor users can cut through a ghoul (zombie) swarm like a hot knife through butter, but be wary of the drawbacks.
Get caught in a bottleneck, nimble rogue, and the game will crush you like a radroach. Come back with a suit of power armor and you may fare better, but if you waked there you're probably out of power and can't walk back. If you make that journy, you've got an expensive repair bill on your hands with materials that have to be found. After a while you might set up a few settlements and find people to do the work for you, but if building houses, beds, farms, and wells for those people isn't your thing, then don't do it.
So what do you do? Like life, find something that suits you. Aimless wandering is what these games are known for, but they're numerous factions, military, technological, or otherwise, that are desperate for your support. These choices bear their own consequences, and that's what makes this game great.
I wouldn't recommend this game to someone who isn't comfortable with great freedom of choice in their journey. Linear gameplay is incredibly rare here, as even the deepest bunker or tallest building is littered with interconnecting rooms, trap doors, access stairways, and rooftops. Tactically oriented players can scout the building with a night vision scope, go up the fire escape to take out the snipers on the roof and enter through the access hatch to find themselves perched on a catwalk that overlooks the baddie littered factory floor below. It's easy pickings from there, but you want to charge in the front door, no one's stopping you.
If you die in there, you'll take more of a hit to your ego than anything. There's no save checkpoints you have to hit to keep yourself backed up, just an autosave feature that'll save you if you forget to hit the quicksave button every now and then. Those of you looking for a challenge might be disgusted that the game's difficulty can be so easily circumvented, but in an age of multiplayer games where everything you do can be compared to other players,this game set the onus of performance sits squarely on your shoulders. Do what you do, and do it well, because you and only you will know that it was good.
A word of warning to my perfectionistic brethren. You can make yourself hate this game if you're not careful. You can only carry so much, and while you can fast travel back to base to dump your scavenged materials, just take tbe ripest fruits and don't spend all day evaluating which items are most deserving. Management aspects like this are fun and rewarding, but they cater to players who want to watch their resources grow over time. Learn to prioritize early on and remember that time is the only resource in scarcity.
Play this game if you enjoy working at making your character good, running across cool looking monsters, interesting people, and epic items that can dish out gratuitous amounts of damage. With corny retro music playing in the background the whole time.

This is a review aimed towards those who are interested in buying the game and are new to the Souls series. If you are a returning player interested in knowing how it compares to the other two games, in my opinion, Dark Souls III is much better than either of the iterations, with more variety than Dark Souls II and much more balanced, fluid gameplay than Dark Souls and much less unfairness in its design choice. Though if you are a masochist that just wants the game to pound you, you may find it less appealing.
__
Dark Souls III, and the Souls series in general is a game that is difficult to serve a purpose, and that is to test your human spirit. It is not insanely and notoriously unfair, but it does paint a picture of you as a simple human being, an insignificant mote of existence in a much grander universe. And it is your job, as the player, to prove to that universe that you are something, that you are capable of becoming powerful, that your human spirit, not your skill or your wits, will survive any arduous journey that they throw at you.
This game is about surviving hardship, moral ambiguity and a dreadful, fearful world. It is about giving you a deep sense of wonder, and just enough tools for you to grow and learn as a player. The gameplay's ability to make you die quickly is not to frustrate you, but rather to make you very aware of your own mortality. And it is this awareness that brings immersion and satisfaction. When almost any enemy can kill you if you are clumsy or slipshod, every enemy that you defeat becomes that much more satisfying to take the heads from.
It's brilliance comes from the level of agency that it gives to the player, whether you outskill a difficult opponent, or resort to cheap tactics and cheesing a for, both give you great pleasure as you learn the ins and outs of surviving in the inhospitable landscape. A player doesn't have to be good to beat the game, they merely have to be patient, and to be aware of their surroundings.
Is the game fun? Yes. But it is often in a way that you do not expect, and it is difficult to describe why something that punishes you so harshly can be so engaging. It is not for everyone, but it doesn't take long to see the game's charm, once you survive the initial shock.
TL;DR: This game excels in putting you in the zone. It is a trial of the human spirit, rather than a game to enjoy for the masses. But if that appeals to you, I strongly recommend this game.

Fallout 4, a sprawling new world for the fans of Fallout to explore. There is quite a mixed bunch of reviews for this game, as to whether or not it actually lives up to what it was supposed to be. I am here in an attempt to set that to rest. Firstly, for a Fallout game, it does fall short on a few mechanics. For example, the RPG elements, including but not limited to dialogue is very cut down in favor of a more first-person shooter style game. However, it is pleasing to see that the Fallout universe is still the same good one we saw in many of the previous games. With crooks, con men, sociopaths, robots, gunslingers, and everything in between making their appearance in this game. Many will claim that this is a good game, but the same can not be said when comparing it to its predecessors. I simply must disagree, this title will pull you in from the start, and consume your life with the seemingly endless amount of side quests and random encounters. Not to mention the settlement building system, which, if you are into, will provide countless more hours of gameplay. This game is well worth the price tag, and will be played for years to come.
