This review in short: don't buy this game, buy Fallout: New Vegas instead.
I was very excited myself for this title, and preordered it with a season pass. Even after over a hundred hours, I cannot make this game enjoyable to play, as much as I WANT it to be fun.
Why?
THE PROS:
- The gunplay is very well done in Fallout 4 compared to previous titles (however mods for previous titles render this point null and void)
THE CONS:
- The graphics even on ultra look less appealing than in older titles that can be modded to look better than this
- Your decisions as a character bear no impact on the story or world around you until the very end of the game
- This far after launch, there are still gamebreaking glitches, and a fair number of them (my pipboy radio is permanently broken)
- It is impossible to play a villainous role in Fallout 4, dialouge is vague and does not impact the story or relations with other characters in any meaningful way
- Role playing in Fallout 4 is virtually impossible in any aspect beyond how your character looks
- The game goes from unbearably hard early on to drool inducingly easy, regardless of difficulty settings
- The game world feels choked and devoid of variety, with city buildings being 90% of the traversable game
- Characters aren't memorable and many aren't interesting or entertaining to interact with
- Weapon variety is painfully absent, as most weapons are either too weak to be used in any meaningful way or rare
- Enemies do not put up a fight or are brutally difficult, there is no middle ground here
If you are looking into buying a Fallout title, buy Fallout: New Vegas instead. It does all of the above far, far better than Fallout 4, and has more to keep you on your toes as you play. In addition, the modding communiuty for New Vegas has much more to offer than this game's.

I think the fact that I have unlocked over half the achievements in less than a week already says quite a bit. Even despite the resolution issues I had with this game since June, after a little while, I kind of just got used to it. Taking that aside, however, I really do like what the game has to offer; a good chunk of it is fanservice, and I feel that there are hits (
) and misses (
) in this regard.
Taking this into account, however, it almost seems as if DS3 expects you to have played the first game to understand some of its lore. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, per se, but I suspect that it can oftentimes lose you if this is the Dark Souls game you start out with (EDIT: this seems to apply moreso to the main game; the first DLC is much less reliant on its predecessors
).
Other than that, some of the positives I've encountered are that a lot of the bosses I've enjoyed (plus their respective OST's, I'm pretty sure I've added about 10 tracks to my Soulsborne YouTube album in just this past week) and level design is pretty good. The world doesn't intertwine in itself like DS1 or Bloodborne, but each area has its own shortcuts to sort of compensate for that.
Some negatives I have with it, however, are that I feel that it is a bit too linear compared to the previous 2 games. Not that the entire game is set on a 100% strict path, but the absence of branching pathways like in the first two games (looking at how you got the Lord Souls in DS1 and the Great Souls in DS2) would likely diminish some of its replayability. Like I said before, the quality/resolution settings require a high end PC, so it can diminish the experience quite a bit if you have a laptop more optimized for anything up to console generation 7 (so Xbox 360/PS3 era). I do know about some balancing issues regarding PvP, but I'm not one to say on this too much since I rarely get invaded (also because I suck horrendously at PvP).
Also, (yes, I'm going to be that guy), the devs really should fix poise; too often I've gotten staggered with a mid build about as easily as someone that would have a light build, and it is annoying especially when I want to try to perform a strong attack with my Exiled Greatsword that takes a couple seconds to charge up.
(EDIT: Poise has finally been adjusted prior to the first DLC, so the complaints on this do not feel as relevant.)
Overall, though, I can't really say much else. As of writing this review, I just got into NG+3, and DS3's replayability is still fairly strong, especially with the Ringed City DLC out now
. The various classes are still there to experiment with (knight, sorcerer, assassin, etc.), so the game can still that degree of replayability as its predecessors (As an example, some weapons like AoA's throwing spear and TRC's Giant Door Shield  can be used for some neat challenge runs.). I still recommend playing this (and the DLC's), especially if you want to see how the game itself plays out in the overall Dark Souls narrative.
It's a great game, if you haven't already bought it. Do it.

I think this game deserves a revitalized review from my end, mostly because I feel as if many discussions have arose from the gameplay and a few issues need to be addressed on a developer to community level. To start, this particular Dark Souls title is incredibly formidable in terms of *enjoyment* more so than the previous titles. With the exception of Dark Souls 1, I found the older titles to be more difficult than fun. Mostly because of the lack of interesting bosses although I found the chariot boss to be interesting. What made Dark Souls 3 enjoyable is a nostalgic return to anor londo, a consistent classic area that is almost iconic to Dark Souls titles asides from the PTSD inducing blight town. It made me incredibly happy to see that developers also implement many "arena" type areas most likely knowing how us players would make use of those fantastic and cinematic spaces ( new players will notice them most likely and older players will immediately want to jump in on the fight club culture ). In addition, the bosses were more or less alluring, interesting, dramatic and lore provoking, nothing less to expect from a game with great lore puzzle pieces!
However, when we talk about gameplay, this is where a lot of us are divided and this is why I will give a neutral opinion. I will put it quite lightly, Dark Souls 3 is not the hardest game but it is the most funnest game. The combat system has been renewed, revisted and almost innovated ontop of bloodborne's rather spam intensive L1 and L2 pvp culture. A few updates have fixed a few weapons that could achieve such skill-less strategies from dominating the pvp meta. Unfortunately, with the introduction of "hyper armor" and the removal of "poise" you'd find players running around with rags, a heavy great weapon with a hyper armor moveset and a quick-parry side arm like a caestus or a buckler. In fact, with the introduction of hornet ring, a Dark Souls classic, dexterity pvp has become more or less a one turn kill phenomena. If you think I am kidding, buy the game, run up to someone and feign a L1 attack, they would most likely parry on the first encounter.
Now if we look to the other side of the argument we also find other people that think Dark Souls 3's combat is of "true skill" where your ability to survive in a violent encounter is one's reaction time, time management, resource management as well as one's ability to execute combos a the right place and the right time. Some daringly state, Dark Souls 3 combat is the epitome of a true skill-based pvp experience and to a degree, I ought to agree wholeheartedly. I think it's fair to say that a lot of us veterans who lay our hearts with Havel thaumaturgy or smough hammer fun times don't exactly find it fair that we're punished for wearing more armor or a mechanical or a fashion level. I think this is where the community has to come together and either agree to adapt to the change or keep being vocal about our dismay and disatisfaction towards the lack of poise. Oh and if you're a battle mage or an arcanist of some kind? Yeah, you'd be happy to know that with the changes to magic, being a mage is difficult, challenging and almost incredibly rewarding. If you can succeed as a battle mage, you have something to be proud of as magic is no longer an 'ez mode' but rather an potent alternative option to dedicated swordplay.
Other than that, if you just started getting into Dark Souls 3, I would strongly suggest you try out the previous titles if you're a lore head and if you're just wanting to see what all these juicy "get good" memes and "gang banger" cosplay rooms are all about, just hop on to Dark Souls 3, you'd be guranteed to have a lot of fun. Jolly cooperation is strongly recommended thanks to the optimization as well! ( No more regedit edits or stupid in-game connection rings ). My point is, Dark Souls 3 is a "great game" but it no where resembles its past titles in the gameplay mechanics department - keep that in mind. ( Directed to both new and old players ) All in all, have fun, "get good" and certainly, "get rekt[ed]."

Ok let me get the good out of the way first before I talk about the bad and there is a lot of bad were it counts in this game. The atmasphere in this game is the best that it has ever been they really did get the single player part of this game right. The veiws are beautiful and the envirment sucks you into the game and just doesn't let go. The bosses are fun and unique but some of them are very gimmicky at times with one of them being a one shot kill if you hit the weak spot and one needing a specific weapon to kill him, these bring down what could have been an epic and fun boss fight but at the same time this game also has the most remeberable bosses of the series ranging from  one that will keep you on your toes, one that punishes you if you start to panic, and one that is just oozing with lore and mistery. These are the things that this game does right and it does it very well but were it starts to mess up is the pvp and the covanents, this is were the bad starts.
The covanents feel like as if they were just slaped on the game at the end of the development cycle, like as if they were just a box on a check list to mark off. It really does seem like as if From Soft didn't even try with the covanent system. They have no dynamic with the enviroment or with eachother, they barely have any reason in the lore to exist in the world. They seem more like glorified venders than anything else, you join them just to get the two covanent items that they offer if you collect 30 offerings and thats it, they don't do anything else. They don't affect how you invade people any more, blades of the darkmoon are just a later game verson of the blue sentinels so you have three covanents that do the exact samething. Watch dogs of farron are in an early part of the game so once you go past a sertaint level you can't even do that covanent anymore. Warriors of Sunlight seem out of place in the world. There is just no dynamic to the covanents, not with the world or each other. They just seem to blend in with eachother as there is little to nothing seperating them from eachother.
Invading is a mess right now as the advantage is heavily stacked in the favor of the host with 80% of the invasions you do are against a full team of players and they will use a seed of the giants because that item is way too easy to get and thats what i think distroyes invasions, seed of the giants being to easy to get and the matchmaking putting you up against three to four people at once.
Poise no long works like how it use to intead they replaced it with hyper armor which is a poor mans pose because it only works while you are in mid swing and that's the problem with it its too slow for ultra weapons to use because faster weapons will just simply stagger them before they can even swing. With this fast weapons have dominated the scene since release, greatswords and bigger get out class by fast small weapons because they can just stagger you before your hyper armor starts. When it comes to pvp its no longer about what you are good with its who can swing faster, and you can win multiple fights by just simply masting R1 until your oppenent dies.
Even with all of these short commings the game is still great, you will have tons of fun playing throught this game and exploring the world and From Soft says that they are going to try and fix all of the problems with how the pvp works. So this game does have a futur just if you want to play nothing but pvp then you are better off just playing Dark souls 2. The pvp is much better in that game and it still has a good number of people playing it but if you want to play through the game with little to no pvp than this game is fantastic and well polished in that specific way.

Dark Souls III, where do I start?
Dark Souls III is an incredible journey, from start to finish, it was definitely worth my 80€, and hopefully even more so with the upcoming DLC.
My first playthrough utilized my standard Strength build and I was playing on a XBOX 360 Controller, so lets get started with the review.
Minor to Major Spoilers ahead, as I'm pretty much just writing stuff as I go along, so be warned if you care about such stuff!
Dark Souls 3 kind of just throws you into it's world, no real explanation given. You get some, to newcomers, real gibberish talk about ash and how the Lords have risen again and start in a very linear area with not much but a few messages on the ground telling you the basic controls.
A few weak enemies litter the relatively straight forward path, only two branching ways are shown from the beginning. Typically for the Souls series, there is one early-on incredibly hard to beat enemy that is not actually the boss of the Tutorial area, that gives a really powerful early-game reward to the players dedicated and skillful enough to beating it.
After the first bonfire there is a small taste of Dark Souls branching paths, yet a clear direction is still visible.
The Tutorial Boss, Iudex Gundyr, is in my opinion simply the best Tutorial boss in the series. He makes you use a lot of what's been explained to you with the messages and requires you to get familiar and used to studying your enemie's moves and attacks.
Upon beating him and proceeding to the Firelink Shrine, the Central disconnected Hub of the Game, the next goal is the High Wall of Lothric.
To sum the rest of the Game up, it gradually becomes more difficult the further you go along, with a few tough nuts to crack along the way, for example powerful Tar-Monsters on the High Wall which can obliterate your HP and have a lot of health.
Dark Souls 3's OST this time around has been mostly handled by Yuka Kitamura, who was previousely responsible for the amazing Score to Sir Alonne's Bossfight in Dark Souls II, giving an untypically, yet fitting "Bombastic" feel to the Boss-Encounters.
- Striking aesthetic with only some minor bad spritework
- Immediate immersion into the typical "Dark Souls"-Atmosphere, a dark and gritty Dark-Fantasy in which nigh-on anyone or anything is hostile towards you.
- A deep yet very hidden Lore, for those keen on discovering new theories.
- Challenging, Easy-to-learn Hard-to-master Combat mechanics with a lot of depth in technique and choice of Build/Weapon
- Enormous variety in Armors/Outfits, Weapons, Shields
- "Epic" Bossfights, due to the Amazing OST by Yuka Kitamura
- Further improvements upon the somewhat clunky-feeling Dark-Souls II (even though a lot of good ideas weren't carried over)
-  Streamlining and un-slacking of needlessly overcomplicated mechanics (i.e. Blue Titanite, Armor Upgrades etc.)
- Good Balance in PVP, due to a lot of viable physical Build-Weapon Combinations and a community actively searching for new tech to make everything work in PVP.
- The best PVP-dueling experience in the Souls series.
- dying a lot!
- Somewhat "lighter" atmosphere, the earlier Souls Games felt way more dreadful, just due to the grittier colour-palette.
- The very vague description of one's ultimate goal can turn off players that look for a more "guided" experience.
- Combat can feel "unfair", due to sometimes awkwardly, or nearly not telegraphed attacks, very strickt dodge or parry timings, and again a lack of understanding of the actual underlying mechanics.
- A lot of weird and unrelatable decisions, such as the complete reworking of Poise
- An at times incredibly toxic playerbase (which game doesen't have that though amirite?)
- The weakest Invasion-based PVP in the series, with countless, sometimes unreasonable limitations upon the Invader.
- dying a lot!
TL;DR: Dark Souls III offers more of the classic Dark Souls Experience, while not being too shy to make major changes to the overall flow of the game. Hidetaka Miyazaki has truly outdone himself with this installment of the series. It is an incredible journey from start to finish, wether you're in it with a friend or two or you are solely exploring the game's world on your own.
It is a journey of encountering problems and applying the age old rule "Adapt and Overcome" to any situation that one may find challenging.
An epic conclusion to a franchise that has gained the status of a true classic!

Fallout 4 is the latest installment in the Fallout series. Is it the ultimate post-post-apocalyptic experience? I would say it falls short of what I had in mind, but is ultimately an excellent game. Let's get what it does right out of the way: the game is set in Boston and reimagines it very well. There are also many small details, or prop placements rather, that tell little stories of their own. The music is engaging and reacts to the environment; propr to Ion Zur for updating the main title with some pretty cool chords. Having the main character speak is also something that surprised me, and it adds an extra layer of immersion. There are many more things I'd like to point out that the game does well, but I think it's best if I mention the pitfalls. The game is still buggy and occasional crashes do happen. The graphics are subpar for 2015, although this can be rectified by installing mods. And the biggest dissapointment of all was that the DLCs were mediocre. While the main story arc was interesting playing through three times, the DLCs didn't engage me. With only two DLCs that I'd consider real story DLCs, I am dissapointed with Bethesda as they focused the bulk of their efforts on creating 'workshop DLCs' which allow players to update settlements. Overall Fallout 4 feels less like an RPG as the previous editions were, and more like a linear adventure game. I would still recommend this game to anyone, especially on sale... I am hoping for Obsidian to create one of their own.

Fallout 4 is the latest installment in the Fallout series. Is it the ultimate post-post-apocalyptic experience? I would say it falls short of what I had in mind, but is ultimately an excellent game. Let's get what it does right out of the way: the game is set in Boston and reimagines it very well. There are also many small details, or prop placements rather, that tell little stories of their own. The music is engaging and reacts to the environment; propr to Ion Zur for updating the main title with some pretty cool chords. Having the main character speak is also something that surprised me, and it adds an extra layer of immersion. There are many more things I'd like to point out that the game does well, but I think it's best if I mention the pitfalls. The game is still buggy and occasional crashes do happen. The graphics are subpar for 2015, although this can be rectified by installing mods. And the biggest dissapointment of all was that the DLCs were mediocre. While the main story arc was interesting playing through three times, the DLCs didn't engage me. With only two DLCs that I'd consider real story DLCs, I am dissapointed with Bethesda as they focused the bulk of their efforts on creating 'workshop DLCs' which allow players to update settlements. Overall Fallout 4 feels less like an RPG as the previous editions were, and more like a linear adventure game. I would still recommend this game to anyone, especially on sale... I am hoping for Obsidian to create one of their own.

This game is far better than people give it credit for.
Does the perk tree restrict your playstyle, as compared to previous games? Yes.
But if you ask me, that's about it.
(all pros and cons are comparative to the previous titles)
Pros:
-Large world, i'm fairly confident it is bigger than both previous games.
-Wide range of customization, character customization was improved drastically in FO4 and im so glad you no longer have to answer useless questions about how you play (what do you see in this picture? oh, a ship? you're a melee fighter!)
-Settlements, too many people use this as a negative. It's extra content, plain and simple. If you don't like it, don't use it. You can play through the entire game and not use a single settlement should you choose. I, however, love the ability to create fortifications and strongholds for the people of the Commonwealth.
-Graphics, this one is self explanatory
-Voiced character, Oh my god people were so excited to hear about this when they announced it some 2-3 years ago. I was too and i still love it. Just because your character doesn't sound like what you wanted him to sound like, doesn't mean it's bad. The voice acting is phenomenal and the writing is good.
-Story, this story is far better than New Vegas', as you actually have some kind of personal connection and will to participate in the events transpiring within the Commonwealth. Similar to 3, it's all about family ties. After you kill Benny in New Vegas, you have literally no other connections to anything happening. You "Choose" to alter the Wasteland just because. It feels completely irrelevant and totally misplaced. Maybe if you had once been the leader of some big gang that ruled the wasteland and that's why Benny shot you, it would actually make sense.
-Combat, Finally the Fallout combat isn't choppy. And holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is it fantastic. Enemies actually taking cover and having smooth movements, it's glorious.
-Modding capability, You can literally do anything you please with this game. Anything.
-Music, they mashed music from both previous games into this one and it is wonderful. Damn i love this music.
Cons:
-Perk Tree, it is very restrictive to your playstyle. In previous titles, you could max the "guns" skill and use any ballistic weapon you please. Now, you have to choose between semi-auto pistols, semi-auto rifles, or automatic rifles/pistols. Granted, you can max them all, but it takes perk points away from other things you could be getting.
-Insane RPG scaling, what i mean by this is, you get too strong too quickly. After about 20 levels, if you maxed but one of the gun skills and potentially the ability to modify them as well (science, guns, blacksmith, etc) then you can basically kill anything you like with little to no trouble. Even if you turn the difficulty up to Very Hard, it's not very hard.
-Power Armor, this♥♥♥♥♥♥is given to you right away, and you can keep it on at all times for the rest of the game. It is absolutely way too strong. Couple this with the RPG scaling and you just become a hulking menace that can kill anything with its bare fists. I never use it, but i do not think it should be so readily available and so damn strong.
-Range of weaponry, without mods, there really aren't that many guns. Are they highly modifiable? for sure. But it simply isn't enough. They should've thrown another 10 or so guns in just to give a little more variety to the weapons.
-Minutemen, ANOTHER SETTLEMENT NEEDS YOUR HELP! Granted, i enjoy defending the people and setting up new homes for the stray folks of the Commonwealth, but this is so god damn repetitive and it NEVER ENDS. Preston Garvey is the FLATTEST CHARACTER EVER.
-DLC, other than Automatron and Far Harbor, these DLCs suck. Filler♥♥♥♥♥♥or badly written stories.
So/So:
-Factions, I really like all of the factions but what bothers me is how some of them are portrayed. The BoS went from the good guys of the Capital Wasteland to, "We'll kill anyone if it means we can stop the Institute and their insane technology!" I didn't like the transition and i still don't. The Minutemen were once great and if you rebuild them, they're still not very good. If you go through with building x amount of settlements and capturing the Castle, they ought to have some sway in the commonwealth. I would've liked to see you create some sort of government out of the Minutemen, and have an ending with them where they kill off the BoS and the Institute and take over for themselves. Something like the "People's Republic of the Commonwealth" maybe. The Institute, man i wish they were actually good people. So much potential wasted because they were evil. Opportunity totally missed. The Railroad is probably the only faction i am 100% okay with.
-Ambient sounds/sound effects, Gun sounds are meh, and enemy sounds are meh too. i just feel like they lack some sort of depth.
Altogether, i'd say this game is well worth the buy. Do not get the season pass, but rather buy the only 2 DLC that matter,  Far Harbor (which is probably their greatest DLC ever) and Automatron. Don't forget to mod the hell out of it, too.

Dark Souls III, where do I start?
Dark Souls III is an incredible journey, from start to finish, it was definitely worth my 80€, and hopefully even more so with the upcoming DLC.
My first playthrough utilized my standard Strength build and I was playing on a XBOX 360 Controller, so lets get started with the review.
Minor to Major Spoilers ahead, as I'm pretty much just writing stuff as I go along, so be warned if you care about such stuff!
Dark Souls 3 kind of just throws you into it's world, no real explanation given. You get some, to newcomers, real gibberish talk about ash and how the Lords have risen again and start in a very linear area with not much but a few messages on the ground telling you the basic controls.
A few weak enemies litter the relatively straight forward path, only two branching ways are shown from the beginning. Typically for the Souls series, there is one early-on incredibly hard to beat enemy that is not actually the boss of the Tutorial area, that gives a really powerful early-game reward to the players dedicated and skillful enough to beating it.
After the first bonfire there is a small taste of Dark Souls branching paths, yet a clear direction is still visible.
The Tutorial Boss, Iudex Gundyr, is in my opinion simply the best Tutorial boss in the series. He makes you use a lot of what's been explained to you with the messages and requires you to get familiar and used to studying your enemie's moves and attacks.
Upon beating him and proceeding to the Firelink Shrine, the Central disconnected Hub of the Game, the next goal is the High Wall of Lothric.
To sum the rest of the Game up, it gradually becomes more difficult the further you go along, with a few tough nuts to crack along the way, for example powerful Tar-Monsters on the High Wall which can obliterate your HP and have a lot of health.
Dark Souls 3's OST this time around has been mostly handled by Yuka Kitamura, who was previousely responsible for the amazing Score to Sir Alonne's Bossfight in Dark Souls II, giving an untypically, yet fitting "Bombastic" feel to the Boss-Encounters.
- Striking aesthetic with only some minor bad spritework
- Immediate immersion into the typical "Dark Souls"-Atmosphere, a dark and gritty Dark-Fantasy in which nigh-on anyone or anything is hostile towards you.
- A deep yet very hidden Lore, for those keen on discovering new theories.
- Challenging, Easy-to-learn Hard-to-master Combat mechanics with a lot of depth in technique and choice of Build/Weapon
- Enormous variety in Armors/Outfits, Weapons, Shields
- "Epic" Bossfights, due to the Amazing OST by Yuka Kitamura
- Further improvements upon the somewhat clunky-feeling Dark-Souls II (even though a lot of good ideas weren't carried over)
-  Streamlining and un-slacking of needlessly overcomplicated mechanics (i.e. Blue Titanite, Armor Upgrades etc.)
- Good Balance in PVP, due to a lot of viable physical Build-Weapon Combinations and a community actively searching for new tech to make everything work in PVP.
- The best PVP-dueling experience in the Souls series.
- dying a lot!
- Somewhat "lighter" atmosphere, the earlier Souls Games felt way more dreadful, just due to the grittier colour-palette.
- The very vague description of one's ultimate goal can turn off players that look for a more "guided" experience.
- Combat can feel "unfair", due to sometimes awkwardly, or nearly not telegraphed attacks, very strickt dodge or parry timings, and again a lack of understanding of the actual underlying mechanics.
- A lot of weird and unrelatable decisions, such as the complete reworking of Poise
- An at times incredibly toxic playerbase (which game doesen't have that though amirite?)
- The weakest Invasion-based PVP in the series, with countless, sometimes unreasonable limitations upon the Invader.
- dying a lot!
TL;DR: Dark Souls III offers more of the classic Dark Souls Experience, while not being too shy to make major changes to the overall flow of the game. Hidetaka Miyazaki has truly outdone himself with this installment of the series. It is an incredible journey from start to finish, wether you're in it with a friend or two or you are solely exploring the game's world on your own.
It is a journey of encountering problems and applying the age old rule "Adapt and Overcome" to any situation that one may find challenging.
An epic conclusion to a franchise that has gained the status of a true classic!

After coming back to this game after several changes to my hardware and software I can happily say this game is a 9/10.
But when I first played it, it was awful. It lacked content, it ran badly on low graphic settings (my computer at the time was midrange and ran most games on high/medium), the console UI made my eyes bleed etc etc. Most insultingly, I had ran it on ultra and it looked like filth. It was a massive letdown after the hype.
Having come back to it now, I can happily say it's absolutely incredible. I'm still running
the game without DLC like on release, the only difference is I now have an i5 6600 (old processor was an A8-7600) and 36 mods for the game, not including the ENB and F4SE which had to be manually downloaded without nexus mod manager. Most of the mods are graphical enhancers (4k texture packs for everything) or they're weapon or armour mods, but each one adds in a crucial gap that the base game missed.
However, because of the fact I had to mod the game so hard just to make it not look and feel disgusting, I have to downvote. Most of the mods I installed are quality of life purely, with only a few filling in content holes, and the most infuriating part of all this is that my FPS really hasn't changed. Hopefully Bethesda learns from this and starts making good games again..
I also advise anyone who wants this to get it, but only when it's on something like the Black Friday sale (67% off! £13 in the UK, or about $20) because it's actually worth it for that kind of price.

While Fallout 4 certainly does not capture the same spirit as Fallout 3 or New Vegas, this game still made me sink 100+ hours into it in just a few weeks.
Pros:
- Fantastic visuals and animations. When I first saw Feral Ghouls crawling up the elevator shafts of an abandoned warehouse, I got chills
- Combat. Guns now feel unique and every shot packs a punch
- Improved enemy AI. Gone are the days of Raiders mindlessly rushing you as you casually melt their faces with a minigun
- Solid voice acting
- Crafting and Base Building systems addictive as hell (but only if you're an OCD hoarder like me)
Cons:
- Totally butchered the sophisticated speech and dialogue systems in the previous games. Literally the 4 options to any conversation are: "Yes, No, Maybe, Ask for more Information"
- Tying all perks to the SPECIAL stats oversimplifies the levelling system
- Automatic weapons with the "Explosive Bullet" attribute are overpowered and effectively break the game
-  HERE'S THE BIG PROBLEM: Questing is much more linear. Your actions have very little consequences on other related NPCS in most cases. In most cases I can almost please every stakeholder in a quest, and they barely comment on my actions. Compare this with the many interactions with the 4 factions in New Vegas. This makes the game essentially more of a Borderlands-esque shooter rather than an RPG in my opinion.
I'm still recommending this game for the sheer amount of content, and for just how much fun I had with it. But for fans of the previous games, you may be let down by the fact that Fallout 4 has been dumbed down to a lite RPG shooter

I have what, for some reason, is still considered to be a controversial opinion of Bethesda's games. Even though I'm not alone in thinking that Bethesda's storywriting is unsatisfying, it's characters are shallow and aren't actually affected by the players desires, and that they seem to have a blatant disregard for the effect that bugs have on the player experience; people still recoil in horror when I say that Bethesda isn't actually good at making games. Now maybe I'm being too cynical, maybe games aren't supposed to reach some 11/10 standard and blow us away consistently, maybe F3, NV and F4 are just stepping stones towards the truly great game we all hope is coming. But let's be honest, we have had open-world games for a long time now, no one can say it's a genre in it's infancy. We've also had RPGs for a long time, pretty much as long as we've had games themselves. So even though there is room to grow and learn, and always the space provided by artistic licence; It's fair to say, that there are some established do's and don'ts for both RPGs and open-world games. And even if you decide as a developer to try and create something from scratch and learn for yourself what to do and not to do; there's still no reason why you can't learn from others who've come before you. I don't know specifically what the vision was, but if they did try to say that they didn't want to follow anyone else's example, so that they could make it from scratch, they don't really have a leg to stand on, as they are already rebooting a cherished and thoroughly developed series of games. So this is our third installment of modern, 3D, seamless (except for fast travel) games from Bethesda. In fact I lie, there's also been the Elder Scrolls series. So why, now that Bethesda has had plenty of time to learn the ins and outs of crafting a gaming experience and beginning to understand what it means to be responsible to, and be in contact with their community; have we gone backwards? Why is Fallout4 the most impressive, best-looking, most in-depth and I dare say best-feeling game in the series, but simultaneously manages to be the most immature, most boring, least replayable game in the series? Now before you go telling your friends that you read half of a negative review on Fallout 4; I do really like this game, I thoroughly enjoy the new crafting and modding system for weapons and armour. I am pleasantly surprised by the quality of the Settlement build/scrap system, I think the combat is relatively visceral and hard-hitting, and that the all-important picking up of objects and grabbing stuff out of containers is at an all time high. But that's about where my love for this game ends, although love I exploring, meeting new characters and trying to judge what type of individual they will be, and just plain killing things; the story is well, really average. The player character will always end up getting around to the outcome that they always would have, regardless of the player's intentions. Your playstyle is always limited by what's actually practical, and what archetype of weapons are the most powerful and least-risky. And most of the characters you meet will just annoy the heck out of you. My favourite companions were actually the robot ones, they were the most animated and unique characters in the whole game! Most voice acting is fantastic, and fits the characters perfectly (props to voice actors) but unfortunately for the hard-working voice actors, the characters are about as shallow as the caps that they trade with. Always saying the most obvious, most idiotic things and always responding to simple situations with strangely complex reactions, or reacting to complex situations as if they were nothing more than kindegarten disagreements. I had hoped that Fallout 4 would bring a refreshing change to the formula we are used to, especially considering we waited 7 years for this game. I hoped we would have discovered mature, deep characters with dialogue that didn't make us want to skip most of their lines. I hoped we would find a choice-based story which would actually allow us to have the kind of effect on the outcome that we are led to believe we are responsible for in the cutscenes and "reputation" we earn throughout the game. Instead we seem like placehloders in different strings of quests, which aren't actually that dependant upon our presence in them.  I hoped that Bethesda would have said: "Yeah so the game files are going to be huge, in order to cope with the massive world we know you wanted." I hoped that they would have decided to not simply say that enough was enough, and that modders will take care of the rest of the bugs, instead of taking a slightly more professional approach to product design. So, yeah, I'm disappointed in Fallout 4, because I wanted it to be more, I think it deserved to be more. I thought Bethesda would grow, and not just keep developing games, but develop the very development itself, so that we could reap the benefits of a more mature studio. One that understands the industry, genre(s) and expectations of their playerbase, a bit more than they did back when Oblivion graced us with it's glory. This is a positive review, because in reality, I'm still playing this game, and will continue to do so for potentially hundreds of hours. But it will be my general love for sneak-kills, explosions, exploring and ultimately MODS that will keep me coming back for more. I look forward to TES:VI and future Fallout titles, but just like I did with Ubisoft, I'm starting to trust Bethesda just a little less.

After all the turmoil and controversy has settled, it is time to give a level-headed opinion.
This game is a big departure from Fallout 3 and New Vegas.  The main protagonist is now voice-acted.  This change makes dialogue feel much more natural and emotional.  It also makes your character feel like a part of the story rather than a godly loot-lugging sock puppet.  However, the dialogue options have been diminished from previous titles, giving you about 4 options to use at any time which seems like a dumbed down version of Mass Effect's system (Paragon, Renegade, Neutral, Interrogate).  Not only this, but many times people will respond the same way regardless of your choice.  Your dialogue choice also seldom has an effect on relationships and how quests progress.
Combat is awesome.  Power Armor has been overhauled but I think it is definitely for the better.  Iron sights have been added (disregarding what Obsidian did for New Vegas as Bethesda is a different studio).  Grenades have a dedicated hotkey.  Sprinting has been added and consumes action points.  VATS has been altered but still acts mostly the same.  Critical strikes are more strategic and less random (you can argue %based crits are better but IMO rng is always poor game design).  There is a layered armor system; shoulder pads and chest armor can be put on over certain lighter clothing options for a unique look and extra special effects.  Best of all, armor and weapons can be modified at crafting stations.  You can get more defense, more damage, different shooting modes, different sights, etc.  New crafting system is a big win for me.
New SPECIAL system is a hit and a miss simultaneously.  Character stats have been removed and have now been integrated with SPECIAL and the perk system.  Honestly, I think this was a good decision as the new systems usurp it entirely and we no longer have an unneccessary layer.  Because SPECIAL is now much more important it encourages you to make a specialized character whereas in Fallout 3 and New Vegas, you would benefit the most from a balanced character.  In fact, you cannot even make a balanced character in the beginning of Fallout 4.  Perks behave similarly to past titles, except this time every perk has a SPECIAL requirement.  This is the first issue of the new perk system.  If you want to roleplay as a very intelligent character who overcomes their fragile physique by modifying their gear to the max, well now you need level 4 strength to add tesla bracers to your power armor.  My reaction to this?  Refer to my avatar.  The second issue is that some of the perks just plain suck.  Rad resistant, refractor, and toughness are terrible.  Most perks are simply stat boosts that don't come with fun bonuses (something New Vegas did well).  The way Local Leader and Cap Collector interact with the new settlement mode is terrible.  Yeah let's get into that.
Settlements are cool.  They're fun if you want to build things and you can mostly ignore it if you're not interested.  Most issues with the settlement system can be easily fixed with simple mods.  However, settlements have had a severe affliction to quantity and quality of towns.  We have Goodneighbor and Diamond City, that's it.
Story is pretty decent.  It starts off very strong, hits a rut when you meet the Minutemen (Mama Murphy WTF Bethesda), picks back up when you get to Diamond City, and then explodes when you are surrounded with men in labcoats.  But after this point things go downhill fast.  The story gets much less interesting after this point and now you're looking at your options of ending the main story.  Well the thing is, you don't have a lot of options.  You want to join the Minutemen and the Railroad?  Nope, they can't get along for some idiotic reason.  What about Minutemen with Brotherhood of Steel?  Nope, that can't happen either.  Basically, you get to choose one faction to kill another faction and that's how the endings go.  You can hardly acquire any variation of any ending; granual control is very lacking.  At least all the endings are very explosive.
The world is amazing.  Downtown Boston is fabulously in shambles similar to DC.  The coasts have washed-up irradiated sea creatures.  Entering the Glowing Sea for the first time is a Fallout experience I wish I could relive.  Textures are decent and the lighting system is spectacular.
At the end of the day, this is a great game.  A lot of people love to hate this game and say "It's a bad game".  It's not my opinion that this is a good game, it is a fact that this is a good game.  My proof:  good gameplay, improved graphics, new mechanics, improved end-game meta, massive open world, player freedom.  Roleplaying has taken a big hit sadly but that doesn't make this a bad game by any means.
Be sure to play Far Harbor.  It addresses a lot of issues I had with the main game (dialogue and story-related).  Make sure to bring Nick with you for the entire ride.

I have what, for some reason, is still considered to be a controversial opinion of Bethesda's games. Even though I'm not alone in thinking that Bethesda's storywriting is unsatisfying, it's characters are shallow and aren't actually affected by the players desires, and that they seem to have a blatant disregard for the effect that bugs have on the player experience; people still recoil in horror when I say that Bethesda isn't actually good at making games. Now maybe I'm being too cynical, maybe games aren't supposed to reach some 11/10 standard and blow us away consistently, maybe F3, NV and F4 are just stepping stones towards the truly great game we all hope is coming. But let's be honest, we have had open-world games for a long time now, no one can say it's a genre in it's infancy. We've also had RPGs for a long time, pretty much as long as we've had games themselves. So even though there is room to grow and learn, and always the space provided by artistic licence; It's fair to say, that there are some established do's and don'ts for both RPGs and open-world games. And even if you decide as a developer to try and create something from scratch and learn for yourself what to do and not to do; there's still no reason why you can't learn from others who've come before you. I don't know specifically what the vision was, but if they did try to say that they didn't want to follow anyone else's example, so that they could make it from scratch, they don't really have a leg to stand on, as they are already rebooting a cherished and thoroughly developed series of games. So this is our third installment of modern, 3D, seamless (except for fast travel) games from Bethesda. In fact I lie, there's also been the Elder Scrolls series. So why, now that Bethesda has had plenty of time to learn the ins and outs of crafting a gaming experience and beginning to understand what it means to be responsible to, and be in contact with their community; have we gone backwards? Why is Fallout4 the most impressive, best-looking, most in-depth and I dare say best-feeling game in the series, but simultaneously manages to be the most immature, most boring, least replayable game in the series? Now before you go telling your friends that you read half of a negative review on Fallout 4; I do really like this game, I thoroughly enjoy the new crafting and modding system for weapons and armour. I am pleasantly surprised by the quality of the Settlement build/scrap system, I think the combat is relatively visceral and hard-hitting, and that the all-important picking up of objects and grabbing stuff out of containers is at an all time high. But that's about where my love for this game ends, although love I exploring, meeting new characters and trying to judge what type of individual they will be, and just plain killing things; the story is well, really average. The player character will always end up getting around to the outcome that they always would have, regardless of the player's intentions. Your playstyle is always limited by what's actually practical, and what archetype of weapons are the most powerful and least-risky. And most of the characters you meet will just annoy the heck out of you. My favourite companions were actually the robot ones, they were the most animated and unique characters in the whole game! Most voice acting is fantastic, and fits the characters perfectly (props to voice actors) but unfortunately for the hard-working voice actors, the characters are about as shallow as the caps that they trade with. Always saying the most obvious, most idiotic things and always responding to simple situations with strangely complex reactions, or reacting to complex situations as if they were nothing more than kindegarten disagreements. I had hoped that Fallout 4 would bring a refreshing change to the formula we are used to, especially considering we waited 7 years for this game. I hoped we would have discovered mature, deep characters with dialogue that didn't make us want to skip most of their lines. I hoped we would find a choice-based story which would actually allow us to have the kind of effect on the outcome that we are led to believe we are responsible for in the cutscenes and "reputation" we earn throughout the game. Instead we seem like placehloders in different strings of quests, which aren't actually that dependant upon our presence in them.  I hoped that Bethesda would have said: "Yeah so the game files are going to be huge, in order to cope with the massive world we know you wanted." I hoped that they would have decided to not simply say that enough was enough, and that modders will take care of the rest of the bugs, instead of taking a slightly more professional approach to product design. So, yeah, I'm disappointed in Fallout 4, because I wanted it to be more, I think it deserved to be more. I thought Bethesda would grow, and not just keep developing games, but develop the very development itself, so that we could reap the benefits of a more mature studio. One that understands the industry, genre(s) and expectations of their playerbase, a bit more than they did back when Oblivion graced us with it's glory. This is a positive review, because in reality, I'm still playing this game, and will continue to do so for potentially hundreds of hours. But it will be my general love for sneak-kills, explosions, exploring and ultimately MODS that will keep me coming back for more. I look forward to TES:VI and future Fallout titles, but just like I did with Ubisoft, I'm starting to trust Bethesda just a little less.

After all the turmoil and controversy has settled, it is time to give a level-headed opinion.
This game is a big departure from Fallout 3 and New Vegas.  The main protagonist is now voice-acted.  This change makes dialogue feel much more natural and emotional.  It also makes your character feel like a part of the story rather than a godly loot-lugging sock puppet.  However, the dialogue options have been diminished from previous titles, giving you about 4 options to use at any time which seems like a dumbed down version of Mass Effect's system (Paragon, Renegade, Neutral, Interrogate).  Not only this, but many times people will respond the same way regardless of your choice.  Your dialogue choice also seldom has an effect on relationships and how quests progress.
Combat is awesome.  Power Armor has been overhauled but I think it is definitely for the better.  Iron sights have been added (disregarding what Obsidian did for New Vegas as Bethesda is a different studio).  Grenades have a dedicated hotkey.  Sprinting has been added and consumes action points.  VATS has been altered but still acts mostly the same.  Critical strikes are more strategic and less random (you can argue %based crits are better but IMO rng is always poor game design).  There is a layered armor system; shoulder pads and chest armor can be put on over certain lighter clothing options for a unique look and extra special effects.  Best of all, armor and weapons can be modified at crafting stations.  You can get more defense, more damage, different shooting modes, different sights, etc.  New crafting system is a big win for me.
New SPECIAL system is a hit and a miss simultaneously.  Character stats have been removed and have now been integrated with SPECIAL and the perk system.  Honestly, I think this was a good decision as the new systems usurp it entirely and we no longer have an unneccessary layer.  Because SPECIAL is now much more important it encourages you to make a specialized character whereas in Fallout 3 and New Vegas, you would benefit the most from a balanced character.  In fact, you cannot even make a balanced character in the beginning of Fallout 4.  Perks behave similarly to past titles, except this time every perk has a SPECIAL requirement.  This is the first issue of the new perk system.  If you want to roleplay as a very intelligent character who overcomes their fragile physique by modifying their gear to the max, well now you need level 4 strength to add tesla bracers to your power armor.  My reaction to this?  Refer to my avatar.  The second issue is that some of the perks just plain suck.  Rad resistant, refractor, and toughness are terrible.  Most perks are simply stat boosts that don't come with fun bonuses (something New Vegas did well).  The way Local Leader and Cap Collector interact with the new settlement mode is terrible.  Yeah let's get into that.
Settlements are cool.  They're fun if you want to build things and you can mostly ignore it if you're not interested.  Most issues with the settlement system can be easily fixed with simple mods.  However, settlements have had a severe affliction to quantity and quality of towns.  We have Goodneighbor and Diamond City, that's it.
Story is pretty decent.  It starts off very strong, hits a rut when you meet the Minutemen (Mama Murphy WTF Bethesda), picks back up when you get to Diamond City, and then explodes when you are surrounded with men in labcoats.  But after this point things go downhill fast.  The story gets much less interesting after this point and now you're looking at your options of ending the main story.  Well the thing is, you don't have a lot of options.  You want to join the Minutemen and the Railroad?  Nope, they can't get along for some idiotic reason.  What about Minutemen with Brotherhood of Steel?  Nope, that can't happen either.  Basically, you get to choose one faction to kill another faction and that's how the endings go.  You can hardly acquire any variation of any ending; granual control is very lacking.  At least all the endings are very explosive.
The world is amazing.  Downtown Boston is fabulously in shambles similar to DC.  The coasts have washed-up irradiated sea creatures.  Entering the Glowing Sea for the first time is a Fallout experience I wish I could relive.  Textures are decent and the lighting system is spectacular.
At the end of the day, this is a great game.  A lot of people love to hate this game and say "It's a bad game".  It's not my opinion that this is a good game, it is a fact that this is a good game.  My proof:  good gameplay, improved graphics, new mechanics, improved end-game meta, massive open world, player freedom.  Roleplaying has taken a big hit sadly but that doesn't make this a bad game by any means.
Be sure to play Far Harbor.  It addresses a lot of issues I had with the main game (dialogue and story-related).  Make sure to bring Nick with you for the entire ride.

One of the best games I've ever played. Gorgeous graphics, with very impressive and fluid animations for the most part (and a little faster than DS1 and 2 if you didn't like how slow it could be at times). Don't even bother playing with a keyboard; the optimization is a bit better this time around, but it absolutely CANNOT compare with just using and XBox controller. Trust me.
The difficulty seems to be lowered a little this time around, perhaps to be more new-player-friendly, but I'm probably biased since when I first played through this game in April, I'd been on a Souls binge since mid-November; plenty of time to git gud. Don't believe what people say about the "unfair difficulty" of these games - Dark Souls has never been that hard. It's simply been a CHALLENGE, which people all say they like in a game, but as soon as they actually GET a challenge, they complain about it. Try it out for yourself.
The world is pretty large, the largest of the three (I would assume), with rich and varied environments and enemies. The level design is, for me, something of a mixed bag. Dark Souls III is definitely trying to go back to the design of the original Dark Souls, and it does its job pretty well, though there aren't truly any sprawling paths that you can go down whenever you want, like in DS1, and it's not quite as vertical. And while the actual layout of the world makes a LOT more sense than DS2 (elevator up into a lake of lava anyone?), I found myself getting a little annoyed at the FOUR DIFFERENT CATHEDRALS in the game and just too much... cleanliness? I guess that's correct. What I mean is that in DS1, and to a much lesser extent in 2, the world felt OLD, falling into disrepair, with cracks and dust and plant life growing in the buildings. The world here... I don't quite know how to say it... it feels abandoned in a way, but also NOT. It seems very pristine at times compared to DS1, and while that's objectively not a bad thing, for me personally, I'd like a few less big churches and a few more ruins. Despite the personal gripe, the different zones are extremely detailed, paintstakingly so, and just looking around the environment gives you lots of clues as to the zone's lore (more on the superb lore later) and where to go next. There's a specific spot where paying attention and remembering details unlocks a whole ZONE later on. Hell, at one point you can see literally the ENTIRE GAME in one shot! That's absolutely astounding, and one of the best moments in the game.
The PvP is fun. Very meta-y, and the net code it pretty bad, but I enjoy the occasional duel binge. I don't do invasions so I can't speak from experience, but a lot of popular YouTubers seem to think that invasions are crappy and overly unfair to the invader.
Now, the best things about this game, I think, are the story and the bosses. Story first.
The story is sort of vaguely introduced in the opening cutscene, but most of it is learned through talking to the friendly NPCs you meet along your travels and by reading item descriptions. It may seem annoying at first to not have the story told to you like most games do, but I assure you, the Souls universe has some of the deepest, most complex, and most interesting lore out there, with new discoveries and theories being made all the time by a vibrant community of fans. In fact, some people have entire careers based of just the STORY of this game. The voice-acting is superb so you should totally talk to every NPC you can, and the NPC stories themselves, while not quite at the level of DS1 characters all the time, are still very nice and fleshed out. And while DS2 has been largely ignored but for a few items here and there, there are references all over to DS1, expertly placed. It's a not-so-subtle love letter to the people who were fans of this game from the start.
The bosses are AWESOME! Some are certainly better than others, but all of them are very pretty and with astounding sountracks to accompany them. When you play through a game that has no music for the most part, fighting against seemingly overwhelming odds amidst a vibrant and and epic soundtrack is a truly incredible sensation. Never mind the fact that every boss in the game has TWO PHASES! These bosses will be hard, and if you're new to the game, you'll probably die. Sometimes you'll die a LOT. Sometimes it will be very frustrating and it will seem impossible to progress past this point. But may I remind you: people beat this game on New Game +7, naked, using only their fists. So... you can do it, I promise. And when you do finally beat the boss, when you overcome those odds and watch this incredible obstacle fall before you... well, the sense of accomplishment and joy (and admittedly relief, sometimes) is unparalleled in any game I have ever played, ever. It's insane.
So to conclude, while this game is not perfect (and no game is), it is an incredibly rich and immersive experience unrivaled by almost anything out there. In fact, DS1 and 2 are two of the very small handful games that CAN compare with it. It is frustrating at times, but undeniably worth it for the fun you'll have playing it. The perfect way to send off one of the greatest series of all time.

An excellent closure to the series, Dark souls 3 is a good bye letter from From Software to the fans, offering us a memorable journey through the land of Lothric.
-The story is more linear in this game, right after the tutorial you are told your mission: Bring the Lords of Cinder and save the First Flame. on one side the story is not as rich and memorable as the one from the first game, but at the same time i appreciate it, we have done this already in the first games, the game knows it and so it jumps right into the important stuff, there is still a lot to learn from the cities and events through enviroment, dialogues and item descriptions like a proper souls game.
-The level is pretty damn good, overall the enemy placement doesn't feel unfair most of the time, and as it should be, you are almost always able to see what's going to jump into you if you are careful of your sorroundings, the scenarios are amazing, many areas like cathedrals or temples look really well polished and it's really fun to adventure through them, just like in the first game.
-The gameplay is the very sweetspot of Dark Souls 3, fast, aggresive and completely adrenaline-filled combat, shields are once again a viable option, although not as amazing as they were in DaS1, instead rolling has become godlike, with minimum stamina consumption and ridiculous iframes, also this game offers some of the funniest and most badass bosses i have seen in the series, the Nameless King is a fight to remember no doubt. Many complain about the fact that poise doesn't exist in DS3, which means you can go full heavy armor and still get constantly staggered by a dagger attack spamming, but im ok with it, this game is more about timing rolls and proper blocking anyways, also not all Souls games have to be the same
-In terms of graphics, honestly the game is nothing to be amazed with, neither any game of the series, but it is by far the prettiest looking of the series, and the quality of the textures in the areas is not terrible like in DaS1 and 2.
Overall it is not THE BEST Dark souls but that's just because i don't think there is a best one among them all, although i proudly say this is a top quality souls game that will satisfy any challenge-hungry or action lover player out there. fully recommended!

One of the best games I've ever played. Gorgeous graphics, with very impressive and fluid animations for the most part (and a little faster than DS1 and 2 if you didn't like how slow it could be at times). Don't even bother playing with a keyboard; the optimization is a bit better this time around, but it absolutely CANNOT compare with just using and XBox controller. Trust me.
The difficulty seems to be lowered a little this time around, perhaps to be more new-player-friendly, but I'm probably biased since when I first played through this game in April, I'd been on a Souls binge since mid-November; plenty of time to git gud. Don't believe what people say about the "unfair difficulty" of these games - Dark Souls has never been that hard. It's simply been a CHALLENGE, which people all say they like in a game, but as soon as they actually GET a challenge, they complain about it. Try it out for yourself.
The world is pretty large, the largest of the three (I would assume), with rich and varied environments and enemies. The level design is, for me, something of a mixed bag. Dark Souls III is definitely trying to go back to the design of the original Dark Souls, and it does its job pretty well, though there aren't truly any sprawling paths that you can go down whenever you want, like in DS1, and it's not quite as vertical. And while the actual layout of the world makes a LOT more sense than DS2 (elevator up into a lake of lava anyone?), I found myself getting a little annoyed at the FOUR DIFFERENT CATHEDRALS in the game and just too much... cleanliness? I guess that's correct. What I mean is that in DS1, and to a much lesser extent in 2, the world felt OLD, falling into disrepair, with cracks and dust and plant life growing in the buildings. The world here... I don't quite know how to say it... it feels abandoned in a way, but also NOT. It seems very pristine at times compared to DS1, and while that's objectively not a bad thing, for me personally, I'd like a few less big churches and a few more ruins. Despite the personal gripe, the different zones are extremely detailed, paintstakingly so, and just looking around the environment gives you lots of clues as to the zone's lore (more on the superb lore later) and where to go next. There's a specific spot where paying attention and remembering details unlocks a whole ZONE later on. Hell, at one point you can see literally the ENTIRE GAME in one shot! That's absolutely astounding, and one of the best moments in the game.
The PvP is fun. Very meta-y, and the net code it pretty bad, but I enjoy the occasional duel binge. I don't do invasions so I can't speak from experience, but a lot of popular YouTubers seem to think that invasions are crappy and overly unfair to the invader.
Now, the best things about this game, I think, are the story and the bosses. Story first.
The story is sort of vaguely introduced in the opening cutscene, but most of it is learned through talking to the friendly NPCs you meet along your travels and by reading item descriptions. It may seem annoying at first to not have the story told to you like most games do, but I assure you, the Souls universe has some of the deepest, most complex, and most interesting lore out there, with new discoveries and theories being made all the time by a vibrant community of fans. In fact, some people have entire careers based of just the STORY of this game. The voice-acting is superb so you should totally talk to every NPC you can, and the NPC stories themselves, while not quite at the level of DS1 characters all the time, are still very nice and fleshed out. And while DS2 has been largely ignored but for a few items here and there, there are references all over to DS1, expertly placed. It's a not-so-subtle love letter to the people who were fans of this game from the start.
The bosses are AWESOME! Some are certainly better than others, but all of them are very pretty and with astounding sountracks to accompany them. When you play through a game that has no music for the most part, fighting against seemingly overwhelming odds amidst a vibrant and and epic soundtrack is a truly incredible sensation. Never mind the fact that every boss in the game has TWO PHASES! These bosses will be hard, and if you're new to the game, you'll probably die. Sometimes you'll die a LOT. Sometimes it will be very frustrating and it will seem impossible to progress past this point. But may I remind you: people beat this game on New Game +7, naked, using only their fists. So... you can do it, I promise. And when you do finally beat the boss, when you overcome those odds and watch this incredible obstacle fall before you... well, the sense of accomplishment and joy (and admittedly relief, sometimes) is unparalleled in any game I have ever played, ever. It's insane.
So to conclude, while this game is not perfect (and no game is), it is an incredibly rich and immersive experience unrivaled by almost anything out there. In fact, DS1 and 2 are two of the very small handful games that CAN compare with it. It is frustrating at times, but undeniably worth it for the fun you'll have playing it. The perfect way to send off one of the greatest series of all time.

So...
Once again the agony of this dying world is prolonged in this new release of the Dark Souls series. The world is still begging to die, and it's very tired. Yet those who just... refuse to let go will embark once again to a journey to reignite and relink the flame. Some gave up, some even refused to do this task, and the lords have left their thrones. So it's our job... burden... opportunity (it depends how you look at it) to take up this task and relink the flame in a final effort. Is it even worth it? Well... That's up to you to decide because the game has multiple endings. But... my choice was obvious. We have to let it go.
The story is just as familiar as it is strange. And it's up to your thirst of curiosity to find out more about it. Yet this time around everything became more easier to descipher and understand.
The gameplay is once again typical of the franchise with new additions here and there, but overall the same familiar concept.
The graphics are top quality and really enable the display of the intended artistic direction. There is no question about it, this one is the best looking souls game to date.
The level design is mostly smart, but perhaps a bit underwhelming compared to the high expectations. The genius of the DS1 is not returning, nor the brilliant design of DS2 DLC areas, and I don't think it ever will, but that will not make me bash the game just because I saw better. It is still great.
While right now there are no DLC's out yet and I can only talk about what I have in my hands, I can say this: DS3 is a great game, that I would recommend to fans of the franchise and new players alike. Also feels like the most accesible title of the series for new players that can have easier time figuring out the story and getting into the game in general.

So...
Once again the agony of this dying world is prolonged in this new release of the Dark Souls series. The world is still begging to die, and it's very tired. Yet those who just... refuse to let go will embark once again to a journey to reignite and relink the flame. Some gave up, some even refused to do this task, and the lords have left their thrones. So it's our job... burden... opportunity (it depends how you look at it) to take up this task and relink the flame in a final effort. Is it even worth it? Well... That's up to you to decide because the game has multiple endings. But... my choice was obvious. We have to let it go.
The story is just as familiar as it is strange. And it's up to your thirst of curiosity to find out more about it. Yet this time around everything became more easier to descipher and understand.
The gameplay is once again typical of the franchise with new additions here and there, but overall the same familiar concept.
The graphics are top quality and really enable the display of the intended artistic direction. There is no question about it, this one is the best looking souls game to date.
The level design is mostly smart, but perhaps a bit underwhelming compared to the high expectations. The genius of the DS1 is not returning, nor the brilliant design of DS2 DLC areas, and I don't think it ever will, but that will not make me bash the game just because I saw better. It is still great.
While right now there are no DLC's out yet and I can only talk about what I have in my hands, I can say this: DS3 is a great game, that I would recommend to fans of the franchise and new players alike. Also feels like the most accesible title of the series for new players that can have easier time figuring out the story and getting into the game in general.

A wonderful game with satisfying combat and gorgeous aeshetics.  It retains the Souls trademark difficulty but adds layers and layers of UI polish and character fluidity to the formula.
If you're a newcomer and curious about the Souls series, this is the perfect game to start out in.  It fixes some flaws in prior games and further improves upon the aspects that made those games oustanding.  For veterans of the series who have played DS1 and DS2, this game is a proper finale to the everlasting cycle of the Souls games and shouldn't be missed.
My only criticism is that there is a lower number of bosses in DS3 than in DS1/DS2 and that the game is quite unoptimized.

To start off, I'm not a original Fallout gamer. I started at Fallout 3, which is still my favorite (heresy, I know).  I have grown to really like New Vegas, but I haven't played the original series.
This... This isn't either Fallout 3 or New Vegas.  I liked it, but that's the problem. I didn't *love* it. I loved 3 and Vegas. I loved exploring, collecting, the endless missions and especially the humor of Fallout 3.  I loved that my decisions made a difference - even if I didn't know that was going to make a difference in the future.  Sometimes I was surprised.
I'm not surprised here. They crippled the dialogue.  All the big decisions are ham-handed and obvious. Most of your interactions don't matter, except to the extent it's possibly a new person to give you missions.  The new way of dialogue, the "wheel" or whatever, doesn't always clue you in on how you are going to react and limits you to like 3 or 4 responses. Again, not that it matters in most situations.
But, mostly, I'm disappointed in the story and side stories. Most of them are terrible, and didn't hold my interest at all. Part of the fun of Fallout 3 and New Vegas was the fact it was like an action novella.  Fallout 4 is not an equivelant.
Not to say there isnt' enjoyable parts, some of the locations are cool.  The Raiders encampment in the far Northeast was kinda cool. The mine experience was cool (no spoilers).  Some of the guns were cool.  My kids loved making robots with me.
The crafting was cool at first.  I really hate the arbitrary limits on building though. I really want to build my own fortress - but I can't without mods.  I'd run out of "room" before I finish the outer wall.
All in all it's cool, the gameplay is familiar and fine. But, I don't know if I can recommend it at retail. It's just not up to its predecessors, even with the new crafting system.

For anyone looking to get into Dark Souls that hasn't played the series before, do not let it scare you.
I had never played a Dark Souls game before this one, and it is a fantastic game. What you hear about it being a challenge is true, but it is not a negative thing.
The game is rewarding. When you beat an area or defeat a boss, you really feel like you've accomplished something. Each enemy you fight has the potentital to kill you if you aren't careful. Too often in games now the enemy AI is not actually a threat, merely a minor nuisance on the way to a clear cut story. You can master the enemies, but not without a lot of trial and error, aka dying all the time.
There is much more to the game that just difficulty however. Each weapon has it's own unique set of moves and fighting styles. The weapon art in the game is fantastic, and picking a weapon can be as much about style as function if you want it to be. You can PvP and find people using all sorts of different weapons.
There are also hidden items all throughout the game. If you are an easter egg hunter, you are going to love this game. You will find walls that look normal, but fade away when you hit them, and hidden paths and all sorts of little goodies.
The level design is great. Coupled with the difficulty, they add in what essentially amount to checkpoints throughout the level, each one making it easier to get to the main areas final boss. You can really feel the progress you are making as you get better along the way.
This is just a great game overall. The graphics are beautiful, (quite demanding though I will say, but it is well optimized) the gameplay is a ton of fun, and the replay value with new game + is through the roof. I couldn't really be any happier with a game than I am with Dark Souls.
So many games have come out with a lot of hype, but this one lived up to it and thensome for me.
Get this game. I don't know if it'll go on sale, but it's worth the $60 if you ask me.

Dark Souls 3 is quite possibly my favorite game to come out in recent years with few exceptions.
When somebody asks "How hard is it really?", You can always tell them it looks harder than it is.
In fact it is quite difficult once you get to higher levels or take yourself into New game+ (Second playthrough).
The enemies don't scale very much early on in a second playthrough but will still test you by being in potentially different positions of the world and use more of a broad array of attacks and buffs.
Overall i would say DS3 is a lot more difficult than say... Ninja Gaiden Black (if any of you have ever broken controllers over that game you know what i'm talking about).
PVP is quite fun when you have friends. Being invaded by another player is always fun as well when you have a Seed of a giant tree handy!.
Co-op summoning is quite fun as well and can really be good for those who are having trouble with an area or boss.
REMEMBER.
Your build in the beginning does not really matter too much at higher levels!. You can respect 5 times per gameplay and (if patient enough) you can level all the way to 802 i believe. So don't stress about stat points too early!.
Overall; i loved the story (there are multiple endings) as well as the gameplay / graphics as DS3 is using the same engine that was used for Bloodbourne with a few tweaks here and there.

Its been over a year since this game came out and i have almost nothing to complain about anymore. So lets break down what happened shall we?
Most importantly both DLC are out now. They were both pretty awesome but i think some things could have been improved especially with the first DLC which was
.
This DLC introduced two new bosses. While the final boss of the DLC was one of my favourite bosses in the series i can't say the same for the second one. It was basically a copy of Royal Rat Authority from DS2 with addition of 3 wolfs and a npc. Only good thing this boss droped was a item called Champion's Bones which unlocks the PvP arena. And that was one of the big reasons i actually bought this DLC since the only way you can unlock the PvP arena is throught one of the DLCs. The DLC it self took me about 5 hours to complete. Its not too long but if you consider the quality of the DLC and the time you can spend in the arena i would say it was worth it. The second DLC was definetly the better out of those two. I personally think its one of the best DLCs ever made and that DLC is
.
There are four new bosses and a tons of items varying from weapons, spells and even some of the coolest armor sets in the entire series. The bosses in this DLC are some of the best bosses in the souls series. My favourite is probably the Slave Knight Gael which is the finall boss of the entire DLC. Also Demon in Pain & Demon from Below is an awesome boss fight. Its a two stage boss fight in which you fight both Demon in Pain & Demon from Below in the first phase. Once you kill both of the demons they transform in to the Demon Prince which is basically stronger, more agressive version of the first two demons. Then there is Darkeater midir. Without a doubt the strongest boss in the entire game. It has insane on hit combo and extremly high defenses so prepare to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked. First time i fought this boss i was on NG+3 and it took me about 3 - 4 hours to beat him. And then there is the Halflight, Spear of the Church which is another generic NPC boss. However if you play online you won't face the NPC but you will fight against another player. Which can be fun but if you are playing against someone with 500 ping its just pure annoyance. So yeah this DLC took me about 10 hours to complete. Mainly thanks to the Midir. But non the less its hands down one of the best DLCs to this day and for the 15€ you pay for it you get more than enough content.
To summarize things up Dark Souls 3 got a lot of the flaws it had patched. Ashes of Ariandel whilst short added the thing which this game missed the most and that was a PvP arena. The Ringed city was an amazing DLC which added some of the best boss fights in the entire franchise and gave the game an worthy ending which this series deserves. So for me Dark Souls III with the DLCs is 9.5/10 game.
