This game is what you probably expect it to be, combination of Dark Souls and Bloodborne. And it plays out very well, yes it has some flaws but more on them later. Since there is a lot to cover i am going to split this review in to three categories -  Gameplay, Single player and Online play.
Lets start with gameplay. If you played any other souls game you will be familiary with controls and yes there are some tweaks from previous game but its small changes you are going to learn pretty quick. Most noticable difference is that the game is more fast paced thanks to Bloodborne. Another addition to gameplay is weapon art and FP bar (mana). FP bar determines how many spells you can use and it determines how much you can use your weapon art. Weapon art is uniqe skill for every weapon. It differs from backstep with dagger to buffing your sword with fire for a period of time.
One of the strongest part of this game is its lore. Thing with Souls game is that most of the lore is hidden in item description so you should read them if you are interested in it. And best thing about this game is probably its bosses. Every souls game had great bosses but i am pretty confident to say that Dark Souls III has some of the most amazing bosses in ever.
As usual there is a co-op and PvP. Both of them stayed pretty much the same. Which works for co-op but not for PvP. Since the game is fast paced like Bloodborne magic is utterly useless and same goes for miracles and pyromancy (only exeptions are buffs) and that essentialy removes all of those elements from PvP. Another thing that is kinda annoying is a fact you can use estus as invader. Probably the worst part is that there are no PvP arenas. And don't get me wrong i like PvP in this game its just gets repetitive after a while.
All in all Dark Souls III is amazing game with few flaws. Yes the PvP gets repetitive after a while and magic is useless but i don't regret single penny spent on this game. For me its 8/10!

Great successor to the first game (might even be a little bit better in my opinion). All locations seem to be well-made with challenging, creative bosses.  Even at the highest levels with the strongest weapons, enemies in some of the original areas can knock off pretty big chunks of health if you're not careful. One huge improvement is what they did with magic. Instead of a spell or miracle or pyromancy having a set number of times you can cast it, each cast of magic depletes a part of a mana(?) bar, which can be restored without having to constantly rest at bonfires.
If you like the DS series, you'll like DS3.

Before I begin, I would like to say that this review is being written after 5 playthroughs of the game.
Dark souls is a franchise I recently adopted with me picking up Dark Souls, as well as Dark Souls III. And let me say Dark Souls III blew my mind on my initial playthrough. The world, the detail, the soundtraack, and the combat all felt fresh and exciting to me, even as a new player. And if that wasn't enough going for the game, the bosses are considered some of the most thrilling and best designed bosses in any Soulsbourne game.
The lore in Dark Souls III is one of my favourites in any game. The connections to both Dark Souls and Dark Souls II is seamless and intriguing. every area has a purpose and every enemy has a backstory. That said the lore is not all up in your face. It is only there if you want it to be, so it won't be an annoyance if you don't want it to be.
That said, after beating the game once, it is loosing it's flare.
The difficulty of the game decreased for me immensely after my second playthrough. There are only so many strange and  inefficient builds I can use before I get bored. It was almost like I found an easy mode. Hopefully the DLC will revive this in the future, but for now I have lost most will to play.
If I had to some up this game, I would say the first 120 Hours of gameplay will be a thrilling experience, but once you master the bosses, it will be relatively easy.

This is probably the best action game i've ever played, by far.
First, I want to point out that I got this game on PC through steam, and quickly realized it wasn't intended to be played with a keyboard and mouse.  I also crashed multiple times on the lowest settings and also had severe framerate drops (on a pretty decent computer).  I ended up getting a steam refund (thank god that was an option) and getting the game for Xbox One and have since put in about 60 hours.  If you don't have a steam controller and a strong PC, I strongly advise you to look into a different platform.
It's true that this game is difficult.  To my surprise though, it's not that frustrating for me.  I go into the game knowing that some enemies are going to mop the floor with me, sometimes repeatedly.  This was especially true on my first playthrough.  Here are some tips to keep the frustration to a minimum.
one:  Keep the stakes low.  When you die, you drop all of your souls (currency). you have a chance to pick them up near the place you died, but if you die again before you pick them up, they're gone.  For this reason, when you reach a bonfire (checkpoint), make it a habit to go back to the Firelink Shrine (your home base) and spend your souls.
two:  Don't force yourself to play when you're not in the mood.  This game, by nature is very stressful, even when you're doing well.  If you're not eager to play, and you have a sense of dread about a new area, take a break, and don't play until you really want to.
three:  Don't set high expectations.  Nomatter what skill level you are in other games, you will always start as a noob in Dark Souls.  Knowing each enemy is crucial.  You will die a lot on your first playthrough.  Just keep in mind that with every failed attempt, you get a little better.  (by the way, there's no easy-mode difficulty setting)
four:  The key to being good at this game is patience.  It's the times you try to breeze through an area that you get your organs served to you on a plate.  With the way the combat system works, fighting multiple enemies is a terrible idea.  Use a range weapon to lure them one at a time.  There are also a lot of ambushes.  Excersize caution around ledges, doorways and dark areas where enemies might hide.  Also keep in mind that some items are meant to lure you.  If you don't mind spoilers, use online resources.  Watch playthroughs and guides, and read up on the Dark Souls wiki.
The combat in this game is extremely engaging and doesn't get old.  Since every enemy has the potential to ruin your day, it really keeps you on your toes.  The combat is all about timing, and since each enemy has different behavior, attacks and weaknesses, it's crucial to know each enemy.  If your smart, you'll find yourself occasionally taking the time to study how an enemy fights, rather than killing them the first chance you get.  If you love games with intense combat systems, you'll love Dark Souls.
Another thing this game does great is that it has excelent replayability.  There are about ten different character classes that you get to start with.  There are also different styles of combat and classes of weapons.  You can be a greatsword/shield wielding knight, a dual wielding mercenary, a katana wielding assassin, a sourcerer, a stealth archer, etc.  The list goes on and on.  On top of that, when you finish a the game, you have the option to start again from the beginning, keeping your levels and equipment, but having an increased difficulty.  The only thing I feel is missing from this game is the ability to fight bosses multiple times.
There is also multiplayer, which is very well incorporated into the game.  I currently don't have Xbox Live Gold, so I can't talk much about it, but people seem to enjoy it.
The Dark Souls series has a very complex and interesting underlying lore that it leaves you to figure out on your own.  You can learn about the lore through item descriptions, talking to NPCs, ect.  You can also learn alot about the lore through online resources.  There are entire forums dedicated to speculating and discussing the lore.  If you don't want to delve into the lore, you don't have to, but it's a great addition to the game if you find it interesting.
Bottom line, this game is amazing.  This is one of the few games I can play for hours without realizing it.  I highly reccomend it to someone looking for a challenge.

Nuka World was the final edition to Fallout 4’s expansive world. I’m writing this article to share my thoughts on the state of Fallout 4. Some note’s to take before you invest yourselves into my thoughts, I am playing Fallout 4 on a PC with a AMD FX-8350, R9 280x and 16gb of DDR3 Ram. I play Fallout 4 on Ultra without God-Rays, I am running 20 modifications to the game and logged at least 500 hours into Fallout 4 as of writing this. I'm not going to touch at all on the mechanics of the game since that has not changed at all nor anything else that has not changed since release.
Fallout 4 was a fantastic game from the get go for me. I really loved New Vegas and 3 was great too but not my most favorite. However I did find some things I truly missed that New Vegas and Fallout 3 had that Fallout 4 did not. The things that I missed most were…
Expansive weapons list, and no Bethesda your weapon mods don't count as different weapons, Just cause my combat rifle has a longer barrel does not make it the same as my short one.
More dialogue options, This go around I feel like I wasn't able to say the things I would normally say. I like to be as passive aggressive as I can in the Fallout universe as that is my true nature. This go around of Fallout it was Good, eeeehhh…. , Evil. No passive aggressive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ry. This was not a crippling factor for me since I was okay with the good options provided as it was the route I picked when passive aggressive wasn't available in previous Fallout’s
More town’s and cities. To be honest I actually hated the cities in Fallout 3, The only one I somewhat enjoyed was Megaton. Beyond that I didn’t care what happened to any of the citizens in places like Arefu, Rivet City, or even Canterbury Commons. New Vegas was different how ever. The people felt more genuine and had way better back stories. I liked exploring every city and town in New Vegas because everyone had something to share and it was so much easier to connect with the people. I even loved visiting Vault 3 though it was quite the pain to get there… I guess that’s just shows Obsidian has better writers than Bethesda. Fallout 4 had a lack of cities though each city I visited was quite interesting and found myself interested in everyone’s stories. Though I guess it’s just part of the background to the game where (SPOILER) the institute synths ravaged the wasteland and destroyed a lot of the settlements.

When I first started playing Fallout 4 I was very interested in settlement building. I really loved the idea of creating your own encampments of people so I can benefit the land around me and create my own towns. Especially since I was so disappointed in Fallout 3’s lack of character behind settlements. I was also a huge fan of the real time settler mod in Fallout New Vegas so it was quite the extra treat for me when announced. The starting items for settlement building were not bad in Fallout 4, Though a bick lack luster and very rustic but I guess that was okay. As I progressed through the game I was hoping Picket Fences would give me something more clean and neat to build with instead of sheet metal and plywood but alas that was something they never added that I installed a couple mod’s to make up for. Wasteland Workshop, Far Harbor and Contraptions came along and I feel like I got what I was asking for. They added a ton of new pieces and my settlements looked way more unique and clean. Then Vault Tec came out and I was able to build clean furniture and more items for my settlers to do. I feel like settlement building is a lot of fun now without mods. Thought my settlers have absolutely no character to them my buildings do and they’re mine which gives me a lot more pride and excitement about them.
Fallout’s story I feel was not as bad as people made it out to be really. It was way more diverse than Fallout 3’s and almost on par with New Vegas. There were 4 choices to be had all with different ways to end the game. They actually made subtle changes to the commonwealth so it didn’t feel like nothing after the game was completed. This is the one thing I feel people were making mountains out of mole hills with saying it wasn't as good as Fallout 3’s ending. I actually took the time to go back to 3 quickly and went to a save close to the ending where I realised I didn’t have much say in the ending besides (SPOILERS) putting an FEV into the water. Beyond that the main quest line had no significant choice that I remember. Far Harbor even gave more of an expansion on choices and moral ambiguity. Fallout 4 was about what you believed was best for the commonwealth. Though there wasn't a whole lot of backstory behind synths I saw the good in in it by a institute take over though personally I enjoyed the minutemen ending as it was the most american thing to do in the game. Though once the game is complete including DLC I can't help but feel somewhat lonely… But hey look it that more gunners to shoot!
Many people are thrilled that they can be a raider, I however found the raiders to be disgusting and barbaric. But that’s the point of an RPG you get to be what you want. This brought on a whole new dynamic to the game that more people can appreciate. Nuka World was not my cup of tea because I don't particularly like playing the bad guy. Once I wiped out the raiders I grabbed Dogmeat and went back to liberating settlements and killing raiders. It was not a bad DLC at all it was probably my third or fifth favorite DLC iteration in the fallout series when it came to the nitty gritty but again I'm just not the raider type. So now that Fallout 4 is done in a sense I would say that the state of fallout is good it’s still very playable and there’s been a lot of fixes and changed making it my second favorite Fallout after new vegas.

Great game for running around doing chores and crafting/building stuff. However, one thing Bethesda could've improved on for sure: a very complex but concise plotline. The main storyline was very predictable and very short, there were several ways they could've done to make it interesting. For example (SPOILERS): there could've been an interesting quest for Nick Valentine with Kellog in control of his mind; there could've been more to the Minutemen other than you instantly becoming General and taking orders from stupid Preston Gravy to help settlements that you already built to the tee but somehow always ♥♥♥♥ing fail at defending itself (lol); there would be more explanation as to why the Institute kidnapped/killed people or what they did with the original people they'd swap out with synths, that way there's an actual incentive to join the Institute; rebuilding dead settlements like University Point; developing more on your companion characters — each one gives a different outcome to certain events, and actually have the balls to show a funny/awkward sex scene with them instead of "black screening". There were so many good ideas for all these plotlines within the game, but it was almost like they were half baked or rushed. What's interesting after playing earlier fallout games like New Vegas and FO3, which felt like there was a very thick plotline, FO4 feels like a downgrade as far as story. The only thing that was improved from the previous games were the interface design (easier for players to understand where/what♥♥♥♥♥♥is on your screen), better graphics engine, animation is better (although a bit derpy most of the time but hey what game doesn't have derpy animations?), and adding crafting/building element to create settlements.
Games such as the Witcher 3 have so much detail and in depth storylines within the main storyline that it puts the storywriters in FO4 to shame. What happened to the writers in the previous games? Don't get me wrong I play the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Fallout 4  still because of its crafting element (it's like Sims), but again the story was so disappointing. Small side quests have more in depth detail than the main quest. C'mon Bethesda, you're better than this!

Currently this review is still in development but as I experience more and more of the game I will keep on updating this review.
SUMMARY:
Dark Souls 3 is a great game I recommend for new players of the series with the only faults being easy early game bosses and pretty much all bosses in general having a low health bar with all this being topped of with a pretty linear P.V.P. system.
Apart from that I have to say that Dark Souls 3 is a great game with plenty of challenge for newer players but not as much for veterans of the series.
Overall this game is very solid and is deserving of 8/10.
EDIT: The game is great and that's what I already have said. But this game suffers from some very big and quite glaring issues.
The start of this game from the 3rd Area (2nd non-tutorial area) to the 6th area (5th non-tutorial area) are just annoying and slow. The enemies are slow and annoying and are full of horrible concepts that weren't executed right. The places themselves are plain and just ugly. The bosses (not including the 6/5th area boss) are easy.
That entire part of the game is just... Not very fun on consecutive runs.
After that the game is just infinitely better.
Apart from the Dungeon.
I hate that place.
I wish they could have just done something exciting and fun for those 3 areas and not just some bland and not fun areas.
Otherwise this game is great and feels a lot less clunky then Dark Souls 1 and a lot less annoying than Dark Souls 2.
The bonfire placement in this game is needless to say kind of silly. Some bonfires being only 10 metres away.
Apart from these issues and bosses having really small health pools in the start of the game this game is great.

Edit 22/11/2017
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Still one of my favorite games of all time. Insanely fun every time I play, and more so with content mods and a good ENB (Olympus ENB). Worth every hour I put into it, and I suggest that you keep an eye on Fallout 4 VR (and Skyrim Vr / Doom VFR) in the future!
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Upon ascending to the platform above Vault 111, I remember seeing the beautiful world in a state of stupefaction. I had expected that like the worlds of other Fallout games, the Commonwealth would be a grotesque world of greys and browns, yet I saw at once that this one was utterly different.
The Commonwealth is as beautiful as Skyrim. The radiation storms of the Glowing Sea create lightning that dances in the distance as you circumvent Deathclaws and Supermutants entrenched in battle. In the night, formidable power armor-equipped raiders shine their headlamps on Boston's beaches, looking out for mirelurks and ghouls, and the impressive Mass Fusion building towers over all.
The world has true character. It has been lovingly hand-crafted, and it simply feels
. Whether you are exploring Corvega Assembly Plant, various crash sites scattered around the Commonwealth, or the Quincy Ruins, you'll find that each location seems to fit into the world perfectly.
Bethesda's characters are solid. Many of them are outfitted with extensive dialogue, and many are not, but this creates realism; players simply do not
every NPC who walks by to relate their life stories and engage in a lengthy discussion. I've had characters who aren't members of any faction refuse to talk to me or trade solely because they didn't like me. I was fine with that.
The gun and armor customization systems are truly impressive. Through them, you will create mods that you actually
; there is little filler in the game's entirety. You can rename guns as well. On that note, the gunplay is utterly satisfying and is
.
Power armor is fantastic in this iteration. Near the beginning of the game, you will be handed a set of weak, low-tech power armor, and eventually you will work up to the likes of the X-01 suit and cool paint jobs and accessories for your gear.
Concerning followers, I have only played with Dogmeat and Piper, but both have been awesome to work with. It's fun to find bandanas and dog armor for Dogmeat, and Piper has tons of dialogue that add to the game's character. When we were at The Third Rail, for example, Piper appeared quite jealous as I was talking to Magnolia and would insert awkward comments into the conversation. I have heard that other followers are excellent as well.
The story is phenomenal. Your actions throughout truly have an impact on the post-story Commonwealth.
. And riding in the Vertibirds is out-of-this-world cool.
Inon Zur's Fallout 4 score is one of my favorite soundtracks. But even if you decide to turn off the music, Fallout 4 has a myriad of ambient insect, bird, and wind noises that truly make the world come alive.
What I did not like:
Many of the buildings have incredibly ugly textures
The Inner City is poorly optimized
You are often expected to play the "good guy"
Most of the DLC is not worth the price, excluding Far Harbor.
Mods that you should get:
War of the Commonwealth (endless warfare between NPCs makes the world feel real)
Vertibird Overhaul (ride Vertibirds even if unaffiliated with BOS)
True Storms: Legendary Edition (better radiation storms- rain, snow, fog)
What's more, Bethesda (as of November 2016) is tweaking Fallout 4 to make the entire experience available to play on virtual reality devices sometime in 2017.
Put simply, Fallout 4 is easily one of the best open world experiences ever created. I heartily recommend this game.

Now that I've thoroughly played enough DS3 to have an accurate opinion, it's almost as good as the first game.
Almost.
The game's great, and I can't put it down so don't get me wrong, but there are a few things I take issue with. But I will suck this game's♥♥♥♥♥♥at the same time so there's that to look forward to.
While most people will probably say it plays like DS1, I have to disagree. It plays more like Demon's Souls from the PS3 and Bloodborne had a super baby. The magic, or "FP" bar, make a return, and increases via Attunement and the Ember system functions like the Ephemeral Eyes/Stone/I-Don't-Remember from Demon's Souls as well, except not being Embered doesn't half your HP like Soul Form. And really the only other HUD changes are the toolbelt on the start menu, where you can put up to 5 items that you feel shouldn't be in your useable items (White/Red Soapstone, Seperation Crystal, stuff like that.).
PvE is definitely the thing that makes this game shine. DS2 had a lot of boring enemies, so DS3 had to keep things more fresh than Will Smith. And fresh it is. The enemies I've noticed have also been given moves that punish backstab fishing, so From is telling newcomers to "git gud". The weapons you have to dispose of the baddies is also fantastic. I'm especially fond of the dual-weilding weapons, which have replaced Powerstancing (which was something I liked from DS2. RIP Powerstanced Lightning Shotels.) and good god are they ever fun. I won't mention too many, because they're there for you to find, but I'll say my favourite is the Farron Greatsword. Heaven incarnate.
PvP sits in the middle of the Souls series for me, DS1 being kinda sucky while DS2, ironically, being the best. It seems to have the best of both worlds; DS1's play style and DS2's server functionality. While this may sound great, lemme just tell you why it's not as great. Invasions, if you're not dueling with your soapstone, prioritize people co-oping, or if you're a Souls Veteran, Gankers. 9 times outta 10, I'd come across a 3v1 situation, and that's enough for me to break something. I used to be an evil guy in DS2, constantly invading and ruining people's days, but now I'm strapped to the confines of a dueling arena that PvPers have gathered in. It get's bland after a while. Other than the situation of invasions, PvP is enjoyable, given that you've set yourself up properly. Most of the weapons are viable, though some stand out more than others.
Now, normally, I wouldn't talk about Covenants, but it begs to be mentioned. Darkmoon's back, but it's the exact same as... the Blue Sentinels. Y'know. That covenant no one's a part of in DS2. I'd have less issue if it didn't require a total of 30 Concord Proofs for Darkmoon Blade. So future Darkmoons, INVEST EARLY WITH BLUE SENTINELS. They're literally the exact same. Just pray that someone keeps Way of Blue as their covenant. The defence covenants are back too, while more suited for lower leveled PvP. We basically have Forest Hunters and Princess' Guard back, and the resemblance is a bit more uncanny the moment I typed that sentence. Weird.
Finally, this game is the most beautiful looking in the series by far. That is a blessing and a curse. I initally refunded this game because my old laptop couldn't handle it, yet could handle DS1 and DS2:SOTFS. So, after dropping 1.3 grand on a new one, I can actually play it. SO I URGE YOU, MAKE SURE YOU AT LEAST MAKE MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS BEFORE BUYING. It's unfortunate that people with lower power computers will have a hard time with this thing running, and my heart goes out to guys because I know how it feels waiting for this game and then realize you can't play it. That is actually my main critique with the graphics, THEY'RE TOO GOOD.
All in all, 9/10 for the sequel the original game deserved, despite it's short-commings.

Before I begin, I would like to say that this review is being written after 5 playthroughs of the game.
Dark souls is a franchise I recently adopted with me picking up Dark Souls, as well as Dark Souls III. And let me say Dark Souls III blew my mind on my initial playthrough. The world, the detail, the soundtraack, and the combat all felt fresh and exciting to me, even as a new player. And if that wasn't enough going for the game, the bosses are considered some of the most thrilling and best designed bosses in any Soulsbourne game.
The lore in Dark Souls III is one of my favourites in any game. The connections to both Dark Souls and Dark Souls II is seamless and intriguing. every area has a purpose and every enemy has a backstory. That said the lore is not all up in your face. It is only there if you want it to be, so it won't be an annoyance if you don't want it to be.
That said, after beating the game once, it is loosing it's flare.
The difficulty of the game decreased for me immensely after my second playthrough. There are only so many strange and  inefficient builds I can use before I get bored. It was almost like I found an easy mode. Hopefully the DLC will revive this in the future, but for now I have lost most will to play.
If I had to some up this game, I would say the first 120 Hours of gameplay will be a thrilling experience, but once you master the bosses, it will be relatively easy.

Where does one begin to describe the game? There are so many pluses, and so few negatives.
If you enjoy shooter games, this game has it in spades, and is done very well.
If you enjoy an RPG style game, it is here, though not as focused as Fallout 3 and New Vegas. Still, it is a strong component, from my personal view.

The open world RPG of post-apocalyptic scavenging starts again. Similar in vein to its predecessor, Fallout 4 allows you to hop into Power Armor once more to fight against the tyrannies of the Commonwealth.
Once you get underway into the game, you can start to make choices on your gender, face and starting S.P.E.C.I.A.L attributes, levelling them and various other fun perks as you level up towards infinity. That's right, the cap from previous games has been removed, allowing you to buff up as many perks as you want, from Heavy Guns to Robotics Expert to Ninja.
This beautiful world runs on the Creation Engine, so if you liked the visuals in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim then you won't be disappointed. If you're playing the PC or Xbox version, you can modify the game with third-party plugins, using programs such as Nexus Mod Manager and LOOT, enabling even richer experiences, from additional armor, to more quests and customizable skins.
The quests themselves aren't as varied as you'd find in Fallout 3 but do not let that sway you from purchasing the game, nor it's DLCs. The best DLCs include Far Harbor and Nuka-World though the Season Pass is still well worth it if you're an avid fan of Bethesda's games.
The amount of content in this game is still staggering though, from the huge number of weapon customizations, powerful legendary loot, and settlements to craft there is always something to do. Survival mode difficulty cranks things even further up to 11, by really making things challenging, making you think before you fire because, if you die, you instantly go back to when you last slept. A bummer if you haven't slept for ages, but so rewarding when you finally get in bed after shooting 20 feral ghouls in the face. (Ad victoriam!)
Why are you still reading? Grab the game, hop in some jet-packed power armor, and punch that deathclaw in the face!

Easily my favorite game of the series!
Pros of the game:
1. The creativity of the environments, enemies, bosses, weapons, etc.
2. It has throwbacks from Dark Souls 1. Though, I personally don't like very many throwbacks, I found it to be awesome to see places, and characters look so much better.
3. The Bosses. Facing the first boss in this game was probably "the hook" of this game to me. It was incredibly challenging, especially for new Dark Souls players, yet entertaining. As for the rest of the bosses, for there are a few that are too easy or just not fun, i loved them!
4. The graphics... All I have to say is the view when you first get to Irithyll of the Boreal Valley is absolutely breathtaking and the rest of the game just looks amazing!
5. The "learning curve" of this game. What most people say about Dark Souls is "why would you want to play a game where you die a lot." Well, for those who have actually played the game, know that you learn from your deaths. You learn when to parry from this enemy's attack, or this place in a level sets off a trap or ambush, or this chest has a chain facing forward, therefore it's a mimic. It's something that I've always loved about the Souls games, and it continues it in the 3rd game.
The cons in the game:
1. Rolling is super OP, you can get away with virtually anything, by rolling, even if it logically doesn't make sense. (Starting off as a knight, you don't fat roll in the beginning like in Dark Souls 1 & 2)
2. Though there are throwbacks from the first Dark Souls, I also felt that it was a bit "unoriginal" and relied on them a bit... Like Star Wars 7 for example. (THIS DOESN'T HAVE TO BE A CON, IT'S MY PERSONAL PREFERENCE OF IT)
3. I've never felt the urge to ever  explore different kinds of weapons throughout the game. After finding the "Astora Straight Sword" in the 2nd level, I've stuck with it throughout the entire game eventually upgrading it to +10 giving it 322 physical damage with a raw gem. Of course, I've found many amazing weapons, i just never bothered using them, because my sword did so much more damage then the other and I could add any kind of buffs to it as much as i'd like. Idk, it's probably just me.

Fantastic addition to the Soulsborne games. If you are someone who enjoyed Demon Souls, Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2 or Bloodborne, you will enjoy this game.
Pros:
-The combat is amped up in this Souls game. It is faster and features weapon arts which are basically special moves that a weapon can perform and it spices things up.
-The new weapon infusions allow for increased potential on all fronts and not just the elemental or resistance based.
-Loads of armor sets, weapons and Spells.
-Lots of character side quests and stories to unravel.
-Stats are a bit simpler than previous games. You know exactly what each stat does and how it will benefit your character.
-Bosses are well designed and often challenging even after a few trips through the game.
-It has a lot of easter eggs and shout outs to the two previous Dark Souls, particularly in relation to the in game lore.
Cons:
-There aren't many weapon arts that are unique. Many weapons of the same type share the same one or two weapon arts.
-Some vital weapon infusions you don't obtain until VERY late in the game.
-Spells are fairly under powered through the first half of the game.
-The side quests for some characters in this game can be quite difficult to figure out, sometimes leaving you to look them up because there wasn't any real reason you would have figured them out just playing the game.
-The enemies in this game have some of the cheapest design and AI in the series. They will swing through solid objects like walls and floors to hit you. Some moves that are just near impossible to avoid. Lookin at you leaping Ghru...
-There are very few areas in this game that I enjoyed going through. I often found myself saying "I hate this zone..." when progressing in a new playthrough. No one zone stuck out as a zone I loved to go through, they were all a bit tedious or lack luster to me.
-Invasians can get way out of hand in some zones and performing invasions in standard zones can be extremely one sided. In the Farron Keep/Crucifixion Woods, the Wolf covenants invaders are constant if you are embered. But on the other hand, invading in a non covenant related zones you will often invade groups of two or more players with no other invaders to back you up.
Overall, it isn't my absolute favorite in the series (my vote goes to Bloodborne :]  It's a PS4 exclusive though), but it is still fantastic. Anyone who enjoyed the previous ones should definitely pick this up. We have yet to even see the DLC, but it can only really expand on the good that is already here.
Overall Score: 8/10

Easily my favorite game of the series!
Pros of the game:
1. The creativity of the environments, enemies, bosses, weapons, etc.
2. It has throwbacks from Dark Souls 1. Though, I personally don't like very many throwbacks, I found it to be awesome to see places, and characters look so much better.
3. The Bosses. Facing the first boss in this game was probably "the hook" of this game to me. It was incredibly challenging, especially for new Dark Souls players, yet entertaining. As for the rest of the bosses, for there are a few that are too easy or just not fun, i loved them!
4. The graphics... All I have to say is the view when you first get to Irithyll of the Boreal Valley is absolutely breathtaking and the rest of the game just looks amazing!
5. The "learning curve" of this game. What most people say about Dark Souls is "why would you want to play a game where you die a lot." Well, for those who have actually played the game, know that you learn from your deaths. You learn when to parry from this enemy's attack, or this place in a level sets off a trap or ambush, or this chest has a chain facing forward, therefore it's a mimic. It's something that I've always loved about the Souls games, and it continues it in the 3rd game.
The cons in the game:
1. Rolling is super OP, you can get away with virtually anything, by rolling, even if it logically doesn't make sense. (Starting off as a knight, you don't fat roll in the beginning like in Dark Souls 1 & 2)
2. Though there are throwbacks from the first Dark Souls, I also felt that it was a bit "unoriginal" and relied on them a bit... Like Star Wars 7 for example. (THIS DOESN'T HAVE TO BE A CON, IT'S MY PERSONAL PREFERENCE OF IT)
3. I've never felt the urge to ever  explore different kinds of weapons throughout the game. After finding the "Astora Straight Sword" in the 2nd level, I've stuck with it throughout the entire game eventually upgrading it to +10 giving it 322 physical damage with a raw gem. Of course, I've found many amazing weapons, i just never bothered using them, because my sword did so much more damage then the other and I could add any kind of buffs to it as much as i'd like. Idk, it's probably just me.

Fantastic addition to the Soulsborne games. If you are someone who enjoyed Demon Souls, Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2 or Bloodborne, you will enjoy this game.
Pros:
-The combat is amped up in this Souls game. It is faster and features weapon arts which are basically special moves that a weapon can perform and it spices things up.
-The new weapon infusions allow for increased potential on all fronts and not just the elemental or resistance based.
-Loads of armor sets, weapons and Spells.
-Lots of character side quests and stories to unravel.
-Stats are a bit simpler than previous games. You know exactly what each stat does and how it will benefit your character.
-Bosses are well designed and often challenging even after a few trips through the game.
-It has a lot of easter eggs and shout outs to the two previous Dark Souls, particularly in relation to the in game lore.
Cons:
-There aren't many weapon arts that are unique. Many weapons of the same type share the same one or two weapon arts.
-Some vital weapon infusions you don't obtain until VERY late in the game.
-Spells are fairly under powered through the first half of the game.
-The side quests for some characters in this game can be quite difficult to figure out, sometimes leaving you to look them up because there wasn't any real reason you would have figured them out just playing the game.
-The enemies in this game have some of the cheapest design and AI in the series. They will swing through solid objects like walls and floors to hit you. Some moves that are just near impossible to avoid. Lookin at you leaping Ghru...
-There are very few areas in this game that I enjoyed going through. I often found myself saying "I hate this zone..." when progressing in a new playthrough. No one zone stuck out as a zone I loved to go through, they were all a bit tedious or lack luster to me.
-Invasians can get way out of hand in some zones and performing invasions in standard zones can be extremely one sided. In the Farron Keep/Crucifixion Woods, the Wolf covenants invaders are constant if you are embered. But on the other hand, invading in a non covenant related zones you will often invade groups of two or more players with no other invaders to back you up.
Overall, it isn't my absolute favorite in the series (my vote goes to Bloodborne :]  It's a PS4 exclusive though), but it is still fantastic. Anyone who enjoyed the previous ones should definitely pick this up. We have yet to even see the DLC, but it can only really expand on the good that is already here.

Its not the best of the Fallout series, but it is a good edition and fans of the series should definitely play it. The first notable difference is that the game is much more "colorfull" and brighter. It doesn't have the same depressing atmosphere that the other Fallout games have. I believe this has to do with the story line, as it plays into the narrative of rebuilding the world that is pushed quite a lot in the story. It does come with a few new game mechanics such as the changed VATS system, which is now slow motion rather than a full out pause. Power armor is no longer a perk, but is rather treated like a vehicle. Another great new feature is the settlement building. Players can now build their own settlements and populate them with settlers.
What I didn't like about the game, is that it falls into the same trap so many other open-world RPGs fall into. The exploratoin can feel somewhat unrewarding and ultimately becomes just more grinding. Most missions are of the same old "go there, kill this person/retrieve this item" variety and it all becomes a little boring too fast. But as I've said, this is a fault the entire genre suffers from usually and Fallout has always been a defining franchise of said genre.
All in all a great game, and a decent contributor to the franchise. 8.5/10

Easily my favorite game of the series!
Pros of the game:
1. The creativity of the environments, enemies, bosses, weapons, etc.
2. It has throwbacks from Dark Souls 1. Though, I personally don't like very many throwbacks, I found it to be awesome to see places, and characters look so much better.
3. The Bosses. Facing the first boss in this game was probably "the hook" of this game to me. It was incredibly challenging, especially for new Dark Souls players, yet entertaining. As for the rest of the bosses, for there are a few that are too easy or just not fun, i loved them!
4. The graphics... All I have to say is the view when you first get to Irithyll of the Boreal Valley is absolutely breathtaking and the rest of the game just looks amazing!
5. The "learning curve" of this game. What most people say about Dark Souls is "why would you want to play a game where you die a lot." Well, for those who have actually played the game, know that you learn from your deaths. You learn when to parry from this enemy's attack, or this place in a level sets off a trap or ambush, or this chest has a chain facing forward, therefore it's a mimic. It's something that I've always loved about the Souls games, and it continues it in the 3rd game.
The cons in the game:
1. Rolling is super OP, you can get away with virtually anything, by rolling, even if it logically doesn't make sense. (Starting off as a knight, you don't fat roll in the beginning like in Dark Souls 1 & 2)
2. Though there are throwbacks from the first Dark Souls, I also felt that it was a bit "unoriginal" and relied on them a bit... Like Star Wars 7 for example. (THIS DOESN'T HAVE TO BE A CON, IT'S MY PERSONAL PREFERENCE OF IT)
3. I've never felt the urge to ever  explore different kinds of weapons throughout the game. After finding the "Astora Straight Sword" in the 2nd level, I've stuck with it throughout the entire game eventually upgrading it to +10 giving it 322 physical damage with a raw gem. Of course, I've found many amazing weapons, i just never bothered using them, because my sword did so much more damage then the other and I could add any kind of buffs to it as much as i'd like. Idk, it's probably just me.

Fantastic addition to the Soulsborne games. If you are someone who enjoyed Demon Souls, Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2 or Bloodborne, you will enjoy this game.
Pros:
-The combat is amped up in this Souls game. It is faster and features weapon arts which are basically special moves that a weapon can perform and it spices things up.
-The new weapon infusions allow for increased potential on all fronts and not just the elemental or resistance based.
-Loads of armor sets, weapons and Spells.
-Lots of character side quests and stories to unravel.
-Stats are a bit simpler than previous games. You know exactly what each stat does and how it will benefit your character.
-Bosses are well designed and often challenging even after a few trips through the game.
-It has a lot of easter eggs and shout outs to the two previous Dark Souls, particularly in relation to the in game lore.
Cons:
-There aren't many weapon arts that are unique. Many weapons of the same type share the same one or two weapon arts.
-Some vital weapon infusions you don't obtain until VERY late in the game.
-Spells are fairly under powered through the first half of the game.
-The side quests for some characters in this game can be quite difficult to figure out, sometimes leaving you to look them up because there wasn't any real reason you would have figured them out just playing the game.
-The enemies in this game have some of the cheapest design and AI in the series. They will swing through solid objects like walls and floors to hit you. Some moves that are just near impossible to avoid. Lookin at you leaping Ghru...
-There are very few areas in this game that I enjoyed going through. I often found myself saying "I hate this zone..." when progressing in a new playthrough. No one zone stuck out as a zone I loved to go through, they were all a bit tedious or lack luster to me.
-Invasians can get way out of hand in some zones and performing invasions in standard zones can be extremely one sided. In the Farron Keep/Crucifixion Woods, the Wolf covenants invaders are constant if you are embered. But on the other hand, invading in a non covenant related zones you will often invade groups of two or more players with no other invaders to back you up.
Overall, it isn't my absolute favorite in the series (my vote goes to Bloodborne :]  It's a PS4 exclusive though), but it is still fantastic. Anyone who enjoyed the previous ones should definitely pick this up. We have yet to even see the DLC, but it can only really expand on the good that is already here.
Overall Score: 8/10

Dark Souls III is a culmination of some of the best aspects of the previous Souls games, creating a more fitting sequel to the Dark Souls series then Dark Souls II was. Dark Souls III does try to stand out however, bringing faster combat, faster enemies and bosses to the table, while still maintaining a strong emphasis on patience and situational awareness the original Dark Souls had, albeit with a more linear world.
You once again begin the game with a short cutscene, with a little more to go on then in previous installments. The Lords of Cinder have left their thrones, and presumably you’re the one destined to fetch them like a kindergarden teacher gathering children for naptime. You quickly find your way to the Firelink Shrine to meet the new/old cast of characters, who greet you with the usual creepy cackling. Firelink Shrine feels a little more welcoming and safe than previous games, sharing similarities with the Nexus from Demon Souls as it’s almost entirely disconnected from the rest of the gameworld. Although it still carries the themes of Dark Souls unlike Majula from Dark Souls II, this new Firelink Shrine doesn’t really compare to the previous one in my opinion, I much prefered when the hub-area was actually in the centre of the world I was exploring, much like Dark Souls did.
You’ll find in Dark Souls III that it’s exceedingly difficult to go the wrong way, since Firelink Shrine now serves as a disconnected hub-world where you teleport to the areas you’ll be exploring. The world is still intertwined and connected once you’re removed from Firelink Shrine, however these intertwined pathways and shortcuts are only present within their own individual areas, while the original Dark Souls had pathways and shortcuts
their areas. A fine example would be that Blighttown was connected to the Depths, and Drakes Valley, giving you an option of which way you would like to approach Blighttown from. Dark Souls III has linear paths between areas, not offering any options on how to approach them.
Combat is improved in Dark Souls III, boasting far faster combat than previous installments and
, which are a new set of attacks which are specific to the weapon/magic you’re using. However, they’re limited by the new FP bar(Focus Points), this helps to significantly mix up combat style, offering more variety in attacks. As previously mentioned, this faster combat is done in such a way that patience and learning enemy attack patterns is still highly encouraged, and due to the quicker speed of combat, there is less downtime when waiting for an enemy to be vulnerable. It feels different, and will take some adjusting - but it’s a welcome addition in my eyes.
The world this time around feels more like Dark Souls, unlike Dark Souls II. Providing that same depressing and grim beauty we have come to enjoy and love. Dark Souls III goes further with the entire apocalyptic theme, the land of Lothric truly feels like it's dying, like the world is coming to an end. The NPCs also feel much more familiar, some previous NPCs actually returning for this third game. The characters and dialog are much better this time around too, however it still leaves something to be desired, as many of the NPCs have almost nothing to say until the closing hours of the game, honestly giving me some frustration as I was playing. It’s a great improvement from Dark Souls II, but still isn’t much better than the original Dark Souls. Characters are mostly memorable, but much of the dialog is relatively weak.
The typical storytelling and lore returns to Dark Souls III, making the player put it together like a puzzle instead of clearly stating it. It’s also in a similar fashion to the original Dark Souls, not making the same mistakes Dark Souls II made. I was worried when starting Dark Souls III that any mention of previous Souls games in the lore would be fanservice, however it didn’t take long to realize that there was actually a lot of care put into what was mentioned. The only fanservice that I felt was being able to obtain the Sun Set, however this was obtained via a non-obtuse way and wasn’t just found lying about in a chest. Overall Dark Souls III’s lore and story is handled really well, and feels like a good conclusion to the series, regardless of the questions which may remain unanswered.
Dark Souls III isn’t perfect, the linearity compared to the original Dark Souls left me wanting, and many of the mechanics which were previously favored have been heavily altered and changed. Poise being the finest example as it’s essentially non-existent, which seemed to throw a wrench at the PvP community. Many of the covenant systems also seems to be broken or not very useful, which heavily affects the online play. It’s unfortunate that the last supposed Dark Souls game seemed to have really messed up the online play for PvPers, however the PvEers seem largely unaffected by these changes. Aside from these glaring issues, Dark Souls III serves as a wonderful sequel to Dark Souls, offering new aspects to the combat and spicing it up with its speed and variety in attacks. If you have yet to play a Souls game, I suggest playing Dark Souls before Dark Souls III, and treating Dark Souls II as a disconnected additional game, as you don’t need to play it to understand the other two games.
If you enjoyed previous Souls games for its lore and PvE, Dark Souls III provides much of the same with a few welcomed additions, however PvP has been significantly hampered due to the changes with Poise.

However, they’re limited by the new FP bar(Focus Points), this helps to significantly mix up combat style, offering more variety in attacks. As previously mentioned, this faster combat is done in such a way that patience and learning enemy attack patterns is still highly encouraged, and due to the quicker speed of combat, there is less downtime when waiting for an enemy to be vulnerable. It feels different, and will take some adjusting - but it’s a welcome addition in my eyes.
The world this time around feels more like Dark Souls, unlike Dark Souls II. Providing that same depressing and grim beauty we have come to enjoy and love. Dark Souls III goes further with the entire apocalyptic theme, the land of Lothric truly feels like it's dying, like the world is coming to an end. The NPCs also feel much more familiar, some previous NPCs actually returning for this third game. The characters and dialog are much better this time around too, however it still leaves something to be desired, as many of the NPCs have almost nothing to say until the closing hours of the game, honestly giving me some frustration as I was playing. It’s a great improvement from Dark Souls II, but still isn’t much better than the original Dark Souls. Characters are mostly memorable, but much of the dialog is relatively weak.
The typical storytelling and lore returns to Dark Souls III, making the player put it together like a puzzle instead of clearly stating it. It’s also in a similar fashion to the original Dark Souls, not making the same mistakes Dark Souls II made. I was worried when starting Dark Souls III that any mention of previous Souls games in the lore would be fanservice, however it didn’t take long to realize that there was actually a lot of care put into what was mentioned. The only fanservice that I felt was being able to obtain the Sun Set, however this was obtained via a non-obtuse way and wasn’t just found lying about in a chest. Overall Dark Souls III’s lore and story is handled really well, and feels like a good conclusion to the series, regardless of the questions which may remain unanswered.
Dark Souls III isn’t perfect, the linearity compared to the original Dark Souls left me wanting, and many of the mechanics which were previously favored have been heavily altered and changed. Poise being the finest example as it’s essentially non-existent, which seemed to throw a wrench at the PvP community. Many of the covenant systems also seems to be broken or not very useful, which heavily affects the online play. It’s unfortunate that the last supposed Dark Souls game seemed to have really messed up the online play for PvPers, however the PvEers seem largely unaffected by these changes. Aside from these glaring issues, Dark Souls III serves as a wonderful sequel to Dark Souls, offering new aspects to the combat and spicing it up with its speed and variety in attacks. If you have yet to play a Souls game, I suggest playing Dark Souls before Dark Souls III, and treating Dark Souls II as a disconnected additional game, as you don’t need to play it to understand the other two games.
If you enjoyed previous Souls games for its lore and PvE, Dark Souls III provides much of the same with a few welcomed additions, however PvP has been significantly hampered due to the changes with Poise.

This game hurts. Not in the way that previous souls titles do. This game hurts in that it's not the game it should have been. There are technically various ways to approach it, but you can no longer play a real tank character, magic is effectively useless, as it requires you to be completely invested in magic stats and using a very specific set of items and equipment. Pyromancy and Miracles have the same exact issue. I recently reinstalled because I had heard there would be DLC, and I'm hoping the DLC will add in balance changes that fx how awful the PvP is. I've fought maybe 6 people since reinstalling, all of them R1 spamming goons. The two hit stunlock limitation simply made it so that they hit you twice, roll out, roll in, hit you twice again, rinse and repeat. This game lost what made souls pvp fun. Creativity is no longer viable in PvP. It's barely viable in PvE. The game feels unfinished, and the director himself has apologized for it. The armor system is almost entirely pointless, after running some tests I found that the difference between a starting armor set and a late game heavy set was literally 14 points of damage. Honestly, lore wise it doesnt make all that much sense or add a tremendous amount on the series. It's very pretty though. All in all I would not recommend it. Just replay the lightning strike of genius that is the first Dark Souls.

Quick Review after reading some other reviews and having played many hours of this game following the other iterations:
Firstly, Dark souls 3 does not disappoint in the areas of lore, pacing, rich and varied environments, or visuals and audio.
In all of these ways I want to love Dark Souls 3, and most folks seem to agree with that.
It's only some of the diehard older fans of the series like myself that seem to have an issue, and that issue is primarily with the gameplay mechanics. I won't rattle off the myriad of things that other top rated reviews here have mentioned as being changes that some see as unfavorable, like the general issue of the removal of poise or the lack of viable character build choices.
Let me lay it out simply: If you're paying attention, this game's mechanics are so fudged they aren't even consistent with themselves.
Example: Pick up a sword and shield. Approach PvP generic undead soldier who also wields sword and shield. Swing sword, he blocks, you recoil from his shield stability rating, which exceeds the weight/force of your smaller sword's swing. Undead soldier gets a free hit on you.
Then you get invaded. Undead player approaches with dagger. You think, "I'll use my shield!" No, you won't, because the mechanics for PvE combat and the mechanics for PvP combat are literally not the same.
Undead player swings dagger at your shield, hits, and reduces your stamina for taking the hit....and he keeps swinging without pause, because your shield does not recoil any attacks in pvp. Dummy, you shouldn't have bothered bringing it.
...Except you like to play both PvE and PvP...what do you do? Apparently learn the unwritten rules for the differences between PvE and PvP mechanics and conform only to character builds that thrive in both situations after hours of trying to figure out why issues like this exist without any explanation.
As a long time Souls player, I don't consider issues like this minor. I consider them at the very least enormous gripes that generate frustration and break immersion. At the most, and at the current moment, I haven't played this game in awhile because I find this sort of issue to skew my view so negatively.
To me, Dark Souls 3 feels like they superimposed the richness of lore and setting of the best of Souls onto the mechanics of a 7 year old, somewhat fleshed out, forgettable action RPG. That's exactly how it plays for me.
I love it and I hate it. Take it as you will. I hope you find this helpful.

It's hard to give an unbiased review of a Souls game, being the unabashed fan that I am, but let me try and give a short, and hopefully useful breakdown of the pros and cons of the supposedly final entry in the series.
Pros:
-Trademark breathtaking settings
-Punishing difficulty
-Variety of approaches to combat
-Beautiful yet depressing atmosphere
-Nods to previous series entries
-Sorcery is no longer ridiculously overpowered (caveat in the cons, though)
-Beautiful visual design, models, armor, weapons, and monsters
-Visual variety for Fashion Souls
-Co-op changes to matchmaking (passwords!)
-Rich story to discover rather than have fed to you
-Faster paced combat opens new possibilities and approaches
-New weapon types and abilities!
-New Covenant system is very convenient
-Final boss for first DLC is one of the most amazing fights in the series!
Cons:
-More linear than your usual Souls game
-The usual framerate stuttering in some areas
-Changes to sorcery make it significantly less viable
-Somewhat easier than other entries in the series
-A couple of segments and bosses are out and out cheap rather than difficult, which kind of breaks up the spirit of the usual hard but fair model
-Maybe no more Souls games after this!
-Invasions made more complicated by higher limit of summoned friendly phantoms
-DLC is...quite short
Fallout 4 is a legendary collection for everyonr to enjoy.

pros: good bosses, especially the humanoid. They really stepped up after designing some most memorable bosses in Bloodborne DLC. Gerat OST. Good NPCs that I care about. Some areas are memorable and within each level the maps are as awesome as ever. Nicely wrap up the trilogy and brings the story to an end, which so many series failed to do. Quite an emotional journey if you have played the previous games. Lore is still on point and introduced a lot of interesting characters that I am desperately to know more. Most importantly, it finally put an end to one of the biggest running theory in DS universe!!!
cons: combat is way too Bloodborne-ish without proper integration into Souls combat. Namely, smash r1 to victory. Too much nodding to DS1 (can be good or bad, depending on how you see it). And pvp. Don't even get started.
Biggest gripe: way too linear in terms of progression and not enough variability for replay. Instead having viable str, dex and hybrid weapons in all previous games, basically quality reigns supreme.
verdict: Definitely still worth playing and I do not regret the preorder+DLC. But it's weaker than DS1 in story and NPC, and combat-wise weaker than BB. Also, DS2 doesn't exist except for some lore reasons.

Bloodborne 2 is great.
...What was that? This is Dark Souls? Huh, I couldn't tell.
Jokes aside, this is not truly a Dark Souls game.
Don't get me wrong, and let me get this out of the way first: I really do love Dark Souls III.
The different areas of the game, though they do tend to be overbearing on hardware, are beautiful. The atmosphere of each area, including ambient noise, the backdrop, buildings and structures, and geography, tie in with one another perfectly. The controls are smooth and fluent, even on something as clunky as a keyboard and mouse.
But the game is too different from the other two to be considered on par with them as a sequel.
Let's address the elephant in the room; poise.
Hoo boy, From, did you ♥♥♥♥ up royally here.
The poise stat is described in the game as "The ability to withstand attacks without breaking form." Poise is gained by equipping armors and certain weapons and rings, with heavier armors obviously giving more poise. The poise rating can be seen in your character's status menu towards the bottom right of the page.
Now, I'll spare the lecture, because you can look up "Dark Souls 3 poise" on google and see the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that ensues for yourself. But in short, the stat is useless and currently does nothing, and digging through the game's files will reveal that there is actually a line of code turning poise's function off. Due to this fact, you can be stunlocked by literally any enemy in the game, including basic enemies like dagger-wielding hollows, dogs, and rats.
"Well, hey! At least you'll be getting more damage resistance with heavier armor!" Although this is the case, it is only marginally true. Armor comes into play in the same sense as in Dark Souls II and Bloodborne, where armor resistance gives little to no additional protection to incoming damage, to the point where a low level enemy you had problems with at the start has the potential of still giving you problems even if you return to the area with end-game gear and stats.
Any sort of build diversity has been thrown out the window due to magic following the trend of becoming increasingly worse in each game as time goes by, poise and armor in general becoming useless, and more weapons in the game that allow R1 spammers to run rampant without you being able to do anything unless you know how to parry, or they're just extremely bad at the simplest of techniques (surprise surprise, they're not).
>inb4 "git gud scrub"
Professional players like record holders, skilled streamers, and speedrunners have all claimed issues like these
On top of all this, most of the bosses are gimmicky as all hell and just have you exploiting one specific mechanic rather than needing to think your actions through and utilize skill to triumph. Even if there was a boss that needed true skill and thought to beat, the game uses a much more lenient summoning algorythm that allows a person to summon players up to 10-15 levels higher than them, rather than the absolute maximum being 5 levels higher than the host. No matter how bad a host is, they can just summon 3 higher level phantoms to steamroll through the area with zero challenge at all.
tl;dr Dark Souls III is a beautiful game with good controls, but is too easy, all armor sucks, and all build diversity outside of dex builds is gone

I pre-purchased this game a couple of months prior to the release since I was a big fan of the previous 2 soul games. After 100 hours in the game and 4 playthroughs I can say that this is my all time favorite game that I have ever played.
The game got it all. Single player, multiplayer and co-op while playing through the stoey-line, which is quite unique. You play it however you may like to play it, by your own, or with the help of others. There's a lot of different mechanics in the game and with it, it brings an incredibly enjoyable multiplayer. The invading and summoning is great, and truely makes it a souls game when you can ruin someone's hard work by outplaying them. It makes the game unpredictable, which I find lacking in a lot of todays story-line focused games. But Dark souls does this perfectly.
I believe this is the only game that I've actually felt was truely worth $60. Even though the game in itself is incredible, it also brings a fantastic community with it. Subreddits and other forums which discussed the different mechanics behind every weapon, and all the videos about PvP'ing makes for a great experience.
If there's any game I would truely recommend out of all of the 120 games that I own, this is probably my top recommendation.

It's hard to give an unbiased review of a Souls game, being the unabashed fan that I am, but let me try and give a short, and hopefully useful breakdown of the pros and cons of the supposedly final entry in the series.
Pros:
-Trademark breathtaking settings
-Punishing difficulty
-Variety of approaches to combat
-Beautiful yet depressing atmosphere
-Nods to previous series entries
-Sorcery is no longer ridiculously overpowered (caveat in the cons, though)
-Beautiful visual design, models, armor, weapons, and monsters
-Visual variety for Fashion Souls
-Co-op changes to matchmaking (passwords!)
-Rich story to discover rather than have fed to you
-Faster paced combat opens new possibilities and approaches
-New weapon types and abilities!
-New Covenant system is very convenient
-Final boss for first DLC is one of the most amazing fights in the series!
Cons:
-More linear than your usual Souls game
-The usual framerate stuttering in some areas
-Changes to sorcery make it significantly less viable
-Somewhat easier than other entries in the series
-A couple of segments and bosses are out and out cheap rather than difficult, which kind of breaks up the spirit of the usual hard but fair model
-Maybe no more Souls games after this!
-Invasions made more complicated by higher limit of summoned friendly phantoms
-DLC is...quite short
Took some time to get into Fallout 4, but loving it now I am. The ability to upgrade weapons and armor is a good addition, but the settlements can be a pain to manage.

pros: good bosses, especially the humanoid. They really stepped up after designing some most memorable bosses in Bloodborne DLC. Gerat OST. Good NPCs that I care about. Some areas are memorable and within each level the maps are as awesome as ever. Nicely wrap up the trilogy and brings the story to an end, which so many series failed to do. Quite an emotional journey if you have played the previous games. Lore is still on point and introduced a lot of interesting characters that I am desperately to know more. Most importantly, it finally put an end to one of the biggest running theory in DS universe!!!
cons: combat is way too Bloodborne-ish without proper integration into Souls combat. Namely, smash r1 to victory. Too much nodding to DS1 (can be good or bad, depending on how you see it). And pvp. Don't even get started.
Biggest gripe: way too linear in terms of progression and not enough variability for replay. Instead having viable str, dex and hybrid weapons in all previous games, basically quality reigns supreme.
verdict: Definitely still worth playing and I do not regret the preorder+DLC. But it's weaker than DS1 in story and NPC, and combat-wise weaker than BB. Also, DS2 doesn't exist except for some lore reasons.

Dark souls 3 is the first souls game i played, and my personal favorite game of all time. I honestly think i have no nostaligia bias since I played ds1 and 2 after i completed this game. Albeit, I realize that this game would be even better if you are familiar with the previous games lore and atmospheres, since there is tons of fan service (which is not a bad thing for the most part.) If you are a fan of the souls series, there is no doubt you will love atleast the PVE aspects of this game. I think this entry to the series really takes the cake in boss design, world design, asthetics, soundrack, and combat in general. Yes, it is more linear than the previous games, but that isnt a big gripe for me atleast. The combat style is more like bloodborne than previous souls game, its faster paced and it rewards a more aggresive playstyle. The balance isn't perfect, but it never is in a souls game. heavier weapons aren't as powerful and lighter ones for PVE, and sorcery still isn't good (I think pyromancy is in PVP and PVE, but im the minority in saying this) But I do like the FP bar system alot better than spell casts, and the ability to choose how many health estuses you want and how many FP estuses you want. It allows for a little but more variety and customization to you build. Since this is a souls game though, everything is still viable, and you can overcome anything in this game with any weapon, but some are stronger than others. 1 thing for certain I dont really like is the elemental infusions (Fire weapons, Lightning, Dark, Blessed, Ect.) Most of them seem to nerf the damage in almost every scenario, since most enemies are more weak tp physical damage than elemental. Its pretty much better to buff with resin always. The infusions that affect the scaling in terms of strength, dex and luck (Strong, Refined, Sharp, and Hollow gems) are all viable, and reccomended I believe depending on what you are putting levels into. I also like the new idea of pine bundles, that give you a stronger, quickly enabled buff that only lasts a few seconds. It adds an ability to buff during a boss fight or catch an opponenent off guard. The addition of weapons arts is really hit or miss depending on what the weapon is. Many weapons have unique and useful weapon arts, while some weapons just share a rather boring weapon art throughout most of thhe non unipue weapons in its class (IE: straightswords have the same or similar weapon arts, aside from the more unique ones) But, in my opinion, dark souls 3 have the most fluid and engaging comat that isnt clunky like the previous games.
This game ties up the lore and gives an option of an ending that doesnt link the fire or not link it. Its a secret ending that allows you to break the cycle of relinking the fire that has been occuring since gwyn first did it himself. It is the true ending to the game, if you will. This game explains alot of lore from previous games, and also comes jam packed with its own, and its fascinating. There is tons of fan service and many callbacks and things from the previous games. Its basically like a love letter to souls fans. This is a big reason why I think this is such an amazing game. It was my first souls game and I still loved every bit of it. Im sure I would have loved my first playthrough even more if I had some experience with the previous games.
Along with this, there are various NPC questlines that are great and can heavily affect the state of your world and that specific playthrough. Also questlines can affect what ending you can achieve (There are 4 unique endings)
I do think this is the best souls game from software has made. (I have not played Bloodborne or demon's souls yet, if you wish to count those). If there is one gripe I have and many others have, its PVP. The biggest issue is invasions prioritize players that have summons in their world. It is rare to find 1v1 invasions, they are usually 1v3 atleast. This makes it extremely hard to actually kill the host, because of this games faster estus system and rolls taking less stamina than previous games, allowing for easy spam rolling if you are in trouble. Yeah, invasions kinda suck, and im hoping from software can realize this and fix it. I hear alot of people saying that PVP in general sucks, but i dont see why. A common argument is that straight sword = OP and other weapons arent viable. From my experience with PVP (Which isnt a ton, but atleast 10 hours) trying many different weapons, many different weapons have various movesets you can use to your advantage. I understand why the biggest gripe of this game is PVP, but i still love duels and fight clubs and they are extremely easy to find. There are tons of players to do PVP with, and winning duels can get you the covenent rewards, if the constant 1v3 invades arent working.
In conclusion, I think that if you played and enjoyed the other souls games, then you will love this game. If you loved bloodborne, then you will love this game. This game basically fixed everything wrong that ds2 did. It brings back a full, vibrant world that feels occupied and not boringly designed. Theres always something going on and something to look at, which just isnt the case in ds2. I think everybody should play this game, and it lives up to the expectations set by previous souls games, and its a fantastic game on its own. I think this game is easier to get into then the previous titles, but im not sure why. Anyways, buy this game if you havent, its a masterpiece, miyazaki has outdone himself once again.
PS: many people say poise doesnt exist, but it does, it just works different in this game due to the different pace of combat. Yes its weird and there is surely an argument that its bad, but it exists.

The Fallout series is incredible. Since Bethesda took over the series, their open world sandboxes have become one of my favorite game types. Fallout 4 is a beautiful game and one of the greater parts of their lineup. That said, they followed a Bethesda trend in making their level up system simpler, the problem here is that it takes away from the purpose and experience of perks. Instead of gradually earning greater skill through use of objects (a bethesda staple from Morrowind to Skyrim) you instead earn experience and spend it as you please. So, to advance with a gun you have to spend one of your rare perks on gun category, to pick locks and hack computers, same problem.
Beyond this idiotic switch I'd have to say I still quite enjoyed the game. The story mode, if you play it straight through is a bit shorter than previous games, but its fun and entertaining nonethelss, and its always been the story told by the environment that I found truly entertaining. The Commonwealth is vast, though I've heard some complain its smaller than others in the series, I still find myself exploring new ruins and finding new secrets and pieces of lore.
The new features in crafting settlements and changes in upgrading equipment are fun but relatively monotonous and without much definite purpose. Armor upgrades aren't powerfull enough to cause much difference, weapon upgrades, while some are powerful, mostly just served to take away from actual loot variety. The settlement systems revolving quests are fine but they aren't verry engaging, just the same things over and over with little reward.
In all I give Fallout 4 a positive review still, its flaws, while a little dumb if you hold them up against their predacessors are small in the grand scheme of things. the game is still a refreshing play, different from other entreies into the AAA lineup in that it doesn't conform to industry standards, it made its sacrifices in the name of progress. I can't wait to get back to it and even more, to see what the fallout series has in store for us in the future.
8.5/10

I've wasted almost 2 months of my life playing this game as of now. It's fun, it's challenging, it's a new experience every time you start a new journey. Nothing restricts you, the player, from being a certain type of character. If you want to play as a heavy-hitting tank, you can do that. If you want to play as a light-weight mage, you can do that. If you want to play as an archer, you can do that. There is little to no restriction to what type of character you can play as. Each boss, each area is a puzzle. You need to use your limited resources (your healing, your mana, your items) and your head to make your way from area to area, one safepoint to the next, without dying to various foes. If you make a mistake, you are punished. The punishment is a more brute way of teaching the player to be careful, and to learn from their mistake.
After playing a Souls game, in my experience, games like Legend of Zelda seem less difficult and are easier to breeze through. I believe playing a Souls game helps the player grow in skill.
I give this game a 9.5/10.
