Having 100%'ed this game now I feel this is a good time for a review.
TL;DR:
Overall, this game is honestly the best game I've played this year. It's better than the games I played last year too - and it managed to pull me away from Overwatch for basically 3 weeks straight, and I'm still not finished with it, even after 280+ hours.
Very highly recommended, even for newcomers to the series. In fact,
for newcomers to the series, as this game is probably your best way in to what is most definitely one of the best damn game series ever created.
Long(er) version:
Dark Souls 3 is the first Souls game I played that I actually enjoyed - I own Dark Souls 1 & 2, and neither of those immediately grabbed me like Dark Souls 3 did. I didn't have to try nearly as hard to start enjoying DS3 as I did the other two games in the series.
Because of this, if you are a newcomer to the Souls series, I would highly recommend you play this game first to get a feel for the controls and playstyle of the game, then after completing it, go back and play the older games, which is what I am doing now.
As for DS3 itself, I haven't played a game this captivating, both inside and outside the game, in years. The last time a game occupied my everyday thoughts this much was many years ago, back on my old PS3 days with Battlefield 3. I played DS3 for a couple of hours to begin with, and made fair progress. But - the moment I beat the 1st real boss you face, after the "tutorial" boss, I was hooked.
Every time I put my controller down I was immediately thinking what I was going to do next when I played again. I put 60 hours into this game in my first 2 weeks of owning it - whilst also working full time. Like I said, I haven't played a game that captured me this much in years.
The combat system is intuitive, fluid and feels fantastic to play at 60fps. The hitboxes are awesome - a simple search on youtube will reveal to you just how good they are.
The rolling thresholds are gone from the old games, so now you can "fast" roll at 70% equpid load, rather than the 16% from Dark Souls 1.
The graphics are fantastic and very well themed - playing on an Nvidia 770 4GB I can run this game at a solid 60 on high. Walking through one of the later areas of the game that is lit with moonlight looks stunning - you'll know which area I mean when you get there!
The story continues from the previous 2 games, and is as deep and fascinating as ever. You can skip the story completely, by not reading item descriptions and skipping the NPC dialogue. But, if you pay attention and spend some time every now and again reading a few things, you'll quickly become immersed in this game (and series') amazingly deep and thorough story. If anything, I recommend you play the older games just to learn the origins of the some of the bosses and items you find in this game. If not, there are many lore videos on youtube, all worth a watch.
The PvP is... Well, its Dark Souls, so very competitive and sometimes kinda toxic. There is an established meta Soul Level you can stop levelling once you reach - it is at this level you will experience the most varied and plentiful PvP. Invasions are broken, with the invader being at a huge disadvantage, but these can still be fun from time to time, if you get lucky and invade a good host. If you're looking for good, fair PvP, look up honour duels for this game and try some summoning rather than invading - I enjoy honor duels substantially more than invasions, but it all comes down to what type of a PvP experience you are looking for. Poise is
"
", so be careful when using super slow weapons in PvP as enemies with faster weapons will very easily stagger you and get you in a stun lock - not fun at all.
The weapons are varied enough to keep you busy for a long time, if you want to learn and use each. Some weapons that were very good from previous games have been completely borked, but there are many other awesome alternatives you can use that are equally as fun. The armor is good with many blast-from-the-pasts from previous games, allowing you to cosplay as your favourite bosses or make some hideous monstrosity wearing only a loincloth giant fat armor.
Character creation and customisation is also improved from previous games, allowing you to tweak your character to fairly deep measures.
The music - oh man the music. Give the composer a Grammy, please. The boss fights in this game are awesome as they are (well, most anyway..), but the music really takes them to the next level. The music in the forefront of my mind is the track that accompanies the first Lord of Cinder you fight, but all of the tracks are amazing in their own right and perfectly accompany an already fantastic game.
Overall, this game is honestly the best game I've played this year. It's better than the games I played last year too - and it managed to pull me away from Overwatch for basically 3 weeks straight.
Very highly recommended, even for newcomers to the series. In fact,
for newcomers to the series, as this game is your best way in to what is probably one of the best damn game series ever created.

I've heard horror stories from other people that have played the previous two games, but I also witnessed the joy they experienced when they finally defeated that one boss that had wrecked them 15+ times. Dark Souls 3 is a fantastic ending to one of the best action RPG series ever made. A lot of the issues that hardcore fans had of DS2 have been successfully resolved, and Miyazaki again shows how brilliant a game creator he is.
Pros:
1. Bosses. This is the most important thing in this series. The bosses in DS3 are brilliant in every way. The bosses feel so creative in how diverse they are. You have some who are your standards slow, but strong; then there are some who are fast and agility, which Miyazaki obviously took from Bloodborne. Bosses like The Dancer are so different from any other we've had in the Soul's series before.
2. Combat. While the Souls combat doesn't change too much from title to title, in DS3 it is much more responsive and quick. My biggest issues with DS1 was how sluggish your movements were. But you move to fluidly this time around. The biggest change to combat is the magic system. It resembles that of Demon's Souls in that you have a mana bar now, instead of a finite amount of spell uses. It allows for better managing of your spells in my opinion.
3. The world. Oh my god, the world in DS3 is unlike anything we've seen before. Time is basically collapsing upon itself, and so you have locations and people from Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 1, and Dark Souls 2 appearing in the game. Its absolutely incredible. Its the biggest nostalgic trip I've ever seen in a game. And they don't just throw all this in just to appease fans. When you delve into the lore, you find out why all of this is happening. Another great thing DS3 does is bring back the connected world. While the Firelink Shrine is a hub world, the rest of the world fits together so perfectly. Don't get me wrong, its still nowhere near as good as the connected world in Dark Souls 1, but its light years above Dark Souls 2.
4. Music. The music in this game is unbelievable. Dark Souls has always had some of the best music in games, but DS3 takes it to a new level. Take the Abyss Watchers fight; you start off with a nice tempo, but once it hits stage two of the fight, when the boss powers up with fire, the music just goes crazy and it matches the movements of the Abyss Watcher so perfectly. The best music in the game though is in stage two of the final boss. I would never spoil it, but when you hear it, any DS1 fan will lose their mind.
Cons:
1. Poise. I don't whose idea it was to change poise so drastically, but they need to be fired. Poise used to let you stand your ground while being a heavy character, now it basically just lets you have more invincibility frames while rolling. Its pointless, especially if you're a heavy character who can only fat roll.
Overall, DS3 is the best way to end the series. While there is DLC coming, which will likely finish out the story, the main game is just the perfect ending for such an amazing game series. If you're a fan of the series and haven't played it yet, I can't recommend this game enough.

Dark Souls III is the pivotal Dark Souls experience for seasoned veterans and new comers alike. With its minimalist story and timing focused combat, Dark Souls is back and is as brutal as ever.


Dark Souls III establishes beautiful artistic design and relatively low requirements to create a stunning atmosphere. Whether I was making my way through a lonely snow laden valley, or a grimy Undead Village, It all looked great. I loved the returning theme of seeing a distant location on the horizon only to find myself there hours later. Dark Souls III really presents itself well, and I had absolutely no graphical issues with my rig.

Dark Souls games always have had minimal plot development. Dark Souls III is no different. I personally love the minimalist plot, and I urge any gamer who is unsure to try it. The Story really unfolds with extra dialogue from NPCs and through various item descriptions. The Story is best understood through the lore of the land. By learning the various secrets and stories of Lodran, the story of your character will become clearer.

Dark Souls III brings back the hit-and-run tactics of its predecessors, but adds plenty of new additions that work. The basics are the same; blocking and rolling must be timed perfectly to execute properly. Attacks must be planned, enemies patterns mastered, and proper items all come into play. The "Tough but Fair" difficulty is ever present. One slip up can lead to a grisly demise.
A huge new edition is the FP bar. The FP bar is a separate blue bar placed on your HUD that dictates your ability to use magic and special abilities. Every spell or special ability uses some FP, and the only way to regain FP is to drink from the new Ashen Estus Flask. Since Ashen Estus Flasks can only be obtained by trading in normal Estus Flasks the player is forced to make a choice. More HP or more FP?

Dark Souls III is an expansive experience that can easily eat more than 60 hours on a first play through. But most gamers will find themselves coming back to Lodran time and time again. Experimenting with new characters, weapons, play styles and more. Dark Souls III and its DLC are worth every penny, even more so if they are on sale!

With nearly 200 hours into the game, I think it's safe to say that I have a general feel on what I think of the game. Since I have 200 hours in, you'd think that I enjoy this installment quite a bit, and I can say that I did, AT FIRST.
This of course changed after completing my first playthrough, roughly 60 hours into the game. The game, unlike pretty much every installment in the franchise, gets stale after the first playthrough -- not only is there a lack of incentive to enter NG+, but the actual new games and onward are very dissapointing, adding nothing but new upgraded rings. It's a far cry from the brilliant new game experience of the second game, which not only added these upgraded rings, but also changed enemy placement and added new enemies in general (making NG+ feel like an actual new game).
This leads to my next point; Dark Souls III takes heavy inspiration from the first game in the franchise (along with Bloodborne, which I have yet to play). With inspiration can come dependence, and thus, fan service aplenty. This fan service was present in pretty much every aspect of the game, including the story, equipment, environments, etc... It almost made me mad in some parts when I saw blatant references and the like when I was playing through, and in hindsight, nearly half of the game was content that had already been used or covered before in past installments (Dark Souls I in particular -- there was nearly no Dark Souls II fanservice or acknowledgement whatsoever).
Now for my major criticism -- weapon variety. At first glance, one might think that there are a great amount of unique weapons in this game, based off of all of the different weapon types and different backgrounds to certain weapons within these categories. Bully for me (and many others as well), when I learned that there were next to no differences between most of these weapons. Each spear was the same, each dagger was the same, each thrusting sword was the same... You get the idea. The only weapons that had unique properties to them were boss weapons, or weapons wielded by NPCs in the game (and most of these weapons weren't even that good, since they can't be infused or buffed, and generally have unsatisfactory AR). They may have had unique movesets, being the only real catch to using these weapons, but it isn't really worth that much, considering the player can just equip a short sword or thrusting sword and easy mode the game (PvP included). There are really only two viable weapon classes in this game, regardless of all the patching that was made to "nerf" these weapons.
This lack of weapon variety translates into stale PvP, which is what gives these games longevity (at least, in the past). Couple that with a poor matchmaking system, terrible network connectivity, unbalanced rolling, lack of working mechanics (which work as intended, if you know what I mean), and abundance of overpowered mechanics (bleed says hello, and poison says goodbye).
Here are my overall, brief reflections on the game, so you can see how I would rank this game:
PROS:
- Fast-paced combat
- Mostly excellent bosses
- Beautiful character and environmental art
- Slightly primitive but nice graphic fidelity
- Really nicely implemented difficulty curve (the best in the franchise)
- Nice progression (story and gameplay wise) and pacing
- Fashion Souls is as good as ever (although not as great as Dark Souls II's fashion)
- Great level design by area in most cases
- Very atmospheric and mood-setting
- Cool lore (in most cases)
CONS:
- Very limited weapon variety (lack of viable weapons)
- Abundant fan service
- Poor matchmaking and connectivity
- Lack of replay value
- Unbalanced game mechanics in some cases
- Lack of game mechanics in some cases
- Linear, boring world design
- Certain useless Weapon Arts
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who has played any of the past games -- I'm sure that you would still like it. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoy the game, but I do honestly think that it's the worst in the franchise.

TL TR: 10/10 but only with mods, without mods and as of this day of this review  6/10
Regardless of age, this game's amazing community has created some of the best mods to the point where it stands on par with any new triple A release. Without the mods though, this game does feel dated with its visuals and awkward controls. (which can be fixed with the help of mods)

A fair warning, Modding this game does require a bit of learning which might be intimidating. There are many easy to follow guides online/youtube that will walk you step by step though.
The Review:
Note: This review is based off of the stock game, no mods used. Also for mods, you have to play offline of steam with a different EXE thats not connected to Steam, My real playtime hours should be close to 300 hours.
I have logged countless hours into this game and surprisingly still discovering new things about the lore/world
Pros:
-how flexible this game can adapt to any FPS playing style. Run n Gun, sharpshooting, or even a sneaky melee only character, this game not only rewards you but encourges any playing style.
-Linear quests and as well an impressive amount of side quests (but different outcomes) with many ways on tackling it. Linear is a goodthing for such a giant world to keep you away from feeling overwhelmed.
-Branching Storylines with well written backgrounds and reasonings to make the player feel conflicted on choices.
-Many unique weapons, weapon attachments, and outfits to spice things up along the way.
-Best companions in all of Fallout series, a good balance of charming damaged people who have sometime of score to settle, either with others or with their own personal demons. Also you can decide how they will face those stuggles.
CONS:
-Buggy, also some quests can be faulty by pure chance so save often. (There is a single mod that connects all of this)
-Dated Visuals/ limited voice actors/ NPCs ugly and sometimes recycled.
From the screenshots, there game looks like a public restroom, you will hear the same 12 voice actors doing everyline in this game without even changing up their accents or nothing. The NPCs all look fairly similar with one another. (theres mods to make every NPC update and as well unique)
-Awkward Gunplay
Some guns feel a bit too light for my liking, Enemy movement looks unnatural, it likes they are skating on ice which messes up your aim, weapons are too focus on stats which forces you to change different weapons has you level up. Personally I became attached to pistols in the game but had a hardtime sticking with some of them at higher levels. This is odd for a game that encourges you to create your own gameplay style.
-You will become overpowered midway into the game.
If you know what you are doing, it is possible to be OP at level 14 out of 50 (which was the case for me) and I only did around 15 side quests. The problem about being OP in this game is that it breaks the lore of surviving in a harsh wasteland. It will get to the point where quest become chours to do since there is no more real reward other than advancing the story.  The most fun you will have is in the first 10 levels. (there are mods that balances this issue and as well make all weapons dangerous to keep your OP character grounded)
-This world feels very lonely, even with a companion.
This massive world is mostly in the desert, and as you can imagine...sand..and more sand. The towns have great lore to them but the actual presenation will make you feel like you just been catfished. NPCs will boost about the great Vegas Strip but in reality its only around 6 buildings within 2 blocks. Even with fast travel, when you have to make a trip to anywhere, you will be reminded on how dull everything really is due to the lack of activtity in the world. (there are mods to help bring life into the world but personally for me, it still felt a bit dull at times.)
If you need a recommendation of a mod, look up A Tale of Two Wastelands, this mod combines both Fallout 3 and New Vegas into a single game. There are many step by step guides on installing this mod out there.
Rating 10/10

Fanservice Souls III is a game where you are tasked with bringing a bunch of old dudes to their jumbo Lazyboy chairs, so that the barbecue may commence. Along the way you fight a bunch of skrublords, become bros with a vegetable, get staggered by a rat even when wearing armor made of stone, see a cheater roleplaying as an attack helicopter, black crystal out of a gank squad's world, and express admiration of the star around which the earth orbits. Dating simulators don't get much better than this.

-----------------------------------------------
+Combat is faster and smoother (though I still prefer DS1's slower speed and weightier feel)
+Incredible soundtrack, some of the best music in the whole Dark Souls trilogy (I'm glad I preordered to get the OST for free)
+Co-op is the best it's ever been, password feature makes connecting with friends insanely easy (you can even co-op with higher SL friends)
+Weapon arts, while not every weapon has a different attack/ability, is a welcome addition (also strong attacks can be charged)
+New Focus Bar for magic is awesome, choosing whether to keep your estus upgrades in your HP healing one or new blue FP restoring one adds a fair amount of depth (and since weapon arts use FP, it give an incentive for melee players to level Attunement)
+Great level design, well paced, lots of cleverly hidden secrets (though somewhat predictable for Souls vets)
+Bosses are good overall, plenty of outstanding and challenging fights (final boss is awesomesauce)
+Keyboard & Mouse controls are finally good (though sadly no keyboard button icons)
-Too much fanservice, not to mention some of it barely makes sense
-It might be because I'm a veteran, but Dark Souls III is the shortest in the series, taking just over 20 hours to beat the first time, and that's when you take the time to go everywhere
-Despite the great level design, the world itself is very linear, lacking the interconnection of DS1

-Invasions suck, way too many disadvantages for the invader, 7/10 times the host has at least one phantom
-Covenants are underwhelming, there's 2 pairs of covenants that are exactly the same, the other pair's only difference is the areas
-Armor cannot be upgraded, which is a shame because I was hoping they would add the ability to infuse armors with different elements
-The weapon durability system is the same as DS2's, rest at a bonfire to restore durability, only difference is weapons take FOREVER to break, making repair powder useless
-The anticheat system is terrible, at launch innocent players were getting banned, and even though it improved since then, some players are still getting warning messages for no reason
-While not surprising because of the above con, there's a fair amount of cheaters in PVP, takes a while for one to get banned, if at all
-While the PC port is mostly good, the graphical options barely make a difference in terms of performance
=Some enemies like the Pus of Man rely too much on brute force to kill rather than rewarding strategy and patience
=TOO MANY GOSHDANG MIMICS
=Jailers are the most annoying thing to ever exist
=Weapon balance is a heck of a lot better than it was at launch, but some weapons still need buffs or nerfs
="Does not open from this side"
=
=Fat armors still have model clipping issues more awkward than a baby kangaroo painting the end of the world on sandpaper while handstanding on a moped
-----------------------------------------------
Overall, Dark Souls III is an outstanding game, a fitting end to a fantastic series, and a must-have for Dark Souls fans or people who like rewarding RPGs. While it did get quite a few things wrong, the aspects it did right immensely outweigh the negatives.

Fanservice Souls III is a game where you are tasked with bringing a bunch of old dudes to their jumbo Lazyboy chairs, so that the barbecue may commence. Along the way you fight a bunch of skrublords, become bros with a vegetable, get staggered by a rat even when wearing armor made of stone, see a cheater roleplaying as an attack helicopter, black crystal out of a gank squad's world, and express admiration of the star around which the earth orbits. Dating simulators don't get much better than this.

-----------------------------------------------
+Combat is faster and smoother (though I still prefer DS1's slower speed and weightier feel)
+Incredible soundtrack, some of the best music in the whole Dark Souls trilogy (I'm glad I preordered to get the OST for free)
+Co-op is the best it's ever been, password feature makes connecting with friends insanely easy (you can even co-op with higher SL friends)
+Weapon arts, while not every weapon has a different attack/ability, is a welcome addition (also strong attacks can be charged)
+New Focus Bar for magic is awesome, choosing whether to keep your estus upgrades in your HP healing one or new blue FP restoring one adds a fair amount of depth (and since weapon arts use FP, it give an incentive for melee players to level Attunement)
+Great level design, well paced, lots of cleverly hidden secrets (though somewhat predictable for Souls vets)
+Bosses are good overall, plenty of outstanding and challenging fights (final boss is awesomesauce)
+Keyboard & Mouse controls are finally good (though sadly no keyboard button icons)
-Too much fanservice, not to mention some of it barely makes sense
-It might be because I'm a veteran, but Dark Souls III is the shortest in the series, taking just over 20 hours to beat the first time, and that's when you take the time to go everywhere
-Despite the great level design, the world itself is very linear, lacking the interconnection of DS1

-Invasions suck, way too many disadvantages for the invader, 7/10 times the host has at least one phantom
-Covenants are underwhelming, there's 2 pairs of covenants that are exactly the same, the other pair's only difference is the areas
-Armor cannot be upgraded, which is a shame because I was hoping they would add the ability to infuse armors with different elements
-The weapon durability system is the same as DS2's, rest at a bonfire to restore durability, only difference is weapons take FOREVER to break, making repair powder useless
-The anticheat system is terrible, at launch innocent players were getting banned, and even though it improved since then, some players are still getting warning messages for no reason
-While not surprising because of the above con, there's a fair amount of cheaters in PVP, takes a while for one to get banned, if at all
-While the PC port is mostly good, the graphical options barely make a difference in terms of performance
=Some enemies like the Pus of Man rely too much on brute force to kill rather than rewarding strategy and patience
=TOO MANY GOSHDANG MIMICS
=Jailers are the most annoying thing to ever exist
=Weapon balance is a heck of a lot better than it was at launch, but some weapons still need buffs or nerfs
="Does not open from this side"
=
=Fat armors still have model clipping issues more awkward than a baby kangaroo painting the end of the world on sandpaper while handstanding on a moped

Overall, Dark Souls III is an outstanding game, a fitting end to a fantastic series, and a must-have for Dark Souls fans or people who like rewarding RPGs. While it did get quite a few things wrong, the aspects it did right immensely outweigh the negatives.

Please note, this review is the BASE GAME ONLY- I have purchased but not yet explored the DLC.
Like many other people, I was not a huge fan of the main quest. The first half of it or so is great- I couldn't help tunnel-visioning my way through it, desperately trying to see what happens next. The second half, when the quest starts to branch is where it stops being so "omg what happens next!?" and starts being more "really? these are my only options?" I guess the hopeless feeling of "there's no good choice here" does sort of fit the hopeless-wasteland-future narrative, but it really made me feel almost powerless as a player. Three of the four main factions can be summed up with "yeah, we do bad things, but the end totally justifies the means," and the fourth is centered around repeatable quests that consist of "go to x, kill y, use workshop, repeat." Again, it does fit the setting, but it made the RPG aspect of the game seem almost disappointing having to choose between siding with one of three homicidal factions or lolrampage-obliterating said three factions and resigning yourself to playing "The Sims: Wasteland edition."
That being said, this is Fallout. There is so much more to this game than just the main quest. The main quest *is* worth playing the game for- at least once, anyway- but the real gem of Fallout 4 is the open-world I've always loved. There are so many random events you encounter while wandering the wasteland, and so many sidequests, nooks and crannies to explore, all set in the deadly unforgiving post-nuclear-war wasteland we've come to love. There are a wide variety of companions to befriend- some you can even romance- who offer commentary on your current location/battle/choices. You can even adjust the difficulty to make the wasteland just the right amount of unforgiving. I'm over 100 hours in, and I haven't come close to exploring everything. My only real gripe with the wasteland is with the random spawning of enemies. Yes, this absolutely keeps the game from getting stale. However, when a deathclaw just happens to spawn in an area you have to go through for an early-game quest (no, I'm not talking about the first deathclaw you ALWAYS see), it really does feel like you got ♥♥♥♥ed by RNGesus.
TLDR:
9/10 Overall. War never changes. This game is definitely worth buying and playing if you are at all interested in a post-nuclear-war setting.
7/10 Main quest. The main quest is a rollercoaster of "omg what next?!" and "meh whatever" but still worth playing at least once.
9.75/10 Wasteland. Expansive, dangerous open world full of locks to pick, terminals to hack, people to manipulate, things to collect, places to explore, Deathclaws to rip you in half, radiation to melt your face, companions to bond with, and plenty of enemies to blow apart with lasers, bullets, missles, and mininukes.

For once, I'm not really sure what to say. I just loved it.

While I do have my Ups and Downs regarding the game let me start by getting the CONS out of the way.
- Third Game in the series that should of been fine tuned and bug fixed far before release.
- Poise; the most arguable of problems by definition, does NOT work as intended.
- Spamming basic attacks is honestly the way to clear the entire game rather than think critically and measure your swings in any fight.  This INCLUDES PvP.
- The scaling of difficulty with additional phantoms is sub par and should include more black spirit enemies or even higher invasion rates.
- There is no real point in being a white mad phantom other than to troll everyone.  Needs incentive for being summoned and killing enemies AND/or The Host/Phantoms present.
- NG+ rings and Lackluster difficulty change in game enemies item locations etc.
- Estus is difficult to punish due to it's near instant animation and ability to move at walking pace rather than slow walk pace.
- Unlimited summoning; limit summons based on a timer cooldown after two that starts when the first one dies.  about 5 minutes to summon a new phantom once that expires.  Stop the suicide spooky squad.
-Physical Infusions are the only way to really go unless you're recharging FP or HP with them equipped.
-Vitality is an underwhelming stat that essentially is only used to prevent fat rolling for a fashionable armor set and weapon allotment.
Pros
- The game is STILL very pretty.
- Veteran players still found themselves dying despite that it's technically easier than the previous games.
- Weapon arts, dual wielding; powerstance is missed but can be dealt with from Dark Souls II
- Password Matchmaking:  Hey i don't have to make a character to be in your range now!
- Newer armor sets and some returning old ones.
- THE RED EYE ORB RETURNETH!
- You can be a Blue Cop as early as Crucifixion Woods and help the newcomers against invaders... and it's not entirely useless
- Damage types against enemies can matter tremendously so the "know your enemy" aspect makes being a smart Ashen One a boon in a world with things not equally weak to others.
- The Passion for the Fashion is a fire that will never die given the Piecemealing of Sets.
- Bows are pretty neat now. (CROSSBOWS NEED TUMBLE SHOOTING.)
- I can bash with a greatshield for respectable damage. (i need a spiked one now)
- Matchmaking is as balanced as it's gonna get based on weapon and SL respectively.
- Rope Firebombs.
- Resins for everything.
- Double, triple, quad buffer detected? Duel Charm it off.

Believe it or not, this is the second Souls game that I've played (Bloodbourne was my first but we can debate about that some other time). I tried DS2 but the port for the controller was horrible. I thought this was going to have a horrible port too but I was wrong; I was able to play as if I was playing in a console except with better FPS (as long as you have the specs). This game has gained a lot of patches and balancing updates since release, so I can safely say that you won't find much bugs and OP weapons anymore. FromSoftware keeps this game updated, and remember that the first DLC is going to come up some time this Fall.
I've finished the game three time using three different builds. In other words, this game has a LOT of replayability factor because of one main reason: the variety of builds you can use. Once you get bored of PVE, there's always PVP. You will meet a lot of folks wether they be nice or not, it's all fun.
The soundtracks are amazing. All boss fights will be etched to your mind by their signature soundtracks. Just starting from the main menu alone, you know you'll have eargasms all throughout a playthrough.
For the story, I missed out on a lot of hype regarding the lore when I finished this game. It seems you really need to finish DS1 if you want to have a greater feeling of attachment towards the story, but other than that you'll be able to play the game and still understasnd it just fine.
9/10 overall because the gameplay, story, and sountracks are superb, but the DLCs haven't arrived yet. I'm sure this will be a 10/10 once they do.

You start as a worthless dead being that is not even worth setting on fire to preserve the dying world. You set out to go through lost kingdoms, forbidden places and fight unspeakable beings. It is a journey of a game, and it has plenty of places to explore, a large variety of enemies, characters with distinct personalities and motives, and abilities you can use to your liking creating a playstyle that truly fits you.
If you are looking for multiplayer experience then you will have the opportunity to help other players, or invade them or simultaneously both at the same time. There are various in-game groups that will give you motivation via a simple reward system (per assist or per kill, depending on the group) that will give you a currency item, and you will be able to exchange it for something as you level up with that group by offering the currency to it.
I feel that it has the best online community right now, as people are not aggressive in-game, rarely you get to hear someone being angry, frustrated, and generally being an idiot with an attitude. Some players with a microphone (it is optional to enable as a feature) and the subreddit, and wiki on fextralife are full of information, and discussion about the game, from the mechanics to the lore and features.
On the subreddit specifically there's also presence of Namco's community manager, so you can get to know things almost directly from the developers through the community manager. This is a huge plus for me, since I've been a fan of Bungie for a while, since their Halo days where they kept a close tie with their community.
This game will offer you an experience; it will be a challenge in many places, and in others it will be easy fully depending on your playstyle, and ability to adapt quickly to the variety of location and enemies.

I like the game, there is no denying that, especially since I’m close to finishing my fourth playthorugh, yet I can’t be ignorant just because of that. The greatness of every component that makes Dark Souls III is crippled by its poor technical execution and I’m afraid this is a result of the fans’ and journalists’ attitude towards the game. Praising without questioning has given the developers a free pass with the end result being countless bugs and problems that went unfixed throughout an entire series making their way into its finale.
Dark Souls III is a good game that combines most of the great elements of its predecessors into one final blow. The impact of the finale is subject to each gamer perception towards the series. In my case, I said that the best way to improve on the series is to find the balance between its two predecessors while focusing on fixing the problems of the past and Dark Souls III did only half of that. How important each half is? I guess the time spent playing the game can be interpreted as an answer to that.

Generally, the worst thing that can happen to a games series is to run out of ideas and to continue going on only as a revenue maker (Assassin’s Creed?!). If Dark Souls III is the last game of the Souls series, then it is a worthy finale, one that goes out with a boom. It changes just enough in terms of mechanics to make the gameplay feel more fluid and refined, while offering the best collection of bosses that sprawl some amazingly designed areas. Although its world may not be as meticulously built as the one of the first game and the future of its online component is uncertain as of now, it is a hell of an experience that kept me addicted for two weeks straight and offered more than enough quality content to leave me satisfied. Despite enjoying it a lot more than Dark Souls II, it hasn’t managed to impress me as much as the first one did, but that’s perhaps because it was my first Souls experience.
On an ending note, I can’t wait to see what From Software will do with the DLCs (expect reviews for those as well!), as in all previous cases they have surpassed the vanilla game experience. What’s more, I’m excited for the possibility of new Souls-based games in different settings that are built on the same design principles.

A challenging experience that gives you the ability to choose how you want to progress through the game. With a variety of classes and gear, online multiplayer and PVP, and a conclusive story, this game is a fanatastic send-off to a fan-favorite franchise.
The story is left for you to uncover and has you choose how you want to progress in the game. The map feels singular as everything is connected and is crafted in a way to be semi-linear to ensure you encounter pivotal points in the game, but it provides an open-world feel that still gives you the option to skip one thing and go for another.
The combat varies from weapon to weapon but everyone will be able to find something that suits their playstyle wether it'd be magic, ranged, or melee or all of them! No single experience is the same will be the same as the previous one.
The difficulty of the game enables you to throw in 30 hours AT LEAST(if you don't refund it due to rage like I did before rebuying) while still leaving you unsatisfied and wanting more, allowing for amazing replay value.
For fans of the series and newcomers alike, this game will leave you with a memorable experience and more questions than answers, but a sense of achieving something great upon beating it.

Fallout 4 is a great game, but it's not amazing since the content isn't used to its full potential.  In other words, I get dressed and head out into the wasteland not for quests, or caps, but in hopes of finding Vault-Tec lunchbox confetti and the amusing teddy bear scenes.  If you're into that kind of stuff too, keep an eye out for Jangles The Moon Monkey, comics, bobbleheads, and the first cat in space, Mr. Pebbles.  So, it's still a fun game, despite a dry storyline, and dull decision options within quests.
There are a lot of reviews out there arguing both sides as to whether Fallout 4 is good or bad, some consist of essays written by Fallout veterans, and others consist of a few jumbled words.  I hope my review will be helpful to someone who is searching for something in between.  The knowledge that I'll share consists of things I find interesting about the game, and ofcourse develop further upon my short version of the review.
The difficulty options you can choose from include Very Easy, Easy, Normal, Hard, Very Hard, and Survival.  I started with Survival and stuck with it.  I had a very difficult time at the beginning as the amount of ammo, and medical supplies amongst other things is very limited.  I ventured into the center of the map relatively early, which may have not been one of the smartest ideas.  But I feel like even though it was more challenging than the area you start in, it's a lot more rewarding.  Once I developed a strong presence in the center of the map using settlements, Survival didn't seem so bad.  I have not played Fallout 4 on any of the other difficulty options so I do not know how they compare to Survival, but I feel like the game would be a lot less fun on the other difficulties.  Survival might be really difficult, but it also has a lot of cool features that contribute to why I think Fallout 4 is great.  So I guess I could even say the Survival difficulty is what essentially makes Fallout 4 great, since it has features like:

My initial experience with this game, as a first chose my class, and proceeded to the first boss area, was intimidation. A lot of people say that this game is very difficult and makes everyone rage and whatnot. But to completely honest I felt little to no rage during this game and enjoyed my experience throughout the entire game(exception being the jailers). I quickly was able to pick up the controls(and YES i did use the keyboard and mouse) and noticed myself dying less, and less. As for the rage portion, I was able to look back at my deaths and try not to get mad at them using the trick of telling myself what I did wrong and how I could improve for the next fight. As long as you don't get too fired up when you die (and keep in mind you can usually get your souls back) rage is close to non-existant in this game.
Negative Review Reason #1-Invasions are unbalanced
I would like to start this off by saying, no, no they aren't. People try to invade, and when they fail they claim it is 'unbalanced' because their skill is at a lower level than the host of embers. But they think they have reason behind it when they claim "The invader has half of their normal estus flasks." Yes this is true, but it is also true that both the host and the invader have their advantages and disadvantages. The host may have more estus flasks, but the invaded has the fact that enemies do not target them and the element of surprise. Some people may say "No you're wrong becuase it announces that you're invading!" While this is true it is insignificant because where they know that you will be attacking, they don't know where or when. This is not to mention that if you are invading the odds are in the favor of you having completed the area you are invading in, thus giving you an extended knowlege of enemy placement which gives you the advantage of waiting by some tough enemies. Not to mention that by invading you ARE accepting the risk of any 'unbalances' you see. In summary of the first reason, both the host and invader have advantages and disadvantages.

Honestly I want to counter this statement by just saying "shut up." This game is difficult, that's why in it's genre it says "DIFFICULT", is it too difficult? NO! Any room, boss, etc. CAN be beaten with enough patience and practice. I personally found myself defeating most mobs on my first try. And as for the rage, just don't let it get to you.

After 100 hours I have decided how I feel about this game....
It's absolutely amazing, Fromsoft did it again. Dark Souls 3 has elements from all the games, trying to learn from small mistakes in the past now don't get me wrong this is not a 10/10 would play on an island if this was the last thing I could play in my life and this is why.
In Dark Souls 3 you're hunting down each and every Lord of Cinder and trying to either Link the Flame or let it die out. You know Dark Souls stuff but it's not mostly about the lore that is interesting for most Dark Souls players it's the difficulty of the game. To be honest this game can be pretty hard at times and others not so much, I do love the fact that parrying, backstab and basically every mechanic from the old games just feel so smooth and responsive compared to Dark Souls 2 weird parry where they fall on the ground.
I would say that a lot of the early game bosses are kind of meh after doing about four playthroughs now. My favourite bosses have to be in no particular order. Abyss Watchers, Pontiff, Aldrich, Dancer, Lothric younger prince, Nameless King and of course the Lord of Cinder himself at the end of the game. Not saying the others are bad but they seem too easy and doesn't really give you a challenge. That being said that is my 100% opinion, you might disagree with some of those and that's fine!
Now the epic score of music in this game is beyond amazing. You get so pumped doing these boss battles and your heart starts racing when facing them. It's an experience that I only ever get in Dark Souls games, I have yet to find another series that does the same justice. Graphically this game looks really good too, Bloodborne engine is showing and that's not a bad thing.
On to the PvP side of Dark Souls, can't really comment that much about it. My experiences are usually tons of lag but it's possible that my internet is garbage or I'm just a garbage PvPer. Some people have said that invading is pretty bad, it does seem like it just pairs you into more 1v2 situations then 1v1 which doesn't really seem that fair plus the half estus flask for you but the host has all 15 or whatever amount he has.
The good thing about Dark Souls III is that I don't really have that many complains, it's not a 10/10 game because it can get a bit repetitive after a couple new game plus and the game becomes really easy. That's why a ton of people are excited about the DLC and hell I'm really excited as well, past Dark Souls DLC is great so I hope it lives up to the hype.
In the end Dark Souls III was great, I'll probably update the review later on and if you have serious FPS problems then you'll have to do some Nvidia tweaks which is pretty annoying but if you look around on Google you should be fine so that's an annoying negative about the game.
I hope you guys found this review interesting and hopefully it gives you a broad idea of how the game works. I always recommend checking out videos and coming up with your own opinion if you should buy it or not, personally I would buy it again with the amount of fun I had.

The gameplay in general feels much better. This one's really hard to quantify, but... you can sprint now which is nice? Does that count?
Overall, despite the story that leaves much to be desired, I thoroughly enjoy Fallout 4. It's a lot of fun just screwing around.

With seventy hours into the game, and plans to put in even more, I believe it is time for a review.
Design:Dark Souls III is gorgeous. What, did you want to hear more about the design? Isn't that enough for you to buy it? No? Okay, fine. Dark Souls III has some of the best graphics I've seen in a game to date. It has a Dark Fantasy tone to it, that is done perfectly. My favorite part about the design though it that it varies so much from area to area, and item to item. Every single item looks well made, every enviroment feels detailed and fun to explore. It can feel dark, and depressing, but it can also feel bright and vibrant.
TL;DR: Buy it for them gamfics you filthy casual.
Core Gameplay: Single Player: Although, the multiplayer and single player do merge together, I'm going to spend some time talking about area's, bosses, and weaponry, while staying clear of spoilers, of course. Every single area has varied enemies. These enemies are very well programmed, and each one has weaknesses, and strengths. Many of these strengths are high damage! Many of thier weaknesses are cold steel! But on a more serious note, there are certain elements, that can be added to your weapons through gems, or temporary items. Some enemies, like maggot things, are damaged by fire, where your average dude in armor, is fairly weak to lighting. However, dudes in armor are also very strong against fire, and will smash pyromancers before they get close. Next, bosses. Never before have I seen a game with this many fun and varied bosses. The first Dark Souls game had some annoying re-hashes (I'm looking at you, Stray Demon and friends!) The second Dark Souls game chose quantity over quality, I never asked to fight a boss every five minutes. However, Dark Souls III has some of the coolest looking, most fun to fight, most dynamic, most kill it with fire bosses I've ever seen. Finally, weaponry. This game has a lot of weapons. There, I'm done. Kidding, you think I'd pull that joke twice? Well, I wouldn't. Although many weapons have simmilar attacks, they are very fun to use, and in general balanced... (♥♥♥♥ you estoc, more R1 spam than a short sword) There are exceptions sure, but overall, they are good. The boss weapons especially are fun, and each have unique attacks.
TL;DR: Excellent area's, bosses, and weaponry combine to make the best single player experiance in a Souls game to date.
Core Gameplay: Multiplayer: R1 R1 R1 R1 R1 R1 R1 YOU DIED. That's your multiplayer experiance most of the time. In Dark Souls III you NEED to know how to parry, otherwise, the estoc will find you, and will kill you. All R1 spammer's have on thing in common they don't know how to parry, nor how to not get parried. So just do that. Git gud. Now onto my actual review, instead of advice. The invasions are so ♥♥♥♥ing broken, I'd rather eat broken glass than deal with them. The invasions favor the host so heavily, you are likely to lose, most of the time. You need to learn how to stop ganks, otherwise, you will die. My advice to you is, beat a certain boss, and after that boss, you will come out to a small yard thing. People leave summon signs there, that's where you should pvp. Don't invade there, however, that's not nice.
TL;DR: For the sake of your sanity, don't invade, it's much better to just go to the "arena."
Summary and Rating: Dark Souls III is a great game, one that I believe will stand the test of time, and become a classic. The single player is near perfect, and the multiplayer, with a few patches, could become as good as the other game's multiplayer.
TL;DR: You really like long reviews, huh. Buy the game, it's good.
RATING: 4.5/5

After 100 hours I have decided how I feel about this game....
It's absolutely amazing, Fromsoft did it again. Dark Souls 3 has elements from all the games, trying to learn from small mistakes in the past now don't get me wrong this is not a 10/10 would play on an island if this was the last thing I could play in my life and this is why.
In Dark Souls 3 you're hunting down each and every Lord of Cinder and trying to either Link the Flame or let it die out. You know Dark Souls stuff but it's not mostly about the lore that is interesting for most Dark Souls players it's the difficulty of the game. To be honest this game can be pretty hard at times and others not so much, I do love the fact that parrying, backstab and basically every mechanic from the old games just feel so smooth and responsive compared to Dark Souls 2 weird parry where they fall on the ground.
I would say that a lot of the early game bosses are kind of meh after doing about four playthroughs now. My favourite bosses have to be in no particular order. Abyss Watchers, Pontiff, Aldrich, Dancer, Lothric younger prince, Nameless King and of course the Lord of Cinder himself at the end of the game. Not saying the others are bad but they seem too easy and doesn't really give you a challenge. That being said that is my 100% opinion, you might disagree with some of those and that's fine!
Now the epic score of music in this game is beyond amazing. You get so pumped doing these boss battles and your heart starts racing when facing them. It's an experience that I only ever get in Dark Souls games, I have yet to find another series that does the same justice. Graphically this game looks really good too, Bloodborne engine is showing and that's not a bad thing.
On to the PvP side of Dark Souls, can't really comment that much about it. My experiences are usually tons of lag but it's possible that my internet is garbage or I'm just a garbage PvPer. Some people have said that invading is pretty bad, it does seem like it just pairs you into more 1v2 situations then 1v1 which doesn't really seem that fair plus the half estus flask for you but the host has all 15 or whatever amount he has.
The good thing about Dark Souls III is that I don't really have that many complains, it's not a 10/10 game because it can get a bit repetitive after a couple new game plus and the game becomes really easy. That's why a ton of people are excited about the DLC and hell I'm really excited as well, past Dark Souls DLC is great so I hope it lives up to the hype.
In the end Dark Souls III was great, I'll probably update the review later on and if you have serious FPS problems then you'll have to do some Nvidia tweaks which is pretty annoying but if you look around on Google you should be fine so that's an annoying negative about the game.
I hope you guys found this review interesting and hopefully it gives you a broad idea of how the game works. I always recommend checking out videos and coming up with your own opinion if you should buy it or not, personally I would buy it again with the amount of fun I had.

I'm nominating FO4 for the "Just 5 More Minutes" award, because when I first bought it I literally played for three days straight, stopping only to sleep.
Concerning the legitimate criticism from fans of the series, I'd say to go into it for what it is: more of an action game than an RPG. I had never touched Fallout before I became curious enough to try Fallout 4, and I have thoroughly enjoyed every minute so far. Just accept that it isn't going to be Fallout as you know it, and you may still have fun. (I personally have no interest in kids, and being forced into a 'loving mother' role was really uncool to me. You have no other choice. Every main story voice option is some variation of "I'm worried about my kid." I'm sure this would appeal to parents, though, who could relate to the main character.)
The theme of rebuilding after an apocalypse really resonated with me, though. I am very, very bored of post apocalypse stories about survival. They have been done to death. Right from the start you feel like you're bringing people hope. I really liked that; that your character can bring people together and help rebuild a region.
Related to this, of course, is the settlement building system. It appears to be really hit or miss among my friends. I absolutely loved it. Became sidetracked with it. Kid? What kid. THE COMMONWEALTH IS MY CHILD AND IT NEEDS ME. Some of my friends stopped at the first settlement because they hated it. There doesn't seem to be an in between. I liked going out and scavenging for rare materials initially to make a safe home for my new friends. To give them some comforts that my character knew.
Again, though, this all goes back to how you really aren't given much choice in how to roleplay. I can understand why someone would rather create a raider camp and align with raiders or something. But it simply isn't an option. You have to protect the commonwealth. (For me, this part at least appealed to me! I enjoy being the hero.)
The guns don't have too much variety, but each type dramatically changes gameplay style. I personally went a stealthy, charismatic gunslinger route with silenced pistols. Many other ways to play, though: Up close and personal shotguns, power-armored heavy-gun weilding juggernaut, sniper, Negan; it goes on and on.
The graphics are passable, but nothing to write home about. The trees in particular look abysmal. The whole world is various shades of greyish brown without much variety. It doesn't really encourage you to explore to find that next beautiful region like other open ended RPGs would. However, the inclusion of history-rich sites counteracts this quite well. It's really cool to see "what happened" to historic landmarks. A little bit eery, even. It's pretty neat to explore real places rendered in a game, and that some of the factions mimic major factions in American history is great.
Anyway, this is already really long considering I just want a badge, so I'll wrap it up.
I enjoyed Fallout 4, and do recommend giving it a shot. If you are a longtime Fallout fan and dislike it by comparison to the others, by all means criticize Beth. But I do think that if you go in knowing it will not have the depth you are used to, and you think of it as an action RPG, you could still have fun!

**This review is more about how the game fits into the fallout series not so much on the game itself**
Fallout 4 itself is a great game. However its not great in the areas that made fallout a great franchise.
Fallout games in general are known for typically in depth dialogue, a great level up system, an immersive universe, random funny moments that you wouldn't expect, and tons of things to do ( whether it be exploring or just questing ). Fallout 4 is devoid of almost all of these things. The two things that stand out the most would be that they completely scrapped the old level up system and the fact that there is almost no quests ( other than the same one you get over and over again to help out random settlements which are just boring after the first 3 times ).
Of course there are some good things about the game. The most important one would be the fact that they improved combat far above what it previously was. I don't really know how to describe it but it feels far more satisfying when you beat certain enemies. However this isn't to say that combat is perfect mind you there's plenty of enemies im not the slightest bit worried about ( I'm looking at you deathclaws ) no matter how many rounds it takes to take them down. Deathclaws are something i don't fear anymore maybe its because they where introduced so early in the story and taken down really easily. Or maybe its the fact that they take 8 years go throught the attack animation of their's that i never take any damage from them as long as i move for one second. Regardless they dont hold the same fear as the one shot monsters did back in the originals. It also has settlement building which is pretty cool.
I would be able to recommend this game if it was stand alone and not a sequel to the fallout franchise that i know and love. Assuming your not looking to buy the game as a fallout successor then go right ahead and buy it. For me however i can't recommend this game on that assumption.
TL; DR if you've played the old fallouts and expecting a good sequel to those I'd recommend you pass on this. If your looking for a good stand alone game that is basically just a FPS with some slight RPG aspects then you shouldn't be disappointed.

3. You have HALF your healing/mana items, meaning magic is even more useless and invasions are even more hard.

Though customisation and replayability is severely lacking compared to the previous Dark Souls games, it is definitively the best From Software game yet.
Everything deserves praise.
But personally I think there are some very blunt downsides.
Firstly, I was greatly disappointed by the amount of re-used content from previous games.
Almost half of locations, enemies, weapons, armor and spells was just copied from previous games. With minor barely noticable changes.
Secondly, the game felt like it had little to no difficulty whatsoever in terms of discovery. As if the developers intentionally added methods to make the game all too easy to navigate and cut a lot of corners to reduce both backtracking and freedom of exploration. There's very little challenge in getting around and shortcuts are abundant.
Thirdly, and largely personal preference; The game is simply not hard enough. Online Phantoms make too much of a difference, even ending up solo-ing most bosses whilst the world Host stays in a safe corner and watches.
And there are quite a few 'crutch'-concepts, items and methods to exploit the workings of the game.
Compared to the other Dark Souls, it does not feel like there is any freedom to strategise, just one way, one path.
Though multiple drop-down points and shortcuts are available, they all ultimately lead to the same result.
Barring these three flaws, it is simply one of the greatest games of all time and it should stay that way.

I'm nominating FO4 for the "Just 5 More Minutes" award, because when I first bought it I literally played for three days straight, stopping only to sleep.
Concerning the legitimate criticism from fans of the series, I'd say to go into it for what it is: more of an action game than an RPG. I had never touched Fallout before I became curious enough to try Fallout 4, and I have thoroughly enjoyed every minute so far. Just accept that it isn't going to be Fallout as you know it, and you may still have fun. (I personally have no interest in kids, and being forced into a 'loving mother' role was really uncool to me. You have no other choice. Every main story voice option is some variation of "I'm worried about my kid." I'm sure this would appeal to parents, though, who could relate to the main character.)
The theme of rebuilding after an apocalypse really resonated with me, though. I am very, very bored of post apocalypse stories about survival. They have been done to death. Right from the start you feel like you're bringing people hope. I really liked that; that your character can bring people together and help rebuild a region.
Related to this, of course, is the settlement building system. It appears to be really hit or miss among my friends. I absolutely loved it. Became sidetracked with it. Kid? What kid. THE COMMONWEALTH IS MY CHILD AND IT NEEDS ME. Some of my friends stopped at the first settlement because they hated it. There doesn't seem to be an in between. I liked going out and scavenging for rare materials initially to make a safe home for my new friends. To give them some comforts that my character knew.
Again, though, this all goes back to how you really aren't given much choice in how to roleplay. I can understand why someone would rather create a raider camp and align with raiders or something. But it simply isn't an option. You have to protect the commonwealth. (For me, this part at least appealed to me! I enjoy being the hero.)
The guns don't have too much variety, but each type dramatically changes gameplay style. I personally went a stealthy, charismatic gunslinger route with silenced pistols. Many other ways to play, though: Up close and personal shotguns, power-armored heavy-gun weilding juggernaut, sniper, Negan; it goes on and on.
The graphics are passable, but nothing to write home about. The trees in particular look abysmal. The whole world is various shades of greyish brown without much variety. It doesn't really encourage you to explore to find that next beautiful region like other open ended RPGs would. However, the inclusion of history-rich sites counteracts this quite well. It's really cool to see "what happened" to historic landmarks. A little bit eery, even. It's pretty neat to explore real places rendered in a game, and that some of the factions mimic major factions in American history is great.
Anyway, this is already really long considering I just want a badge, so I'll wrap it up.
I enjoyed Fallout 4, and do recommend giving it a shot. If you are a longtime Fallout fan and dislike it by comparison to the others, by all means criticize Beth. But I do think that if you go in knowing it will not have the depth you are used to, and you think of it as an action RPG, you could still have fun!

Despite its strong points and a well-sung return to formula, Dark Souls III seems lacking in comparison to its forebears.
Demon's Souls was the starting point, Dark Souls was the flawed masterpiece, Dark Souls 2 was the red-haired middle child, Bloodborne was the amazing Lovecraftian acid trip and Dark Souls 3 is.... well, it's basically Dark Souls again.
If you loved the first Dark Souls and just wanted to play it again, but with Bloodborne-esque bosses, then this one's got you covered.
For people expecting the variety and horror that Bloodborne evoked, you're going to be very disappointed. The lore has some bright sparks in bosses like Aldrich and Oceiros, and the game remains fun, but strangely there's less motivation to continue past NG+.
The world feels less like a vast connected whole than the others, but it doesn't reach the "elevator to hell" level that Dark Souls 2 managed (which is honestly a great thing). The environments tend to repeat themselves a bit, with a rampant issue of "too many damn cathedrals" which I'm surprised the devs didn't catch onto.
The game's art design brims with Miyazaki's touch, but the lore is more of the same, the gameplay hasn't evolved to any significant degree and honestly you're better off playing Dark Souls 1 again.
It might seem like I'm slagging it off, but I've got a good 93 hours in it, and it contains one of the hardest bosses I've ever fought so get it if you legitimately can never have enough Dark Souls.

With over 470h in this game, I still find it as fun as the first time I played it and I haven't even used any mods nor have I started any of the DLC quests. While it is true that Fallout 4 doesn't have as many quests as Fallout 3 or FNV had, they are still very well written and fun to play through. Each of them (except the radiant ones) feel very unique. It actually feels more fun and rewarding to play them than to finish them. Game world is fantastically designed and gives a great sense of scale. I'd also say this is by far the most immersive Fallout world to date. Every enterable building has it's own story. It feels as almost every piece of clutter, even at the most random locations has been put there to subtly pique your interest and make you think of it's possible backstory. This amazing immersion achieved by visual design is further enhanced by the sound design which I find to be mindblowing. Regarding the main quest chain, I'll just say that I liked it and found it very interesting.

Though customisation and replayability is severely lacking compared to the previous Dark Souls games, it is definitively the best From Software game yet.
Everything deserves praise.
But personally I think there are some very blunt downsides.
Firstly, I was greatly disappointed by the amount of re-used content from previous games.
Almost half of locations, enemies, weapons, armor and spells was just copied from previous games. With minor barely noticable changes.
Secondly, the game felt like it had little to no difficulty whatsoever in terms of discovery. As if the developers intentionally added methods to make the game all too easy to navigate and cut a lot of corners to reduce both backtracking and freedom of exploration. There's very little challenge in getting around and shortcuts are abundant.
Thirdly, and largely personal preference; The game is simply not hard enough. Online Phantoms make too much of a difference, even ending up solo-ing most bosses whilst the world Host stays in a safe corner and watches.
And there are quite a few 'crutch'-concepts, items and methods to exploit the workings of the game.
Compared to the other Dark Souls, it does not feel like there is any freedom to strategise, just one way, one path.
Though multiple drop-down points and shortcuts are available, they all ultimately lead to the same result.
Barring these three flaws, it is simply one of the greatest games of all time and it should stay that way.

Dark Souls 3 has both upsides and downsides compared to the previous titles.
As it's own game, it is great, but still very rough on newcommers.
Several game mechanics are once again not being explained and without help from other players or a guide, the avarage player is going to miss even entire areas with their own bosses and items on his/her first playthrough(s).
However Souls-Veterans are also going to face a few new mechanics as well.
The game's world is both beautiful and dark. Sometimes even both at the same time. There are countless different enemy designs and fighting through the areas was mostly challanging and fun.
Especially the bosses later in the game are very tough, some even frustratingly hard.
Dark Souls is known to be harsh but fair, this also applies to Dark Souls 3 for the most part. However there are also occasions, where I had to question, if that stunlock, gigantic hitbox or speed is really reasonable. Overall it is still fair, but some moments left a bitter taste.
Dark Souls 3 plays in the same world as the other 2 titles, therefore many different weapons and items make a return and a couple of npcs are directly from the other games.
However Dark Souls 3 also recycles/reuses many of the ideas, it goes so far that some of the moments already felt like fanservice for players that also played through the other games. It is not necessarily bad, but to me it seemed really forced sometimes.
Something else that I missed were connections between areas. Unlike in Dark Souls 1, the world's areas all feel very seperated, even though they are technically very close to each other. Also the player does not have to look for cross-area connections, because he can teleport to other discovered areas right from the get go.
Connecting to specific players got easier, now you can just use a password in the Menu's settings, instead of having to use a ring or even change your whole download region in the steam settings.
This only applies to Summon Signs though, as long as you're online and you meet the conditions, you can end up being assaulted by other players.
PvP exists in 2 ways, either random invasions, where one player appears in a different player's game to kill him, or as dueling, where players summon other players as enemy into their world on purpose via Red Summon Signs.
Invasions prioritize hosts that have coop partners at their side, which helps PvE players, but makes the job difficult for those who want to ambush other players in their world.
The online experience tends to suffer from latency issues, mostly relevant for PvP. A Region Lock exists, but it doesn't seem to do anything (similar to how it was in previous titles).
I did not enjoy the PvP as much as in Dark Souls 2 for multiple reasons:
- Most of my favorite weapons are bad for PvP in the current Patch, because of inferior damage and/or speed, which means I have to use something that I don't enjoy using, when I want to win.
- A large number of weapon movesets got straight up copied from other weapons and there is a high number of weapon moves that are either situational or just completely outclassed/useless
- Especially the strong attacks on many weapons are only useful, when the opponent is far away, because they are much slower than light attacks without giving much of an advantage, therefore the combat loses a lot of depth
Dark Souls 3 is still definitely worth playing for the PvE content already, but it is a shame that the PvP is lackluster. Hopefully things will change over the next months with the upcomming dlc content and further patches.

If you have never played a Fallout game, I would actually recommend starting with Fallout: New Vegas, but I would say that I enjoyed Fallout 4 as much or more than Fallout 3.
The settlement building feature is something unique to Fallout 4.  Some people love it, some people think its a complete waste fo time.  I am somewhere in the middle, I think its a fun and interesting diversion.  This is somethign you shoudl think about if you are considering gettign the season pass or individual DLC since it is the primary component of several of them.  I got the Season pass before I knew what the DLC would be and I got it before they raised the price of it, so I feelk I got my moneys worth on it, but for others,
if you like/love the idea of settlement building, then the season pass is a great deal.  If you just want more gameplay, then you can get just Far Harbor and Nuka-world for a bit less than the season pass.  Both Far Harbor and Nuka-world are worthwhile purchases.  I think I enjoyed Nuka-world a bit more, but I also have a soft spot for amusement parks.
Automotron is somewhere in between.  It does offer a bit more gameplay (but nowhere as much as the two I mentioned above).  It also has a few settlement building things, but its main draw is the ability to create robot companions.  Robot companions don't have any side quest story lines liek the human ones, but they can be very useful in combat.  I enjoyed the Automotron storyline as well even though it was only a couple missions and new locations.
I have not explored the Vault-Tec workshop DLC, so I can't comment on it (think it is supposed to have a quest though).  The Contraptions and Wasteland workshop add stuff I may or may not ever get around to using, but if you do plan to get Far Harbor and Nuka-World, then its not much more to get the full season pass and that makes the other stuff much more reasonable cost even if you only use a bit of it.

When I finished Dark Souls II earlier this year, I criticized it for having lackluster level design and a dull story especially when compared to the amazing precedent that was set with the original Dark Souls. Hidetaka Miyazaki, who directed Demon's Souls and Dark Souls was busy making Bloodborne while Dark Souls 2 was in development and I think his presence was missed. DS2 wasn't terrible, but it didn't quite have the magic of the first game. Miyazaki's magic, while difficult to describe, was something I immediately felt when I started Dark Souls 3. I think it's most noticeable in the level and enemy design. From Software in general has an unrivaled expertise in 3D level design. If you ever want to see video game level design's version of the Mona Lisa, you need to check out some of From Software's offerings from DS1 and DS3
Not only are the environments created in a very mechanically and structurally pleasing way, but the visuals are top notch here as well. As much as DS3's world in concerned with killing you, it's also just as concerned with having you admire its beauty. DS3 has some of the most breathtaking mountains, valleys, lakes and castles I've ever seen in a video game. It can be hard to admire the scenery with the constant threat of death right in front of you, but if you have a chance to stop and take it in, Dark Souls 3 is quite a sight to behold. It's also quite proficient at one of my favorite things to see done well: environmental storytelling. Want to get an idea of how old DS3's Firelink Shrine is? Head below the shrine and see the massive crypt filled with the remains of past fire keepers. Stuff like that really helps with player immersion and bringing the game world to life
The game mechanics are mostly what you'd come to expect if you've played any of From Software's similar offerings. It does seem like the team made a decision to push the combat mechanics more in the direction of DS1 than DS2. Gone is DS2's health bar reduction on every death. Enemies now respawn indefinitely like DS1. Also "humanity", which is now called "ember" is a binary state, again just like DS1. The primary new mix up to the gameplay formula comes in the form of weapon arts. Weapon arts are unique skills that are tied to your left hand item and can range from temporary buffs to entirely new unique moves. Often times your left hand item will be a shield which may have a shield bash or shield parry as like the previous Dark Souls games, or your shield may even default to your right hand weapon's weapon art skill as is the case when you have nothing at all equipped in the left hand slot. Most weapon arts consume your magic meter as well which also gives non magic classes incentive to put points into leveling up their magic bar. I found weapon arts to be a welcome addition to the Souls formula that adds interesting and unique skills and abilities and makes experimenting around with different equipment load outs even more fun and interesting
The strange and alluring mystique of Dark Souls' lore is back in full force. As I wandered through the Dark Souls 3's various mysterious locations, I found myself reading the item descriptions of various weapons and armor I picked up for additional lore. I was even drawn to watching several YouTube videos explaining the backstories of several bosses and NPC and theorizing on their connections. There are also several tie ins and reoccurring characters from the first Dark Souls so veterans of the series are in for a few surprising pay-offs especially for those who are deeply invested in the lore.
If this truly is the last Souls game we get, it is certainly a worthy send off for the series. Level design, audiovisuals, gameplay and lore are all top notch here and in some cases arguably the best we've seen of the Dark Souls series. This is one of my favorite games of the year so far and a must play for fans of these games who are up for one more challenge.
