Dark souls has always been centered around the idea of never ending cycles, when one king dies another will take his place. That cycle brings us to Dark Souls 3, and a new king has been crowned. However, with any cycle, comes repetition and there are many aspects of Dark souls 3 that have been seen and played through in previous games. The repetition is apparent, but Dark Souls 3 delivers the most refined combat yet, a beautiful yet gloomy new area to explore, and some of the most incredible boss fights the series can offer.
One of the greatest pieces of any souls game is the world and it’s atmosphere. The land of Lothric is what you will be exploring in Dark Souls 3, and it exceeds expectations. You could be exploring a medieval ruin, reminiscent of Dark Souls, or be walking the streets of a Gothic town taken right from Bloodborne. The mix of aesthetic styles from previous games creates a dark but fun world to travel through and take all of your enemies souls. Also, not only is the style fantastic, but the graphics in the game are of the highest quality in a souls game, and really takes it one step further to immerse you in the dark world of Lothric.
All these looks, however, mean nothing without the gameplay that will pull you through. Lucky enough for us, the Dark Souls combat we all know and love is back, but more refined with weapon arts and a hint of Bloodborne. Weapon arts are weapon specific moves that can range from a damage buff on an axe, to a quick parry with a sword. These moves use FP, the replacement for mana which can only be regenerated through the use of ashen estus flasks, as well as stamina. They are powerful moves that offer more variety in combat, but if you aren’t in to upgrading your FP, weapon art probably wont be for you. Another clear adjustment to the combat is the influence of Bloodborne. Fighting is now slightly faster, and rewards more aggressive builds. Gone are the days where a shield means complete safety, though they are still very useful, and now you will eventually be rolling and dodging to save your life. These small but impactful additions allowed for an even more enjoyable and open ended combat experience, leaving me wanting more even after completing new game plus, or journey 2.
However, mechanics aren’t the only thing that makes combat fun. Tough and exciting, the enemies in Dark Souls 3 complete the combat experience. There are many familiar enemies as well as new unique monsters, all giving the rage and joy we have come back to time and again. The one problem I have with enemies in Dark Souls 3 is, from my experience, mobs and especially knights are actually harder than the bosses themselves. Not many bosses gave me trouble in Dark souls 3, other than the final fight and the optional champion Gundyr, only dying two or three times at most to any given boss. The random knights however killed me probably around 15 times through out the full game, and even mobs like the crocodile wolf hybrids could kill me multiple times. I understand that other souls games are like this, but in Dark Souls 3 it seems like the difficulty was turned a lot more to the mobs. This didn’t take away from how exceedingly enjoyable the boss fights were, and many of the bosses you battle in Dark Souls 3 quickly became my favorites. The epic fights put you into what looks like fantastical set pieces, creating an atmosphere unmatched by other games. These fights also feel a lot more smooth and fair, which I believe is the reason for them feeling easier. If you can pinpoint the boss’ attacks and weaknesses, you are rewarded quickly after with his soul and the iconic bonfire.
The Last major aspect of any Dark Souls game is, of course, the PvP. It works much like any previous games, and not a lot has changed. You can summon people to help you, or you can invade and be invaded. Though, there is a new ‘wild card’ type that is purple and they can either help or kill you. Fighting other players is also generally the same, but I did notice that there was some delay when attempting to hit other players. Other than the sometimes frustrating delay, PvP is overall enjoyable but not refreshing.
As much as I loved Dark Souls 3 as a whole, there is a problem that could not go unnoticed, and that was on the technical side. I heard there are some fps problems on console, but I played on PC and I was at a steady 60 frames the entire time, so no complaints there. What I noticed was many annoying bugs that did effect the game in some instances. One example is when I died and I had 140,000 souls on my character. I went to go get them back and I took one of the elevators. Suddenly, my character falls through the floor on the elevator, ultimately to his death. There were also some problems with clipping, and the most agitating was locking on to larger bosses. The lock on almost never stays on larger bosses and can make your character look in the wrong direction and take unintended or unfair damage. This was definitely the only major gripe I have with Dark Souls 3, and I hope some of these bugs are fixed soon.
If what we have all been hearing is true, and Dark Souls 3 truly is the last Souls game, then the cycle has ended on a high note. Other than the frustrating bugs, FromSoftware has created the best Dark Souls to date. It has the satisfying and tactical combat that has been perfected from game to game. The dark, atmospheric Lothric is immense amounts of fun to explore, and the Bosses are some of the best iv’e seen. Any souls fan, rpg fan, and even action/adventure fan would be missing out if they over looked Dark Souls 3.

WOW. This game is so far behind Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2 it's astounding. Besides the obvious visual upgrade (which is nice), everything else about this game just feels... strained. Combat is no longer smooth and skill focused, but the same difficulty with facreroll stupidity thrown in. It's not even a matter of difficulty; the AI has been programmed to 'always on, 100%'. There are no openings. There is no skill based dodging, attacks hit everything. There is no learning the opponents moves, they each have dozens they can chain endlessly in any order. This game took a great concept- a difficult game that you expect to die in, but can be beaten with perceverence and skill and turned it into a luck based madhouse.

EDIT 4/19/2017:  Dark Souls III has received a lot of patches, and had two DLC drops since my original review was written, and I just want to say that having clocked a few hundred hours in the game, my recommendation stands strong.  I had loads of fun with PvP, ultimately, and found that that any gap in balance could be overcome with grit and determination.  They've brought poise into the game as a hyper armor mechanic that is only active during certain frames, an interesting change, and not necessarily a step in either direction, but one that shows they are open to community feed back, and really eager to make a game we can all enjoy.
The game still has some pretty harsh balancing issues, don't get me wrong, but there is so much to love. The PvE experience is god damn incredible.  A lot of my favorite souls bosses are found in this installment, the areas are gorgeous, and I just generally enjoyed the hell out of this game.  The lore is interesting, and I grew to love the PvP, even with its balancing issues.  And the secrets hidden throughout it! My first time discovering Archdragon Peak, fighting Darkeater Midir, and so many other things, will always stick with me.
If you have the opportunity to play this game, and have any love for Action RPGs at all, take it and give it a chance.

TL;DR: Dark Souls III is a great game definitely worth playing, but not perfect.  I'm a long-term Souls fan, so I'm a bit passionate about this, and my negative comments should definitely be taken with a grain of salt, as they're fairly specific (and from a place of love).
Dark Souls III has by far the most beautiful visuals in the series, in the same wonderfully dark theming Souls games always have, the same fantastic gameplay beloved in the other installments of the Souls series, and adds another massive time sink for Souls fans needing a fix to sink their teeth into.
And it has some incredibly enjoyable lore! I really loved the story elements in this one.  Not only that, it has some of the best cinematic moments in the series, by far.  The addition of weapon arts really gives this game its own unique signature in the series, although power stancing has, sadly, been removed.   This game is much more of a direct sequel to Dark Souls I, and plays off of it in many ways, so those who didn't like the changes in Dark Souls II will be more comforted in this installment.
These are by no means deal breakers, but with how much I love this series, I'd be remiss not to mention what felt like steps backwards.  It's fairly well publicised that poise is just gone in this game.  Not altered, like Dark Souls II, completely removed.  Basically every weapon will stun for two hits in PvP (unless it's some broken combo) and stun endlessly on most enemies in PvE.  The combat as a whole has been just a tad simplified; its new speed has reduced complexity, and many of its weapon classes are objectively inferior.  Between the removal of poise and the unbalanced weapon classes, a lot of player choice feels as though its been removed.  Most of all, casting has been more or less eradicated as a viable PvP aspect.  Every spell can be dodged, Focus Points limit their ability to sustainably battle, and even when they do hit, spells just aren't as significant as a good straight sword two-hit R1/Right Bumper combo.
I could go on about a few more negatives, all of them equally nitpicky Souls geek things, but the point is that the game is just feels a little less deep than Dark Souls I or II, specifically in the PvP.  It's still incredibly enjoyabale, especially outside of the multiplayer, but if you're anything like me, the reduction of viability of using axes or spells (or whatever you want to use that day) will irk you.  I just feel that the loss of viable build diversity is very sad.
I do love this game, and strongly recommend it.  But it lost a few things that I really enjoyed in previous installments.

I'm not a fan of the writing at times, particularly the endings. The game is buggy and I've had to mess around with settings for hours at a time to prevent slowdown or crashes, and use console commands to help find missing companions or fix bugged quests. The sidequests are often repetitive and aren't very interesting for the most part, generally consisting of travelling to location X and shooting whichever faction or race that happens to be stationed there - there's not a lot of ways to use your stats to talk your way around missions for different results, it's mostly just a bunch of shooting. The base building can be interesting, though as you may expect from a Bethesda game it's impossible to get things quite how you like them, as parts of buildings will often float above the ground or not quite line up the way you imagined, so it's nigh impossible to make anything looking remotely neat and tidy.
But.
I'm 200 hours in. The visuals and sound allow for a really cathartic experience: much like Skyrim before it, I love picking a random location on my map and just walking there, to see what I'll encounter along the way. It serves as a great distraction that you can lose yourself in for hours at a time, something very valuable these days. Does it innovate and push the franchise forward like Fallout 3 did before it? No, not really. It's basically exactly what I expected, no more no less, and I'm perfectly okay with that.

Hello!
Thinking to purchase Dark Souls 3 for some reason?
One thing about it I can't emphasize enough. This game does not tell you how to play it AT ALL.
There's this game called Frisbee. You throw a disc that flies through the air into a basket from far away. Whoever does it in the least amount of throws wins.
You now know more about Frisbee than you will learn about this game the entire time you play it.
Maybe the unique style of story telling and atmosphere? The experience of discovering the game's lore and secrets on your own?
Don't buy it. This game doesn't really have a story. Not a coherent one anyway. You just do the thing you did in the last games. Link the Fire, or don't. And this time you use the people who have linked the fire in the past as kindling to do that this time. For some reason.
Outside of that, there are 2 or 3 NPC interactions of note in the whole game. At least, ones that you'll find anyway. The game hides any and all information of all kinds from the player, so interacting with the NPC side quests isn't something you can deliberately do without a guide. And, among the NPC's that actually exist in the game, almost all of them are vendors that are obscurely, and somewhat unfairly hidden (but are crucial to the game, particularly for certain kinds of character builds) that you will talk to once, before they become normal vendors in the hub area. At which point, they do nothing but sell you stuff.
The story of this game is you kill monsters in a fading world. And also maybe make huge world ending or saving decisions you know nothing about.
Looking to buy it for the PvE difficulty? The experience of making your own character's stats and gathering gear for them?
The game has an astonishing lack of weapon variety. Which would be alright, except that almost every weapon in a given category almost always has the same moveset and utility. The primary difference is how the weapons scale with your stats. And even then, most weapons in a given category are roughly the same.
Additionally, because the game hides info like it does, it's very hard to know if you're doing well or not. It's hard to compare your weapons and damage because the materials to upgrade them with are rare. At least, the materials to make a weapon viable for where you are in the game, are rare. Especially so if you have a unique character that doesn't get basic physical damage scaling. You can completely miss the ability to make a viable setup you want, because  the game hid the materials and vendors to make it from you.
Disregarding all that difficulty, there's still a balance issue. There are weapons that are objectively better than others.
Also, good luck making a non warrior. Magic of every kind does potato damage, the magic bar doesn't regenerate, and is hard to hit anything with without dying.
The enemy designs are inconsistent. They constantly follow different rules from foe to foe. Sometimes enemies don't get stunned when you hit them, sometimes they do. Some of them have near instant attacks that require immediate evading or blocking, and some of them also have extremely delayed attacks that throw you off. Either, you get hit by the delayed attacks because you tried to get away from something you expected to come out almost instantly, or watch for the regular speed attacks, and get hit by something that's literally faster than is possible for a human brain to react to. They are placed in levels that are only designed in the most ridiculous ways possible, only to kill you.
This game puts giant pyrokinetic witches that can shoot through walls, right by a dark alley, where the corners you can't see have invisible enemies that will pop out and hit you as you walk past.
It's fun in a sense. But plenty of it isn't fair. In a different game, that wouldn't be such a huge problem. This game's concept is BASED around the concept of hard but fair. Every enemy needing to adhere to the same rules the player does. Only, this particular iteration's enemies choose when they don't have to follow the rules.
Maybe you're into PvP?
Almost all the people left playing are using the strongest possible setups, because almost everyone that has picked this game up has dropped it. The people remaining are still having fun either screwing around, or have to use the best stuff just to have a chance. So expect to see a lot of the same weapons and tactics.
The PvP is very...basic. Not easy, but not complicated. Very hard because of all the moves and tricks to consider. Most of which you will rarely use.

Veterans
The game definitely feels like Dark Souls 1 which is good and bad depending on your preference. The PVE experience is enthralling and very detailed. Enemies do not have magnets attached to their weapons like in Dark Souls 2 and they are not mindless (ahem...Black Knight DS1) creatures. They have a good mix of strength and their tracing is balanced.  The game introduces new starting classes such as the Assassin and has added a new player stat called Luck.  Rolling feels a bit floaty which is good depending on what Dark Souls you like. The graphics are a huge step up from previous games. I am aware the Dark Souls series is not about graphics but some areas in the game are just jaw dropping.  As for the story...its Dark Souls, figure it out. Bosses aren't too difficult but not too easy. Its a good balance EXCEPT for gimmick bosses. e.g Hit this thing to kill boss instantly/take away huge amount of health. PVP has returned as strong as ever with a meta of SL 120. The game is frequently patched so overpowered weapons are balanced accordingly.  It is a wonderful game and I greatly recommend any Souls veteran play and savor it. Its been confirmed as the last of the series so enjoy it.
NOTE: NG+ does not change very much, a bit disappointing
New Players
Dark Souls this time around has been more friendly to noobies. The level design isn't confusing and you generally know where to go next. If this is your first RPG you are in for a ride a unique ride however I HIGHLY recommend you play at least Dark Souls 1 to grab an overall feel for the franchise. The game isn't overally difficult but it is NOT easy.
Conclusion: It is a must buy for veterans. New players are welcome as it is not too hard but Dark Souls is a niche series so don't force yourself to like it.

Fallout 4 is a solid entry in one of the greatest and most enduring series in video game history. It has flaws aplenty, but detractors to this game too-often overlook its merits, of which there are many.
The graphics are fastastic for a Bethesda open-world game, with detailed models, robust environments, and some truly jaw-dropping vistas that are not only gorgeous, but a true representation of the Fallout experience.
The combat is the best the series has ever seen. The weapon variety is undeniable. The VATS system has been refined to near-perfection. Enemy AI, while far from perfect, is vastly improved over previous games.
The crafting system is a welcome addition to the franchise, and a fully-featured one. It is fairly intuitive, but certainly does suffer from the constraints of Fallout's authentic, albiet aging, user interface. While the settlements are fun to build and manage, a lack of stakes or hooks to the main narrative leave them flat compared to other activities.
The main flaw is the story, which admittedly is weak, even by Bethesda's standards. The developers clearly tried to walk the line between Fallout 3's emotional story beats and New Vegas' deep branching storylines, and as a result, the narrative is muddled and lacking in depth. There are moments of heft, but overall, the protagonist feels detached from the conflicts consuming The Commonwealth. The voice acting, while competent, does few favors for the scattershot writing. That being said, there are a few genuniely impressive turns in the second act, before the uninspired and at times confusing resolution. The radiant quest system is my biggest gripe with the series, taking the uniqueness and discovery out of progression and replacing it with a sterile, paint-by-numbers slog that removes the reward of completion.
As to complaints of a lack of RPG elements - they are valid. Most quests are resolved at the end of a rifle, and investing deeply in non-combat skills only makes progression more difficult. There are times where speech, stealth, or science can move the quest forward, but typically only to the next combat encounter. It's not as bad as some of game's harshest critics would have you believe, but the ability to role-play as you could in  New Vegas or even Fallout 3 is all but gone from this game.
Fallout 4 is a fantastic game, and without the sky-high expectations and the curse of Bethesda's pedigree, would likely be seen much more favorably. There are moments that are absolutely worth the price of admission, but they are too few in what could have been a masterpiece of modern role-playing. As someone whose glasses are very rose-tinted for anything Fallout, this game has and continues to have plenty to offer me, but it may be a while before I start anew in the depths of Vault 111.

The game can be fun, its largely well designed, the world is incredibly detailed and spooky, but the few things it does wrong are such major ♥♥♥♥ups that it turns the game into a frustrating mess.
Demons Souls and Dark Souls 1 were challenging (we dont talk about DS2, its like the deus ex: invisible war of souls games) and yes they♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off at times too when something was really tricky, but it was a good kind of a frustration, getting through the frustratingly hard part felt great.
DS3 really just leaves a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ taste in my mouth even after clearing a hard part, partially because I keep dying of stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Enemies can hit through walls, no matter how thick they are, lockon is erratic and has a mind of its own, enemies have massive hitboxes even when they are small dudes and they can bodyblock you in the many tight corners of the areas which naturally causes the camera to go crazy. Getting stuck and the camera preventing you from seeing anything, then dying. Yeah thats fun. Camera was always an issue, but in this game it somehow becomes a problem far too often. Its not an ocasional little annoyance, its a near constant thing no matter what camera setting you choose.
As for PvP, oh boy have they done goof'd, but everyone already knows that.

It was never this common in the previous games which made invades actually kind of exciting. You never expected it and it was a surprise. Now its something that happens like clockwork whenever you use an ember. Its messed up. Theres no anticipation, no surprise to it. You just know that its going to happen very quickly after you use an ember, with a 100% certainty.

The sequel to Dark Souls 1 that we deserved.
I love the series - and so, let's get down to the things I dislike about the game.
>>RANT BEGINS<<
*Extremely linear in comparison to Dark Souls 1, and extremely short in comparison to Dark Souls 2
*I was never a fan of sorcery, or how overpowered it seemed to be in the previous game. For some reason, though, sorcery seems to have been gimped considerably, way more than I'd like. Being an effective sorcerer now requires full commitment with very little in the way of build flexibility or room to explore. You'll still melt most everything in the game - but it will feel significantly less fun.
*From seems to have delighted in nerfing Faith to oblivion for a long time now, and this game may just be the worst example yet. As of Patch 1.09, there are actually A COUPLE actual Faith weapons, and offensive miracles are MARGINALLY useful in certain controlled circumstances, now. Before recent patches, it was entirely useless.
*Most weapons seem recycled from the previous two games, with not much in the way of new weapons. Though there are plenty of boss weapons, Dark Souls 3 seems to have largely ignored the Dark Souls 2 quality-of-life improvements that made boss weapons actually useful. As it stands, very few of them are even viable. The same can be said for most offensive spells, as well.
*The Poise reworking means that heavy armor is now almost meaningless, save for large weapons' hyper-armor. Anything but the lightest of armors feels like a waste.
*Although I am not fond of Dark Souls 2 in general, I have to admit that that game went to considerable lengths to make most weapon builds viable. Dark Souls 3 seems to have thrown all of that out of the window. Cookie-cutter builds are sadly all too common as a result, with not a lot of the flexibility, variability and surprise aspect that PvP (and even PvE) had in the second installment.
*NPCs seem to have considerably less dialogue this time around.
*Covenants are mostly broken and largely meaningless.
>>RANT ENDS<<
With all that said? Dark Souls 3 is a wonderful game, and feels like a true successor to the original Dark Souls, even if it doesn't quite manage to be as good as the first installment. The controls feel amazing, the enemy and boss design are as strong as ever - if not stronger - and the world and lore are worthy of the name. Weapon Arts add an interesting layer to combat, Focus Bars instead of Spell Casts (as it was in Demon's Souls) increase flexibility. The music -might- just be the best in the series (though that's obviously heavily subjective). NPCs have less dialogue overall, but almost every single one of them has a questline to pursue. In truth, these may not feel like groundbreaking changes from the first game, and really, they aren't. Yet, Dark Souls was never really about innovation for the sake of innovation, but solid design polished to a mirror sheen. And even though Dark Souls 3 has a few flecks of tarnish, it is a fitting and satisfying closing to this beloved, genre-spawning series, and even with it's flaws, it's better than most games out there.

Easily the best out of the souls trilogy (and Demon's Souls) on the PvE side. Very few bosses retain the old "hit it between attacks until it dies" setup: most of them have cool defeat/damage conditions, area hazards, or greatly mix up their movesets part way through the fight. The non-boss parts are also greatly improved: areas feel connected again like they were in DS1, you've got less of the easy trash mob encounters and more stuff that actually makes you think, and there's a large set of optional zones to explore.
PvP on the other hand was pretty lacklustre for me this time around. The sin system is gone, as are blue eye orbs, and yet for some reason there's -two- Blue Sentinel covenants that both only act as Way of Blue helpers. One of the auto-invading covenants is basically dead due to being in a low-level area (unlike Bell Keepers who had two areas to invade to prevent this problem), and interesting summoned-pvp covenants have been done away with: instead of Dragons and Rat King, you've got people who are essentially just a red summon sign that could help you with PvE if they -really- wanted to (hint: they never do). Also, darkwraiths no longer have a dueling arena, PvE covenants are gone, the original poise stat was removed and replaced with a renamed agility, and the balancing just isn't what it was in Scholar of the First Sin.
Overall, the game stands as my favorite because the PvP has always taken a backseat to the PvE or me, and this one's PvE is hands-down the best of the series. But, if you just play the PvE as a means of reaching the main PvP zones, you may want to consider sticking with Scholar (assuming people still play it actively, I haven't checked).

You unearth on the graveyard among ash and bones. No rest for the undead again. Or you can use the fancy The Ashen One as your new Maiden in Black calls you, or unkindled as everyone else does. There’s a nitpicking explanation for the difference between unkindled and undead. The short version is: you tried to link the fire like Gwyn did in the first game, but was found unworthy of the task. You’ve turned into ash and not into cinder like those who were capable of performing the task. Now you rise again because those who unlike you were good enough as a kindling (Lords of Cinder) have abandoned their thrones. The massive boulders shaped into armchairs that are left in the Firelink Shrine look like distant relatives of tombstones in Hunter’s Dream from Bloodborne. Or rather even archstones from Demon’s Souls since Firelink Shrine now looks a lot more like Nexus (but has a secret dark counterpart like Hunter’s Dream did).
The only thing in common (besides the obligatory bonfire) between the old and new location is the complaining knight. This ever present character of hub locations for the series gives you riddled insights on what to do next and reminds you that any hope for success is futile. In the first game he’s greeted you when you got out of the introductory zone. Now he’s at the end of it. He’s at the borderline between abstract time-space of your base of operations and that real fight that begins according to the messages left by other players.
The funniest joke of Dark Souls III is how it reverses the common trope of video games. Your usual path is upwards, from the faubourgs, forests and bogs to the final castle of the ultimate evil. Here you start in it and slowly descend to the foothill and further into the depths where more dangers lurk. That makes you question who you are. And that is the right question for the series, but as usual this mystery is open to interpretation (and largely depends on your actions and choices). It’s easy to miss even though you’re told directly about it by the NPC. Details like this tend to not be the focus of your attention, which usually is centered on how to deal with the hordes of dangerous enemies trying to stab you on your way to the next bonfire.
In the transition from one zone to the other there will be time to just admire the view.
Dark Souls III is like a happy marriage: the tricks aren’t really new, but it still is titillating and enjoyable. And most importantly you don’t wanna trade this comfort for something new because you’re convinced that nothing can be better.
In a way this game is more accessible than ever, more robust and fluent. No more riddles about starting gifts; access to the multiplayer is not so far behind the tricky boss fight and AN incredibly punishing (for a beginner) zone. Now you just purchase your white sign soapstone from a vendor in Firelink Shrine. You don’t even have to find and rescue this seller of marvelous goods, handmaiden. She’s just there. But then again, you have to know what it is you’re buying. You have to know if it’s better to stock up poison-reducing items or packs for arrows for sneaky dragon-killing. You have to be a veteran of the series for that particular pricy key in her stock to immediately catch your attention. Yes, Dark Souls III is a tad easier, but only if you’ve already come prepared with the knowledge and loaded with nostalgia. Only then the silhouette of a blacksmith sitting further in the underground cave besides the handmaiden will make your heart beat faster.
Self-quoting and straight-up repetition of elements from previous titles is yesterday’s news about FromSoftware games. If anything, that’s admirable how essentially doing the same very hardcore and niché thing again and again they’ve gained such a widespread acknowledgment. It’s still a far cry from your typical AAA experience, but for a long-time fan it looks more like a remix, like a fevered dream filled with all those memories blended together than a new adventure. The series are at the point of calling exciting new feature a re-introduction of mana bar which wasn’t present in the series since Demon’s Souls. Well, it’s blue and shows you the amount of mana you spend to cast spells, which isn’t that exciting. What’s more interesting is that you also use it for special 2-handed weapon attacks. This introduces you to the new mechanic of balancing two types of estus-flasks if you use spells or goes completely unnoticed if you only use these special attacks occasionally and stick to the old ways. This is how it goes: a bit of this, a touch of that, familiar NPC making a return, a poisonous bog, an underground cavern, a jail with an NPC trapped behind a locked door. Everything is chopped, sliced and added to the brew.
There’s NPC that kills other NPC and revenge invasion, though implications are far less dramatic. There is a simplistic puzzle with the two elevators far less decorated than in Bloodborne. You do things the same way, look for familiar clues. You jump off the elevators when you see those platforms you can jump off to. If you get bored, the ability to choose a new playstyle is there. It’s worth noting though that attributes’ reallocation is accessible way far into the game as opposed to Dark Souls II. You can easily miss it altogether on discover it at the point when there’s just four bosses left, and all of them are just pathetic ♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Anyway you’re free to choose from melee to magic to bow to something even more exotic. And when you fail with your build optimisation you can always just throw toxic feces at enemy knights. Dozens of armor sets, weapons and rings — enough to justify a replay. You were curious to try out that mechanic that you’ve missed on previous playthrough anyway.
Second playthrough with the comfort of coming prepared. Now you know which chests are mimics and have time to chuckle at “Regret!” message at the dead end. The structure of the world comes back into focus. Vertically stretched layout with intersections, connections, elevators, traps, closed doors and completely cut-off zones. Geography makes sense now.
Even two bonfires mere few dozens of steps away from each other actually make sense when you consider the shortcut you discover later. The story of Dark Souls series revolves around endless cycles of misery and futility of any attempts to overcome it. You’re not even sure if that is the irony or the prophecy of some kind for the company and its games.

The game was an absolute pleasure to play. The gameplay is ripe with immersive lore and eccentric chaaracters. Combat is both balanced and varied, and there are numerous ways to pick apart an opponent, whether through brute strength, sorcery, magic, miracles, or anything one can think of. Boss characters are diverse and propel the story at a reasonable pace, bringing incredibly varied environments to the game along with a sullen, grim milieu of hopelessness, contrasted by the ubiquitous theme of fire. Of course, Dark Souls never fails to present players with challenging gameplay, which critics always seem to conflate with artificial difficulty, though never justly. Overall, the game is perhaps the Magnum Opus of From Soft, and this swan song is one to remember.

While all previous Bethesda RPG titles gave your character some backstory elements, the core of the game still allowed you to play an unique individual. In Fallout 4, you're always the same guy/girl. You have dialog choices, but none of them seem to impact the world around you in any significant unique way. So whats left is a choice of which faction you want to end the game with. And even then, all the ending are pretty much the same in execution. You basicly get a different uniform and a slightly different ending.
NPC interaction in Fallout 4 seems also to create a distance between you and the characters you're interacting with. The contrast between the animated dialog sequences and the stunted, normal AI behaviour is just to big. Entering one of your settlements and just seeing the inhabitants standing around at random locations, only seeming to start moving in a zombie like fashion when the time comes to go to sleep, just really breakes the immersion. It seems so far removed from the village's in Skyrim. People seem to have stuff to do there. They where going out to get food, took walks, and with mods even ran and took shelter in the rain. And that bring me to another point.
This has been the LEAST moddable Betheda Fallout game so far! Don't expect great mods like custom AI behaviour or a flawlessly working Alternate start. There is no scipt extender as far as I know of, so also no custom item sorting.
We will probably never see great mods like frostfall or hunterborn for Fallout 4.
We are also stuck with the grind heavy building system, which is the one and only reason I did spend as much time in this game as I did.
So whats left is a basicly a mostly linear advanture FPS, with a lot of grinding posibilies. Which can be nice, but I don't think is what most people want out of their Fallout experience. I, personally, want to play around in a post apocalyptic retro-futuristic sandbox.
So in the end I do recommend this game. It is not a bad game. It was obviously made with care and skill.
But I do hope Bethesda will listen to the feedback they've gotten and really look to make the next RPG more of an RPG, or at the least give the community the opportunnity to mod it more to their own tastes.

Easily the best out of the souls trilogy (and Demon's Souls) on the PvE side. Very few bosses retain the old "hit it between attacks until it dies" setup: most of them have cool defeat/damage conditions, area hazards, or greatly mix up their movesets part way through the fight. The non-boss parts are also greatly improved: areas feel connected again like they were in DS1, you've got less of the easy trash mob encounters and more stuff that actually makes you think, and there's a large set of optional zones to explore.
PvP on the other hand was pretty lacklustre for me this time around. The sin system is gone, as are blue eye orbs, and yet for some reason there's -two- Blue Sentinel covenants that both only act as Way of Blue helpers. One of the auto-invading covenants is basically dead due to being in a low-level area (unlike Bell Keepers who had two areas to invade to prevent this problem), and interesting summoned-pvp covenants have been done away with: instead of Dragons and Rat King, you've got people who are essentially just a red summon sign that could help you with PvE if they -really- wanted to (hint: they never do). Also, darkwraiths no longer have a dueling arena, PvE covenants are gone, the original poise stat was removed and replaced with a renamed agility, and the balancing just isn't what it was in Scholar of the First Sin.
Overall, the game stands as my favorite because the PvP has always taken a backseat to the PvE or me, and this one's PvE is hands-down the best of the series. But, if you just play the PvE as a means of reaching the main PvP zones, you may want to consider sticking with Scholar (assuming people still play it actively, I haven't checked).

One more minute, one more try, one last push forward. A mantra forms as you struggle. Against insurmountable odds stacked against you. Enemies who have the strength to kill you in a myriad of ways. And traps to fall into the pit of death, restarting the cycle of life once more?
For what purpose? For death once again?
Clearly the path is riddled with the absence of kindness. In it’s place suffering and pain continue.
Welcome to Dark Souls III
Where each player has to struggle time and time again to go beyond the obstacles being brought forth. Being the third in the Souls franchise to complete the ‘Dark Soul’s’ trilogy Miyazaki (the director of the soul’s series). Ends the game with brutal efficiency alike to throwing tantrums and giving up until the brink. When wait you realize the enlightened moment to reach in and grasp victory within your bare hands.
It is a feeling. That is incredibly and hard to describe as most satisfying to face someone grotesque or something challenging to truly test the mettle of your being. And when the dust settles and your breath slows you realize with a feeling of elation and most appreciation the feeling of accomplishment and achievement wrought with everything you have given upon. Soul and body to forge a weapon against your adversary.
It is a sigh of relief. And the cycle continues.
My journey in DSIII is ironically(given the similar state’s of my adventures in the soul series) full of pain, suffering coinciding with accomplishment, the feeling to turn one more corner to find what riches are in store. To risk the feeling of danger once more for one more step forward. When unknowingly we tempt fate and destiny and like horror movies; when the tension is at the most highest with the suspense hanging like a thread we realize our greatest regret and realize our utmost folly in our deaths. And upon loss discover our bet to go all in was all for naught. And to recover our greedy souls as sustenance is one try.
But, the game doesn’t end that way. You can as always in the souls series summon for help. But, be wary of the summons for they could either help or hinder your efforts to progress through the game. Albeit with the incoming invaders when you go online. Should you risk for help at the risk of more danger? It is always and constant ever present question your capabilities. And DSIII re-emphasizes this purpose to forge ahead and question “Can you do it?” and “Can I do it?”
The questions have always been at the forefront of the “Soul series” And continue to test time and time again your ability to traverse through such odds. Be it as 1 vs. All or any number.
The appealing nature of the “Soul Series” in its entirety has emphasized straightforwardness to provide you with the basics and let you go on your journey. There is no holding your hands like a toddler. These types of games hold your hand and throw you off a cliff without the slightest hesitation and make you discover from the first moment in the air, that you will get ♥♥♥♥ed up in more ways than one. And if you’re asking for an easy mode, well you just have to practice to get good and become better than your enemies. Each entry to the franchise introduces new enemies, bosses, areas, items, Npc’s, lore, and more. Yet it has maintained the tradition of the hp bar, the stamina bar, and your utilities of carrying weapons, slight UI changes, and different covenants. There is no new mechanic to engross you to play the game because of this brand spanking new mechanic. The same formula is used. And if it isn’t broken, why should it be fixed?
To look on the unappealing nature of the “Soul Series” I would say the brutal difficulty of direction. With a stab of unknown frustration to venture forth into the world, let it be said DSIII is punishingly to rattle yourself out of focus. When you need focus to play DSIII.
While other games usually contain some narrative, or npc to guide you to a certain location in order to progress through the story. Dark souls have maintained a no hands policy, and it may prove frustrating to some (like I was). Nevertheless, there is simplicity for the Soul’s formula to continue coupled with complexing and in some cases daunting direction to go in the right path. With the flourishing enemy variety to jump your bones and struggle against...
May seem difficult to some, more so unappealing due to its harsh treatment. DSIII remains, in its defense the game treats the player with some respect and expects the same respect be given to it as well. The online portion is a mixed bag in itself as well concerning invaders who intrude upon your session and if successful in killing you will restart you to the nearest bonfire, crushing your soul-progress and your souls in the place where you died. I admit this mechanic when I was first introduced was the bane of my existence and continues to be so in DSIII because I suck at pvping with people. Yet, there are moments when I appreciate it such a mechanic when I reverse the gank with summoning some comrades with me.
“Dark Souls is like Insanity, you keep playing it over and over again expecting to beat it and or win. But, what you don’t realize Dark Souls has already BEATEN YOU.”

Dark Souls 3 Is a fantastic game that has wonderful game play and a great story if you care. the game play is done in a style similar to Bloodborne  (fast paced) but that's the keyword, similar. It has fast paced combat that still maintains the Dark Souls style. The game itself is absolutely beautiful and the lore is superb. Speaking of the lore, it's pretty much entirely optional. The base of the lore (without spoiler) is pretty much the world works in cycles and you have to bring back the people who linled the fire lords of cinder, the people who restarted the cycle. You gain access to the lore via item descriptions and dialogue and it's well worth investing your time into. The soundtrack is absolutely amazing, complimenting the boss fights they go with perfectly. Some issues with the game are however the online. More specifically the invasion system. Pretty much there are hackers,  like in any other game but they can make you have to rebuy the game because it corrupts your game data, plus there are numerous bugs and glitches, but none too game play altering. Overall I'd definitely recommend this game, and give it an arbitrary rating of 9/10.

Warning: I have played this game mainly on ps4, and I decided to give it a second chance on pc for the presence of richer and more complex mods.
Even if Fallout 4 is a very good fps game, it is a really bad role playing game, with dull quests, short dungeons, poor weapon and armor variety (even taking in consideration the possibility to modify and personalize both weapons and armor). In this game Bethesda has focused too much in settlement developement and management. The atmosphere is not as grim as in Fallout 3, with a richer color palette resulting in a strange post-apocaliptic world.
- From the rpg point of view the skill improvements through use have been deleted, there's no weapon and armor decay and the dialogue system with voiced player character is quite poor, with a real lack of choice and consequences. There is not the option to be the "bad guy", under every point of view. Fortunately a survival mode has been implemented and it's quite good, even if in my opinion it's too punishing.
- The quests, both main and side ones, are really dull, short, boring, without real story twists and surprises. Radiant quests are even haunting. You'll learn to hate Preston Garvey and the damned Minutemen! There is lack of interesting npcs, even if the followers have been greatly improved since Fallout 3 and Skyrim. They will approve or disapprove your choices and actions, even if they are going to remain loyal no matter what you're going to do!
- The settlement system is in my opinion well implemented. Even too much! You can really lose many hours building structures and defenses and almost whatever you want, even if there is a building limit for every settlement. Once you reach it the game will disable the possibility to build even the smallest feature. The settlers however are really boring and will bother you with help requests. Some of them will make you desire to kill them after 10 minutes (Jun and marcy Long, I'm talking to you!)
- the combat system is much more dinamic, fun to play, and the possibility to improve your weapons and armor makes it shine like never before. Pity the holstered weapons are invisible (and this was for me one of the most annoying problems of the game, because it breaks the immersion)
- the dungeons consist in big structures that can be accessed often in various ways, but at the end they are quite linear and repetitive. The metro tunnels are quite short and have dead end: you cannot go from point "A" to point "B" through them. This is another problem I really disliked a lot, since I adored the Fallout 3 metro tunnels.
- the atmosphere of the game is lighter, brighter and is not aided by the graphic compartment, quite poor if compared to modern fps and rpg games (an incredible rpg is the Witcher 3, 5 years ahead of every bethesda game in almost every aspect)
- there are too many loading screens. Every ♥♥♥♥ing time I enter a city, a structure or a closed building (often even small rooms) there is an immersion breaking loading screen. I hated them deeply.
Well, this is my review. Not very detailed but sincere. If you are looking for a good fps Fallout 4 is for you. If you are searching for a good rpg with immersive atmosphere and good story search elsewhere.
AFTER PLAYING FALLOUT 4 ON PC A LITTLE BIT, THOUGH...
Well, here is the second part of the review.
I must say that if played with the right mods the game offers a much better experience than vanilla version, on ps4.
- Graphics and audio: With the advent of the High res textures dlc, I must say the game is much more pleasant to explore; the pc version shows a cleaner and much more beautiful graphic compartment, and the audio, with the aid of a good pair of headphones, offers a much more immersive gameplay experience as well.
- From the modding point of view: I've mainly installed weapons related mods, wich add more realistic & powerful carabines, AKs and whatever, which make easier to kill enemies, but much easier to be killed by them as well... I've lost count of the number of times I've been killed with a single shot! I was not a fan of the weapons available in the official game, so this new range of firearms refreshes the gameplay a lot, even if the abovementioned weapons aren't lore-friendly at all, being extremely advanced if compared to the official ones.
- Gameplay and adventures: In this second playthrough, avoiding the Minutemen and the other factions like Hell, specially their radiant s.h.i.t.t.y quests, the overall exploration thing runs better & smoother. I see just what I want to see, I do just what I want to do! "...and it just works!" like a certain very famous game designer said some times ago.
- DLCs & stuff: I've explored the Vault 88 available from the dlc, and I've found it amazing for two good reasons:
1) the cave that I can transform into my personal vault is HUGE!
2) the cave has 3 (THREE!!!) different entrances, that render it as a wonderful subterranean passage from point "A" to point "B" and/or point "C". At last, finally, some sort of subterranean passage! I missed so much the Metro dungeons of Fallout 3! At least this reminds me them a little bit!
I've not explored the other DLCs on this platform, because I'm still fooling around in the main map of the game just to see how it works on my new pc, and I don't like building bases & setlements everywhere. I've already tried it on ps4 and the experience wasn't that amazing, at least for me.
Well, this is it for now. I could add some more impressions in the future, but the overall evaluation tends to remain the same, even if I'm discovering some really good features of Fallout 4. This game shows a really astounding series of features and details, that show the incredible talent of the Bethesda Devs and game designer (Todd Howard) in bringing to digital life wonderful worlds, but with Fallout 4 many flaws (that I have already written and listed above in the first part of this review) still fight back its many wonders, leaving me confused and with a single simple question: is Fallout 4 great or not?

"Ironically Hollow" is how I'd describe the last addition to the Dark Souls series.
Sure you do the same old thing, gotta link that fire...and that's it.
In the last games it had truly memorable and landscape where the Lore was easy to tease out without excessive digging to at the very least have a general feel.
In this final incarnation there are very forgettable characters and unfortunately no lore to speak of..
Where would Hollow apply then?
In short, the Games combat mechanics are solid and functional.  Not quite the same as the last games but it works.
But that's just it.  There's only the gameplay, there's only the combat.  There is no true gratification for completion of a Goal in this game, only relief it's done..
There's no lore, items or real NPC's to call it's own, just borrowed assets and a disgusting excess of fanservice for the first game.
I feel nothing for my character or his intereactions.  There's only 2 NPC's in the entire game I give a half♥♥♥♥♥♥about and only one of them is original to this game alone instead of a fanservice Clone.
PvE (Player versus environment) works fine and is simply enough.  A few enemies and placements feel utterly unfair and/or cheap with either excessive numbers or limitless attacks.  But overall it is manageable with a little practice and memorization to the point of triviality.
However, PvP (Player versus Player) has always been one of the bigger selling points of these games and here is one of the biggest shortcomming of this Game.  If you invade the game has slanted victory to the side of the Host as it should be, but they went much too far.  The invader will have a 30% reduction of thier max hp when entering someones world (this i'm fine with), yet the more Phantoms a Host has the more priority they have to be invaded.
If you're alone you can go hours without seeing a single invader unless you find a red sign(willing invasion) and call them in.  Even then only one Invader can enter a Hosts world when they can have upward of 4 friendlies without opening up the chance for a second hostile phantom.
This is without mentioning an item that turns all enemies on the map hostile towards the invader.  Or the fact the invader must retrieve thier Souls from the location they died in the other world.  PvP just feels so empty and frustrating.  80% of the time you'll be fighting a 3v1 Battle which stunts one of the most important aspects of the Dark souls series, replayability.  Even in PvE there is virtually no replayability, you can beat the game hundreds of times.  With each defeat of the final boss you can enter a NG+ where the enmies gain slightly more health and damage.  But that's it...you can find rings that are improved versions of lesser ones, but that only stretches to NG+2 before hitting a cap when the upgraded Rings themselves offer little benefit over the base ones.
Once you've played through the game once, that's it, there's nothing else left to see...
Even when the DLC drops I have no intention of returning unless it is absolutely phenominal.  I regret buying the Season Pass.
I understand Miyazaki (The founder and crator of the Souls series) wanted it to end here, but it shouldn't feel that way..
I've followed the series since Demons Souls was brought to North America by Atlas.  I've loved the series as a whole and played thousands of hours in it.  Yet just as the first flame is dying, this game lacks a spark.  It's just a husk, and I feel nothing but disappointment in how it is ending..
With that said, I can't recommend this game.  Yes, I played hundreds of hours in it, but that should only make my point stronger.  Very little of all that time was I genuinely enjoying myself instead of struggling to find something to like in a series that has been a part of my life for almost a decade.
Much like the Warrior of Firelink Shrine and his DS3 clone.  I'm simply...Crestfallen.

Alright, it's been over a year. About time I write a review for this game.
At the time of writing, I have 488 hours logged on steam. But by my estimate, the actual number should be around 600 hours because I played for a few months in offline mode to prevent any forced patches from breaking my game.
I'm also not interesting in playing beta tester. I would rather wait until F4SE and other mods are updated before patching the game.
About rating, I'm going to give this game a thumbs up because I obviously got my money's worth in play time.
(And I'm not even done with the game yet. I'm taking a break, after which I plan to resume playing my evil melee character.)
However, I wish I could give it a neutral recomendation instead.
This game has been plagued with issues since day one.
I'm actually one of the lucky one's on this regard. Some people can't even start it even today...
Anyway for a few months around the start of 2016 the CTD's got so bad the game became unplayable.
Then around May, if I recall correctly, one of the patches managed to bring the CTD's back to manageable levels.
One per day at most.
I've had a lot of fun with the DLC's since. In fact, I think Automatron, Far Harbour and Nuka World really helped redeem the game as far as freedom of choice is concerned.
That's a big problem with the base game. It's not really possible to play a consistently evil character without the DLC's.
They really screwed up on that one... what I do is I mostly play a sarcastic♥♥♥♥♥♥and I try to rationalize that atitude into the personality I made for the character.
Anyway, let's do pro's and con's and wrap this review.
Pro's:
- Art direction is good, unfortunately the game needs mods, ini tweeks and enb or reshade for the excelence of the art to show.
- Guns are fun to use.
- World is really dense with tons of places to explore. They clearly put a lot of effort into this.
- Interesting followers. My favorite is Cait.
- All lines are voiced. I'm actually in the minority that enjoys having a voiced portagonist, despite the issues it causes.
- Strong modding community.
Con's:
- Game looks bad without mods, ini tweeks and enb or reshade. And the shadows look atrocious until they are fixed with ini tweaks.
- I don't enjoy using melee weapons outside of V.A.T.S. I feel like they are too stiff. They don't offer enough attack variations to be fun. Not to me anyway.
- Ocasional CTD's.
- The rainbow textures bug on AMD GPU's. Not game breaking but unimmersive as f*ck.
- Hard to play anything but a goodie goodie boy scout without the DLC's.
- Only 4 choices in conversations. Not to mention the simplification of the choices. Thank god for mods...
- Main quest motives are weak. I have no reason to care about Shaun.
Very good game!!!

The pluses
+Improved Combat System
+Voice acting
+Weapon Customization
+The Game’s factions
+NPC Followers I actually like and care about
+The Mods, so much modding
+Hours of playable content
+Hair physics
The Minuses
-Mass effect dialog wheel that doesn’t reflect what you’re character says
-Glitchy graphics that take forever to load in high res textures, or fail to load them in at all
-Glitchy and buggy everything else (typical Bethesda game)
-The game occasionally strong arms you into doing quests and picking sides with no real warning.
-Settlement system not well implemented.
Is it flawed?  Yes but is it terrible?  Not by a long shot, fact I think this has been my favorite Fallout game so far.  And yes I said my favorite Fallout game, despite what others would say about this not being a “True Fallout Game” simply because they don’t like some of the mechanics.  This game stays very true to the lore of the franchise, even with some of the more absurd bits, like Vault Experiments.
Sure there were some stumbles here and there, like the settlement system, and the Mass Effect Dialog tree.
But for me there where definitely more hits then misses.
For starters the combat system is a hell of a lot better, and a lot more fun this time around, VATS is still effective, but a non-vats run is quite doable.
Though the story is a bit rushed and sputters a little at the beginning I ultimately felt the main story here, inspired by the likes of Blade Runner, Terminator, and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep, better then the one found in Fallout 3 or Skyrim.  I found the narrative about the nature of AI quite compelling, and each of the three main factions has valid points about their positions.
Taking a cue from such games as The Witcher, Dragon Age, and of course Bethesda Studios own work on past Elder Scrolls games, the game does away with a measurable morality system and offers no easy answers.  It ultimately leaves the “right thing” open to your interpretation
The voiced protagonist decision was certainly a controversial one, but I think, while it would fail in a game like Elder Scrolls, it works in a Fallout game, both Taylor’s and Delaney’s voice work is superb, to point you may find yourself doing a male and female playthrough.  Just to here they’re different reactions.
Rolling Skills into perks was also a controversial decision, but I think it helps to put more emphasis on the SPECIAL attribute system, and helps deal with the master of everything issue, something that 3 and New Vegas had problems with.  Sure you could still take every perk eventually, but odds are you’ve finished the main quest and most side quest long before that happens.
All in all, it has it’s issues, but if you want an action packed game that provides hundreds of hours of exploration, you can’t go wrong with this one.

If you're a diehard Fallout fan all the way back from Fallout 1, then this probably isn't the game for you. Bethesda made this into more of one of their open-world FPS games and less of what Interplay did for it with the RPG aspects. Way less.
BUT I'm not at all saying this game isn't good. It's actually really fun. The story is great, the graphics are great, the guns, the enemies, the characters, the voice acting are all great. The perk system is... okay! They removed putting in skill points into certain skills such as "Guns" and "Barter" etc. You just point points into perks now. It's probably my main gripe about the game, but it didn't stop me from replaying the game about 4 times. The Settlement system is okay too. Nothing spectacular (in fact, you probably need to add mods to make it really good) but it's something new and interesting to work with the game.
The DLC's are better than you may think. They aren't as great as New Vegas' 4 story DLC's, buuuuut at least two of these DLC's are very story driven with totally new maps involved, and the other two add some story, but also add very cool stuff to the game. Customize your own ROBOTS. Build your own VAULT. Sweetness.
So yeah, there's more to talk about, but the other reviews got that covered. Give the game a chance. It still has some of that Fallout charm. If it goes on sale, definitely consider picking up the base game. There's enough stuff to do in the base game that you don't even need the DLC's. (Buy them though. They're good!)

"Ironically Hollow" is how I'd describe the last addition to the Dark Souls series.
Sure you do the same old thing, gotta link that fire...and that's it.
In the last games it had truly memorable and landscape where the Lore was easy to tease out without excessive digging to at the very least have a general feel.
In this final incarnation there are very forgettable characters and unfortunately no lore to speak of..
Where would Hollow apply then?
In short, the Games combat mechanics are solid and functional.  Not quite the same as the last games but it works.
But that's just it.  There's only the gameplay, there's only the combat.  There is no true gratification for completion of a Goal in this game, only relief it's done..
There's no lore, items or real NPC's to call it's own, just borrowed assets and a disgusting excess of fanservice for the first game.
I feel nothing for my character or his intereactions.  There's only 2 NPC's in the entire game I give a half♥♥♥♥♥♥about and only one of them is original to this game alone instead of a fanservice Clone.
PvE (Player versus environment) works fine and is simply enough.  A few enemies and placements feel utterly unfair and/or cheap with either excessive numbers or limitless attacks.  But overall it is manageable with a little practice and memorization to the point of triviality.
However, PvP (Player versus Player) has always been one of the bigger selling points of these games and here is one of the biggest shortcomming of this Game.  If you invade the game has slanted victory to the side of the Host as it should be, but they went much too far.  The invader will have a 30% reduction of thier max hp when entering someones world (this i'm fine with), yet the more Phantoms a Host has the more priority they have to be invaded.
If you're alone you can go hours without seeing a single invader unless you find a red sign(willing invasion) and call them in.  Even then only one Invader can enter a Hosts world when they can have upward of 4 friendlies without opening up the chance for a second hostile phantom.
This is without mentioning an item that turns all enemies on the map hostile towards the invader.  Or the fact the invader must retrieve thier Souls from the location they died in the other world.  PvP just feels so empty and frustrating.  80% of the time you'll be fighting a 3v1 Battle which stunts one of the most important aspects of the Dark souls series, replayability.  Even in PvE there is virtually no replayability, you can beat the game hundreds of times.  With each defeat of the final boss you can enter a NG+ where the enmies gain slightly more health and damage.  But that's it...you can find rings that are improved versions of lesser ones, but that only stretches to NG+2 before hitting a cap when the upgraded Rings themselves offer little benefit over the base ones.
Once you've played through the game once, that's it, there's nothing else left to see...
Even when the DLC drops I have no intention of returning unless it is absolutely phenominal.  I regret buying the Season Pass.
I understand Miyazaki (The founder and crator of the Souls series) wanted it to end here, but it shouldn't feel that way..
I've followed the series since Demons Souls was brought to North America by Atlas.  I've loved the series as a whole and played thousands of hours in it.  Yet just as the first flame is dying, this game lacks a spark.  It's just a husk, and I feel nothing but disappointment in how it is ending..
With that said, I can't recommend this game.  Yes, I played hundreds of hours in it, but that should only make my point stronger.  Very little of all that time was I genuinely enjoying myself instead of struggling to find something to like in a series that has been a part of my life for almost a decade.
Much like the Warrior of Firelink Shrine and his DS3 clone.  I'm simply...Crestfallen.

As a product in and of itself, Dark Souls III is excellent. Were it not for the monumentally stupid decision to remove poise, the fundamentals of the game would be by far the best in the series. Actions are faster, recovery seems more natural, healing is back to just being estus flasks, and magic uses a pretty ingenius mixture of the Demon's Souls mana bar and the estus flask system. Covenants no longer require a ring slot and can be switched out at anytime. The game is beautiful, with significantly darker coloration and lighting than Dark Souls 2. DS3 also gets rid of one of my least favorite aspects of DS2, the terribly ugly font. (The menu system is a bit worse, though not by a particularly noticeable margin.)
The level design is for the most part great. Even when it is not quite so great, it is leagues above the worst levels in DS1/DS2. Enemy placement seems to have finally returned to a more natural and fair level--in DS3 you regularly fight more than 6 enemies at once, but it never feels quite as ridiculous as it was in DS2 because the enemies are designed with this in mind. I should note however that some enemies break this mold, and that is not the only thing that they break. There are a small handful of enemies in the game that seem to blatantly ignore collision and conventional movement mechanics, which can make them seem unfair. This is most noticeable in the game's various dogs, which constantly clip into walls. There was even one point where I was exploring an area above a basement and a dog floated through the ceiling of the basement and jumped at me. I have a screenshot of an instance where I was playing with my friend and a Valkyrie enemy literally spun himself right into the inside of a wall and got permanently stuck. I would accept this kind of thing in a game like New Vegas, which has a more humorous universe, but in a game like Dark Souls, this lack of polish is kind of shocking. It's like the gargoyles in Anor Londo from DS1--if they didn't fly right, why put them in the game at all. In spite of this I would still say DS3 has better enemies than any of the other souls games. The Evangelists, Irythlll swordswomen and Demon Pyromancers being particularly capable and enjoyable enemies to fight.
It's only with perspective of the previous games that DS3 reveals some pretty pervasive flaws. Tonally, the game is a complete mess. Dark Souls 1 was about a world crumbling to dust, Dark Souls 2 was about desolation and the hopelessness of an endless curse. After finishing it and all it's side-content, I...honestly don't know what Dark Souls 3 was about. Areas have vastly different stories and justifications, which is good, but also bad--it literally feels like you're walking through entirely different worlds, which is not helped by the linear world design. NPC stories are complete absurdity, the only character in the entire game that mostly acts within reasonable standards is Siegward, who is quite literally Siegmeyer with a different name. I would be more ok with this if the NPCs were vendor-lobotomites like Majula in DS2, but not only is it a chore to even
your vendors, but many of them can actually reach a
state of being by completing their questline. This includes the "good" endings. I can very well imagine people never finding the miracle vendor during their first playthrough, they are so out of the way that it is outright ridiculous. (More reason to believe that From hates Faith builds, I guess.) The hex vendor is also extraordinarily difficult to find, though I can at least understand this as hexes are supposed to be end-game level spells.
The game seems to want the player to spend a long period of time around the Firelink Shrine, which is why you can only level up at the firekeeper unlike DS1. This is also the likely reasoning for why there are far more bonfires in this game than any other souls title. Yes, even DS2. Tension is effectively murdered by this. And for what, I wonder? The Firelink Shrine is very annoying to navigate, significantly worse than the hub worlds in any of the previous game. Walls are everywhere which makes it hard to ever get a complete grasp of where the vendors are. I should also mention that the Firekeeper in DS3 is by far the worst hub lady in the series. I am starting to get very tired of this archtype, they rarely offer anything at all other than things the player should already be able to do.
Speaking of archtypes, I don't actually mind the "fanservice" in the game, which is a common complaint. I don't exactly think it's brilliant storytelling, but for the most part the archtypes in the game are clear improvements to the characters they orignated from. Hawkwood is the only Crestfallen Warrior in the series that I can actually tolerate.
If this really is the last Souls game, I can understand Miyazaki wanting to give some finality to his favorite creations. The stuff that
new in the game is extremely compelling. Nearly all of the bosses in the game have excellent environmental storytelling. I also loved that all of the bosses in the game, even the really bizzare ones, had a clear impact on the world around them. This compared to DS2's constant feeling of "Why am I fighting this guy again?"

Over all a fun Fallout game that has potential to be a good time sink should it suit you. The gun play part of the game seems to be pretty solid, Though I can not attest to melee builds my self. Being able to upgrade and improve your weapons and armor as you level and skill up lets your gear improve with you and last longer, can keep your favorites around for a long time.  Mod support helps to extend time of enjoyment by adding to the game as well as fixing it up or correcting what you feel was done wrong when it was made.

Pros and cons below, take them as you will.
Pros.
Good amount of open world land area to explore and find missions to do in.
Gun play over all seems clean and well done, for a non shooter it is good.
Supports different play styles and builds to get the job done.
Some of the story missions are good and make you feel you did something.
The settlement system works pretty good and lets you make a base or home to your liking.
Classic physics bugs still a plenty, They can be super funny and good for a laugh.
Skill point system is pretty good, You can after enough time max all options and gives many ways to boost your self as you level up and play the game.
Cons.
The RPG side of Fallout 4 is lack luster over all (feels gutted) and the speech options are just as bad.
Having a voiced player character can take away from feeling YOU are the one going about the wasteland.
The classic glitches that can be loved also exist as the bad, get stuck in walls, floors, game freezes, crashes, Etc. Save and save often.
Personally the main core game story arc was less fun then some of the side missions.
The colors used in Far Harbor DLC are ... the wrong shades of green and grey.
Load screens for such small dungeons seems very out of place these days.
Texture load distance for high res seems to not happen far enough away, billboards are a good example ~20 feet to see high res.
The game engine needs to die and a new one made, It had its time but it is showing its age and slapping more bits onto it is not viable anymore.

Let me Preface with this
I am a huge fan of Dark Souls and Bloodborne, (I've sunk well over 1k hours into each) I have played the second DS and didn't like it (Big suprise) and was looking forward to this one with optimisim and was hugely dissappointed
Dark Souls 3 Is unbalanced
I feel as if I am playing an early build where tweaking and rebalancing is in its early stages,
Keep in mind
I have multiple max all stat (all 99) characters I went to NG+9 and invested many hours into this game
(Note I do not have very much PVP experience but I do have some. I am mostly reffering to Offline play in this review)
1) Poise is non existant and worthless.
Poise was a major factor in combat in DS 1. It allowed you to take hits without being staggered; if you had a high enough poise value. This allowed you to effectively trade blows with Mobs and Players. You could initiate an attack and not be staggered during the animation. Hyper armor is present in DS3 but it's situational at best. This leads to stunlock gameplay. The best/ultimate/only viable strategy for PvE is to equip all light armor and a weapon with good range and wide sweeping attacks to stagger every enemy in the vacinity and stun lock all of them. I.E. in the Boreal valley I used all light armor and the Wolf knight Great Sword to stagger ever enemy encounter before they staggered me and I got through the area unscathed. However if I tried to use heavier armor and trade blows I would loose everytime. So why bother using heavy armor at all? This brings up two more issues. Sheilds being useless, and enemy aggression/overall combat pacing.
2)Shields.
Sheilds have alway been a very usefull offensive and defensive item in previous souls games. The ability to throw up a shield and block an attack was invaluable. Enemy's blows could bounce off your shield and staggr your opponent creating an opening for you. Depending on the sheild taking a blow would not consume much stamina. However in DS3 I was onlyable to take 2 or 3 hits before my gaurd was broken on most normal sheilds. Thiswouldn't be a problem if the enemies werent so aggressive, but more on thatlater. The offensive side to sheilds in previous souls games in the Parry/Riposte Mechanic which also suffers in this game. I mastered Parrying in DS1 and as a result I could combat most enemies no problem. However in this game the parrying is almost entirely luck based. Enemies swing so quickly parrying is very difficult to perform. Especially when enemies have multi hit combos. Combined with the lack of poise and the stamina cosumed in blocking, screwing up a parry can cost you a fight. Great sheilds are also usless. They too consume a great amount of stamina when blocking attacks leading to frequent guard breaks.
3) Enemy Aggression
This is more of a personal opinion but I feel it still holds weight. Enemies are much more aggressive than they have ever been in a souls game. many enemies have multihit combos that result in the player being stunlocked due to the lack of poise. blocking does not help because your guard breaks easily. Rolling is the only efficient method to combat. Armor and sheilds are way to underpowered to deal with the aggressive enemies of DS3
All of these issues lead to only one viable playstyle. Light rolling, and heavy weapons. Using Heavy armor is pointless as it yields no benefit. Shields can only block a few attacks at best before your guard is broken so why bother with them. The lack of poise leads to a stunlock gameplay.
It feels as if I am playing bloodborne with a Souls skin. From should have made another bloodborne since they obviously wanted to
4)Map design
What is porbably my favorite design feature of DS 1 was the intricate map design. The waps were wooven together vertically which allowed for shortcuts and hidden passage ways. it was really interesting to explore the map and see how it folded back in on itself and how it flowed. Just the oter day I was playing DS 1 through again and I noticed that you can see Lost Izalith from the Tomb of The Giants bonfire. It made the map feel titly knit and jammed packed. Being forced to explore the map and every nook and cranny due to the inability to fast travel early on made me very familliar with themap. I now have it memorizeed like the back of my hand and can navigate it very quickly. However DS3 is rather linear. The map doesnt come together and suprise you like DS1 did. Its not a major issue I'm Just dissappointed slightly
5) Hub World
DS2 and 3 adopted a HUB approach to the game design. they forced you to return to a certain area to level up, upgrade weapons, and to purchase items. While in DS3 merchants, blacksmiths, andbonfires were all over the map. You could all your weapon upgrading, repairs, and leveling up from any bonfire. This allowed the game to flow and didnt interupt the exploration at all.
