As a Souls veteran I came into this game with a degree of skepticism. The second game was a love hate sort of thing for me. While it was fun there was always this nagging feeling that it just wasn't pure Dark Souls. While I had loved melee combat in 1. In 2 I was almost afraid of it. Add in how OP magic was in 2 and I quickly turned into a 300+ lightning spear slinging mess. I had a massive great sword that was for show. The real danger was the chime in my left hand. Then here comes 3 and I have to say it was a really good return to my Dark Souls roots. The combat harkens back to the first game and with it came my love of melee combat. It is where this game shines. At first there was some rust but as I play more the instincts and skills have started to come back. I feel like I haven't missed a beat. Which is what made 2 so frustrating. It was like re learning how to walk in this new and very odd feeling mess. If you loved 1's combat this is for you. The only thing that I find lacking is the level design. In the 1st one the whole world is interconnected in multiple places. You can get to multiple places from different areas. The game is stacked vertically not laid out horizontally. 3's map is very linear. There really isn't much deviation. Just follow the path an you'll get there. The only place I found disorienting was Farrons Keep. Other than that it is really easy to find out where to go.

So I sort of took an unintentional break from this game because of many other releases that have come out that I have also been looking forward to but once I came back it drew me in again.  Plus the addition of the DLCs are making it more of a time suck. I can't get enough of this game.  Yeah it sucks that the devs decided modding the game (even if it's to make it look better) shuts down the achievements but there are ways around that now.  I just wish I had more time to invest in all of my games I'm currently working on.  Such is life.

Fallout 4 was my first introduction to the Fallout franchise, but I think it was a good one. The story was amazing and I always have that tug to play it over and over again. The acheievements created a challenge, (and I still haven't managed to 100% them) a challenge I was willing to take on, and it was fun! Fallout 4 wasn't too hard nor was it too easy. I truly enjoyed the building mechanic, and I could just build for hours on hours if I had the time. Dark Souls is the Elvis of modern gaming. Not like Elvis at the end, but right around the peak. They found their formula, they refined it about as far as they can go, picking and choosing everything so it all comes together into something quite a lot of people like. They experimented and tweaked and worked with feedback to keep things fresh and satisfying.
But I think From knows how that song and dance goes. That's why this is the last one, and I'm glad for that. Plenty of people may still want more of this, and I can perfectly understand why. It's fun, it's solid, it's got some real creativity in it. But we've had more of this. Lots more.
I love this game and this series, and that's why I'm glad this is the last one. It's great to end on a high note, and I can't wait to see what From decides to do next.

In this review:
I'm addressing the only aspects of the game I think are the best. For all other things you think the game has and what to read about, or a pros n cons type of review, you came to the wrong place.
I had one big problem with Dark Souls 1 and Dark Souls 2. Neither of them managed to mantain an above average level of interestingness throu out the whole game (at least for me). They had great innovating ideas as for the storytelling strategy goes, being them based on an enviormental way of selling the information needed to understand the lore behind the events happening at the moment. We all know those games had a great gameplay mechanic quirk that worked all game long, but it felt really repetitive. whether you started the game at Firelink Shrine or Anor Londo, the moveset nor the general look of the enemies changed much. Don't get mistaken, the lore behind those in-game places was astonishing, but the picture behind was over used throu out the game. In conclusion, they both needed variety on enemies.
Dark Souls III completly change that fact, and to an amazing result. It not only had tons of different character models for all enemies in games, they also had completly different movesets, forcing you to spend time or patience understanding them all. That, plus the new hyper bloodborne-type game speed, made this game a different type of difficulty. Before, after dying a few times to the same enemies, you understood there was nothing to do other than keep dying until you get how to win, or farm ultil you get the level to continue. In this game, the speed makes the learning curve really faster, and the enemies variety makes it more interesting than before. Basically, It makes failure interesting
Hope this addressed topic is of use to you. I tried to speak about something new.

Well, it looks like From Software never gave us the balancing that this game needed nor did they do anything with their optimization issues, and instead just continued building on the existing metas ignoring the other balancing issues.  None of the issues I name below were ever fixed.  As such, I am changing my tentative negative to a permanent negative review of this game.  Avoid DS3 to save your sanity (especially multiplayer), play DS1 instead.  Its still better than DS2 though.
Short version:  The brainchild of Dark Souls and Bloodbourne, with all the positives and negatives that come with it.
At this time, this review exists to only talk about my major grievences of the game which currently need updates.  The review will be updated to be positive once these issues are fixed.  Game balancing in regards to previous titles is sort of broken at the moment.  Its like the game was released without testing multiplayer or ingame balancing first.  Basically, I'm waiting for balancing fixes and currently the game, while fun, is not in a satisfying state.
Some things of note:
1) Poise is heavily altered from the traditional "hit-stun resistance" to "i-frame-loss resistance."  Many enemies already have insanely high natural hitstun resistance, making singleplayer quite frustrating given how easily you can get stunned yourself.  In multiplayer, hitstun has become a major issue because every weapon in the game, regardless of hit power, can stumble on hit, allowing few animations except on the heavier weapons to complete.  Faster hitting weapons have huge advantages because they can chainstun.  Currently whoever hits first with the faster hitting weapon has a massive, massive advantage.
2) The meta (straight swords) is so strong and so easily reached it outclasses most other weapons by large margins.  This is largely due to the problems with hitstun.  Most players only use the meta at the moment.
3) Sorceries, miracles, and to some extent pyromancies have been extremely nerfed in this game.  Balancing in regards to them in even just single player is ridiculous.  The main issue is that most enemies in the game are faster than in previous installments, leaving less downtime for casting spells.  Its especially big an issue on boss fights.  Another major issue is that spell strength scaling has changed; most spells are very weak until late game and require very heavy stat investment, and even still most spells are useless.
4) Optimization is relatively poor and the game suffers massive memory leaks.  The game is also a HUGE memory hog and unless you have more than 8 gigs of memory you will probably be throttling the game through your hard drive.
5) Given the game is around release and the balancing on the game, a large part of the playerbase is currently engaging in "dishonorable" behavior.  It is not recommended to play at this time because of that.
6) The PvP system doesn't really work anymore because of some major inherent design flaws. A) The police force against invaders is dependent on being able to invade and protect a player while the invasion is happening, instead of previous systems where players with sin (invaders) were invaded (by the police) to be punished for their sin.  This makes it very, very hard to be summoned as a blue phantom; its simply a matter of being too context sensitive resulting in a low number of positive hits for being summoned, with a large number of players that want to be summoned all at the same time.  B) Many areas with auto-invade covenants, such as Watchdogs of Farron and Aldritch Faithful are only really going to get invasions within set level ranges, and outside of those level ranges invasions will likely be into heavily white phantomed worlds. C) The main method a player has for defending themselves from invasions is to summon as many white phantoms as they possibly can, and there is no penalty for doing so.  Unfortunately, this almost always results in ganks.
This review will be changed to positive once these issues are addressed.  Rest assured, these issues are slowly being fixed by the devs and I am confident they will all be addressed.  The only real issue is just waiting for that to happen, so at this time I say wait a bit before buying.

When i first purchased dark souls 3, i couldn't contain my hype.
I had watched hours upon hours of lore videos, and played countless hours in the original game.
After beating the emotional rollercoaster that was the massive open world
of DS1, I booted up the third game and was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants with wonder at the nods to the first game and the detailed areas. As the game progressed however, my excitement soon turned to disgust.
The open world of dark souls which made it such a unique yet difficult experience is a tradition not held by it's successors. Where DS1 felt like a true grand adventure in a massive interconnecting world filled with peril at every turn, the constant warping to other areas and back to firelink has made this entire game linear and a
. Look at any area map for this game and compare it to that of the first: you travel in a straight line to your final objective of rekindling the fire, boom pow good job everyone goes home. DS1 however,  kept basic linear traits but allowed experienced players to explore a MASSIVE world at their own PACE. It taught those that ventured too far that that wasn't the right way, and didn't spoon feed players in progression nearly as hard as this third installment. For some, this may be a personal thing, but i quickly lost interest in secondary runs because of the inability to mix up my adventure.
The game features overhauled, quicker gameplay in spirit of the PS4 exclusive bloodborne, which is both an advancement and a burden. Some, including myself as an ultra greatsword wielder, feel like the game is balanced towards fast swinging weapons (due to the "removal" of poise cough cough), and personally i found a secondary playthrough with a longsword alone let me breeze through the game. My ultragreatsword "Guts" build struggled considerably with the removal of pancaking and his incredibly slow attacks, and both PvP and PvE to be a living hell. It's clear that miracles and spells, favorites of mine from the original, have little to NO use and deal minimal damage unless a fragile, pure build for their stats are made, making fun and interesting hybrid builds, which the game even encourages at the character creation screen, useless.
I pushed onwards however, and wound up at the end of my linear path only to be plauged with something that made me have to uninstall the game entirely.
While it may be a personal problem, it appears i am not the only one. Between computer freezes, graphics card crashes, sound crackling, and sometimes outright broken controller inputs, the game ran like complete♥♥♥♥♥on my far from poor computer configuration. My PvE sunbro character was BANNED from online due to constant freezing and crashing due to the poor optimization. These issues have apparently been addressed, but the sour taste left in my mouth after experiencing the unbalanced and downright unplayable launch period makes me have no strive to boot up the game again.
Despite these cons, the game was remarkably impressive within the first few hours: the first boss alone had my heart racing with his swift and excellently animated attacks. Seeing the new firelink for the first time blew me away, and as i took things slow i learned the story of those i killed, and in the end found myself an errandboy yes, but an errandboy of destiny. If one looks close enough, the substance and depth of previous souls games IS there. In the stories and the small details of lore left behind in item descriptions and the land itself. Some may say the game relies heavily on the nostalgia of the first game, and in that sense they aren't wrong: it does. But seeing the world of DS1 evolve after countless links to the fire still holds a sense of wonder. The streamlined combat is fluid and fun depending on weapon choice, and seeing the new areas is a blast to experience.
Replayability however, is non existant.
Nonetheless, i simply can't reccomend this game to either first timers OR veterans. The adventure has faded just like the flame, and FROM seeks to grasp the flickering embers and rekindle the fire. In my personal opinon they have failed in their mission, creating a husk of their previous work as a last attempt to creating something the fans would enjoy.
Yet they walk away from a fire filled with unbalanced PvP, hackers softbanning people, and an unpolished world that I personally hope they will correct with the upcoming DLC.
If you are a souls newcomer, Demon's and the original Dark Souls are must plays. If you are hungering for more, feel free to pick up the second or this game. However, I can't say they wont leave you with a bad taste in your mouth to end the series out, for they certainly have left one in mine.

Dark Souls is one of those things that many already have formulated some kind of opinion on already, good or bad.  If you are truly new to the series though it probably would be worth your time to play the others first, as there are moments that you will appreciate more with a bit of context.
For the people that have been down this road before, there are  things you may want to know:
As you may have heard -- poise has changed.  This could be a big thing or it may not affect you at all if you gravitate toward caster or lightly armored builds.  No longer can you trust in heavy♥♥♥♥♥armour to protect you from staggering.  Supposedly it helps hyper-armor (the heavy weapon attack animation invincibility, it think?) but that is currently up for debate.  All we know is that the dev’s aren’t going to change it.
If you played 2: Pyromancy is the new Hex, enjoy!  If you  haven’t (played 2), maybe don’t bother getting any pyromancy spells because they are very stat-dependant now: Faith and Int.  So instead invest in a crossbow and bolts; that is probably going to be a better selection for ranged attacks if you are not going to invest in other stats.  Bows and arrows are still pretty great... poison arrows less so.
The game is faster but not unbearably so.  Just dodge more and you’re fine.  Learn to run-in attack, and roll out instead of hanging around the boss’ backside.  Also remember that the poise problem does more or less go both ways,  It is easier to stagger some enemies than it may appear, just watch for the big wind-ups (as it won’t commonly stop them).
As always prepare for frustration, glory, and a lot of creepy laughing.

Dark Souls III is my favourite game in the series (just), but I will try to be as objective as possible when listing my positives and negatives of the game:
Pros:
- Enemy Diversity: One major fault of Dark Souls II was that all the enemies were pretty similar, this is because all enemies were practically at their core dudes in armour; whilst there was some variety (dragons and giants ect.) the majority of enemies were very similar. However this is not the case in Dark Souls III as enemies feel very distinct and also fit the area they're located in well.
- NPC's: The NPC's in Dark Souls III are very interesting and have other applications than "dude who sells magic" ect. these NPC's also have intersting questlines, that thankfully don't include killing lots of bosses with said NPC (I'm looking at you DS2). NPC's also pop up throughout the game and you're not limiting to only finding NPC's in locations near the starting location, these leads to a continually exciting storyline where multiple puzzles must be figured out to unlock all vendors and NPC's. Furthermore NPC's are interesting with developed storylines that engage the player.
- Locations: The locations in Dark Souls III are generally interesting and fully developped with multiple entwining routes and difficult puzzles to solve; I feel that the areas are sometimes quite small, but this is made up by the multiple routes that need to be taken to fully discover an area. However there is one area I find dull and boring, and that area is called the Catacombs of Carthus - to me it feels dull and there are little discerning features to its many hallways and therefore it is easy to get lost and lose track of what is going on. This is a minor gripe, as I feel this fault is made up comepletely by the other areas, as the others are beautifull and feel right at home in the Dark Souls universe. Another positive of the locations is the sheer effort that goes into optional areas: it is nice to see so much effort put into areas such as Archdragon Peak that most players will miss, and this shows a total dedication in creating a vibrant world on FromSoft's part.
- Music: The music in Dark Souls III feels suitably epic for the occasion, whether it be uncovering unique locations or fighting a challeging boss.
- Fashion Souls: For me (and many other players), much of the enjoyment of a Souls game stems from the ability to create cool looking characters. Dark Souls III readily supplies us "Fashion Soulers" with a large supply of weapons and armour combinations to work with, as well as indepth character creation that allows a huge number of different looking characters to be made.
- Replayability: Most importantly for me, Dark Souls III has many different playstyles and branching storylines to complete that make me want to continually experiment and I have already racked up a total of five complete games so far (more to come)! PvP also represents a huge part of replayability for me, this is because after fighting the same bosses multiple times they become predictable this is not true with PvP, this is because players are always coming up with new and interesting builds and it is fun to test different builds to see how they work.
Now onto the cons:
- PvP feels oversimplified: Whilst I did mention how much I enjoy the PvP of Dark Souls III earlier, I do feel that many of the great features included in previous games have been removed. One thing I enjoyed in Dark Souls II was the dual weilding feature as I felt that this gave builds lots of variety and meant that moveset was often more important than damage. Also in Dark Souls III the poise function is severly limited and I think it only really affects i-frames for roling (or something like that) this limits the functionality of heavy armour as the only really affect resistances and absorption now, since heavy armour require a large stat investment it is now much better to stick with lighter armour as the investment required to use heavy armour is not worth it anymore.
- Overall the game feels more "new player" friendly: Anyone who has played the origional Dark Souls will remember the infamous graveyard, which was full of high level enemies and placed right next to the main hub of the game, this meant that new players often spent ages battling hordes of powerful skeletons before realising that a much easier path existed that lead you to where the game actually wanted you to go. However in Dark Souls III there is the introduction to a hub area disconnected to the rest of the world (like the Nexus in Demon Souls) and from that location you can only warp to one location which is full of enemies designed for your level. In fact the only way I think you can raise the difficulty by progressing to an area would be to activate a shortcut to the Dancer boss. Another point about how the game is easier to learn is the removal of armour leveling, in previous titles to had to upgrade your armour alongside your weapons whereas that feature is removed in Dark Souls III. Perhaps the idea behind this is to encourage players to experiment with armour, however I dislike this as I feel any mistakes you made in chosing what to upgrade you should be stuck with (or grind your way out of).
- Lack of an interconnected world: Whilst I mentioned that the idividual locations were all unique and interesting they feel stabled onto each other and not representitive of a world. In Dark Souls I you would be always discovering shortcuts and passages between locations, whereas whilst there are shortcuts in Dark Souls III (a lot of them in fact) they are often localised to one area and do not allow travel between locations. Part of the problem I believe is the use of immediate bonfire warping, as this means players are not continually travelling between locations and there is not that much of a need to make all the locations fit together, coupled with a world withouht that many multiple paths each playthrough will generally take you in the same route.
- Fan Service: This could really go in either pros or cons: Dark Souls III includes references to multiple souls games and even uses location already explored in Dark Souls I (albiet with empathise on a different part of that location). Ultimately the references in the game could either awe you are leave you unsatisfied with the lack of new content (although there is a lot of that). Whilst I believe the references to other games don't detract from the experience others may think otherwise, so I decided to include this in my review.
Overall however I believe Dark Souls III is a great game and builds upon the postitives of all souls games (and bloodborne), and whilst it will never be as interconnected as the origional Dark Souls it more than makes up for that in fast combat coupled with weapon and armour variety.

Dark souls 3 is a fitting end to the dark souls series. I personally enjoyed it more than 2, and possibly more than the original. However, for as good of a game as it is, it is not without faults. PVP at the moment  is not as balanced as DS2, there is a distinct lack of a poise mechanic that makes heavy weapons less viable. There are fewer viable weapons in general in Dark Souls 3, which seems to me to be a return to Dark Souls 1 in a bad way.
However, despite a couple shortcomings this game is fantastic. Hitboxes for the most part feel smooth and perfect (I had an arrow go in-between my legs without hitting me), it is visually stunning in places, and combat is still as smooth as souls fans expect. In fact, combat in 3 is more fast paced, more akin to bloodborne, which kind of adds an extra element of difficulty to those souls fans who haven't played bloodborne. The game also has some  of the most memorable boss fights in all of the souls games. If you're a souls fan on the fence on whether to buy it: Do it.

This game is so close to being good, but just isn't. It has so many issues with it that it's inexcusable. You can have fun with it, there are good parts to it, but it's just overwelmingly covered with issues and bad design that all the fun or accomplishment you would feel just turns to frustration and tedium.
I'm not going to bother with the good, it's there and it's nothing new from the last games. Other people have already said the good, I'm going to say the bad and why it's not worth it.
1. Camera. It's SO BAD in this game. It just does not work, and you will die SO MANY TIMES because it ♥♥♥♥ed up. And large enemy causes it to freak out and turn oddly, and it's so zoomed in half the time that you can't see what bosses are even doing. In addition to that a lot of regular enemies freak the camera out if you get to close, and cause it to 180 and this not only is disorienty but causes sudden changes to your controls and will easily get you hit/killed. They also have this stupid system called "cinematic camera" on by default that only makes your camera lean forward and lock into place on some attacks. Thankfully you can turn it off.
2.Lock-on. It's crap. Not only is it a short as ♥♥♥♥ range, but it just randomly unlocks all the time. Oh man, and enemy walked behind another enemy/lamp post better unlock. Oh man, that enemy slightly jumped, better unlock. Oh hey, you're close to this enemy, better unlock. Lock on goes above your head on a large enemy? Unlock. How in the world did they ♥♥♥♥ this mechanic up so bad?
3.Poise. More then enough has been said about this, it doesn't work past the first point. All that one point does is give you access to your weapons hyper armor (that some have) and nothing else. Litterally that's it, no one has found any proof whatsoever that it does anything more. And all we've gotten from Fromsoftware is "it's working as intended" which I'm sure is just like durability was "working as intended" in DS2.
4.Enemy AI. This is largely a problem because of Poise. Enemies just attack relentlessly, over and over and over without stop, and with barely any (if any in some cases) openings to hit back. Enemies get their own poise because "♥♥♥♥ you", or just randomly break out of flinching cause why not and endlessly attack you. It's boring and frustraiting. Several bosses, are just walls because they never stop attacking. Ever. Every little hit stuns you making these enemies more frustraiting than they need to be.
5.Boss tells. They're really not there. The game is so fast, that they either don't have tells for most of their attacks or they're so fast and similar that you can't tell before hand. The few tells that are there are for the slowball attacks. This is more a gripe than an issue, but still. You more have to guess than actually know what attack a boss will use a good 70% of the time.
6.Armor. You can't upgrade armor in this game, and I really haven't found any armor that's better than stuff you get early on. If anything there's more cosmetic armor than actually decent armor. This would be fine, if even the most common of enemies weren't one shotting me since mid game. I'm not glass cannon either, roughly 1k health with the best armor I can use (without fat rolling) and still bosses easily one shot, and most enemies either do 60% or one shot as well. More often then not it just feels like I'm outstatted rather than killed through a misstake.
7.Online. Two covenants don't even work right now, or at least they don't work for older characters. Maybe they do now. But in addition to that there's a glitch where friendly phantoms can't enter boss doors. It's not even a rare glitch, and there are some bosses where it pretty much always happens from what I've heard/experienced.
8.Parrying. Doesn't work right, half the time even when you do successfully parry (not a partial block/parry, a full fledged knock them back and go into a reposte parry) you still take damage as if you failed. It's not a rare occurance, and it's terrible. In a game where player poise doesn't exist, and enemies spam attacks the one mechanic you could use doesn't work reliably.
9.Shortcuts. All of them, ALL OF THEM, are anything but short. Anytime you die and have to redo a boss, or go back to an area it's an easy 2+min treck back to a boss or an area, and that's if you run past all the enemies.
10.Area size. The game is huge. Areas are huge, and can get very convoluted. For anyone who likes to explore everything and do everything, this quickly becomes annoying and tedious. You will miss things, npc, whole areas, etc beacuse you didn't notice a small thing/something was invisible and will inevitably have to backtrack and try to find it or just miss it forever. It's also great that some mandatory things are hidden past tiny little hidden areas, that's great. What doesn't help is the games almost obsesive tendancy to have areas that slow you down. Forcing you to a walk/fat roll way to travel and wasting even more time in those areas.
This game is easily the worst of the three dark souls games because of these issues. Even the basic systems that worked flawlessly in the last systems are unreliable in this game (camera, lock on). I just can't recommend this, beacuse of all these issues. The game has lost all fun or fullfillment because it never feels like a challenge is hard for the right reasons. The game feels like it was designed with certain mechanics in place and working, and then had them removed on launch. It's just bad.

Dark Souls III is currently the latest game in the Dark Souls series. If this is your first Dark Souls game, you need to know that Dark Souls is well-known for its extremely hard difficulty, frustrating deaths, and slow grinding progress (because you'll lose everything if you fail to retrieve your dropped souls - or 'money'). In short, it's just completely merciless to the player. If you're a hardcore gamer that loves challenges, I heavily recommend this for you. Dark Souls is the type of game where the difficulty overwhelms the fun, so if you're a casual gamer looking to rekt some AIs easily and be a hero that saves the universe - don't buy this game. Know that your character will die a lot in this game. I mean, A LOT. So if you're the type of person that crushes things around you when you're frustrated, I also don't recommend this game for you to save your stuff.
You'll start with creating your character and choosing a class. And then, the slaughtering will start. Arguably overpowered enemies - usually in the form of monsters - will start popping out as you progress through the map and you'll gain 'souls' when you defeat them. You can spend your collected souls as soon as you find some kind of a 'checkpoint', usually in the form of a large area that consists of a blacksmith, a store, a bonfire (respawn point), and an NPC to upgrade your stats. You'll get to purchase weapons, armors, power-ups, stats, etc. in these checkpoints to give you a better fighting chance against the enemies. Each time you die, you'll drop ALL of your collected souls and you'll have to retrieve it the next time you respawn. If you die again, then you'll not be able to retrieve the souls you collected the first time you died. Only the last pack of souls will be dropped and retrievable. When you successfully dominates an 'area', you'll have to beat a boss fight to gain access to the next 'area'. Usually, the bosses are extremely overpowered and it'll take more than 10 retries to beat them. This is basically what you'll do the whole game. Walk - kill enemies - die - grind souls - die - purchase stuff - fight bosses - die - repeat.
Graphics are way better than Dark Souls II. It's really nice to look at and overall, it's great. The main advantage of the game is the difficulty. Some of you, like me, may think "What? Who finds getting killed over and over again, getting frustrated, punching stuff around you, or even throwing your CPU out of the window because you are p*ssed off as 'fun'?". Well, people have different ideas of 'fun'. There are hundreds of thousands or even millions of players that loves the Dark Souls franchise. The overwhelming difficulty is what makes Dark Souls unique. Its PS4-only cousin, Bloodborne, also gained huge attention from gamers due to similar gameplay style. I personally don't find getting killed over and over again or fighting against overpowered enemies as 'fun' but I find the game greatly trains my mentality - it desensitized me from failure, which will be important in my pursue of success. But know this: this game is not all about death and failures. You'll learn how to fight with your brain instead of blindly slashing everywhere. Yes, Dark Souls is skill-based. You'll have to get used on using the roll, heavy slash, light slash, shields, bows, utiliteies, etc. if you want to be able to progress through the game. They are not easy at all to master.
Storyline is confusing. It's best not to put your hope on the story-driven part. The game lacks explanation about the previous installment stories. You can always look at YouTube to catch up with the stories but IMHO, it's not a nicely written story. It's short, lacks details, lacks plot twists, and it's just way too 'mainstream and predictable'. As for the soundtrack, it's empty as usual. I expected epic songs for these kinds of games but apparently, they still think almost-no-soundtracks is good. The overwhelming difficulty itself is NOT a disdvantage - it is purely based on your gaming style preference. The second noticable disadvantage is the lack of new weapons in the shops. I may not have progressed far but when I meet a 'checkpoint',  I couldn't find anything useful in there. I might have to enchant weapons and all but I haven't quite understood the mechanism. Should it be a disadvantage? I don't know. I might be too stupid to understand the whole mechanism in 5 hours or maybe the game itself lacks tutorials for new players that are not familiar with Dark Souls.
It all depends on your gaming preference. Some people enjoy Dark Souls, some people don't. Make sure you look at the gameplay first on YouTube or whatever before purchasing this game just to make sure you won't waste your money. I personally like this game and recommend it for everyone regardless of your gaming preference because everyone needs to be desensitized from failures. But you might think it's not necessary because you already have a super safe life and a tremendous amount of parent's money. Just make sure you watch the gameplay first before purchasing it.

Doesn't work right, half the time even when you do successfully parry (not a partial block/parry, a full fledged knock them back and go into a reposte parry) you still take damage as if you failed. It's not a rare occurance, and it's terrible. In a game where player poise doesn't exist, and enemies spam attacks the one mechanic you could use doesn't work reliably.
9.Shortcuts. All of them, ALL OF THEM, are anything but short. Anytime you die and have to redo a boss, or go back to an area it's an easy 2+min treck back to a boss or an area, and that's if you run past all the enemies.
10.Area size. The game is huge. Areas are huge, and can get very convoluted. For anyone who likes to explore everything and do everything, this quickly becomes annoying and tedious. You will miss things, npc, whole areas, etc beacuse you didn't notice a small thing/something was invisible and will inevitably have to backtrack and try to find it or just miss it forever. It's also great that some mandatory things are hidden past tiny little hidden areas, that's great. What doesn't help is the games almost obsesive tendancy to have areas that slow you down. Forcing you to a walk/fat roll way to travel and wasting even more time in those areas.
This game is easily the worst of the three dark souls games because of these issues. Even the basic systems that worked flawlessly in the last systems are unreliable in this game (camera, lock on). I just can't recommend this, beacuse of all these issues. The game has lost all fun or fullfillment because it never feels like a challenge is hard for the right reasons. The game feels like it was designed with certain mechanics in place and working, and then had them removed on launch. It's just bad.

As a fan of the fallout series, I love this game. Only the controls for building settlements give me a feeling like "this is made for console and not for pc". Besides that, I would definitly recommend this game.

This time around the Wastelannd really feels different, yet there's still something eerily familiar about it. The comabat has been completley overhauled from Fallout 4, it really makes gunfights much more enjoyable. The whole game seems to be a smoother experience, even the way you loot has been streamlined. Armor is now different, instead of set pieces you can now customize your arm, leg, chest, and head pieces to mix and match to make the armor you want. There are still set pieces, but they're generally not as good as the new armor system. Power armor now features the "Power" part of it. Powered by rare fusion cores, power armor is now a commodity that provides huge amounts of damage resistance (100-200x the amount of your normal armor). Along with all of this there is a new armor modding system. Using scraps that you find in the Commonwealth you can enhance your armor, making it stronger, lighter, making it work for your play style. This system can be completley ignored and you'll still be fine, since many types of modded armor can be purchased or discovered on dead enemies.
Weapons are also different this time around. The first change that Fallout veterans will notice is the removal of the weapon condition system. You no longer have to worry about your weapon breaking due to overuse. This may bother some veterans, but it honestly just removes an annoyance from the game, particuarly late game. I can remember in FNV my primary was a gauss rifle, and I would use it so much and it was only obtainable from the BoS (a rare faction) that keeping it's condition up was an annoyance. I would have to travel back to the BoS Bunker, and then spend my caps on repairing it. Another new addition is weapon modding. Similarly to the armor modding system you can use junk scrounged in the Wasteland to apply new mods to your weapons to make it more powerful, accurate, and to make it work for you. Don't want to bother with this? That's fine. you can buy pre modded weapons or find them in the wastes.
The Commonwealth is a much more open place than the Capital Wasteland, or even the Mojave. Towns are no longer small, five building settlements, and downtown Boston is a vastly different place than it's DC counterpart. Unlike DC there aren't huge rubble piles blocking your path, forcing you to venture through the dreaded Metro to reach your destination. There's also a sense of vertiaclity that hasn't been present in previous titles. When assaulting a building in downtown there are often numerous floors with super mutants or raiders shooting down on you. Enhancing this is a jet pack that can be modded onto your power armor, allowing for quick hops around to reach distant enemies. It's a nice change of pace.
Additionaly there is the settelment building system. The great thing about it is that it can be completley ignored. Just like the new crafting systems, if you don't want to bother finding all the junk needed to do this, the game doesn't penalize you. If you do choose to invest in it, it's easy to lose yourself for hours building settlements and decorating them to your heart's content. The biggest problem with this is that many of the more in depth systems, like inter- settlement caravans are never explained in game and you have to read the in menu help book. It's this that makes it feel like this system may have been tacked on towards the end of development just so the devs could say "We have a settlement building system now, we're kind of like Minecraft!". That's not to say that it isn't great fun, because it most certainly is.
When it comes to enemy variety it seems like there are less enemies total, but within each enemy type there are different levels of them. For example, there's not just "Raider", there's "Raider Scum". "Raider Veteran", "Raider Scavenger", and many more. Same with super mutants and the other enemies in the game. The problem is, each tier just seems more bullet spongey than the last, other than that it doesn't feel like a different enemy type.
The biggest problem that Fallout 4 has is that it doesn't feel truly innovative. Look at the jump that was made between TES IV and TES V. Side by side they barley look like the same game series. So while Fallout 4 is most certainley a different game than that of it's predecessors, it still feels eerily similar to FO3 and FNV, excpet dumbed down. The new dialouge system works poorly, the options given don't always represent what your character will actually say, and in some cases what your character says won't change the responses of the NPCs.
Despite this Fallout 4 is still a fantastic game that you can easily lose yourself in for hours on end, and it is absolutley worth it's asking price. Is it GOTY? Maybe, but to me The Witcher 3 still deserves that title this year. The game has so much potential for modding and there are so many fantastic directions the DLC could go. But at its core, it still fails as an RPG worthy of following up New Vegas. It is a first person shooter with light RPG elements. Nothing wrong with that, it just means it lacks a lot of the charm that made New Vegas and Fallout 3 great. Still though, I get the feeling that my time in the Commonwealth is just begining and I can't wait to explore it more.

May as well start the review with the cards on the table, that is the 600 and some odd hours I spent in DS2. More importantly, I wrote a lengthy negative review for DS2 and continued to be drawn towards the game, amassing those hours. Like many fans of the series I missed out on DS1 due to bad port, but I enjoyed the pants off Demon Souls. This one didn't go so well with me and I guess I'd like to explain why below, if your interested. Making no effort to hide any spoilers..
We kick right off the game rolling into the first boss which probably caused a heap of refunds for those that didn't spend those few important test-hours in character creation. Really not sure what the idea was with this boss, but it was not the right choice for boss number one. This boss returns near the end of the game once again to show you how having loads of stamina and a very fast weapon is the only way for success in Dark Souls 3 boss fights. And it also shows how bad animations and glitchy enemy-arm-must-autolock-player-model-no-matter-what-way-he-is-facing looks like on the screen. And eww, nowhere in this review will I be saying anything about difficulty, same went for that DS2 review. (prefer the word frustration)
The odd mechanics continue forward with the same layers that I must be frankly tired of by now. Entire zones with poison effects, stunlock situations abound, zones with auto-targetting projectiles raining from the sky on the other end of the map, enemies seemingly without stamina bars and unlimited magics/projectiles, enemies full capability to strike through walls and objects (the ai makes full attempts to use this feature). For comparison, the character you play has trouble wielding a sword in a hallway as swinging it bounces wildy off the walls. Best advice for a new player of this game, don't think for a second that the enemies play by the same game world rules as you do. Some of this I expected to be the same from DS2 and it was, so I shouldn't have the right to complain.
Probably the biggest no-no for me is this fast-forward feel to the game. I read this is some kind of Bloodborne feature but never played that game. Pushing the fast forward button on Dark Souls after releasing three prior games in the souls series with slow-methodical gameplay, why? Say hello to the horrible camera controls, now in high speed. Watch as high-speed bosses flip around arenas causing the camera to lose its mind. (sigh)...nevermind your dead again.
I don't know what happened. All I can say is I have zero interest in entering new game plus mode. (which has been a staple feature in the series) For new players, you can re-enter the game in new game plus mode with your character beefed up and play through a harder version. But with the flashbacks of the bosses, the camera, the who-made-these-decisions face palms?
Armor no longer can be upgraded which is great, as there wasn't enough materials in the game to do it anyway. Unfortunately it seems armor-with-buffs doesn't really exist anymore. (just one or two items) Dual wielding weapons seems to be removed, which is a shame it was fun to dual wield ultra great swords in DS2. (or hammers, or morning stars...etc) Archery has been nerfed big time with arrow stacks at 99 arrows instead of 999. 99 arrows doesn't get you to the next bonfire unless you run pass everything, and running pass enemies doesn't earn souls to buy more arrows. Just started using magic after finishing the game, so not going to comment on fighting bosses solo with it. All I can say is you have to use fast weapons in the boss arenas, and have lots of stamina to survive. (see fast-forwarded gameplay above)
There's more but I must be about out of room by now. Thanks for reading and hopefully this was helpful to some extent. (I feel better after putting it into words)

If you want to play solo offline go for it, like I stated earlier, the game is beautiful and satisfying.  But, if you want to play coop with friends for the PVE experience it will just suck plain and simple.  I will not recommend this game because FROM software has an elitist attitude about this game and punishes coop PVE players.  Recently they just patched the game to make invasions occur even more frequently so now in coop all you will be doing is playing PVP; frankly, it sucks. While i am putting yes as my recommendation, I am going to state that my actual statement is a MAYBE
PVE: If you are looking into this game for the primary purporse of being a single/coop player game then i would 100% recommend this. The level design is cool, the bosses are for the most part challeging, and over it is a great experience.
PvP: If you are here for the PVP, like i was, then you will most likely be dissapointed in the game. Mechanincally the pvp is the best in the series, however there are some major issues keeping it from being good. The first one is Invasions, you can pretty much only invade coop worlds now, meaning you are always in a 2v1 or higher with some very rare exceptions. The host of the world also has a 25% health boost that you dont have, so they are also at a constant advantage. There is no more 1v1 arenas like there were in dark souls 2, so duels come exclusively from summon signs. These are actually pretty good, but there is one major problem. There is no variety. Any split weapon damage (Like say any kind of elemental damage) does a very significant amount less to a player than a standard phys damage weapon. In addition unlike dark souls 2, which let you buff the elemental weapon in order to boost its damage' you cant buff elemental weapons at all. This severly limits pyro, faith, and int builds, making them nearly worthless in pvp. Past that the amount of actually good or even decent weapons in pvp also feels very limited. Spells in this game are also really really bad in pvp, with only buff spells even being useful. I had 200+ hours in Dark souls 2 pvp just from the amount of builds i could do. This game already has me bored simply because there is no variety. If you want this game for PvP you will most likely run out of things to do sooner rather than later.

As a big fan of Dark Souls I and Dark Souls II, I am greatly pleased with Dark Souls III. The gameplay is closer to DS2 than DS1. The game mechanics are great. I love the idea of using focus to cast spells instead of having a certain amount of casts like in the previous games. Magic is a valuable playstyle.
I found the bosses' design more creative than those from DS2, although there weren't as much bosses. There weren't any cheap copies like there were in the previous two games (like asylum demon/demon firesage, Dragonslayèer knights, Ornstein/old dragonslayer) and the boss fights was interesting and diverse. There were very difficult bosses and easy bosses as well.
Enemies keep respawning (like DS1, unlike DS2). The poison mechanic is also changed in that it works wat slower than the previous games, making it less dangerous. Items are easier to use and the interface in general is great.
There are a lot of callbacks to Dark Souls 1, which you might or might not find a good thing. There aren't as many DS2 callbacks, if I remember. Story wise, it's the same as DS1 & DS2 in that there's no clear story, but the story is hidden instead.
The combat system is great, but there're some instances that were very annoying and just seemed unfair. There have been countless times when my attacks were deflected by the wall or a pillar, but there weapons sometimes hit you straight through a solid wall.
There are some other negative points about this game, though. First of all, the game's map isn't as intertwined as DS1's. Also, at the beginning, the game might feel a bit linear, although that changes after the first couple of area's. In the different area's, there are a lot of shortcuts that can be opened (by opening a door or kicking a ladder). When it comes to the world, one other problem I have is the amount of swamp-like/watery area's, which are very annoying cause they slow you down and might poison you. There are at least 5 area's that I can think of (I won't spoil which ones).
Another problem there is are online covenant-related issues. There are some covenants that appear not to work (Blue Sentinels, Darkmoon, ... ). These covenants are supposed to send you to other players when they're attacked by invading players, yet you never get summoned. Cause some of these covenants don't work as they should, farming the items required to deepen your relation with the covenant becomes a big hassle because their drop rates are extremely small (I'm looking at the Proof of a concord Kept item).
The camera sometimes screws you over when tracking an enemy (I'm looking at the Nameless King). I have played this game with my controller, so I can't say anything about the pc (mouse/keyboard) controls.
There're a lot of other positive and negative elements in this game that I haven't mentioned yet because I currently can't think of them. Also, I might have mentioned more negative points (and went in more depth with them) than positive points, but don't let that mislead you about the quality and greatness of the game.
Overall, I loved this game and if you enjoyed the previous Dark Souls games, I advise you to purchase this game as well.

When I first started this game I was really excited to play because of all the good things that were said about it. Especially after the monstrosity that is Dark souls 2. It obviously had a lot of problems, but also introduced a lot of cool new feature Thankfully Dark souls 3 has fixed most of those issues. Dark souls 3 really feels like a dark souls game to me, which dark souls 2 didn't. The classic firelink shrine is back as well as plenty of others like Anor Londo. I enjoyed playing through the pve part of the game and loved what it had to offer. That is until i started to fiddle with the pvp. The pvp is an absolute clown fiesta. Your either going to have a blast or your going to be punting your dog across the room out of sheer anger. The latency can get pretty annoying and you will get hit by something that clearly didn't hit you. Parrying is also a lot easier now and hornet ring is back. But every game has its downsides. One downside to this installment is poise. The poise stat is still there but it no longer does anything. Instead we have something known as "hyper armor". Which is basically just i-frames in which you cannot be staggered. A lot of really heavy weapon's attacks have hyperarmor. This can be looked at as a good thing or a bad thing. Personally I like the concept but dislike that poise is literally a useless stat. Another downside is obviously the netcode for pvp. The netcode is probably the worst it has been in all of the dark souls. Pvping is really just complete♥♥♥♥♥♥compared to the other because of how bad the netcode is. It basically forces FROM to nerf certain op pvp weapons because they are unable to fix the core mechanics of the game. I've still got some enjoyment out of it though. Anyways, I would definitely recommend this game if you enjoyed any of the others. Goodluck out there and have fun.

Fallout 4 is one of the best open world RPGs to come out in years (In my opinion). The game world if stuffed with treasure waiting to be discovered along with loads of weapon and armor mods and collectables with in game bonuses, along with lots of great weapons for destroying foes! This is the first game that Bethesda has created that actually rewards you for spending time creating your character, because when you activate a dialogue, your character and the person you are talking to come into view and what unfolds during the discussion is much like a mini cutscene, so you can enjoy watching your character, whom you created, interacting with others instead of being a voiceless tool, like in other Bethesda games.
In Fallout 4 you are free to do anything you want, however you want to do it. You can choose who you ally yourself with and who you destroy, much like the other Fallout games. Newly introduced to the fallout series though, is the basebuilding mechanics. You can create your own settlements to protect, grow and house settlers as well as grow food, purify water and just make the overall world a better, more "lived in" place. You can make your own house, however large or complex you want, given you have the materials. Materials are scrapped from the junk found lying around the wasteland, some of which are rare, which can be used to create the most powerful items and most useful settlement items.
If you are looking for a game that you can potentially get lost in for days, this is a great choice, it is very immersive and great fun.

This was the first Dark Souls game I ever actually played through properly. The difficulty is massively hyped and my brother told me not to bother because he said I'd just rage and not enjoy it.

Some of the bosses were massively difficult while I was learning the mechanics and getting better at dodging (in particular), but even when I got absolutely stumped, I could summon help and after enough tries, beat the boss.
Some people have complained about the game comparing it to previous iterations or talking about poise being broken (it is), but from a pure new player's point of view, this turned out to be a fun game. I'm a better-than-average gamer, so take that into account, but given enough effort and the will/determination to succeed, anyone can beat this game.
It's not for the faint of heart or for people who truly frustrate easily, but it's immensely satisfying to succeed.

Generally not a very good game.
The lore is obscure and not understandable. Most maps have pretty much the same undead boohoo-ghosty theme.
The combat mechanics are generally poorly designed and leaves pretty much only a single viable combat strategy: Rolling to become invinsible during the roll and then hacking your opponent once you've rolled enough to make them lower their guard. Blocking or spell casting seems redundant. Furthermore you'll find your character often use a kick-move instead of your input attack. The kick is probably intended to be a shield-breaker, but shows up in the midst of strike combination - often with one own's demise as a result.
Moreover, the combat system features an obnoxious "stun effect" of being hit by an enemy blow. While this might be realistic it makes the outcome of a fight rather predictable, since you're often not able to avoid any further strikes once you've been hit once - cause you've been "stunned".
Also, many boss fights require you to die serveral times in order to learn the attack moves of the boss, so you'll be able to roll-and-hack effectively. This is time consuming and rather pointless, since you'll be able to roll-and-hack your way through the game eventually.
If you haven't played Dark Souls before, you'll undoubtedly need to seek out some advice online. Here you'll learn that the Dark Souls community is mainly comprised of very condensending and elitist people, who will tell you to "git gud" even if you're completly new to the game.
On the positive side though, the graphics are amazing, and especially the music of certain bossfights makes the fights a lot more intense and is a nice addition to the whole gloomy sorrow theme of the game. Also i like the idea of having a game that is not actually a walk-in-the-park to complete, but abovementioned combat mechanics sort of makes the game more anoying to play rather than actually difficult to play.
All in all i'd say that if you're not a fan of the Dark Souls series, and/or don't have 200+ hours to put into learning the whole scheme of things, go buy another game. There are penty of better thought-out games out there, where a casual can have more fun and more memorable experiences.

I want to love this game, but the game doesnt love me, other players, or even itself.
With a lot of the weapons, you can feel the sheer lack of creativity, the lack to make a fancy moveset that feels good and functions good like weve seen in many other previous installments such as a lot of Dark Souls 1 as well as Dark Souls 2s dlc weapons. This game lacks polish and origonal design, alot being borrowed from other games.
The crucified ogres in the crucifixion woods use Father Gascoins moveset from Bloodborne, most enemies weve seen before or seen variations of before as well.
Movesets feel really bad in a lot of cases, they feel rushed and underdeveloped as if someone really didnt care too much when making them for a lot of weapons, very limp.
I got this same type of feeling when I played Dark Souls 2, alot of weapons felt "floaty" and rather unsatasfying. You could call it rose tinted glasses but weapons in Dark Souls 1 felt better, and even Demons Souls. Dark Souls 3 focuses more on giving you nostalgia than trying to wow you with creativity. One of the most creative areas of the game is Lothric Castle, the first and one of the last areas was one of those few creative areas I felt good about. Dark Souls 3s level design feels rather unappealing in a lot of ways but is generally okay, there couldve been more love and creativity in a lot of areas and I feel like they really didnt try to get crazy. The Catacombs are the catacombs, the demon ruins are the demon ruins, anor londo is anor londo, undead settlement is bloodborne. I can feel the lack of fun and the more pressure being put on them by Bamco.
The game is filled with untested or generally missing mechanics, hyper armor is finnicky on a lot of weapons and poise is 100% absent, people keep testing to find out what it does and so far every single one has been disproven. Some enemies and some areas are flatout ruined by this missing poise, the fire breathed from a dragon staggers you every quarter of a second, enemies like the Thrall are scarier than some bosses too.
You can mash your way through this game with r1 where as in Dark Souls 1, you could still do that but id be confident in saying its harder to do, even if you stacked defense and poise. People are afraid of poise returning to dark souls 3 but they forget that the backstab issues from dark souls 1 are fixed in this game and those issues wouldnt return, the stunlocks are gone and wont return as well.
Now this just makes it all feel worse on top of everything ive listed.
There is so much cut content from this game that im absolutely certain is going to be pushed into dlc, saved by bamco for extra dlc money. Youve got finished weapons, finished armor, all with stats and descriptions too. Im amazed at the lack of UNFINISHED cut content in the game.
Maybe the DLCs will be better with Bamco taking a step back away from the pushed release date, but as it stands right now I dont think this game is worth buying and playing and I myself will be stopping until the DLCs release and even then, if the game still isnt fixed I might not come back for a year or so to see if any of the actual game mechanical issues get fixed.
I played a lot of Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3, ive played Demon Souls and I have not yet played Bloodborne to my own distress. I can confidently say this game is not very good at its current state and itll be a good long while before that changes, as I have said above.
Thank you for reading and I hope you can understand my point of view.

If you've never played a Dark Souls game before, this is a great one to start with.
PROS: First things first; I say its a good start, because it is the easiest in the series. The motions are fluid, if a bit restrictive (once you play it, you understand what i mean), the graphics are amazing, the game is REALY well optimized, and, true to form, this game will make you want to play more, even as you have your a$$ handed to you. Even the first boss is a nice tutorial into the game. The enemies are a for the most part predictable, but dont let that fool you. Almost every enemy has one move that looks like another, but attacks at different times, which can make parrying and dodging a bit difficult if you don't pay attention.
CONS: OFFLINE: One of the major cons per gameplay is the F***ING CAMERA! it can go haywire at the most inopportune moments, which in a game series known for difficulty, can screw you over fast. TIP: You can rely on the camera but always be aware of your surroundings. If the enemy goes out of lock and you can't see him, it helps to know where he probably is and to know where the escape routes are.
Poise is basically nonexistant in this game compared to the others. With the heaviest armor (tested with a few invasions for authenticity) you will still flinch with the weakest weapon hit. Armor is basically just to help get another 2-3% damage reduction, which admittedly CAN mean the difference between crouching over and dying and surviving with a couple hit points.
The worst aspect of this game is by far the anti-cheating system in place to "protect" online players from hackers. You can only realy expect the anti cheating sytem to work on people who were HIT with hacked weapons or people who PICK UP hacked weapons that other players drop. Trust me, the anti cheating system is the BIGGEST F*** YOU to honest players I have ever seen. Oh yeah, and just so I dont forget to say it, the anti cheating system will PERMA BAN you. Not for a week, not for a month, not for a year, FOREVER.
Now although the cons might seem to outweigh the pros, I will still recomend this to people. The hackers, do seems to be dwindiling in numbers now that the game has been out for a while, and I personally love the game and gameplay far too much to just stop. My only suggestion is that, until FROM fixes the cheat problem to something much more manageable, THIS GAME IS NOT WORTH FULL PRICE. It is worth a buy , but wait till you can get everything for about 40 bucks (DLC INCLUDED).  Once they fix the cheating system then I will say that it is worth full price.

Fallout 4 is one of the best open world RPGs to come out in years (In my opinion). The game world if stuffed with treasure waiting to be discovered along with loads of weapon and armor mods and collectables with in game bonuses, along with lots of great weapons for destroying foes! This is the first game that Bethesda has created that actually rewards you for spending time creating your character, because when you activate a dialogue, your character and the person you are talking to come into view and what unfolds during the discussion is much like a mini cutscene, so you can enjoy watching your character, whom you created, interacting with others instead of being a voiceless tool, like in other Bethesda games.
In Fallout 4 you are free to do anything you want, however you want to do it. You can choose who you ally yourself with and who you destroy, much like the other Fallout games. Newly introduced to the fallout series though, is the basebuilding mechanics. You can create your own settlements to protect, grow and house settlers as well as grow food, purify water and just make the overall world a better, more "lived in" place. You can make your own house, however large or complex you want, given you have the materials. Materials are scrapped from the junk found lying around the wasteland, some of which are rare, which can be used to create the most powerful items and most useful settlement items.
If you are looking for a game that you can potentially get lost in for days, this is a great choice, it is very immersive and great fun.

A few months ago, I engaged in a sort of 'Dark Souls marathon'. So I still remember how it feels to play Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2. My review will take that in account so there will be comparisons ;)
So this Dark Souls 3 is a good game. What stroke me the most was the pace of fights and the way you press the keys to deliver damage. It is closer to Dark Souls 1 than Dark Souls 2 - which had bad response.
Fights and hits are dynamic, although casting magic spells sometimes feels like you're playing a dumb mage. Finding an angle can be a pain. Targeting an enemy doesn't help much, mainly because you can't target from too far ; playing a mage requires a bit of practice (or getting used to) when it comes to cast a spell before the enemy hits you.
Targeting is a real downside to the game, as well as the camera... It is sometimes hard to run and target an enemy ; sometimes you select and deselect one because you spammed your key too fast as the game wouldn't lock your target... But, you can get past this matter.
The maps are good. Although at times, you feel like wandering to unlock a shortcut. I didn't find the level design crazy awesome, perhaps simply 'good'. It feels a bit like Dark Souls 1, in fact there is a zone that you played in the first one !
Bosses are good and some are unique in a way ; it's always interesting to fight a boss in a Dark Souls :)
Some of them will give you a hard time. However, some others are easily killable when you summon someone, or an IA. In those cases, killing a boss doesn't feel really rewarding.
However I felt like the game aims a bit at newcomers to the serie, to be noob-friendly. It is hard, but it almost feels like a regular RPG. Or slowly getting to it...
Overall I do recommend it, especially when it comes to sales ; and most of all to Dark Souls' players !

Down in the "safety" of the vault i instantly start exploring this small vault, that feels so big. My baby is taken from me and ohh boy my feelings... Only an hour into the game and I had already started having feelings for the charactes.
I'm finally out of the vault after 200 years. I know look into the wasteland of Boston. It felt so real. After then having played the game for a while i start interacting with all the major factions in the game; Brotherhood of Steel, The Institute, Commonwealth Minutemen and The Railroad. I start seeing all different perspectives on the Synths and also the wasteland. I play some different missions for all the factions, but one faction was right just for me. Now i only play for that faction and that's all im thinking about. As i get promoted and so on, it motivates me to keep playing for that faction.
Then all of a sudden after not realizing how fast time has gone by I'm at the ending. It made me so sad. I had chosen The Brotherhood of Steel, and now i had to kill my son. All this time i was going around looking for my son. Checking different towns and factions. It was not that i didn't know it woul'd come to this, i was just not prepared. The game had gotten me so hooked i had forgotten it was a game. So when it finally came to the ending it was harsh...
If you're looking for a good single player game to play then i advise you to play Fallout 4. Never have i been felling so much for the characters inside a game it was quite crazy. It's not an experience you woul'd want to miss out on and the game is very long.

-People you summon might be ice-skating around and the same goes for invaders, hitting you with no animation and being impossible to attack. When being summoned to another hosts world you might have similar problems with lagging and even NPCs being statues taking dmg 5 seconds after being hit.

6/8/16 - This will be a list of Pro's and Con's and a small or big blob of information with a very short TL:DR right after it. It's a lover of the souls games so take this gamer's review with some speculation/salt.
Pro
-Smooth silky gameplay, far better than it's first two father and mother.
-Slightly (Or massive depending on your PC specs) improved visuals.
-Better PVE in terms of connectivity and bosses.
-Weapons arts. Basically each weapons have some sort of special attack making it slighty more unqiue than it's predecessors.
-Soul Memory no longer exists.
-NG and NG+ and onward can be played and invaded.
-Summoning in PVE can be done with anyone so long as a password is added. Doing this scales both players levels.
-New addition of different types of phantoms (Good one's being the Mad phantom and Ald. Faithful)
-Enemies no longer have a spawn limit and will respawn like enemies from DS1.
-The ending of the game is a nod to the previous souls players, much the entire game is but the end boss truly is a sight to behold. Brought a tear to my eye and worthy of a positive I should think.
There are plenty more but these are more or less (Exception of the last one) which I think are Objective good for the game.
Con
-No poise (Working as intended? A joke)
-Variety in PVP. A serious lack of originality. You'll see mostly Dark Swords, UGS's, Rapier's, and Caestus's. (It's obvious why but truly not a big issue for some. Depending on who you ask magic I.E, Mircale users, Pyromancers and Sorcerers have issues in terms of builds).
-Ease of game. Dark Souls is usually known for it's difficult gameplay, I however have found it to be satisfactory but others I hear aren't having the ball breaking experience like the previous games (Especially those Bloodborne DLC fanatics).
-Minor bugs still exist and this game had a far cry from a good launch experience.
-Once you clear a boss in that area you can't be invaded in it. (Trivial I know but I've been reading reddit forums and friends tell me it's an issue).
-Darkmoon Cov, Blue Sent, and Watchdog's apparently have connectivity issues. In these terms I mean they usually don't get summoned in for fights partly because these Covenant's depend on an area to invade or a particular condition for an invasion aswell as the normal invade requirement. (Blue's have to have people in the way of the blue covenant to even be summoned, Watch Dog's have to have people walk around in a area so they can be summoned however this conflicts with the whole "You killed a boss here? looks like you won't be invaded here ever until you beat the game again and go through this area".)
-Advantages are usually in favor of the Host during invasions. This barring the fact they aren't alone. Things like Giant seeds, Dark Moons, Blue Sentinels, White phantom summons, Yellow phantom summons, and possibly more that I don't even know about or haven't mentioned. Gank squads are the norm now and if you invade you must be prepared to fight more than one person usually. Especially since invasions are primed for multiple people in one game.
Now I know there are plenty more postitives and negatives and I know that I haven't listed a lot of them here, probably because most are people's nitpicks and are mostly subjective in my eyes. Phantom ranges on some weapons, invaders who invade have to walk back to their souls, dried finger adds and extra helpful phantom as well as a chance to be invaded by two phantoms, armor upgrades no longer exist, invaders have estus, blah blah blah. I won't list these and many more for they can be argued both ways. I think the game is more than what I thought I was going to get. I absolutely play this tons and will for the ongoing future assuming the game continues it's course or gets better (Which I hope it does). In short I think this game is a solid Seven. Now before you get angry just hear me out. A five is average, anything below is below what is normally accepted in games. If your a six then you've pretty much flown above most games. While Dark Souls 3 is far from perfect I think it strives pretty damn hard for a high ranking and totally is better than most games out there.
TL:DR - Game's good, beware of issues with game mechanics and PVP could be done better. PVE is good though.

If the first Dark Souls depicted a world gracefully drifting towards the apocalypse, Dark Souls 3 shows one on a spiraling, feverish descent directly into it. It’s a fierce and punishing behemoth that dares you to take a step forward before knocking you back, again and again and again. But with a bleak, yet beautiful world that’s enthralling to explore and packed with secrets to find, I always felt compelled to come back, eager for that familiar thrill of overcoming even the most exacting challenges.
Dark Souls 3 does suffer from occasional framerate dips and a few underwhelming boss fights, but beyond that, its epic scale, aggressive obstacles, and rich development of existing lore make it the grandest and fiercest Dark Souls adventure yet.
The Kingdom of Lothric and the lands that lie beyond contain some of the most visually striking places developer From Software has ever crafted. Even though many of its locations do recycle ideas from familiar locales (like the Catacombs and yet another poison swamp), they're distinguished well enough to feel distinct from their past game parallels. There was never a moment when I didn’t feel captivated by their strong sense of place and the amount of gorgeous detail put into each environment. I stared out in awe atop the crumbling medieval stronghold of the High Wall, taking in the view of its surrounding valleys and snow-capped mountains, while all around me the fort’s frenzied denizens turned to stone and wood mid-prayer. I trudged through the poison swamps of the Road of Sacrifices while battling seething, cross-bearing beasts, braved Irithyll’s chilling, Tower of Latria-like dungeon, and got lost in a multi-story maze of curse-ridden bookshelves in the Grand Archives.
Every level is not only full of breathtaking architectural marvels and the most minute environmental embellishments, but also dense with things to do and see from moment to moment. But those views are more intense than Dark Souls 3 can handle – dramatic framerate dips (which we saw even on an ultra-high-end PC with two GeForce GTX Titan Zs) caused a lot of these fantastic looking areas to drag along, sometimes down to 20 to 25 FPS. But the rest of the time, when it is running at a smooth 60 (on PC only), Dark Souls 3 is a sight to see.
Exploration of the aforementioned places is the cornerstone of this series, and Dark Souls 3’s world does a lot to reward an inquisitive and thorough nature. You could spend hours in a single area, diligently investigating every dark corner or side road, and be consistently rewarded with some interesting story revelation, new gear, mini bosses, and even entire secret areas. Illusory walls make a triumphant return, driving me to compulsively slash away at suspicious-looking dents or bricks in search of precious equipment. I got a pretty high rate of return on doing that, too, from the earliest levels to the very late game. Crystal lizards also must have had a breeding season, because there are a ton of them slithering around, ripe for the slaying and with lots of twinkling titanite for leveling up special weapons.
Dark Souls 3’s world isn’t as openly interconnected as that of Dark Souls 1 (where you can freely move between high and low-level areas), but individual areas still weave their own branching paths together seamlessly, creating twisting mazes of overlapping passages and shortcuts that were a joy to lose myself in. Perhaps it’s because of this lack of interconnectivity that Dark Souls 3 feels larger than the first game. Early and late-game levels don’t directly connect as often, so the more you progress linearly from level to level, the farther it seems like you’ve journeyed.
Your progress is marked by massive landmarks, which lend the world a cohesive quality. In several early levels, I could maintain sight of the High Wall from which I’d originally come; while trying to extinguish a series of beacons as part of the entry process for a boss, I scaled a huge ladder through the thick canopy of trees blocking my view and could see clearly where I was in relation to the first level. I recalled seeing nearly this exact place too, from another spot on the High Wall.
This solid sense of space and geography elevates Dark Souls 3’s level design beyond the relatively weak blueprint of Dark Souls 2, making a mostly triumphant return to the kind of large-scale, world-focused journey of Dark Souls 1. Perhaps the only things sadly missing from Dark Souls 3’s environments are the kind of interesting platforming challenges present in places like Dark Souls 1’s Sen’s Fortress or Crystal Cave.
