Daaaaaaaaaaaaaaaark Souls 3.
If you enjoy the Demon's/Dark/Bloodborne formula, then I believe you will enjoy this game.  I write this at almost 60 hours having just finished my first play through.  I started a sorcerer build and a melee build and eventually took the sorcerer build to completion.  I finished around SL 95 with 3 weapons @ +10 and a lot of the game covered.  My first playthrough is clocked in at around 45 hours.
Dark Souls 3 is an RPG that takes you through a dying world that will punish you over and over for little mistakes but when you're finished it will feel amazing.  To me, there isn't another series like this in gaming.  I've enjoyed every hour spent in the Souls/Borne series despite how excruciating it can be at times.
Gameplay: Start by selecting your class and making your character.  The starting class doesn't matter much as you'll be able to create whatever you want by the end of your first game.  The game allows you to respect 5 times per play through, but you can figure out how to get there (or just google but it involves a covenant).  Game follows the predecessors where you play a single character in either melee/mage/mix/really whatever you want to do.  You can dual wield, you can run sword and shield, you can get the biggest weapon in the game eventually and run around two handing that, you can run staff/chime and sword.  You explore the world gaining more ground via bonfires which let you teleport around the world to save time.
There is no pausing.  All weapons/armor have weights to them, they have different looks, different animations and it let's the game have a lot of different combinations.  "Fashion Souls" exists for a reason.
Bosses: The series is known for its bosses and I don't think this entry disappoints.  There are excellent bosses that are all varied.  I believe in my first play through I found all of them, as in there are a bunch of optional areas/bosses that you could miss/skip if you wanted to.  There are also 'mini' bosses scattered through out the game which are usually just protecting special items.
Invading / Coop:
The souls series has pvp and coop.  PVP happens via invading live gameplay through either items or covenants where you can invade someones game before a boss and fight them and kill them.  You can only invade someone who is 'alive'.  This means that they haven't died.  When you die in Souls games your HP is reduced and you're "hollow".  You can become 'alive' again via various means.  PVP also happens through several covenants either in attacking or defending roles.  Coop happens by summoning other players at random, or via password with friends or via covenant to sometimes help defend yourself when you're invaded.  You could play offline and avoid all of this but what fun is that?  I'm not that great and die to most PVPers but I don't avoid it.
Graphics: GTX780, I'm maxed on everything and have good FPS as far as I can tell.  Have only had visible drops here and there.
Audio: On board audio, just average.  Nothing that stands out too much.

**This review is by a Dark Souls player, for Dark Souls players**
Does it have problems? Yes. Didn't all of the Dark Souls games have noticeable problems so soon after launch? Yes. Will these problems be fixed, like in the other Souls games? Well, probably not.
This game is a good game. It has it's issues like all of the other souls games, but it does hold up pretty well on it's own. The issue I have with this game are the fundamental mechanics. Primarily the way defence works. I won't go into detail, but basically the defence is split into two separate integers: a flat defence that increases only as you level up and wear armor (any armor, as all armor in the same category (head, torso, legs, hands) gives the same flat increase to flat defence), and a percentage based integer that increases by the armor you wear, rings that buff/debuff armor, and spell buffs. First of all, I don't have any idea why they would decide to go about this, why they would try to make this one thing so complicated that no one person could understand just by looking at, when they had it perfectly so simple from the other games. Second, this is a serious detriment to the other mechanics that they reused from the other games. Split damage (damage with at least two different damage types, as in physical + any elemental, or any combination of any damage type) is seriously affected. It's no longer about "use a magic type attack to deal more damage to magic susceptible enemies", it's now "buff physical as much as possible to deal high damage to everything". I'll write more about this late, but look this stuff up, it's disgusting.

I won't go into detail, but basically the defence is split into two separate integers: a flat defence that increases only as you level up and wear armor (any armor, as all armor in the same category (head, torso, legs, hands) gives the same flat increase to flat defence), and a percentage based integer that increases by the armor you wear, rings that buff/debuff armor, and spell buffs. First of all, I don't have any idea why they would decide to go about this, why they would try to make this one thing so complicated that no one person could understand just by looking at, when they had it perfectly so simple from the other games. Second, this is a serious detriment to the other mechanics that they reused from the other games. Split damage (damage with at least two different damage types, as in physical + any elemental, or any combination of any damage type) is seriously affected. It's no longer about "use a magic type attack to deal more damage to magic susceptible enemies", it's now "buff physical as much as possible to deal high damage to everything". I'll write more about this late, but look this stuff up, it's disgusting.

Daaaaaaaaaaaaaaaark Souls 3.
If you enjoy the Demon's/Dark/Bloodborne formula, then I believe you will enjoy this game.  I write this at almost 60 hours having just finished my first play through.  I started a sorcerer build and a melee build and eventually took the sorcerer build to completion.  I finished around SL 95 with 3 weapons @ +10 and a lot of the game covered.  My first playthrough is clocked in at around 45 hours.
Dark Souls 3 is an RPG that takes you through a dying world that will punish you over and over for little mistakes but when you're finished it will feel amazing.  To me, there isn't another series like this in gaming.  I've enjoyed every hour spent in the Souls/Borne series despite how excruciating it can be at times.
Gameplay: Start by selecting your class and making your character.  The starting class doesn't matter much as you'll be able to create whatever you want by the end of your first game.  The game allows you to respect 5 times per play through, but you can figure out how to get there (or just google but it involves a covenant).  Game follows the predecessors where you play a single character in either melee/mage/mix/really whatever you want to do.  You can dual wield, you can run sword and shield, you can get the biggest weapon in the game eventually and run around two handing that, you can run staff/chime and sword.  You explore the world gaining more ground via bonfires which let you teleport around the world to save time.
There is no pausing.  All weapons/armor have weights to them, they have different looks, different animations and it let's the game have a lot of different combinations.  "Fashion Souls" exists for a reason.
Bosses: The series is known for its bosses and I don't think this entry disappoints.  There are excellent bosses that are all varied.  I believe in my first play through I found all of them, as in there are a bunch of optional areas/bosses that you could miss/skip if you wanted to.  There are also 'mini' bosses scattered through out the game which are usually just protecting special items.
Invading / Coop:
The souls series has pvp and coop.  PVP happens via invading live gameplay through either items or covenants where you can invade someones game before a boss and fight them and kill them.  You can only invade someone who is 'alive'.  This means that they haven't died.  When you die in Souls games your HP is reduced and you're "hollow".  You can become 'alive' again via various means.  PVP also happens through several covenants either in attacking or defending roles.  Coop happens by summoning other players at random, or via password with friends or via covenant to sometimes help defend yourself when you're invaded.  You could play offline and avoid all of this but what fun is that?  I'm not that great and die to most PVPers but I don't avoid it.
Graphics: GTX780, I'm maxed on everything and have good FPS as far as I can tell.  Have only had visible drops here and there.
Audio: On board audio, just average.  Nothing that stands out too much.

A typical Bethesda game in the line of Skyrim or Fallout 3.   If you have played either of these games you know what to expect.
Pros: Like most Bethesda games, they craft a great, detailed and interesting sandbox for you to play in and explore.  There are tons of little details to find, and the combat has been greatly improved from fallout 3, to the point where I do not feel the need to rely on VATS.  Of course, it is very easy to break the gameplay if you want to, as things are not very well balanced.  However I don't find that a bad thing as it is nice to beable to reach a god-like level without cheating.  The addition of settlements will be hit or miss for people, but I quite enjoy it.  You can spend a lot of time building up small towns in the wasteland and it gives you a lot of power to make things the way you would like while still fitting in mostly with the game world.  Though a note, that mods are extremely recommended if you plan to build settlements.
Lastly, Mods make this game like most Bethesda games.  Give them a try and they will transform your game experience and add many more hours.
Cons: The usual is true here too, the main story completely wastes a very good premise.  Instead of exploring what should be obvious themes of humanity ('What makes us human?') and the role of science/religion in coping with disaster, these become superficial and only touched on in isolated incidents.  If you aren't interested in story then this won't matter to you, and even then it's not a deal breaker, just disappointing.
Additionaly, while stills of the game look great, the animations are horrifying at times.  The first time Piper talks and it looks like her teeth are trying to escape her mouth always creeps me out.
Conclusion:  Worth the price of admission.

After having played this game for literally HUNDREDS of hours, I think I can finally give my opinions about it. It is very much not a perfect game, and (in my opinion) not as complex as previous Fallout games. The action and world are vastly improved, as are the animations. What I find Fallout 4 lacks is depth. The NPC interactions are closer to Mass Effect than other Bethesda games in the sense that you are limited to up to 4 conversation choices and the camera changes as if it plays out a scene. This was perfectly fine for Mass Effect, but sort of feels out of place in a Fallout game. The camera changes are a nice touch, but the limited conversation options just don't feel right after playing New Vegas. The story has potential, but the endings (storywise) were sort of a letdown after all the buildup; just sort of, "Okay, you did it." I'd have loved a continuation like Fallout 3 had with the Broken Steel DLC.
One thing that may have overshadowed the gameplay is Crafting. Whether it's weapons or settlements, there's a lot to do. I'm pretty sure that most of my hours were devoted to settlements. I found another minigun? Cool. A crate of Wonderglue and Duct Tape? HELL YES.
The DLC's add a lot to the experience, but I wound up being more excited for more workshop options. The workshop builder itself is a MASSIVE PAIN. I've had to thoroughly research how to use it and it's a perfectionist's nightmare. All I want is clipping ability and an option to turn snapping on and off. If you play it, you'll know what I mean, but I powered through it and wound up with massive settlements that are at least 5-10 times over the size limit (useful little tricks used).
Overall, I experienced a lot with this game. I really did have fun with it and enjoyed exploring a beautifully thought-out world with danger around almost every corner (and Power Armor. Can't forget that.) and ANOTHER SETTLEMENT NEEDS OUR HELP!

As a game, disregarding all Fallout and Bethesda RPG bias, the game is solid, no refutation.
Now, as a "RPG game"? No. As a "Fallout game"? No. As the sequel we were all waiting for? Maybe.
The problem with the Fallout series is there is so much variation between the "trinity" (Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas and Fallout 4), stating the quality of the game based on the other two is simply unfair. So this review will simply break down the game as A) A video game but also importantly for any sequel in a franchise B) A family member of the Fallout universe.
I break down this rewiew using the three "G's" of gaming.
Graphics:
- Graphically, the other Fallout games don't compare. Most RPGs and even shooters struggle to meet the same standards while also being OPEN WORLD. Sure, "Doom" has beautiful visuals but is not nearly as open world as Fallout, and really is a linear progresson. "Battlefield 4" yes, open world, is not nearly as beautiful and arguably finds itself with more graphical glitches and lacks the precison of detail Fallout 4 does.
Gameplay:
- Now as far as game play goes, it follows the basic formula of any other Bethesda RPG or any other Fallout. Got yourself a pip boy, there are weapons, armor, etc. Now Fallout 4 takes an interesting spin on the old crafting systems by actually making them useful. Crafting weapons and armor is so extremely satisfying. Also, all that useless scrap♥♥♥♥♥♥in the other games HAS PURPOSE NOW! There are just more weapon choices, variability and most important to me in RPGs, armor variation. Skyrim in all honestly lacked armor variation within the vanilla game. Shooting just feels superior compared to the other games, and in quite honestly I feel like I am playing a solid shooter like Call of Duty or battlefield with how smooth each weapon fires. Melee weapons are also so much better compared to the other games like, I think even Skyrim could use a tip or two.
Genre:
- Let's start with the genre as an RPG. Yikes. All RPGs get the nice cope out of saying "it's up to the player to determine how role play there game becomes" but it's difficult when RPGs strip players of the basic necessities. For instance, every chat interaction with characters in the game can be broken down with the formula "Good/Humble, Mean/Bad, Inquisitive and Silence" Literally. You feel like an NPC talking to other people's characters.
- In addition, the quests get very... boring. Everyone loves to♥♥♥♥♥♥on Preston but for good reason, the settlement quests are god awful. In general, the first story arc you are FORCED to interact with (whether or not you try your hardest to side step it) is with the faciton known as the Minutemen, which you will find have 2 interesting quests and the rest is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t boring redundant same old same old. Honestly, every faction feels somewhat boring, as Fallout 3 fans will feel as their Brotherhood of Steel is not the knights in tech armor they remember but just racist♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the Institute is just oblivious to emotion and the Railroad well... just like the name implies. Now where the game does do well is with the character story arcs. The worst part of the factions, is the lack of them. Why can't I be a raider? Fallout New Vegas let you join multiple gangs and even Caeser's Legion. The Gunners in Fallout 4? Just another group to gun down. Raiders, Mutants, Gunners, all the enemies might as well be the same model because nothing about the unique enemies makes them feel unique and purposeful.
- Every "ending" with the game feels satisfying enough, to the point where I feel like my decisions matter and I have reason to go back and replay through the other endings. The story of every companion (besides what I like to call spontaneous companions like Strong, which even they have enough personality) is extremely interesting. Piper, Nick and even Danse are all real, cool characters with depth. Now again, I can't vouche for every character because those like Preston, or the Institute Director  are just dull, flat and static characters which really need to be dynamic because they hinder the story.
- Now let's discuss the genre as a Fallout game. Yeah there are Fallout elements, stories, characters, etc. I always said Fallout New Vegas really strayed away from the core lore of the Fallout series but I was wrong. Dead wrong. Fallout 4 just does not feel very much like a Fallout game. There are factions like the Raiders or The Gunners who could have stories and purpose to the lore, but simply lack it. Another note, as previously mentioned with enemies are the Mutants. I don't see the centaurs of the other games or tons of cool vaults with their own weird thing to them. You don't see either of that really. Sure Fallout 4 retains some quirky Fallout moments like the idea of Hancock being a colonial mayor ghoul or the feel of a wasteland town like Diamond City, but those are all too few. These qualities should be common like in Fallout 3. The one redeemeing part of the game is the emphasis on the Old World. Nick's story and even the main character's provide a lot of background knowledge on the Pre-War world which I greatly appreciate considering Fallout New Vegas lacked a lot of that.
- If anything, Fallout 4 is a better shooter than RPG. Guns feel great, killing feels great, all combat feels great. The new talent system really rewards players in a unique way of the ranks, but again, IT LITERALLY A BETHESDA STANDARD: aka, 1-100 skills. Those just DONT EXIST. That should be the clearest indicator of this being a shooter with a really great story, rather than an RPG.
Overall, I give Fallout 4 7/10. Game runs well, looks great, and plays fantastic. But the game isn't amazing for the reasons as advertised, or for the reasons of being a Fallout game. The game feels too distant from the franchise and more importantly too distant from the RPG genre all together.

86/100 - Overall, Fallout 4 is a good game. However, if you're wondering whether or not Fallout 4 is better than the older Fallout 3 or Fallout New Vegas games, the answer is no. The fact is that although Fallout 4 got a lot right in terms of the story, world design, setting, combat, crafting, automatron crafting, settlement building, etc. and although it is still an enjoyable and fun game to play in its own right; Fallout 4 is also lacking in some areas while needing improvements in others.
For example compared to the previous two Fallout games in the series, Fallout 4 is lacking / missing key RPG elements of the previous games (or at the very least is lacking said RPG elements to the degree in which they were previously implemented). These missing elements include but are not limited to the lack of RPG character building and dialogue choices which matter.
Specifically, for Fallout 4 this means that we have limited dialogue choices and responses in which to interact with via a dialogue wheel. If I were to speculate, this was probably done due to the implementation of voice overs in Fallout 4 for the character dialogue (versus the silent protagonist and text dialogue choices of the previous 2 games in the series). Nevertheless, the fact remains that RPG mechanics are a must for any Fallout or Elder Scrolls game as they represent one of the key pillars / foundations / signatures of said IPs and it is this same signature / pillar (in combination with others) which as a whole uniquely distinguish and help make a Fallout game feel like Fallout and an Elder Scrolls game feel like Elder Scrolls. Does this mean that Fallout 4 did not feel like a Fallout game? The answer is no. In fact, as a whole (up to about 70 - 80%) Fallout 4 did feel like a Fallout game but at the same time with the removal of said RPG mechanics it also (in my opinion) represents an unnecessary regression / change in the wrong direction as well as a dilution of the Fallout brand, a disappointment, and unnecessary distraction which prevents one from becoming truly immersed in and enjoying what could have been a truly great game.
As for needed improvements, I would recommend that the developers add in an option within the menu or game settings to turn off radiant / repeatable quests. I also recommend that the settlement building and mechanics system as a whole needs a lot of improvement as well.
Specifically: 1) increase default settlement item limits. Note: Currently, I use the console to work around this and to manually increase the settlement item cap for each settlement. 2) Add a scrap all settlement junk and debris with one button click (2 button clicks if there is a scrap all confirmation) as an option to save time clearing a settlement lot while keeping the existing manual scrap feature for those who prefer to use it instead. 3) allow fencing and some types of objects to clip into the ground (in terms of item collision) so depending on the uneven terrain ... and if this feature is implemented fences and walls would no longer float in the air due to uneven terrain. 4) Add in an option within the menu to temporarily turn off settlement building ... automatic wall and other automatic object snapping such that when constructing settlements (such as buildings, walls, etc) one will have the option / flexibility / ease of use / quicker, reliable, and more accurate way to snap an object to any object that they want. Basically, the idea is to make settlements easier / simple to build without having to constantly deal with and fight with object snapping and collision issues which are detrimental to and plagues the Fallout 4 settlement building system.
5) allow fencing to be quickly placed around the perimeter such as drag / hold mouse click while placing it AND OR the option to purchase with one click at higher cost automatic / pre-made fencing that will automatically surround the entire perimeter of the lot with fencing including 1-2 entrances and exits. 6) Add in a system that significantly overhauls / improves and makes settlement management quicker, faster, and easier to manage (such as viewing and managing all settlers within a settlement in bulk via one in-game menu versus the current system which involves speaking to each settler you wish to manage ... one settler at a time). With this new system also allow the settler's job role, bed assignment, etc. settings to all be configured via in-game menu as well as add in separate in-game settlement options for setting and configuring the default job roles for new settlers as well as for managing existing settlers as well as adding in the ability to configure default settler gear, weapons, etc. for new settlers. For example, depending on which job role a settler has such as guard vs farming the game would check the settlement settings and depending on said settings ... assign the appropriate workshop item gear to a settler (after they join the settlement) such as giving an npc combat armor vs clothing ... pipe pistol vs rifle or shotgun.
7) Fix AI pathing issues. Ex: Fix pathing issues such that settlement enemies do not spawn inside settlement walls nor warp through walls. Ex: Fix it such that settlers do not end up warping to top of building after waking up in the morning and becoming trapped on top of their homes. Ex: Fix it such that AI / settlers and supply line personnel will always use the entrances and exits that are available (within a settlement) and not attempt to warp through or become stuck at fencing or walls and being unsure of where to go or what the best path is. 8) Fix it such that mods do not break nor prevent Steam achievements from being earned.
In closing, Fallout 4 has a lot of potential and the makings of a truly great game. However, it needs more development work, support, and polishing of existing features to accomplish this. Nevertheless, in its current state I would still recommend Fallout 4. As I said above, it is a good game and is enjoyable. It just needs some improvements and polishing to make it as good if not better than the previous two games.

This game feels like a step down from Fallout: New Vegas however it can be entertaining all the same, I have enjoyed playing it despite some frustrations. I'm a sucker for the setting so I enjoyed it despite how much I am about to complain!
Fallout 4 combines the inherantly fun exploration of a cool setting with a myriad of strange and at times baffling design choices, not to mention a whole mess of bugs which unfortunately seem to have become the standard. (Get the unofficial patch mod, you won't regret it!)
Whilst the shooter mechanics have vastly improved, pretty much every other facet of combat is worse than New Vegas; melee combat is woeful, an almost naked raider can deflect a swing from a super sledge with their bare arms, Feral ghouls always initiate combat with a horrifically jerky set of animations which sends them teleporting forwards straight through any attempt to hit them. Gun perks have been carved up into a strange combination of PISTOLS, RIFLES, AUTOMATIC WEAPONS leaving semi automatic 2 handed weapons straight up just better than everything else. You can no longer simply equip a grenade, it is on a hotkey.
The towns in the game are almost non existant, the Settlement mechanic pretty much means you have to build the towns yourself! As a result there is a lack of vendors early game. Enjoy having no ammo if you choose to use automatic weapons. Whilst a fun distraction for a while, Settlement building is quite unpolished and janky to the point where it can be very frustrating.
Power Armor is very cool, however you probably won't use it often.
The SPECIAL and perk system is a mess, some perks are straight up bad, some perks are locked behind arbitrary SPECIAL requirements.
The writing is straight up bad at times, Kid in a Fridge is such a bad quest.
Overall you get the sense Bethesda made Fallout 4 to experiment with a bunch of weird mechanics and shipped it as a game. Unfortunately they shipped it as a main series game in a much loved franchise. I sincerely hope that next time, they actually figure out what game they want to make, instead of throwing random features at a wall and seeing what sticks.

After having played this game for literally HUNDREDS of hours, I think I can finally give my opinions about it. It is very much not a perfect game, and (in my opinion) not as complex as previous Fallout games. The action and world are vastly improved, as are the animations. What I find Fallout 4 lacks is depth. The NPC interactions are closer to Mass Effect than other Bethesda games in the sense that you are limited to up to 4 conversation choices and the camera changes as if it plays out a scene. This was perfectly fine for Mass Effect, but sort of feels out of place in a Fallout game. The camera changes are a nice touch, but the limited conversation options just don't feel right after playing New Vegas. The story has potential, but the endings (storywise) were sort of a letdown after all the buildup; just sort of, "Okay, you did it." I'd have loved a continuation like Fallout 3 had with the Broken Steel DLC.
One thing that may have overshadowed the gameplay is Crafting. Whether it's weapons or settlements, there's a lot to do. I'm pretty sure that most of my hours were devoted to settlements. I found another minigun? Cool. A crate of Wonderglue and Duct Tape? HELL YES.
The DLC's add a lot to the experience, but I wound up being more excited for more workshop options. The workshop builder itself is a MASSIVE PAIN. I've had to thoroughly research how to use it and it's a perfectionist's nightmare. All I want is clipping ability and an option to turn snapping on and off. If you play it, you'll know what I mean, but I powered through it and wound up with massive settlements that are at least 5-10 times over the size limit (useful little tricks used).
Overall, I experienced a lot with this game. I really did have fun with it and enjoyed exploring a beautifully thought-out world with danger around almost every corner (and Power Armor. Can't forget that.) and ANOTHER SETTLEMENT NEEDS OUR HELP!

As a game, disregarding all Fallout and Bethesda RPG bias, the game is solid, no refutation.
Now, as a "RPG game"? No. As a "Fallout game"? No. As the sequel we were all waiting for? Maybe.
The problem with the Fallout series is there is so much variation between the "trinity" (Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas and Fallout 4), stating the quality of the game based on the other two is simply unfair. So this review will simply break down the game as A) A video game but also importantly for any sequel in a franchise B) A family member of the Fallout universe.
I break down this rewiew using the three "G's" of gaming.
Graphics:
- Graphically, the other Fallout games don't compare. Most RPGs and even shooters struggle to meet the same standards while also being OPEN WORLD. Sure, "Doom" has beautiful visuals but is not nearly as open world as Fallout, and really is a linear progresson. "Battlefield 4" yes, open world, is not nearly as beautiful and arguably finds itself with more graphical glitches and lacks the precison of detail Fallout 4 does.
Gameplay:
- Now as far as game play goes, it follows the basic formula of any other Bethesda RPG or any other Fallout. Got yourself a pip boy, there are weapons, armor, etc. Now Fallout 4 takes an interesting spin on the old crafting systems by actually making them useful. Crafting weapons and armor is so extremely satisfying. Also, all that useless scrap♥♥♥♥♥♥in the other games HAS PURPOSE NOW! There are just more weapon choices, variability and most important to me in RPGs, armor variation. Skyrim in all honestly lacked armor variation within the vanilla game. Shooting just feels superior compared to the other games, and in quite honestly I feel like I am playing a solid shooter like Call of Duty or battlefield with how smooth each weapon fires. Melee weapons are also so much better compared to the other games like, I think even Skyrim could use a tip or two.
Genre:
- Let's start with the genre as an RPG. Yikes. All RPGs get the nice cope out of saying "it's up to the player to determine how role play there game becomes" but it's difficult when RPGs strip players of the basic necessities. For instance, every chat interaction with characters in the game can be broken down with the formula "Good/Humble, Mean/Bad, Inquisitive and Silence" Literally. You feel like an NPC talking to other people's characters.
- In addition, the quests get very... boring. Everyone loves to♥♥♥♥♥♥on Preston but for good reason, the settlement quests are god awful. In general, the first story arc you are FORCED to interact with (whether or not you try your hardest to side step it) is with the faciton known as the Minutemen, which you will find have 2 interesting quests and the rest is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t boring redundant same old same old. Honestly, every faction feels somewhat boring, as Fallout 3 fans will feel as their Brotherhood of Steel is not the knights in tech armor they remember but just racist♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the Institute is just oblivious to emotion and the Railroad well... just like the name implies. Now where the game does do well is with the character story arcs. The worst part of the factions, is the lack of them. Why can't I be a raider? Fallout New Vegas let you join multiple gangs and even Caeser's Legion. The Gunners in Fallout 4? Just another group to gun down. Raiders, Mutants, Gunners, all the enemies might as well be the same model because nothing about the unique enemies makes them feel unique and purposeful.
- Every "ending" with the game feels satisfying enough, to the point where I feel like my decisions matter and I have reason to go back and replay through the other endings. The story of every companion (besides what I like to call spontaneous companions like Strong, which even they have enough personality) is extremely interesting. Piper, Nick and even Danse are all real, cool characters with depth. Now again, I can't vouche for every character because those like Preston, or the Institute Director  are just dull, flat and static characters which really need to be dynamic because they hinder the story.
- Now let's discuss the genre as a Fallout game. Yeah there are Fallout elements, stories, characters, etc. I always said Fallout New Vegas really strayed away from the core lore of the Fallout series but I was wrong. Dead wrong. Fallout 4 just does not feel very much like a Fallout game. There are factions like the Raiders or The Gunners who could have stories and purpose to the lore, but simply lack it. Another note, as previously mentioned with enemies are the Mutants. I don't see the centaurs of the other games or tons of cool vaults with their own weird thing to them. You don't see either of that really. Sure Fallout 4 retains some quirky Fallout moments like the idea of Hancock being a colonial mayor ghoul or the feel of a wasteland town like Diamond City, but those are all too few. These qualities should be common like in Fallout 3. The one redeemeing part of the game is the emphasis on the Old World. Nick's story and even the main character's provide a lot of background knowledge on the Pre-War world which I greatly appreciate considering Fallout New Vegas lacked a lot of that.
- If anything, Fallout 4 is a better shooter than RPG. Guns feel great, killing feels great, all combat feels great. The new talent system really rewards players in a unique way of the ranks, but again, IT LITERALLY A BETHESDA STANDARD: aka, 1-100 skills. Those just DONT EXIST. That should be the clearest indicator of this being a shooter with a really great story, rather than an RPG.
Overall, I give Fallout 4 7/10. Game runs well, looks great, and plays fantastic. But the game isn't amazing for the reasons as advertised, or for the reasons of being a Fallout game. The game feels too distant from the franchise and more importantly too distant from the RPG genre all together.

War. War Never Changes. I've played every Fallout game since Fallout 3 religiously. Though i've played Fallout 1 and 2 a little, I never got into them. But once Fallout 3 came out, I was amazed and encaptured into it. I spent countless hours into sidequests and little tedious tasks to level myself up. Then New Vegas came out and I played that through and through up until Fallout 4's release.
Here's the Bad, lets just get it out of the way: The Story was WAY to predictable and kinda a copy and paste of Fallout 3, just reversed. I'm not giving anymore away, as i've already said way too much.
Glitches, every Bethesda game has them, and some of them are just horrible, and others are humorous. I've happened to manage to find ways to get myself stuck or quests just bugged out and I couldn't ever complete them, including storyline quests, which resulted in me creating a fresh new game inorder to actually be able to complete the storyline.
The Good: Graphics, some people care about graphics, some don't. I like how the game get's prettier and NPC's have some more fluidity to them in their conversations and they actually look like people, and not silly putty stretched over a robot.
Settlements, you can build your own safehaven and practically live there. Place stores, earn caps, produce your resources, become self sufficient. You can find a good spot to hunker down and hoard all your junk into to later mod  your weapons.
New Mechanics and added features, have you not seen the power armor? It's actual POWER ARMOR, though sadly I rarely use it because I love to be stealthy. The moment you step into the suit everything gets easier and you absorb so much damage and become a walking tank... almost. Your armor breaks and such, so keep it repaired.
I did more of a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor review, but I hope it's atleast something that helps with someone's purchase. If you are here for a good story and want to be amazed, the game is good.
Or hell if you wanna turn this into your own pleasure filled game like how some people do with skyrim, kudos to you.

In truth I came into this with high hopes. I enjoyed it sure, but when I looked toward the others and saw the modding community I just had to stop and realize what it was I had just got.
The Storylines were decent, however there was in truth only 2 endings. And one of the climactic events was just reliving the end of Fallout 3.
The Customization was good... Ish. After awhile you notice you only want one thing. And most of the time people want Power Armor - I did not. Leaving me with a need for mods to fill that gap of decent armor without being super bulky.
The settler system... Okay let's be honest, that is all they wanted you to focus on. This is the main point of the game to them. Fallout shelter was such a big hit that they needed to make it into a 3 dimentional world. It was lackluster and in the end you notice that it is just a waste of time. But hey, My 30 Settlers with Power Armor are cool... I guess...
Overall Gameplay - Noticable improvements for action and constant play, however Dungeons itself are just... Dull to say the least.
OVERALL REVIEW - It was a shame storywise, however good for at least one playthrough. You can enjoy it while it is there, but even the DLC leaves a hole where it should be filled. I feel Fallout New Vegas and Fallout 3 was where the Peak was, now we are on the slow decline.  I recommend for awhile... But trust me, don't fall for the hype it was given.

I'm sure this review isn't going to change the mind of anyone teetering on whether or not to purchase it, but here goes.  This game IS NOT my favorite Fallout game by a long shot.
The crafting system is something I absolutely hate and I believe that there is little to no explanation on how to use it (I would hate it even if there was.  Just informing others what to expect).  Crafting is too complicated and I wish it was kept more to weapons and not settlements.  If I wanted to play Sim City then I would have purchased it.
Another downside in my opinion was the randon jobs system in regard to one character in particular (Preston). This seemed very much like padding to make the game longer to me.  I am in no way opposed to padding a game as long as it is kept interesting, the way it was done here was more annoying than anything.  Being that I am a completionist in games like this, It took me far too long to realize that the random jobs would just keep on coming.  Bad on you Bethesda.
To the shock and horror of other Fallout fans, I actually enjoyed the combat system.  VATS was an option and not a necessity like it was in 3 and New Vegas.  I like the to have the option to go in guns blazing or to use a more slow, turn-based, & methodical approach if I wanted.
Moral of the story is that this game is NOT perfect and it is NOT (even close) to being the best Fallout game, it is still a darn good game in its own right.  I would suggest picking it up (especially during a sale).

While it's not as good as Fallout: New Vegas, it's still a good Fallout game.  Like previous Fallout games (3, NV), it's a first person shooter style game, with a fairly sizeable open world.  It doesn't have quite as much character customization as previous titles (more limited Perks, lack of Traits), but it does retain the weapon customization that was prominent in previous titles.
Another reason it's not as good as NV is the lack of Karma in making decisions.  Allegiance to various factions is now a more hidden stat as well (you don't have a Pip Boy readout of your faction reputations), and you can't fully ally with multiple factions, either.  The decision making in 4 is much more straightforward and simplistic compared to NV, which is a plus for gamers more into exploration/combat, and a minus for those interested in the role playing depth that NV had.
The settlement system is fairly robust, which is useful, but it does have it's drawbacks, such as parts not aligning well at times, and NPCs tying themselves to the wrong vertical level  in the mesh, resulting in them being half buried in the floor at times (not that it impedes them any, they just walk around half buried).
So, is it worth getting?  If you like the Fallout games, it's a fairly good game, albeit a bit more linear than previous titles, so I'd say yes.  Are the DLCs worth getting?  Far Harbor is good, Nuka World has it's bad points (such as being based around making one binary decision in one way, with the other decision basically closing off the main quest line altogether), the rest (Automatron, Vault Tech, Wasteland Workshop, Contraptions) are good if you're into the settlement stuff, but can be passed over if you aren't.
That being said, it's also basically a dead game now.  It's no longer being developed, so no new DLCs, and given that long standing bugs have never been fixed, it's not likely to receive more updates.  On the other hand, people are still developing mods for it, so some of those bugs are being fixed and improvements being made, just not by the official publisher.
Bottom line, I like the game and recommend at least the base game.  DLCs are either optional (FH/NW) or only recommended for builders (all the others).

Fallout 4 is a fun game making some welcome updates to the game such as the leveling system, major improvement to graphics, and features. I liked most of the side quests in the game, but found themain story to be sort of a repeat of Fallout 3 as you're once again tasked to look for a missing family member. There is a faction system available allowing the player to join groups such as the Minute Men or Brotherhood of Steel gaining unique items and perks. While the faction system can add another reason to replay the game, Fallout New Vegas did it better such as if a player♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a faction too much they would send hitmen to kill you. A majority of missions can be completed by killing enemies, but there are some quests which allow opposite approaches such as through speech.
Settlement customization can be a fun and at times irritating distraction as somtimes objects would refuse to snap to position correctly. The settlement options can be deep with multiple items availaible from gates to homes so you won't have similar settlements unless you choose. The weapon and armor customization are just as deep as the settlement's as there different items to make particular improvements. Almost every weapon has some type of item that can improve stability, sight, or power. Armor cusotmizations can contain items for stealth or damage resistances that can be added to accomadate how you play.
Companions also make a return in Fallout 4 as there are multiple characters available to follow you into the wastelands such as a super mutant or cheerfully murderous robot. Each companion is unique in there own way from their backgrounds to their likes and dislikes and will provide certain perks that range from sort of usefull to okay. While I like the addition of the fully voiced character, I would have liked to have better dialogue description as to get a better idea of what the character would say. I liked Fallout 4 so I would recommend buying it, but please avoid buying that darn season pass and just buy the story dlc if you don't care for customizing settlements.

I have played Fallout 4 two hundred twenty-five hours and counting. I wanted to write this review well after Fallout 4 had been released, all of the DLC had been released, and when the modding community had really had a good opportunity to get a foothold in. Fallout 4 is an amazing game all in all. To those people who were giving this game 0's and 10's on the very first day it was released, within the first 10 minutes of playing, all I got to say is that those reviews don't help ANYONE. A game like this takes time to grow.
Gameplay probably features the biggest changes and improvements of the Fallout series. Improvements can be found from various aspects of the game, from combat, exploration, crafting and character building. Compared to Fallout 3, the combat is much more responsive, faster and dynamic. Enemy variation is amazing in Fallout 4 and it was often surprising to see new features and abilities added to already known enemy types. Crafting is one of the biggest and greatest part of Fallout 4. As soon I saw the new crafting system of Fallout 4 in E3, I knew it was going to be great and sure wasn’t disappointed. With Automatron DLC you can also build your own robots, and go far as building your own kickass Sentry Bot. With the improved crafting looting and exploration became more important and rewarding. Junk rarity was also in great balance, I often found myself missing needed materials which then motivated me go out to explore the wasteland. With the new crafting system also came the settlement mode, which allowed players to create their own towns and settlements. To me the vanilla settlement mode was dull in many ways. Either way the settlement mode can a lot of fun with mods, allowing you to actually craft something genuine and incredible. The leveling and perk system was also redesigned. While there was nothing wrong with the previous system, the new system was a welcome change.
In general, the atmosphere in Fallout 4 is subtler than in previous entries. Commonwealth felt much brighter and hopeful than the desolate Capital Wasteland or Mojave Desert. This is likely due to the more vibrant weathers. To improve immersion, Bethesda did a nice job of reducing the amount of loading screens. Abandoned towns now could be explored without having to struggle through the 5 second loading screen every now and then.
I personally enjoyed the main plot, mainly because I didn’t expect much of it I got what I expected. Most of the main storyline was very good, it definitely had some memorable moments, difficult choices and the total length of the story wasn’t too bad. As for side content and quests, which were usually good but often hard to find. Radiant quests in Fallout 4 have a large role. The highly criticized voiced protagonist and the new dialogue system didn’t bother me, which did undoubtedly pose problems. But to me they were welcome changes, which felt like taking one step back and two steps forward.
While Fallout 4 did sacrifice some of its predecessors RPG elements, it still turned out to be one of the best open-world shooter that I’ve played. Fallout did change for better or worse, but as for me, it’s still a Fallout game, and a damn good one.

I have delayed writing this review for quite some time, gathering my thoughts, nuances of the game, but finally I'm ready to give my humble opinion.
Out of all Bethesda Fallout games to date, this one is the winner in my book, with Fallout NV in close second place.
First and foremost this game is immensely huge, 172h in it, and still I barely scratched the surface of this game…
Even more so if you are playing it on survival difficulty. You will understand why I said that, and why it is actually the best way to play this game.
Aside from that, Fallout 4 has really good quality of background environmental sounds/music. Voice acting could be little bit better, but don't get me wrong it is still quite good.
Graphics are quite better compared to previous Bethesda Fallout games, especially if you are a high-end hardware user, but this is mostly a subjective thing (what one expects from the game/engine.)
Introduction of settlement building is quite refreshing, and really adds up to the game. It makes you feel connected to the game in ways, you never realized it could. But this can also be the biggest source of fun and frustration in game...
Lastly this game has a huge modding community, with quite a large number of mods that can seriously enhance the game even more, both with graphics/ui, sounds etc… which I strongly advise to use.

Although a far cry from other Fallout games, it still is a solid Bethesda title. Fallout veterans are likely to be disappointed. I recommend buying it on sale.
+ Enormous open world
+ Captivating story with a few twists
+ Improved gunplay
+ Likeable companions
+ Crafting and customisation
+/- Infinite radiant side-quests
+/- Dumbed down gameplay mechanics
+/- Settlements (time-consuming, micromanagement hell – many will enjoy it though)
+/- Changes to power armour (it's more like a vehicle than armour)
- It's a shooter with RPG elements, not the other way around
- Graphics are bland and the game isn't well-optimised
- VATS is nearly useless
- Little to no quest variety
- Bugs and other nuisances
Fallout 4... Never before has a game left me with such mixed feelings. Although I very much enjoyed playing it (as well as other Bethesda titles in the past), I have to say that this game is a major disappointment.
Nevertheless, let us focus on the pros first. The world is huge and it is very easy to be immersed in it. There is an awful lot of locations to visit, quests to do, and enemies to kill. The gunplay is a vast improvement to the previous Fallout games and, while being clearly designed for consoles (mouse acceleration and input lag are real until one edits some files), it is solid. There also are plenty of crafting and customisation options, so if you watched Full Metal Jacket and you always wanted to have your very own Charlene*, this game lets you do that. I also liked the available companions (there's nothing that screams bad*ss more than having a personal butler fight alongside you) and the main plot a lot.
This game definitely caters to a casual gamer – the RPG mechanics the Fallout series were known for have been significantly dumbed down. One does not have to plan their levelling strategy, since the protagonist can be the master-of-all-trades, given enough XP (there's no level cap and some quests can be done indefinitely). Speaking of key changes, the power armour feels more like a car you can enter and roam the wasteland. While inside, one cannot perform certain actions (like crafting) and the armour requires an external power source called fusion core to function. Settlements are a result of Bethesda jumping on the survival bandwagon and while the idea itself is not bad per se, the execution seems half-baked to me. Firstly, the basic mechanics are not explained to the player. And secondly, settlers are not the sharpest knives in the drawer and, as a result, settlements are a micromanagement hell. With that said, watching a settlement grow can be fun.
My biggest gripe with the game is that it is no longer a proper RPG. The dialogue lines have been replaced with the dialogue wheel (thanks Biower for ruining dialogues since 2007). One can no longer be the devil incarnate (or even a raider for that matter). The new perk system also is a step backwards in my opinion. VATS no longer stops time (only slows it down) and is borderline useless, unless one decides to spend a lot of points in perception. Speaking of shortcomings, infinite radiant side-quests are the bulk of the game – there are few well-designed, interesting quests. And lastly, AI of both enemies and companions leaves a lot to be desired.
In conclusion, Fallout 4 is a terrible Fallout. Does it make it a bad game? Certainly not, but it is not what it says on the tin. Bethesda tried to appeal to the widest audience possible and they certainly succeeded in this regard. To all fellow Fallout fanatics: try not to think you are playing a Fallout game and you will most likely enjoy it.
*One can rename any weapon they own.

With a little over 500 hours’ worth of gameplay Fallout 4 has been one hell of an adventure. From a visual standpoint Bethesda has taken what they have used in the past and created a believable post-apocalyptic Boston. If you have the computer to run it maxed out the whole experience is a gorgeous cinematic landscape full of hidden gems. There is so much to explore outside the main questline, and that’s without the DLC. While you can finish off the main story in about 20 hours, I highly recommend spending time just wandering through Boston and the surrounding areas. The subtle nods to the history of Boston and previous Fallout games help complete this cinematic story. For the most part the DLC is worth the extra cash if you can afford it. Far Harbor and Nukaworld absolutely expand the already large universe. Oh and if you like building stuff? Settlements and vault construction are engrossing and keep you trying to perfect each to keep NPC’s happy and well cared for, or not your call. Can’t wait for Bethesda to surprise us with Fallout 5.

So I wanted to make sure that I gave this game a fair shake before giving it a review, so after 600+ hours here it is:
Pros:
+lore
+some quests particularly those found in side quests and dlcs such as Far Harbor and Nuka-World
+settlement building
+Drinking Buddy
+content per money spent
+improved graphics
+survival mode
Cons:
-old failing engine, somewhat unstable game
-buggy/glitchy quests
-buggy areas
-atmosphere is less immersive than it could of been
-forced story path made it feel different than previous games
-M next to modded saves/modded saves have achievements disabled
-dialog wheel is a let down
Other thoughts:
-Mods really provide the atmosphere that this game should of had from the get go, but mods tend to make the engine even more unstable. True Storms causes texture glitches to become more frequent and annoying. Expanding Settlements causes crashing to desktop to be more frequent. Unofficial patch was not completed at the time of writing this because they found a glitch they could not fix. Hopefully bethesda helps them, but probably not ;(
-Although this game is glitchy, there is nothing game breaking that will prevent completion of main story line. Crashes to desktop do exist and quests becoming bugged occur somewhat frequently. The ability to use the ingame console is extremely helpful in most situations where bugs become problems. I had issues where certain groups would begin to attack me for no reason when they shouldn't of been aggressive and I ended up having to reload a previous save. I really wish they'd let this engine die and come up with something better and less buggy. I'm still not a fan of how quests may not be reset correctly even with console or how the game engine seems to be less than friendly with the frames per second in some places.
Overall: 7/10 Game is entertaining but the engine's bugs hold it back. Bethesda has done some things that make the game less mod friendly. If you can overlook those flaws and the dialog wheel or just mod the dialog wheel, you'll have a great time. It's a must for those who are fans of the lore and the series.

If you are new to the Fallout franchise, this game is for you. if you are very familiar with previous Fallout games, this game is still good but might dissapoint you depending on what type of player you are.
Fallout 4 is amazing when it comes to combat, weapon/armor customization, going around looting, intriguing lore and also the settlement workshop. But... the RPG element is lacking in this game (atleast compared to previous titles). You now have only 4 dialogue options, there are only 1 type of dialogue "skill checks" (charisma), there are very few actually interesting perks to invest your perk points in (there's 6 different perks that boost your damage with a certain weapon type by 20%) and last but not least, the quests are just... meh. I have heard som people complaining about that the player character actually has a voice, which i can't see how it's a problem and i actually liked that i actually got to hear a dialogue (the choices where few mind you) from 2 people and not just an NPC.
So in summary: Combat: 9+/10 Weapon/Armor customization: 8+/10 Open world: 7+/10 Quest/Dialogue options: 5/10 Level system/Perks: 4/10 Quests: 4/10
So out of these 6 points i decided to include the average score is 6/10 but to be honest, if i would just rate this game out of the blue, i'd give it atleast 8.5/10 although there's plenty of pros and cons about this games that i did not mention.

This game has received a lot of hate from the fanbois, but as one of them, let me tell you: I love it!  Survival is really where I've had the most fun, but also the most frustration due to bugs.
Pros:
The graphics and animations are truly beautiful, and help you to feel immersed in the story.  And there is a story, despite what some of the reviews will have you believe.  On the whole, it's pretty good, too.
Needing to keep hydrated, fed and rested in Survival is a nice component, made even better by the fact that healing takes time.  To help balance this out, you can hide behind objects and peek out, just like the enemy will.
You CAN choose to spec your character in different ways, and this WILL have different effects on your gameplay - again, despite the claims of naysayers.  But now choice of direction is much more important (particularly in survival).  If you spec into a sneaky sniper, don't expect him to survive close combat with melee enemies (duh!).
The crafting is the best in any Fallout game, including being able to build up settlements (which helps you feel like you're really taming that wasteland), and modding your weapons and armour to do what you need them to do.
There are some fantastic additions way over and above any previous title.  The first time you equip Power Armour, and it OPENS UP AND YOU CLIMB IN?  Just...wow!  You can also fire flares into the sky, to bring Minutemen allies to a fight, call down artillery on enemy positions, call in other allied groups, and best of all FLY OVER THE WASTELAND in a vertiberd, dealing death to enemies below with the door-mounted minigun.  Those views - just breathtaking!
With the Automatron mod, you can take good old Codsworth or Marie, and add to their already impressive abilities with additional weaponary, armour, etc.  Oh hell, is that a Super Mutant Behemoth?!  'It was, Sir...past tense' - Codsworth, dusting off his bowler hat, and cooling his rapid fire lasers.
The wasteland is MASSIVE compared to earlier games.  You will actually need those settlements as bases, and will need to plan your journeys.  Riding in a vertiberd is a godsend, but often comes late in most players playthroughs.
Cons:
The bugs!  Oh god, the bugs!  The first time I played it through, it was almost unplayable even when not on Survival, because of the amount of times the game would hang up when trying to enter or leave a settlement.  And Preston ****ing Garvey would NEVER accompany me due to an incredibly frustrating but well documented and known common bug.  Bethesda, fix that ****, it's important that key content like companions WORKS.
On Survival, it's so bad I'm contemplating jacking it in, even though I've somehow made it to Level 34.  The current problem?  The story requires me to visit the town of Goodneighbour.  I can't.  The game hangs up every time I try to enter.  Searching google for help, some people found a workaround to this (again, common!) bug by jumping into the settlement from a neibouring building.  But when I try to enter those buildings - the game hangs up!  Comeon Bethesda!
The other cons are really relatively minor.  The ability to gain affinity with factions, from FONV, is gone, which is a shame.  Dialogue is no longer affected by your stats (No more Intel 1 characters saying 'Me Vault Dweller.  Me smash').  And while the Commonwealth has a beautiful mix of funny, sad and bitter-sweet side quests and data entries to explore, your decisions have limited impact on how things go down until the very last one...
Summary:
On the whole, this is the best FallOut game to date, no doubt, but is plagued with well documented bugs that - let's face it - Bethesda isn't going to fix.  Because you already bought the game.  And that's a pretty ****ty choice of theirs.  At least it's not the gigantic dissapointment Rome Total War 2 and X Rebirth were.  On the other hand, THOSE games have been largely fixed.

Being a die-hard Fallout fan i was bound to be happy with a new Fallout, but also got disappointed in some very Fallout-esque points.
First of all let me start by saying:this is a Fallout game, it got the humor, the guts, glory and guns right on. But Bethesda seems to be letting go the RPG part of the game, there is one thing i HATED with a burning passion is that my actions have close to zero influence in the overall mood of the world, best example is when you meet Piper and the Mayor of Diamond City, no matter what you tell the fatso he will reply the same thing, remember Bethesda? Remember the time when if you cackled too much about your vault the super mutants could track it more easily? I sure do. Now, what killed my mood hands down is when "X"(i will not spoiler) is found to be a synth inside the BoS, and "Y" orders you to kill it, if you kill it, its fine, if you don't all you gotta do is pass a speech check and bingo blango you still can come back to the  BoS and get promoted! That's preposterous! There is no consequence, there is no bad ending. But i suppose i'm over-extending myself, bottom line, if you are a hardcore Fallout fan you will most likely enjoy it, if you never played Fallout you will love it.
Pros:
>Voice-acting is over-the-top(you can't find a NPC with the same voice as another)
>Sound effects
>Aiming system
>Crafting and modding
>Modding community
Cons:
>Graphics engine is ancient
>Poorly optimized
>Lore inconsistency
>Your actions have very little impact in the world.

Fallout 3 was "Oblivion with guns," Fallout: New Vegas was "Oblivion with guns - in Vegas!"  If you're being honest with yourself, you'll admit that Fallout 4 is "Skyrim with lasers."  Hell, Maxson is basically Ulfric Stormcloak with a Midwestern accent.
That being said, it is still a great game.  The updated perk system allows for a much more customizable hero/heroine, the story is surprisingly well-written, and you'll find yourself genuinely caring for your companions and the fate of the Commonwealth.  I don't even care about the real Boston so that's saying something.
The humor is more subtle this time than it was in New Vegas and definitely more than it was in the first two games, which bordered on dark comedy.  You still have Protectrons shouting "EXTERMINATE!" when you get too close to them, though, and there are other sci-fi references if you know what you're looking for.
It's not perfect, though.  Again, the engine is an upgraded version of the Morrowind engine.  Which is fine, but it's hard to tell if we are in an "what ain't broke" situation or if Bethesda is actually starting to run out of ideas.  Getting rid of the karma counter is great, as it was poorly implemented in Fallout 3, but again your supposed moral "options" are "save the world while being a great guy/gal" or "save the world while being a rude jerk."
It's nice that there's only one paragon faction - the Minute Men, and the others have their own gray areas (the Railroad are well-intentioned extremists, the Brotherhood of Steel is flirting with neo-Nazism, and the Institute is going to save the world whether they want it or not).  They've definitely implemented a "play as the bad guys" plan much better than Fallout: New Vegas did, in which the Caesar's Legion path was limited and filled with buggy quests.
Settlement building is fun at first but it quickly turns into a full-blown plot tumor, in which you have to start delaying your various quests in order to save and upgrade your settlements.  You also find yourself wanting to slap the settlers when they grouse about not having enough food despite there being hundreds of ears of corn in your workbench and half-a-dozen young men sitting on the couch and staring into space, waiting for orders from you, personally, who might be the General of the Minutemen or Director of the Institute by this point.  I know it's a game but the "micromanage the populace" issue really breaks immersion.
These are minor gripes in an otherwise great game.  Highly recommended for anyone that enjoyed the previous Fallout games or Skyrim.

Fallout 4 is the latest entry in the popular Fallout series and was developed by Bethesda Game Studios themselves, as opposed to the previous game, New Vegas, which was made by Obsidian Entertainment. This time around the player takes control of a character named the Sole Survivor, who lived with his family in Massachusetts during the last few days before the Nuclear Wars. Having woken up after a long cryogenic slumber in a now barren wasteland known as the Commonwealth, the Survivor must now adapt to the new reality and rescue his/her son from a mysterious organization.
It's pretty clear that the developers of Fallout 4 attempted to craft a Fallout game that would get the same good reception as New Vegas, while introducing several successful elements from The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim at the same time. The result is a game not as good as New Vegas was, but that is leagues better than Fallout 3.
While you can still create a character with his/her own S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats and have a great perks selections while levelling up, the developers' decision to remove skills and give your character a fixed background really hurt the roleplaying angle of Fallout 4 in the long run. This isn't helped by the game following the Skyrim's formula a bit too well: the majority of the quests and side quests you are given are simply about clearing dungeons of enemies or going there to help some NPC or retrive a McGuffin. The only non-combat skill you can use during dialogue is charisma, which allows you to turn few quests the way you want them to or simply ask the quest givers for more money. Therefore, Fallout 4 never gets as immersive as New Vegas was and the potential to replay the game with a different character is vastly reduced.
The two strongest suits of Fallout 4 are, however, the general presentation and the general overhaul to combat. The world of Fallout has never looked so "gorgeous" and varied and exploring the Commonwealth is, for the most part, something you'll wish to do at lenght. Shooting and melee weapons handling have been considerably improved from both Fallout 3 and New Vegas and Fallout 4 feels like an excellent shooter in its own right. You can also leave your own mark on your gear more thanks to the introduction of armor pieces (which you can wear over your current outfit for extra protection or nice side effects) and weapon mods (nearly all the weapons you can use have interchangeable parts in order for you to change their parameters as you see fit, to better tailor them to your own playstyle).
The most important addition Fallout 4 makes to the series is its deeper crafting system. On top of your ability to craft and improve both armor, outfits and weapons, you can also collect materials scattered through all the Commonwealth and build lasting machines and elements of the scenery in fixed settlement areas and leave your own mark on the world. Truth be told, however, crafting in Fallout 4 is as immersive and fun to perform as you decide it will be: weapons and armor crafting can at times appear completely useless, since you can find the strongest gear right in the game's world easily, and the whole settlement mechanic will appeal to some, but also be annoying to others (it doesn't help that the main quest at times forces you to build stuff and the hunting for component can be, at times, incredibly frustrating).
As I mentioned above, the story angle of Fallout 4 is definitely leagues better than the abysmal one provided in Fallout 3, but it never quite reaches the heights of New Vegas. The first part of your story, which is about following your son's steps and try to find him, is the strongest suit of the narrative: after that, the game tries to offer a "factions at war" scenario in the same vein as New Vegas, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.
In the very end, the enjoyment you can gain from Fallout 4 depends a lot on your own personal preference when videogames, and the Fallout series, are concerned. If you like a more action-oriented Fallout looking stunning, then you'll adore Fallout 4. If you care more about the roleplaying angle, you'll be inevitably disappointed sooner or later. If you occupy the middle ground, then Fallout 4 is definitely a good purchase and a solid game

There was a guy who frequently bought cheeseburgers at McDonalds. One day, he read a mcdonalds ad in the newspaper for a new cheeseburger. This new cheeseburger was advertised to have a bigger, juicer and tastier beef patty than the old cheeseburgers.
Now after seeing the advert he goes to McDonalds and pays full price for the burger; which cost more than the old cheeseburger.
When he unwrapped the wrapper for his cheeseburger, he was greeted by a smaller beef patty that just tasted like the old one, four hamburger buns and there were twice the pickles than in the old one.
The main focus of the fallout franchise was about the freedom of choice, how choices you make impacted the world around you and this is what immersed people in the Universe of Fallout. Everywhere in the story and side quests, it always forces you to be somewhat "moral". You can barely be evil in this game, the freedom of choosing whether to be evil or good is butchered by the game being more linear rather than non-linear. The Karma system which was one of the main aspects of the previous games is no more already.
While I don't mind having a voiced protagonist, it really restricts the amount of content of all the quests as the voice actor can only record a limited amount of lines during the time is used for developing the game. So naturally and unintentionally, the main and side quests have become even more linear because of this restriction.
The gameplay is definitely an improvement over the old games, it feels more exiciting to put on a suit of power armor and the fights feel much more engaging. However I've noticed bandits and supermutants throwing grenades at walls only for them to bounce back on themselves. The A.I. is the only thing about combat that Bethesda didn't quite get.
There is a large and noticeable amount of game breaking bugs. There are killer abadoned cars that suddenly fly towards you and kill you, corpses turning inside out and moving up the damn walls like the excorcist and dogmeat is suddenly phases through the elevator floor plumetting 10 stories down. These are just a few bugs you encounter in the entire game.
Bethesda really tried to mimic the features that made alot of the blockbuster games out there succesful, yet all they did was create a messy, chaotic game with littered with bugs in every corner. While the concepts in this game are great, they just seem very unpolished and incomplete. I just feel that Bethesda missed out on taking Fallout 4's hidden potential and turning it into what could've been a better game.
Fallout 4 was advertised to be a polished, RPG game but what I bought was the opposite of what was advertised. What disturbs me isnt how Fallout 4 lacked content, but how everyone is just willing to shell out money for incomplete games nowadays.

These Fallout games do not require knowledge of previous entries in the series to understand them or enjoy them, so Fallout 4 is as good a place as any to step into the wasteland and have some fun. Fallout 4 has a lot of cool stuff going on for it, from its weapons, to its armor, to its factions, to some of its quests, to some of its DLC, to just wandering the wasteland early in the game and leveling up. There is a lot to get into here.
Post-apocalyptic settings can be risky when it comes to fiction. Unless you just like watching people suffer, it can be a bit of a downer playing in a post-apocalyptic setting for any significant length of time. However, with Fallout 4, the tone of the game is very satirical...like how RoboCop had an awful "New Detroit" that you would never want to live in, that is terribly violent and often bleak, but there are so many snarky jokes like "I'd buy that for a dollar," the "6000 SUX" and its in-movie commercial, and more. Fallout does that in its own style, using over-the-top patriotism with certain "old world" tech, computer communications that are less than serious, and quests that put a smile on your face. I really like how you're in a horrible environment, but it still feels so charming despite all of that.
The leveling system is the best of any that Fallout has seen to date. In the prior games, you have to study the manual or an online guide to find out what levels you need to have which attitbutes at which values, and which skills you need to pick up at which time to be able to have the option to take other skills. Nope. That's awful. Only masochistic/hardcore people who want everything to be a pain in the rear and leave everything to chance...including whether or not your character you've spent 80+ hours playing is any good or not, would like such as system. If that's you, then you'll hate Fallout 4's leveling because it's designed so you have a big, animated chart you can scroll around, showing you different levels of different skills, what levels you need to get each thing at, etc. It's wonderful!
For any creeps who want to claim "Ohhh but your character can just max everything out and is good at everything with the new leveling system because you can level up past 200!" that's nice. If someone is willing to put the time and effort into playing the game THAT long, then so be it. I have played this game for hundreds of hours, and my character just hit level 100, as I recall. I could wreck the most powerful enemy in the game in one shot about 200 hours back, so even if I did max my character out, it doesn't matter. More importantly, I am nowhere close to maxing my character out, and I would have to play several hundred more hours to do it. =/
Basically, this game is Skyrim but sci-fi and with more focus. By that, I mean the quests and everything else is less distracting and I am always able to finish these recent Fallout games, whereas the Elder Scrolls games I either never finish or take forever to get through them due to not sticking with them long enough out of eventual boredom. The world of Fallout just sucks me in and keeps me interested, though.
One thing that's new to Fallout in this game is settlement-building. You will meet a weirdo guy named Preston Garvey in the game who will generally force missions on you to go scout out a settlement and set it up. It's pretty fun the first few times, though your settlement can be attacked...which is really annoying when you set up a tower-defense-style maze, only to realize that if you're away from your base, the game just spawns the enemies inside your base so that all of your mega deathtrap lasers and rocket launchers lining your entrance never fire and the enemy just slaughters all of your settlers and breaks your stuff you built.
You will get paged to come defend these bases often, and it gets really old. I loved the settlements, but when I have to personally go fight at them despite dumping mounds of auto turrets in the bases and setting up uber deathtrap entrances, I lost a lot of that love. I feel like a Fallout 5 or equivalent could really improve on settlements, and they could easily be one of the best parts of the game. All the freedom of choice of its predecessors is gone, it's not so much an open world RPG as a linear game with a fairly big map.
