Fallout 4 is the latest entry in the popular Fallout series and was developed by Bethesda Game Studios themselves, as opposed to the previous game, New Vegas, which was made by Obsidian Entertainment. This time around the player takes control of a character named the Sole Survivor, who lived with his family in Massachusetts during the last few days before the Nuclear Wars. Having woken up after a long cryogenic slumber in a now barren wasteland known as the Commonwealth, the Survivor must now adapt to the new reality and rescue his/her son from a mysterious organization.
It's pretty clear that the developers of Fallout 4 attempted to craft a Fallout game that would get the same good reception as New Vegas, while introducing several successful elements from The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim at the same time. The result is a game not as good as New Vegas was, but that is leagues better than Fallout 3.
While you can still create a character with his/her own S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats and have a great perks selections while levelling up, the developers' decision to remove skills and give your character a fixed background really hurt the roleplaying angle of Fallout 4 in the long run. This isn't helped by the game following the Skyrim's formula a bit too well: the majority of the quests and side quests you are given are simply about clearing dungeons of enemies or going there to help some NPC or retrive a McGuffin. The only non-combat skill you can use during dialogue is charisma, which allows you to turn few quests the way you want them to or simply ask the quest givers for more money. Therefore, Fallout 4 never gets as immersive as New Vegas was and the potential to replay the game with a different character is vastly reduced.
The two strongest suits of Fallout 4 are, however, the general presentation and the general overhaul to combat. The world of Fallout has never looked so "gorgeous" and varied and exploring the Commonwealth is, for the most part, something you'll wish to do at lenght. Shooting and melee weapons handling have been considerably improved from both Fallout 3 and New Vegas and Fallout 4 feels like an excellent shooter in its own right. You can also leave your own mark on your gear more thanks to the introduction of armor pieces (which you can wear over your current outfit for extra protection or nice side effects) and weapon mods (nearly all the weapons you can use have interchangeable parts in order for you to change their parameters as you see fit, to better tailor them to your own playstyle).
The most important addition Fallout 4 makes to the series is its deeper crafting system. On top of your ability to craft and improve both armor, outfits and weapons, you can also collect materials scattered through all the Commonwealth and build lasting machines and elements of the scenery in fixed settlement areas and leave your own mark on the world. Truth be told, however, crafting in Fallout 4 is as immersive and fun to perform as you decide it will be: weapons and armor crafting can at times appear completely useless, since you can find the strongest gear right in the game's world easily, and the whole settlement mechanic will appeal to some, but also be annoying to others (it doesn't help that the main quest at times forces you to build stuff and the hunting for component can be, at times, incredibly frustrating).
As I mentioned above, the story angle of Fallout 4 is definitely leagues better than the abysmal one provided in Fallout 3, but it never quite reaches the heights of New Vegas. The first part of your story, which is about following your son's steps and try to find him, is the strongest suit of the narrative: after that, the game tries to offer a "factions at war" scenario in the same vein as New Vegas, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.
In the very end, the enjoyment you can gain from Fallout 4 depends a lot on your own personal preference when videogames, and the Fallout series, are concerned. If you like a more action-oriented Fallout looking stunning, then you'll adore Fallout 4. If you care more about the roleplaying angle, you'll be inevitably disappointed sooner or later. If you occupy the middle ground, then Fallout 4 is definitely a good purchase and a solid game

These Fallout games do not require knowledge of previous entries in the series to understand them or enjoy them, so Fallout 4 is as good a place as any to step into the wasteland and have some fun. Fallout 4 has a lot of cool stuff going on for it, from its weapons, to its armor, to its factions, to some of its quests, to some of its DLC, to just wandering the wasteland early in the game and leveling up. There is a lot to get into here.
Post-apocalyptic settings can be risky when it comes to fiction. Unless you just like watching people suffer, it can be a bit of a downer playing in a post-apocalyptic setting for any significant length of time. However, with Fallout 4, the tone of the game is very satirical...like how RoboCop had an awful "New Detroit" that you would never want to live in, that is terribly violent and often bleak, but there are so many snarky jokes like "I'd buy that for a dollar," the "6000 SUX" and its in-movie commercial, and more. Fallout does that in its own style, using over-the-top patriotism with certain "old world" tech, computer communications that are less than serious, and quests that put a smile on your face. I really like how you're in a horrible environment, but it still feels so charming despite all of that.
The leveling system is the best of any that Fallout has seen to date. In the prior games, you have to study the manual or an online guide to find out what levels you need to have which attitbutes at which values, and which skills you need to pick up at which time to be able to have the option to take other skills. Nope. That's awful. Only masochistic/hardcore people who want everything to be a pain in the rear and leave everything to chance...including whether or not your character you've spent 80+ hours playing is any good or not, would like such as system. If that's you, then you'll hate Fallout 4's leveling because it's designed so you have a big, animated chart you can scroll around, showing you different levels of different skills, what levels you need to get each thing at, etc. It's wonderful!
For any creeps who want to claim "Ohhh but your character can just max everything out and is good at everything with the new leveling system because you can level up past 200!" that's nice. If someone is willing to put the time and effort into playing the game THAT long, then so be it. I have played this game for hundreds of hours, and my character just hit level 100, as I recall. I could wreck the most powerful enemy in the game in one shot about 200 hours back, so even if I did max my character out, it doesn't matter. More importantly, I am nowhere close to maxing my character out, and I would have to play several hundred more hours to do it. =/
Basically, this game is Skyrim but sci-fi and with more focus. By that, I mean the quests and everything else is less distracting and I am always able to finish these recent Fallout games, whereas the Elder Scrolls games I either never finish or take forever to get through them due to not sticking with them long enough out of eventual boredom. The world of Fallout just sucks me in and keeps me interested, though.
One thing that's new to Fallout in this game is settlement-building. You will meet a weirdo guy named Preston Garvey in the game who will generally force missions on you to go scout out a settlement and set it up. It's pretty fun the first few times, though your settlement can be attacked...which is really annoying when you set up a tower-defense-style maze, only to realize that if you're away from your base, the game just spawns the enemies inside your base so that all of your mega deathtrap lasers and rocket launchers lining your entrance never fire and the enemy just slaughters all of your settlers and breaks your stuff you built.
You will get paged to come defend these bases often, and it gets really old. I loved the settlements, but when I have to personally go fight at them despite dumping mounds of auto turrets in the bases and setting up uber deathtrap entrances, I lost a lot of that love. I feel like a Fallout 5 or equivalent could really improve on settlements, and they could easily be one of the best parts of the game. I have to admit, it can be a bit addicting even in Fallout 4, despite the issues I mentioned.
Lastly, the story in the game is pretty decent. It kept me more interested than the story in Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas, but Fallout 4's actual ending is really, really weak. Other than that, it's quite nice, though. Overall, I can't deny that I had a lot of fun with this game, though given its size, I don't know if I'll ever play through it all again someday or not. I played long enough to say that I got my money's worth and had a good time, though.

DISCLAIMER: Take this review with huge grain of salt. Most recent game I completed recently was from 2013, and I missed out on whole previous gaming generation (excluding Skyrim, TF2 and few other games) before that.
So, Fallout 4. I waited for it impatiently ever since I saw E3 demo back in the day, and my hype was growing stronger with every review I've read. I couldn't play it though - my PC was far too weak to play recent games, and my situration didn't allow for upgrade.
But recentlyy, I've managed to get a new PC and finally play this game.
I'll cut the chase:  I hated this game at first. I kept pressing tab (habbit I've got Skyrim) after I finished looting enemies, which kept bringing up PipBoy. Also, fight. At first I couldn't grasp how much it changed since New Vegas - enemies were moving too fast, V.A.T.S didn't help much and I spent more time running away than actually putting up a fight in first few hours of gameplay. Hell, getting to Diamond City took me well over an hour of constant running from ghouls, bloatflys and those huge mosquito things. First potential companion I've met - Piper - I hated from start (I still hate ehr by the way). Constant nagging of Preston also added to my frustration.
But, hours passed. I slowly got used to modern-ess of this game and I can honestly say - I like it and I would recommend it to anyone who's looking for Fallout-themed sandbox FPS with minor RPG and RTS elements. Combat is okay, graphics are really pretty (but game is unoptimized like hell), soundtrack is 10/10.
If you're looking for good Fallout game though, this is not a game you're looking for. Check out New Vegas or Fallout 1&2 instead. Bethesda was trying to step up their game, but results pale in comparison with achievements of Black Isle Studios (Fallout 1&2) and Obsidian Entertaiment (Fallout: New Vegas).

Bethesda have done with the Fallout series what they did with the Elder Scrolls series. They’ve improved the sound, graphics and animations, but simplified the games so they appeal to a wider audience and are adapted to run on console systems. In
, we have great graphics, but the story and rpg aspects that were present in earlier Fallout games have diminished and the emphasis now is for the player to experience a "Fallout-themed" open world setting.
In
the player's ability to have a meaningful influence on the Fallout world is greatly reduced when compared to earlier games. The only obvious, lasting influence you can have on the Fallout 4 world is to create settlements by scavenging for junk materials from ruined towns and cities. The feature allows you to create and furnish buildings, do farming, rig up generators and create defences. But there's no intricate plot you can become entangled in, and very little in the way of interaction with npcs, factions and politics. You have only four choices when interacting with an npc, offered by an on-screen menu containing pre-determined phrases (clearly designed with consoles in mind). Unlike Fasllout New Vegas, NPCs are now pretty much divided into good and bad. Ones that want to kill you, and ones that don't.
Another significant change with Fallout 4 is the continuous update cycle for the game, which can be seen as a way of taking control of the platform. The updates bring little value for the end-user on a PC, but often have the effect of breaking mods, especially those that rely on the script extender (F4SE). One of the more recent updates introduced the Creation Club, which many see as the beginning of paid mods on an increasingly controlled platform, replacing the open-ended modding possibility that all Bethesdas' games had previously been famous for.
I enjoy playing Fallout 4, despite the negative things I have written. However, since the game is now subject to change through its continuous updates, user experience can deteriorate and so can peoples' review ratings.

For a moment, please ignore the fact that I've over 1,000 hours spent with this game.
Fallout 4 is like a drug addiction.
Despite all the quirks you endure/exhibit while using, you still get a high that, to you, outweighs the fact you make yourself look like an insufferable jerk or you play a game that is one.
In time, you become so accustomed and desensitized by it, you keep on coming back to it to fill a void.
You don't try other games/methods since they involve effort to learn from scratch.
You eventually reach a point when you look back at all the time, money, rotting teeth, or what-have-you, that you'll never get back.
If you can only afford one game for the next 1-2 years, Fallout 4 might be the one for you.
Otherwise, if you want to experience variety and true high-quality games that aren't rife with game-breaking bugs, go play some indie games, the gateway drug into gaming's clean-highs.

The world of Fallout 4 seems much larger and more explorable than even other installements in the series, which are remakably open ended. The addition of settlements is a nice way to break up what would otherwise be extended periods of time spent either aimlessly wandering or running around looking for specific things. I also believe Bethesda's choice to include the developer character  modeling system is a very welcome change to character creation, and give a lot more power to the player.
While the new crafting system can be daunting at first, it very quickly becomes both normal, and nearly indespensibe in the game, while also giving you a reason to hold on to that tin can. That being said, this also does reduce the need for trading items, as you can find most things in the wasteland and will be reluctant to sell anyting, in case you need the parts.
The leveling system is probably the one thing that I would have prefered they left asis. Where I see the benifits of their new system, especially dealing with the hacking/lockpicking mechanics, I still belive that the point based system is better than the purely perks based one.
Overall, I spent over $200, as I bought a gamestop bundle to get the pip-boy edition pre order, which is a lot of money. However I would still say that Fallout 4 was worth every penny.

Fallout 4 is almost my favorite Fallout game. New Vegas slightly edges it out because of its viable non-combat builds and for the faction-reputation system.
Fallout 4 took all the crappy stuff from 3 and threw it out the window. No more silent protagonist. No more awkward conversations with stiff NPCs. No more forever-wandering-the-wastes.
The character creation is so much more streamlined in Fallout 4. Although I think some of the perks are a bit underpowered relative to others, I think the "hidden skills" system is far better than investing skill points tediously into skills.
The world is way more fleshed out than Fallout 3.  It just feels more real to me. Around every corner is a notable landmark or hidden stash. When I just wanted to explore, there were tons of side quests to encounter and bases to claim.
The story and its primary factions are pretty cool. Much better than the plot of Fallout 3. Because affiliating yourself with a faction is a large part of the main story, I really enjoyed playing through the game multiple times to see how each faction's plot differed from the rest. I couldn't even tell you what the last half of Fallout 3's story is, and I played it through almost 3 times. Also, Fallout 4's ending is waaaay less anticlimactic than its predecessors (imo, New Vegas's ending was just okay, and 3's ending was downright terrible).
I see this game getting a lot of hate, which is a total shame. I loved it from start to finish, and can't wait to play it through a 3rd and 4th time!

The world of Fallout 4 seems much larger and more explorable than even other installements in the series, which are remakably open ended. The addition of settlements is a nice way to break up what would otherwise be extended periods of time spent either aimlessly wandering or running around looking for specific things. I also believe Bethesda's choice to include the developer character  modeling system is a very welcome change to character creation, and give a lot more power to the player.
While the new crafting system can be daunting at first, it very quickly becomes both normal, and nearly indespensibe in the game, while also giving you a reason to hold on to that tin can. That being said, this also does reduce the need for trading items, as you can find most things in the wasteland and will be reluctant to sell anyting, in case you need the parts.
The leveling system is probably the one thing that I would have prefered they left asis. Where I see the benifits of their new system, especially dealing with the hacking/lockpicking mechanics, I still belive that the point based system is better than the purely perks based one.
Overall, I spent over $200, as I bought a gamestop bundle to get the pip-boy edition pre order, which is a lot of money. However I would still say that Fallout 4 was worth every penny.

Fallout 4 is almost my favorite Fallout game. New Vegas slightly edges it out because of its viable non-combat builds and for the faction-reputation system.
Fallout 4 took all the crappy stuff from 3 and threw it out the window. No more silent protagonist. No more awkward conversations with stiff NPCs. No more forever-wandering-the-wastes.
The character creation is so much more streamlined in Fallout 4. Although I think some of the perks are a bit underpowered relative to others, I think the "hidden skills" system is far better than investing skill points tediously into skills.
The world is way more fleshed out than Fallout 3.  It just feels more real to me. Around every corner is a notable landmark or hidden stash. When I just wanted to explore, there were tons of side quests to encounter and bases to claim.
The story and its primary factions are pretty cool. Much better than the plot of Fallout 3. Because affiliating yourself with a faction is a large part of the main story, I really enjoyed playing through the game multiple times to see how each faction's plot differed from the rest. I couldn't even tell you what the last half of Fallout 3's story is, and I played it through almost 3 times. Also, Fallout 4's ending is waaaay less anticlimactic than its predecessors (imo, New Vegas's ending was just okay, and 3's ending was downright terrible).
I see this game getting a lot of hate, which is a total shame. I loved it from start to finish, and can't wait to play it through a 3rd and 4th time!

I was a huge fan of 3, preordered New Vegas special edition, and preordered 4 Pip Boy Edition with season pass.
I got about halfway through the campaign and got bored. The main problem is that the dialogue system overhaul ruined the immersion. Your choices are positive, negative, sarcastic, and funny. The dialogue choices make the questlines seem rigid and don't offer much leeway.
I forced myself through the campaign and didn't touch it again until DLC came out. Automatron was way too quick of a story and didn't bring too much new content. Didn't play Wasteland Workshop because I wasn't too interested in the building system. I was able to play about an hour of Far Harbor, but I haven't wanted to pick up the game again. DLC's in general were bland and nothing like the ones in 3 and NV.

Fallout 3 was a complete game changer for me. It really showed me what an immersive experience a decent first person RPG could be. As a consequence my personal hype levels for 4 were at a peak when they revealed the game. Upon having thrashed it into the ground, unlocked every achievement and sampled every aspect of the DLC, I can honestly say I have enjoyed the experience. I went all the way to level 100, finished every alternative ending and completed pretty much every quest it threw at me. I will step back into it soon to sample Survival mode, and when they release the VR compatibility it may well be the killer app many of us need to commit to VR.
I do have a few criticisms of the game, but in truth they probably only exist because I regard Fallout 3 so highly. The overall story here just didn't seem as epic and involving as that of the previous game. I think this is a consequence of having so many different endgames. In 3 it was one way or the other. Here it's one of 4 ways via multiple intersections, some of which are very dull and badly written conclusions to what by all accounts is an epic journey. Also I didn't like the lack of a visible karma system in the pipboy (the thing that tells you whether your good or bad or somewhere inbetween). I realise this is represented in the way your relationships with the various characters unfold, but not having a visual reference to how holy / evil you is something I miss.
Overall, a solid experience. As many have said on here and elsewhere, it's not an amazing RPG as the way the story and your character arc plays out is quite linear. However the central loop of roam, kill, loot, repeat is still fully intact, the soundtrack is incredible, and the gun play and first person action elements of the game are tight and an evolution from previous games.

Just a quick note: I own none of the DLC
This game was in development for so long, and somehow it still feels incomplete.  Oh, sure you can build up your settlements, have crops and defense and structures, but most of the time it's just downright frustrating to do any of that.  There's no grid to snap walls, floors, or anything to.  The only time they snap is to another wall or floor, and why is it that cables have this predetermined curve to them, causing them to sometimes be unplaceable because the curve passes through the ground or something when in reality that's not at all what would happen?  And why when I'm building can't I float around like I've turned off collision so I don't have to build a set of stairs just to be able to put something up on a roof?
The variety of enemies from previous titles is gone.  New Vegas gave the player a vast and easily encountered number of different factions.  In Fallout 4, the majority of enemy factions basically comes down to Ghouls, (which the game even sometimes reminds the player during a random loading screen are not zombies) Super Mutants, and Raiders.  Occasionally, the player will have to deal with Gunners and during the more story-driven quests, Synths, but that's about it.  Those are the most common enemies in the game, and they're the most common by quite a lot.
Of course, it's possible this wouldn't be so bothersome if it weren't for the fact that by its own design, the game forces these enemy factions to be encountered extremely often.  There is an abysmal amount of side quests in this game, as it seems instead focus has been placed on giving the player repeatable quests to either defend a settlement by building up its defenses, help a settlement get one of its members back after they were kidnapped, usually by a settlement of Raiders somewhere, clear out a location filled with Ghouls, or stop Super Mutants from raiding a settlement again by clearing them out of a location, too.  Wash, rinse, repeat, indefinitely.  When I walked onto a pier and randomly discovered the "Here There Be Monsters" quest I nearly cried at the thought of being able to do something other than clear out a dungeon.
The skill system has been absolutely decimated.  There are no more skills.  Now there are only perks.  One weakness I've found of the Fallout games has always been that they never really hammer home any sense of really building your character into one specific thing.  You have the ability to put points into whatever skills you want, resulting in just making your character generally better at everything.  Some people really like this, and I can understand that completely, but never was the problem with this system so glaring until now.  Skills have turned into perks, and also perks are still perks.  The Guns skill has now been broken up and scattered all over the tree into several different perks, whereas before there were not only perks relating to guns, but a skill designated for them, too.  Some of these new perks, however, are just completely pointless.  Lockpicking, for example, progresses exactly as it used to, except now, because everything is locked to a certain level, it's impossible to be able to open master locks until a certain level is achieved, which makes no sense and makes the whole system feel incredibly watered down.  In previous games, you could just max out any skill as quickly as you desired.  It makes leveling feel unrewarding as your choices in what you can do have become way more limited.
One positive thing I'd like to mention is the very creative way that junk works.  You can now pick up pretty much any item you find and sell it or store it at a workbench and use its base materials to help you build things around your settlements.  It's a very nice way to give a bit more interactivity to the world the player is in, as it allows you to do more with those objects than just pick them up and toss them around.
Overall, despite everything I've said, this is still a fun game, though I can't really play it for many hours at a time due to the never-ending bombardment of settlement quests.  The weapon and armor customization is really good, though it is annoying being forced to wait until a certain level so the next rank of the armorer or science perk can be met in order to do more things with the customizing.  The story isn't half bad, even if it is a bit short, and the outside environments are fantastic as long as you don't look to closely at them.  However, I still can't recommend this game, for the detailed reasons above, as well as some other minor things (unfinished roofs, building textures warping into each other, the super mutants voices have somehow gotten even more irritating, etc.).  Hopefully the next Fallout will be able to fix at least some of these problems.

Fallout 3 was a complete game changer for me. It really showed me what an immersive experience a decent first person RPG could be. As a consequence my personal hype levels for 4 were at a peak when they revealed the game. Upon having thrashed it into the ground, unlocked every achievement and sampled every aspect of the DLC, I can honestly say I have enjoyed the experience. I went all the way to level 100, finished every alternative ending and completed pretty much every quest it threw at me. I will step back into it soon to sample Survival mode, and when they release the VR compatibility it may well be the killer app many of us need to commit to VR.
I do have a few criticisms of the game, but in truth they probably only exist because I regard Fallout 3 so highly. The overall story here just didn't seem as epic and involving as that of the previous game. I think this is a consequence of having so many different endgames. In 3 it was one way or the other. Here it's one of 4 ways via multiple intersections, some of which are very dull and badly written conclusions to what by all accounts is an epic journey. Also I didn't like the lack of a visible karma system in the pipboy (the thing that tells you whether your good or bad or somewhere inbetween). I realise this is represented in the way your relationships with the various characters unfold, but not having a visual reference to how holy / evil you is something I miss.
Overall, a solid experience. As many have said on here and elsewhere, it's not an amazing RPG as the way the story and your character arc plays out is quite linear. However the central loop of roam, kill, loot, repeat is still fully intact, the soundtrack is incredible, and the gun play and first person action elements of the game are tight and an evolution from previous games.

Hmm. Fallout 4 leaves me very conflicted. With Fallout New Vegas being my favourite RPG ever, I was very much looking forward to Fallout 4 initially. Fallout 3 was alright I thought but lacked a lot of a depth and had some horrendous writing. I had hoped Bethesda would look at what made New Vegas so well recieved and take some notes, but as it turns out it's like that game never existed. Fallout 4 is a "refined" Fallout 3 with extra stuff on top, and retains a lot of that game's flaws.
There have been written many things by angry 1/2/NV zealots already on the internet so I'll keep this fairly brief.
+ Fantastic graphics and art style. Some may find the 50's aestethic a little overdone, but it suits the game perfectly. Animation is way better than the old gamebryo games and it does a ton for the feel of the game. I still have my qualms about how everything still looks broken down and dirty 200+ years after the bombs fell, but whatever.
+ Great soundtrack and music, both atmospheric sounds and ingame radio.
+ Hell yeah the brotherhood is awesome in this game.
+ Well crafted locations and world map, but Bethesda really should look at introducing some variety into their dungeon design. It feels very Elder Scrolls, and not necessarily in a good way.
/ Settlement system feels half baked. Building things in first person is fiddly and non-precise, your settlers can't do anything yourself, and you need to keep doing this yourself in every single settlement you want populated. If you like me found it really boring, and just wanted to skip it, you have to ignore one of the factions. But that's ok because they were the generic good guy faction anyway which I wasn't interested in. :)
/ Gun and armor crafting is initially very rewarding, but scavenging is kind of boring and mid-late game there's pretty much zero reason to change your gun setup around. It doesn't make much sense to use something outside of what you have specialised into.
/ Ńo traits, they removed skills, remade the perks and special system and somehow made a much less compelling version of it all. It's not objectively terrible, but I see very little merit in it.
/ The main story and general writing is a definite step above Fallout 3, but that isn't saying much.
/ Skyrim-esque legendary system, which is both good because it allows some extra specialisation, and bad because it bloats the game with useless things and leaves you with extremely few interesting unique guns.
- Abysmal dialogue system. This goes against everything that's Fallout. In all the previous games you can have long meaningful discussions with NPCs and you don't mind it one bit because they're so well written. In Fallout 4, you're given no real choice in dialogue, and have very little way of affecting what you're saying. You may have seen the joke about Fallout 4 conversations having 4 choices, Yes, Yes (sarcastic), Tell me more (also yes) and No (actually yes). The really sad thing is just how true it is.
- I really don't like the voiced protagonist either, mainly because it's just reading aloud what I've already read on screen, and also because it simply does not suit all characters.
- The game is incredibly combat heavy and lacks any nuance. Where as NV gave you a lot of morally interesting choices and many different ways to resolve quests, you just shoot your way through things 99% of the time in this game. Gone are the mostly pacifist runs, or smooth talker builds.
- Faction reputation is gone and you can be super best buddies with all the factions at once without consequense until the extreme late game. This is super boring and doesn't make much sense at all.
- Actually, the factions are just boring overall.
- The followers at least have have a little more personality than Fallout 3's cardboard cutouts, but they're almost all identical in the way they talk and interact with you. In NV each companion had a very fulfilling and well written quest and would react to you very differently depending on what you did. In FO4 it feels very video-gamey and not like an interesting character you want to know. Disappointing.
Ultimately, I enjoyed Fallout 4 for the positives it does have, and all the new things that it brought, even if I didn't end up liking all of them in the end. A newcomer to the series may not see the flaws I pointed out as very critical. But I do not feel much of an urge to play anymore, not until I get the DLC I'm interested in anyway (very little of it). It's a fine game, but not what I wanted it to be, I guess.

I last played Fallout 4 in January and I began to wonder... how is it that I am approaching a year of not playing a game in one of my favorite series?
Short version of what I saw is that Fallout 4 (base game only) is lacking in the sense of emotion, discovery, and value. Whenever I play it, I feel like it is more of a shooter that I have been given an open map to run around in. Yes, there are are still some quests that are interesting but almost everything gets solved the same way at the end no matter what options you take: kill them dead. The crafting system is a bit of nuisance but settlement building wasn't even as close as amazing as it was promissed. It does look a lot nicer visually because everything isn't grey or brownish but it just doesn't have that RPG feel to it. The factions aren't really different to eachother because you don't see much change in the environment or characters besides someone getting nuked based on your choice. I will give credit for the way power armor works now because before it seemed like just a metal suit when it was pretty much described as a walking tank but now it is exactly like a walking tank. It is ridiculous how weak the suits are unless you upgrade them extensively but this is new so I can forgive it somewhat.
Compared to the other 3D Fallout games, New Vegas and Fallout 3, most of what I thought that was lacking in FO4 were in these games. My judgement on Fallout 4 may be biased based on having higher expectations due to the other two games but I feel that it has reason since Bethesda did have these games to look at and figure out what people liked. I am aware that New Vegas falls under Obsidian but I'm sure you can still learn a lot about the game by reading reviews on it and playing it. Fallout 3 had many things right except the faction system, good vs bad end-game choices, and length but it still deserves more praise than 4. You get stuck with the Brotherhood but unless you are truly against being the good guy, you won't be complaining at all. The biggest thing that stood out to me was how long my interest in the games lasted. To this day I can easily say I have over 1000 hours on New Vegas w/ all DLC (mostly on the PS3) and over a few hundred for Fallout 3 w/ Broken Steel and Anchorage DLC (also on PS3).
. It's ridiculous how much they expect you to spend on Fallout 4 DLC to make the game seem more complete when you should already get most of it buying the game.

The problem with sequels is that too many fanboys expect them to carry their predecessors' baggage around with them. Fallout and Fallout 2 are pure RPGs, and are two of the greatest games of all time. Fallout 3 and New Vegas tried to shoehorn an FPS into the Fallout formula, with varying degrees of success. With Fallout 4, Bethesda has chosen to forge ahead and create a pure shooter with some RPG elements based on Black Isle's lore. It's a brave decision, and the game they made is great when judged on its own merits. The problem is that when you tack a number onto the name of a beloved franchise, your game doesn't get judged on its own merits. If Bethesda had called this game something else and sold it as a Fallout spinoff instead of a Fallout sequel, the current 77% positive reviews would be closer to 95%.

A lot of good points, too bad that for one improvement from the previous games, there's two or three regressions in different domains.
Yes, the game accumulates a lot of pros, and in almost every domain : the new artistic direction is awesome, the settlement construction is relatively fun, the gunplay is finally feeling right, and the wasteland is always compelling to explore.
Sadly, it ends here : in almost every other category the game fails to deliver something even equivalent to Fallout 3, which is sad given that almost a decade separates the two games :
:
Writing is the quintessential point in a good RPG, or rather
. With a storyline that'll make a summer blockbuster sound philosophical, a cast of unidimensional characters (which includes the PC, as Bethesda did anything in their power to prevent you from appropriating it) and a crippled dialogue system, the game looks like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of an Hollywood summer flick and a korean MMO, taking the moralizing tone and manichean storyline from the first and the endless randomly generated fetch quests from the latter.
Nothing that you do is actually important to the game world, and apparently now the Wasteland is so harsh that any NPC that is not a villain will automatically appreciate you, treat you as a hero and give you Freebie (Hello Danse that made me join him on a big operation 3 mins after meeting me, and Preston Garvey that entrusts you, the player, to liberate the wasteland all by yourself, a mere 10 minutes after a scripted action sequence (which breaks easily).
The quests are all prety bland and the same. Go there, shoot everyone, bring back the McGuffin. Again, and again. No more glimpses of Wasteland weirdness, no more infiltration, no more talking your way out of a situation, no more stealh (except in combats, to rack up a crit or two). That's right. Whatever type of character you play, you'll always heroically save the day by killing all the baddies.
Positive : the fast loot menu is great.
Negative : everything else.
The new stats system is awful and dumbed down, and overwhelms you with a lot of choices that don't matter : "hmmm... should I take +5% dmg resist or +5% rad resist ?" and your stats have little to no inluence on the storyline, dissociating these two elements further (no more Low-INT run where you play a retard or high-charisma characters talking their way out of the most awkward situations)
Most of the mechanics that made Fallout a game about survival simply disappeared (like weapon durability, ammo types, damage thresholds, and a decent basic needs system). The only alternative is a "Survival mode" that is more frustrating than challenging.
The new artistic direction is great with weapons, buildings and vehicles appearing more varied, and showing more "volume". Everything from the guns you fire to the environment you explore feels heavy and really there, ethers from the carboardy models from Fallout 3/NV.
The graphics themselves are good and the "new" engine performs well even on lower end systems. It's because Bethesda gave up on this part and used a refurbished iD Tech as their renderer, which is a big step up from their 2001 pipeline.
Even with that, everything is not perfect and you need to mess up with the config files to change even simple things like screen resolution or FoV. Not to mention the immense disappointment of 144hz monitor users that con't get the best out of their hardware. Bethesda doesn't care for both low-end and high-end hardware users.
The environmental soundtrack is great, and the choice of radio songs is still good. The addition of clasical music is a welcomed idea. However the voice acting is very inconsistent, and the crappy dialogue system doestn't help making things credible. That's a lot of burnt money  that could've went to other departments (like Q&A, programming, or maybe to hire professional writers instead of the poor lonely intern).
Overall the game disappoints, even though it has a lot of good elements. If you look for a good FPS go ahead, but you're warned, the game istn't anything more. Till the moddig scene develops that is.

Positive:
+ The gun accuracy is better than in FO3, which was a much needed fix
+ Better combat than FO3
+ Beatiful enviroment, great immersion
+ The sound effects are good
Negative:
- The inventory:
** While you are juggling hundreds of items and storing the bad ones, from a simple listed inventory, you can't EQUIP the item from there. You have to exit and go back to inventory, find the same item AGAIN and then equip it. It doubles the time you are already wasting sorting your inventory................
- Your companion is braindead:
** The entire game your companion is trying to hump your leg. He gets in your way so much it gets very tiresome to even have him around. He blocks doorways, he pushes you out of cover. Seriously you should bring him to the metro and chain him to a heavy object while he's looking the other way because he slows you down more than the helps you.
He's so obnoxious it makes the game feel sluggish and unresponsive because hes just there, in your way.
** Also an FPS
does not mix with grenades. You'll notice that 10 minutes into the game. You can't command him to stay the same minute you get attacked. The whole game mechanic is just really stupid.
- Bugs: 5 minutes into the game I find a dead something in the water which kept splashing water. This bug is visible everywhere in the game. Can't patch an obvious bug like that really ?
-Loading: Lots of loading screens. Some games have no loading screens...
- The controls: Oh my goodness !?! How can a developer like Bethesda publish a game that won't even let you remap your keys properly. That just shows how little self respect they have as a developer.
** For a game with endless weapons and weapon modifications it is extremely sad to see you can't remap hotbar buttons. Weapons are in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 0 ° -. The first thing I do in ANY shooter game is remap the grenade buttons. You can't remap squad in Fallout4. So you will be pressing the wrong buttons A LOT.
** Half the time you get a message 'do you want to exit this window', which you can't disable. Extremely annoying, even immersion breaking.
** Some people use AZERTY and not QUERTY keyboards. If you use AZERTY, you need to remap WASD. For build-mode this does not work ! This means even the basic directional controls can't be managed properly. I mean WTF... I'd expect this from a small developer console to PC ported game but not from FALLOUT4.
** Sometimes you have to press TAB to exit.
Sometimes you have to press ESC to exit.
Sometimes you have to press W to exit.
You will press the wrong button a lot, and you will see the menu when you don't want it a lot. Also immersion breaking.
- Navigation:
You can go anywhere on the map, even on rooftops, on cars, wherever. And when you run into an old log, you will be stopped in your tracks. The character should have been able to just step over it without interrupting your walk. It just makes the game feel very sluggish and unresponsive....again. The gameplay would have been a lot different if logs didn't stop you walking.
- Map:
Initially I found the map to be a lot smaller than Fallout4, but there seem to be plenty of buildings to scavange and explore.
Conclusion:
------------
The story seems much shallower than FO3. You go from the introduction to the game to shooting miniguns in like an hour. The content seems copy pasted, nothing new.
I own all Fallout games. FO4 has a lot of issues. It's sad that the controls are such a mess and the game feels so sluggish and unresponsive.
After I've played StarWars Battlefront I can't even go play Fallout4 because when come from a responsive game to Fallout4 it plays like you're in a swimmingpool full of glue, trying to run. It's very tiresome.
I guess I'll have to go write a MOD or code some AutoHotKey to fix my Fallout4 controls because Bethesda payed someone who probably never played a videogame in his life to program the controls.

Fallout 4, is more "Streamlined" than any other fall out game. It's basically gone from being an RPG to being single-player call of duty.
That is to say the story aspect of it which made Fallout New Vegas and fallout 3 so great, isn't there in the slightest. The Sim's city feature of the game is a joke, all it really does is waste some of your time so you feel like there is more content in the game before you ultimately realize it's not worth your time beyond making a single outpost which is just for your player home. The combat is a bit better which i do appreciate but this is honestly the only good thing about this game. I played so many hours of this because i love the previous fallouts and i just wanted this to be great and i was always looking for a different way to try to play this game to improve it and i couldn't the base game is the problem.
The makers of the game also got lazy, so many quests and NPC's are basically just copied and pasted. Every quest is usually go to this place kill a bunch of people and then grab something or turn something on. They would have thought this means there is more content and interesting gameplay hours. But when your doing the same thing over and over again, it is the opposite of fun.
I would not recommend this game, even for somebody with far too much free time (The only thing this game is good for is wasting time) I won't be buying any DLC for this, or the next fallout game. Probably not even the next elder scrolls game if bethesda keeps on with this "Streamlining" this act of trying to appeal to a larger audience and make more money for their producers while ultimately alienating their loyal fans who played previous installments of their franchises.

A good game with plenty of improvements, but many changes and simplifications that for me have hurt the overall experience of learning the game, as it has taken away alot of choice and progression and replaced it with mindless grinding via murdering things that move.
The new weapon system, while very customisable, takes away the fun in the hunt for that one part you always want (mine was the hunting rifle scope in NV) and instead gives you a whole branch of guns in one find, making most weapons you find boring and repetitive as there is nothing at all unique about them. And the weapon legendary system? Man I dislike it so much, instead of a unique weapon, you get the same thing with a random 'power' attached to it, giving it no lore to the game and sometimes completly stupid things like a Double-barrel break open shotgun... that you dont have to reload... im sure theres a lot of other stupid examples but that one always triggers me.
One thing they did try was voicing the protagonist, a good try but there was nowhere near enough choice in conversations with npcs (I do get a kick out of the sarcasm lines though) as you were always either a good samaritan or a sarcastic jerk, never evil, maybe a little borderline with cash demands but nothing out of the ordinary of standard human behaviour.
The world they made, was definately fantastic, but it lacked story depth, it only gave small pieces in some audio logs or notes, but nothing to follow. The settlement building idea, a good idea definately, but the npcs dont really travel or go exploring or anything, they kind of just loiter. The building system works quite well (DLC workshop add-ons seemed kinda half baked) its more the settler and raider system that definatly could use a good looking at as when your not physically in a area, settlement raiders can bypass all defences and start in the middle of your settlement.
What Fallout 4 lacks for me is a need to learn the mechanics of it, its too straight forward, with the previous Fallouts or even the older Elder Scrolls titles on your first playthrough you'd usually pick a random set of stats and get a damn good story that was challenging but fun with plenty of choice, so when you finnally did a second playthrough, you switch things up, have a better stat card from the get go and make a new set of choices, based on what you learnt from the last playthrough. I felt Fallout 4 was lacking very much in that department.
Overall, I guess I expected more of the great story telling I got from the last 2 titles but was dissapointed with it instead. I understand that simplifying mechanics makes the game more accessible but it also takes away the learning curve that make some games so great, especially ones that are to be considered rpgs (or at least were anyway).
I love the Fallout universe like crazy but feel more could of been done with the resources they had on hand.
If your new to the Fallout universe I suggest playing one of the older titles before this one if your into character building and the likes, but if you want a fairly simple game I reccomend Fallout 4 with thumbs up, but as a person who has played previous titles I cant bring myself to press the thumbs up button.

** For a game with endless weapons and weapon modifications it is extremely sad to see you can't remap hotbar buttons. Weapons are in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 0 ° -. The first thing I do in ANY shooter game is remap the grenade buttons. You can't remap squad in Fallout4. So you will be pressing the wrong buttons A LOT.
** Half the time you get a message 'do you want to exit this window', which you can't disable. Extremely annoying, even immersion breaking.
** Some people use AZERTY and not QUERTY keyboards. If you use AZERTY, you need to remap WASD. For build-mode this does not work ! This means even the basic directional controls can't be managed properly. I mean WTF... I'd expect this from a small developer console to PC ported game but not from FALLOUT4.
** Sometimes you have to press TAB to exit.
Sometimes you have to press ESC to exit.
Sometimes you have to press W to exit.
You will press the wrong button a lot, and you will see the menu when you don't want it a lot. Also immersion breaking.
- Navigation:
You can go anywhere on the map, even on rooftops, on cars, wherever. And when you run into an old log, you will be stopped in your tracks. The character should have been able to just step over it without interrupting your walk. It just makes the game feel very sluggish and unresponsive....again. The gameplay would have been a lot different if logs didn't stop you walking.
- Map:
Initially I found the map to be a lot smaller than Fallout4, but there seem to be plenty of buildings to scavange and explore.
Conclusion:
------------
The story seems much shallower than FO3. You go from the introduction to the game to shooting miniguns in like an hour. The content seems copy pasted, nothing new.
I own all Fallout games. FO4 has a lot of issues. It's sad that the controls are such a mess and the game feels so sluggish and unresponsive.
After I've played StarWars Battlefront I can't even go play Fallout4 because when come from a responsive game to Fallout4 it plays like you're in a swimmingpool full of glue, trying to run. It's very tiresome.
I guess I'll have to go write a MOD or code some AutoHotKey to fix my Fallout4 controls because Bethesda payed someone who probably never played a videogame in his life to program the controls.

Normally, I feel like Fallout games get better with time. I bought Fallout 4 around launch and sunk a good number of hours into it. It was buggy, ugly, clunky, and kind of tedious but it had a certain addicting aspect that kept me coming back. Upon completing most of the main quest lines I immediately felt no motivation to keep playing. I didn't care about exploring. I didn't care about making an awesome base. The game no longer had any draw.
So almost a year after launch I saw all the DLC on sale for pretty cheap. Hey, with some mods and DLC, this game should be a treat to play, right? Eh...
First off, mods do help. Somewhat. They add many quality of life elements that are missing from the game and some tweaks that are hard to live without. However I don't feel this game received enough traction to attract the quality of mods and conversions we have seen in previous Bethesda games. The depth isn't there or at least I haven't found it yet.
Second off, the DLC kinda sucks. I've played a good way through most of them and they feel like very cheap addons that do little to help expand upon the game's mechanics or story in any meaningful way. Oh nice, I can build more things in my base. But base building is still clunky as hell. There are some new items strewn across the DLC but nearly enough in my opinion. The few bits of content added across the DLCs doesn't do a whole like to breath new life into this game. It's more of the same. I was playing my way through one of them when the game crashed about 3 times in a row. Before I could load it up again BAM. I lost all motivation to play the game again.
Which brings me to my conclusion:
Almost a year after the launch of this game it is buggy, ugly, clunky, and kind of tedious. It still crashes on me, though not as much. There are still random framerate drops despite my GTX 980. Quests bug out. Things disappear at random. If I wasn't playing on PC with the ability to console-correct some of these issues the main story quest for the Nuka World DLC would have been unplayable.
This is definitely a game that you can put a good number of hours into. There is a lot to do. But it’s all pretty much the same. If you can get it for cheap then there may be some value in it for you. But it’s basically cheap all-you-can-eat food. Sure, there’s lots of it, but it all tastes the same and none of it is really any good.

The problem with sequels is that too many fanboys expect them to carry their predecessors' baggage around with them. Fallout and Fallout 2 are pure RPGs, and are two of the greatest games of all time. Fallout 3 and New Vegas tried to shoehorn an FPS into the Fallout formula, with varying degrees of success. With Fallout 4, Bethesda has chosen to forge ahead and create a pure shooter with some RPG elements based on Black Isle's lore. It's a brave decision, and the game they made is great when judged on its own merits. The problem is that when you tack a number onto the name of a beloved franchise, your game doesn't get judged on its own merits. If Bethesda had called this game something else and sold it as a Fallout spinoff instead of a Fallout sequel, the current 77% positive reviews would be closer to 95%.

A lot of good points, too bad that for one improvement from the previous games, there's two or three regressions in different domains.
Yes, the game accumulates a lot of pros, and in almost every domain : the new artistic direction is awesome, the settlement construction is relatively fun, the gunplay is finally feeling right, and the wasteland is always compelling to explore.
Sadly, it ends here : in almost every other category the game fails to deliver something even equivalent to Fallout 3, which is sad given that almost a decade separates the two games :
:
Writing is the quintessential point in a good RPG, or rather
. With a storyline that'll make a summer blockbuster sound philosophical, a cast of unidimensional characters (which includes the PC, as Bethesda did anything in their power to prevent you from appropriating it) and a crippled dialogue system, the game looks like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of an Hollywood summer flick and a korean MMO, taking the moralizing tone and manichean storyline from the first and the endless randomly generated fetch quests from the latter.
Nothing that you do is actually important to the game world, and apparently now the Wasteland is so harsh that any NPC that is not a villain will automatically appreciate you, treat you as a hero and give you Freebie (Hello Danse that made me join him on a big operation 3 mins after meeting me, and Preston Garvey that entrusts you, the player, to liberate the wasteland all by yourself, a mere 10 minutes after a scripted action sequence (which breaks easily).
The quests are all prety bland and the same. Go there, shoot everyone, bring back the McGuffin. Again, and again. No more glimpses of Wasteland weirdness, no more infiltration, no more talking your way out of a situation, no more stealh (except in combats, to rack up a crit or two). That's right. Whatever type of character you play, you'll always heroically save the day by killing all the baddies.
Positive : the fast loot menu is great.
Negative : everything else.
The new stats system is awful and dumbed down, and overwhelms you with a lot of choices that don't matter : "hmmm... should I take +5% dmg resist or +5% rad resist ?" and your stats have little to no inluence on the storyline, dissociating these two elements further (no more Low-INT run where you play a retard or high-charisma characters talking their way out of the most awkward situations)
Most of the mechanics that made Fallout a game about survival simply disappeared (like weapon durability, ammo types, damage thresholds, and a decent basic needs system). The only alternative is a "Survival mode" that is more frustrating than challenging.
The new artistic direction is great with weapons, buildings and vehicles appearing more varied, and showing more "volume". Everything from the guns you fire to the environment you explore feels heavy and really there, ethers from the carboardy models from Fallout 3/NV.
The graphics themselves are good and the "new" engine performs well even on lower end systems. It's because Bethesda gave up on this part and used a refurbished iD Tech as their renderer, which is a big step up from their 2001 pipeline.
Even with that, everything is not perfect and you need to mess up with the config files to change even simple things like screen resolution or FoV. Not to mention the immense disappointment of 144hz monitor users that con't get the best out of their hardware. Bethesda doesn't care for both low-end and high-end hardware users.
The environmental soundtrack is great, and the choice of radio songs is still good. The addition of clasical music is a welcomed idea. However the voice acting is very inconsistent, and the crappy dialogue system doestn't help making things credible. That's a lot of burnt money  that could've went to other departments (like Q&A, programming, or maybe to hire professional writers instead of the poor lonely intern).
Overall the game disappoints, even though it has a lot of good elements. If you look for a good FPS go ahead, but you're warned, the game istn't anything more. Till the moddig scene develops that is.

I suppose I have been programmed to love this game, but !@#$ it, I love this game. When I hear this games ambient music, my brain just starts getting pumped up. Here are some things I would say to a newcomer:
1. DO NOT START PLAYING TILL YOU ARE READY to play
The game reaches down and grabs whatever you have down there in the first 20 minutes of gameplay. Good, Bad, or indifferent the "problem/conflict" is almost immediate. This isn't just the whole nuclear fallout thing, it’s another element.
2. Get immersed! Noise Canceling Headphones, Dark Room, your best PC, and some time! 3D optional, but not a requirement. Give this game a real chance, and give yourself a real chance to get into this universe. How seriously you take a game is how seriously you escape. Personally, I need an escape from my reality, and this game did it. Well take the past tense out of that, it still does!
3. Get all the mods first. The gameplay DLCs are based on what level you are, so unless you want to start over, I would get the DLCs first, then start playing. It keeps things linear. It is NOT a requirement as the game has a great non-linear freebase to it, and it won't change the story much, but it is better to have them at the started.
4. The Virgin Playthrough....
The game has AMAZING mods, and I am just now after hundreds of hours diving in. This game also has some of the strangest bugs I have ever seen in a finished game. They are not bad or not functional, but they are just strange. Things like dead characters dying and sticking assfirst out of the ground somehow, and dialog beings strangely slow, then immediately fast....
Play the game through the end 1 time before you mod. It keeps it stable, or as stable as it can be unmodded, and gives you perspective of what you are changing.
5. Look Forward
I can't wait till the next edition of Fallout! This one is grossly different from the other games, but here is the best part.... because you can mod the game, you can get Fallout 1-3 features in Fallout 4 with mods! The framework of this game is just awesome, and I can't wait to see what is in store for us next. I just hope the trend is up!

Background: This was my first Fallout Game Ever. I was talked into buying this one because I have spent nearly 500 hours in Skyrim, Oblivion, and Morrowind and was told this was the Post Nuclear Version of Skyrim. Boy were they Right...
Guns, Guns, Guns: Man do I love guns. Big ones, small ones, weird ones, and a Man portable...holy crap that's a nuke on my shoulder! Gun Crafting is a major part of the game and I 100% recommend doing so. High level of Customization to fit your play style. Also Crafting can let you produce silenced weapons for stealth gameplay.
Its an RPG!:  Skill Trees, Stats, Percentages, loot tables, and crazy odd A.I. decisions make this game enjoyable and very customizable to a wide range of playstyles.
Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System(V.A.T.S): So after playing Fallout 4 like it was Skyrim I randomly miss clicked the VATS button on my keyboard and was immediately confused by a feature I had heard about and seen on images on
but had completely forgotten about its existence. Immediately my brain said this is how you cheat. Now don't get me wrong, I understand it is a feature that is meant to enhance gameplay, but it isn't for me.  Anyways it lets you slow down time and view percentages-to-hit on your targeted enemy and you let the game take over aiming for you. That's really an AimBot. No Thanks.
Social Mechanics: The game uses your Stats and a Reputation system to determine how Story NPCs interact with you. Of course there are many scripted enemies and monstrous beasts that will just break you for being you.  Perks you can unlock can enhance and change NPC Attitude as well.
Note: I have not played the Expansions.
Final Thoughts: Given its my first Fallout Game I would have to say I did enjoy my time because I played it like Skyrim. No VATS, Stealthy, Sniping.  It's not everyone's cup of tea, this game.
As Always watch gameplay Videos before Buying!

By far the weakest entry in the fallout series, interms of story, and well being an rpg. But for what it is, it's still a solid game. I love how power armor, crafting/upgrading, and combat works. Which in all honesty, is something i wish the other two games did just as good. mostly the combat. Plus, while i WAS annoyed that there was no level cap, it atleast works better for this kinda game, since you don't HAVE to keep improving your character if you don't want too. where as if this was a game like Skyrim... oooh boy.
to be honest there was only two issues i had with this game; it's lackluster nature as a main fallout game. As well as it's unrealised story. To behonest though? this story could've been better suited too a spinoff within the fallout universe, rather than a main game. The Sole Survivor feels more like a set protagonist than he does a blank slate. Sure, the other fallout protags had quick little backstories, but even then you had soooo much leg room for making your own character. But since this doesn't wanna decide whether or not the Sole Survivor is a actuall character, or just a blank slate for the player, it just kinda feels... off. infact, that's my opinion on the whole game. It wants to do one thing, but HAS to do the other.
again; if this storyline was used for a fallout spinoff game, it would've been better. The characters, and overall plot could've gotten better focus. Because yeah, it has a ♥♥♥♥♥ON of potential. but it just feels... unrealised.
As for what could be done in 5 (or whatever the hell it's gunna be called) i have some suggestions. Firstly; have a good balance of story and a badass overworld. If the devs of witcher 3 can do both, on their FIRST ATTEMPT, there is no excuse. the best things about 3 and 4 are their hubworlds. While the best thing in New Vegas was it's story and characters, and how you as the player affected that story. Witcher 3 meanwhile, succeeded in both. even if you have to work with obsideon again, it'd be really awesome if we can have the ebst of both worlds.

after 37 hours of playtime trying to get Fallout 4 to work, I still can't get it to run properly. I've tried everything from going into the ini files to verifying the game's cache multiple times. I've tried everything possible, and the game still won't run properly. After experimenting with the files, I've managed to get the game to a stable frame rate when going into densely populated areas, but loading screens take minutes to load up, and most of the time don't even load up at all. I've tried running the vanilla game, and it still won't work. The main problem is the extremely long loading screens, but their are also several glitches that make the game almost unplayable.
Main problems with the game are as follows:
- game not starting up, forcing me to log out of steam, and log back in to get it working.
- texture bugs
- infinite loading screens (I'm not being sarcastic)
- extremely long loading screens the longer I play (ranging from 40 seconds to 3 minutes)
- head not able to move vertically (the only way I could fix this was verifying the game's cache)
- several compatability issues with Nvidia (I'm currently on the Gforce GTX 1070, which is a very modern video card)
Seconday Problems:
- shooting mechanics can sometimes be wonky (not getting proper hit registration, etc)]
- RPG mechanics are really limited and aren't as well polished as other Bethesda games
- settlement building is basically unplayable without mods (unplacable items, items not snapping to one another, etc)
- facial textures not up to date with other games (best example is the character known as 'Mama Murphy')
All in all, if you can get this game to work, it's really fun. But if you can't, then you're out of luck. I'd highly reccommend buying this game on console, as mods are now able to be installed, and you have a much higher chance of this working. This was the game that really tested my time and patience, but ultimately, it won.

I'm going to go against the consensus and recommend this game.
If you come in expecting tough decisions and consequences like the Witcher series (or even Fallout 3), you will be disappointed. While there are still some consequences (The Institute vs Everyone Else), the choices made seemed mechanical and inorganic. It's like flipping a switch and seeing 2 distinct outcomes for the Commonwealth.
The quests provided are go here/kill that person/get that object back for both sides. You feel like you are a servant doing whatever Bethesda wanted you to do. The linear path has already been set for you, and you only must walk in it. You don't feel significant. Every settlement you save feel more like a task/job than a heroic thing to do. NPC replies in a pre-scripted way as if you're working as opposing to following your own destiny.
Don't expect to find Witcher-level consequences here. In the Witcher, every choice has a deeper and implicit meaning to it. You can choose to be a kind, compassionate, generous person and you would find villagers thanking you wherever you go. On the other hand, you can choose to be a work-for-hire, being indifferent to what's happening around you and seeing the consequences directly - merchants getting locked up by bandits, peasants being beaten up and looted by the guards, for example.
In Fallout, you would simply not see that NPC again. Some might make remarks of what you do, but you'll hear the same thing repeatedly that it loses its meaning. The dialogues you'll hear becomes noises in the end.
But, as a shooter, Fallout 4 is an excellent game. The combat mechanics no longer have a mechanical/clunky feel compared to Fallout 3. You can sprint, you can use iron sights, and the weapon customization mechanic is deep and rewarding. Finding a better receiver/scope/ammo slot for your sniper feels rewarding. You feel like if you’re out there, constantly improving and becoming a more powerful person at every step since you depart Vault 111 and enter the Wasteland.
You are constantly reminded that the Wasteland is a barbaric and lawless place – where blood and bullet triumphs diplomacy and compassion. You will find raider gangs trying to invade your settlement. They are ruthless – They’re out there to kill you. And you will win. By blood and iron. For every raider, you have triumphed, for every of their settlement you’ve taken, you will feel more powerful. You will find bottlecaps, weapons, or even rare magazines that give you bonuses. And this, is what makes you more powerful. You will find yourself indomitable when you find that silent advanced receiver to your combat rifle. 77 to 130 damage.
So, in summary, don’t think of Fallout 4 as a traditional RPG. Instead, think of it as a loot-combat game (like Diablo) and you’ll enjoy it.

Overall, the Games only worth it to mess around with mods. This is just another beloved RPG being cut down to appeal to the masses rather than the fans. This game has really killed my excitement for TES VI, and overall ruined my memories of the series.

I have over 1000 hours in this game according to STEAM.  I bet I have at least half that much again that STEAM doesn't know about because I played off-line.  Perhaps just from that you'll guess what I think of this game.  I find the fighting challenging but not discouraging, the exploring interesting and not monotonous, the construction theme - building settlements - rewarding, and the main quest line suitably engaging.  Side quests can get a bit repetitive but I enjoy hiking across the wasteland and dealing with the natives as I pursue side quests so I don't mind.  I have encountered a couple of game glitches in all the time I've put into wandering around what's left of Massachusetts, but the console and a wiki help me smooth those rough edges as they come up.  After having completed all the quests a couple of times with different characters and difficulty levels I also find the console useful to keep my interest up.  Did you know you can create as many enemies as you want, where you want them, with the console?   It's a great way to test your settlement defenses and it's loads of fun to watch those defenses put to extreme testing.
I particularly enjoy the huge playscapes that Bethesda creates.   Morrowind, Skyrim, Massachusetts - they've all been a blast to randomly wander through and discover the treasures and traps the designers have left for me to stumble upon.  The wide variety of quests help provide some structure but these games define what open world means - I can go where I want, just following my nose, at any time.  I also like that it's not all fighting.  Not long into these games I actually have to go looking for someone or something to target, giving me plenty of leisure to explore buildings, caves, and countryside for useful items and interesting NPCs.  In this game, the added bonus of being able to repeatedly design defensible settlements that can create their own food/water/power was a powerful improvement over prior Bethesda games.  Turns out I like to build even more than I like to blow stuff up!  I would like the settlers to actually appreciate the effort I put into their home more but no matter how nice I make it their happiness is only based on full bellies and a bed out of the rain.  Streetlamps, bedroom furniture, and paintings on the wall make no impression on them.  Crafting is almost as rewarding as it is in Skyrim, the leveling and perk system shows polish learned from Bethesda's prior games, and the interface is clear, intuitive, and easy to use.
Recommended.  Highly recommended.

Bugs and not just Radroaches or Bloatfly's

My experiences are about Fallout 4 on survival difficulty.
Fallout 4 was more or less fine until the survival mode update.  After the update, console commands were disabled.  This wouldn't normally be a problem, but recent Fallout games aren't known for being completely free of bugs.  Up until this point it wasn't too bad. There were a few times I got stuck in objects, with no way out other than loading a previous save.
I was willing to overlook this until recently. The game has been getting buggier.  I've been playing a few hundred hours on the same character, and one of the side quests is incompleteable because the next part of the quest won't trigger.  Furthermore, reentering places with latched doors and other nonstandard locking mechanisms can result in glitches that prevent their use and resulting in getting stuck since sometimes there's no other way out.
Another bug is that the game now stalls pretty frequently when using VATS.  The only way to do anything after this happens is to logoff of the computer and relogin.
None of this would be too much of a problem, however survival mode disables the save feature, requiring use of a bed to sleep/save.  The fact that sleeping for short durations can result in sickness and reduction of adrenaline makes it detrimental until the character is tired.  Getting stuck in an object, blocked by a door, or any other annoying bugs that force loading a save when the last save is a while ago is not fun.  All this makes me question why bethesda would disable the console on such a bug ridden game.

After 340.8 hours played...
I STILL love this game!
I backed off of the settlement building, as I pretty much have everything set up how I want it.
I bought it full price (it went on sale the next day)
I still have a TON of Far Harbor and ALL of NukaWorld to explore.
The main thing I really like as far as the storyline goes is that, depending on how you (the player) feel about various factions is pretty much the difference between the good guys and the bad guys.

-Combat is refined,fluid and feels great.
-World has something new to find around every corner
-Mods make the game's purchase worth it
-This game runs like a.ss. Ive experienced lag in some older games due to the engine being so old, imagine that with a "next gen" game. random drops to 30fps and sometimes even lower, and 60fps lock.
-Game was clearly made for console, doesnt control too well with a KBM, especially the pipboy.
-Artificial Difficulty. Game is pretty easy for the most part, but sometimes an insanely powerful enemy comes out of nowhere, forcing me to run or get killed. I think I remember Howard talking about this before the game was out, saying its a good thing. It's not.
-Remember when I said theres something new around every corner? Well thats backfiring right back at them now. I'll give an example, I was wandering around and found a gunfight between two different people who looked the exact same. Im interested, I save then I go over to them. I cant talk to either one, they dont even notice me so I shoot one of them. He's dead. thats it. the other guy walks off. I reload my save, shoot guy no.2. then the same thing again. thats it. I just move on dissapointed. This is just one example of all the horribly written events mashed into the game.
-ZERO choices with actual meaning. Apart from the endings, theres no actual choices in this game. Its just following a path. Honestly its sad how the series has came from the originals. I remember really feeling like I can do whatever I want and there being a billion different ways to do ___ quest in 1/2. Now all you can do is the set way, following the set story. Speaking of.
-The story's writing is a.ss. Did they really give up the RP from the RPG for this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Two Worlds has a better story.
-The leveling system's been dumbed down for casuals, only perks now, no karma at all.
Overall, the Games only worth it to mess around with mods. This is just another beloved RPG being cut down to appeal to the masses rather than the fans. This game has really killed my excitement for TES VI, and overall ruined my memories of the series.

I have over 1000 hours in this game according to STEAM.  I bet I have at least half that much again that STEAM doesn't know about because I played off-line.  Perhaps just from that you'll guess what I think of this game.  I find the fighting challenging but not discouraging, the exploring interesting and not monotonous, the construction theme - building settlements - rewarding, and the main quest line suitably engaging.  Side quests can get a bit repetitive but I enjoy hiking across the wasteland and dealing with the natives as I pursue side quests so I don't mind.  I have encountered a couple of game glitches in all the time I've put into wandering around what's left of Massachusetts, but the console and a wiki help me smooth those rough edges as they come up.  After having completed all the quests a couple of times with different characters and difficulty levels I also find the console useful to keep my interest up.  Did you know you can create as many enemies as you want, where you want them, with the console?   It's a great way to test your settlement defenses and it's loads of fun to watch those defenses put to extreme testing.
I particularly enjoy the huge playscapes that Bethesda creates.   Morrowind, Skyrim, Massachusetts - they've all been a blast to randomly wander through and discover the treasures and traps the designers have left for me to stumble upon.  The wide variety of quests help provide some structure but these games define what open world means - I can go where I want, just following my nose, at any time.  I also like that it's not all fighting.  Not long into these games I actually have to go looking for someone or something to target, giving me plenty of leisure to explore buildings, caves, and countryside for useful items and interesting NPCs.  In this game, the added bonus of being able to repeatedly design defensible settlements that can create their own food/water/power was a powerful improvement over prior Bethesda games.  Turns out I like to build even more than I like to blow stuff up!  I would like the settlers to actually appreciate the effort I put into their home more but no matter how nice I make it their happiness is only based on full bellies and a bed out of the rain.  Streetlamps, bedroom furniture, and paintings on the wall make no impression on them.  Crafting is almost as rewarding as it is in Skyrim, the leveling and perk system shows polish learned from Bethesda's prior games, and the interface is clear, intuitive, and easy to use.
Recommended.  Highly recommended.
