I've always been quite conflicted about Fallout 4.
On the other hand it has a bunch of really good new features. The new crafting and building systems are really good and fit the world of Fallout perfectly. The combat is actually really damn fun this time. The characters and the world are mostly great. There are also some minor cool new features like the new loot menu. And of course there's content for hundreds of hours and the replayability is solid. On top of that there are tons of great mods which fix Bethesda's shortcomings and add new features and content.
But it's also kind of a one step forward, two steps back -situation. The main characters are fully voiced, which is great, but this dumbs down the dialogue quite a bit. The quests are also quite linear, lacking the complexity and open nature of previous Fallout titles. And the engine sucks big time, there are tons of nasty technical difficulties and it's buggy as f*ck.
It's a solid game, but it could've been so much better.

I think Fallout 4 is a fun game and they improved the areas that needed fixing in my opinon. Those being animations, gun play, crafting system, and a color pallete that isn't brown(fallout nv) or greenish grey (Fallout 3).
Where Fallout 4  went backwards is with, cities, rpg mechanics and quests.
In the base game the only cities that you dont have to build are Diamond City, Covenant, or Vault 81 ( I think thats all of them). Which aggrevates me, because I love exploring and finding new cities and talking with the people and learning some of the lore.
The rpg mechanics have been dumbed down alot which stinks. Early on in the game leveling up has a meaning but in the later levels 40 and up you tend to be a jack of all trades which is were you can really see how dumbed down the mechanics are. Also less of a focus on building your character seeing as how you can just put points in your special stats when you level up if you choose to do so.
Last but not least are the quests. There are quite a few good quests in fallout 4, but there are also a lot of go here kill this quests that will repeat. This is fine as it gives you something to do, but it is also bad because instead of doing said quest and getting a cool piece of loot or stat boost you just get money which I think further waters down the rpg feel.
With fallout 4 Bethesda improved in some areas and backslid in others. I personally can look past the bad and enjoy myself in the game. If you are on the fence about buying it or waiting I would suggest watching a few lets plays and deciding for yourself. I personally would not buy the seasonpass for 50 dollars though. I love the dlcs but I dont think they are worth 50 ( I got the season pass when it was 25 dollars so take that for what it is worth).

Pros
+ A similar size map to previous games but with a lot more locations and unmarked locations.
+ A survival mode reminiscent of Hypothermia and Realistic Needs mods from Skyrim.
+ Codsworth can say your name (simple but fun to hear).
+ Loot respawns after a few days so you can technically play indefinitely .
+ Weapon modding is a great addition as it was via mods in NV and F3.
+ Plenty of factions to choose from.
+ A large variety of companions (but I don't have the  heart to tell Dogmeat to go home and wait for me)
+ Great atmospheric music (as always)
+ Legendary enemies and effects extend the replayability to much compared to simply having unique weapons.
+ Huge level cap.
+ Finally the Vault Dweller has a voice.
+ Constructing settlements. Probably the most satisfying element of the game.
+ Huge selection of perks to choose from.
+ Great DLC (although I wish they'd create more).
+ Limitless missions.
Cons
- Removal of karma system.
- The main factions want your to kill the others when you get to a certain point in the main storyline.
- Lack of end game content once the main story is complete.
- Rather dull and muddy textures.
- Radio station playlists could be longer.
- You can make many game breaking character builds.
- Far too much settlement build focused DLC.
- A lack of variety with weapons (especially melee and unarmed).
- Poor optimization and performance (especially in downtown Boston).
Overall an amazing game, yes certain things are missing that we loved in previous games, but so much has been added. I'm nearing 900 hours and still haven't resorted to heavily modding the game. I added an ENB mod once and a few other bits here and there, but mainly texture based mods. I've not felt any need to add any extra content mods. Short Review:
It's an action-adventure game with reminiscent roleplaying aspects pretending to be a Fallout RPG. 6/10 I do not recommend this as a Fallout game.
If this game was based in a different universe with all of these gameplay aspects and wasn't called Fallout. 9/10 I would recommend this if it was something else.
Don't get me wrong, this is a fun game, but this isn't a Fallout game no matter the disguise or title. I especially love the modding capability.
Long Review with bits of spoilers:
This game is nothing like the first 2 Fallouts (obviously) and this game is not even like Fallout 3 or Fallout New Vegas.
The voiced character option I didn't mind, but I was hoping they would have at least two maybe three voices for male and female that way I can at least attempt to make a unique character that doesn't feel like a character everyone else can make.
Skills don't matter becasue they don't exist. Perks don't matter because you can acquire all of them by reaching level 256 I believe. Roleplaying for immersion feels pointless since there's barely any choice in dialogue. There's a sarcastic option 50% of the time in conversations, then there is 2-3 ways to say, "yes." And sometimes, when there's only 2 options to say, "yes," there's an option to say, "maybe later" when asked to do a task, and very rarely there is an option to simply say, "no." There are no evil choices in this game. There are good ones, then there are stupid ones. The is a UI mod that fixes this so it's not just a few words but the actual lines that are said  so you know what your character is saying and I 100% recommend that.
Lore wise, the game just keeps retconning and adds new things that don't make sense, like another version of powered armour, which would have made better sense if it was known as the Brotherhoods modern version by combining T-45 and T-51 together to make their own, and that would explain why all the Brotherhood wears is T-60 only, but no the T-60 was made during the Great War.
Bethesda also removed any trace of the Enclave ever existing or having any influence in the Commonwealth, no small recon outposts just for interaction, or a remnant that has an ability to join any faction depending on which way you sway them, like in New Vegas. Only Enclave guy is in Far Harbor and he worships Atom.
The story is almost exactly the same as Fallout 3, except you're the Father/Mother looking for the son that technically left you in the Vault. But your son is known as Father so technically speaking Father left you in the vault. Sadly, Father is not voiced by Liam Neeson.
Extremely limited number of weapons, unless you have mods like I do, then you've got a complement of 100+ extra weapons to the ones that already exist. But if you don't have mods, then, while the weapons are neat that they have in this game, they're missing a lot of the older models that Fallout originally had that added on and gave it the retro-40's era look.
Only Factions that matter are Institute, Brotherhood, and Minutemen. Railroad are just useful idiots for their clothes upgrades, and that one pistol, besides that they're worthless. Minutemen align with the player so it doesn't matter who you pick, Institute or Brotherhood, they're both good factions, but Institute is better. Too bad you can't go for a 3 way alliance between the Institute, Brotherhood, and Minutemen. Only 3 way alliance you can form is with the Brotherhood, Minutemen, and the Railroad, which is just lame.
I liked the Robots DLC just because I can make all the robots I want.
I liked the Fisherman DLC because I can shoot things with harpoons, and I made peace between the synths, the Atom fanatics, and the Fishermen. Then I called the Institue in to reclaim the Synths, because robots that think they're human are dangerous.
The Nuka Cola Raider DLC was lackluster. Not so exciting, but I liked the AK which was a nice touch, but not as good as the AK's I got from mods.
This is also the 5th time I had to write a review for this game because apparently it didn't submit my very detailed with specifics review. So let us hope it submits this one this time.

The good:
- Fantastic doggo. Top notch. It can even wear clothes.
- They've clearly invested a lot into settlement construction, if that's your kind of thing.
The bad:
- The story is awful; the kind of awful that thinks it's important and good. Just because the main character has a child that I see for five minutes does not make me invested in that child, Bethesda.
- The main character is railroaded into a very particular story role, which robs the player of the type of freedom we expect from Bethesda and Fallout. If you thought your dad was the most boring part of Fallout 3 (and it was) then this is that times a hundred.
- The main character is also railroaded into a particular gameplay style, with the skill system changed for the worse and character customisation flattened out. You are going to be a shootperson whether you like it or not.
- Quests boil down to: go here, shoot some things, get loot. No depth, no nuance, no talking your way into or out of things.
- The world feels flat and dead. So you've been living in this diner for years, and still haven't removed the skeletons from the seats?
- There are some good ideas and seeds of companions here (Nick Valentine is a particular standout) but the game never truly delivers on them.
- If you're not into settlement construction (I'm not) be prepared to be pestered forever about it.
Overall: save your money, play New Vegas.

From the get go, you are pigeonholed into the role of a generic straight man on an insanely pedestrian quest to avenge a dead wife and a kidnapped son. And the truth is, I just don't care. It feels so contrived. It takes away from the immersion because I can hardly roleplay as the character I would like to be.
If the tradeoff for full voice acting is a shoehorned story and the loss of most RPG elements, then it's clearly not worth it. It's probably the first game I've ever modded from the get-go because the "vanilla" experience is so excruciatingly dull.
The only thing that this game has going for it are the graphics, which are a massive improvement over previous entries in the series. I'd recommend picking up
or
(my favourite) instead of Fallout 4 because this buggy mess isn't really worth it even on sale at -75%.
Oh, and one last thing... In 2016, it's simply unacceptable to be so behind the times as to not to include a single LGBT character in a role-playing game. No, wait, there are two lesbian NPCs, but they can't be interacted with, and they literally get nuked roughly 2 minutes into the game. Aside from that, in the year 2287, there are no gay characters. None. Zero. Nada. Sure, your character and companions can get a little bi-curious, if you catch my drift, but come on... Would it have been really so hard to redub just a handful of lines to allow for a gay or lesbian main character?
But given this is a game in which the inclusion of a female playable character was a last minute afterthought due to public backlash, none of this is surprising. Stay away from this lazy attempt at an RPG unless you've already beaten the previous two entries in the series, and you're in desperate need of some more post-apocalyptic gameplay.

No choice compared to . .  what?  II've played allegedly choice heavy games like the Witcher 3 and Baldur's Gate.  Fallout 4 has about as much choice as them. but they present it in a less straightforward manner so I'm guessing most people just don't notice how many options they have.
The lack of stats was annoying at first, but I stopped minding in about thirty minutes because the perk system is interesting and has significant effects.   The characters are really well written this time around, and the story seems like a huge upgrade over Fallout 3 or New Vegas, so I'm not sure where those complaints are coming from.  Maybe it falls apart past the 55 hour mark and I haven't reached the collapse yet, but I doubt it.
In general, the game takes away slideshows and summaries and hand-holding and just makes things happen in the world, and people, used to announcements telling them how their decisions affected the world, don't seem to notice.

I enjoyed playing Fallout 4 but it wasn't everything I hoped it would be. Coming from playing both Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas I was hoping for something in a similar vein. Fallout 4 can be considered an RPG but the role playing elements that defined the previous games are noticeably lacking in some areas. For the first time you play a fully voiced protagonist simply referred to as the Sole Survivor.
The main story starts off intriguingly with your wife being killed and your son being taken from Vault 111 where you have been cryogenically frozen for the past several years. But when you finally leave the vault to search for him the story soon starts to faint to the background as you explore the wasteland better known as the Commonwealth. This isn't necessarily a bad thing as you are free to do anything you want from this point on, which is after all a trademark of the Fallout series, but it does take away any form of emotional attachment to the story. Besides that though you will encounter some interesting characters along the way and there are some good side quests to undertake. There are several factions you can align with and there is an interesting sub-plot about synths and a mysterious organization called the Institute which also links back to the main story.
Coming back to the role playing element, by having a fully voiced protagonist Bethesda unfortunately made the decision to severely dumb down the whole dialogue system making it difficult to sometimes react the way you want to, or in worse cases limits you from making a particular decision as the dialogue option you choose hardly reflects what the protagonist will actually say. They also got rid of several other important elements like karma and overall just simplified a lot of things.
What Bethesda undoubtedly did get right this time around is the combat. It's been much improved and the game actually feels much more like a first person shooter. Weapons feel great and killing enemies using the well known VATS system is very satisfying. The whole crafting system seems more like an afterthought though. I'll admit I had some fun with it but when you look beyond the basic stuff of managing a settlement you see it's just not very complex and there are a lot of annoying restrictions to it.
Another thing they got right is the Commonwealth itself. It's really detailed, there are a lot of places to explore and overall the world just feels really immersive. Graphically I would say the game looks really good, definitely an upgrade to the previous games but you can't help but notice that some areas are less detailed than others and you'll occasionally bump into some lazy texture work. Performance is generally okay, at least if you have the hardware to run it and if you tweak the settings a lot. Using default settings however can lead to a lot of annoying fps drops, texture glitches and lighting problems, and so I would therefor rate the quality of the PC port itself as being quite average.
In the end I would say that Fallout 4 is still a pretty good entry to the series despite it's flaws. Looking at it as a first person shooter with some RPG elements to it and a decent story with a compelling and detailed open world to explore, I'd say it's worth your time and money.

I enjoyed playing Fallout 4 but it wasn't everything I hoped it would be. Coming from playing both Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas I was hoping for something in a similar vein. Fallout 4 can be considered an RPG but the role playing elements that defined the previous games are noticeably lacking in some areas. For the first time you play a fully voiced protagonist simply referred to as the Sole Survivor.
The main story starts off intriguingly with your wife being killed and your son being taken from Vault 111 where you have been cryogenically frozen for the past several years. But when you finally leave the vault to search for him the story soon starts to faint to the background as you explore the wasteland better known as the Commonwealth. This isn't necessarily a bad thing as you are free to do anything you want from this point on, which is after all a trademark of the Fallout series, but it does take away any form of emotional attachment to the story. Besides that though you will encounter some interesting characters along the way and there are some good side quests to undertake. There are several factions you can align with and there is an interesting sub-plot about synths and a mysterious organization called the Institute which also links back to the main story.
Coming back to the role playing element, by having a fully voiced protagonist Bethesda unfortunately made the decision to severely dumb down the whole dialogue system making it difficult to sometimes react the way you want to, or in worse cases limits you from making a particular decision as the dialogue option you choose hardly reflects what the protagonist will actually say. They also got rid of several other important elements like karma and overall just simplified a lot of things.
What Bethesda undoubtedly did get right this time around is the combat. It's been much improved and the game actually feels much more like a first person shooter. Weapons feel great and killing enemies using the well known VATS system is very satisfying. The whole crafting system seems more like an afterthought though. I'll admit I had some fun with it but when you look beyond the basic stuff of managing a settlement you see it's just not very complex and there are a lot of annoying restrictions to it.
Another thing they got right is the Commonwealth itself. It's really detailed, there are a lot of places to explore and overall the world just feels really immersive. Graphically I would say the game looks really good, definitely an upgrade to the previous games but you can't help but notice that some areas are less detailed than others and you'll occasionally bump into some lazy texture work. Performance is generally okay, at least if you have the hardware to run it and if you tweak the settings a lot. Using default settings however can lead to a lot of annoying fps drops, texture glitches and lighting problems, and so I would therefor rate the quality of the PC port itself as being quite average.
In the end I would say that Fallout 4 is still a pretty good entry to the series despite it's flaws. Looking at it as a first person shooter with some RPG elements to it and a decent story with a compelling and detailed open world to explore, I'd say it's worth your time and money.

The monetization of user-made content is a controversial topic and has once again reared its ugly head with the launch of Fallout 4's Creation Club.
This program is doomed to cause a rift in the modding community, ending support for non-CC modders by giving rise to a hierarchy of Bethesda-sponsored creators. Said creators are compensated with a lump sum while Bethesda reaps continuous profit from their work. In addition, forcing the player to download packages that potentially interfere with how their game runs and locking them behind a paywall is *not* good for business, as it damages the company's relationship with the consumer and negatively weighs on the stability of the game.
The Creation Club was a mistake. It is an aberration of marketing that must be rectified. In the words of the immortal Liberty Prime: "DEMOCRACY IS NON-NEGOTIABLE."

I can't believe how many people have crawled out of the woodwork to bad mouth this game because the dialogue is weak, or because player choices are less immersive than in New Vegas. Many of the recent "would not recommend" reviews come from people who have more than 200 hours of playtime. How could a game that keeps someone busy for that long possibly earn a "would not recommend" rating?
Fallout 4 provides an amazing framework for in game building and settlement management, enormous amounts of non-violent content ( as well as the best violent content of any Fallout game), and some of the best weapon/armor  modifications of any game I've ever seen. Does it have weaknesses? Yes, of course it does. Do those weaknesses amount to a “would not recommend” rating? NO! If you are still on the fence about this game I recommend a careful analysis of the recent negative comments. Ask yourself how someone who gets more than 300 hours of playtime out of a game could possibly justify a negative review. If you hate it why play it?
I’ve played this game for about 400 hours and I love it. I just hope Bethesda doesn’t listen to all this negative crap and eliminate in game building, settlement construction, and weapon/armor modification in favor of immersive dialogue. Immersive dialogue is important but Fallout 4 represents a focus on building. Weak dialogue, which is a problem in Fallout 4, does not justify a “would not recommend” rating.

Lots of negative reviews for this game but for good reason.
If you bought or are looking to buy Fallout 4 because its a Fallout game-you might be disapointed. I personally am a huge Fallout fan but i also appreciate open world shooters with a hell lot of freedom
WHICH IS WHAT THIS GAME IS.
Alot of "fallout" aspects are gone or modified but the game shines in its new inovated aspects such as teh vastly improved combat, freedom, customazion (oh the customization).
If youre looking for a great open world shooter with your own twist in every playthrough- this is your game.
If you're looking for a cookie cut out of the previous fallout games with boosted graphics, you'll still enjoy it but you will also dislike the game.

I played 30 hours of this game when it first released and put it down, now that I don't have much expectations I decided to resume playing it where I left. I can't stop and I'm enjoying this game, exploring taking my time. And I'm still not done the main story line yet! I think it's the good way to play it, not just run straight to the finish line and miss out on all the other side quests. If you're looking to buy this and never played Fallout before and looking to spend some time alone living a virtual experience, it's totally rewarding to put a few dozen hours in this world. The only thing that could set this aside is maybe Skyrim Special Edition coming out next week.

This game is so much fun. The graphics are beautiful, and they've cranked up the combat quality from Fallout 3 and New Vegas.
The downside, is that nearly EVERYTHING in the game outside the cities wants to kill you. With the exception of a few wandering caravan traders.
The game is immersive with several very interesting diverging plot points with different factions vying for your attention.
The worst part is at the end of the quest line, you're pretty much required to kill EVERY other faction that isn't the main one you've chosen.
Still, it's worth the price of admission. The DLC is a ton of fun, very well done, adding tons of hours to the gameplay. I highly recommend this game

possibly the most meh bethesda game. Certainly the most meh I've played. The engine and mechanic upgrades are in fact pretty expansive and bring a lot to the table but... the changes have also taken away a lot of stuff in suprising ways. The focus on unique companion affinity was cool and it meant playing a certain way with certain characters but it hurt the moding comunity as companions now became too much trouble to make. the voiced MC was just a bad move in the end and the dialogue options as many have said are horribly limmiting. The combat system is magnificent, but comes with a trade off. I now spend most game time running around going pew pew for kicks because the story and quests are all lacking and uncompelling. The main story couldve been left out and long term we all wouldnt have noticed. The DLC's all are far too pricey for what they bring to the table and the main game cost, while worth the production cost, is not worth it considering what it buys you elsewhere. this paired with the dying or silent modding comunity and I'm left really not able to recomend this to anyone. If you want a fallout game, I suggest going to NV. If you want a bethesda game, skyrim is getting a hd update. I really do wish this game were worth wasting more time in, but theres just better and cheaper stuff out there. that is as unbiased a look as I can give.

The game is very repetitive and unoriginal. The difficulty level in the game is merely how many times you have to shoot things to kill them. As you move into the later stages, and your character reaches higher levels, you can find yourself having to shoot enemies literaly hundreds of times. When your character reaches a high level the enemies can't really hurt you so every fight is just several minutes of repetitive shooting of the enemies, with almost no danger of being killed. The game is also very buggy, with crashes, and freezes occuring almost every  time you fast travel, or go through a door or anything involving changes of location other than walking.
I would not reccommend this game at all, in fact I reccommend NOT buying this game.
